Diagram: a trait object is a fat pointer.

Left, two elements of `parts: Vec<Box<dyn Render>>`. Each element is two pointers side by side: a "data ptr" and a "vtable ptr".
- parts[0]: the data ptr points to `Text("hello")` on the heap; the vtable ptr points to the vtable for (Text, Render).
- parts[1]: the data ptr points to `Checkbox(true)` on the heap; the vtable ptr points to the vtable for (Checkbox, Render).

Middle, the two vtables. Each has rows: drop, size and align, render, label.

Right, where the rows point:
- Text's `render` row -> `Text::render`. Text's `label` row -> the trait's default `label`, compiled for Text (Text does not override it).
- Checkbox's `render` row -> `Checkbox::render`. Checkbox's `label` row -> `Checkbox::label` (its override).

Caption: `part.label()` on parts[0] follows the vtable ptr, reads the "label" row and calls it with the data ptr as `self`. Row order and whether vtables are shared are compiler details. On 64-bit each pointer is 8 bytes, so the fat pointer is 16.

// Exercise 1: a mixed zoo (reference solution)
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex1_zoo.rs && ./main --test-threads=4

trait Animal {
    fn name(&self) -> String;
    fn sound(&self) -> String;
    // Default: "<name> says <sound>"
    fn speak(&self) -> String {
        format!("{} says {}", self.name(), self.sound())
    }
}

struct Dog;
struct Cat {
    name: String,
}
struct Parrot {
    word: String,
}

impl Animal for Dog {
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        String::from("dog")
    }
    fn sound(&self) -> String {
        String::from("woof")
    }
}

impl Animal for Cat {
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        self.name.clone()
    }
    fn sound(&self) -> String {
        String::from("meow")
    }
}

impl Animal for Parrot {
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        String::from("parrot")
    }
    fn sound(&self) -> String {
        self.word.clone()
    }
    fn speak(&self) -> String {
        format!("{0}! {0}!", self.word)
    }
}

fn zoo() -> Vec<Box<dyn Animal>> {
    vec![
        Box::new(Dog),
        Box::new(Cat { name: "Tom".into() }),
        Box::new(Parrot { word: "hello".into() }),
    ]
}

fn chorus(animals: &[Box<dyn Animal>]) -> String {
    let lines: Vec<String> = animals.iter().map(|a| a.speak()).collect();
    lines.join("; ")
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn default_speak_uses_each_types_own_name_and_sound() {
        assert_eq!(Dog.speak(), "dog says woof");
        assert_eq!(Cat { name: "Kit".into() }.speak(), "Kit says meow");
    }

    #[test]
    fn parrot_overrides_speak() {
        let p = Parrot { word: "hi".into() };
        assert_eq!(p.sound(), "hi");
        assert_eq!(p.speak(), "hi! hi!");
    }

    #[test]
    fn zoo_holds_three_different_types() {
        let z = zoo();
        let names: Vec<String> = z.iter().map(|a| a.name()).collect();
        assert_eq!(names, ["dog", "Tom", "parrot"]);
    }

    #[test]
    fn chorus_goes_through_the_vtable() {
        assert_eq!(chorus(&zoo()), "dog says woof; Tom says meow; hello! hello!");
        assert_eq!(chorus(&[]), "");
    }
}

// Exercise 2: rules as boxed closures (reference solution)
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex2_rules.rs && ./main --test-threads=4

type Rule = Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool>;

fn max_len(n: usize) -> Rule {
    Box::new(move |s| s.len() <= n) // usize is Copy: copied in
}

fn without(word: &str) -> Rule {
    let word = word.to_string(); // own a copy; the closure must be 'static
    Box::new(move |s| !s.contains(word.as_str()))
}

fn one_of(allowed: Vec<String>) -> Rule {
    Box::new(move |s| allowed.iter().any(|a| a == s)) // the Vec is moved in
}

fn passes_all(rules: &[Rule], text: &str) -> bool {
    rules.iter().all(|r| r(text))
}

fn count_passing(rules: &[Rule], words: &[&str]) -> usize {
    words.iter().filter(|w| passes_all(rules, w)).count()
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn single_rules() {
        assert!(max_len(3)("abc"));
        assert!(!max_len(3)("abcd"));
        assert!(without("x")("abc"));
        assert!(!without("bc")("abc"));
        let r = one_of(vec!["red".into(), "blue".into()]);
        assert!(r("red") && !r("green"));
    }

    #[test]
    fn rule_outlives_the_string_it_was_made_from() {
        let rule = {
            let temp = String::from("oops");
            without(&temp)
        }; // `temp` is dropped here; the rule must still work
        assert!(rule("fine"));
        assert!(!rule("oops!"));
    }

    #[test]
    fn rules_of_different_closure_types_in_one_vec() {
        let rules: Vec<Rule> = vec![max_len(5), without("z"), Box::new(|s: &str| !s.is_empty())];
        assert!(passes_all(&rules, "abc"));
        assert!(!passes_all(&rules, "abcdef"));
        assert!(!passes_all(&rules, ""));
        assert!(passes_all(&[], "anything"));
        assert_eq!(count_passing(&rules, &["ok", "zoo", "toolong", "", "fine"]), 2);
    }
}

// Exercise 3: a traffic signal with the state pattern (reference solution)
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex3_signal.rs && ./main --test-threads=4

trait Light {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light>;
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str;
    // Default: most lights stay on for 30 seconds.
    fn seconds(&self) -> u32 {
        30
    }
}

struct Red;
struct Green;
struct Yellow;

impl Light for Red {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Green)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "red"
    }
}

impl Light for Green {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Yellow)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "green"
    }
}

impl Light for Yellow {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Red)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "yellow"
    }
    fn seconds(&self) -> u32 {
        5
    }
}

struct Signal {
    light: Option<Box<dyn Light>>,
}

impl Signal {
    fn new() -> Signal {
        Signal { light: Some(Box::new(Red)) }
    }

    fn advance(&mut self) {
        // take() leaves None behind, giving us the owned Box to consume.
        let old = self.light.take().unwrap();
        self.light = Some(old.next());
    }

    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        self.light.as_ref().unwrap().color()
    }

    fn run_for(&mut self, n: usize) -> u32 {
        let mut total = 0;
        for _ in 0..n {
            total += self.light.as_ref().unwrap().seconds();
            self.advance();
        }
        total
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn cycle_of_colours() {
        let mut s = Signal::new();
        let mut seen = vec![s.color()];
        for _ in 0..3 {
            s.advance();
            seen.push(s.color());
        }
        assert_eq!(seen, ["red", "green", "yellow", "red"]);
    }

    #[test]
    fn default_and_overridden_seconds() {
        assert_eq!(Red.seconds(), 30);
        assert_eq!(Green.seconds(), 30);
        assert_eq!(Yellow.seconds(), 5);
    }

    #[test]
    fn run_for_adds_up_and_moves_on() {
        let mut s = Signal::new();
        assert_eq!(s.run_for(3), 65);
        assert_eq!(s.color(), "red");
        assert_eq!(s.run_for(0), 0);
        assert_eq!(s.run_for(2), 60);
        assert_eq!(s.color(), "yellow");
    }
}

> `trait Shape: Debug { ... }` says "every type that implements `Shape` must also implement `Debug`". `Debug` is a supertrait of `Shape`.

## 1. Two ways to abstract

You already know one way to write code that works for many types: generics (sub-module 09). `fn show<T: Display>(item: &T)` works for any `T` that implements `Display`. The compiler handles it by monomorphisation: it writes one copy of `show` for every concrete type you call it with, `show::<i32>`, `show::<String>` and so on. Each copy knows its type exactly, so every call is a direct call that can be inlined. This is static dispatch: the method is chosen at compile time.

Generics have one limit: each use picks one type. A `Vec<T>` holds values of a single type `T`. A function returning `impl Trait` returns one concrete type, even if the caller cannot name it. So how do you keep a text box, a checkbox and a button in one list and call `render` on each?

Rust's answer is a trait object, written `dyn Trait`. A trait object stands for "some value of a type that implements `Trait`; which type is decided at run time". There is only one copy of the code that uses it, and each method call is looked up at run time. This is dynamic dispatch.

Generics (`T: Trait`)Trait objects (`dyn Trait`)

Method chosenat compile timeat run time, through a vtable

Copies of your functionone per concrete typeone

Inliningyesusually not

Mixed types in one `Vec`noyes: `Vec<Box<dyn Trait>>`

The Rust Book (ch. 18.2, "Using Trait Objects to Allow for Values of Different Types") builds a GUI library this way. Our `widgets.rs` is a small version of it:

```
let parts: Vec<Box<dyn Render>> =
    vec![Box::new(Text("hello".into())), Box::new(Checkbox(true))];
for part in &parts {
    println!("{}", part.render()); // which render? decided per element, at run time
}
```

The `Vec` still holds one type: `Box<dyn Render>`. What differs is the type inside each box.

## 2. Behind a pointer: fat pointers and vtables

A `Text` and a `Checkbox` have different sizes. So what size is a `dyn Render`? There is no single answer: `dyn Render` is an unsized type (its size is not known at compile time). Rust can only store values whose size it knows, on the stack, in a struct field or in a `Vec` slot. That is why a trait object always sits behind a pointer: `&dyn Render`, `&mut dyn Render` or `Box<dyn Render>`.

That pointer is a fat pointer: two machine words.

- A data pointer to the value itself (the `Checkbox` on the heap, or wherever it lives).

- A vtable pointer to a table the compiler built for that pair (concrete type, trait).

A vtable ("virtual method table") holds the information needed to use the value without knowing its type: how to drop it, its size and alignment, then one entry per trait method, each pointing at the machine code for that type's version of the method.

Two boxed trait objects. Each element of `parts` is a data pointer plus a vtable pointer. Each (type, Render) pair has its own vtable whose rows point at that type's code.

A call such as `part.label()` does three things at run time: follow the vtable pointer, read the `label` row, call the function found there with the data pointer as `self`. That indirect call is the cost of dynamic dispatch: one extra memory read, and the compiler usually cannot inline the call because it does not know which function it will be.

You can see the "fat" part directly. `static_vs_dyn.rs` prints the sizes of a thin and a fat reference:

```
&i32: 8 bytes, &dyn Display: 16 bytes
```

These numbers are for a 64-bit machine (8-byte pointers). The rule is "two pointers instead of one", not "16 bytes". The exact layout of a vtable (row order, whether two values of the same type share one vtable) is a compiler detail you never rely on.

A `Box<dyn Trait>` also costs a heap allocation per value, because each value must live somewhere the box can point to. A borrowed `&dyn Trait` needs no allocation: `let one: &dyn Render = &Text("plain".into());` in `widgets.rs` points at a value that is already somewhere.

## 3. `Sized` and `?Sized`

Every generic parameter has a hidden bound: `T: Sized`, "the size of `T` is known at compile time". That is almost always what you want, since the function may need to store a `T`. But it means this generic function cannot be called with a trait object:

```
fn show_any<T: Display>(item: &T) -> String { format!("[{item}]") }

let m: Box<dyn Display> = Box::new(7);
show_any(m.as_ref()); // T would be `dyn Display`, which is not Sized
```

```
error[E0277]: the size for values of type `dyn std::fmt::Display` cannot be known at compilation time
```

Write `T: ?Sized` ("`T` may or may not be sized") to remove the hidden bound. This is fine here because `show_any` only ever touches `T` through a reference `&T`, which is a pointer of known size:

```
fn show_any<T: Display + ?Sized>(item: &T) -> String { format!("[{item}]") }
```

Now `T` can be `dyn Display`, or `str` (another unsized type you have used since 03 behind `&str`).

## 4. Choosing between generics and trait objects

SituationUseWhy

A function used with one type at a timegeneric `T: Trait` or `impl Trait`fastest; no allocation; inlinable

A list (or field) holding several types at once`Vec<Box<dyn Trait>>`a `Vec<T>` has exactly one `T`

Types chosen at run time (from a config file, user input, plugins)`Box<dyn Trait>`the compiler cannot know the type

Want less generated code (many types, big function)`&dyn Trait`one copy instead of one per type

A small, fixed set of kinds you controlan `enum`see section 9

A common mistake is to think `Vec<T>` with `T: Trait` can hold "anything that implements `Trait`". It cannot: `T` is one type, chosen by the caller. Only `dyn Trait` erases the concrete type.

## 5. Default methods through `dyn`

A trait may give a method a default body. In `widgets.rs`, `label` has a default and `Checkbox` overrides it:

```
trait Render {
    fn render(&self) -> String;
    fn label(&self) -> String { String::from("(unnamed)") }
}
impl Render for Checkbox {
    fn render(&self) -> String { /* ... */ }
    fn label(&self) -> String { String::from("checkbox") }
}
```

How does a vtable deal with this? Every vtable has a row for every trait method, defaults included. For `Checkbox` the `label` row points at `Checkbox::label`. For `Text`, which does not override it, the row points at the default body compiled for `Text`. A default method is like a small generic function: the compiler makes one copy of it per implementing type.

This explains what happens when a default calls another method of the same trait. Inside the copy compiled for `Text`, `self` is a `&Text`, so `self.render()` calls `Text::render`; the type is known there, so that inner call is static. Only the outer call through the trait object goes through the vtable.

To predict what a default method does for a type, read it as if you had pasted its body into that type's `impl` block. Every `self.method()` inside it then resolves to that type's own `method`, overridden or not.

## 6. Dyn compatibility: which traits can be objects

A vtable is a fixed list: one row per method, each pointing at one function. Some methods cannot fit in such a list, so a trait containing them cannot be used as `dyn Trait`. Such a trait is not dyn compatible (older texts say "not object safe"). The main rules, from the Rust Reference:

Method shapeProblem for a vtable

`fn copy(&self) -> Self`The caller must reserve space for the returned `Self`, but behind `dyn` its size is unknown.

`fn put<V: ToString>(&mut self, v: V)`A generic method is a family of functions, one per `V`. A fixed list cannot hold an open-ended family.

`fn new() -> Self` (no `self`)There is no value, so no vtable to look in.

Uncomment both `doubled` lines in `dyn_compat.rs` to see the error:

```
error[E0038]: the trait `Shape` is not dyn compatible
  ...because method `doubled` references the `Self` type in its return type
```

There are two ways out.

- Keep the method off the vtable with `where Self: Sized`. The trait becomes dyn compatible again, and the method can still be called on concrete types, but not on a `dyn Shape`. `dyn_compat.rs` does this with `doubled_sized`.

- Change the method's shape so it fits in a vtable: return `Box<dyn Shape>` instead of `Self`, or take `&dyn ToString` (or a `String`) instead of a generic `V`. Each costs something: a heap allocation, a conversion, or a second dynamic call.

`Box<dyn Trait>` does not make an incompatible trait compatible. The problem is the trait's methods, not where the object is stored.

## 7. Supertraits

`trait Shape: Debug { ... }` says "every type that implements `Shape` must also implement `Debug`". `Debug` is a supertrait of `Shape`. Two consequences:

- Code that has a `Shape` may use `Debug` too. Debug's method joins Shape's vtable, so `println!("{:?}", shapes[0])` works on a `Box<dyn Shape>`.

- Because the supertrait's methods join the vtable, the supertrait must be dyn compatible as well. `Debug` and `Display` are. `Clone` is not (`clone` returns `Self`), and neither is `Default` (`default()` has no `self` and returns `Self`). So `trait Shape: Clone` makes `dyn Shape` impossible.

```
use std::fmt::Debug;
trait Shape: Debug { fn area(&self) -> f64; }

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Square(f64);
impl Shape for Square { fn area(&self) -> f64 { self.0 * self.0 } }
// impl Shape for Square requires Square: Debug, which the derive provides.
```

## 8. Boxed closures and `'static`

Every closure has its own unnamed type, even two closures with the same signature (10). So a list of closures needs a trait object: `Vec<Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool>>`. `Fn`, `FnMut` and `FnOnce` are traits like any other.

A rule you will meet often: in a struct field or in a function's return type, `Box<dyn Trait>` is short for `Box<dyn Trait + 'static>`. `'static` here means "the value inside does not borrow anything that could go away". A closure meets it if every captured value is owned by the closure: copied in, cloned in or moved in. It fails if it captures a reference to a local variable or to a parameter.

```
fn prefix_rule(prefix: &str) -> Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool> {
    let owned = prefix.to_string();                // the closure gets its own copy
    Box::new(move |s| s.starts_with(owned.as_str()))
}
```

If the closure used `prefix` directly, it would hold a borrow that only lives as long as the caller's string, and the compiler refuses:

```
error: lifetime may not live long enough
  returning this value requires that `'1` must outlive `'static`
```

`move` moves whatever the closure names. If the variable is itself a reference (`prefix: &str`, `limit: &u32`), `move` moves the reference into the closure. The closure still borrows. To own the data, copy or clone it out first: `let limit = *limit;` or `let owned = prefix.to_string();`.

A `&dyn Fn(..)` parameter, by contrast, may borrow freely: it is only used during the call. Writing other lifetimes, such as `Box<dyn Fn() + 'a>`, is covered in 14.

## 9. Consuming a trait object; trait objects vs enums

A method may take its receiver as `self: Box<Self>`. It then consumes the box: after the call, the object is gone. The Book's state pattern (ch. 18.3, "Implementing an Object-Oriented Design Pattern") uses this so a state transition uses up the old state. `state.rs` is adapted from it:

```
trait State {
    fn submit(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn State>;
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str;
}
impl State for Draft {
    fn submit(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn State> { Box::new(Review) }
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str { "draft" }
}
```

`self: Box<Self>` is dyn compatible: the receiver is a pointer of known size, so the call can go through the vtable. The catch is that you must own the box to call it. A shared or mutable borrow of a box is not enough; you cannot move a box out from behind a reference. When the box sits inside something else, take it out first:

Where the box livesHow to take it out

`Option<Box<dyn State>>``opt.take()` leaves `None` behind

a field or variable of a type with a default`std::mem::take(&mut x)` (11)

a `Vec<Box<dyn T>>`, all of it`v.drain(..)` or `mem::take(&mut v)`, which leave it empty

a `Vec`, one element`v.remove(i)` or `v.pop()`

### Trait objects or an enum?

The same states could be an `enum State { Draft, Review, Published }` with `match` in each operation. The two designs make different changes cheap:

ChangeTrait objectsEnum + match

Add a new kind (type / variant)one new type and its `impl`; no other code changesedit every `match`

Add a new operationadd a method to the trait and to every typeone new function with one `match`; the compiler checks every case

Types from outside your crate (plugins)yesno: the set is closed

Cost per callvtable call, heap allocation per boxa `match` on a tag; no allocation needed

## 10. Check yourself

Ask the Tutor about any of these. Try to answer first.

- Why must `dyn Trait` always sit behind a pointer? What are the two halves of that pointer?

- Why can a trait with `fn copy(&self) -> Self` not be a trait object, while `fn copy(&self) -> Box<dyn Trait>` is fine?

- A default method calls `self.unit()`. For a type that overrides `unit`, which `unit` runs, and why?

- Why does a closure stored in a `Box<dyn Fn()>` field have to own what it captures?

- What would you gain and lose by rewriting `state.rs` as an enum?

Sources: adapted from The Rust Programming Language, ch. 18.2 and ch. 18.3, Rust by Example, "Returning Traits with dyn" and the Rust Reference, "Dyn compatibility" (MIT/Apache-2.0).

[entity 908 · fat-pointer.png · diagram]
Diagram: a trait object is a fat pointer.

Left, two elements of `parts: Vec<Box<dyn Render>>`. Each element is two pointers side by side: a "data ptr" and a "vtable ptr".
- parts[0]: the data ptr points to `Text("hello")` on the heap; the vtable ptr points to the vtable for (Text, Render).
- parts[1]: the data ptr points to `Checkbox(true)` on the heap; the vtable ptr points to the vtable for (Checkbox, Render).

Middle, the two vtables. Each has rows: drop, size and align, render, label.

Right, where the rows point:
- Text's `render` row -> `Text::render`. Text's `label` row -> the trait's default `label`, compiled for Text (Text does not override it).
- Checkbox's `render` row -> `Checkbox::render`. Checkbox's `label` row -> `Checkbox::label` (its override).

Caption: `part.label()` on parts[0] follows the vtable ptr, reads the "label" row and calls it with the data ptr as `self`. Row order and whether vtables are shared are compiler details. On 64-bit each pointer is 8 bytes, so the fat pointer is 16.

// Exercise 2: rules as boxed closures (reference solution)
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex2_rules.rs && ./main --test-threads=4

type Rule = Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool>;

fn max_len(n: usize) -> Rule {
    Box::new(move |s| s.len() <= n) // usize is Copy: copied in
}

fn without(word: &str) -> Rule {
    let word = word.to_string(); // own a copy; the closure must be 'static
    Box::new(move |s| !s.contains(word.as_str()))
}

fn one_of(allowed: Vec<String>) -> Rule {
    Box::new(move |s| allowed.iter().any(|a| a == s)) // the Vec is moved in
}

fn passes_all(rules: &[Rule], text: &str) -> bool {
    rules.iter().all(|r| r(text))
}

fn count_passing(rules: &[Rule], words: &[&str]) -> usize {
    words.iter().filter(|w| passes_all(rules, w)).count()
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn single_rules() {
        assert!(max_len(3)("abc"));
        assert!(!max_len(3)("abcd"));
        assert!(without("x")("abc"));
        assert!(!without("bc")("abc"));
        let r = one_of(vec!["red".into(), "blue".into()]);
        assert!(r("red") && !r("green"));
    }

    #[test]
    fn rule_outlives_the_string_it_was_made_from() {
        let rule = {
            let temp = String::from("oops");
            without(&temp)
        }; // `temp` is dropped here; the rule must still work
        assert!(rule("fine"));
        assert!(!rule("oops!"));
    }

    #[test]
    fn rules_of_different_closure_types_in_one_vec() {
        let rules: Vec<Rule> = vec![max_len(5), without("z"), Box::new(|s: &str| !s.is_empty())];
        assert!(passes_all(&rules, "abc"));
        assert!(!passes_all(&rules, "abcdef"));
        assert!(!passes_all(&rules, ""));
        assert!(passes_all(&[], "anything"));
        assert_eq!(count_passing(&rules, &["ok", "zoo", "toolong", "", "fine"]), 2);
    }
}

trait Light {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light>;
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str;
    // Default: most lights stay on for 30 seconds.
    fn seconds(&self) -> u32 {
        30
    }
}

struct Red;
struct Green;
struct Yellow;

impl Light for Red {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Green)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "red"
    }
}

impl Light for Green {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Yellow)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "green"
    }
}

impl Light for Yellow {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Red)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "yellow"
    }
    fn seconds(&self) -> u32 {
        5
    }
}

struct Signal {
    light: Option<Box<dyn Light>>,
}

impl Signal {
    fn new() -> Signal {
        Signal { light: Some(Box::new(Red)) }
    }

    fn advance(&mut self) {
        // take() leaves None behind, giving us the owned Box to consume.
        let old = self.light.take().unwrap();
        self.light = Some(old.next());
    }

    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        self.light.as_ref().unwrap().color()
    }

    fn run_for(&mut self, n: usize) -> u32 {
        let mut total = 0;
        for _ in 0..n {
            total += self.light.as_ref().unwrap().seconds();
            self.advance();
        }
        total
    }
}

## 1. Two ways to abstract

You already know one way to write code that works for many types: generics (sub-module 09). `fn show<T: Display>(item: &T)` works for any `T` that implements `Display`. The compiler handles it by monomorphisation: it writes one copy of `show` for every concrete type you call it with, `show::<i32>`, `show::<String>` and so on. Each copy knows its type exactly, so every call is a direct call that can be inlined. This is static dispatch: the method is chosen at compile time.

Generics have one limit: each use picks one type. A `Vec<T>` holds values of a single type `T`. A function returning `impl Trait` returns one concrete type, even if the caller cannot name it. So how do you keep a text box, a checkbox and a button in one list and call `render` on each?

Rust's answer is a trait object, written `dyn Trait`. A trait object stands for "some value of a type that implements `Trait`; which type is decided at run time". There is only one copy of the code that uses it, and each method call is looked up at run time. This is dynamic dispatch.

Generics (`T: Trait`)Trait objects (`dyn Trait`)

Method chosenat compile timeat run time, through a vtable

Copies of your functionone per concrete typeone

Inliningyesusually not

Mixed types in one `Vec`noyes: `Vec<Box<dyn Trait>>`

The Rust Book (ch. 18.2, "Using Trait Objects to Allow for Values of Different Types") builds a GUI library this way. Our `widgets.rs` is a small version of it:

```
let parts: Vec<Box<dyn Render>> =
    vec![Box::new(Text("hello".into())), Box::new(Checkbox(true))];
for part in &parts {
    println!("{}", part.render()); // which render? decided per element, at run time
}
```

The `Vec` still holds one type: `Box<dyn Render>`. What differs is the type inside each box.

## 2. Behind a pointer: fat pointers and vtables

A `Text` and a `Checkbox` have different sizes. So what size is a `dyn Render`? There is no single answer: `dyn Render` is an unsized type (its size is not known at compile time). Rust can only store values whose size it knows, on the stack, in a struct field or in a `Vec` slot. That is why a trait object always sits behind a pointer: `&dyn Render`, `&mut dyn Render` or `Box<dyn Render>`.

That pointer is a fat pointer: two machine words.

- A data pointer to the value itself (the `Checkbox` on the heap, or wherever it lives).

- A vtable pointer to a table the compiler built for that pair (concrete type, trait).

A vtable ("virtual method table") holds the information needed to use the value without knowing its type: how to drop it, its size and alignment, then one entry per trait method, each pointing at the machine code for that type's version of the method.

Two boxed trait objects. Each element of `parts` is a data pointer plus a vtable pointer. Each (type, Render) pair has its own vtable whose rows point at that type's code.

A call such as `part.label()` does three things at run time: follow the vtable pointer, read the `label` row, call the function found there with the data pointer as `self`. That indirect call is the cost of dynamic dispatch: one extra memory read, and the compiler usually cannot inline the call because it does not know which function it will be.

You can see the "fat" part directly. `static_vs_dyn.rs` prints the sizes of a thin and a fat reference:

```
&i32: 8 bytes, &dyn Display: 16 bytes
```

These numbers are for a 64-bit machine (8-byte pointers). The rule is "two pointers instead of one", not "16 bytes". The exact layout of a vtable (row order, whether two values of the same type share one vtable) is a compiler detail you never rely on.

A `Box<dyn Trait>` also costs a heap allocation per value, because each value must live somewhere the box can point to. A borrowed `&dyn Trait` needs no allocation: `let one: &dyn Render = &Text("plain".into());` in `widgets.rs` points at a value that is already somewhere.

## 3. `Sized` and `?Sized`

Every generic parameter has a hidden bound: `T: Sized`, "the size of `T` is known at compile time". That is almost always what you want, since the function may need to store a `T`. But it means this generic function cannot be called with a trait object:

```
fn show_any<T: Display>(item: &T) -> String { format!("[{item}]") }

let m: Box<dyn Display> = Box::new(7);
show_any(m.as_ref()); // T would be `dyn Display`, which is not Sized
```

```
error[E0277]: the size for values of type `dyn std::fmt::Display` cannot be known at compilation time
```

Write `T: ?Sized` ("`T` may or may not be sized") to remove the hidden bound. This is fine here because `show_any` only ever touches `T` through a reference `&T`, which is a pointer of known size:

```
fn show_any<T: Display + ?Sized>(item: &T) -> String { format!("[{item}]") }
```

Now `T` can be `dyn Display`, or `str` (another unsized type you have used since 03 behind `&str`).

## 4. Choosing between generics and trait objects

SituationUseWhy

A function used with one type at a timegeneric `T: Trait` or `impl Trait`fastest; no allocation; inlinable

A list (or field) holding several types at once`Vec<Box<dyn Trait>>`a `Vec<T>` has exactly one `T`

Types chosen at run time (from a config file, user input, plugins)`Box<dyn Trait>`the compiler cannot know the type

Want less generated code (many types, big function)`&dyn Trait`one copy instead of one per type

A small, fixed set of kinds you controlan `enum`see section 9

A common mistake is to think `Vec<T>` with `T: Trait` can hold "anything that implements `Trait`". It cannot: `T` is one type, chosen by the caller. Only `dyn Trait` erases the concrete type.

## 5. Default methods through `dyn`

A trait may give a method a default body. In `widgets.rs`, `label` has a default and `Checkbox` overrides it:

```
trait Render {
    fn render(&self) -> String;
    fn label(&self) -> String { String::from("(unnamed)") }
}
impl Render for Checkbox {
    fn render(&self) -> String { /* ... */ }
    fn label(&self) -> String { String::from("checkbox") }
}
```

How does a vtable deal with this? Every vtable has a row for every trait method, defaults included. For `Checkbox` the `label` row points at `Checkbox::label`. For `Text`, which does not override it, the row points at the default body compiled for `Text`. A default method is like a small generic function: the compiler makes one copy of it per implementing type.

This explains what happens when a default calls another method of the same trait. Inside the copy compiled for `Text`, `self` is a `&Text`, so `self.render()` calls `Text::render`; the type is known there, so that inner call is static. Only the outer call through the trait object goes through the vtable.

To predict what a default method does for a type, read it as if you had pasted its body into that type's `impl` block. Every `self.method()` inside it then resolves to that type's own `method`, overridden or not.

## 6. Dyn compatibility: which traits can be objects

A vtable is a fixed list: one row per method, each pointing at one function. Some methods cannot fit in such a list, so a trait containing them cannot be used as `dyn Trait`. Such a trait is not dyn compatible (older texts say "not object safe"). The main rules, from the Rust Reference:

Method shapeProblem for a vtable

`fn copy(&self) -> Self`The caller must reserve space for the returned `Self`, but behind `dyn` its size is unknown.

`fn put<V: ToString>(&mut self, v: V)`A generic method is a family of functions, one per `V`. A fixed list cannot hold an open-ended family.

`fn new() -> Self` (no `self`)There is no value, so no vtable to look in.

Uncomment both `doubled` lines in `dyn_compat.rs` to see the error:

```
error[E0038]: the trait `Shape` is not dyn compatible
  ...because method `doubled` references the `Self` type in its return type
```

There are two ways out.

- Keep the method off the vtable with `where Self: Sized`. The trait becomes dyn compatible again, and the method can still be called on concrete types, but not on a `dyn Shape`. `dyn_compat.rs` does this with `doubled_sized`.

- Change the method's shape so it fits in a vtable: return `Box<dyn Shape>` instead of `Self`, or take `&dyn ToString` (or a `String`) instead of a generic `V`. Each costs something: a heap allocation, a conversion, or a second dynamic call.

`Box<dyn Trait>` does not make an incompatible trait compatible. The problem is the trait's methods, not where the object is stored.

## 7. Supertraits

`trait Shape: Debug { ... }` says "every type that implements `Shape` must also implement `Debug`". `Debug` is a supertrait of `Shape`. Two consequences:

- Code that has a `Shape` may use `Debug` too. Debug's method joins Shape's vtable, so `println!("{:?}", shapes[0])` works on a `Box<dyn Shape>`.

- Because the supertrait's methods join the vtable, the supertrait must be dyn compatible as well. `Debug` and `Display` are. `Clone` is not (`clone` returns `Self`), and neither is `Default` (`default()` has no `self` and returns `Self`). So `trait Shape: Clone` makes `dyn Shape` impossible.

```
use std::fmt::Debug;
trait Shape: Debug { fn area(&self) -> f64; }

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Square(f64);
impl Shape for Square { fn area(&self) -> f64 { self.0 * self.0 } }
// impl Shape for Square requires Square: Debug, which the derive provides.
```

## 8. Boxed closures and `'static`

Every closure has its own unnamed type, even two closures with the same signature (10). So a list of closures needs a trait object: `Vec<Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool>>`. `Fn`, `FnMut` and `FnOnce` are traits like any other.

A rule you will meet often: in a struct field or in a function's return type, `Box<dyn Trait>` is short for `Box<dyn Trait + 'static>`. `'static` here means "the value inside does not borrow anything that could go away". A closure meets it if every captured value is owned by the closure: copied in, cloned in or moved in. It fails if it captures a reference to a local variable or to a parameter.

```
fn prefix_rule(prefix: &str) -> Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool> {
    let owned = prefix.to_string();                // the closure gets its own copy
    Box::new(move |s| s.starts_with(owned.as_str()))
}
```

If the closure used `prefix` directly, it would hold a borrow that only lives as long as the caller's string, and the compiler refuses:

```
error: lifetime may not live long enough
  returning this value requires that `'1` must outlive `'static`
```

`move` moves whatever the closure names. If the variable is itself a reference (`prefix: &str`, `limit: &u32`), `move` moves the reference into the closure. The closure still borrows. To own the data, copy or clone it out first: `let limit = *limit;` or `let owned = prefix.to_string();`.

A `&dyn Fn(..)` parameter, by contrast, may borrow freely: it is only used during the call. Writing other lifetimes, such as `Box<dyn Fn() + 'a>`, is covered in 14.

## 9. Consuming a trait object; trait objects vs enums

A method may take its receiver as `self: Box<Self>`. It then consumes the box: after the call, the object is gone. The Book's state pattern (ch. 18.3, "Implementing an Object-Oriented Design Pattern") uses this so a state transition uses up the old state. `state.rs` is adapted from it:

```
trait State {
    fn submit(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn State>;
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str;
}
impl State for Draft {
    fn submit(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn State> { Box::new(Review) }
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str { "draft" }
}
```

`self: Box<Self>` is dyn compatible: the receiver is a pointer of known size, so the call can go through the vtable. The catch is that you must own the box to call it. A shared or mutable borrow of a box is not enough; you cannot move a box out from behind a reference. When the box sits inside something else, take it out first:

Where the box livesHow to take it out

`Option<Box<dyn State>>``opt.take()` leaves `None` behind

a field or variable of a type with a default`std::mem::take(&mut x)` (11)

a `Vec<Box<dyn T>>`, all of it`v.drain(..)` or `mem::take(&mut v)`, which leave it empty

a `Vec`, one element`v.remove(i)` or `v.pop()`

### Trait objects or an enum?

The same states could be an `enum State { Draft, Review, Published }` with `match` in each operation. The two designs make different changes cheap:

ChangeTrait objectsEnum + match

Add a new kind (type / variant)one new type and its `impl`; no other code changesedit every `match`

Add a new operationadd a method to the trait and to every typeone new function with one `match`; the compiler checks every case

Types from outside your crate (plugins)yesno: the set is closed

Cost per callvtable call, heap allocation per boxa `match` on a tag; no allocation needed

## 10. Check yourself

Ask the Tutor about any of these. Try to answer first.

- Why must `dyn Trait` always sit behind a pointer? What are the two halves of that pointer?

- Why can a trait with `fn copy(&self) -> Self` not be a trait object, while `fn copy(&self) -> Box<dyn Trait>` is fine?

- A default method calls `self.unit()`. For a type that overrides `unit`, which `unit` runs, and why?

- Why does a closure stored in a `Box<dyn Fn()>` field have to own what it captures?

- What would you gain and lose by rewriting `state.rs` as an enum?

Sources: adapted from The Rust Programming Language, ch. 18.2 and ch. 18.3, Rust by Example, "Returning Traits with dyn" and the Rust Reference, "Dyn compatibility" (MIT/Apache-2.0).

[entity 908 · fat-pointer.png · diagram]
Diagram: a trait object is a fat pointer.

Left, two elements of `parts: Vec<Box<dyn Render>>`. Each element is two pointers side by side: a "data ptr" and a "vtable ptr".
- parts[0]: the data ptr points to `Text("hello")` on the heap; the vtable ptr points to the vtable for (Text, Render).
- parts[1]: the data ptr points to `Checkbox(true)` on the heap; the vtable ptr points to the vtable for (Checkbox, Render).

Middle, the two vtables. Each has rows: drop, size and align, render, label.

Right, where the rows point:
- Text's `render` row -> `Text::render`. Text's `label` row -> the trait's default `label`, compiled for Text (Text does not override it).
- Checkbox's `render` row -> `Checkbox::render`. Checkbox's `label` row -> `Checkbox::label` (its override).

Caption: `part.label()` on parts[0] follows the vtable ptr, reads the "label" row and calls it with the data ptr as `self`. Row order and whether vtables are shared are compiler details. On 64-bit each pointer is 8 bytes, so the fat pointer is 16.

// Exercise 1: a mixed zoo (reference solution)
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex1_zoo.rs && ./main --test-threads=4

trait Animal {
    fn name(&self) -> String;
    fn sound(&self) -> String;
    // Default: "<name> says <sound>"
    fn speak(&self) -> String {
        format!("{} says {}", self.name(), self.sound())
    }
}

struct Dog;
struct Cat {
    name: String,
}
struct Parrot {
    word: String,
}

impl Animal for Dog {
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        String::from("dog")
    }
    fn sound(&self) -> String {
        String::from("woof")
    }
}

impl Animal for Cat {
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        self.name.clone()
    }
    fn sound(&self) -> String {
        String::from("meow")
    }
}

impl Animal for Parrot {
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        String::from("parrot")
    }
    fn sound(&self) -> String {
        self.word.clone()
    }
    fn speak(&self) -> String {
        format!("{0}! {0}!", self.word)
    }
}

fn zoo() -> Vec<Box<dyn Animal>> {
    vec![
        Box::new(Dog),
        Box::new(Cat { name: "Tom".into() }),
        Box::new(Parrot { word: "hello".into() }),
    ]
}

fn chorus(animals: &[Box<dyn Animal>]) -> String {
    let lines: Vec<String> = animals.iter().map(|a| a.speak()).collect();
    lines.join("; ")
}

#[cfg(test)]

    fn zoo_holds_three_different_types() {
        let z = zoo();
        let names: Vec<String> = z.iter().map(|a| a.name()).collect();

    }

// Exercise 2: rules as boxed closures (reference solution)
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex2_rules.rs && ./main --test-threads=4

type Rule = Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool>;

fn max_len(n: usize) -> Rule {
    Box::new(move |s| s.len() <= n) // usize is Copy: copied in
}

fn without(word: &str) -> Rule {
    let word = word.to_string(); // own a copy; the closure must be 'static
    Box::new(move |s| !s.contains(word.as_str()))
}

fn one_of(allowed: Vec<String>) -> Rule {
    Box::new(move |s| allowed.iter().any(|a| a == s)) // the Vec is moved in
}

fn passes_all(rules: &[Rule], text: &str) -> bool {
    rules.iter().all(|r| r(text))
}

fn count_passing(rules: &[Rule], words: &[&str]) -> usize {
    words.iter().filter(|w| passes_all(rules, w)).count()
}

// Exercise 3: a traffic signal with the state pattern (reference solution)
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex3_signal.rs && ./main --test-threads=4

trait Light {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light>;
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str;
    // Default: most lights stay on for 30 seconds.
    fn seconds(&self) -> u32 {
        30
    }
}

struct Red;
struct Green;
struct Yellow;

impl Light for Red {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Green)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "red"
    }
}

impl Light for Green {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Yellow)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "green"
    }
}

impl Light for Yellow {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Red)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "yellow"
    }
    fn seconds(&self) -> u32 {
        5
    }
}

struct Signal {
    light: Option<Box<dyn Light>>,
}

impl Signal {
    fn new() -> Signal {
        Signal { light: Some(Box::new(Red)) }
    }

    fn advance(&mut self) {
        // take() leaves None behind, giving us the owned Box to consume.
        let old = self.light.take().unwrap();
        self.light = Some(old.next());
    }

    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        self.light.as_ref().unwrap().color()
    }

    fn run_for(&mut self, n: usize) -> u32 {
        let mut total = 0;
        for _ in 0..n {
            total += self.light.as_ref().unwrap().seconds();
            self.advance();
        }
        total
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn cycle_of_colours() {
        let mut s = Signal::new();
        let mut seen = vec![s.color()];
        for _ in 0..3 {
            s.advance();
            seen.push(s.color());
        }
        assert_eq!(seen, ["red", "green", "yellow", "red"]);
    }

    #[test]
    fn default_and_overridden_seconds() {
        assert_eq!(Red.seconds(), 30);
        assert_eq!(Green.seconds(), 30);
        assert_eq!(Yellow.seconds(), 5);
    }

    #[test]
    fn run_for_adds_up_and_moves_on() {
        let mut s = Signal::new();
        assert_eq!(s.run_for(3), 65);
        assert_eq!(s.color(), "red");
        assert_eq!(s.run_for(0), 0);
        assert_eq!(s.run_for(2), 60);
        assert_eq!(s.color(), "yellow");
    }
}

## 1. Two ways to abstract

You already know one way to write code that works for many types: generics (sub-module 09). `fn show<T: Display>(item: &T)` works for any `T` that implements `Display`. The compiler handles it by monomorphisation: it writes one copy of `show` for every concrete type you call it with, `show::<i32>`, `show::<String>` and so on. Each copy knows its type exactly, so every call is a direct call that can be inlined. This is static dispatch: the method is chosen at compile time.

Generics have one limit: each use picks one type. A `Vec<T>` holds values of a single type `T`. A function returning `impl Trait` returns one concrete type, even if the caller cannot name it. So how do you keep a text box, a checkbox and a button in one list and call `render` on each?

Rust's answer is a trait object, written `dyn Trait`. A trait object stands for "some value of a type that implements `Trait`; which type is decided at run time". There is only one copy of the code that uses it, and each method call is looked up at run time. This is dynamic dispatch.

Generics (`T: Trait`)Trait objects (`dyn Trait`)

Method chosenat compile timeat run time, through a vtable

Copies of your functionone per concrete typeone

Inliningyesusually not

Mixed types in one `Vec`noyes: `Vec<Box<dyn Trait>>`

The Rust Book (ch. 18.2, "Using Trait Objects to Allow for Values of Different Types") builds a GUI library this way. Our `widgets.rs` is a small version of it:

```
let parts: Vec<Box<dyn Render>> =
    vec![Box::new(Text("hello".into())), Box::new(Checkbox(true))];
for part in &parts {
    println!("{}", part.render()); // which render? decided per element, at run time
}
```

The `Vec` still holds one type: `Box<dyn Render>`. What differs is the type inside each box.

## 2. Behind a pointer: fat pointers and vtables

A `Text` and a `Checkbox` have different sizes. So what size is a `dyn Render`? There is no single answer: `dyn Render` is an unsized type (its size is not known at compile time). Rust can only store values whose size it knows, on the stack, in a struct field or in a `Vec` slot. That is why a trait object always sits behind a pointer: `&dyn Render`, `&mut dyn Render` or `Box<dyn Render>`.

That pointer is a fat pointer: two machine words.

- A data pointer to the value itself (the `Checkbox` on the heap, or wherever it lives).

- A vtable pointer to a table the compiler built for that pair (concrete type, trait).

A vtable ("virtual method table") holds the information needed to use the value without knowing its type: how to drop it, its size and alignment, then one entry per trait method, each pointing at the machine code for that type's version of the method.

Two boxed trait objects. Each element of `parts` is a data pointer plus a vtable pointer. Each (type, Render) pair has its own vtable whose rows point at that type's code.

A call such as `part.label()` does three things at run time: follow the vtable pointer, read the `label` row, call the function found there with the data pointer as `self`. That indirect call is the cost of dynamic dispatch: one extra memory read, and the compiler usually cannot inline the call because it does not know which function it will be.

You can see the "fat" part directly. `static_vs_dyn.rs` prints the sizes of a thin and a fat reference:

```
&i32: 8 bytes, &dyn Display: 16 bytes
```

These numbers are for a 64-bit machine (8-byte pointers). The rule is "two pointers instead of one", not "16 bytes". The exact layout of a vtable (row order, whether two values of the same type share one vtable) is a compiler detail you never rely on.

A `Box<dyn Trait>` also costs a heap allocation per value, because each value must live somewhere the box can point to. A borrowed `&dyn Trait` needs no allocation: `let one: &dyn Render = &Text("plain".into());` in `widgets.rs` points at a value that is already somewhere.

## 3. `Sized` and `?Sized`

Every generic parameter has a hidden bound: `T: Sized`, "the size of `T` is known at compile time". That is almost always what you want, since the function may need to store a `T`. But it means this generic function cannot be called with a trait object:

```
fn show_any<T: Display>(item: &T) -> String { format!("[{item}]") }

let m: Box<dyn Display> = Box::new(7);
show_any(m.as_ref()); // T would be `dyn Display`, which is not Sized
```

```
error[E0277]: the size for values of type `dyn std::fmt::Display` cannot be known at compilation time
```

Write `T: ?Sized` ("`T` may or may not be sized") to remove the hidden bound. This is fine here because `show_any` only ever touches `T` through a reference `&T`, which is a pointer of known size:

```
fn show_any<T: Display + ?Sized>(item: &T) -> String { format!("[{item}]") }
```

Now `T` can be `dyn Display`, or `str` (another unsized type you have used since 03 behind `&str`).

## 4. Choosing between generics and trait objects

SituationUseWhy

A function used with one type at a timegeneric `T: Trait` or `impl Trait`fastest; no allocation; inlinable

A list (or field) holding several types at once`Vec<Box<dyn Trait>>`a `Vec<T>` has exactly one `T`

Types chosen at run time (from a config file, user input, plugins)`Box<dyn Trait>`the compiler cannot know the type

Want less generated code (many types, big function)`&dyn Trait`one copy instead of one per type

A small, fixed set of kinds you controlan `enum`see section 9

A common mistake is to think `Vec<T>` with `T: Trait` can hold "anything that implements `Trait`". It cannot: `T` is one type, chosen by the caller. Only `dyn Trait` erases the concrete type.

## 5. Default methods through `dyn`

A trait may give a method a default body. In `widgets.rs`, `label` has a default and `Checkbox` overrides it:

```
trait Render {
    fn render(&self) -> String;
    fn label(&self) -> String { String::from("(unnamed)") }
}
impl Render for Checkbox {
    fn render(&self) -> String { /* ... */ }
    fn label(&self) -> String { String::from("checkbox") }
}
```

How does a vtable deal with this? Every vtable has a row for every trait method, defaults included. For `Checkbox` the `label` row points at `Checkbox::label`. For `Text`, which does not override it, the row points at the default body compiled for `Text`. A default method is like a small generic function: the compiler makes one copy of it per implementing type.

This explains what happens when a default calls another method of the same trait. Inside the copy compiled for `Text`, `self` is a `&Text`, so `self.render()` calls `Text::render`; the type is known there, so that inner call is static. Only the outer call through the trait object goes through the vtable.

To predict what a default method does for a type, read it as if you had pasted its body into that type's `impl` block. Every `self.method()` inside it then resolves to that type's own `method`, overridden or not.

## 6. Dyn compatibility: which traits can be objects

A vtable is a fixed list: one row per method, each pointing at one function. Some methods cannot fit in such a list, so a trait containing them cannot be used as `dyn Trait`. Such a trait is not dyn compatible (older texts say "not object safe"). The main rules, from the Rust Reference:

Method shapeProblem for a vtable

`fn copy(&self) -> Self`The caller must reserve space for the returned `Self`, but behind `dyn` its size is unknown.

`fn put<V: ToString>(&mut self, v: V)`A generic method is a family of functions, one per `V`. A fixed list cannot hold an open-ended family.

`fn new() -> Self` (no `self`)There is no value, so no vtable to look in.

Uncomment both `doubled` lines in `dyn_compat.rs` to see the error:

```
error[E0038]: the trait `Shape` is not dyn compatible
  ...because method `doubled` references the `Self` type in its return type
```

There are two ways out.

- Keep the method off the vtable with `where Self: Sized`. The trait becomes dyn compatible again, and the method can still be called on concrete types, but not on a `dyn Shape`. `dyn_compat.rs` does this with `doubled_sized`.

- Change the method's shape so it fits in a vtable: return `Box<dyn Shape>` instead of `Self`, or take `&dyn ToString` (or a `String`) instead of a generic `V`. Each costs something: a heap allocation, a conversion, or a second dynamic call.

`Box<dyn Trait>` does not make an incompatible trait compatible. The problem is the trait's methods, not where the object is stored.

## 7. Supertraits

`trait Shape: Debug { ... }` says "every type that implements `Shape` must also implement `Debug`". `Debug` is a supertrait of `Shape`. Two consequences:

- Code that has a `Shape` may use `Debug` too. Debug's method joins Shape's vtable, so `println!("{:?}", shapes[0])` works on a `Box<dyn Shape>`.

- Because the supertrait's methods join the vtable, the supertrait must be dyn compatible as well. `Debug` and `Display` are. `Clone` is not (`clone` returns `Self`), and neither is `Default` (`default()` has no `self` and returns `Self`). So `trait Shape: Clone` makes `dyn Shape` impossible.

```
use std::fmt::Debug;
trait Shape: Debug { fn area(&self) -> f64; }

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Square(f64);
impl Shape for Square { fn area(&self) -> f64 { self.0 * self.0 } }
// impl Shape for Square requires Square: Debug, which the derive provides.
```

## 8. Boxed closures and `'static`

Every closure has its own unnamed type, even two closures with the same signature (10). So a list of closures needs a trait object: `Vec<Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool>>`. `Fn`, `FnMut` and `FnOnce` are traits like any other.

A rule you will meet often: in a struct field or in a function's return type, `Box<dyn Trait>` is short for `Box<dyn Trait + 'static>`. `'static` here means "the value inside does not borrow anything that could go away". A closure meets it if every captured value is owned by the closure: copied in, cloned in or moved in. It fails if it captures a reference to a local variable or to a parameter.

```
fn prefix_rule(prefix: &str) -> Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool> {
    let owned = prefix.to_string();                // the closure gets its own copy
    Box::new(move |s| s.starts_with(owned.as_str()))
}
```

If the closure used `prefix` directly, it would hold a borrow that only lives as long as the caller's string, and the compiler refuses:

```
error: lifetime may not live long enough
  returning this value requires that `'1` must outlive `'static`
```

`move` moves whatever the closure names. If the variable is itself a reference (`prefix: &str`, `limit: &u32`), `move` moves the reference into the closure. The closure still borrows. To own the data, copy or clone it out first: `let limit = *limit;` or `let owned = prefix.to_string();`.

A `&dyn Fn(..)` parameter, by contrast, may borrow freely: it is only used during the call. Writing other lifetimes, such as `Box<dyn Fn() + 'a>`, is covered in 14.

## 9. Consuming a trait object; trait objects vs enums

A method may take its receiver as `self: Box<Self>`. It then consumes the box: after the call, the object is gone. The Book's state pattern (ch. 18.3, "Implementing an Object-Oriented Design Pattern") uses this so a state transition uses up the old state. `state.rs` is adapted from it:

```
trait State {
    fn submit(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn State>;
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str;
}
impl State for Draft {
    fn submit(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn State> { Box::new(Review) }
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str { "draft" }
}
```

`self: Box<Self>` is dyn compatible: the receiver is a pointer of known size, so the call can go through the vtable. The catch is that you must own the box to call it. A shared or mutable borrow of a box is not enough; you cannot move a box out from behind a reference. When the box sits inside something else, take it out first:

Where the box livesHow to take it out

`Option<Box<dyn State>>``opt.take()` leaves `None` behind

a field or variable of a type with a default`std::mem::take(&mut x)` (11)

a `Vec<Box<dyn T>>`, all of it`v.drain(..)` or `mem::take(&mut v)`, which leave it empty

a `Vec`, one element`v.remove(i)` or `v.pop()`

### Trait objects or an enum?

The same states could be an `enum State { Draft, Review, Published }` with `match` in each operation. The two designs make different changes cheap:

ChangeTrait objectsEnum + match

Add a new kind (type / variant)one new type and its `impl`; no other code changesedit every `match`

Add a new operationadd a method to the trait and to every typeone new function with one `match`; the compiler checks every case

Types from outside your crate (plugins)yesno: the set is closed

Cost per callvtable call, heap allocation per boxa `match` on a tag; no allocation needed

## 10. Check yourself

Ask the Tutor about any of these. Try to answer first.

- Why must `dyn Trait` always sit behind a pointer? What are the two halves of that pointer?

- Why can a trait with `fn copy(&self) -> Self` not be a trait object, while `fn copy(&self) -> Box<dyn Trait>` is fine?

- A default method calls `self.unit()`. For a type that overrides `unit`, which `unit` runs, and why?

- Why does a closure stored in a `Box<dyn Fn()>` field have to own what it captures?

- What would you gain and lose by rewriting `state.rs` as an enum?

[entity 908 · fat-pointer.png · diagram]
Diagram: a trait object is a fat pointer.

Left, two elements of `parts: Vec<Box<dyn Render>>`. Each element is two pointers side by side: a "data ptr" and a "vtable ptr".
- parts[0]: the data ptr points to `Text("hello")` on the heap; the vtable ptr points to the vtable for (Text, Render).
- parts[1]: the data ptr points to `Checkbox(true)` on the heap; the vtable ptr points to the vtable for (Checkbox, Render).

Middle, the two vtables. Each has rows: drop, size and align, render, label.

Right, where the rows point:
- Text's `render` row -> `Text::render`. Text's `label` row -> the trait's default `label`, compiled for Text (Text does not override it).
- Checkbox's `render` row -> `Checkbox::render`. Checkbox's `label` row -> `Checkbox::label` (its override).

Caption: `part.label()` on parts[0] follows the vtable ptr, reads the "label" row and calls it with the data ptr as `self`. Row order and whether vtables are shared are compiler details. On 64-bit each pointer is 8 bytes, so the fat pointer is 16.

// Exercise 1: a mixed zoo (reference solution)
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex1_zoo.rs && ./main --test-threads=4

trait Animal {
    fn name(&self) -> String;
    fn sound(&self) -> String;
    // Default: "<name> says <sound>"
    fn speak(&self) -> String {
        format!("{} says {}", self.name(), self.sound())
    }
}

struct Dog;
struct Cat {
    name: String,
}
struct Parrot {
    word: String,
}

impl Animal for Dog {
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        String::from("dog")
    }
    fn sound(&self) -> String {
        String::from("woof")
    }
}

impl Animal for Cat {
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        self.name.clone()
    }
    fn sound(&self) -> String {
        String::from("meow")
    }
}

impl Animal for Parrot {
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        String::from("parrot")
    }
    fn sound(&self) -> String {
        self.word.clone()
    }
    fn speak(&self) -> String {
        format!("{0}! {0}!", self.word)
    }
}

fn zoo() -> Vec<Box<dyn Animal>> {
    vec![
        Box::new(Dog),
        Box::new(Cat { name: "Tom".into() }),
        Box::new(Parrot { word: "hello".into() }),
    ]
}

fn chorus(animals: &[Box<dyn Animal>]) -> String {
    let lines: Vec<String> = animals.iter().map(|a| a.speak()).collect();
    lines.join("; ")
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn default_speak_uses_each_types_own_name_and_sound() {
        assert_eq!(Dog.speak(), "dog says woof");
        assert_eq!(Cat { name: "Kit".into() }.speak(), "Kit says meow");
    }

    #[test]
    fn parrot_overrides_speak() {
        let p = Parrot { word: "hi".into() };
        assert_eq!(p.sound(), "hi");
        assert_eq!(p.speak(), "hi! hi!");
    }

    #[test]
    fn zoo_holds_three_different_types() {
        let z = zoo();
        let names: Vec<String> = z.iter().map(|a| a.name()).collect();
        assert_eq!(names, ["dog", "Tom", "parrot"]);
    }

    #[test]
    fn chorus_goes_through_the_vtable() {
        assert_eq!(chorus(&zoo()), "dog says woof; Tom says meow; hello! hello!");
        assert_eq!(chorus(&[]), "");
    }
}

// Exercise 2: rules as boxed closures (reference solution)
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex2_rules.rs && ./main --test-threads=4

type Rule = Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool>;

fn max_len(n: usize) -> Rule {
    Box::new(move |s| s.len() <= n) // usize is Copy: copied in
}

fn without(word: &str) -> Rule {
    let word = word.to_string(); // own a copy; the closure must be 'static
    Box::new(move |s| !s.contains(word.as_str()))
}

fn one_of(allowed: Vec<String>) -> Rule {
    Box::new(move |s| allowed.iter().any(|a| a == s)) // the Vec is moved in
}

fn passes_all(rules: &[Rule], text: &str) -> bool {
    rules.iter().all(|r| r(text))
}

fn count_passing(rules: &[Rule], words: &[&str]) -> usize {
    words.iter().filter(|w| passes_all(rules, w)).count()
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn single_rules() {
        assert!(max_len(3)("abc"));
        assert!(!max_len(3)("abcd"));
        assert!(without("x")("abc"));
        assert!(!without("bc")("abc"));
        let r = one_of(vec!["red".into(), "blue".into()]);
        assert!(r("red") && !r("green"));
    }

    #[test]
    fn rule_outlives_the_string_it_was_made_from() {
        let rule = {
            let temp = String::from("oops");
            without(&temp)
        }; // `temp` is dropped here; the rule must still work
        assert!(rule("fine"));
        assert!(!rule("oops!"));
    }

    #[test]
    fn rules_of_different_closure_types_in_one_vec() {
        let rules: Vec<Rule> = vec![max_len(5), without("z"), Box::new(|s: &str| !s.is_empty())];
        assert!(passes_all(&rules, "abc"));
        assert!(!passes_all(&rules, "abcdef"));
        assert!(!passes_all(&rules, ""));
        assert!(passes_all(&[], "anything"));
        assert_eq!(count_passing(&rules, &["ok", "zoo", "toolong", "", "fine"]), 2);
    }
}

// Exercise 3: a traffic signal with the state pattern (reference solution)
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex3_signal.rs && ./main --test-threads=4

trait Light {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light>;
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str;
    // Default: most lights stay on for 30 seconds.
    fn seconds(&self) -> u32 {
        30
    }
}

struct Red;
struct Green;
struct Yellow;

impl Light for Red {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Green)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "red"
    }
}

impl Light for Green {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Yellow)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "green"
    }
}

impl Light for Yellow {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Red)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "yellow"
    }
    fn seconds(&self) -> u32 {
        5
    }
}

struct Signal {
    light: Option<Box<dyn Light>>,
}

impl Signal {
    fn new() -> Signal {
        Signal { light: Some(Box::new(Red)) }
    }

    fn advance(&mut self) {
        // take() leaves None behind, giving us the owned Box to consume.
        let old = self.light.take().unwrap();
        self.light = Some(old.next());
    }

    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        self.light.as_ref().unwrap().color()
    }

    fn run_for(&mut self, n: usize) -> u32 {
        let mut total = 0;
        for _ in 0..n {
            total += self.light.as_ref().unwrap().seconds();
            self.advance();
        }
        total
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn cycle_of_colours() {
        let mut s = Signal::new();
        let mut seen = vec![s.color()];
        for _ in 0..3 {
            s.advance();
            seen.push(s.color());
        }
        assert_eq!(seen, ["red", "green", "yellow", "red"]);
    }

    #[test]
    fn default_and_overridden_seconds() {
        assert_eq!(Red.seconds(), 30);
        assert_eq!(Green.seconds(), 30);
        assert_eq!(Yellow.seconds(), 5);
    }

    #[test]
    fn run_for_adds_up_and_moves_on() {
        let mut s = Signal::new();
        assert_eq!(s.run_for(3), 65);
        assert_eq!(s.color(), "red");
        assert_eq!(s.run_for(0), 0);
        assert_eq!(s.run_for(2), 60);
        assert_eq!(s.color(), "yellow");
    }
}

## 1. Two ways to abstract

You already know one way to write code that works for many types: generics (sub-module 09). `fn show<T: Display>(item: &T)` works for any `T` that implements `Display`. The compiler handles it by monomorphisation: it writes one copy of `show` for every concrete type you call it with, `show::<i32>`, `show::<String>` and so on. Each copy knows its type exactly, so every call is a direct call that can be inlined. This is static dispatch: the method is chosen at compile time.

Generics have one limit: each use picks one type. A `Vec<T>` holds values of a single type `T`. A function returning `impl Trait` returns one concrete type, even if the caller cannot name it. So how do you keep a text box, a checkbox and a button in one list and call `render` on each?

Rust's answer is a trait object, written `dyn Trait`. A trait object stands for "some value of a type that implements `Trait`; which type is decided at run time". There is only one copy of the code that uses it, and each method call is looked up at run time. This is dynamic dispatch.

Generics (`T: Trait`)Trait objects (`dyn Trait`)

Method chosenat compile timeat run time, through a vtable

Copies of your functionone per concrete typeone

Inliningyesusually not

Mixed types in one `Vec`noyes: `Vec<Box<dyn Trait>>`

The Rust Book (ch. 18.2, "Using Trait Objects to Allow for Values of Different Types") builds a GUI library this way. Our `widgets.rs` is a small version of it:

```
let parts: Vec<Box<dyn Render>> =
    vec![Box::new(Text("hello".into())), Box::new(Checkbox(true))];
for part in &parts {
    println!("{}", part.render()); // which render? decided per element, at run time
}
```

The `Vec` still holds one type: `Box<dyn Render>`. What differs is the type inside each box.

## 2. Behind a pointer: fat pointers and vtables

A `Text` and a `Checkbox` have different sizes. So what size is a `dyn Render`? There is no single answer: `dyn Render` is an unsized type (its size is not known at compile time). Rust can only store values whose size it knows, on the stack, in a struct field or in a `Vec` slot. That is why a trait object always sits behind a pointer: `&dyn Render`, `&mut dyn Render` or `Box<dyn Render>`.

That pointer is a fat pointer: two machine words.

- A data pointer to the value itself (the `Checkbox` on the heap, or wherever it lives).

- A vtable pointer to a table the compiler built for that pair (concrete type, trait).

A vtable ("virtual method table") holds the information needed to use the value without knowing its type: how to drop it, its size and alignment, then one entry per trait method, each pointing at the machine code for that type's version of the method.

Two boxed trait objects. Each element of `parts` is a data pointer plus a vtable pointer. Each (type, Render) pair has its own vtable whose rows point at that type's code.

A call such as `part.label()` does three things at run time: follow the vtable pointer, read the `label` row, call the function found there with the data pointer as `self`. That indirect call is the cost of dynamic dispatch: one extra memory read, and the compiler usually cannot inline the call because it does not know which function it will be.

You can see the "fat" part directly. `static_vs_dyn.rs` prints the sizes of a thin and a fat reference:

```
&i32: 8 bytes, &dyn Display: 16 bytes
```

These numbers are for a 64-bit machine (8-byte pointers). The rule is "two pointers instead of one", not "16 bytes". The exact layout of a vtable (row order, whether two values of the same type share one vtable) is a compiler detail you never rely on.

A `Box<dyn Trait>` also costs a heap allocation per value, because each value must live somewhere the box can point to. A borrowed `&dyn Trait` needs no allocation: `let one: &dyn Render = &Text("plain".into());` in `widgets.rs` points at a value that is already somewhere.

## 3. `Sized` and `?Sized`

Every generic parameter has a hidden bound: `T: Sized`, "the size of `T` is known at compile time". That is almost always what you want, since the function may need to store a `T`. But it means this generic function cannot be called with a trait object:

```
fn show_any<T: Display>(item: &T) -> String { format!("[{item}]") }

let m: Box<dyn Display> = Box::new(7);
show_any(m.as_ref()); // T would be `dyn Display`, which is not Sized
```

```
error[E0277]: the size for values of type `dyn std::fmt::Display` cannot be known at compilation time
```

Write `T: ?Sized` ("`T` may or may not be sized") to remove the hidden bound. This is fine here because `show_any` only ever touches `T` through a reference `&T`, which is a pointer of known size:

```
fn show_any<T: Display + ?Sized>(item: &T) -> String { format!("[{item}]") }
```

Now `T` can be `dyn Display`, or `str` (another unsized type you have used since 03 behind `&str`).

## 4. Choosing between generics and trait objects

SituationUseWhy

A function used with one type at a timegeneric `T: Trait` or `impl Trait`fastest; no allocation; inlinable

A list (or field) holding several types at once`Vec<Box<dyn Trait>>`a `Vec<T>` has exactly one `T`

Types chosen at run time (from a config file, user input, plugins)`Box<dyn Trait>`the compiler cannot know the type

Want less generated code (many types, big function)`&dyn Trait`one copy instead of one per type

A small, fixed set of kinds you controlan `enum`see section 9

A common mistake is to think `Vec<T>` with `T: Trait` can hold "anything that implements `Trait`". It cannot: `T` is one type, chosen by the caller. Only `dyn Trait` erases the concrete type.

## 5. Default methods through `dyn`

A trait may give a method a default body. In `widgets.rs`, `label` has a default and `Checkbox` overrides it:

```
trait Render {
    fn render(&self) -> String;
    fn label(&self) -> String { String::from("(unnamed)") }
}
impl Render for Checkbox {
    fn render(&self) -> String { /* ... */ }
    fn label(&self) -> String { String::from("checkbox") }
}
```

How does a vtable deal with this? Every vtable has a row for every trait method, defaults included. For `Checkbox` the `label` row points at `Checkbox::label`. For `Text`, which does not override it, the row points at the default body compiled for `Text`. A default method is like a small generic function: the compiler makes one copy of it per implementing type.

This explains what happens when a default calls another method of the same trait. Inside the copy compiled for `Text`, `self` is a `&Text`, so `self.render()` calls `Text::render`; the type is known there, so that inner call is static. Only the outer call through the trait object goes through the vtable.

To predict what a default method does for a type, read it as if you had pasted its body into that type's `impl` block. Every `self.method()` inside it then resolves to that type's own `method`, overridden or not.

## 6. Dyn compatibility: which traits can be objects

A vtable is a fixed list: one row per method, each pointing at one function. Some methods cannot fit in such a list, so a trait containing them cannot be used as `dyn Trait`. Such a trait is not dyn compatible (older texts say "not object safe"). The main rules, from the Rust Reference:

Method shapeProblem for a vtable

`fn copy(&self) -> Self`The caller must reserve space for the returned `Self`, but behind `dyn` its size is unknown.

`fn put<V: ToString>(&mut self, v: V)`A generic method is a family of functions, one per `V`. A fixed list cannot hold an open-ended family.

`fn new() -> Self` (no `self`)There is no value, so no vtable to look in.

Uncomment both `doubled` lines in `dyn_compat.rs` to see the error:

```
error[E0038]: the trait `Shape` is not dyn compatible
  ...because method `doubled` references the `Self` type in its return type
```

There are two ways out.

- Keep the method off the vtable with `where Self: Sized`. The trait becomes dyn compatible again, and the method can still be called on concrete types, but not on a `dyn Shape`. `dyn_compat.rs` does this with `doubled_sized`.

- Change the method's shape so it fits in a vtable: return `Box<dyn Shape>` instead of `Self`, or take `&dyn ToString` (or a `String`) instead of a generic `V`. Each costs something: a heap allocation, a conversion, or a second dynamic call.

`Box<dyn Trait>` does not make an incompatible trait compatible. The problem is the trait's methods, not where the object is stored.

## 7. Supertraits

`trait Shape: Debug { ... }` says "every type that implements `Shape` must also implement `Debug`". `Debug` is a supertrait of `Shape`. Two consequences:

- Code that has a `Shape` may use `Debug` too. Debug's method joins Shape's vtable, so `println!("{:?}", shapes[0])` works on a `Box<dyn Shape>`.

- Because the supertrait's methods join the vtable, the supertrait must be dyn compatible as well. `Debug` and `Display` are. `Clone` is not (`clone` returns `Self`), and neither is `Default` (`default()` has no `self` and returns `Self`). So `trait Shape: Clone` makes `dyn Shape` impossible.

```
use std::fmt::Debug;
trait Shape: Debug { fn area(&self) -> f64; }

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Square(f64);
impl Shape for Square { fn area(&self) -> f64 { self.0 * self.0 } }
// impl Shape for Square requires Square: Debug, which the derive provides.
```

## 8. Boxed closures and `'static`

Every closure has its own unnamed type, even two closures with the same signature (10). So a list of closures needs a trait object: `Vec<Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool>>`. `Fn`, `FnMut` and `FnOnce` are traits like any other.

A rule you will meet often: in a struct field or in a function's return type, `Box<dyn Trait>` is short for `Box<dyn Trait + 'static>`. `'static` here means "the value inside does not borrow anything that could go away". A closure meets it if every captured value is owned by the closure: copied in, cloned in or moved in. It fails if it captures a reference to a local variable or to a parameter.

```
fn prefix_rule(prefix: &str) -> Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool> {
    let owned = prefix.to_string();                // the closure gets its own copy
    Box::new(move |s| s.starts_with(owned.as_str()))
}
```

If the closure used `prefix` directly, it would hold a borrow that only lives as long as the caller's string, and the compiler refuses:

```
error: lifetime may not live long enough
  returning this value requires that `'1` must outlive `'static`
```

`move` moves whatever the closure names. If the variable is itself a reference (`prefix: &str`, `limit: &u32`), `move` moves the reference into the closure. The closure still borrows. To own the data, copy or clone it out first: `let limit = *limit;` or `let owned = prefix.to_string();`.

A `&dyn Fn(..)` parameter, by contrast, may borrow freely: it is only used during the call. Writing other lifetimes, such as `Box<dyn Fn() + 'a>`, is covered in 14.

## 9. Consuming a trait object; trait objects vs enums

A method may take its receiver as `self: Box<Self>`. It then consumes the box: after the call, the object is gone. The Book's state pattern (ch. 18.3, "Implementing an Object-Oriented Design Pattern") uses this so a state transition uses up the old state. `state.rs` is adapted from it:

```
trait State {
    fn submit(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn State>;
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str;
}
impl State for Draft {
    fn submit(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn State> { Box::new(Review) }
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str { "draft" }
}
```

`self: Box<Self>` is dyn compatible: the receiver is a pointer of known size, so the call can go through the vtable. The catch is that you must own the box to call it. A shared or mutable borrow of a box is not enough; you cannot move a box out from behind a reference. When the box sits inside something else, take it out first:

Where the box livesHow to take it out

`Option<Box<dyn State>>``opt.take()` leaves `None` behind

a field or variable of a type with a default`std::mem::take(&mut x)` (11)

a `Vec<Box<dyn T>>`, all of it`v.drain(..)` or `mem::take(&mut v)`, which leave it empty

a `Vec`, one element`v.remove(i)` or `v.pop()`

### Trait objects or an enum?

The same states could be an `enum State { Draft, Review, Published }` with `match` in each operation. The two designs make different changes cheap:

ChangeTrait objectsEnum + match

Add a new kind (type / variant)one new type and its `impl`; no other code changesedit every `match`

Add a new operationadd a method to the trait and to every typeone new function with one `match`; the compiler checks every case

Types from outside your crate (plugins)yesno: the set is closed

Cost per callvtable call, heap allocation per boxa `match` on a tag; no allocation needed

- Why must `dyn Trait` always sit behind a pointer? What are the two halves of that pointer?

- Why can a trait with `fn copy(&self) -> Self` not be a trait object, while `fn copy(&self) -> Box<dyn Trait>` is fine?

- A default method calls `self.unit()`. For a type that overrides `unit`, which `unit` runs, and why?

- Why does a closure stored in a `Box<dyn Fn()>` field have to own what it captures?

Diagram: a trait object is a fat pointer.

Left, two elements of `parts: Vec<Box<dyn Render>>`. Each element is two pointers side by side: a "data ptr" and a "vtable ptr".
- parts[0]: the data ptr points to `Text("hello")` on the heap; the vtable ptr points to the vtable for (Text, Render).
- parts[1]: the data ptr points to `Checkbox(true)` on the heap; the vtable ptr points to the vtable for (Checkbox, Render).

Middle, the two vtables. Each has rows: drop, size and align, render, label.

Right, where the rows point:
- Text's `render` row -> `Text::render`. Text's `label` row -> the trait's default `label`, compiled for Text (Text does not override it).
- Checkbox's `render` row -> `Checkbox::render`. Checkbox's `label` row -> `Checkbox::label` (its override).

Caption: `part.label()` on parts[0] follows the vtable ptr, reads the "label" row and calls it with the data ptr as `self`. Row order and whether vtables are shared are compiler details. On 64-bit each pointer is 8 bytes, so the fat pointer is 16.
