Diagram: a trait object is a fat pointer.

Left, two elements of `parts: Vec<Box<dyn Render>>`. Each element is two pointers side by side: a "data ptr" and a "vtable ptr".
- parts[0]: the data ptr points to `Text("hello")` on the heap; the vtable ptr points to the vtable for (Text, Render).
- parts[1]: the data ptr points to `Checkbox(true)` on the heap; the vtable ptr points to the vtable for (Checkbox, Render).

Middle, the two vtables. Each has rows: drop, size and align, render, label.

Right, where the rows point:
- Text's `render` row -> `Text::render`. Text's `label` row -> the trait's default `label`, compiled for Text (Text does not override it).
- Checkbox's `render` row -> `Checkbox::render`. Checkbox's `label` row -> `Checkbox::label` (its override).

Caption: `part.label()` on parts[0] follows the vtable ptr, reads the "label" row and calls it with the data ptr as `self`. Row order and whether vtables are shared are compiler details. On 64-bit each pointer is 8 bytes, so the fat pointer is 16.

// Exercise 1: a mixed zoo (reference solution)
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex1_zoo.rs && ./main --test-threads=4

trait Animal {
    fn name(&self) -> String;
    fn sound(&self) -> String;
    // Default: "<name> says <sound>"
    fn speak(&self) -> String {
        format!("{} says {}", self.name(), self.sound())
    }
}

struct Dog;
struct Cat {
    name: String,
}
struct Parrot {
    word: String,
}

impl Animal for Dog {
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        String::from("dog")
    }
    fn sound(&self) -> String {
        String::from("woof")
    }
}

impl Animal for Cat {
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        self.name.clone()
    }
    fn sound(&self) -> String {
        String::from("meow")
    }
}

impl Animal for Parrot {
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        String::from("parrot")
    }
    fn sound(&self) -> String {
        self.word.clone()
    }
    fn speak(&self) -> String {
        format!("{0}! {0}!", self.word)
    }
}

fn zoo() -> Vec<Box<dyn Animal>> {
    vec![
        Box::new(Dog),
        Box::new(Cat { name: "Tom".into() }),
        Box::new(Parrot { word: "hello".into() }),
    ]
}

fn chorus(animals: &[Box<dyn Animal>]) -> String {
    let lines: Vec<String> = animals.iter().map(|a| a.speak()).collect();
    lines.join("; ")
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn default_speak_uses_each_types_own_name_and_sound() {

        assert_eq!(Cat { name: "Kit".into() }.speak(), "Kit says meow");
    }

    fn parrot_overrides_speak() {
        let p = Parrot { word: "hi".into() };
        assert_eq!(p.sound(), "hi");
        assert_eq!(p.speak(), "hi! hi!");
    }

    #[test]
    fn zoo_holds_three_different_types() {
        let z = zoo();
        let names: Vec<String> = z.iter().map(|a| a.name()).collect();
        assert_eq!(names, ["dog", "Tom", "parrot"]);
    }

    #[test]
    fn chorus_goes_through_the_vtable() {
        assert_eq!(chorus(&zoo()), "dog says woof; Tom says meow; hello! hello!");
        assert_eq!(chorus(&[]), "");
    }

// Exercise 2: rules as boxed closures (reference solution)
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex2_rules.rs && ./main --test-threads=4

type Rule = Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool>;

fn max_len(n: usize) -> Rule {
    Box::new(move |s| s.len() <= n) // usize is Copy: copied in
}

fn without(word: &str) -> Rule {
    let word = word.to_string(); // own a copy; the closure must be 'static
    Box::new(move |s| !s.contains(word.as_str()))
}

fn one_of(allowed: Vec<String>) -> Rule {
    Box::new(move |s| allowed.iter().any(|a| a == s)) // the Vec is moved in
}

fn passes_all(rules: &[Rule], text: &str) -> bool {
    rules.iter().all(|r| r(text))
}

fn count_passing(rules: &[Rule], words: &[&str]) -> usize {
    words.iter().filter(|w| passes_all(rules, w)).count()
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn single_rules() {
        assert!(max_len(3)("abc"));
        assert!(!max_len(3)("abcd"));
        assert!(without("x")("abc"));
        assert!(!without("bc")("abc"));
        let r = one_of(vec!["red".into(), "blue".into()]);
        assert!(r("red") && !r("green"));
    }

    #[test]
    fn rule_outlives_the_string_it_was_made_from() {
        let rule = {
            let temp = String::from("oops");
            without(&temp)
        }; // `temp` is dropped here; the rule must still work
        assert!(rule("fine"));
        assert!(!rule("oops!"));
    }

    #[test]
    fn rules_of_different_closure_types_in_one_vec() {
        let rules: Vec<Rule> = vec![max_len(5), without("z"), Box::new(|s: &str| !s.is_empty())];
        assert!(passes_all(&rules, "abc"));
        assert!(!passes_all(&rules, "abcdef"));
        assert!(!passes_all(&rules, ""));
        assert!(passes_all(&[], "anything"));
        assert_eq!(count_passing(&rules, &["ok", "zoo", "toolong", "", "fine"]), 2);
    }
}

// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex3_signal.rs && ./main --test-threads=4

trait Light {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light>;
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str;
    // Default: most lights stay on for 30 seconds.
    fn seconds(&self) -> u32 {
        30
    }
}

struct Red;
struct Green;
struct Yellow;

impl Light for Red {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Green)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "red"
    }
}

impl Light for Green {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Yellow)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "green"
    }
}

impl Light for Yellow {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Red)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "yellow"
    }
    fn seconds(&self) -> u32 {
        5
    }
}

struct Signal {
    light: Option<Box<dyn Light>>,
}

impl Signal {
    fn new() -> Signal {
        Signal { light: Some(Box::new(Red)) }
    }

    fn advance(&mut self) {
        // take() leaves None behind, giving us the owned Box to consume.
        let old = self.light.take().unwrap();
        self.light = Some(old.next());
    }

    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        self.light.as_ref().unwrap().color()
    }

    fn run_for(&mut self, n: usize) -> u32 {
        let mut total = 0;
        for _ in 0..n {
            total += self.light.as_ref().unwrap().seconds();
            self.advance();
        }
        total
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn cycle_of_colours() {
        let mut s = Signal::new();
        let mut seen = vec![s.color()];
        for _ in 0..3 {
            s.advance();
            seen.push(s.color());
        }
        assert_eq!(seen, ["red", "green", "yellow", "red"]);
    }

    #[test]
    fn default_and_overridden_seconds() {
        assert_eq!(Red.seconds(), 30);
        assert_eq!(Green.seconds(), 30);
        assert_eq!(Yellow.seconds(), 5);
    }

    #[test]
    fn run_for_adds_up_and_moves_on() {
        let mut s = Signal::new();
        assert_eq!(s.run_for(3), 65);
        assert_eq!(s.color(), "red");
        assert_eq!(s.run_for(0), 0);
        assert_eq!(s.run_for(2), 60);
        assert_eq!(s.color(), "yellow");
    }
}

## 1. Two ways to abstract

You already know one way to write code that works for many types: generics (sub-module 09). `fn show<T: Display>(item: &T)` works for any `T` that implements `Display`. The compiler handles it by monomorphisation: it writes one copy of `show` for every concrete type you call it with, `show::<i32>`, `show::<String>` and so on. Each copy knows its type exactly, so every call is a direct call that can be inlined. This is static dispatch: the method is chosen at compile time.

Generics have one limit: each use picks one type. A `Vec<T>` holds values of a single type `T`. A function returning `impl Trait` returns one concrete type, even if the caller cannot name it. So how do you keep a text box, a checkbox and a button in one list and call `render` on each?

Rust's answer is a trait object, written `dyn Trait`. A trait object stands for "some value of a type that implements `Trait`; which type is decided at run time". There is only one copy of the code that uses it, and each method call is looked up at run time. This is dynamic dispatch.

Generics (`T: Trait`)Trait objects (`dyn Trait`)

Method chosenat compile timeat run time, through a vtable

Copies of your functionone per concrete typeone

Inliningyesusually not

Mixed types in one `Vec`noyes: `Vec<Box<dyn Trait>>`

The Rust Book (ch. 18.2, "Using Trait Objects to Allow for Values of Different Types") builds a GUI library this way. Our `widgets.rs` is a small version of it:

```
let parts: Vec<Box<dyn Render>> =
    vec![Box::new(Text("hello".into())), Box::new(Checkbox(true))];
for part in &parts {
    println!("{}", part.render()); // which render? decided per element, at run time
}
```

The `Vec` still holds one type: `Box<dyn Render>`. What differs is the type inside each box.

## 2. Behind a pointer: fat pointers and vtables

A `Text` and a `Checkbox` have different sizes. So what size is a `dyn Render`? There is no single answer: `dyn Render` is an unsized type (its size is not known at compile time). Rust can only store values whose size it knows, on the stack, in a struct field or in a `Vec` slot. That is why a trait object always sits behind a pointer: `&dyn Render`, `&mut dyn Render` or `Box<dyn Render>`.

That pointer is a fat pointer: two machine words.

- A data pointer to the value itself (the `Checkbox` on the heap, or wherever it lives).

- A vtable pointer to a table the compiler built for that pair (concrete type, trait).

A vtable ("virtual method table") holds the information needed to use the value without knowing its type: how to drop it, its size and alignment, then one entry per trait method, each pointing at the machine code for that type's version of the method.

Two boxed trait objects. Each element of `parts` is a data pointer plus a vtable pointer. Each (type, Render) pair has its own vtable whose rows point at that type's code.

A call such as `part.label()` does three things at run time: follow the vtable pointer, read the `label` row, call the function found there with the data pointer as `self`. That indirect call is the cost of dynamic dispatch: one extra memory read, and the compiler usually cannot inline the call because it does not know which function it will be.

You can see the "fat" part directly. `static_vs_dyn.rs` prints the sizes of a thin and a fat reference:

```
&i32: 8 bytes, &dyn Display: 16 bytes
```

These numbers are for a 64-bit machine (8-byte pointers). The rule is "two pointers instead of one", not "16 bytes". The exact layout of a vtable (row order, whether two values of the same type share one vtable) is a compiler detail you never rely on.

A `Box<dyn Trait>` also costs a heap allocation per value, because each value must live somewhere the box can point to. A borrowed `&dyn Trait` needs no allocation: `let one: &dyn Render = &Text("plain".into());` in `widgets.rs` points at a value that is already somewhere.

## 3. `Sized` and `?Sized`

Every generic parameter has a hidden bound: `T: Sized`, "the size of `T` is known at compile time". That is almost always what you want, since the function may need to store a `T`. But it means this generic function cannot be called with a trait object:

```
fn show_any<T: Display>(item: &T) -> String { format!("[{item}]") }

let m: Box<dyn Display> = Box::new(7);
show_any(m.as_ref()); // T would be `dyn Display`, which is not Sized
```

```
error[E0277]: the size for values of type `dyn std::fmt::Display` cannot be known at compilation time
```

Write `T: ?Sized` ("`T` may or may not be sized") to remove the hidden bound. This is fine here because `show_any` only ever touches `T` through a reference `&T`, which is a pointer of known size:

```
fn show_any<T: Display + ?Sized>(item: &T) -> String { format!("[{item}]") }
```

Now `T` can be `dyn Display`, or `str` (another unsized type you have used since 03 behind `&str`).

## 4. Choosing between generics and trait objects

SituationUseWhy

A function used with one type at a timegeneric `T: Trait` or `impl Trait`fastest; no allocation; inlinable

A list (or field) holding several types at once`Vec<Box<dyn Trait>>`a `Vec<T>` has exactly one `T`

Types chosen at run time (from a config file, user input, plugins)`Box<dyn Trait>`the compiler cannot know the type

Want less generated code (many types, big function)`&dyn Trait`one copy instead of one per type

A small, fixed set of kinds you controlan `enum`see section 9

A common mistake is to think `Vec<T>` with `T: Trait` can hold "anything that implements `Trait`". It cannot: `T` is one type, chosen by the caller. Only `dyn Trait` erases the concrete type.

## 5. Default methods through `dyn`

A trait may give a method a default body. In `widgets.rs`, `label` has a default and `Checkbox` overrides it:

```
trait Render {
    fn render(&self) -> String;
    fn label(&self) -> String { String::from("(unnamed)") }
}
impl Render for Checkbox {
    fn render(&self) -> String { /* ... */ }
    fn label(&self) -> String { String::from("checkbox") }
}
```

How does a vtable deal with this? Every vtable has a row for every trait method, defaults included. For `Checkbox` the `label` row points at `Checkbox::label`. For `Text`, which does not override it, the row points at the default body compiled for `Text`. A default method is like a small generic function: the compiler makes one copy of it per implementing type.

This explains what happens when a default calls another method of the same trait. Inside the copy compiled for `Text`, `self` is a `&Text`, so `self.render()` calls `Text::render`; the type is known there, so that inner call is static. Only the outer call through the trait object goes through the vtable.

To predict what a default method does for a type, read it as if you had pasted its body into that type's `impl` block. Every `self.method()` inside it then resolves to that type's own `method`, overridden or not.

## 6. Dyn compatibility: which traits can be objects

A vtable is a fixed list: one row per method, each pointing at one function. Some methods cannot fit in such a list, so a trait containing them cannot be used as `dyn Trait`. Such a trait is not dyn compatible (older texts say "not object safe"). The main rules, from the Rust Reference:

Method shapeProblem for a vtable

`fn copy(&self) -> Self`The caller must reserve space for the returned `Self`, but behind `dyn` its size is unknown.

`fn put<V: ToString>(&mut self, v: V)`A generic method is a family of functions, one per `V`. A fixed list cannot hold an open-ended family.

`fn new() -> Self` (no `self`)There is no value, so no vtable to look in.

Uncomment both `doubled` lines in `dyn_compat.rs` to see the error:

```
error[E0038]: the trait `Shape` is not dyn compatible
  ...because method `doubled` references the `Self` type in its return type
```

There are two ways out.

- Keep the method off the vtable with `where Self: Sized`. The trait becomes dyn compatible again, and the method can still be called on concrete types, but not on a `dyn Shape`. `dyn_compat.rs` does this with `doubled_sized`.

- Change the method's shape so it fits in a vtable: return `Box<dyn Shape>` instead of `Self`, or take `&dyn ToString` (or a `String`) instead of a generic `V`. Each costs something: a heap allocation, a conversion, or a second dynamic call.

`Box<dyn Trait>` does not make an incompatible trait compatible. The problem is the trait's methods, not where the object is stored.

## 7. Supertraits

`trait Shape: Debug { ... }` says "every type that implements `Shape` must also implement `Debug`". `Debug` is a supertrait of `Shape`. Two consequences:

- Code that has a `Shape` may use `Debug` too. Debug's method joins Shape's vtable, so `println!("{:?}", shapes[0])` works on a `Box<dyn Shape>`.

- Because the supertrait's methods join the vtable, the supertrait must be dyn compatible as well. `Debug` and `Display` are. `Clone` is not (`clone` returns `Self`), and neither is `Default` (`default()` has no `self` and returns `Self`). So `trait Shape: Clone` makes `dyn Shape` impossible.

```
use std::fmt::Debug;
trait Shape: Debug { fn area(&self) -> f64; }

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Square(f64);
impl Shape for Square { fn area(&self) -> f64 { self.0 * self.0 } }
// impl Shape for Square requires Square: Debug, which the derive provides.
```

## 8. Boxed closures and `'static`

Every closure has its own unnamed type, even two closures with the same signature (10). So a list of closures needs a trait object: `Vec<Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool>>`. `Fn`, `FnMut` and `FnOnce` are traits like any other.

A rule you will meet often: in a struct field or in a function's return type, `Box<dyn Trait>` is short for `Box<dyn Trait + 'static>`. `'static` here means "the value inside does not borrow anything that could go away". A closure meets it if every captured value is owned by the closure: copied in, cloned in or moved in. It fails if it captures a reference to a local variable or to a parameter.

```
fn prefix_rule(prefix: &str) -> Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool> {
    let owned = prefix.to_string();                // the closure gets its own copy
    Box::new(move |s| s.starts_with(owned.as_str()))
}
```

If the closure used `prefix` directly, it would hold a borrow that only lives as long as the caller's string, and the compiler refuses:

```
error: lifetime may not live long enough
  returning this value requires that `'1` must outlive `'static`
```

`move` moves whatever the closure names. If the variable is itself a reference (`prefix: &str`, `limit: &u32`), `move` moves the reference into the closure. The closure still borrows. To own the data, copy or clone it out first: `let limit = *limit;` or `let owned = prefix.to_string();`.

A `&dyn Fn(..)` parameter, by contrast, may borrow freely: it is only used during the call. Writing other lifetimes, such as `Box<dyn Fn() + 'a>`, is covered in 14.

## 9. Consuming a trait object; trait objects vs enums

A method may take its receiver as `self: Box<Self>`. It then consumes the box: after the call, the object is gone. The Book's state pattern (ch. 18.3, "Implementing an Object-Oriented Design Pattern") uses this so a state transition uses up the old state. `state.rs` is adapted from it:

```
trait State {
    fn submit(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn State>;
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str;
}
impl State for Draft {
    fn submit(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn State> { Box::new(Review) }
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str { "draft" }
}
```

`self: Box<Self>` is dyn compatible: the receiver is a pointer of known size, so the call can go through the vtable. The catch is that you must own the box to call it. A shared or mutable borrow of a box is not enough; you cannot move a box out from behind a reference. When the box sits inside something else, take it out first:

Where the box livesHow to take it out

`Option<Box<dyn State>>``opt.take()` leaves `None` behind

a field or variable of a type with a default`std::mem::take(&mut x)` (11)

a `Vec<Box<dyn T>>`, all of it`v.drain(..)` or `mem::take(&mut v)`, which leave it empty

a `Vec`, one element`v.remove(i)` or `v.pop()`

### Trait objects or an enum?

The same states could be an `enum State { Draft, Review, Published }` with `match` in each operation. The two designs make different changes cheap:

ChangeTrait objectsEnum + match

Add a new kind (type / variant)one new type and its `impl`; no other code changesedit every `match`

Add a new operationadd a method to the trait and to every typeone new function with one `match`; the compiler checks every case

Types from outside your crate (plugins)yesno: the set is closed

Cost per callvtable call, heap allocation per boxa `match` on a tag; no allocation needed

## 10. Check yourself

Ask the Tutor about any of these. Try to answer first.

- Why must `dyn Trait` always sit behind a pointer? What are the two halves of that pointer?

- Why can a trait with `fn copy(&self) -> Self` not be a trait object, while `fn copy(&self) -> Box<dyn Trait>` is fine?

- A default method calls `self.unit()`. For a type that overrides `unit`, which `unit` runs, and why?

- Why does a closure stored in a `Box<dyn Fn()>` field have to own what it captures?

- What would you gain and lose by rewriting `state.rs` as an enum?

Diagram: a trait object is a fat pointer.

Left, two elements of `parts: Vec<Box<dyn Render>>`. Each element is two pointers side by side: a "data ptr" and a "vtable ptr".
- parts[0]: the data ptr points to `Text("hello")` on the heap; the vtable ptr points to the vtable for (Text, Render).
- parts[1]: the data ptr points to `Checkbox(true)` on the heap; the vtable ptr points to the vtable for (Checkbox, Render).

Middle, the two vtables. Each has rows: drop, size and align, render, label.

Right, where the rows point:
- Text's `render` row -> `Text::render`. Text's `label` row -> the trait's default `label`, compiled for Text (Text does not override it).
- Checkbox's `render` row -> `Checkbox::render`. Checkbox's `label` row -> `Checkbox::label` (its override).

Caption: `part.label()` on parts[0] follows the vtable ptr, reads the "label" row and calls it with the data ptr as `self`. Row order and whether vtables are shared are compiler details. On 64-bit each pointer is 8 bytes, so the fat pointer is 16.

// Exercise 1: a mixed zoo (reference solution)
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex1_zoo.rs && ./main --test-threads=4

trait Animal {
    fn name(&self) -> String;
    fn sound(&self) -> String;
    // Default: "<name> says <sound>"
    fn speak(&self) -> String {
        format!("{} says {}", self.name(), self.sound())
    }
}

struct Dog;
struct Cat {
    name: String,
}
struct Parrot {
    word: String,
}

impl Animal for Dog {
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        String::from("dog")
    }
    fn sound(&self) -> String {
        String::from("woof")
    }
}

impl Animal for Cat {
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        self.name.clone()
    }
    fn sound(&self) -> String {
        String::from("meow")
    }
}

impl Animal for Parrot {
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        String::from("parrot")
    }
    fn sound(&self) -> String {
        self.word.clone()
    }
    fn speak(&self) -> String {
        format!("{0}! {0}!", self.word)
    }
}

fn zoo() -> Vec<Box<dyn Animal>> {
    vec![
        Box::new(Dog),
        Box::new(Cat { name: "Tom".into() }),
        Box::new(Parrot { word: "hello".into() }),
    ]
}

fn chorus(animals: &[Box<dyn Animal>]) -> String {
    let lines: Vec<String> = animals.iter().map(|a| a.speak()).collect();
    lines.join("; ")
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn default_speak_uses_each_types_own_name_and_sound() {
        assert_eq!(Dog.speak(), "dog says woof");
        assert_eq!(Cat { name: "Kit".into() }.speak(), "Kit says meow");
    }

    #[test]
    fn parrot_overrides_speak() {
        let p = Parrot { word: "hi".into() };
        assert_eq!(p.sound(), "hi");
        assert_eq!(p.speak(), "hi! hi!");
    }

    #[test]
    fn zoo_holds_three_different_types() {
        let z = zoo();
        let names: Vec<String> = z.iter().map(|a| a.name()).collect();
        assert_eq!(names, ["dog", "Tom", "parrot"]);
    }

    #[test]
    fn chorus_goes_through_the_vtable() {
        assert_eq!(chorus(&zoo()), "dog says woof; Tom says meow; hello! hello!");
        assert_eq!(chorus(&[]), "");
    }
}

// Exercise 2: rules as boxed closures (reference solution)
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex2_rules.rs && ./main --test-threads=4

type Rule = Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool>;

fn max_len(n: usize) -> Rule {
    Box::new(move |s| s.len() <= n) // usize is Copy: copied in
}

fn without(word: &str) -> Rule {
    let word = word.to_string(); // own a copy; the closure must be 'static
    Box::new(move |s| !s.contains(word.as_str()))
}

fn one_of(allowed: Vec<String>) -> Rule {
    Box::new(move |s| allowed.iter().any(|a| a == s)) // the Vec is moved in
}

fn passes_all(rules: &[Rule], text: &str) -> bool {
    rules.iter().all(|r| r(text))
}

fn count_passing(rules: &[Rule], words: &[&str]) -> usize {
    words.iter().filter(|w| passes_all(rules, w)).count()
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn single_rules() {
        assert!(max_len(3)("abc"));
        assert!(!max_len(3)("abcd"));
        assert!(without("x")("abc"));
        assert!(!without("bc")("abc"));
        let r = one_of(vec!["red".into(), "blue".into()]);
        assert!(r("red") && !r("green"));
    }

    #[test]
    fn rule_outlives_the_string_it_was_made_from() {
        let rule = {
            let temp = String::from("oops");
            without(&temp)
        }; // `temp` is dropped here; the rule must still work
        assert!(rule("fine"));
        assert!(!rule("oops!"));
    }

    #[test]
    fn rules_of_different_closure_types_in_one_vec() {
        let rules: Vec<Rule> = vec![max_len(5), without("z"), Box::new(|s: &str| !s.is_empty())];
        assert!(passes_all(&rules, "abc"));
        assert!(!passes_all(&rules, "abcdef"));
        assert!(!passes_all(&rules, ""));
        assert!(passes_all(&[], "anything"));
        assert_eq!(count_passing(&rules, &["ok", "zoo", "toolong", "", "fine"]), 2);
    }
}

// Exercise 3: a traffic signal with the state pattern (reference solution)
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex3_signal.rs && ./main --test-threads=4

trait Light {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light>;
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str;
    // Default: most lights stay on for 30 seconds.
    fn seconds(&self) -> u32 {
        30
    }
}

struct Red;
struct Green;
struct Yellow;

impl Light for Red {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Green)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "red"
    }
}

impl Light for Green {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Yellow)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "green"
    }
}

impl Light for Yellow {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Red)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "yellow"
    }
    fn seconds(&self) -> u32 {
        5
    }
}

struct Signal {
    light: Option<Box<dyn Light>>,
}

impl Signal {
    fn new() -> Signal {
        Signal { light: Some(Box::new(Red)) }
    }

    fn advance(&mut self) {
        // take() leaves None behind, giving us the owned Box to consume.
        let old = self.light.take().unwrap();
        self.light = Some(old.next());
    }

    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        self.light.as_ref().unwrap().color()
    }

    fn run_for(&mut self, n: usize) -> u32 {
        let mut total = 0;
        for _ in 0..n {
            total += self.light.as_ref().unwrap().seconds();
            self.advance();
        }
        total
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn cycle_of_colours() {
        let mut s = Signal::new();
        let mut seen = vec![s.color()];
        for _ in 0..3 {
            s.advance();
            seen.push(s.color());
        }
        assert_eq!(seen, ["red", "green", "yellow", "red"]);
    }

    #[test]
    fn default_and_overridden_seconds() {
        assert_eq!(Red.seconds(), 30);
        assert_eq!(Green.seconds(), 30);
        assert_eq!(Yellow.seconds(), 5);
    }

    #[test]
    fn run_for_adds_up_and_moves_on() {
        let mut s = Signal::new();
        assert_eq!(s.run_for(3), 65);
        assert_eq!(s.color(), "red");
        assert_eq!(s.run_for(0), 0);
        assert_eq!(s.run_for(2), 60);
        assert_eq!(s.color(), "yellow");
    }
}

Copies of your functionone per concrete typeone

Inliningyesusually not

Mixed types in one `Vec`noyes: `Vec<Box<dyn Trait>>`

The Rust Book (ch. 18.2, "Using Trait Objects to Allow for Values of Different Types") builds a GUI library this way. Our `widgets.rs` is a small version of it:

```
let parts: Vec<Box<dyn Render>> =
    vec![Box::new(Text("hello".into())), Box::new(Checkbox(true))];
for part in &parts {
    println!("{}", part.render()); // which render? decided per element, at run time

The `Vec` still holds one type: `Box<dyn Render>`. What differs is the type inside each box.

## 2. Behind a pointer: fat pointers and vtables

A `Text` and a `Checkbox` have different sizes. So what size is a `dyn Render`? There is no single answer: `dyn Render` is an unsized type (its size is not known at compile time). Rust can only store values whose size it knows, on the stack, in a struct field or in a `Vec` slot. That is why a trait object always sits behind a pointer: `&dyn Render`, `&mut dyn Render` or `Box<dyn Render>`.

That pointer is a fat pointer: two machine words.

- A data pointer to the value itself (the `Checkbox` on the heap, or wherever it lives).

- A vtable pointer to a table the compiler built for that pair (concrete type, trait).

A vtable ("virtual method table") holds the information needed to use the value without knowing its type: how to drop it, its size and alignment, then one entry per trait method, each pointing at the machine code for that type's version of the method.

Two boxed trait objects. Each element of `parts` is a data pointer plus a vtable pointer. Each (type, Render) pair has its own vtable whose rows point at that type's code.

A call such as `part.label()` does three things at run time: follow the vtable pointer, read the `label` row, call the function found there with the data pointer as `self`. That indirect call is the cost of dynamic dispatch: one extra memory read, and the compiler usually cannot inline the call because it does not know which function it will be.

You can see the "fat" part directly. `static_vs_dyn.rs` prints the sizes of a thin and a fat reference:

```
&i32: 8 bytes, &dyn Display: 16 bytes
```

These numbers are for a 64-bit machine (8-byte pointers). The rule is "two pointers instead of one", not "16 bytes". The exact layout of a vtable (row order, whether two values of the same type share one vtable) is a compiler detail you never rely on.

A `Box<dyn Trait>` also costs a heap allocation per value, because each value must live somewhere the box can point to. A borrowed `&dyn Trait` needs no allocation: `let one: &dyn Render = &Text("plain".into());` in `widgets.rs` points at a value that is already somewhere.

## 3. `Sized` and `?Sized`

Every generic parameter has a hidden bound: `T: Sized`, "the size of `T` is known at compile time". That is almost always what you want, since the function may need to store a `T`. But it means this generic function cannot be called with a trait object:

```
fn show_any<T: Display>(item: &T) -> String { format!("[{item}]") }

let m: Box<dyn Display> = Box::new(7);
show_any(m.as_ref()); // T would be `dyn Display`, which is not Sized
```

```
error[E0277]: the size for values of type `dyn std::fmt::Display` cannot be known at compilation time
```

Write `T: ?Sized` ("`T` may or may not be sized") to remove the hidden bound. This is fine here because `show_any` only ever touches `T` through a reference `&T`, which is a pointer of known size:

```
fn show_any<T: Display + ?Sized>(item: &T) -> String { format!("[{item}]") }
```

Now `T` can be `dyn Display`, or `str` (another unsized type you have used since 03 behind `&str`).

## 4. Choosing between generics and trait objects

SituationUseWhy

A function used with one type at a timegeneric `T: Trait` or `impl Trait`fastest; no allocation; inlinable

A list (or field) holding several types at once`Vec<Box<dyn Trait>>`a `Vec<T>` has exactly one `T`

Types chosen at run time (from a config file, user input, plugins)`Box<dyn Trait>`the compiler cannot know the type

Want less generated code (many types, big function)`&dyn Trait`one copy instead of one per type

A small, fixed set of kinds you controlan `enum`see section 9

A common mistake is to think `Vec<T>` with `T: Trait` can hold "anything that implements `Trait`". It cannot: `T` is one type, chosen by the caller. Only `dyn Trait` erases the concrete type.

## 5. Default methods through `dyn`

A trait may give a method a default body. In `widgets.rs`, `label` has a default and `Checkbox` overrides it:

```
trait Render {
    fn render(&self) -> String;
    fn label(&self) -> String { String::from("(unnamed)") }
}
impl Render for Checkbox {
    fn render(&self) -> String { /* ... */ }
    fn label(&self) -> String { String::from("checkbox") }
}
```

How does a vtable deal with this? Every vtable has a row for every trait method, defaults included. For `Checkbox` the `label` row points at `Checkbox::label`. For `Text`, which does not override it, the row points at the default body compiled for `Text`. A default method is like a small generic function: the compiler makes one copy of it per implementing type.

This explains what happens when a default calls another method of the same trait. Inside the copy compiled for `Text`, `self` is a `&Text`, so `self.render()` calls `Text::render`; the type is known there, so that inner call is static. Only the outer call through the trait object goes through the vtable.

To predict what a default method does for a type, read it as if you had pasted its body into that type's `impl` block. Every `self.method()` inside it then resolves to that type's own `method`, overridden or not.

## 6. Dyn compatibility: which traits can be objects

A vtable is a fixed list: one row per method, each pointing at one function. Some methods cannot fit in such a list, so a trait containing them cannot be used as `dyn Trait`. Such a trait is not dyn compatible (older texts say "not object safe"). The main rules, from the Rust Reference:

Method shapeProblem for a vtable

`fn copy(&self) -> Self`The caller must reserve space for the returned `Self`, but behind `dyn` its size is unknown.

`fn put<V: ToString>(&mut self, v: V)`A generic method is a family of functions, one per `V`. A fixed list cannot hold an open-ended family.

`fn new() -> Self` (no `self`)There is no value, so no vtable to look in.

Uncomment both `doubled` lines in `dyn_compat.rs` to see the error:

```
error[E0038]: the trait `Shape` is not dyn compatible
  ...because method `doubled` references the `Self` type in its return type
```

There are two ways out.

- Keep the method off the vtable with `where Self: Sized`. The trait becomes dyn compatible again, and the method can still be called on concrete types, but not on a `dyn Shape`. `dyn_compat.rs` does this with `doubled_sized`.

- Change the method's shape so it fits in a vtable: return `Box<dyn Shape>` instead of `Self`, or take `&dyn ToString` (or a `String`) instead of a generic `V`. Each costs something: a heap allocation, a conversion, or a second dynamic call.

`Box<dyn Trait>` does not make an incompatible trait compatible. The problem is the trait's methods, not where the object is stored.

## 7. Supertraits

`trait Shape: Debug { ... }` says "every type that implements `Shape` must also implement `Debug`". `Debug` is a supertrait of `Shape`. Two consequences:

- Code that has a `Shape` may use `Debug` too. Debug's method joins Shape's vtable, so `println!("{:?}", shapes[0])` works on a `Box<dyn Shape>`.

- Because the supertrait's methods join the vtable, the supertrait must be dyn compatible as well. `Debug` and `Display` are. `Clone` is not (`clone` returns `Self`), and neither is `Default` (`default()` has no `self` and returns `Self`). So `trait Shape: Clone` makes `dyn Shape` impossible.

```
use std::fmt::Debug;
trait Shape: Debug { fn area(&self) -> f64; }

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Square(f64);
impl Shape for Square { fn area(&self) -> f64 { self.0 * self.0 } }
// impl Shape for Square requires Square: Debug, which the derive provides.
```

## 8. Boxed closures and `'static`

Every closure has its own unnamed type, even two closures with the same signature (10). So a list of closures needs a trait object: `Vec<Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool>>`. `Fn`, `FnMut` and `FnOnce` are traits like any other.

A rule you will meet often: in a struct field or in a function's return type, `Box<dyn Trait>` is short for `Box<dyn Trait + 'static>`. `'static` here means "the value inside does not borrow anything that could go away". A closure meets it if every captured value is owned by the closure: copied in, cloned in or moved in. It fails if it captures a reference to a local variable or to a parameter.

```
fn prefix_rule(prefix: &str) -> Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool> {
    let owned = prefix.to_string();                // the closure gets its own copy
    Box::new(move |s| s.starts_with(owned.as_str()))
}
```

If the closure used `prefix` directly, it would hold a borrow that only lives as long as the caller's string, and the compiler refuses:

```
error: lifetime may not live long enough
  returning this value requires that `'1` must outlive `'static`
```

`move` moves whatever the closure names. If the variable is itself a reference (`prefix: &str`, `limit: &u32`), `move` moves the reference into the closure. The closure still borrows. To own the data, copy or clone it out first: `let limit = *limit;` or `let owned = prefix.to_string();`.

A `&dyn Fn(..)` parameter, by contrast, may borrow freely: it is only used during the call. Writing other lifetimes, such as `Box<dyn Fn() + 'a>`, is covered in 14.

## 9. Consuming a trait object; trait objects vs enums

A method may take its receiver as `self: Box<Self>`. It then consumes the box: after the call, the object is gone. The Book's state pattern (ch. 18.3, "Implementing an Object-Oriented Design Pattern") uses this so a state transition uses up the old state. `state.rs` is adapted from it:

```
trait State {
    fn submit(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn State>;
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str;
}
impl State for Draft {
    fn submit(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn State> { Box::new(Review) }
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str { "draft" }
}
```

`self: Box<Self>` is dyn compatible: the receiver is a pointer of known size, so the call can go through the vtable. The catch is that you must own the box to call it. A shared or mutable borrow of a box is not enough; you cannot move a box out from behind a reference. When the box sits inside something else, take it out first:

Where the box livesHow to take it out

`Option<Box<dyn State>>``opt.take()` leaves `None` behind

a field or variable of a type with a default`std::mem::take(&mut x)` (11)

a `Vec<Box<dyn T>>`, all of it`v.drain(..)` or `mem::take(&mut v)`, which leave it empty

a `Vec`, one element`v.remove(i)` or `v.pop()`

### Trait objects or an enum?

The same states could be an `enum State { Draft, Review, Published }` with `match` in each operation. The two designs make different changes cheap:

ChangeTrait objectsEnum + match

Add a new kind (type / variant)one new type and its `impl`; no other code changesedit every `match`

Add a new operationadd a method to the trait and to every typeone new function with one `match`; the compiler checks every case

Types from outside your crate (plugins)yesno: the set is closed

Cost per callvtable call, heap allocation per boxa `match` on a tag; no allocation needed

Ask the Tutor about any of these. Try to answer first.

- Why must `dyn Trait` always sit behind a pointer? What are the two halves of that pointer?

- Why can a trait with `fn copy(&self) -> Self` not be a trait object, while `fn copy(&self) -> Box<dyn Trait>` is fine?

- A default method calls `self.unit()`. For a type that overrides `unit`, which `unit` runs, and why?

- Why does a closure stored in a `Box<dyn Fn()>` field have to own what it captures?

- What would you gain and lose by rewriting `state.rs` as an enum?

trait Animal {
    fn name(&self) -> String;
    fn sound(&self) -> String;
    // Default: "<name> says <sound>"
    fn speak(&self) -> String {
        format!("{} says {}", self.name(), self.sound())
    }
}

struct Dog;
struct Cat {
    name: String,
}
struct Parrot {
    word: String,
}

impl Animal for Dog {
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        String::from("dog")
    }
    fn sound(&self) -> String {
        String::from("woof")
    }
}

impl Animal for Cat {
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        self.name.clone()
    }
    fn sound(&self) -> String {
        String::from("meow")
    }
}

impl Animal for Parrot {
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        String::from("parrot")
    }
    fn sound(&self) -> String {
        self.word.clone()
    }
    fn speak(&self) -> String {
        format!("{0}! {0}!", self.word)
    }
}

fn zoo() -> Vec<Box<dyn Animal>> {
    vec![
        Box::new(Dog),
        Box::new(Cat { name: "Tom".into() }),
        Box::new(Parrot { word: "hello".into() }),
    ]
}

fn chorus(animals: &[Box<dyn Animal>]) -> String {
    let lines: Vec<String> = animals.iter().map(|a| a.speak()).collect();
    lines.join("; ")
}

// Exercise 2: rules as boxed closures (reference solution)
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex2_rules.rs && ./main --test-threads=4

type Rule = Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool>;

fn max_len(n: usize) -> Rule {
    Box::new(move |s| s.len() <= n) // usize is Copy: copied in
}

fn without(word: &str) -> Rule {
    let word = word.to_string(); // own a copy; the closure must be 'static
    Box::new(move |s| !s.contains(word.as_str()))
}

fn one_of(allowed: Vec<String>) -> Rule {
    Box::new(move |s| allowed.iter().any(|a| a == s)) // the Vec is moved in
}

fn passes_all(rules: &[Rule], text: &str) -> bool {
    rules.iter().all(|r| r(text))
}

fn count_passing(rules: &[Rule], words: &[&str]) -> usize {
    words.iter().filter(|w| passes_all(rules, w)).count()
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn single_rules() {
        assert!(max_len(3)("abc"));
        assert!(!max_len(3)("abcd"));
        assert!(without("x")("abc"));
        assert!(!without("bc")("abc"));
        let r = one_of(vec!["red".into(), "blue".into()]);
        assert!(r("red") && !r("green"));
    }

    #[test]
    fn rule_outlives_the_string_it_was_made_from() {
        let rule = {
            let temp = String::from("oops");
            without(&temp)
        }; // `temp` is dropped here; the rule must still work
        assert!(rule("fine"));
        assert!(!rule("oops!"));
    }

    #[test]
    fn rules_of_different_closure_types_in_one_vec() {
        let rules: Vec<Rule> = vec![max_len(5), without("z"), Box::new(|s: &str| !s.is_empty())];
        assert!(passes_all(&rules, "abc"));
        assert!(!passes_all(&rules, "abcdef"));
        assert!(!passes_all(&rules, ""));
        assert!(passes_all(&[], "anything"));
        assert_eq!(count_passing(&rules, &["ok", "zoo", "toolong", "", "fine"]), 2);
    }
}

trait Light {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light>;
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str;
    // Default: most lights stay on for 30 seconds.
    fn seconds(&self) -> u32 {
        30
    }
}

struct Red;
struct Green;
struct Yellow;

impl Light for Red {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Green)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "red"
    }
}

impl Light for Green {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Yellow)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "green"
    }
}

impl Light for Yellow {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Red)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "yellow"
    }
    fn seconds(&self) -> u32 {
        5
    }
}

struct Signal {
    light: Option<Box<dyn Light>>,
}

impl Signal {
    fn new() -> Signal {
        Signal { light: Some(Box::new(Red)) }
    }

    fn advance(&mut self) {
        // take() leaves None behind, giving us the owned Box to consume.
        let old = self.light.take().unwrap();
        self.light = Some(old.next());
    }

    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        self.light.as_ref().unwrap().color()
    }

    fn run_for(&mut self, n: usize) -> u32 {
        let mut total = 0;
        for _ in 0..n {
            total += self.light.as_ref().unwrap().seconds();
            self.advance();
        }
        total
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn cycle_of_colours() {
        let mut s = Signal::new();
        let mut seen = vec![s.color()];
        for _ in 0..3 {
            s.advance();
            seen.push(s.color());
        }
        assert_eq!(seen, ["red", "green", "yellow", "red"]);
    }

    #[test]
    fn default_and_overridden_seconds() {
        assert_eq!(Red.seconds(), 30);
        assert_eq!(Green.seconds(), 30);
        assert_eq!(Yellow.seconds(), 5);
    }

    #[test]
    fn run_for_adds_up_and_moves_on() {
        let mut s = Signal::new();
        assert_eq!(s.run_for(3), 65);
        assert_eq!(s.color(), "red");
        assert_eq!(s.run_for(0), 0);
        assert_eq!(s.run_for(2), 60);
        assert_eq!(s.color(), "yellow");
    }
}

pub fn long_words_upper(text: &str, min_chars: usize) -> Vec<String> {

    text.split_whitespace()

CREATE OR REPLACE PACKAGE BODY xxap_uninv_accr_pkg AS
-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- XX AP Uninvoiced Receipts Accrual (XXAP_UNINV_ACCR)
-- Month end: expense receipts delivered in the period and not yet invoiced,
-- written to XXAP_UNINV_ACCR_LINES for the accrual journal.
-- Run by the close team from XX Payables Close (all operating units).
-- v2.1  03-2024  : expense accounts only
-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

  PROCEDURE run (errbuf        OUT VARCHAR2,
                 retcode       OUT VARCHAR2,
                 p_period_name IN  VARCHAR2) IS

    CURSOR c_receipts (cp_start DATE, cp_end DATE) IS
      SELECT rt.transaction_id,
             rt.quantity,
             rt.po_unit_price,
             pd.code_combination_id,
             pd.org_id,
             ph.segment1  po_number,
             ph.vendor_id
        FROM rcv_transactions  rt,
             po_distributions  pd,
             po_headers        ph
       WHERE rt.transaction_type       = 'DELIVER'
         AND rt.transaction_date      >= cp_start
         AND rt.transaction_date       < cp_end + 1
         AND pd.po_distribution_id     = rt.po_distribution_id
         AND pd.accrue_on_receipt_flag = 'N'
         AND ph.po_header_id           = pd.po_header_id;

    l_start    DATE;
    l_end      DATE;
    l_billed   NUMBER;
    l_account  gl_code_combinations.segment3%TYPE;
    l_rows     PLS_INTEGER := 0;
    l_written  PLS_INTEGER := 0;
  BEGIN
    mo_global.init('PO');

    SELECT start_date, end_date
      INTO l_start, l_end
      FROM gl_periods
     WHERE period_set_name = 'XX_CALENDAR'
       AND period_name     = p_period_name;

    DELETE FROM xxap_uninv_accr_lines
     WHERE period_name = p_period_name;

    FOR r IN c_receipts (l_start, l_end) LOOP

      -- quantity already invoiced against this receipt
      SELECT NVL(SUM(aid.quantity_invoiced), 0)
        INTO l_billed
        FROM ap_invoice_distributions aid
       WHERE aid.rcv_transaction_id = r.transaction_id;

      -- natural account of the charge account
      SELECT gcc.segment3
        INTO l_account
        FROM gl_code_combinations gcc
       WHERE gcc.code_combination_id = r.code_combination_id;

      IF l_account BETWEEN '5000' AND '7999'          -- expense accounts only
         AND r.quantity > l_billed THEN
        INSERT INTO xxap_uninv_accr_lines
          (period_name, org_id, po_number, vendor_id, rcv_transaction_id,
           natural_account, code_combination_id, uninvoiced_qty, accrual_amount,
           created_by, creation_date)
        VALUES
          (p_period_name, r.org_id, r.po_number, r.vendor_id, r.transaction_id,
           l_account, r.code_combination_id, r.quantity - l_billed,
           ROUND((r.quantity - l_billed) * r.po_unit_price, 2),
           fnd_global.user_id, SYSDATE);
        l_written := l_written + 1;
      END IF;

      l_rows := l_rows + 1;
      IF MOD(l_rows, 500) = 0 THEN
        COMMIT;
      END IF;
    END LOOP;

    COMMIT;
    fnd_file.put_line(fnd_file.log, l_rows || ' receipt lines read, ' || l_written || ' accrual lines written');
    retcode := '0';
  EXCEPTION
    WHEN OTHERS THEN
      ROLLBACK;
      errbuf  := SQLERRM;
      retcode := '2';
  END run;

END xxap_uninv_accr_pkg;
/

CREATE OR REPLACE PACKAGE BODY xxap_uninv_accr_pkg AS
-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- XX AP Uninvoiced Receipts Accrual (XXAP_UNINV_ACCR)
-- Month end: expense receipts delivered in the period and not yet invoiced,
-- written to XXAP_UNINV_ACCR_LINES for the accrual journal.
-- Run by the close team from XX Payables Close (all operating units).
-- v2.1  03-2024  : expense accounts only
-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

  PROCEDURE run (errbuf        OUT VARCHAR2,
                 retcode       OUT VARCHAR2,
                 p_period_name IN  VARCHAR2) IS

    CURSOR c_receipts (cp_start DATE, cp_end DATE) IS
      SELECT rt.transaction_id,
             rt.quantity,
             rt.po_unit_price,
             pd.code_combination_id,
             pd.org_id,
             ph.segment1  po_number,
             ph.vendor_id
        FROM rcv_transactions  rt,
             po_distributions  pd,
             po_headers        ph
       WHERE rt.transaction_type       = 'DELIVER'
         AND rt.transaction_date      >= cp_start
         AND rt.transaction_date       < cp_end + 1
         AND pd.po_distribution_id     = rt.po_distribution_id
         AND pd.accrue_on_receipt_flag = 'N'
         AND ph.po_header_id           = pd.po_header_id;

    l_start    DATE;
    l_end      DATE;
    l_billed   NUMBER;
    l_account  gl_code_combinations.segment3%TYPE;
    l_rows     PLS_INTEGER := 0;
    l_written  PLS_INTEGER := 0;
  BEGIN
    mo_global.init('PO');

    SELECT start_date, end_date
      INTO l_start, l_end
      FROM gl_periods
     WHERE period_set_name = 'XX_CALENDAR'
       AND period_name     = p_period_name;

    DELETE FROM xxap_uninv_accr_lines
     WHERE period_name = p_period_name;

    FOR r IN c_receipts (l_start, l_end) LOOP

      -- quantity already invoiced against this receipt
      SELECT NVL(SUM(aid.quantity_invoiced), 0)
        INTO l_billed
        FROM ap_invoice_distributions aid
       WHERE aid.rcv_transaction_id = r.transaction_id;

      -- natural account of the charge account
      SELECT gcc.segment3
        INTO l_account
        FROM gl_code_combinations gcc
       WHERE gcc.code_combination_id = r.code_combination_id;

      IF l_account BETWEEN '5000' AND '7999'          -- expense accounts only
         AND r.quantity > l_billed THEN
        INSERT INTO xxap_uninv_accr_lines
          (period_name, org_id, po_number, vendor_id, rcv_transaction_id,
           natural_account, code_combination_id, uninvoiced_qty, accrual_amount,
           created_by, creation_date)
        VALUES
          (p_period_name, r.org_id, r.po_number, r.vendor_id, r.transaction_id,
           l_account, r.code_combination_id, r.quantity - l_billed,
           ROUND((r.quantity - l_billed) * r.po_unit_price, 2),
           fnd_global.user_id, SYSDATE);
        l_written := l_written + 1;
      END IF;

      l_rows := l_rows + 1;
      IF MOD(l_rows, 500) = 0 THEN
        COMMIT;
      END IF;
    END LOOP;

    COMMIT;
    fnd_file.put_line(fnd_file.log, l_rows || ' receipt lines read, ' || l_written || ' accrual lines written');
    retcode := '0';
  EXCEPTION
    WHEN OTHERS THEN
      ROLLBACK;
      errbuf  := SQLERRM;
      retcode := '2';
  END run;

END xxap_uninv_accr_pkg;
/

CREATE OR REPLACE PACKAGE BODY xxap_uninv_accr_pkg AS
-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- XX AP Uninvoiced Receipts Accrual (XXAP_UNINV_ACCR)
-- Month end: expense receipts delivered in the period and not yet invoiced,
-- written to XXAP_UNINV_ACCR_LINES for the accrual journal.
-- Run by the close team from XX Payables Close (all operating units).
-- v2.1  03-2024  : expense accounts only
-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

  PROCEDURE run (errbuf        OUT VARCHAR2,
                 retcode       OUT VARCHAR2,
                 p_period_name IN  VARCHAR2) IS

    CURSOR c_receipts (cp_start DATE, cp_end DATE) IS
      SELECT rt.transaction_id,
             rt.quantity,
             rt.po_unit_price,
             pd.code_combination_id,
             pd.org_id,
             ph.segment1  po_number,
             ph.vendor_id
        FROM rcv_transactions  rt,
             po_distributions  pd,
             po_headers        ph
       WHERE rt.transaction_type       = 'DELIVER'
         AND rt.transaction_date      >= cp_start
         AND rt.transaction_date       < cp_end + 1
         AND pd.po_distribution_id     = rt.po_distribution_id
         AND pd.accrue_on_receipt_flag = 'N'
         AND ph.po_header_id           = pd.po_header_id;

    l_start    DATE;
    l_end      DATE;
    l_billed   NUMBER;
    l_account  gl_code_combinations.segment3%TYPE;
    l_rows     PLS_INTEGER := 0;
    l_written  PLS_INTEGER := 0;
  BEGIN
    mo_global.init('PO');

    SELECT start_date, end_date
      INTO l_start, l_end
      FROM gl_periods
     WHERE period_set_name = 'XX_CALENDAR'
       AND period_name     = p_period_name;

    DELETE FROM xxap_uninv_accr_lines
     WHERE period_name = p_period_name;

    FOR r IN c_receipts (l_start, l_end) LOOP

      -- quantity already invoiced against this receipt
      SELECT NVL(SUM(aid.quantity_invoiced), 0)
        INTO l_billed
        FROM ap_invoice_distributions aid
       WHERE aid.rcv_transaction_id = r.transaction_id;

      -- natural account of the charge account
      SELECT gcc.segment3
        INTO l_account
        FROM gl_code_combinations gcc
       WHERE gcc.code_combination_id = r.code_combination_id;

      IF l_account BETWEEN '5000' AND '7999'          -- expense accounts only
         AND r.quantity > l_billed THEN
        INSERT INTO xxap_uninv_accr_lines
          (period_name, org_id, po_number, vendor_id, rcv_transaction_id,
           natural_account, code_combination_id, uninvoiced_qty, accrual_amount,
           created_by, creation_date)
        VALUES
          (p_period_name, r.org_id, r.po_number, r.vendor_id, r.transaction_id,
           l_account, r.code_combination_id, r.quantity - l_billed,
           ROUND((r.quantity - l_billed) * r.po_unit_price, 2),
           fnd_global.user_id, SYSDATE);
        l_written := l_written + 1;
      END IF;

      l_rows := l_rows + 1;
      IF MOD(l_rows, 500) = 0 THEN
        COMMIT;
      END IF;
    END LOOP;

    COMMIT;
    fnd_file.put_line(fnd_file.log, l_rows || ' receipt lines read, ' || l_written || ' accrual lines written');
    retcode := '0';
  EXCEPTION
    WHEN OTHERS THEN
      ROLLBACK;
      errbuf  := SQLERRM;
      retcode := '2';
  END run;

END xxap_uninv_accr_pkg;
/

CREATE OR REPLACE PACKAGE BODY xxap_uninv_accr_pkg AS
-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- XX AP Uninvoiced Receipts Accrual (XXAP_UNINV_ACCR)
-- Month end: expense receipts delivered in the period and not yet invoiced,
-- written to XXAP_UNINV_ACCR_LINES for the accrual journal.
-- Run by the close team from XX Payables Close (all operating units).
-- v2.1  03-2024  : expense accounts only
-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

  PROCEDURE run (errbuf        OUT VARCHAR2,
                 retcode       OUT VARCHAR2,
                 p_period_name IN  VARCHAR2) IS

    CURSOR c_receipts (cp_start DATE, cp_end DATE) IS
      SELECT rt.transaction_id,
             rt.quantity,
             rt.po_unit_price,
             pd.code_combination_id,
             pd.org_id,
             ph.segment1  po_number,
             ph.vendor_id
        FROM rcv_transactions  rt,
             po_distributions  pd,
             po_headers        ph
       WHERE rt.transaction_type       = 'DELIVER'
         AND rt.transaction_date      >= cp_start
         AND rt.transaction_date       < cp_end + 1
         AND pd.po_distribution_id     = rt.po_distribution_id
         AND pd.accrue_on_receipt_flag = 'N'
         AND ph.po_header_id           = pd.po_header_id;

    l_start    DATE;
    l_end      DATE;
    l_billed   NUMBER;
    l_account  gl_code_combinations.segment3%TYPE;
    l_rows     PLS_INTEGER := 0;
    l_written  PLS_INTEGER := 0;
  BEGIN
    mo_global.init('PO');

    SELECT start_date, end_date
      INTO l_start, l_end
      FROM gl_periods
     WHERE period_set_name = 'XX_CALENDAR'
       AND period_name     = p_period_name;

    DELETE FROM xxap_uninv_accr_lines
     WHERE period_name = p_period_name;

    FOR r IN c_receipts (l_start, l_end) LOOP

      -- quantity already invoiced against this receipt
      SELECT NVL(SUM(aid.quantity_invoiced), 0)
        INTO l_billed
        FROM ap_invoice_distributions aid
       WHERE aid.rcv_transaction_id = r.transaction_id;

      -- natural account of the charge account
      SELECT gcc.segment3
        INTO l_account
        FROM gl_code_combinations gcc
       WHERE gcc.code_combination_id = r.code_combination_id;

      IF l_account BETWEEN '5000' AND '7999'          -- expense accounts only
         AND r.quantity > l_billed THEN
        INSERT INTO xxap_uninv_accr_lines
          (period_name, org_id, po_number, vendor_id, rcv_transaction_id,
           natural_account, code_combination_id, uninvoiced_qty, accrual_amount,
           created_by, creation_date)
        VALUES
          (p_period_name, r.org_id, r.po_number, r.vendor_id, r.transaction_id,
           l_account, r.code_combination_id, r.quantity - l_billed,
           ROUND((r.quantity - l_billed) * r.po_unit_price, 2),
           fnd_global.user_id, SYSDATE);
        l_written := l_written + 1;
      END IF;

      l_rows := l_rows + 1;
      IF MOD(l_rows, 500) = 0 THEN
        COMMIT;
      END IF;
    END LOOP;

    COMMIT;
    fnd_file.put_line(fnd_file.log, l_rows || ' receipt lines read, ' || l_written || ' accrual lines written');
    retcode := '0';
  EXCEPTION
    WHEN OTHERS THEN
      ROLLBACK;
      errbuf  := SQLERRM;
      retcode := '2';
  END run;

END xxap_uninv_accr_pkg;
/

WHAT A COMPLETE ANSWER TO THE STAGE ABOVE LOOKS LIKE:
No statement is slow; the statements run too many times. The SUM on AP_INVOICE_DISTRIBUTIONS ran 1,412,806 times at about 9.7 ms each (13,720 s, 92% of the 14,961 s run), mostly single-block reads (1.9 million db file sequential read waits): one index probe on AP_INVOICE_DISTRIBUTIONS_N17 plus one table block per receipt line. The GL_CODE_COMBINATIONS lookup ran 1,412,806 times (610 s) and the INSERT 331,020 times (403 s); the driving cursor itself took only 180 s. The plan's FILTER on MO_GLOB_ORG_ACCESS_TMP is the multi-org security predicate, paid on every execution. 1.4 million executions is India's volume: before June the same loop ran about 95,000 times, which is the old 10 minutes. The fix is the shape of the program, not one statement: one set-based statement that reads the period's deliveries once, joins to invoiced quantities aggregated once per receipt (GROUP BY rcv_transaction_id, as an inline view or a join), joins GL_CODE_COMBINATIONS instead of looking it up, and writes the result with a single INSERT ... SELECT (at minimum BULK COLLECT with FORALL). In batch code, read the _ALL tables with an explicit org_id filter taken from the operating units the request may process, rather than paying the security predicate per row; drop the commits inside the loop. Expected run: a few passes over about 1.4 million rows with hash joins, minutes rather than hours. Proof: run old and new against the same clone snapshot and compare line by line (period, org, receipt, quantity, amount); every difference explained.

NEVER say any of these, in any wording::
  - rows times cost
  - ORACLE_PROCESS_ID
  - queue time
  - too many times
  - GROUP BY rcv_transaction_id
  - set-based statement

You may point at where to look. You may not name the mechanism or the fix. If your sentence would let them answer without thinking, rewrite it.

I’d go straight to the trace and say the time is overwhelmingly in the two SQL statements executed once per receipt row, not in the fetch from the cursor itself.

The clearest line is the AP invoice lookup:
- `SELECT NVL(SUM(AID.QUANTITY_INVOICED), 0) FROM AP_INVOICE_DISTRIBUTIONS AID WHERE AID.RCV_TRANSACTION_ID = :B1`
- `Execute 1412806`
- `Fetch 1412806`
- `elapsed 13598.93`
- `disk 1906288`
- `query 11302448`
- `db file sequential read 1906288`

That says this statement ran 1,412,806 times and spent about 13,599 seconds elapsed, which is the bulk of the 4+ hour run. The access path itself is an index range scan on `AP_INVOICE_DISTRIBUTIONS_N17`, so the issue is not a missing index in the obvious sense; it is the repeated single-row lookup pattern at huge scale.

The second SQL has the same shape:
- `SELECT GCC.SEGMENT3 FROM GL_CODE_COMBINATIONS GCC WHERE GCC.CODE_COMBINATION_ID = :B1`
- `Execute 1412806`
- `Fetch 1412806`
- `elapsed 510.82`
- `query 4238418`

That one is much smaller, but still executed 1.4 million times. Together they confirm the package is doing row-by-row SQL inside the loop.

What I’d change in the program:
- Eliminate the per-row `SELECT SUM(...)` and precompute invoiced quantity in a set-based query or inline view joined to the receipt cursor.
- Eliminate the per-row lookup of `gl_code_combinations.segment3` by joining it in the cursor up front.
- Ideally rewrite the whole thing as one set-based `INSERT INTO xxap_uninv_accr_lines ... SELECT ...` with aggregation and filters applied in SQL, instead of PL/SQL looping.

So the main fix is not a tweak; it’s a rewrite from row-by-row processing to set-based SQL.

WHAT A COMPLETE ANSWER TO THE STAGE ABOVE LOOKS LIKE:
No statement is slow; the statements run too many times. The SUM on AP_INVOICE_DISTRIBUTIONS ran 1,412,806 times at about 9.7 ms each (13,720 s, 92% of the 14,961 s run), mostly single-block reads (1.9 million db file sequential read waits): one index probe on AP_INVOICE_DISTRIBUTIONS_N17 plus one table block per receipt line. The GL_CODE_COMBINATIONS lookup ran 1,412,806 times (610 s) and the INSERT 331,020 times (403 s); the driving cursor itself took only 180 s. The plan's FILTER on MO_GLOB_ORG_ACCESS_TMP is the multi-org security predicate, paid on every execution. 1.4 million executions is India's volume: before June the same loop ran about 95,000 times, which is the old 10 minutes. The fix is the shape of the program, not one statement: one set-based statement that reads the period's deliveries once, joins to invoiced quantities aggregated once per receipt (GROUP BY rcv_transaction_id, as an inline view or a join), joins GL_CODE_COMBINATIONS instead of looking it up, and writes the result with a single INSERT ... SELECT (at minimum BULK COLLECT with FORALL). In batch code, read the _ALL tables with an explicit org_id filter taken from the operating units the request may process, rather than paying the security predicate per row; drop the commits inside the loop. Expected run: a few passes over about 1.4 million rows with hash joins, minutes rather than hours. Proof: run old and new against the same clone snapshot and compare line by line (period, org, receipt, quantity, amount); every difference explained.

  - rows times cost
  - ORACLE_PROCESS_ID
  - queue time
  - too many times
  - GROUP BY rcv_transaction_id
  - set-based statement

I’d go straight to the trace and say the time is overwhelmingly in the two SQL statements executed once per receipt row, not in the fetch from the cursor itself.

The clearest line is the AP invoice lookup:
- `SELECT NVL(SUM(AID.QUANTITY_INVOICED), 0) FROM AP_INVOICE_DISTRIBUTIONS AID WHERE AID.RCV_TRANSACTION_ID = :B1`
- `Execute 1412806`
- `Fetch 1412806`
- `elapsed 13598.93`
- `disk 1906288`
- `query 11302448`
- `db file sequential read 1906288`

That says this statement ran 1,412,806 times and spent about 13,599 seconds elapsed, which is the bulk of the 4+ hour run. The access path itself is an index range scan on `AP_INVOICE_DISTRIBUTIONS_N17`, so the issue is not a missing index in the obvious sense; it is the repeated single-row lookup pattern at huge scale.

The second SQL has the same shape:
- `SELECT GCC.SEGMENT3 FROM GL_CODE_COMBINATIONS GCC WHERE GCC.CODE_COMBINATION_ID = :B1`
- `Execute 1412806`
- `Fetch 1412806`
- `elapsed 510.82`
- `query 4238418`

That one is much smaller, but still executed 1.4 million times. Together they confirm the package is doing row-by-row SQL inside the loop.

What I’d change in the program:
- Eliminate the per-row `SELECT SUM(...)` and precompute invoiced quantity in a set-based query or inline view joined to the receipt cursor.
- Eliminate the per-row lookup of `gl_code_combinations.segment3` by joining it in the cursor up front.
- Ideally rewrite the whole thing as one set-based `INSERT INTO xxap_uninv_accr_lines ... SELECT ...` with aggregation and filters applied in SQL, instead of PL/SQL looping.

So the main fix is not a tweak; it’s a rewrite from row-by-row processing to set-based SQL.

WHAT A COMPLETE ANSWER TO THE STAGE ABOVE LOOKS LIKE:
No statement is slow; the statements run too many times. The SUM on AP_INVOICE_DISTRIBUTIONS ran 1,412,806 times at about 9.7 ms each (13,720 s, 92% of the 14,961 s run), mostly single-block reads (1.9 million db file sequential read waits): one index probe on AP_INVOICE_DISTRIBUTIONS_N17 plus one table block per receipt line. The GL_CODE_COMBINATIONS lookup ran 1,412,806 times (610 s) and the INSERT 331,020 times (403 s); the driving cursor itself took only 180 s. The plan's FILTER on MO_GLOB_ORG_ACCESS_TMP is the multi-org security predicate, paid on every execution. 1.4 million executions is India's volume: before June the same loop ran about 95,000 times, which is the old 10 minutes. The fix is the shape of the program, not one statement: one set-based statement that reads the period's deliveries once, joins to invoiced quantities aggregated once per receipt (GROUP BY rcv_transaction_id, as an inline view or a join), joins GL_CODE_COMBINATIONS instead of looking it up, and writes the result with a single INSERT ... SELECT (at minimum BULK COLLECT with FORALL). In batch code, read the _ALL tables with an explicit org_id filter taken from the operating units the request may process, rather than paying the security predicate per row; drop the commits inside the loop. Expected run: a few passes over about 1.4 million rows with hash joins, minutes rather than hours. Yes — I think you mean the `MO_GLOB_ORG_ACCESS_TMP` row source showing up under the AP invoice lookup, and likely the same kind of MOAC access check under the driving query.

In the plan for:

`SELECT NVL(SUM(AID.QUANTITY_INVOICED), 0) FROM AP_INVOICE_DISTRIBUTIONS AID WHERE AID.RCV_TRANSACTION_ID = :B1`

I see:
- `TABLE ACCESS FULL MO_GLOB_ORG_ACCESS_TMP`

That is the multi-org access control filter EBS adds in AP/PO context. It’s there to enforce the current org access set for the APPS session.

Does it matter to the rewrite? Not really to the logic, but yes to how I’d rewrite it:
- I would keep the same EBS security context / MOAC initialization (`mo_global.init('PO')`) behavior.
- I would not try to bypass it.
- But I would avoid calling that SQL millions of times, because even a small security check becomes expensive when it is executed 1.4 million times.

So the step is a security/access filter, not business logic. It matters because it contributes overhead and because any rewrite has to preserve org filtering, but it’s not the root cause by itself.

Fair enough, and preserving the security context rather than working around it is the right instinct.

So you did the rewrite. It now runs in 6 minutes, and you ran parity on three periods, June, July and August: the new output matches the old program's output line for line, same receipts, same quantities, same amounts. Everyone signs off.

Then the India controller comes back. They say India's August uninvoiced accrual should be somewhere around 5.1 crore. Your report shows 1.92 crore for the India operating unit. The US and UK numbers nobody is disputing.

Two things on the desk in front of you. First, the August output summary from the rewrite: by operating unit, India has far fewer accrual lines than its receipt volume would suggest, and the natural accounts appearing on the India lines are a narrow set. Second, the two Accounting Flexfield structures in this instance: the US and UK ledgers share one structure where segment3 is the natural account, and the India ledger was implemented on its own structure with a different segment order, so segment3 there holds something else entirely and the natural account sits elsewhere.

Why is India low, and why didn't your parity testing catch it?

WHAT A COMPLETE ANSWER TO THE STAGE ABOVE LOOKS LIKE:
No statement is slow; the statements run too many times. The SUM on AP_INVOICE_DISTRIBUTIONS ran 1,412,806 times at about 9.7 ms each (13,720 s, 92% of the 14,961 s run), mostly single-block reads (1.9 million db file sequential read waits): one index probe on AP_INVOICE_DISTRIBUTIONS_N17 plus one table block per receipt line. The GL_CODE_COMBINATIONS lookup ran 1,412,806 times (610 s) and the INSERT 331,020 times (403 s); the driving cursor itself took only 180 s. The fix is the shape of the program, not one statement: one set-based statement that reads the period's deliveries once, joins to invoiced quantities aggregated once per receipt (GROUP BY rcv_transaction_id, as an inline view or a join), joins GL_CODE_COMBINATIONS instead of looking it up, and writes the result with a single INSERT ... SELECT (at minimum BULK COLLECT with FORALL). In batch code, read the _ALL tables with an explicit org_id filter taken from the operating units the request may process, rather than paying the security predicate per row; drop the commits inside the loop. Expected run: a few passes over about 1.4 million rows with hash joins, minutes rather than hours. Yes — I think you mean the `MO_GLOB_ORG_ACCESS_TMP` row source showing up under the AP invoice lookup, and likely the same kind of MOAC access check under the driving query.

In the plan for:

`SELECT NVL(SUM(AID.QUANTITY_INVOICED), 0) FROM AP_INVOICE_DISTRIBUTIONS AID WHERE AID.RCV_TRANSACTION_ID = :B1`

I see:
- `TABLE ACCESS FULL MO_GLOB_ORG_ACCESS_TMP`

That is the multi-org access control filter EBS adds in AP/PO context. It’s there to enforce the current org access set for the APPS session.

Does it matter to the rewrite? Not really to the logic, but yes to how I’d rewrite it:
- I would keep the same EBS security context / MOAC initialization (`mo_global.init('PO')`) behavior.
- I would not try to bypass it.
- But I would avoid calling that SQL millions of times, because even a small security check becomes expensive when it is executed 1.4 million times.

So the step is a security/access filter, not business logic. It matters because it contributes overhead and because any rewrite has to preserve org filtering, but it’s not the root cause by itself.

That has to be raised with finance now, not just fixed in code. The fix: never hard-code a segment number. Find each operating unit's ledger and chart of accounts (HR_OPERATING_UNITS or the OU's ledger, then GL_LEDGERS.CHART_OF_ACCOUNTS_ID), find the natural-account segment from the flexfield qualifier GL_ACCOUNT (FND_FLEX_APIS.GET_SEGMENT_COLUMN or the segment qualifier setup), and select expense accounts by account type (GL_CODE_COMBINATIONS.ACCOUNT_TYPE = 'E') rather than by number range. India is low because the package is filtering on the wrong segment for the India ledger.

In the code, the business test is:

```plsql
SELECT gcc.segment3
  INTO l_account
  FROM gl_code_combinations gcc
 WHERE gcc.code_combination_id = r.code_combination_id;

IF l_account BETWEEN '5000' AND '7999' THEN
```

That only works for the US/UK structure where segment3 is the natural account. For India, segment3 is something else, so a lot of valid expense receipts never pass the `BETWEEN '5000' AND '7999'` test. That would explain both symptoms you mentioned:
- India has far fewer accrual lines than the receipt volume suggests
- the natural accounts on the India lines are a narrow set, basically only the ones where whatever is in segment3 happens to fall into that range by coincidence

Why parity didn’t catch it:
- I only tested against the old program’s output, so the rewrite matched the old bug exactly.
- The old program was already wrong for India, because it was hard-coded to `segment3` instead of using the ledger’s actual account structure.
- So line-for-line parity against legacy output can still miss a functional defect if the legacy logic is bad for a subset of ledgers.

What I’d change:
- Stop hard-coding `gcc.segment3` as the natural account.
- Resolve the natural account based on the accounting flexfield structure for the org/ledger, or derive it from the account segment definition instead of assuming position 3.
- Re-test with India-specific cases, not just parity against the old output.

So the root cause is a structure assumption baked into the code, and parity passed because it was validating equivalence to the same incorrect logic.

move_object.report_notes:
Across the question the candidate showed genuine senior-level diagnostic instinct. On the opening they read the package accurately and unprompted: the cursor over the PO and receiving tables, both per-row SELECT INTOs, the row-by-row insert and the periodic commit, and framed the slowdown correctly as volume scaling against per-row cost. They needed the request history read out to them before separating the late start from the actual run time, but once given the numbers they drew the right conclusion and treated the scheduling delay as a separate conversation with the close team.

On the trace they were strong and specific: quoted the 1,412,806 executions, the 13,598 seconds on the AP sum, the single block read waits, and concluded correctly that no statement is individually slow so the program shape is the problem, proposing a set-based single pass with an insert select. They missed the in-loop commits and did not spot the multi-org temp table in the plan until pointed at the row source lines; once prompted they identified it as the MOAC policy and said it must be preserved, but did not go on to filter the _ALL tables by org explicitly in batch code, and never quantified cost per execution against India's volume.

The flexfield defect was their best stage: diagnosed unprompted from the hard-coded segment and the 5000 to 7999 range, explained why the assumption fails for the India ledger and why parity testing against a defective baseline proved nothing, and proposed deriving the account segment from the ledger's flexfield structure. They stopped short of selecting by account type rather than a numeric range, and crucially did not raise that three months of accruals are understated in GL and finance must be told now, which had to be prompted.

On the final DBA change they produced a well-organised governance answer: refuse an ad hoc production change the night before close, demand the exact diff, clone evidence, rollback and backout, parity and India-specific functional checks, and business sign-off rather than DBA sign-off alone. They were rightly sceptical of a hint as symptom tuning on row-by-row SQL and noted its fragility. However they did not do the arithmetic on the UAT figure in the exhibit: the improved run time still lands past the cut-off because the executions remain, which is the core judgement the stage was testing. They also did not challenge DBMS_STATS being called directly against AP and PO tables, nor the histogram implications or the risk of changing standard AP and PO plans the night before close, and did not raise the ongoing DML and patch maintenance cost of adding a custom index to a core AP table, or the fragility of a hint naming an index by name. No concrete plan for close night either.

Overall: fast, evidence-grounded analyst, very good on code and trace, excellent on the functional defect, sound on change control process, but thinner on EBS-specific platform standards and on converting numbers in an exhibit into a go/no-go decision. Prompting was needed twice across the question, both times on exhibit detail rather than reasoning.
move_object.response: That's a sound governance answer, and the instinct to refuse an ad hoc patch the night before close is right. Two things I'd have wanted you to push on: the UAT figure they quote in their own header is worth doing the arithmetic on against the cut-off before you even argue about process, and I'd have liked you to look harder at how those statistics calls are being made on core AP and PO tables and what that could do to standard programs the night before close. But you got there on the risk of hinting inside row-by-row SQL and on who needs to sign off. That's all we have time for. Thanks for working through it so openly, particularly the reading of the trace and the account segment issue, which you got quickly. Someone will be back in touch about next steps.

messages.content: Right, so the settings page is basically split into a server read and a client submit, and that’s where I’d look first. `app/settings/page.tsx` does an `await getSettings()` on every render, then passes those values into `SettingsForm`; the form itself is in `app/settings/settings-form.tsx`, and when you hit save it calls the server action in `app/settings/actions.ts`, which parses the form and then `await putSettings(parsed.values)`. So the write path seems to reach the API, at least in principle. The reason a reload still shows the old values feels like caching somewhere on the read side, not the form state: `getSettings()` is probably being memoized or cached in `lib/settings`, or the route is being statically cached by Next because there’s no obvious `noStore`/revalidation in the page. Since the app is built once and then run in three `next start` containers with separate `.next` directories, if the settings data is being cached at build/render level in each container, one save would not invalidate the other containers, and even the same container may keep serving the stale server component output. I’d point specifically at `app/settings/page.tsx` for the read, `app/settings/actions.ts` for the write, and then `lib/settings` / `lib/settings-schema` as the likely place where caching or fetch options are hiding. On the header issue, `app/layout.tsx` wraps the whole app in `AccountProvider`, but `app/account-provider.tsx` fetches `/api/account` from the browser after hydration, so the badge is client-populated and could briefly show the wrong cached state if the browser or some shared response is involved; the route handler is `app/api/account/route.ts`, which reads the `sid` cookie and then calls `getAccountSummary(sid)`. So the stale name smell is separate, but the settings bug itself is almost certainly that the settings read path is cached and never invalidated after `putSettings`.
