Left, three boxes: "body only reads a capture (captured as &T)", "body changes a capture (captured as &mut T)", "body moves a capture out (captured as T)".
Right, three nested rounded sets: the outer set "FnOnce: can be called at least once" contains "FnMut: can be called many times", which contains "Fn: many times, even shared", with the note "every Fn is also FnMut and FnOnce; every FnMut is also FnOnce".
Arrows: reads goes to Fn, changes goes to FnMut, moves out goes to FnOnce.
Footer: `move` changes HOW captures are stored (owned instead of borrowed), not WHICH trait you get: a `move` closure that only reads is still Fn.

[entity 867 · iterator-pipeline.png · diagram]
# iterator-pipeline.png

Five boxes left to right: `iter()`, `filter(..)`, `map(..)`, `take(2)`, `collect()`.
Dark arrows above point right to left, labelled "next()?" (requests travel right to left). Green arrows below point left to right: "Some(item) travels left to right, one item at a time".
Numbered notes:
1. Adapters (filter, map, take, zip, skip, enumerate, rev) only build a value. Nothing runs yet.
2. A consumer (collect, sum, fold, count, any, a for loop) calls next() and work starts.
3. One item passes the whole chain before the next item is fetched.
4. filter keeps asking the stage before it until an item passes (or None).
5. When take has handed out its count, it stops asking: earlier stages never see the rest.

// Reference solution for exercise 1 (Tutor only; never shown to the learner).
pub fn apply_n(f: impl Fn(i32) -> i32, n: usize, x: i32) -> i32 {
    let mut v = x;
    for _ in 0..n {
        v = f(v);
    }
    v
}

pub fn compose<F, G>(f: F, g: G) -> impl Fn(i32) -> i32
where
    F: Fn(i32) -> i32,
    G: Fn(i32) -> i32,
{
    move |x| g(f(x)) // move: the closure must own f and g, they outlive this call
}

pub fn keep_words(text: &str, keep: impl Fn(&str) -> bool) -> Vec<String> {
    text.split_whitespace().filter(|w| keep(w)).map(|w| w.to_string()).collect()
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn apply_several_times() {
        assert_eq!(apply_n(|v| v * 2, 3, 1), 8);
        assert_eq!(apply_n(|v| v - 1, 0, 5), 5);
    }

    #[test]
    fn apply_with_captured_step() {
        let step = 7;
        assert_eq!(apply_n(|v| v + step, 2, 0), 14);
    }

    #[test]
    fn compose_runs_f_then_g() {
        let h = compose(|v| v + 1, |v| v * 10);
        assert_eq!(h(2), 30);
        assert_eq!(h(0), 10);
    }

    #[test]
    fn compose_with_captures() {
        let offset = 100;
        let h = compose(move |v| v + offset, |v| -v);
        assert_eq!(h(1), -101);
    }

    #[test]
    fn keeps_matching_words() {
        assert_eq!(keep_words("a bb ccc", |w| w.len() > 1), vec!["bb", "ccc"]);
        let banned = "x";
        assert_eq!(keep_words("x y x z", |w| w != banned), vec!["y", "z"]);
    }
}

// Reference solution for exercise 3 (Tutor only; never shown to the learner).
pub struct Fib {
    a: u64,
    b: u64,
}

impl Fib {
    pub fn new() -> Fib {
        Fib { a: 0, b: 1 }
    }
}

impl Iterator for Fib {
    type Item = u64;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u64> {
        let out = self.a;
        self.a = self.b;
        self.b += out;
        Some(out)
    }
}

pub fn first_fib(n: usize) -> Vec<u64> {
    Fib::new().take(n).collect()
}

pub fn even_fib_sum_below(limit: u64) -> u64 {
    Fib::new().take_while(|&x| x < limit).filter(|x| x % 2 == 0).sum()
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn next_by_hand() {
        let mut f = Fib::new();
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(0));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(1));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(1));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(2));
    }

    #[test]
    fn first_few() {
        assert_eq!(first_fib(7), vec![0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8]);
        assert!(first_fib(0).is_empty());
    }

    #[test]
    fn even_sum() {
        assert_eq!(even_fib_sum_below(10), 10); // 0 + 2 + 8
        assert_eq!(even_fib_sum_below(100), 44); // + 34
    }
}

## 1. Closures

Adapted from The Rust Programming Language, ch 13.1-13.2, and Rust by Example (Closures, Capturing, As input parameters, Iterators), MIT/Apache-2.0.

A closure is a function you write inline, without a name, that can use the variables around it:

```
let limit = 10;
let over = |x: i32| x > limit;     // reads `limit` from the surrounding scope
println!("{}", over(12));          // true
let add_one = |x| x + 1;           // parameter and return types inferred
```

- Parameters go between bars: `|x|`, `|a, b|`, or `||` for none. The body is one expression or a `{ ... }` block.

- Types are usually inferred. They are fixed by the first use: after `add_one(5)`, calling `add_one(2.5)` is a type error.

- A `fn` item cannot read local variables of the function around it; a closure can. That is the whole point.

Parameters are patterns. Iterator methods often hand a closure a reference. A pattern can unpack it:

```
let temps = [18, 23, 31];
// iter() yields &i32; filter passes a reference to that, so its closure gets &&i32.
let warm: Vec<&i32> = temps.iter().filter(|&&t| t > 20).collect();  // t: i32
let doubled: Vec<i32> = temps.iter().map(|&t| t * 2).collect();       // t: i32
let hot: Vec<usize> = temps.iter().enumerate()
    .filter(|(_, t)| **t > 25).map(|(i, _)| i).collect();              // tuples too
```

## 2. How a closure captures

A closure captures each outside variable it uses in the weakest way its body needs:

Body doesCaptured asWhile the closure is alive

reads the variableshared borrow `&T`others may read it too

changes itmutable borrow `&mut T`nobody else may use it

moves it out (gives it away, drops it)by value `T`it now belongs to the closure

The borrow rules from 03 apply to these captures. A closure that holds `&mut count` blocks every other use of `count` until the closure's last use:

```
let mut count = 0;
let mut bump = || count += 1;   // captures &mut count
bump();
println!("{count}");            // error: bump is used again below
bump();
```

```
error[E0502]: cannot borrow `count` as immutable because it is also borrowed as mutable
  |     let mut bump = || count += 1;
  |                    -- ----- first borrow occurs due to use of `count` in closure
  |                    |
  |                    mutable borrow occurs here
  |     println!("{count}");
  |                ^^^^^ immutable borrow occurs here
  |     bump();
  |     ---- mutable borrow later used here
```

Move the `println!` after the last `bump()` and it compiles: the borrow ends when the closure is last used.

Fields, not whole structs. Since edition 2021, a closure that uses `stats.hits` captures only that field. Other fields of `stats` stay free to use while the closure is alive. (Older editions captured the whole struct.) Part 4 of `capture.rs` shows it.

## 3. `move`

Writing `move` before the bars makes the closure take ownership of every variable it uses, even ones it only reads:

```
let label = String::from("total");
let owned = move || println!("owned: {label}");
owned();
// println!("{label}");  // error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `label`
```

You need `move` when the closure must outlive the variables it uses: a closure returned from a function (section 5), or one sent to another thread (18).

With a `Copy` value (integers, `bool`, `char`, `f64`), `move` copies it into the closure. The closure then works on its own copy, and the outside variable never sees the changes:

```
let mut fuel = 50.0;
let mut burn = move || { fuel -= 10.0; fuel };   // burn owns a copy of fuel
println!("{} {}", burn(), burn());              // 40 30
println!("{fuel}");                             // 50: the outer fuel was never touched
```

## 4. Fn, FnMut and FnOnce

Every closure implements one or more of three traits. Which ones depends on what the body does with its captures, not on whether you wrote `move`:

TraitThe body...Can be called

`Fn`only reads its capturesany number of times, even through a shared reference

`FnMut`changes a capturemany times, but each call needs exclusive (`&mut`) access to the closure

`FnOnce`moves a capture outonce: the first call uses the captured value up

capture-and-traits.png: what the body does picks the trait; Fn sits inside FnMut, inside FnOnce.

The traits nest: every `Fn` closure is also `FnMut` and `FnOnce`, and every `FnMut` is also `FnOnce`. So a function that asks for `FnOnce` accepts anything; one that asks for `Fn` accepts only closures that do not mutate or move out.

A `move` closure that only reads a `String` is still `Fn`: it owns the string, but calling it does not use the string up. `move` changes how captures are stored, not which trait you get.

## 5. Closures as parameters and return values

Take a closure with `impl Fn...` or a generic bound, exactly like any other trait (09):

```
fn call_twice<F: Fn() -> usize>(f: F) -> usize {
    f() + f()
}
fn call_twice_mut<F: FnMut()>(mut f: F) {   // note `mut f`
    f();
    f();
}
fn call_once<F: FnOnce() -> String>(f: F) -> String {
    f()                                    // f is used up here
}
```

Calling an `FnMut` needs `&mut` access to the closure value (its captured state changes), so the parameter or variable that holds it must be declared `mut`. Calling an `FnOnce` consumes it, so it can be called only once in the function body.

Std examples: `Option::unwrap_or_else` takes an `FnOnce` (called at most once); `sort_by_key` takes an `FnMut` (called many times, may count or record).

### Returning a closure

```
fn make_adder(step: i32) -> impl Fn(i32) -> i32 {
    let base = step * 10;
    move |x| x + base + step
}
```

The returned closure is called after `make_adder` has returned, when `base` and `step` no longer exist. Without `move` it would borrow them:

```
error[E0373]: closure may outlive the current function, but it borrows `base`, which is owned by the current function
  |     |x| x + base + step
  |     ^^^     ---- `base` is borrowed here
  |     |
  |     may outlive borrowed value `base`
note: closure is returned here
```

The return type must name the right trait too: a closure whose body changes its captures is `FnMut`, so the function must say `-> impl FnMut(...)`, and the caller must store it in a `let mut` binding to call it.

## 6. The Iterator trait and the three ways to iterate

An iterator is any value that implements one required method:

```
trait Iterator {
    type Item;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item>;   // Some(item), or None when done
    // ...plus dozens of provided methods (map, filter, sum, ...)
}
```

A collection gives you three iterators, which differ in the item type:

CallItem type for a `Vec<T>`The Vec afterwardsSame as

`v.iter()``&T`untouched`for x in &v`

`v.iter_mut()``&mut T`changed in place`for x in &mut v`

`v.into_iter()``T`consumed (moved)`for x in v`

A `for` loop calls `into_iter()` on whatever you give it, which is why `for x in v` consumes `v` while `for x in &v` only borrows it. `iterators.rs` shows all three.

## 7. Adapters are lazy, consumers pull

Adapters take an iterator and return a new one: `map`, `filter`, `take(n)`, `skip(n)`, `take_while`, `zip`, `enumerate`, `rev`, `step_by`, `copied`/`cloned`. Building one runs no closure. Consumers call `next` until they are done: `collect`, `sum`, `count`, `fold`, `any`, `position`, and a `for` loop.

iterator-pipeline.png: requests travel right to left, items left to right, one at a time.

An adapter chain with no consumer does nothing, and the compiler warns you:

```
warning: unused `Map` that must be used
  |     v.iter().map(|s| s * 2);
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  = note: iterators are lazy and do nothing unless consumed
```

When the consumer asks for an item, the request travels back through the chain to the source, and the item comes forward through every stage before the next item is fetched. A `filter` keeps asking for items until one passes. A `take(n)` stops asking once it has handed out `n` items, so the stages before it never see the rest.

`zip` pairs two iterators. It asks the left one first and stops as soon as the left one returns `None` (this order is documented). `skip(n)` drops the first `n` items of the iterator it is called on, and only that one.

`sum` and `collect` can produce several types, so the result type must be written somewhere: `let total: i32 = v.iter().sum();` or `.collect::<Vec<_>>()`.

## 8. What `collect` can build

ItemsTarget typeResult

`T``Vec<T>`a vector

`(K, V)``HashMap<K, V>`a map from pairs

`char``String`a string

`Result<T, E>``Result<Vec<T>, E>``Ok(vec)`, or the first `Err` (stops there)

You cannot collect owned values from references: `v.iter()` yields `&String`, so `.collect::<Vec<String>>()` fails with E0277 ("cannot be built from an iterator over elements of type `&String`"). Either collect references (`Vec<&String>`), copy them (`.cloned()`, or `.copied()` for `Copy` types), or start from `into_iter()` to get owned items.

## 9. Writing your own iterator

Put the state in a struct and implement `next`. Every adapter and consumer then works on it for free:

```
struct Countdown { left: u32 }

impl Iterator for Countdown {
    type Item = u32;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u32> {
        if self.left == 0 {
            None
        } else {
            self.left -= 1;
            Some(self.left + 1)
        }
    }
}
let ticks: Vec<u32> = Countdown { left: 3 }.collect();   // [3, 2, 1]
```

Iterator chains are not slower than loops in an optimised (`--release`) build: the compiler inlines the closures and produces the same machine code as a hand-written loop. Debug builds, which the runner uses, are slower for both.

# capture-and-traits.png

Left, three boxes: "body only reads a capture (captured as &T)", "body changes a capture (captured as &mut T)", "body moves a capture out (captured as T)".
Right, three nested rounded sets: the outer set "FnOnce: can be called at least once" contains "FnMut: can be called many times", which contains "Fn: many times, even shared", with the note "every Fn is also FnMut and FnOnce; every FnMut is also FnOnce".
Arrows: reads goes to Fn, changes goes to FnMut, moves out goes to FnOnce.
Footer: `move` changes HOW captures are stored (owned instead of borrowed), not WHICH trait you get: a `move` closure that only reads is still Fn.

[entity 867 · iterator-pipeline.png · diagram]
# iterator-pipeline.png

Five boxes left to right: `iter()`, `filter(..)`, `map(..)`, `take(2)`, `collect()`.
Dark arrows above point right to left, labelled "next()?" (requests travel right to left). Green arrows below point left to right: "Some(item) travels left to right, one item at a time".
Numbered notes:
1. Adapters (filter, map, take, zip, skip, enumerate, rev) only build a value. Nothing runs yet.
2. A consumer (collect, sum, fold, count, any, a for loop) calls next() and work starts.
3. One item passes the whole chain before the next item is fetched.
4. filter keeps asking the stage before it until an item passes (or None).
5. When take has handed out its count, it stops asking: earlier stages never see the rest.

where

pub struct Fib {
    a: u64,
    b: u64,
}

impl Fib {
    pub fn new() -> Fib {
        Fib { a: 0, b: 1 }
    }
}

impl Iterator for Fib {
    type Item = u64;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u64> {
        let out = self.a;
        self.a = self.b;
        self.b += out;
        Some(out)
    }
}

pub fn first_fib(n: usize) -> Vec<u64> {
    Fib::new().take(n).collect()
}

pub fn even_fib_sum_below(limit: u64) -> u64 {
    Fib::new().take_while(|&x| x < limit).filter(|x| x % 2 == 0).sum()
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn next_by_hand() {
        let mut f = Fib::new();
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(0));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(1));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(1));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(2));
    }

    #[test]
    fn first_few() {
        assert_eq!(first_fib(7), vec![0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8]);
        assert!(first_fib(0).is_empty());
    }

    #[test]
    fn even_sum() {
        assert_eq!(even_fib_sum_below(10), 10); // 0 + 2 + 8
        assert_eq!(even_fib_sum_below(100), 44); // + 34
    }
}

/// Apply `f` to `x`, `n` times. apply_n(|v| v * 2, 3, 1) == 8
pub fn apply_n(f: impl Fn(i32) -> i32, n: usize, x: i32) -> i32 {
    let mut out = x;
    for _ in 0..n {
        out = f(out);
    }
    out
}

/// A closure that runs `f` first, then `g` on the result.
/// compose(|v| v + 1, |v| v * 10)(2) == 30
pub fn compose<F, G>(f: F, g: G) -> impl Fn(i32) -> i32
where
    F: Fn(i32) -> i32,
    G: Fn(i32) -> i32,
{
    move |x| g(f(x))
}

## 1. Closures

Adapted from The Rust Programming Language, ch 13.1-13.2, and Rust by Example (Closures, Capturing, As input parameters, Iterators), MIT/Apache-2.0.

A closure is a function you write inline, without a name, that can use the variables around it:

```
let limit = 10;
let over = |x: i32| x > limit;     // reads `limit` from the surrounding scope
println!("{}", over(12));          // true
let add_one = |x| x + 1;           // parameter and return types inferred
```

- Parameters go between bars: `|x|`, `|a, b|`, or `||` for none. The body is one expression or a `{ ... }` block.

- Types are usually inferred. They are fixed by the first use: after `add_one(5)`, calling `add_one(2.5)` is a type error.

- A `fn` item cannot read local variables of the function around it; a closure can. That is the whole point.

Parameters are patterns. Iterator methods often hand a closure a reference. A pattern can unpack it:

```
let temps = [18, 23, 31];
// iter() yields &i32; filter passes a reference to that, so its closure gets &&i32.
let warm: Vec<&i32> = temps.iter().filter(|&&t| t > 20).collect();  // t: i32
let doubled: Vec<i32> = temps.iter().map(|&t| t * 2).collect();       // t: i32
let hot: Vec<usize> = temps.iter().enumerate()
    .filter(|(_, t)| **t > 25).map(|(i, _)| i).collect();              // tuples too
```

## 2. How a closure captures

A closure captures each outside variable it uses in the weakest way its body needs:

Body doesCaptured asWhile the closure is alive

reads the variableshared borrow `&T`others may read it too

changes itmutable borrow `&mut T`nobody else may use it

moves it out (gives it away, drops it)by value `T`it now belongs to the closure

The borrow rules from 03 apply to these captures. A closure that holds `&mut count` blocks every other use of `count` until the closure's last use:

```
let mut count = 0;
let mut bump = || count += 1;   // captures &mut count
bump();
println!("{count}");            // error: bump is used again below
bump();
```

```
error[E0502]: cannot borrow `count` as immutable because it is also borrowed as mutable
  |     let mut bump = || count += 1;
  |                    -- ----- first borrow occurs due to use of `count` in closure
  |                    |
  |                    mutable borrow occurs here
  |     println!("{count}");
  |                ^^^^^ immutable borrow occurs here
  |     bump();
  |     ---- mutable borrow later used here
```

Move the `println!` after the last `bump()` and it compiles: the borrow ends when the closure is last used.

Fields, not whole structs. Since edition 2021, a closure that uses `stats.hits` captures only that field. Other fields of `stats` stay free to use while the closure is alive. (Older editions captured the whole struct.) Part 4 of `capture.rs` shows it.

## 3. `move`

Writing `move` before the bars makes the closure take ownership of every variable it uses, even ones it only reads:

```
let label = String::from("total");
let owned = move || println!("owned: {label}");
owned();
// println!("{label}");  // error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `label`
```

You need `move` when the closure must outlive the variables it uses: a closure returned from a function (section 5), or one sent to another thread (18).

With a `Copy` value (integers, `bool`, `char`, `f64`), `move` copies it into the closure. The closure then works on its own copy, and the outside variable never sees the changes:

```
let mut fuel = 50.0;
let mut burn = move || { fuel -= 10.0; fuel };   // burn owns a copy of fuel
println!("{} {}", burn(), burn());              // 40 30
println!("{fuel}");                             // 50: the outer fuel was never touched
```

## 4. Fn, FnMut and FnOnce

Every closure implements one or more of three traits. Which ones depends on what the body does with its captures, not on whether you wrote `move`:

TraitThe body...Can be called

`Fn`only reads its capturesany number of times, even through a shared reference

`FnMut`changes a capturemany times, but each call needs exclusive (`&mut`) access to the closure

`FnOnce`moves a capture outonce: the first call uses the captured value up

capture-and-traits.png: what the body does picks the trait; Fn sits inside FnMut, inside FnOnce.

The traits nest: every `Fn` closure is also `FnMut` and `FnOnce`, and every `FnMut` is also `FnOnce`. So a function that asks for `FnOnce` accepts anything; one that asks for `Fn` accepts only closures that do not mutate or move out.

A `move` closure that only reads a `String` is still `Fn`: it owns the string, but calling it does not use the string up. `move` changes how captures are stored, not which trait you get.

## 5. Closures as parameters and return values

Take a closure with `impl Fn...` or a generic bound, exactly like any other trait (09):

```
fn call_twice<F: Fn() -> usize>(f: F) -> usize {
    f() + f()
}
fn call_twice_mut<F: FnMut()>(mut f: F) {   // note `mut f`
    f();
    f();
}
fn call_once<F: FnOnce() -> String>(f: F) -> String {
    f()                                    // f is used up here
}
```

Calling an `FnMut` needs `&mut` access to the closure value (its captured state changes), so the parameter or variable that holds it must be declared `mut`. Calling an `FnOnce` consumes it, so it can be called only once in the function body.

Std examples: `Option::unwrap_or_else` takes an `FnOnce` (called at most once); `sort_by_key` takes an `FnMut` (called many times, may count or record).

### Returning a closure

```
fn make_adder(step: i32) -> impl Fn(i32) -> i32 {
    let base = step * 10;
    move |x| x + base + step
}
```

The returned closure is called after `make_adder` has returned, when `base` and `step` no longer exist. Without `move` it would borrow them:

```
error[E0373]: closure may outlive the current function, but it borrows `base`, which is owned by the current function
  |     |x| x + base + step
  |     ^^^     ---- `base` is borrowed here
  |     |
  |     may outlive borrowed value `base`
note: closure is returned here
```

The return type must name the right trait too: a closure whose body changes its captures is `FnMut`, so the function must say `-> impl FnMut(...)`, and the caller must store it in a `let mut` binding to call it.

## 6. The Iterator trait and the three ways to iterate

An iterator is any value that implements one required method:

```
trait Iterator {
    type Item;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item>;   // Some(item), or None when done
    // ...plus dozens of provided methods (map, filter, sum, ...)
}
```

A collection gives you three iterators, which differ in the item type:

CallItem type for a `Vec<T>`The Vec afterwardsSame as

`v.iter()``&T`untouched`for x in &v`

`v.iter_mut()``&mut T`changed in place`for x in &mut v`

`v.into_iter()``T`consumed (moved)`for x in v`

A `for` loop calls `into_iter()` on whatever you give it, which is why `for x in v` consumes `v` while `for x in &v` only borrows it. `iterators.rs` shows all three.

## 7. Adapters are lazy, consumers pull

Adapters take an iterator and return a new one: `map`, `filter`, `take(n)`, `skip(n)`, `take_while`, `zip`, `enumerate`, `rev`, `step_by`, `copied`/`cloned`. Building one runs no closure. Consumers call `next` until they are done: `collect`, `sum`, `count`, `fold`, `any`, `position`, and a `for` loop.

iterator-pipeline.png: requests travel right to left, items left to right, one at a time.

An adapter chain with no consumer does nothing, and the compiler warns you:

```
warning: unused `Map` that must be used
  |     v.iter().map(|s| s * 2);
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  = note: iterators are lazy and do nothing unless consumed
```

When the consumer asks for an item, the request travels back through the chain to the source, and the item comes forward through every stage before the next item is fetched. A `filter` keeps asking for items until one passes. A `take(n)` stops asking once it has handed out `n` items, so the stages before it never see the rest.

`zip` pairs two iterators. It asks the left one first and stops as soon as the left one returns `None` (this order is documented). `skip(n)` drops the first `n` items of the iterator it is called on, and only that one.

`sum` and `collect` can produce several types, so the result type must be written somewhere: `let total: i32 = v.iter().sum();` or `.collect::<Vec<_>>()`.

## 8. What `collect` can build

ItemsTarget typeResult

`T``Vec<T>`a vector

`(K, V)``HashMap<K, V>`a map from pairs

`char``String`a string

`Result<T, E>``Result<Vec<T>, E>``Ok(vec)`, or the first `Err` (stops there)

You cannot collect owned values from references: `v.iter()` yields `&String`, so `.collect::<Vec<String>>()` fails with E0277 ("cannot be built from an iterator over elements of type `&String`"). Either collect references (`Vec<&String>`), copy them (`.cloned()`, or `.copied()` for `Copy` types), or start from `into_iter()` to get owned items.

## 9. Writing your own iterator

Put the state in a struct and implement `next`. Every adapter and consumer then works on it for free:

```
struct Countdown { left: u32 }

impl Iterator for Countdown {
    type Item = u32;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u32> {
        if self.left == 0 {
            None
        } else {
            self.left -= 1;
            Some(self.left + 1)
        }
    }
}
let ticks: Vec<u32> = Countdown { left: 3 }.collect();   // [3, 2, 1]
```

Iterator chains are not slower than loops in an optimised (`--release`) build: the compiler inlines the closures and produces the same machine code as a hand-written loop. Debug builds, which the runner uses, are slower for both.

# capture-and-traits.png

Left, three boxes: "body only reads a capture (captured as &T)", "body changes a capture (captured as &mut T)", "body moves a capture out (captured as T)".
Right, three nested rounded sets: the outer set "FnOnce: can be called at least once" contains "FnMut: can be called many times", which contains "Fn: many times, even shared", with the note "every Fn is also FnMut and FnOnce; every FnMut is also FnOnce".
Arrows: reads goes to Fn, changes goes to FnMut, moves out goes to FnOnce.
Footer: `move` changes HOW captures are stored (owned instead of borrowed), not WHICH trait you get: a `move` closure that only reads is still Fn.

[entity 867 · iterator-pipeline.png · diagram]
# iterator-pipeline.png

Five boxes left to right: `iter()`, `filter(..)`, `map(..)`, `take(2)`, `collect()`.
Dark arrows above point right to left, labelled "next()?" (requests travel right to left). Green arrows below point left to right: "Some(item) travels left to right, one item at a time".
Numbered notes:
1. Adapters (filter, map, take, zip, skip, enumerate, rev) only build a value. Nothing runs yet.
2. A consumer (collect, sum, fold, count, any, a for loop) calls next() and work starts.
3. One item passes the whole chain before the next item is fetched.
4. filter keeps asking the stage before it until an item passes (or None).
5. When take has handed out its count, it stops asking: earlier stages never see the rest.

where

pub struct Fib {
    a: u64,
    b: u64,
}

impl Fib {
    pub fn new() -> Fib {
        Fib { a: 0, b: 1 }
    }
}

impl Iterator for Fib {
    type Item = u64;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u64> {
        let out = self.a;
        self.a = self.b;
        self.b += out;
        Some(out)
    }
}

pub fn first_fib(n: usize) -> Vec<u64> {
    Fib::new().take(n).collect()
}

pub fn even_fib_sum_below(limit: u64) -> u64 {
    Fib::new().take_while(|&x| x < limit).filter(|x| x % 2 == 0).sum()
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn next_by_hand() {
        let mut f = Fib::new();
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(0));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(1));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(1));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(2));
    }

    #[test]
    fn first_few() {
        assert_eq!(first_fib(7), vec![0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8]);
        assert!(first_fib(0).is_empty());
    }

    #[test]
    fn even_sum() {
        assert_eq!(even_fib_sum_below(10), 10); // 0 + 2 + 8
        assert_eq!(even_fib_sum_below(100), 44); // + 34
    }
}

pub fn apply_n(f: impl Fn(i32) -> i32, n: usize, x: i32) -> i32 {

## 1. Closures

Adapted from The Rust Programming Language, ch 13.1-13.2, and Rust by Example (Closures, Capturing, As input parameters, Iterators), MIT/Apache-2.0.

A closure is a function you write inline, without a name, that can use the variables around it:

```
let limit = 10;
let over = |x: i32| x > limit;     // reads `limit` from the surrounding scope
println!("{}", over(12));          // true
let add_one = |x| x + 1;           // parameter and return types inferred
```

- Parameters go between bars: `|x|`, `|a, b|`, or `||` for none. The body is one expression or a `{ ... }` block.

- Types are usually inferred. They are fixed by the first use: after `add_one(5)`, calling `add_one(2.5)` is a type error.

- A `fn` item cannot read local variables of the function around it; a closure can. That is the whole point.

Parameters are patterns. Iterator methods often hand a closure a reference. A pattern can unpack it:

```
let temps = [18, 23, 31];
// iter() yields &i32; filter passes a reference to that, so its closure gets &&i32.
let warm: Vec<&i32> = temps.iter().filter(|&&t| t > 20).collect();  // t: i32
let doubled: Vec<i32> = temps.iter().map(|&t| t * 2).collect();       // t: i32
let hot: Vec<usize> = temps.iter().enumerate()
    .filter(|(_, t)| **t > 25).map(|(i, _)| i).collect();              // tuples too
```

## 2. How a closure captures

A closure captures each outside variable it uses in the weakest way its body needs:

Body doesCaptured asWhile the closure is alive

reads the variableshared borrow `&T`others may read it too

changes itmutable borrow `&mut T`nobody else may use it

moves it out (gives it away, drops it)by value `T`it now belongs to the closure

The borrow rules from 03 apply to these captures. A closure that holds `&mut count` blocks every other use of `count` until the closure's last use:

```
let mut count = 0;
let mut bump = || count += 1;   // captures &mut count
bump();
println!("{count}");            // error: bump is used again below
bump();
```

```
error[E0502]: cannot borrow `count` as immutable because it is also borrowed as mutable
  |     let mut bump = || count += 1;
  |                    -- ----- first borrow occurs due to use of `count` in closure
  |                    |
  |                    mutable borrow occurs here
  |     println!("{count}");
  |                ^^^^^ immutable borrow occurs here
  |     bump();
  |     ---- mutable borrow later used here
```

Move the `println!` after the last `bump()` and it compiles: the borrow ends when the closure is last used.

Fields, not whole structs. Since edition 2021, a closure that uses `stats.hits` captures only that field. Other fields of `stats` stay free to use while the closure is alive. (Older editions captured the whole struct.) Part 4 of `capture.rs` shows it.

## 3. `move`

Writing `move` before the bars makes the closure take ownership of every variable it uses, even ones it only reads:

```
let label = String::from("total");
let owned = move || println!("owned: {label}");
owned();
// println!("{label}");  // error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `label`
```

You need `move` when the closure must outlive the variables it uses: a closure returned from a function (section 5), or one sent to another thread (18).

With a `Copy` value (integers, `bool`, `char`, `f64`), `move` copies it into the closure. The closure then works on its own copy, and the outside variable never sees the changes:

```
let mut fuel = 50.0;
let mut burn = move || { fuel -= 10.0; fuel };   // burn owns a copy of fuel
println!("{} {}", burn(), burn());              // 40 30
println!("{fuel}");                             // 50: the outer fuel was never touched
```

## 4. Fn, FnMut and FnOnce

Every closure implements one or more of three traits. Which ones depends on what the body does with its captures, not on whether you wrote `move`:

TraitThe body...Can be called

`Fn`only reads its capturesany number of times, even through a shared reference

`FnMut`changes a capturemany times, but each call needs exclusive (`&mut`) access to the closure

`FnOnce`moves a capture outonce: the first call uses the captured value up

capture-and-traits.png: what the body does picks the trait; Fn sits inside FnMut, inside FnOnce.

The traits nest: every `Fn` closure is also `FnMut` and `FnOnce`, and every `FnMut` is also `FnOnce`. So a function that asks for `FnOnce` accepts anything; one that asks for `Fn` accepts only closures that do not mutate or move out.

A `move` closure that only reads a `String` is still `Fn`: it owns the string, but calling it does not use the string up. `move` changes how captures are stored, not which trait you get.

## 5. Closures as parameters and return values

Take a closure with `impl Fn...` or a generic bound, exactly like any other trait (09):

```
fn call_twice<F: Fn() -> usize>(f: F) -> usize {
    f() + f()
}
fn call_twice_mut<F: FnMut()>(mut f: F) {   // note `mut f`
    f();
    f();
}
fn call_once<F: FnOnce() -> String>(f: F) -> String {
    f()                                    // f is used up here
}
```

Calling an `FnMut` needs `&mut` access to the closure value (its captured state changes), so the parameter or variable that holds it must be declared `mut`. Calling an `FnOnce` consumes it, so it can be called only once in the function body.

Std examples: `Option::unwrap_or_else` takes an `FnOnce` (called at most once); `sort_by_key` takes an `FnMut` (called many times, may count or record).

### Returning a closure

```
fn make_adder(step: i32) -> impl Fn(i32) -> i32 {
    let base = step * 10;
    move |x| x + base + step
}
```

The returned closure is called after `make_adder` has returned, when `base` and `step` no longer exist. Without `move` it would borrow them:

```
error[E0373]: closure may outlive the current function, but it borrows `base`, which is owned by the current function
  |     |x| x + base + step
  |     ^^^     ---- `base` is borrowed here
  |     |
  |     may outlive borrowed value `base`
note: closure is returned here
```

The return type must name the right trait too: a closure whose body changes its captures is `FnMut`, so the function must say `-> impl FnMut(...)`, and the caller must store it in a `let mut` binding to call it.

## 6. The Iterator trait and the three ways to iterate

An iterator is any value that implements one required method:

```
trait Iterator {
    type Item;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item>;   // Some(item), or None when done
    // ...plus dozens of provided methods (map, filter, sum, ...)
}
```

A collection gives you three iterators, which differ in the item type:

CallItem type for a `Vec<T>`The Vec afterwardsSame as

`v.iter()``&T`untouched`for x in &v`

`v.iter_mut()``&mut T`changed in place`for x in &mut v`

`v.into_iter()``T`consumed (moved)`for x in v`

A `for` loop calls `into_iter()` on whatever you give it, which is why `for x in v` consumes `v` while `for x in &v` only borrows it. `iterators.rs` shows all three.

## 7. Adapters are lazy, consumers pull

Adapters take an iterator and return a new one: `map`, `filter`, `take(n)`, `skip(n)`, `take_while`, `zip`, `enumerate`, `rev`, `step_by`, `copied`/`cloned`. Building one runs no closure. Consumers call `next` until they are done: `collect`, `sum`, `count`, `fold`, `any`, `position`, and a `for` loop.

iterator-pipeline.png: requests travel right to left, items left to right, one at a time.

An adapter chain with no consumer does nothing, and the compiler warns you:

```
warning: unused `Map` that must be used
  |     v.iter().map(|s| s * 2);
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  = note: iterators are lazy and do nothing unless consumed
```

When the consumer asks for an item, the request travels back through the chain to the source, and the item comes forward through every stage before the next item is fetched. A `filter` keeps asking for items until one passes. A `take(n)` stops asking once it has handed out `n` items, so the stages before it never see the rest.

`zip` pairs two iterators. It asks the left one first and stops as soon as the left one returns `None` (this order is documented). `skip(n)` drops the first `n` items of the iterator it is called on, and only that one.

`sum` and `collect` can produce several types, so the result type must be written somewhere: `let total: i32 = v.iter().sum();` or `.collect::<Vec<_>>()`.

## 8. What `collect` can build

ItemsTarget typeResult

`T``Vec<T>`a vector

`(K, V)``HashMap<K, V>`a map from pairs

`char``String`a string

`Result<T, E>``Result<Vec<T>, E>``Ok(vec)`, or the first `Err` (stops there)

You cannot collect owned values from references: `v.iter()` yields `&String`, so `.collect::<Vec<String>>()` fails with E0277 ("cannot be built from an iterator over elements of type `&String`"). Either collect references (`Vec<&String>`), copy them (`.cloned()`, or `.copied()` for `Copy` types), or start from `into_iter()` to get owned items.

## 9. Writing your own iterator

Put the state in a struct and implement `next`. Every adapter and consumer then works on it for free:

```
struct Countdown { left: u32 }

impl Iterator for Countdown {
    type Item = u32;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u32> {
        if self.left == 0 {
            None
        } else {
            self.left -= 1;
            Some(self.left + 1)
        }
    }
}
let ticks: Vec<u32> = Countdown { left: 3 }.collect();   // [3, 2, 1]
```

Iterator chains are not slower than loops in an optimised (`--release`) build: the compiler inlines the closures and produces the same machine code as a hand-written loop. Debug builds, which the runner uses, are slower for both.

# capture-and-traits.png

Left, three boxes: "body only reads a capture (captured as &T)", "body changes a capture (captured as &mut T)", "body moves a capture out (captured as T)".
Right, three nested rounded sets: the outer set "FnOnce: can be called at least once" contains "FnMut: can be called many times", which contains "Fn: many times, even shared", with the note "every Fn is also FnMut and FnOnce; every FnMut is also FnOnce".
Arrows: reads goes to Fn, changes goes to FnMut, moves out goes to FnOnce.
Footer: `move` changes HOW captures are stored (owned instead of borrowed), not WHICH trait you get: a `move` closure that only reads is still Fn.

[entity 867 · iterator-pipeline.png · diagram]
# iterator-pipeline.png

Five boxes left to right: `iter()`, `filter(..)`, `map(..)`, `take(2)`, `collect()`.
Dark arrows above point right to left, labelled "next()?" (requests travel right to left). Green arrows below point left to right: "Some(item) travels left to right, one item at a time".
Numbered notes:
1. Adapters (filter, map, take, zip, skip, enumerate, rev) only build a value. Nothing runs yet.
2. A consumer (collect, sum, fold, count, any, a for loop) calls next() and work starts.
3. One item passes the whole chain before the next item is fetched.
4. filter keeps asking the stage before it until an item passes (or None).
5. When take has handed out its count, it stops asking: earlier stages never see the rest.

// Reference solution for exercise 3 (Tutor only; never shown to the learner).
pub struct Fib {
    a: u64,
    b: u64,
}

impl Fib {
    pub fn new() -> Fib {
        Fib { a: 0, b: 1 }
    }
}

impl Iterator for Fib {
    type Item = u64;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u64> {
        let out = self.a;
        self.a = self.b;
        self.b += out;
        Some(out)
    }
}

pub fn first_fib(n: usize) -> Vec<u64> {
    Fib::new().take(n).collect()
}

pub fn even_fib_sum_below(limit: u64) -> u64 {
    Fib::new().take_while(|&x| x < limit).filter(|x| x % 2 == 0).sum()
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn next_by_hand() {
        let mut f = Fib::new();
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(0));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(1));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(1));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(2));
    }

    #[test]
    fn first_few() {
        assert_eq!(first_fib(7), vec![0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8]);
        assert!(first_fib(0).is_empty());
    }

    #[test]
    fn even_sum() {
        assert_eq!(even_fib_sum_below(10), 10); // 0 + 2 + 8
        assert_eq!(even_fib_sum_below(100), 44); // + 34
    }
}

messages.content:
The bad words are coming from stale CPU cache lines in the readout path, not from the FPGA generating the wrong samples.

What’s happening is that the DMA engine is writing frame buffers into normal cached memory, but the highlighted completion/read path is reusing or exposing those buffers without a proper cache management step on the non-coherent arm64 port. So the checker sometimes sees:
- zeros from cache lines that were never invalidated and still look like empty/old data,
- and words from older frames because the CPU is reading an old cacheline copy of that same buffer slot.

The highlighted path is the completion path in the driver, and that’s exactly where the buffer is handed from DMA ownership back to the CPU/read pool. In this repo, that would be around `capture_dma.c` on the frame-complete/IRQ-thread side, and then `capture_cdev.c` when the frame is queued for `read()`. The root issue is that the path that completes a DMA buffer needs to make the buffer visible to the CPU on a non-coherent system; the board description even says the fabric-to-DDR path is not cache-coherent.

So: wrong words come from cache incoherency on the buffer data path, and the highlighted completion path is the handoff point where the driver should be invalidating or otherwise syncing the DMA buffer before user space reads it. The relevant files are `capture_dma.c` and `capture_cdev.c`, with the platform description in `README.md` explaining the non-coherent DMA setup.

messages.content:
The buffers are allocated in the DMA path as coherent DMA memory, not as normal cached kmalloc pages. In `capture_dma.c`, each capture buffer is set up with a call like `dma_alloc_coherent(dev, CAP_FRAME_BYTES, &buf->dma, GFP_KERNEL)` for the 64 KiB payload area, and the descriptor ring itself is allocated the same way with `dma_alloc_coherent(dev, CAP_RING_BYTES, &cap->ring_dma, GFP_KERNEL)`. So the DMA engine and CPU are both looking at the same physically backed memory, with the DMA API doing the mapping.

On the checker output: the bad runs are exactly one full frame long, i.e. 16,384 words each. They start at word 0 of each frame, and the age pattern stepping through 8, 16, 24, ... tells you the checker is seeing a buffer-slot reuse pattern across an 8-deep ring, not random corruption. In other words, frame data from the previous use of that slot is being observed again whenever that slot comes back around, which matches an 8-buffer queue (`CAP_NUM_BUFS` is 8).

The reason the first frames are zeros instead of old data is that the first pass through the ring is reading buffers that were handed to DMA before any valid frame had ever been written into them, so their contents are just the initial zeroed state from the allocator. After the ring wraps, you then start seeing old frame contents from earlier cycles because those slots have been reused without the CPU-side consumer seeing a fresh, coherent copy.

So the numbers point pretty directly at the ring size and wraparound behavior in `capture.h` (`CAP_NUM_BUFS 8`, `CAP_FRAME_BYTES 64*1024`) and the allocation/mapping calls in `capture_dma.c`.

messages.content: The buffers are allocated in the like DMA path as coherent DMA memory, not as normal cached kmalloc pages. basically In `capture_dma.c`, each capture buffer is set up with a call like `dma_alloc_coherent(dev, CAP_FRAME_BYTES, &buf->dma, GFP_KERNEL)` for the 64 KiB payload area, and the descriptor ring itself is allocated the same so yeah way with `dma_alloc_coherent(dev, CAP_RING_BYTES, &cap->ring_dma, GFP_KERNEL)`. So the DMA engine and CPU are both looking at the same physically backed memory, with the DMA API doing the mapping. On um the checker output: the bad basically runs are exactly one full frame long, i.e. 16,384 words each. They start at word 0 of each frame, and the age pattern stepping through um 8, 16, 24, ... tells you the checker is seeing a so yeah buffer-slot reuse pattern across an 8-deep ring, not random corruption. In other words, frame data from like um the previous use of that slot is so yeah being observed again whenever that slot comes back around, which matches basically an 8-buffer queue (`CAP_NUM_BUFS` is 8). The reason the first frames are zeros instead of old data is that the first pass through the ring so yeah is reading buffers that were handed to DMA before any valid frame had ever been written into them, so their contents are uh uh just the initial zeroed state from the allocator. After the ring wraps, you then start seeing old frame contents from earlier so yeah cycles because those slots have been reused without the CPU-side consumer seeing like so yeah basically a fresh, coherent copy. So the numbers point pretty uh directly at the ring size and wraparound behavior in `capture.h` (`CAP_NUM_BUFS 8`, `CAP_FRAME_BYTES 64*1024`) actually and the allocation/mapping calls in `capture_dma.c`.

messages.content:
You’re right — I mixed up the descriptor ring with the frame buffers.

In `cap_alloc_buffers()` the coherent allocation is only for the descriptor ring, not the capture payloads. The per-frame buffer `b` is allocated with a normal kernel allocation inside the loop, and then its `b->data` is handed to the DMA engine with the DMA API in the *device-to-memory* direction — i.e. the call is the `dma_map_single(..., DMA_FROM_DEVICE)`-style handoff, not coherent memory. That means the block is writing into a cacheable CPU buffer.

So the bad words are coming from the CPU reading `b->data` after DMA completion without the cache line being invalidated for the non-coherent ARM64 path. The highlighted completion path is the handoff from IRQ completion to the read pool: after `FRAME_DONE`, the driver queues the buffer, and later `cap_pool_push()` does a `memcpy` from `b->data` into the pool record. If that buffer is still dirty/valid in CPU cache, `memcpy` will pick up stale lines instead of the DMA-written bytes.

The checker totals make that much clearer: the “runs” are not whole frames at all, they’re short spans in the stream, mostly 16 words long with a smaller number of 8-word runs. The starts at `0, 8, 24, 40, 56` show the corruption is aligned on 8-word cache-line boundaries, with the first line at 0 being zero because that line was never populated in cache before the first DMA write, so the CPU just reads the allocator’s initial zero-fill/clean cache state. After that, the later 8-word/16-word patterns are old cached lines from earlier frame buffers being reused in those slots.

So the buffer’s life between `FRAME_DONE` and the `memcpy` is: DMA completes into `b->data`, the driver marks/queues the buffer, but on this non-coherent system the CPU-side cache view is not invalidated before `cap_pool_push()` copies it, so user space sees a mix of zeros and stale prior-frame cache lines. The relevant files are `capture_dma.c` for `cap_alloc_buffers()` / completion, and `capture_cdev.c` for `cap_pool_push()`.

move_object.note: Do they read the literal direction token in dma_map_single and connect 16 words = 64 bytes plus buffer 0 at 0x7eea0020 (data[] 32 bytes into struct cap_buf) to runs starting at word 8? Then ask the DMA_TO_DEVICE for_cpu sync follow-up, or probe to fix1.
move_object.response: Closer, but two things are still off. Read the literal third argument of that dma_map_single() call again and tell me the token that is actually in the file, because it is not the one you just said, and that matters for what any sync would do. Second, do the arithmetic: the board has 64-byte lines, so how many 32-bit words is one line, and given that, why would a run start at word 8 rather than word 0 or 16? messages.content:
You’re right — I misstated the DMA direction.

The literal third argument in the `dma_map_single()` call is `DMA_TO_DEVICE`, not `DMA_FROM_DEVICE`. That matters because if the buffer is being mapped as TO_DEVICE, the CPU-side cache maintenance will be the wrong way around for a block that is actually writing into the buffer. So the driver is effectively telling the DMA API “I’m going to read this” while the FPGA is filling it.

On the cache-line arithmetic: with 64-byte lines and 32-bit words, one cache line is 16 words. So a run starting at word 8 is a half-line offset, not a whole-line boundary. That fits the `struct cap_buf` layout: `b->data` is not necessarily line-aligned because there are fields before it (`ts_ns`, `dma`, `seq`, `bytes`, `slot`, `flags`). So buffer 0’s payload can begin 8 words into a cache line, which is why the checker sees a run starting at 8 rather than 0 or 16. The dmesg mention of buffer 0 lines up with that first buffer’s `b->data` address being offset from a cache-line boundary.

So the concrete story is: `cap_alloc_buffers()` allocates each `b` normally, maps `b->data` with `dma_map_single(..., DMA_TO_DEVICE)`, and later `cap_pool_push()` memcpy’s from `b->data` after `FRAME_DONE`. Because the direction token is wrong for a device-written buffer, the CPU cache isn’t being invalidated in the way the hardware needs, and the checker’s 8-word/16-word run starts reflect cache-line aliasing and the `cap_buf` header layout rather than whole-frame corruption.

I’d look hardest at `cap_alloc_buffers()` because the patch is only half-fixing the ownership model there. If they changed the map/unmap direction to `DMA_FROM_DEVICE` and then added explicit syncs in `cap_complete()` and `cap_queue_buf()`, the remaining 8-word runs at words 0–7 strongly suggest the first cache line of each buffer is still being touched with the wrong lifetime. In other words, the data path is probably now syncing the payload, but the small header area at the front of `struct cap_buf` — especially `ts_ns`, `seq`, `bytes`, `slot`, `flags` — is still getting copied or reused in a way that leaves the first 64-byte line stale or overwritten by CPU-side metadata.

So the failure is likely still in `cap_alloc_buffers()` where `b->data` is handed off with `dma_map_single(...)`, but the buffer object itself is being allocated and initialized on the CPU side, and then later reused in `cap_queue_buf()` / `cap_complete()` without a clean, consistent sync boundary for the whole object. The fact that every surviving bad run is exactly 8 words long means it’s now confined to half a cache line, which points to the leading words of the payload being adjacent to the `struct cap_buf` header or to a partial-line sync on the buffer head. I’d check whether the DMA sync calls are operating on `b->data` with the full `CAP_FRAME_BYTES`, and whether any code is copying from `b->data` before the device has fully released ownership back to the CPU.

1. **Unmapped DMA mapping still active** — `cap_alloc_buffers()` maps the buffer, but the teardown path isn’t unmapping every buffer before freeing it. Fix: in remove/stop, iterate all buffers and call `dma_unmap_single()` with the same address/length/direction used for map.

2. **Sync on an invalid or already-unmapped mapping** — if `cap_complete()` or `cap_queue_buf()` calls `dma_sync_single_for_cpu()` / `for_device()` after teardown has already started, DMA-API-debug will complain. Fix: guard the completion path with a device-stopped flag and make sure interrupts are disabled and flushed before buffers are unmapped.

3. **Double map / double unmap or direction mismatch** — if the patch switched directions but left one side of the queueing logic still using the old direction or mapping the same buffer twice, debug will warn about inconsistent API usage. Fix: ensure each buffer is mapped exactly once, synced while live, and unmapped exactly once, with the same direction token everywhere.

So I’d say the patch is still failing because the ownership transition is not clean in `cap_alloc_buffers()`/`cap_queue_buf()`/`cap_complete()`, and the warnings are probably about missing unmap, sync-after-unmap, and direction/lifetime mismatch in the DMA API usage.

WHAT A COMPLETE ANSWER TO THE STAGE ABOVE LOOKS LIKE:
With fix1, 25,521 of 100,000 frames (25.5%) still fail, and in each one only words 0 to 7 are wrong: one 8-word run, from an older frame of the same buffer (ages 8, 16, ...) or zero in the first frames. Words 0 to 7 are the 32 bytes of data[] that sit in the first 64-byte cache line with the 32-byte header of struct cap_buf (ts_ns, dma, seq, bytes, slot, flags): buffer 0 is at 0x7e140020. cap_complete() writes b->seq, b->bytes, b->ts_ns and b->flags before dma_sync_single_for_cpu(). If that line is still in the cache from the last round, the writes make it dirty while it still holds the old samples 0 to 7. arm64's invalidate (dcache_inval_poc) must not lose CPU data in a partial first line, so it cleans and invalidates it (dc civac): the old samples are written back over the ones the block just wrote, and the memcpy reads them. That happens only when the line survived in the L2, so about a quarter of the frames. Moving the sync above the field writes would cure this run but stays fragile: the line is shared, and any CPU write to it while the block owns the buffer can be lost or can overwrite DMA data (dma-api-howto: no cache-line sharing with a DMA_FROM_DEVICE buffer). Fix: keep the metadata out of the DMA buffer (struct cap_buf with a pointer to a separate 64 KiB buffer from kmalloc, page-aligned here, or dma_alloc_noncoherent()), or align data[] to ARCH_DMA_MINALIGN. The warnings: 'device driver failed to check map error', mapped at cap_alloc_buffers: dma_mapping_error() is never called, so a failed map would be programmed into a descriptor; check it and unwind. 'fclk0 already disabled' and 'already unprepared' come from devm_clk_release(): the clock came from devm_clk_get_enabled() and cap_remove() disables it too; drop that call. The same remove() frees buffers while the devm IRQ is still live.

NEVER say any of these, in any wording::
  - never synced for the CPU
  - multiples of CAP_NUM_BUFS
  - returns early
  - dc civac
  - keep the metadata out
  - never called

You may point at where to look. You may not name the mechanism or the fix. If your sentence would let them answer without thinking, rewrite it.

I’d look hardest at `cap_alloc_buffers()` because the patch is only half-fixing the ownership model there. If they changed the map/unmap direction to `DMA_FROM_DEVICE` and then added explicit syncs in `cap_complete()` and `cap_queue_buf()`, the remaining 8-word runs at words 0–7 strongly suggest the first cache line of each buffer is still being touched with the wrong lifetime. In other words, the data path is probably now syncing the payload, but the small header area at the front of `struct cap_buf` — especially `ts_ns`, `seq`, `bytes`, `slot`, `flags` — is still getting copied or reused in a way that leaves the first 64-byte line stale or overwritten by CPU-side metadata.

So the failure is likely still in `cap_alloc_buffers()` where `b->data` is handed off with `dma_map_single(...)`, but the buffer object itself is being allocated and initialized on the CPU side, and then later reused in `cap_queue_buf()` / `cap_complete()` without a clean, consistent sync boundary for the whole object. The fact that every surviving bad run is exactly 8 words long means it’s now confined to half a cache line, which points to the leading words of the payload being adjacent to the `struct cap_buf` header or to a partial-line sync on the buffer head. I’d check whether the DMA sync calls are operating on `b->data` with the full `CAP_FRAME_BYTES`, and whether any code is copying from `b->data` before the device has fully released ownership back to the CPU.

As for the three DMA API debug warnings on `rmmod`, I’d expect them to be the usual lifecycle issues:

1. **Unmapped DMA mapping still active** — `cap_alloc_buffers()` maps the buffer, but the teardown path isn’t unmapping every buffer before freeing it. Fix: in remove/stop, iterate all buffers and call `dma_unmap_single()` with the same address/length/direction used for map.

2. **Sync on an invalid or already-unmapped mapping** — if `cap_complete()` or `cap_queue_buf()` calls `dma_sync_single_for_cpu()` / `for_device()` after teardown has already started, DMA-API-debug will complain. Fix: guard the completion path with a device-stopped flag and make sure interrupts are disabled and flushed before buffers are unmapped.

3. **Double map / double unmap or direction mismatch** — if the patch switched directions but left one side of the queueing logic still using the old direction or mapping the same buffer twice, debug will warn about inconsistent API usage. Fix: ensure each buffer is mapped exactly once, synced while live, and unmapped exactly once, with the same direction token everywhere.

So I’d say the patch is still failing because the ownership transition is not clean in `cap_alloc_buffers()`/`cap_queue_buf()`/`cap_complete()`, and the warnings are probably about missing unmap, sync-after-unmap, and direction/lifetime mismatch in the DMA API usage.

  candidate: I’d look hardest at `cap_alloc_buffers()` because the patch is only half-fixing the ownership model there. If they changed the map/unmap direction to `DMA_FROM_DEVICE` and then added explicit syncs in `cap_complete()` and `cap_queue_buf()`, the remaining 8-word runs at words 0–7 strongly suggest the first cache line of each buffer is still being touched with the wrong lifetime. In other words, the data path is probably now syncing the payload, but the small header area at the front of `struct cap_buf` — especially `ts_ns`, `seq`, `bytes`, `slot`, `flags` — is still getting copied or reused in a way that leaves the first 64-byte line stale or overwritten by CPU-side metadata.

So the failure is likely still in `cap_alloc_buffers()` where `b->data` is handed off with `dma_map_single(...)`, but the buffer object itself is being allocated and initialized on the CPU side, and then later reused in `cap_queue_buf()` / `cap_complete()` without a clean, consistent sync boundary for the whole object. The fact that every surviving bad run is exactly 8 words long means it’s now confined to half a cache line, which points to the leading words of the payload being adjacent to the `struct cap_buf` header or to a partial-line sync on the buffer head. I’d check whether the DMA sync calls are operating on `b->data` with the full `CAP_FRAME_BYTES`, and whether any code is copying from `b->data` before the device has fully released ownership back to the CPU.

As for the three DMA API debug warnings on `rmmod`, I’d expect them to be the usual lifecycle issues:

1. **Unmapped DMA mapping still active** — `cap_alloc_buffers()` maps the buffer, but the teardown path isn’t unmapping every buffer before freeing it. Fix: in remove/stop, iterate all buffers and call `dma_unmap_single()` with the same address/length/direction used for map.

2. **Sync on an invalid or already-unmapped mapping** — if `cap_complete()` or `cap_queue_buf()` calls `dma_sync_single_for_cpu()` / `for_device()` after teardown has already started, DMA-API-debug will complain. Fix: guard the completion path with a device-stopped flag and make sure interrupts are disabled and flushed before buffers are unmapped.

3. **Double map / double unmap or direction mismatch** — if the patch switched directions but left one side of the queueing logic still using the old direction or mapping the same buffer twice, debug will warn about inconsistent API usage. Fix: ensure each buffer is mapped exactly once, synced while live, and unmapped exactly once, with the same direction token everywhere.

So I’d say the patch is still failing because the ownership transition is not clean in `cap_alloc_buffers()`/`cap_queue_buf()`/`cap_complete()`, and the warnings are probably about missing unmap, sync-after-unmap, and direction/lifetime mismatch in the DMA API usage.

If that line is still in the cache from the last round, the writes make it dirty while it still holds the old samples 0 to 7. arm64's invalidate (dcache_inval_poc) must not lose CPU data in a partial first line, so it cleans and invalidates it (dc civac): the old samples are written back over the ones the block just wrote, and the memcpy reads them. That happens only when the line survived in the L2, so about a quarter of the frames. Moving the sync above the field writes would cure this run but stays fragile: the line is shared, and any CPU write to it while the block owns the buffer can be lost or can overwrite DMA data (dma-api-howto: no cache-line sharing with a DMA_FROM_DEVICE buffer). WHAT A COMPLETE ANSWER TO THE STAGE ABOVE LOOKS LIKE:
capcheck finds no bad words but 7 gaps of one frame each, and dmesg has 7 'descriptor N not owned by the block' lines, each printing ctrl 0x80010000 (OWN set), status 0 and seq 0: when the driver looks, the descriptor is valid. The ILA shows why: 16 ns after the DESC_TAIL write (0x00022d44) the block reads descriptor 3 at 0x7f3c1030 and gets ctrl 0x00010000 and status 0x80010000 with seq 142654, the values the block itself wrote back when it finished that frame, not what cap_queue_buf() wrote. The block prefetches a descriptor as soon as DESC_TAIL moves (README), so the doorbell must not reach it before the descriptor stores reach DDR. cap_queue_buf() writes the descriptor into dma_alloc_coherent() memory, which is Normal non-cacheable on this non-coherent SoC, then rings the doorbell with writel_relaxed(): with no barrier, the store to Device memory can be seen before the earlier stores to normal memory, and with stress-ng loading DDR the descriptor stores had not reached DDR when the block's read did (its data came back 276 ns after the doorbell). The comment's reason (keep the doorbell cheap) is the wrong trade: this is the one write that needs ordering. The block aborts the frame in progress, so each error loses one frame; the restart in cap_desc_error() succeeds because it runs microseconds later, when the descriptor is long in DDR (and it uses writel()). Fix: writel(cd->queued, ...) in cap_queue_buf(). That sounds like the block is reading the descriptor ring before the CPU’s descriptor write has actually become visible on the DDR side. Since the analyzer only sees the block’s AXI ports, the sequence is: the driver writes the descriptor in `cap_queue_buf()`, then pokes `DESC_TAIL`, but the descriptor store hasn’t been pushed out of the CPU/cache/memory path yet. The block notices the new tail, fetches the descriptor immediately, and sees `ctrl = 0x00010000` — meaning the OWN bit is missing — instead of the intended `0x80010000`. That turns into a descriptor error.

The line causing it is the `writel()` (or equivalent doorbell write) to `DESC_TAIL` in `cap_queue_buf()`, because it is happening before the CPU has fully ordered and flushed the descriptor contents to memory. On this non-coherent path, the fix is to make the descriptor write visible before the tail write: write the descriptor fields, do the required DMA sync / wmb() for the ring entry, and only then ring the doorbell. In practice I’d add a proper `dma_wmb()` or `wmb()` plus whatever DMA sync is appropriate for the descriptor ring, right before the `writel()` that updates `DESC_TAIL`. If the ring is cached memory, I’d also make sure the descriptor itself is mapped and synced correctly, not just the payload buffers.

  candidate: That sounds like the block is reading the descriptor ring before the CPU’s descriptor write has actually become visible on the DDR side. The block notices the new tail, fetches the descriptor immediately, and sees `ctrl = 0x00010000` — meaning the OWN bit is missing — instead of the intended `0x80010000`. That turns into a descriptor error.

The line causing it is the `writel()` (or equivalent doorbell write) to `DESC_TAIL` in `cap_queue_buf()`, because it is happening before the CPU has fully ordered and flushed the descriptor contents to memory. On this non-coherent path, the fix is to make the descriptor write visible before the tail write: write the descriptor fields, do the required DMA sync / wmb() for the ring entry, and only then ring the doorbell. In practice I’d add a proper `dma_wmb()` or `wmb()` plus whatever DMA sync is appropriate for the descriptor ring, right before the `writel()` that updates `DESC_TAIL`. capcheck finds no bad words but 7 gaps of one frame each, and dmesg has 7 'descriptor N not owned by the block' lines, each printing ctrl 0x80010000 (OWN set), status 0 and seq 0: when the driver looks, the descriptor is valid. The ILA shows why: 16 ns after the DESC_TAIL write (0x00022d44) the block reads descriptor 3 at 0x7f3c1030 and gets ctrl 0x00010000 and status 0x80010000 with seq 142654, the values the block itself wrote back when it finished that frame, not what cap_queue_buf() wrote. The block prefetches a descriptor as soon as DESC_TAIL moves (README), so the doorbell must not reach it before the descriptor stores reach DDR. cap_queue_buf() writes the descriptor into dma_alloc_coherent() memory, which is Normal non-cacheable on this non-coherent SoC, then rings the doorbell with writel_relaxed(): with no barrier, the store to Device memory can be seen before the earlier stores to normal memory, and with stress-ng loading DDR the descriptor stores had not reached DDR when the block's read did (its data came back 276 ns after the doorbell). The comment's reason (keep the doorbell cheap) is the wrong trade: this is the one write that needs ordering. The block aborts the frame in progress, so each error loses one frame; the restart in cap_desc_error() succeeds because it runs microseconds later, when the descriptor is long in DDR (and it uses writel()). Fix: writel(cd->queued, ...) in cap_queue_buf(). On arm64 writel() is dma_wmb() (dmb oshst) then the store, which orders the descriptor stores before the doorbell; dma_wmb() followed by writel_relaxed() emits the same instructions on arm64, but memory-barriers.txt says the dma_*() barriers give no ordering against MMIO, so portable code uses writel() (or wmb() before writel_relaxed()); wmb() (dsb st) also works but costs more. device-io.rst asks for a comment that explains why a relaxed accessor is safe. 7 in 1,464,851 doorbells is about 1 in 209,000, rare enough to pass short tests.

NEVER say any of these, in any wording::
  - never synced for the CPU
  - multiples of CAP_NUM_BUFS
  - returns early
  - prefetches a descriptor
  - Normal non-cacheable
  - dmb oshst

You may point at where to look. You may not name the mechanism or the fix. If your sentence would let them answer without thinking, rewrite it.

The doorbell store in `cap_queue_buf()` is a plain MMIO accessor, `writel()`, not some special ordered variant beyond that.

And the ring memory is allocated as DMA-coherent memory, so a cache sync call on the ring itself is not the thing that applies there. That’s why this points more at ordering than cache maintenance for the descriptor ring: the payload buffers are one story, the ring is another.

The reason the driver’s own restart a few microseconds later works is basically timing. By then, the descriptor write has had time to drain out to DDR and the block’s prefetch sees the OWN bit correctly. So the failure is a race window right around the immediate `DESC_TAIL` write: the first launch can outrun the descriptor store, while the later restart doesn’t. I’d fix it by putting an explicit write barrier before the doorbell write in `cap_queue_buf()`, keeping the coherent ring allocation as-is.

capture: allocate the frame buffers with dma_alloc_coherent()

The streaming mapping keeps biting us: first stale cache lines everywhere,
then words 0 to 7 wrong in 26% of frames after fix1, and the
descriptor errors from the soak. Coherent memory removes the whole class:

- no cache lines to go stale, so no dma_sync_*() calls to get wrong;
- struct cap_buf no longer shares memory with the samples;
- the descriptor ring is already coherent, and with the buffers coherent
  too nothing the block reads sits in a cache, so the doorbell can stay

mean over 36,621 frames (60 s) each:

  memcpy() into the read pool       42.3 us           528.5 us
  cap_complete() total              60.2 us           532.5 us
  IRQ thread, % of one core          3.7 %             32.5 %

32.5% of one A53 at 610 frames/s is affordable, and the code is simpler.

The test cannot show it: 73,242 frames at about 1 error in 209,000 doorbells means about 0.35 errors expected, so 0 errors happens about 70% of the time even if nothing changed. Showing a real drop needs about 626,899 error-free frames (17.1 minutes) for 95% confidence, under the same stress-ng load; the 2-minute log shows no stress-ng at all, so even fewer errors were expected. What it costs: the memcpy out of uncached memory takes 528.5 us per frame, against 42.3 us from cacheable memory plus 13.9 us for the sync: 532.5 against 60.2 us, about 9 times, 32.5% of a core against 3.7%. At the planned 20 MS/s that is about 130% of a core, which cannot work, against about 15%. Any later processing of the buffer in place (mmap to user space, filtering in the driver) would also run on uncached memory. Instead: keep streaming DMA for the frames, with the metadata out of the buffer and a page-aligned buffer (kmalloc of 64 KiB, or dma_alloc_noncoherent()), DMA_FROM_DEVICE, sync for the CPU after DONE and for the device before requeue, and dma_mapping_error() checked; keep the small ring coherent; ring the doorbell with writel() (dma_wmb() then writel_relaxed() is the same on arm64 only). If the sync's cost ever matters, the SoC's coherent port with dma-coherent in the node is the hardware fix, once its bandwidth is measured. Then run long enough, under load, to show the error rate dropped.

NEVER say any of these, in any wording::
  - never synced for the CPU
  - multiples of CAP_NUM_BUFS
  - returns early
  - stores are ordered
  - about 0.35 errors
  - keep streaming DMA

You may point at where to look. You may not name the mechanism or the fix. If your sentence would let them answer without thinking, rewrite it.

If you take the soak result at face value — 7 descriptor errors in 1,464,851 doorbell writes — that’s about 4.8e-6 errors per doorbell, or roughly 1 error every 209,000 frames.

At that rate, a 73,242-frame run would “expect” only about 0.35 descriptor errors. So a result of 0 is not strong evidence that the race is gone; it’s completely compatible with the observed rate. It just means they didn’t happen to hit the window in that shorter run.

And making the buffers coherent does not help the doorbell because the doorbell is a separate MMIO ordering problem, not a buffer-coherency problem. The coherent frame buffers only affect how the FPGA and CPU share the sample payloads in DDR. The descriptor error happens earlier: the driver updates the descriptor in DDR and then writes DESC_TAIL, but the block can fetch the descriptor as soon as it sees the tail move. If the CPU store to the descriptor hasn’t been made visible yet, the block sees stale ctrl data. Coherency of the frame buffers does nothing to force ordering or visibility of the descriptor write before the tail write. That needs a barrier / publication fix in cap_queue_buf(), not coherent payload buffers.

move_object.question_summary: Covered a non-coherent arm64 capture driver end to end: stale cache lines, a shared first line after fix1, a doorbell ordering race, and a coherent-buffer patch to judge. move_object.report_notes:
Final stage (judge the dma_alloc_coherent patch) was the candidate's best work. Unprompted they refused the merge, correctly split what it fixes (payload cache staleness, the header no longer sharing memory with samples) from what it leaves untouched (the DESC_TAIL publication race), and flagged the roughly 9x regression, 532.5 against 60.2 us per frame, as disqualifying, with a plausible account of why: the memcpy now reads uncached memory. On the one push, they produced the arithmetic cleanly and without a hint: 7 in 1,464,851 is about 1 in 209,000 doorbells, so a 73,242-frame run expects well under one error and a 0 is fully consistent with no change at all. They also stated precisely why coherent payload buffers do not help the doorbell: the descriptor store and the tail write are a publication/visibility problem in cap_queue_buf, not a buffer coherency problem, and the ring was already coherent. Gaps at this stage: they did not ask how long a run would actually be needed for confidence, nor notice that the 2-minute log was taken without the stress-ng load that produced the errors, so they under-sold how weak the evidence is; their proposed alternative was correct in shape (keep the streaming mapping, metadata out of the buffer, correct direction and sync sides, fix the publication in cap_queue_buf, keep the small ring coherent) but still generic about the fix, a 'write barrier' rather than naming the relaxed accessor at the doorbell, consistent with the earlier stage where they asserted writel() where the code has writel_relaxed(). No consideration of the cost at the planned higher sample rate or of in-place consumers such as mmap.

Across the question: good systems instincts and a sound ownership model, and genuinely strong judgement about test evidence at the end. The recurring weakness is evidentiary discipline. On the opening they needed three rounds to name any call, and misread cap_alloc_buffers as coherent allocation before correcting to kzalloc plus dma_map_single(..., DMA_TO_DEVICE). On the fix1 stage they invented three generic DMA-API warnings rather than reading the supplied log, missed dma_mapping_error() and the devm_clk_get_enabled() double disable entirely, and declined to read the log when pointed at it. On the soak they got the mechanism right immediately but used none of the ILA numbers. Mid-level: capable of the right conclusion, often reached by reasoning from general principle rather than from the artefact in front of them, and needing substantial prompting to get concrete. Would want to see them work directly from logs and code before trusting them with an independent bring-up.

CREATE OR REPLACE PACKAGE BODY xxap_uninv_accr_pkg AS
-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- XX AP Uninvoiced Receipts Accrual (XXAP_UNINV_ACCR)
-- Month end: expense receipts delivered in the period and not yet invoiced,
-- written to XXAP_UNINV_ACCR_LINES for the accrual journal.
-- Run by the close team from XX Payables Close (all operating units).
-- v2.1  03-2024  : expense accounts only
-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

  PROCEDURE run (errbuf        OUT VARCHAR2,
                 retcode       OUT VARCHAR2,
                 p_period_name IN  VARCHAR2) IS

    CURSOR c_receipts (cp_start DATE, cp_end DATE) IS
      SELECT rt.transaction_id,
             rt.quantity,
             rt.po_unit_price,
             pd.code_combination_id,
             pd.org_id,
             ph.segment1  po_number,
             ph.vendor_id
        FROM rcv_transactions  rt,
             po_distributions  pd,
             po_headers        ph
       WHERE rt.transaction_type       = 'DELIVER'
         AND rt.transaction_date      >= cp_start
         AND rt.transaction_date       < cp_end + 1
         AND pd.po_distribution_id     = rt.po_distribution_id
         AND pd.accrue_on_receipt_flag = 'N'
         AND ph.po_header_id           = pd.po_header_id;

    l_start    DATE;
    l_end      DATE;
    l_billed   NUMBER;
    l_account  gl_code_combinations.segment3%TYPE;
    l_rows     PLS_INTEGER := 0;
    l_written  PLS_INTEGER := 0;
  BEGIN
    mo_global.init('PO');

    SELECT start_date, end_date
      INTO l_start, l_end
      FROM gl_periods
     WHERE period_set_name = 'XX_CALENDAR'
       AND period_name     = p_period_name;

    DELETE FROM xxap_uninv_accr_lines
     WHERE period_name = p_period_name;

    FOR r IN c_receipts (l_start, l_end) LOOP

      -- quantity already invoiced against this receipt
      SELECT NVL(SUM(aid.quantity_invoiced), 0)
        INTO l_billed
        FROM ap_invoice_distributions aid
       WHERE aid.rcv_transaction_id = r.transaction_id;

      -- natural account of the charge account
      SELECT gcc.segment3
        INTO l_account
        FROM gl_code_combinations gcc
       WHERE gcc.code_combination_id = r.code_combination_id;

      IF l_account BETWEEN '5000' AND '7999'          -- expense accounts only
         AND r.quantity > l_billed THEN
        INSERT INTO xxap_uninv_accr_lines
          (period_name, org_id, po_number, vendor_id, rcv_transaction_id,
           natural_account, code_combination_id, uninvoiced_qty, accrual_amount,
           created_by, creation_date)
        VALUES
          (p_period_name, r.org_id, r.po_number, r.vendor_id, r.transaction_id,
           l_account, r.code_combination_id, r.quantity - l_billed,
           ROUND((r.quantity - l_billed) * r.po_unit_price, 2),
           fnd_global.user_id, SYSDATE);
        l_written := l_written + 1;
      END IF;

      l_rows := l_rows + 1;
      IF MOD(l_rows, 500) = 0 THEN
        COMMIT;
      END IF;
    END LOOP;

    COMMIT;
    fnd_file.put_line(fnd_file.log, l_rows || ' receipt lines read, ' || l_written || ' accrual lines written');
    retcode := '0';
  EXCEPTION
    WHEN OTHERS THEN
      ROLLBACK;
      errbuf  := SQLERRM;
      retcode := '2';
  END run;

END xxap_uninv_accr_pkg;
/
