move_object.report_notes:
Three stages on one driver (boot splat, lockdep on st->lock, interrupt storm).

Stage 1 (boot splat): opened with the generic shape (a hard handler may not sleep, push work to a thread) but could not extract anything from the boot log, citing no line at all: no mutex.c:585, no preempt_count 10001, no irqs_disabled 128, no HARDIRQ-ON-W to IN-HARDIRQ-W on cfg_lock registered at qadc_probe. Only after being pointed at qadc_wdog_period did they name mutex_lock(&st->cfg_lock) and correctly explain why a sleeping lock is illegal there, then correctly walked qadc_hardirq to qadc_wdog_kick to qadc_wdog_period. Production behaviour stayed abstract: said it usually works because the path is short and the lock is usually free, but never explained why the contended case is fatal, never named qadc_reset_work holding cfg_lock across two I2C writes and usleep_range, and never tied it to the CPU0 detail. Fix direction was right but vague. Two substantial hints needed.

Stage 2 (lockdep on st->lock): again said they could not read the report and opened with a wrong guess (lock ordering between two locks). Once the lines were read to them they recovered well: one lock, hard handler taking it on the same CPU as a process-context holder, interrupted task cannot release, CPU wedged until the hardware watchdog reboots, correctly linked to the README note that the GPIO interrupt lands on CPU0 and to the field freezes. Missed that the reporting task was on CPU1 so lockdep flagged the pattern without an actual hang. Fix for latest_show was correct and concrete: spin_lock_irqsave over a snapshot, formatting outside the lock. The audit of the other call sites was weak even after a direct push: the timer callback was waved through as safe if it uses a spinlock and does not sleep, missing that it too can be interrupted on the same CPU and needs the irqsave variant, and they never looked at the second attribute, missing that it takes no lock at all over a 64-bit counter on a 32-bit CPU.

Stage 3 (interrupt storm): first answer again declined to read the files and offered only the shape, mentioning shared, level-triggered and a vague ONESHOT. I read out the numbers. Their second answer used them qualitatively but misread 5,002 and 4,002 as the expected 100 Hz rate, and did not compute 243,963 interrupts for 2,000 conversions, roughly 122 per conversion, nor interpret 82 and 162 entries per conversion as the line staying asserted through the ~300 us I2C read. After a direct push on the arithmetic and on the repeated identical CH0 to CH3 bytes, they corrected cleanly: 1,000 expected per ADC, so the extra samples are spurious; the thread is entered more than once per real conversion, reads stale data, and hands a sample to the core on every entry regardless of whether the device produced one. They proposed reading STATUS first, accepting data only when DRDY is set, and clearing the ready condition exactly once per conversion. They did not get to the return value consequence (always returning IRQ_HANDLED, and what IRQ_NONE would buy), did not explain the mask and unmask behaviour of a level line without the oneshot flag, did not spot the dummy primary handler that worked around the kernel's refusal, did not explain why a 0x49 conversion holds the line low twice as long, and did not note that every sharer must agree on the flag.

Overall: underlying model of execution contexts and of a shared level-triggered line is real and, once the data is in front of them in prose, they reason accurately and self-correct without defensiveness. The serious weakness in this interview was investigative: across all three stages they never once cited a line, number or filename unprompted, repeatedly stating they could not read the attachments, and each core reading had to be handed to them. Every stage needed at least two direct prompts. Grading what was demonstrated: solid conceptual mid-level knowledge, well below mid-level evidence gathering from logs, captures and source.
move_object.response: Good, that is the reading. The sample counts are the tell: about 1,000 real conversions per ADC in that window against 5,002 and 4,002 recorded, so most of what the core is being handed is not a new conversion at all, and the capture backs you up with the same CH0 to CH3 bytes coming back and reads landing after RDY has already gone high. Checking STATUS before accepting data, and letting what the thread hands back to the core reflect that check, is exactly the direction. I am going to stop the clock on this one here. One thing worth saying before we move on: the analysis you gave each time was sound once the numbers were in front of you, but in all three parts I had to read the log, the report and the capture out to you before anything specific came back. In this kind of work, the digging through the log and the trace is most of the job, so that is the part I would want to see you do unaided. Thanks for working through it, we will pick up with the next question.

If the request in qadc_probe is set up in a way that leaves the line asserted or retriggers on an already-low shared line, you can get repeated interrupts and CPU0 load.

The specific places I’d inspect are the request_threaded_irq() call in qadc_probe and the read in qadc_irq_thread(): if the driver is not fully clearing the device condition for every interrupt, the GPIO can keep re-firing. I’d change the IRQ setup to the correct shared/oneshot form and make sure the threaded handler fully drains the device state before returning.
  ai: Fine, I will read you the numbers. Line 63, gpio-mxc 17, Level, shared by 1-0048 and 1-0049, goes from 44,792,380 to 45,036,343 over the ten second window, all of it on CPU0. Both ADCs run at 100 Hz, and in that same window 1-0048 samples go up by 5,002 and 1-0049 by 4,002. On the capture, RDY sits low for 317 us in one case and 622 us in another, and the debug GPIO toggled at entry to the hard handler shows 82 entries in the first and 162 in the second, roughly one every 3.8 us the whole time RDY is low. So: what do those three sets of numbers each tell you, and which line in the request and which part of the thread body get you each one?

    the gap you named: No numbers used: no 243,963 interrupts per 10 s versus 2,000 conversions, no 82/162 handler entries per conversion, no duplicate-sample reading of the shared line and the thread's return value.
  candidate: Those numbers say the interrupt line is being serviced over and over while the physical RDY line is still low, so the GPIO interrupt is effectively retriggering in a storm instead of being handled once per conversion.

- The interrupt counter jump on CPU0 shows the line is firing far more often than the ADC sample rate would suggest.
- The fact that both ADC sample counts only rise by about 5,002 and 4,002 in 10 seconds says the conversions themselves are roughly in the expected range for 100 Hz, so the extra IRQs are not extra samples.
- The capture numbers — RDY low for 317 us / 622 us, with 82 / 162 hard-handler entries in that window — show the same low level is causing many interrupt entries before the handler gets the line cleared.

The specific cause is the threaded IRQ read path: in qadc_irq_thread() the driver reads only 8 bytes from QADC_REG_DATA, not the STATUS byte at 0x00 plus DATA. Per the README, RDY is released only when the read includes the last DATA byte and completes at STOP, but because the line is shared and level-low, the GPIO interrupt can immediately re-enter until the device finally deasserts the line.

The other contributing line is the request in qadc_probe(): the IRQ is requested as a shared level interrupt, so if the handler doesn’t fully clear the source on the first pass, the shared GPIO line remains asserted and keeps re-firing on CPU0.

What I would change:

1. In qadc_irq_thread(), read from QADC_REG_STATUS and fetch STATUS + DATA together, so the read path definitely clears DRDY every time.
2. Make sure the IRQ is requested with the proper ONESHOT semantics for a threaded shared level IRQ, so the line is masked until the thread finishes.
3. If needed, also verify the handler drains both ADCs’ pending ready state correctly, since they share the same GPIO line.

So the numbers are telling us: sample rate is fine, but IRQ rate is exploding because the level-low RDY source is not being fully cleared in the threaded handler, and CPU0 is paying for every retrigger.
  ai: Hold on one number there. You said the sample counts look about right for 100 Hz. Do that arithmetic out loud for me: ten seconds, 100 Hz, per ADC, versus the 5,002 and 4,002 that were actually recorded. And while you are at it, the capture lists the bytes of each transaction: several reads come back with exactly the same CH0 to CH3 values as the previous read of that same ADC, and some happen after RDY has already gone back high. Fair enough, here are the pieces. The patch deletes qadc_hardirq entirely: request_threaded_irq now passes NULL for the primary with IRQF_SHARED | IRQF_ONESHOT, the thread does the I2C read, takes the timestamp at its own start, and kicks the watchdog at the end. st->lock is converted from a spinlock to a mutex everywhere, including inside qadc_wdog_expired, which is still the timer callback. qadc_remove now does: cancel_work_sync(&st->reset_work); del_timer_sync(&st->wdog); then takes cfg_lock and calls qadc_hw_config(st, 0).

The log: interrupts are down to about 200 a second, stall_test says PASS for both ADCs, unbind_loop 50 of 50 no crash. But dmesg has a BUG: sleeping function called from invalid context at mutex.c:585, pid 0, swapper/1, preempt_count 101, trace going qadc_wdog_expired from call_timer_fn from run_timer_softirq from handle_softirqs, followed by a lockdep inconsistent {SOFTIRQ-ON-W} -> {IN-SOFTIRQ-W} on &st->lock. And after the unbind loop, four of these: ODEBUG: free active (active state 0) object type timer_list hint qadc_wdog_expired, from kfree, from devres_release_group, from i2c_device_remove under unbind_store.

So: sign off or not, and what are those two telling you?

messages.content:
I would not sign off on it as written.

The test results are encouraging, but the log is still showing two real problems:

1. `BUG: sleeping function called from invalid context ... qadc_wdog_expired ... run_timer_softirq`
   - That tells me `qadc_wdog_expired()` is now trying to take the mutex from timer/softirq context.
   - A mutex is not allowed there. So converting `st->lock` from spinlock to mutex everywhere is not safe because the timer callback still runs in softirq context.
   - That matches the lockdep report: `SOFTIRQ-ON-W -> IN-SOFTIRQ-W` on `&st->lock`.

2. `ODEBUG: free active (active state 0) object type timer_list ... qadc_wdog_expired ... from devres_release_group`
   - That says the timer object is being freed while it is still active or not fully torn down.
   - So `qadc_remove()` is not stopping the watchdog timer in a way that guarantees the callback cannot still run before the device-managed resources are released.

What I would write in `remove()` is to stop anything that can re-arm or race first, and to make sure the timer cannot fire again before teardown completes. In practice I would want the watchdog timer canceled before freeing anything it can touch, and I would not use a mutex in the timer path.

As for the work split:
- Hard handler: if you keep a hard handler at all, it should do only the minimal IRQ bookkeeping and wake the thread. But given the new `IRQF_ONESHOT | NULL` setup, I think removing the hard handler is fine.
- Thread: do the I2C read, timestamping, sample storage, and watchdog kick there.
- Timer callback: it must not take a mutex. It should only set state and schedule work, or otherwise use a spinlock/atomic path that is safe in softirq context.

So the patch looks closer, but I would reject it until the timer-side locking is fixed and the teardown path guarantees the watchdog timer cannot fire after remove starts.

move_object.response: Good, the softirq half is right. Stay on the ODEBUG for a moment, because it is sharper than it looks. remove() already called del_timer_sync on that timer, and that call does wait for the callback and leaves the timer inactive. Yet by the time devres frees the memory the object is active again. So who armed it in between? Walk me through what is still running at that point in an unbind, and while you are there tell me what the kernel would have done here if debug objects had not been compiled in.

messages.content:
I think the thing re-arming it is the work item started from the timer path. `del_timer_sync()` waits for `qadc_wdog_expired()` itself, but that callback calls `schedule_work(&st->reset_work)`, and the work can still run after `remove()` has returned from the timer cancel and moved on.

So in an unbind, the sequence is roughly:
- unbind starts, new IRQs are stopped by the core/device removal path
- `qadc_remove()` calls `cancel_work_sync(&st->reset_work)` and `del_timer_sync(&st->wdog)`
- the timer callback may already have run before `del_timer_sync()` returns, and it may have queued `reset_work`
- then the workqueue thread runs `qadc_reset_work()`, which calls `qadc_wdog_kick(st)` at the end and re-arms the timer
- after that, devres starts freeing the device-managed objects, but the timer has already been armed again, so debugobjects sees an active timer being freed

If debug objects were not compiled in, I think this would have turned into a silent use-after-free or a later crash instead of the explicit ODEBUG warning. The timer would still be armed against freed memory, so the next expiry could call back into freed state.

To fix it, I would make `remove()` stop and flush the reset work path in the right order so nothing can re-arm the watchdog after `del_timer_sync()`, or have the work path check a removed/shutting-down flag before kicking the timer.

move_object.response: The work path is one route, and you are right that cancelling the work before the timer leaves a window. But check the assumption you opened with: you said new IRQs are stopped by the core before qadc_remove() runs. Is that actually true for an interrupt that was requested with devm_request_threaded_irq? messages.content:
No, I don’t think that assumption is safe. With `devm_request_threaded_irq()`, the IRQ is not necessarily torn down before `qadc_remove()` runs; devres unwind happens after the driver’s remove callback returns. So while `remove()` is executing, the threaded IRQ for this device can still be running or be scheduled again.

Because the line is shared with the other ADC at 0x49, the thread can also be invoked by interrupts that are really for the other device, and it can still call `qadc_wdog_kick(st)` or otherwise touch this device’s timer/state while teardown is in progress.

So the timer getting re-armed in between `del_timer_sync()` and devres freeing the memory can come from the IRQ thread itself, not only from the reset work. That means `remove()` needs to mark the device as shutting down first, and the threaded IRQ path needs to check that flag before re-arming the watchdog or doing any work that survives past removal. I’d also want the IRQ disabled or freed explicitly before the final resource release, rather than relying on devm cleanup order alone.

Missed that the reporting task was on CPU1 so no actual hang occurred.

Stage 3 (storm): used 243,963 in 10 s and the 82/162 handler entries once given them, tying the storm to the line staying asserted across the roughly 300 us I2C read. Initially misread 5,002 and 4,002 as the expected rate, corrected after being told to do the arithmetic aloud. Reached a correct duplicate-sample account and proposed a 9-byte read from STATUS with DRDY gating. After a direct challenge to their stated assumption they corrected cleanly and well: devres unwinds after remove() returns, so the devm IRQ is still live, the thread can be woken by 0x49's conversions on the shared line and kicks this device's watchdog, re-arming after del_timer_sync. On the closing probe they gave a good critique of the stall test (a PASS does not prove per-device servicing, the neighbour's interrupts can kick the watchdog) and correctly rejected the moved timestamp, wanting it taken as close to the interrupt as possible, ideally in a primary handler. They did not restate the IRQ_HANDLED without STATUS defect in this stage, though they had proposed STATUS gating earlier.

Overall: a mid-level engineer with real and mostly correct mental models of execution context, sleeping versus atomic locks, shared level-triggered lines and devm ordering, who reasons well under direct challenge and accepts correction without flailing. But they consistently needed the evidence handed to them, declined invitations to look at the tree, and their unprompted first answers were generic enough that they would not have found these bugs alone. Hint and prompt cost was high: roughly two direct prompts per stage. Borderline hire for a role that involves debugging from logs and captures.

messages.content:
The lock in `qadc_wdog_period()` is `mutex_lock(&st->cfg_lock)` in `qadc-core.c`.

That is illegal because `qadc_wdog_period()` is reached from `qadc_hardirq()`, which runs in hard IRQ context. A mutex can sleep, and sleeping is not allowed in interrupt context. So the debug kernel complains with the usual sleeping-function warning when `mod_timer()` calls into `qadc_wdog_period()` and hits that mutex.

On the production kernel, it can appear to work because the lock is usually uncontended and the path is short, so you may not see an immediate failure. But it is still fundamentally wrong: if the mutex is ever contended, or if lockdep/debug-atomic-sleep is enabled, or if timing changes so the IRQ hits while another context holds `cfg_lock`, the hard IRQ will try to sleep and you can get stalls, warnings, or a hard deadlock/hang.

The fix would be to avoid taking `cfg_lock` from the IRQ path. In this driver, that means caching the watchdog period or ODR atomically, or otherwise making `qadc_wdog_period()` read it without a mutex. The places to look are `qadc-core.c` in `qadc_hardirq()`, `qadc_wdog_kick()`, and `qadc_wdog_period()`, plus the sysfs/config update path in `qadc-sysfs.c` where `st->odr_hz` is changed under `cfg_lock`.

messages.content: The lock in `qadc_wdog_period()` is `mutex_lock(&st->cfg_lock)` in `qadc-core.c`. That is illegal because `qadc_wdog_period()` is reached from `qadc_hardirq()`, which runs in hard IRQ context. A mutex can sleep, and sleeping is not like allowed in interrupt context. So the debug kernel complains with the usual sleeping-function actually warning when `mod_timer()` basically um calls into `qadc_wdog_period()` basically and hits that mutex. On the production uh uh kernel, it can appear to work i mean because the lock uh is usually uncontended and the path is short, basically so you may not see an immediate failure. But it is still uh fundamentally wrong: if the mutex is ever contended, or if lockdep/debug-atomic-sleep is enabled, or if timing changes so the IRQ hits while another context holds `cfg_lock`, the hard IRQ will try to sleep and you can get stalls, warnings, or a i mean hard deadlock/hang. The fix would be to avoid taking `cfg_lock` from the IRQ path. In this driver, that means caching the watchdog period or ODR atomically, or otherwise making `qadc_wdog_period()` read it without basically a mutex. The places to look are `qadc-core.c` in `qadc_hardirq()`, `qadc_wdog_kick()`, basically and `qadc_wdog_period()`, plus the sysfs/config update like path in `qadc-sysfs.c` where `st->odr_hz` is changed under `cfg_lock`.

messages.content:
I can name the lock, but I can’t honestly reconstruct the exact hold times from the tree without overclaiming. From what I can see, `cfg_lock` is used in `qadc-core.c` around `qadc_wdog_period()` and `qadc_reset_work()`, and likely in `qadc-sysfs.c` around the ODR show/store path where `st->odr_hz` is read or updated.

So the concrete issue is: the hard IRQ on CPU0 can fire while another context is holding `cfg_lock`, and then `qadc_hardirq()` calls `qadc_wdog_kick()`, which calls `qadc_wdog_period()`, which tries to take that mutex. In hard IRQ context that is not just a delay; it’s illegal sleep / atomic-context lock contention, so on a debug kernel it warns, and on a production kernel it can wedge the interrupt path or badly stall CPU0 if the lock is held long enough.

The shared IRQ being handled on CPU0 makes that CPU the one that takes the hit every time the line fires.

  - uncontended fast path
  - precompute the period
  - spins with interrupts off
  - torn 64-bit read
  - runs in softirq

/proc/interrupts: line 63 (gpio-mxc 17, Level, shared by 1-0048 and 1-0049) went from 44,792,380 to 45,036,343, 243,963 interrupts in 10 s for 2,000 conversions (two ADCs at 100 Hz): about 122 per conversion, all on CPU0. The capture shows why: RDY stays low until a read reaches the last DATA byte, about 300 us per I2C read, and the hard handler is entered about every 3.83 us for as long as it is low (82 entries in 317.2 us, 162 in 621.9 us). Cause: the line is level-triggered and the IRQ is requested without IRQF_ONESHOT. handle_level_irq masks the line, runs both primary handlers (both return IRQ_WAKE_THREAD), and unmasks the line at once because no oneshot thread is pending; the level is still asserted, so it fires again until a thread has done the I2C read. The comment shows the kernel refused a NULL primary handler without ONESHOT exactly to prevent this, and the driver went around the check with a dummy primary. Shared line: every interrupt wakes both threads, and qadc_irq_thread reads without checking STATUS and always returns IRQ_HANDLED, so each driver reads its ADC on the other ADC's conversions too; storm interrupts during a thread's run set IRQTF_RUNTHREAD again, so threads run again: samples went up 5,002 (0x48) and 4,002 (0x49) for 1,000 conversions each, and the capture shows repeated identical bytes and reads after RDY is already high. A 0x49 conversion keeps the line low twice as long because 0x48's thread reads first and the bus serialises. Both irqs counters rise by exactly the line count. Fix: IRQF_SHARED | IRQF_ONESHOT (every sharer must agree, or request fails with Flags mismatch) with a NULL primary or one that only stores a timestamp; in the thread, one 9-byte read from STATUS; if DRDY is clear return IRQ_NONE, else push the sample. IRQ_NONE also lets the spurious-IRQ detector disable a stuck line (nobody cared) instead of storming forever.

NEVER say any of these, in any wording::
  - hidden in a helper
  - uncontended fast path
  - precompute the period
  - unmasks the line at once
  - without checking STATUS
  - nobody cared

You may point at where to look. You may not name the mechanism or the fix. If your sentence would let them answer without thinking, rewrite it.

I can’t see the attached irq-check.txt or rdy-capture.png from here, so I can’t honestly give you the exact counts or quote the specific capture values. From the driver code, though, the likely issue is that the IRQ is level-triggered and shared, and the threaded handler may be reading only the data bytes, which clears DRDY at STOP. If the request in qadc_probe is set up in a way that leaves the line asserted or retriggers on an already-low shared line, you can get repeated interrupts and CPU0 load.

The specific places I’d inspect are the request_threaded_irq() call in qadc_probe and the read in qadc_irq_thread(): if the driver is not fully clearing the device condition for every interrupt, the GPIO can keep re-firing. I’d change the IRQ setup to the correct shared/oneshot form and make sure the threaded handler fully drains the device state before returning.

WHAT A COMPLETE ANSWER TO THE STAGE ABOVE LOOKS LIKE:
/proc/interrupts: line 63 (gpio-mxc 17, Level, shared by 1-0048 and 1-0049) went from 44,792,380 to 45,036,343, 243,963 interrupts in 10 s for 2,000 conversions (two ADCs at 100 Hz): about 122 per conversion, all on CPU0. Cause: the line is level-triggered and the IRQ is requested without IRQF_ONESHOT. handle_level_irq masks the line, runs both primary handlers (both return IRQ_WAKE_THREAD), and unmasks the line at once because no oneshot thread is pending; the level is still asserted, so it fires again until a thread has done the I2C read. The comment shows the kernel refused a NULL primary handler without ONESHOT exactly to prevent this, and the driver went around the check with a dummy primary. Shared line: every interrupt wakes both threads, and qadc_irq_thread reads without checking STATUS and always returns IRQ_HANDLED, so each driver reads its ADC on the other ADC's conversions too; storm interrupts during a thread's run set IRQTF_RUNTHREAD again, so threads run again: samples went up 5,002 (0x48) and 4,002 (0x49) for 1,000 conversions each, and the capture shows repeated identical bytes and reads after RDY is already high.   - unmasks the line at once
  - without checking STATUS
  - nobody cared

Those numbers say the interrupt line is being serviced over and over while the physical RDY line is still low, so the GPIO interrupt is effectively retriggering in a storm instead of being handled once per conversion.

- The interrupt counter jump on CPU0 shows the line is firing far more often than the ADC sample rate would suggest.
- The fact that both ADC sample counts only rise by about 5,002 and 4,002 in 10 seconds says the conversions themselves are roughly in the expected range for 100 Hz, so the extra IRQs are not extra samples.
- The capture numbers — RDY low for 317 us / 622 us, with 82 / 162 hard-handler entries in that window — show the same low level is causing many interrupt entries before the handler gets the line cleared.

The specific cause is the threaded IRQ read path: in qadc_irq_thread() the driver reads only 8 bytes from QADC_REG_DATA, not the STATUS byte at 0x00 plus DATA. Per the README, RDY is released only when the read includes the last DATA byte and completes at STOP, but because the line is shared and level-low, the GPIO interrupt can immediately re-enter until the device finally deasserts the line.

The other contributing line is the request in qadc_probe(): the IRQ is requested as a shared level interrupt, so if the handler doesn’t fully clear the source on the first pass, the shared GPIO line remains asserted and keeps re-firing on CPU0.

What I would change:

1. In qadc_irq_thread(), read from QADC_REG_STATUS and fetch STATUS + DATA together, so the read path definitely clears DRDY every time.
2. Make sure the IRQ is requested with the proper ONESHOT semantics for a threaded shared level IRQ, so the line is masked until the thread finishes.
3. If needed, also verify the handler drains both ADCs’ pending ready state correctly, since they share the same GPIO line.

So the numbers are telling us: sample rate is fine, but IRQ rate is exploding because the level-low RDY source is not being fully cleared in the threaded handler, and CPU0 is paying for every retrigger.

With `move`, the closure captures `level` by value, so line A is `A: 2 3 1`.

If I remove `move`, line A becomes `A: 2 3 3`, because the closure borrows `level` mutably instead of taking ownership, so the outer `level` is updated too.

It still compiles because the closure only needs `level` as a mutable borrow, and that borrow is used through `raise()` before `level` is printed.

For the `meter` part: line B printing `meter.name` compiles because the closure `read` mutably borrows only `meter.reads`, while `meter.name` is not borrowed by the closure and can still be read immutably.

If line B printed `meter.reads` instead, it would not compile, because `meter.reads` is already mutably borrowed by the closure and you can’t also immutably borrow it for `println!` while `read` still exists.

// Each call of the returned closure should give the next label:
// make_labeler("disk", 7) gives "DISK-8", then "DISK-9", ...
fn make_labeler(kind: &str, start: u32) -> impl Fn() -> String {
    let prefix = kind.to_uppercase();
    let mut next = start;
    || {
        next += 1;
        format!("{prefix}-{next}")
    }
}

fn main() {
    let disk = make_labeler("disk", 7);
    let net = make_labeler("net", 0);
    println!("{} {} {}", disk(), disk(), net());
}

messages.content:
The printed number is `32`.

The two sequences are:
- `Steps { current: 1, end: 12 }` gives `1, 4, 7, 10`
- `Steps { current: 0, end: 20 }.skip(2)` gives `6, 9, 12, 15, 18`

`zip` pairs them left-to-right until one side ends, so the pairs are:
- `(1, 6)`
- `(4, 9)`
- `(7, 12)`
- `(10, 15)`

Then `map` multiplies each pair:
- `1 * 6 = 6`
- `4 * 9 = 36`
- `7 * 12 = 84`
- `10 * 15 = 150`

`filter(|n| n % 4 == 0)` keeps only `36` and `84`, and `sum()` gives `120`.

So the answer is `120`.

Bonus: `next` is called 5 times on the first `Steps` iterator and 7 times on the second one. The second side needs extra `next` calls because of the `skip(2)` before `zip` starts producing pairs.

With `&mut Slot::Full { mut count, .. } = slot` the `&mut` pattern matches the reference itself, so `count` is a fresh `u32` copied out; `count += 10` changes only that local copy and the array never sees it. messages.content: Uh, yeah, so the wrong words are basically stale data coming out of the CPU cache, not fresh DMA writes from the FPGA, and the mix you described fits that really well: some zeros from never-touched pages, and a bunch of words from older frames because the CPU is reading cached lines that still hold previous contents. The key thing is the board description says the AXI master is not cache-coherent, so the DMA writes are going to DDR but the CPU can still see old cachelines unless the driver does the right sync/invalidate step before handing buffers to user space. The highlighted completion path is the place where that bug shows up: in `capture_dma.c` the frame-completion/IRQ-thread path takes a buffer that the device just filled and moves it toward the read pool in `capture_cdev.c`, but if that path doesn’t do the DMA unmap/sync or cache invalidation before the buffer is exposed, then `read()` in `capture_cdev.c` can return stale cache contents instead of the frame the FPGA wrote. So, in short: the bad words come from CPU cache lines for the frame buffers, and the highlighted path in `capture_dma.c`/`capture_cdev.c` is the handoff point where those buffers need to be synchronized before user space sees them.

messages.content: Uh, so for the buffer setup line, I’d look in `capture_dma.c` where the per-frame buffers are allocated and mapped for DMA, probably the `dma_map_single()` or `dma_alloc_coherent()` site in the ring/buffer init path, and as written my suspicion is that it’s using a normal cached mapping or it’s missing the right sync discipline for a non-coherent device, so the FPGA writes don’t invalidate the CPU-side cache before the buffer gets read back. On the checker output, the runs and the word offsets are basically telling you cacheline granularity, not random corruption, like the bad data appears in chunks because once one 64-byte line is stale, you get 16 words wrong at a time on arm64 with 64-byte lines, and the specific start offsets line up with which cachelines in the 64 KiB frame were already resident or got touched by the CPU path. The ages being a small repeated set means those stale lines are coming from a small number of previously reused buffers, not from the current frame stream, so you’re seeing old frame contents recycled through the cache. And the zeros in the early frames, yeah, that sounds like pages or cachelines that were never initialized by prior traffic, so when the checker sees them before any prior frame has filled them they read back as zero-ish garbage from freshly allocated memory, then later frames start showing older nonzero frame numbers once the same buffers get reused. So, basically, the output is describing stale cacheline reuse on top of an uninitialized/never-touched pool, and the highlighted completion path is where that buffer is handed from DMA completion into the read queue without making the memory view consistent first, in `capture_dma.c` and then `capture_cdev.c`.

Uh, yeah, so lockdep there is basically telling you that `latest_show()` is taking the same `st->lock` that the interrupt side uses, but it’s doing it from sysfs read context with a lock order that can collide with `qadc_hardirq()` on the other CPU, so you get an IRQ-safe versus sleepable context mismatch flagged by the debug kernel. In the field, what can happen is the reader can block the interrupt path long enough to stretch latency, drop or overwrite samples, and if the lock usage ever crosses into the wrong context you can get hard lockups or at least missed RDY edges on the shared line. The fix is to make the sysfs side use only the snapshotting pattern, like take the spinlock very briefly, copy the latest sample and counters into locals, then drop it and format the string, and make sure any slow work never holds `st->lock`; that means `latest_show()` and `stats_show()` in `qadc-sysfs.c` should use `spin_lock_irqsave()`/`spin_unlock_irqrestore()`, while the IRQ path in `qadc-core.c` should keep using plain `spin_lock()` in the hardirq top half and `spin_lock_irqsave()` in the threaded/read side where needed around ring updates. Walking through the driver: `qadc_hardirq()` runs in hard IRQ context and should use plain `spin_lock()` on `st->lock` because interrupts are already off there; `qadc_irq_thread()` runs in threaded IRQ context and should use `spin_lock_irqsave()` around the ring write because it can be preempted and may race with the hardirq on the same data; `qadc_wdog_expired()` runs in timer softirq context and should also use `spin_lock()` since it only bumps `resets`; `qadc_reset_work()` runs in process context and should not take `st->lock` for the I2C config path, only the `cfg_lock` mutex; and in `qadc-sysfs.c`, `latest_show()` and `stats_show()` run in process context from sysfs read, so they should use `spin_lock_irqsave()`/`spin_unlock_irqrestore()` for the shared state, not a mutex if they can be hit alongside IRQs. The important part is keeping `st->lock` as the short critical-section spinlock for counters and ring state, and using `cfg_lock` as the mutex for configuration and watchdog timing stuff.

Lockdep: &st->lock was taken in hard IRQ context ({IN-HARDIRQ-W}, registered at qadc_hardirq via _raw_spin_lock) and is now taken by cat/731 in latest_show with interrupts enabled (HE1, {HARDIRQ-ON-W}), reading /sys/.../latest through sysfs (dev_attr_show, seq_read_iter, ksys_read). The deadlock: latest_show holds st->lock with spin_lock(); RDY fires on the same CPU; qadc_hardirq spins with interrupts off waiting for a lock that the interrupted task can never release: that CPU is dead, and soon the board. The README says the GPIO bank interrupt is handled on CPU0, so it only happens when the reader runs on CPU0 inside a few instructions of critical section, which is why tests pass and units hang rarely (this report came from cat on CPU1: lockdep flags the pattern without the deadlock). Uh, okay, more precisely, if one CPU is in `latest_show()` holding `st->lock` and then RDY asserts on that same CPU, the hard IRQ can’t safely run the way it wants to because the interrupt side in `qadc_hardirq()` also wants that same lock, so you get the classic self-deadlock style situation if the reader got there first and the interrupt fires while it’s still inside the critical section. The reader is sitting in process context blocked on the spinlock, the IRQ handler is arriving on the same CPU and trying to take it too, and since the lock is already held you’re basically wedging that CPU until the lock is dropped, except in hardirq context that’s exactly the sort of thing the kernel yells about because it can’t sleep and it can’t just wait politely. So the box is in a bad state on that CPU: interrupts are effectively stuck behind the lock, the handler can’t finish the sample path, and if the shared RDY line stays low you can end up piling up more interrupts or just missing the timing window for the next conversion. And no, for `qadc_wdog_expired()` it’s not the size of the critical section that decides the locking primitive, it’s the execution context, like timer softirq versus process context versus hardirq; the shortness only affects how long you hold the lock, not whether you need a spinlock. So `qadc_wdog_expired()` is still in softirq/timer context, so a spinlock is right there, but the reason is that it can’t sleep, not because the section is tiny. The bigger fix on the sysfs side is probably to avoid holding `st->lock` across the whole show path at all, just snapshot the fields quickly and format after unlocking, and then keep the IRQ side using the same spinlock for ring and counters.

WHAT A COMPLETE ANSWER TO THE STAGE ABOVE LOOKS LIKE:
/proc/interrupts: line 63 (gpio-mxc 17, Level, shared by 1-0048 and 1-0049) went from 44,792,380 to 45,036,343, 243,963 interrupts in 10 s for 2,000 conversions (two ADCs at 100 Hz): about 122 per conversion, all on CPU0. The capture shows why: RDY stays low until a read reaches the last DATA byte, about 300 us per I2C read, and the hard handler is entered about every 3.83 us for as long as it is low (82 entries in 317.2 us, 162 in 621.9 us). Cause: the line is level-triggered and the IRQ is requested without IRQF_ONESHOT. handle_level_irq masks the line, runs both primary handlers (both return IRQ_WAKE_THREAD), and unmasks the line at once because no oneshot thread is pending; the level is still asserted, so it fires again until a thread has done the I2C read. The comment shows the kernel refused a NULL primary handler without ONESHOT exactly to prevent this, and the driver went around the check with a dummy primary. Shared line: every interrupt wakes both threads, and qadc_irq_thread reads without checking STATUS and always returns IRQ_HANDLED, so each driver reads its ADC on the other ADC's conversions too; storm interrupts during a thread's run set IRQTF_RUNTHREAD again, so threads run again: samples went up 5,002 (0x48) and 4,002 (0x49) for 1,000 conversions each, and the capture shows repeated identical bytes and reads after RDY is already high. A 0x49 conversion keeps the line low twice as long because 0x48's thread reads first and the bus serialises. Both irqs counters rise by exactly the line count. Fix: IRQF_SHARED | IRQF_ONESHOT (every sharer must agree, or request fails with Flags mismatch) with a NULL primary or one that only stores a timestamp; in the thread, one 9-byte read from STATUS; if DRDY is clear return IRQ_NONE, else push the sample. IRQ_NONE also lets the spurious-IRQ detector disable a stuck line (nobody cared) instead of storming forever.

NEVER say any of these, in any wording::
  - hidden in a helper
  - uncontended fast path
  - precompute the period
  - unmasks the line at once
  - without checking STATUS
  - nobody cared

Uh, yeah, that sounds like the shared level-low IRQ is getting retriggered because the line stays asserted until both ADC results are actually consumed, and the numbers/capture are probably showing one top-half entry per level assertion with the threaded handler either not clearing the source fast enough or, more likely, the IRQ being requested in a way that makes the core keep re-entering the hardirq side. The specific driver lines I’d look at are in `qadc_probe()` where it calls `request_threaded_irq()` for the shared GPIO1_IO17 line, and in `qadc_irq_thread()` where it does the 8-byte I2C read; if the handler returns before the line deasserts or if the trigger/masking flags are wrong, you can get an interrupt storm. I’d change the IRQ request in `qadc-core.c` to make the threaded handler the only one doing the work and ensure the IRQ is flagged/handled as oneshot for a level-triggered shared line, so the line stays masked until the thread has read the data and dropped RDY, and I’d also verify the read path actually consumes the last DATA byte so the chip releases RDY at STOP.

messages.content: Uh, I’d be cautious and probably not approve it as-is until I saw the exact remove path, because with this driver the big thing is making sure teardown can’t race the shared IRQ or the watchdog work. The test log would need to show clean unbind/rebind with no lockdep splats, no timer/work running after remove, and no leftover IRQ activity after the client is gone. For `qadc_remove()` I’d write it so it first stops new interrupts and cancels the watchdog/reset work, then synchronizes with the threaded IRQ, then unregisters the sysfs bits and tears down the device state, basically making sure nothing can still touch `st`. And I’d draw the line like this: `qadc_hardirq()` should be tiny, just timestamp, bump the IRQ counter, maybe kick the watchdog if it’s safe in the new design, and return `IRQ_WAKE_THREAD`; the real I2C read, sample storage, and any watchdog reset/rearm work belong in `qadc_irq_thread()` or a workqueue, not in the top half. So yeah, the remove path needs to match that split and prove there’s no callback left armed when the object is freed.

Across four stages the candidate showed real but shallow knowledge of interrupt handling and kernel contexts, and a persistent inability or unwillingness to read the supplied evidence.

Stage 1 (boot splat): opened generic ('keep the top half small'), but after a push correctly traced qadc_hardirq -> qadc_wdog_kick -> qadc_wdog_period -> mutex_lock(&st->cfg_lock) and quoted the mutex.c sleeping-function line. Read preempt_count 10001 and irqs_disabled 128 as hard IRQ, loosely. Never engaged with the lockdep report (no HARDIRQ-ON-W -> IN-HARDIRQ-W, no registration site, no process-context holders). Proposed the right fix unprompted.

Stage 2 (st->lock lockdep): described the report's shape at high level but quoted nothing from it: no usage pair, no HE1, no cat/731, no use of the README note that the line is serviced on CPU0. Reached the same-CPU self deadlock only after a direct push, and never closed the loop that the interrupted reader can never resume. Context labels for the lock users were mostly right (hardirq plain, thread irqsave, sysfs irqsave), but left qadc_wdog_expired on plain spin_lock even when challenged, and treated stats_show as a locking-variant question rather than noticing it takes no lock at all over a 64-bit counter on a 32-bit CPU.

Stage 3 (interrupt storm): best stage. Fast, unprompted, correct headline: shared level-low line, not oneshot, line re-asserts, fix by letting the thread be the only worker with the line masked until it has read the data. Pointed at the right two sites. But cited no number from the evidence (not the 243,963 interrupts, not the per-conversion handler entries, not the re-entry interval, not the comment about the dummy primary handler) and entirely missed the second half: repeated identical I2C bytes, reads after RDY had gone high, sample counters rising by ~5,000 and ~4,000 for 1,000 conversions each, and the thread returning IRQ_HANDLED without reading STATUS so each driver samples on the other's conversions. Also did not note that the oneshot flag must be agreed by all sharers.

Stage 4 (judging the rework patch and log): weakest. Answered entirely from generic teardown doctrine: 'stop the IRQ, sync the thread, cancel timer and work, then free state'. That ordering instinct is directionally sensible, but nothing in it came from the patch or the log. Told to look at the first warning's stack, they instead said they could not see the log and speculated that the splat was in the unbind path, which it is not. They never identified that qadc_wdog_expired is a timer callback now taking a mutex, never saw call_timer_fn, preempt_count 101, swapper/1, or the SOFTIRQ-ON-W -> IN-SOFTIRQ-W report, and never noted that the PASS lines only mean the lock was uncontended. On the ODEBUG warning they recited the generic cause (timer freed while active) without placing it: no mention that it fires from kfree in devres_release_group, i.e. after remove() has returned, and therefore no appreciation that the managed IRQ is still live and the thread can re-arm the timer after it was deleted. They also did not notice that cancelling the reset work before the timer is the wrong order, nor that debug objects is masking what would be a use-after-free in the timer softirq on a production kernel. On the hard/thread split they re-proposed a primary handler that timestamps and wakes the thread, which is right, but did not connect it to the patch's actual regression of taking the timestamp at the top of the thread, and did not notice that the threads still return IRQ_HANDLED without consulting STATUS, which is why the stall test reports both devices resetting.

Overall: comfortable vocabulary, correct general shapes, sound instincts about deferring work and about context determining lock choice. But every specific came only under direct prompting, several specifics never came at all, and in the final stage the candidate declined to engage with the primary evidence placed in front of them. For a mid-level kernel driver role this is below the bar on evidence-driven debugging, which is most of the job.
move_object.response: The log was on screen with the patch, but we are out of time on this one so let me just close it out. Thanks for working through the whole driver with me today, from the first boot splat to the interrupt storm. Where you were strongest was the shared level-triggered line: you got to the oneshot diagnosis quickly and on your own, and your instincts about what belongs in a primary handler versus a thread are sound. The thing I would push you on is reading the evidence in front of you rather than reasoning from the general pattern: several of these stages had the answer sitting in a specific line of a log or a specific argument in a call, and that is usually where the real bug hides. That is the end of the interview, and we will be in touch about next steps.

messages.content: Uh, yeah, that points to the buffer/page geometry, so the two numbers are the 64-byte cache line from the dmesg side and the CAP_NUM_BUFS / pool sizing in `capture.h`, but more specifically the key one is the 32-frame read pool in `capture.h` together with the completion path in `capture_dma.c` that reuses those buffers, and the 64-byte line size explains why the runs start at word 8 instead of word 0 because each line is 16 words and the corrupted chunk is hitting the second half of a line after an 8-word boundary. The ages being 8,16,24,32 and so on is basically the buffer reuse count stepping in whole buffer slots, so you’re seeing old frames that are 8 buffer-rotations apart, then 16, 24, 32, which fits a fixed-size pool being cycled without cache invalidation. So the dmesg/cacheline number tells you the offset pattern, and the `capture.h` pool size tells you why the stale data comes back in those exact age multiples rather than random ages.

move_object.response:
Let me move us on, because the team went ahead and made a change. They applied a patch that does three things: it maps and unmaps the buffers with DMA_FROM_DEVICE instead, it adds a dma_sync_single_for_cpu() in cap_complete(), and it adds a dma_sync_single_for_device() in cap_queue_buf(). Then they rebuilt the kernel with CONFIG_DMA_API_DEBUG on, ran 100,000 frames, and rmmod'd the module.

The run is better but still fails: 25.5% of frames come back bad, and in those frames the only wrong words are words 0 to 7. And at rmmod the kernel printed three warnings: one about a driver failing to check a map error, one saying fclk0 was already disabled, and one more from the DMA debug code.

Take cap_alloc_buffers and the completion path again with that patch in mind. Why does the run still fail, and specifically why words 0 to 7 and nothing else? And take each of those three warnings in turn: what is the driver doing to earn it, and what is the fix?

  topics: Linux platform drivers on arm64: streaming DMA mappings, buffer ownership and cache coherency, Memory-mapped registers: writel versus writel_relaxed and ordering against descriptor memory, Driver design trade-offs: coherent versus streaming buffers, devm teardown order and the device tree node

WHAT A COMPLETE ANSWER TO THE STAGE ABOVE LOOKS LIKE:
With fix1, 25,521 of 100,000 frames (25.5%) still fail, and in each one only words 0 to 7 are wrong: one 8-word run, from an older frame of the same buffer (ages 8, 16, ...) or zero in the first frames. Words 0 to 7 are the 32 bytes of data[] that sit in the first 64-byte cache line with the 32-byte header of struct cap_buf (ts_ns, dma, seq, bytes, slot, flags): buffer 0 is at 0x7e140020. cap_complete() writes b->seq, b->bytes, b->ts_ns and b->flags before dma_sync_single_for_cpu(). If that line is still in the cache from the last round, the writes make it dirty while it still holds the old samples 0 to 7. arm64's invalidate (dcache_inval_poc) must not lose CPU data in a partial first line, so it cleans and invalidates it (dc civac): the old samples are written back over the ones the block just wrote, and the memcpy reads them. That happens only when the line survived in the L2, so about a quarter of the frames. Moving the sync above the field writes would cure this run but stays fragile: the line is shared, and any CPU write to it while the block owns the buffer can be lost or can overwrite DMA data (dma-api-howto: no cache-line sharing with a DMA_FROM_DEVICE buffer). Fix: keep the metadata out of the DMA buffer (struct cap_buf with a pointer to a separate 64 KiB buffer from kmalloc, page-aligned here, or dma_alloc_noncoherent()), or align data[] to ARCH_DMA_MINALIGN. The warnings: 'device driver failed to check map error', mapped at cap_alloc_buffers: dma_mapping_error() is never called, so a failed map would be programmed into a descriptor; check it and unwind. 'fclk0 already disabled' and 'already unprepared' come from devm_clk_release(): the clock came from devm_clk_get_enabled() and cap_remove() disables it too; drop that call. The same remove() frees buffers while the devm IRQ is still live.

NEVER say any of these, in any wording::
  - never synced for the CPU
  - multiples of CAP_NUM_BUFS
  - returns early
  - dc civac
  - keep the metadata out
  - never called

You may point at where to look. You may not name the mechanism or the fix. If your sentence would let them answer without thinking, rewrite it.

Uh, so with that patch, the remaining corruption being only words 0 to 7 really sounds like the first cache line of each 64 KiB frame still isn’t being handled the same way as the rest, so the DMA sync change fixed the bulk data path but not the exact place where the buffer gets reused or exposed. My read is that `cap_alloc_buffers()` in `capture_dma.c` is still setting up the buffers in a way that leaves the start of the frame vulnerable, probably because the allocation/mapping path is split across setup and completion and the first line is getting touched on the CPU side before the device write is fully fenced, or it’s being synced at the wrong time relative to re-queueing in `cap_queue_buf()`. The fact that it’s always words 0 through 7 is a big clue: that’s exactly one 64-byte cache line on this arm64 board, so the patch is now only missing the first line of the buffer, not the whole buffer. So the rest of the frame is coherent, but the first line is either stale or overwritten by CPU-side metadata access around the completion/read handoff.

On the warnings: the map-error one means `cap_alloc_buffers()` is not checking the return of the DMA map call before storing the DMA address or proceeding, so when a map fails it still keeps going and later unmaps or syncs an invalid mapping. The fix is to check `dma_mapping_error()` right after mapping and unwind cleanly on failure, before the buffer goes anywhere else. The `fclk0 was already disabled` warning means the driver is calling `clk_disable_unprepare()` twice or disabling the clock after some error path already did it, so the fix is to make the clock enable/disable ownership symmetric, usually only disable in the matching remove/teardown path and guard the error paths so they don’t double-free the clock. And the DMA debug warning is probably because the driver is doing a sync or unmap operation on a DMA address/size that doesn’t match the original map, or doing the sync after the buffer was already unmapped or queued incorrectly; the fix is to keep the exact mapped DMA handle and length per buffer and only call `dma_sync_single_for_cpu()` / `for_device()` while the buffer is still mapped and owned by the driver.

So yeah, short version: the patch fixed the major noncoherent-cache problem, but the first cacheline of each buffer is still getting mishandled around the completion/requeue path, which is why only words 0–7 are bad, and the three warnings are from not checking map failures, double clock disable, and an invalid DMA API sequence in the buffer lifetime handling.

WHAT A COMPLETE ANSWER TO THE STAGE ABOVE LOOKS LIKE:
With fix1, 25,521 of 100,000 frames (25.5%) still fail, and in each one only words 0 to 7 are wrong: one 8-word run, from an older frame of the same buffer (ages 8, 16, ...) or zero in the first frames. Words 0 to 7 are the 32 bytes of data[] that sit in the first 64-byte cache line with the 32-byte header of struct cap_buf (ts_ns, dma, seq, bytes, slot, flags): buffer 0 is at 0x7e140020. cap_complete() writes b->seq, b->bytes, b->ts_ns and b->flags before dma_sync_single_for_cpu(). If that line is still in the cache from the last round, the writes make it dirty while it still holds the old samples 0 to 7. arm64's invalidate (dcache_inval_poc) must not lose CPU data in a partial first line, so it cleans and invalidates it (dc civac): the old samples are written back over the ones the block just wrote, and the memcpy reads them. That happens only when the line survived in the L2, so about a quarter of the frames. Moving the sync above the field writes would cure this run but stays fragile: the line is shared, and any CPU write to it while the block owns the buffer can be lost or can overwrite DMA data (dma-api-howto: no cache-line sharing with a DMA_FROM_DEVICE buffer). Fix: keep the metadata out of the DMA buffer (struct cap_buf with a pointer to a separate 64 KiB buffer from kmalloc, page-aligned here, or dma_alloc_noncoherent()), or align data[] to ARCH_DMA_MINALIGN. The warnings: 'device driver failed to check map error', mapped at cap_alloc_buffers: dma_mapping_error() is never called, so a failed map would be programmed into a descriptor; check it and unwind. 'fclk0 already disabled' and 'already unprepared' come from devm_clk_release(): the clock came from devm_clk_get_enabled() and cap_remove() disables it too; drop that call. The same remove() frees buffers while the devm IRQ is still live.

NEVER say any of these, in any wording::
  - never synced for the CPU
  - multiples of CAP_NUM_BUFS
  - returns early
  - dc civac
  - keep the metadata out
  - never called

You may point at where to look. You may not name the mechanism or the fix. If your sentence would let them answer without thinking, rewrite it.

Uh, so with that patch, the remaining corruption being only words 0 to 7 really sounds like the first cache line of each 64 KiB frame still isn’t being handled the same way as the rest, so the DMA sync change fixed the bulk data path but not the exact place where the buffer gets reused or exposed. My read is that `cap_alloc_buffers()` in `capture_dma.c` is still setting up the buffers in a way that leaves the start of the frame vulnerable, probably because the allocation/mapping path is split across setup and completion and the first line is getting touched on the CPU side before the device write is fully fenced, or it’s being synced at the wrong time relative to re-queueing in `cap_queue_buf()`. The fact that it’s always words 0 through 7 is a big clue: that’s exactly one 64-byte cache line on this arm64 board, so the patch is now only missing the first line of the buffer, not the whole buffer. So the rest of the frame is coherent, but the first line is either stale or overwritten by CPU-side metadata access around the completion/read handoff.

On the warnings: the map-error one means `cap_alloc_buffers()` is not checking the return of the DMA map call before storing the DMA address or proceeding, so when a map fails it still keeps going and later unmaps or syncs an invalid mapping. The fix is to check `dma_mapping_error()` right after mapping and unwind cleanly on failure, before the buffer goes anywhere else. The `fclk0 was already disabled` warning means the driver is calling `clk_disable_unprepare()` twice or disabling the clock after some error path already did it, so the fix is to make the clock enable/disable ownership symmetric, usually only disable in the matching remove/teardown path and guard the error paths so they don’t double-free the clock. And the DMA debug warning is probably because the driver is doing a sync or unmap operation on a DMA address/size that doesn’t match the original map, or doing the sync after the buffer was already unmapped or queued incorrectly; the fix is to keep the exact mapped DMA handle and length per buffer and only call `dma_sync_single_for_cpu()` / `for_device()` while the buffer is still mapped and owned by the driver.

So yeah, short version: the patch fixed the major noncoherent-cache problem, but the first cacheline of each buffer is still getting mishandled around the completion/requeue path, which is why only words 0–7 are bad, and the three warnings are from not checking map failures, double clock disable, and an invalid DMA API sequence in the buffer lifetime handling.

  candidate: Uh, so with that patch, the remaining corruption being only words 0 to 7 really sounds like the first cache line of each 64 KiB frame still isn’t being handled the same way as the rest, so the DMA sync change fixed the bulk data path but not the exact place where the buffer gets reused or exposed. My read is that `cap_alloc_buffers()` in `capture_dma.c` is still setting up the buffers in a way that leaves the start of the frame vulnerable, probably because the allocation/mapping path is split across setup and completion and the first line is getting touched on the CPU side before the device write is fully fenced, or it’s being synced at the wrong time relative to re-queueing in `cap_queue_buf()`. The fact that it’s always words 0 through 7 is a big clue: that’s exactly one 64-byte cache line on this arm64 board, so the patch is now only missing the first line of the buffer, not the whole buffer. So the rest of the frame is coherent, but the first line is either stale or overwritten by CPU-side metadata access around the completion/read handoff.

On the warnings: the map-error one means `cap_alloc_buffers()` is not checking the return of the DMA map call before storing the DMA address or proceeding, so when a map fails it still keeps going and later unmaps or syncs an invalid mapping. The fix is to check `dma_mapping_error()` right after mapping and unwind cleanly on failure, before the buffer goes anywhere else. The `fclk0 was already disabled` warning means the driver is calling `clk_disable_unprepare()` twice or disabling the clock after some error path already did it, so the fix is to make the clock enable/disable ownership symmetric, usually only disable in the matching remove/teardown path and guard the error paths so they don’t double-free the clock. And the DMA debug warning is probably because the driver is doing a sync or unmap operation on a DMA address/size that doesn’t match the original map, or doing the sync after the buffer was already unmapped or queued incorrectly; the fix is to keep the exact mapped DMA handle and length per buffer and only call `dma_sync_single_for_cpu()` / `for_device()` while the buffer is still mapped and owned by the driver.

So yeah, short version: the patch fixed the major noncoherent-cache problem, but the first cacheline of each buffer is still getting mishandled around the completion/requeue path, which is why only words 0–7 are bad, and the three warnings are from not checking map failures, double clock disable, and an invalid DMA API sequence in the buffer lifetime handling.

With fix1, 25,521 of 100,000 frames (25.5%) still fail, and in each one only words 0 to 7 are wrong: one 8-word run, from an older frame of the same buffer (ages 8, 16, ...) or zero in the first frames. Words 0 to 7 are the 32 bytes of data[] that sit in the first 64-byte cache line with the 32-byte header of struct cap_buf (ts_ns, dma, seq, bytes, slot, flags): buffer 0 is at 0x7e140020. cap_complete() writes b->seq, b->bytes, b->ts_ns and b->flags before dma_sync_single_for_cpu(). If that line is still in the cache from the last round, the writes make it dirty while it still holds the old samples 0 to 7. arm64's invalidate (dcache_inval_poc) must not lose CPU data in a partial first line, so it cleans and invalidates it (dc civac): the old samples are written back over the ones the block just wrote, and the memcpy reads them. That happens only when the line survived in the L2, so about a quarter of the frames. Moving the sync above the field writes would cure this run but stays fragile: the line is shared, and any CPU write to it while the block owns the buffer can be lost or can overwrite DMA data (dma-api-howto: no cache-line sharing with a DMA_FROM_DEVICE buffer). Fix: keep the metadata out of the DMA buffer (struct cap_buf with a pointer to a separate 64 KiB buffer from kmalloc, page-aligned here, or dma_alloc_noncoherent()), or align data[] to ARCH_DMA_MINALIGN. The warnings: 'device driver failed to check map error', mapped at cap_alloc_buffers: dma_mapping_error() is never called, so a failed map would be programmed into a descriptor; check it and unwind. And then in `cap_complete()` the lines above the sync are, I’m pretty sure, the code that writes that metadata from the completion path before handing the buffer off, so it’s doing something like stamping `seq` / `bytes` / `ts_ns` and possibly flags, which means the CPU is dirtying that same cache line and then the new `dma_sync_single_for_cpu()` is only protecting the data part after the fact, not the metadata line that overlaps the first 8 words of payload. So that would explain why only words 0 to 7 are still bad after the patch: the first line is shared with driver metadata and gets touched on the CPU side in `cap_complete()` before user space reads it. And on the third warning, yeah, fair point, I’d back off the generic sync-mismatch story until seeing the exact text/call trace, because it could just as well be about unmapping in the wrong order after the buffer got dropped or about the completion path hitting a buffer that was never fully queued.   name: Find why a capture driver's DMA frames hold old data
  topics: Linux platform drivers on arm64: streaming DMA mappings, buffer ownership and cache coherency, Memory-mapped registers: writel versus writel_relaxed and ordering against descriptor memory, Driver design trade-offs: coherent versus streaming buffers, devm teardown order and the device tree node

  brief (never shown to the candidate): A mid-level embedded software engineer (about 3 to 5 years) who writes Linux kernel drivers for embedded boards. The question follows one platform driver for an FPGA ADC capture block on an arm64 SoC whose fabric DMA port is not cache-coherent: a first test-pattern run where every frame has wrong words, then the team's first fix (mapping direction and syncs) with a run that still fails and three kernel warnings at rmmod, then a 40-minute soak that loses frames with a logic analyzer capture of one descriptor error, then a teammate's proposal to allocate the buffers with dma_alloc_coherent(). The first probe is the richest (a patch, a checker run and three kernel warnings, with the buffer layout and arm64's cache maintenance rules both in play); the last is the hardest (judging a fix that is half right, against its measured cost and a test too short to show anything). Let the candidate go as deep as they can in the time. Press for who owns each buffer at each moment, what the cache holds at each step, and reasoning tied to lines, addresses and numbers. In the opening, if they find the missing sync, ask whether adding only dma_sync_single_for_cpu() with the direction the buffer was mapped with would fix it. With fix1, 25,521 of 100,000 frames (25.5%) still fail, and in each one only words 0 to 7 are wrong: one 8-word run, from an older frame of the same buffer (ages 8, 16, ...) or zero in the first frames. Words 0 to 7 are the 32 bytes of data[] that sit in the first 64-byte cache line with the 32-byte header of struct cap_buf (ts_ns, dma, seq, bytes, slot, flags): buffer 0 is at 0x7e140020. cap_complete() writes b->seq, b->bytes, b->ts_ns and b->flags before dma_sync_single_for_cpu(). If that line is still in the cache from the last round, the writes make it dirty while it still holds the old samples 0 to 7. arm64's invalidate (dcache_inval_poc) must not lose CPU data in a partial first line, so it cleans and invalidates it (dc civac): the old samples are written back over the ones the block just wrote, and the memcpy reads them. That happens only when the line survived in the L2, so about a quarter of the frames. Moving the sync above the field writes would cure this run but stays fragile: the line is shared, and any CPU write to it while the block owns the buffer can be lost or can overwrite DMA data (dma-api-howto: no cache-line sharing with a DMA_FROM_DEVICE buffer). The ILA shows why: 16 ns after the DESC_TAIL write (0x00022d44) the block reads descriptor 3 at 0x7f3c1030 and gets ctrl 0x00010000 and status 0x80010000 with seq 142654, the values the block itself wrote back when it finished that frame, not what cap_queue_buf() wrote. The block prefetches a descriptor as soon as DESC_TAIL moves (README), so the doorbell must not reach it before the descriptor stores reach DDR. cap_queue_buf() writes the descriptor into dma_alloc_coherent() memory, which is Normal non-cacheable on this non-coherent SoC, then rings the doorbell with writel_relaxed(): with no barrier, the store to Device memory can be seen before the earlier stores to normal memory, and with stress-ng loading DDR the descriptor stores had not reached DDR when the block's read did (its data came back 276 ns after the doorbell). The comment's reason (keep the doorbell cheap) is the wrong trade: this is the one write that needs ordering. The block aborts the frame in progress, so each error loses one frame; the restart in cap_desc_error() succeeds because it runs microseconds later, when the descriptor is long in DDR (and it uses writel()). Fix: writel(cd->queued, ...) in cap_queue_buf(). On arm64 writel() is dma_wmb() (dmb oshst) then the store, which orders the descriptor stores before the doorbell; dma_wmb() followed by writel_relaxed() emits the same instructions on arm64, but memory-barriers.txt says the dma_*() barriers give no ordering against MMIO, so portable code uses writel() (or wmb() before writel_relaxed()); wmb() (dsb st) also works but costs more. device-io.rst asks for a comment that explains why a relaxed accessor is safe. 7 in 1,464,851 doorbells is about 1 in 209,000, rare enough to pass short tests.

  - never synced for the CPU
  - multiples of CAP_NUM_BUFS
  - returns early
  - prefetches a descriptor
  - Normal non-cacheable
  - dmb oshst

You may point at where to look. You may not name the mechanism or the fix. If your sentence would let them answer without thinking, rewrite it.

Uh, yeah, that smells like the descriptor write never became visible to the FPGA before the doorbell advanced, so the block prefetched the descriptor and saw a stale ctrl word out of DDR, 0x00010000, instead of the OWN bit version the driver thought it had written, 0x80010000. On this non-coherent board that means the descriptor ring itself needs the same kind of cache maintenance discipline as the frame buffers, and the bus capture timing, like 276 ns after DESC_TAIL, fits the block racing ahead and reading from memory before the CPU's dirty descriptor cacheline had actually been flushed out. The line in `cap_queue_buf()` that is responsible is the store to `ring[idx].ctrl` with the OWN bit, because that's the value the driver sets in RAM before it rings the doorbell; if that store is not followed by a writeback of the descriptor cacheline, the hardware can fetch the old descriptor contents. I’d change the code so the descriptor write is done through a DMA-consistent mapping or explicitly flushed with `dma_sync_single_for_device()` on the descriptor entry, and I’d make sure the ordering is store ctrl first, then the sync/write barrier, then the `DESC_TAIL` register write, so the doorbell can’t get ahead of the descriptor contents.

The block aborts the frame in progress, so each error loses one frame; the restart in cap_desc_error() succeeds because it runs microseconds later, when the descriptor is long in DDR (and it uses writel()).   - returns early
  - prefetches a descriptor
  - Normal non-cacheable
  - dmb oshst

Stage 3 (soak, 7 descriptor errors in 1.46 million doorbells, ILA capture): correctly read the capture as the block reading a stale descriptor before the driver's writes landed, and correctly stated the required order, descriptor stores then doorbell. But diagnosed it as missing cache maintenance on the ring, which is wrong because the ring is coherent memory. Pointed at the doorbell twice and asked to name the line as written, they first proposed dma_sync_single_for_device on the descriptor, then invented a wmb() that is not in the function and concluded the ordering was already fine and the cause lay elsewhere. Needed heavy prompting at every stage, and in the last stage invented code rather than reading what was there, which is the most concerning signal. The comment's reason (keep the doorbell cheap) is the wrong trade: this is the one write that needs ordering. messages.content: Uh, so starting at the highlighted handler, that runs in hard IRQ context first, and then the actual I2C read is deferred into the threaded IRQ handler, so the warning is basically the debug kernel catching that the interrupt path is doing something that can sleep or otherwise isn’t safe in hardirq context. On this board that shared RDY line fires both ADCs together, so if the top half does anything heavyweight, like taking a mutex, calling into I2C, or kicking the watchdog the wrong way, the debug kernel will complain and the production kernel could end up with IRQ latency spikes, missed samples, or even lockups if the handler ever blocks while interrupts are off. The fix is to keep the hardirq top half tiny, just timestamp and schedule the thread, and move anything that can sleep into the threaded handler or workqueue, with the locking split so the top half only uses spinlock and the bottom half uses mutex or sleepable I2C calls. I’d look in `qadc-core.c` for the IRQ handler split and the watchdog/reset path, and in `qadc-sysfs.c` if any sysfs write path is taking the same locks around config changes.

messages.content: Uh, so usually it works because the interrupt only lands when the code path is fast enough and the mutex isn’t contended, like the bad sleep is there but it doesn’t always get exercised in a way the debug kernel catches, and on production it just kind of slips by unless the timing lines up badly. What has to line up is basically the shared RDY interrupt firing while `qadc_hardirq()` is already in hardirq context and `qadc_wdog_kick()` hits that `cfg_lock` path at the wrong moment, so if the timer lock or whatever is hot you get the splat, but if not it seems fine. I’d change it by not calling `qadc_wdog_kick()` from the hardirq at all, and instead defer it to the threaded IRQ or a work item, so `qadc_hardirq()` just timestamps and bumps counters, and then `qadc_irq_thread()` or the reset work kicks the watchdog after the I2C read, in `qadc-core.c`.

With a direct push they located the actual path: qadc_hardirq -> qadc_wdog_kick -> qadc_wdog_period taking mutex_lock(&st->cfg_lock), and quoted the mutex.c sleeping-function line and the trace ordering. Twenty minutes later, when tools/qadc-mon.sh started up, lockdep fired again, and this time the report points at latest_show in qadc-sysfs.c, with qadc_hardirq on the other side of it.

// Write `parse`: turn the words of a typed command into a Command.
// Use ONE match on `words` with slice patterns. Rules:
//   no words                                   -> Empty
//   exactly "quit" or exactly "exit"           -> Quit
//   "go" then exactly one of north/south/east/west -> Go(direction)
//   "take" then at least one item              -> Take { first: first item, more: how many items follow it }
//   any other words                            -> Unknown(first word)
// No indexing with [i] and no .len() checks on `words` (rest.len() of a
// sub-slice you bound is fine).

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
enum Command {
    Empty,
    Quit,
    Go(String),
    Take { first: String, more: usize },
    Unknown(String),
}

fn parse(words: &[&str]) -> Command {
    match words {
        [] => Command::Empty,
        ["quit"] | ["exit"] => Command::Quit,
        ["go", dir @ ("north" | "south" | "east" | "west")] => Command::Go(dir.to_string()),
        ["take", first, rest @ ..] => Command::Take { first: first.to_string(), more: rest.len() },
        [word, ..] => Command::Unknown(word.to_string()),
    }
}

fn main() {
    let inputs: [&[&str]; 6] = [&[], &["go", "north"], &["go", "up"], &["take", "key", "map"], &["take"], &["exit"]];
    for words in inputs {
        println!("{words:?} -> {:?}", parse(words));
    }
}

fn classify(pair: (i32, i32)) -> String {
    match pair {
        (x, y) if x == y => format!("diagonal {x}"),
        (0, 0) => String::from("origin"),
        (x, 0) | (0, x) if x < 0 => format!("negative axis {x}"),
        (x, 0) | (0, x) => format!("axis {x}"),
        (n @ 1..=9, _) => format!("small first {n}"),
        _ => String::from("other"),
    }
}

        println!("{p:?} -> {}", classify(p));
    }
}

trait Meter {
    fn value(&self) -> u32;
    fn unit(&self) -> String {
        String::from("units")
    }
    fn report(&self) -> String {
        format!("{} {}", self.value(), self.unit())
    }
}

struct Count(u32);
struct Bytes(u32);

impl Meter for Count {
    fn value(&self) -> u32 {
        self.0
    }
}

impl Meter for Bytes {
    fn value(&self) -> u32 {
        self.0 / 1024
    }
    fn unit(&self) -> String {
        String::from("KiB")
    }
}

fn main() {

struct Filters {
    rules: Vec<Box<dyn Fn(u32) -> bool>>,
}

impl Filters {
    fn add_limit(&mut self, limit: &u32) {
        self.rules.push(Box::new(move |n| n <= *limit));
    }

    fn passes(&self, n: u32) -> bool {
        self.rules.iter().all(|rule| rule(n))
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut filters = Filters { rules: Vec::new() };
    filters.rules.push(Box::new(|n| n % 2 == 0));
    let limit = 10;
    filters.add_limit(&limit);
    let items = [4, 7, 12, 8];
    let kept: Vec<u32> = items.into_iter().filter(|&n| filters.passes(n)).collect();
    println!("{kept:?}");
}

For the arm `Some((x, 0)) => ...`, the pattern is doing several things at once when a value reaches it:

- It checks the outer enum/variant is `Some`, not `None`.
- It checks that the `Some` contains a 2-tuple.
- It checks the second element of that tuple is exactly `0`.
- It binds the first element of the tuple to the name `x`.
- It only allows the arm to run if all of those checks succeed.

So a single pattern can both test structure and extract data at the same time.

What a pattern can do that an `==` comparison cannot is destructure and bind pieces of the value in one step. `==` can only say whether two values are equal as a whole; it does not let you match nested shapes like `Some((_, 0))`, ignore parts with `_`, or bind subparts like `x` while matching.

With patterns, the compiler can check the match is exhaustive and warn you about missing cases, and it can also check for unreachable or redundant arms. With a plain chain of `if ... == ...` tests, it generally can’t prove that you covered every possible shape of the value.

That’s a big practical difference: a `match` gives you a kind of static coverage check. The compiler can tell you, for example, that you forgot `None`, or that one arm can never run because an earlier one already caught it.

Patterns also let the compiler enforce that the shape you’re matching is valid at the point of use, including binding only when the structure matches. With `if` chains, you usually end up doing those checks manually, and the compiler can’t reason about the whole decision tree as well.

fn route(cmd: &String, fallback: &str) -> String {
    match cmd.as_str() {

const STOP: &str = "stop";

fn route(cmd: &String, fallback: &str) -> String {
    match cmd.as_str() {
        STOP => String::from("halt"),
        c @ ("go" | "run") => format!("move ({c})"),
        fallback => format!("fallback {fallback}"),
        other => format!("unknown {other}"),
    }
}

fn main() {
    let default = "wait";
    for word in ["stop", "run", "wait", "jump"] {
        println!("{}", route(&String::from(word), default));
    }
}

The missing cases are: `Signal::Level(100)` and `Signal::Pulse { width: 0..=10, repeat: false }`.

The guarded `Pulse` arm counts for nothing in exhaustiveness checking because the compiler does not treat a guard as guaranteed. Even if the pattern shape matches, the guard might fail, so that arm cannot be used to prove all `Pulse` values are covered.

A fix without `_` is to split the `Pulse` case into unguarded arms that cover both possibilities explicitly:

- `Signal::Pulse { repeat: true, .. }`
- `Signal::Pulse { width: 0..=10, repeat: false }`
- `Signal::Pulse { width, repeat: false } if *width > 10`

That way every `Pulse` is covered by the pattern structure itself.

`_` would be the worse fix because it hides the structure the compiler could otherwise verify. It makes the match look complete without telling the reader which values are actually intended, and it can accidentally swallow cases you meant to handle separately.

const STOP: &str = "stop";

fn route(cmd: &String, fallback: &str) -> String {
    match cmd.as_str() {
        STOP => String::from("halt"),
        c @ ("go" | "run") => format!("move ({c})"),
        f if f == fallback => format!("fallback {fallback}"),
        other => format!("unknown {other}"),
    }
}

    let default = "wait";
    for word in ["stop", "run", "wait", "jump"] {
        println!("{}", route(&String::from(word), default));
    }
}
