WHAT A COMPLETE ANSWER TO THE STAGE ABOVE LOOKS LIKE:
With fix1, 25,521 of 100,000 frames (25.5%) still fail, and in each one only words 0 to 7 are wrong: one 8-word run, from an older frame of the same buffer (ages 8, 16, ...) or zero in the first frames. Words 0 to 7 are the 32 bytes of data[] that sit in the first 64-byte cache line with the 32-byte header of struct cap_buf (ts_ns, dma, seq, bytes, slot, flags): buffer 0 is at 0x7e140020. cap_complete() writes b->seq, b->bytes, b->ts_ns and b->flags before dma_sync_single_for_cpu(). If that line is still in the cache from the last round, the writes make it dirty while it still holds the old samples 0 to 7. arm64's invalidate (dcache_inval_poc) must not lose CPU data in a partial first line, so it cleans and invalidates it (dc civac): the old samples are written back over the ones the block just wrote, and the memcpy reads them. That happens only when the line survived in the L2, so about a quarter of the frames. Moving the sync above the field writes would cure this run but stays fragile: the line is shared, and any CPU write to it while the block owns the buffer can be lost or can overwrite DMA data (dma-api-howto: no cache-line sharing with a DMA_FROM_DEVICE buffer). Fix: keep the metadata out of the DMA buffer (struct cap_buf with a pointer to a separate 64 KiB buffer from kmalloc, page-aligned here, or dma_alloc_noncoherent()), or align data[] to ARCH_DMA_MINALIGN. The warnings: 'device driver failed to check map error', mapped at cap_alloc_buffers: dma_mapping_error() is never called, so a failed map would be programmed into a descriptor; check it and unwind. 'fclk0 already disabled' and 'already unprepared' come from devm_clk_release(): the clock came from devm_clk_get_enabled() and cap_remove() disables it too; drop that call. The same remove() frees buffers while the devm IRQ is still live.

NEVER say any of these, in any wording::
  - never synced for the CPU
  - multiples of CAP_NUM_BUFS
  - returns early
  - dc civac
  - keep the metadata out
  - never called

You may point at where to look. You may not name the mechanism or the fix. If your sentence would let them answer without thinking, rewrite it.

Header only. `cap_alloc_buffers()` maps `buf->data` starting after `struct adc_capture_hdr` in `struct cap_buf`.

So sync/copy misses words 0..7 of the frame payload. Likely the header area stays stale / unflushed.

Warnings: DMA API misuse. Missing map-error check, maybe wrong unmap size / direction, and sync on the wrong subrange.

Files: `capture.h`, `capture_dma.c`, `capture_cdev.c`.

move_object.question_summary: Worked one arm64 capture driver bug: stale data in DMA frames, through the seed (first failing run) and one probe (fix1 with syncs, 25.5% of frames with words 0 to 7 wrong, three rmmod warnings). Got to the right general area, cache staleness and the first cache line of the buffer, but pinned very little to actual lines, addresses or numbers, and several concrete claims were wrong. move_object.report_notes:
Scope covered: seed plus one probe of a four stage question; time ran out at the first probe.

Seed: the candidate reached the correct general diagnosis quickly, that the CPU was reading stale cached data rather than what the block had written, and that the read side sits in the completion copy path. They correctly tied the reported ages of 8, 16 and 24 to the ring wrapping through eight buffers, which was the one number they connected. Against that, two concrete claims were wrong: they said the buffers came from dma_alloc_coherent per buffer when cap_alloc_buffers uses kzalloc plus dma_map_single, and they assumed buffer 0 was 64 KiB aligned when dmesg prints an address 32 bytes into the struct. They introduced 32 KiB D-cache aliasing and cache colouring, which is not the mechanism here. They never named the zeroing allocation as the source of the zero words, never identified DMA_TO_DEVICE as the wrong direction for a capture, and never named the ownership calls needed around the copy. Two prompts for specifics moved them very little.

Probe (fix1, 25.52% of frames with an 8 word run at words 0 to 7, three rmmod warnings): the answer was a short header only note. They did get to the structurally important observation that the payload does not start at the top of struct cap_buf and that the first words share space with the header region, which is the right place to be looking. But they stopped there and did not carry it through: no mention of the 64 byte line, no use of the printed buffer 0 address, no account of what cap_complete writes before the sync (b->seq, b->bytes, b->ts_ns, b->flags) or why that matters for a partly covered line, and no explanation of why it is roughly a quarter of frames rather than all of them. Their proposed cause, a sync on the wrong subrange or a wrong unmap size, is not what the patch shows: the map, sync and unmap all use CAP_FRAME_BYTES consistently and the directions in the diff are consistent. On the warnings they correctly identified the missing dma_mapping_error check in the allocation path, which is one of the three, but they guessed wrong unmap size and direction for the other two rather than reading the call traces, which point clearly at devm_clk_release and a double disable of the clock in remove. No fix was proposed: nothing about separating the metadata from the mapped region or about alignment, and nothing about the devm teardown ordering.

Overall: sound instincts about where cache coherency bugs live and a real, if partial, insight into the struct layout. Weak on evidence discipline. Across both stages the candidate repeatedly asserted mechanisms without checking them against the code and logs placed in front of them, and several assertions were contradicted by the first few lines of those files. Answers stayed at the level of category labels, DMA API misuse, cache staleness, rather than specific calls at specific points with a stated cost. For a mid level kernel driver role this is below the bar on the diagnostic rigour the question was testing, though the general direction finding was adequate. Prompting required was high, and two explicit requests for a line or a number produced little movement.
move_object.response: That is the right neighbourhood on the layout: you have spotted that the payload does not begin at the top of the structure, and that is genuinely where the remaining 8 words come from. I would have wanted you to carry it the rest of the way, using the buffer 0 address in the dmesg line and what cap_complete writes just before the sync, and the warnings are worth reading off their call traces rather than inferring: the two clock ones have a very specific origin in the teardown path. We are out of time, so I will stop us there. Thanks for working through it out loud, and for sticking with the trail from the first run to the patched one.

  name: Find why a capture driver's DMA frames hold old data
  topics: Linux platform drivers on arm64: streaming DMA mappings, buffer ownership and cache coherency, Memory-mapped registers: writel versus writel_relaxed and ordering against descriptor memory, Driver design trade-offs: coherent versus streaming buffers, devm teardown order and the device tree node
  seniority: mid
  brief (never shown to the candidate): A mid-level embedded software engineer (about 3 to 5 years) who writes Linux kernel drivers for embedded boards. The question follows one platform driver for an FPGA ADC capture block on an arm64 SoC whose fabric DMA port is not cache-coherent: a first test-pattern run where every frame has wrong words, then the team's first fix (mapping direction and syncs) with a run that still fails and three kernel warnings at rmmod, then a 40-minute soak that loses frames with a logic analyzer capture of one descriptor error, then a teammate's proposal to allocate the buffers with dma_alloc_coherent(). The first probe is the richest (a patch, a checker run and three kernel warnings, with the buffer layout and arm64's cache maintenance rules both in play); the last is the hardest (judging a fix that is half right, against its measured cost and a test too short to show anything). Let the candidate go as deep as they can in the time. Press for who owns each buffer at each moment, what the cache holds at each step, and reasoning tied to lines, addresses and numbers. In the opening, if they find the missing sync, ask whether adding only dma_sync_single_for_cpu() with the direction the buffer was mapped with would fix it. Strong candidates name specific things: dma_map_single(..., DMA_TO_DEVICE) in cap_alloc_buffers and no sync before cap_pool_push() copies b->data; 16-word runs starting at word 8; ages of 8, 16, 24; zero words in the first frames; buffer 0 at 0x7eea0020, 32 bytes into struct cap_buf; 25.5% of frames with only words 0 to 7 wrong after fix1; b->seq, b->bytes and b->ts_ns written before the sync; the partial first line in arm64's invalidate; 'device driver failed to check map error'; 'fclk0 already disabled' from devm_clk_get_enabled() plus clk_disable_unprepare() in cap_remove(); ctrl 0x80010000 in dmesg against ctrl 0x00010000 returned to the block 276 ns after the DESC_TAIL write; writel_relaxed() in cap_queue_buf(); 7 errors in about 1.46 million doorbells; 532.5 against 60.2 us per frame; 0 errors in 73,242 frames. If an answer names nothing from the files, ask for one line or number before moving on. A candidate who says 'it is a cache problem, flush it', 'make it volatile', 'add mb()' or 'use coherent memory' without saying which call, at which point, and what it costs has not answered; ask what the checker would show afterwards. Don't explain the DMA API, arm64 cache maintenance, memory barriers or the code to the candidate.

With fix1, 25,521 of 100,000 frames (25.5%) still fail, and in each one only words 0 to 7 are wrong: one 8-word run, from an older frame of the same buffer (ages 8, 16, ...) or zero in the first frames. Words 0 to 7 are the 32 bytes of data[] that sit in the first 64-byte cache line with the 32-byte header of struct cap_buf (ts_ns, dma, seq, bytes, slot, flags): buffer 0 is at 0x7e140020. cap_complete() writes b->seq, b->bytes, b->ts_ns and b->flags before dma_sync_single_for_cpu(). If that line is still in the cache from the last round, the writes make it dirty while it still holds the old samples 0 to 7. arm64's invalidate (dcache_inval_poc) must not lose CPU data in a partial first line, so it cleans and invalidates it (dc civac): the old samples are written back over the ones the block just wrote, and the memcpy reads them. That happens only when the line survived in the L2, so about a quarter of the frames. Moving the sync above the field writes would cure this run but stays fragile: the line is shared, and any CPU write to it while the block owns the buffer can be lost or can overwrite DMA data (dma-api-howto: no cache-line sharing with a DMA_FROM_DEVICE buffer). Fix: keep the metadata out of the DMA buffer (struct cap_buf with a pointer to a separate 64 KiB buffer from kmalloc, page-aligned here, or dma_alloc_noncoherent()), or align data[] to ARCH_DMA_MINALIGN. The warnings: 'device driver failed to check map error', mapped at cap_alloc_buffers: dma_mapping_error() is never called, so a failed map would be programmed into a descriptor; check it and unwind.   - returns early
  - dc civac
  - keep the metadata out
  - never called

struct Filters {
    rules: Vec<Box<dyn Fn(u32) -> bool>>,
}

impl Filters {
    fn add_limit(&mut self, limit: &u32) {
        self.rules.push(Box::new(move |n| n <= *limit));
    }

    fn passes(&self, n: u32) -> bool {
        self.rules.iter().all(|rule| rule(n))
    }

What it does when a value reaches it:

What it does when a value reaches it:
1. Checks the value is `Some(...)`.

The compiler gets exhaustiveness and reachability checking from patterns, which a chain of `==` comparisons can’t really provide.

With `match`, the compiler can see all possible shapes of the value and verify that every case is handled, or warn if some arm is impossible or redundant. It can also tell when two patterns overlap or when a later arm can never be reached.

An `if` / `else if` chain of `==` checks is just runtime boolean logic. The compiler usually can’t reason about it as a complete set of cases, so it can’t reliably prove coverage, missing branches, or unreachable branches in the same way.

fn route(cmd: &String, fallback: &str) -> String {
    match cmd.as_str() {

        other => format!("unknown {other}"),

Seed stage was strong and unprompted: the candidate read the snapshot correctly, placed all 300 items in ERROR at PO_AME_APPRV_PROCESS / GET_NEXT_APPROVER, and used the zero count at NOTIFY_APPROVER to rule out the mailer and the worklist as causes. They proposed a clean trace through WF_ITEMS and WF_ITEM_ACTIVITY_STATUSES into the error stack and then into the AME transaction for a single purchase order, and tied the failure to Friday's rule deployment and the new cost centres without being led.

First probe exposed a weakness: they over-read the uniformity of the failures as a systemic rule or code defect and reached for backing out Friday's deployment as the first action, without reconciling that against the error text. One nudge to read across the messages moved them properly: they recognised the named cost centres as Friday's twelve, located the fault in the owner data the rule depends on rather than in the engine, and proposed a sound check comparing distinct cost centres in the errors against the twelve with a branch for anything outside that set. They did not volunteer testing on a single purchase order before acting.

Second probe on recovery was good. They separated cause from recovery, explicitly refused a blind mass resubmit from the UI, proposed testing a recovery path on one or two items first, driving the stuck items back through the workflow admin tools or API from the errored activity, and working in small throttled batches with verification that items move out of ERROR and approvers actually receive work. They also thought about the operational consequence of releasing 300 approvals at once. On the follow up about items that leave error but produce nothing in the worklist, they correctly went to activity history first, asked whether the item reached the notification activity, and named running the workflow background process plus checking notification processing. They did blur mailer and worklist slightly, suggesting a down mailer would leave the worklist empty, which is not right, and they used loose language about resubmission or launching the notification activity. Never proposed touching PO tables directly at any point.

Overall: senior-level diagnostic reading of workflow state, sound recovery discipline, one prompted correction on the first probe and one gentle pull to surface the background process. Minor imprecision on mailer versus worklist.

I’d start by classifying the 41 mismatches in the recon and then line that up with the consumer log.

From the recon:
- 37 are **Paid in portal, open in D365**
- 4 are **Paid in D365, not paid in portal**

That already tells me it’s not a random sync drift, it’s a status propagation problem in both directions.

What stands out in the 37 row table is that they all look very similar:
- portal status = **Paid**
- portal updated_at is clustered around **09:14:05–09:14:29**
- D365 status = **Open**
- D365 last settlement = **PR-0929-02 reversed 09:13**

So I’d suspect the portal got the payment-posted events, but then later got the reversal events and either didn’t apply them, or applied them inconsistently.

The log supports that pretty strongly:
- at **09:02** the projection applies `VendPaymentPosted ... PaymentRunId=PR-0929-02 ... -> applied invoice=INV-5101 status=PAID`
- same pattern continues for the other invoices in that run
- at **09:13:40** the same invoices start getting `VendPaymentReversed ... PaymentRunId=PR-0929-02 ... -> applied invoice=INV-5101 status=APPROVED`

That means the consumer is definitely seeing reversal events and updating the portal side back to Approved for at least those invoices. So for the 37 cases, my first thought is: **the portal projection did receive the reversal and changed state, but the reconciliation export still shows Paid at 18:00 because either the projection/export is stale, or there’s a write-order / replay / snapshot issue around those rows.**

I’d specifically check these things:
1. **Does the portal DB actually have those invoices as Paid at 18:00, or is the export stale?**
   - compare portal table row timestamps with the recon cutoff.
2. **Did the reversal event land after the payment event in the same consumer partition / item order?**
   - the log shows the reversal comes later, so if ordering is wrong, that’s a clue.
3. **Are the 4 opposite-direction mismatches the mirror image of the same problem?**
   - since they are `Paid in D365, not paid in portal`, I’d look for invoices where D365 committed settlement but the portal projection didn’t get or didn’t apply the `VendPaymentPosted` event.
4. **Check whether the portal projection is using eventual consistency but the finance export is taking a point-in-time snapshot that races with consumer lag.**
   - but the log only shows about a minute gap between posted and reversed, so lag alone doesn’t fully explain why the recon is still off at 18:00.

The architecture file and the morning log together point me to the projection layer, not D365 itself:
- D365 says those invoices were settled then reversed on PR-0929-02
- the portal consumer is the component translating events into portal status
- the mismatch pattern is tightly grouped by the same payment run, which usually means a shared event-processing issue, not isolated invoice corruption

So my working theory would be: **there’s a bug or timing issue in the portal projection around reversals for PR-0929-02, causing the portal to leave invoices in Paid while D365 shows them as Open after reversal.**

If I had to prove it, I’d take one invoice like `INV-5101` and trace:
- raw event stream for `BusinessEventId` / `ControlNumber`
- portal projection row history
- the exact state at 18:00 used by the export

And then I’d compare that with the 4 opposite mismatches to see if they’re the same run in the opposite direction.

What stands out in the 37 row table is that they all look very similar:
- portal status = **Paid**
- portal updated_at is clustered around **09:14:05–09:14:29**

- at **09:02** the projection applies `VendPaymentPosted ... PaymentRunId=PR-0929-02 ... -> applied invoice=INV-5101 status=PAID`
- same pattern continues for the other invoices in that run
- at **09:13:40** the same invoices start getting `VendPaymentReversed ... PaymentRunId=PR-0929-02 ... -> applied invoice=INV-5101 status=APPROVED`

That means the consumer is definitely seeing reversal events and updating the portal side back to Approved for at least those invoices. So for the 37 cases, my first thought is: **the portal projection did receive the reversal and changed state, but the reconciliation export still shows Paid at 18:00 because either the projection/export is stale, or there’s a write-order / replay / snapshot issue around those rows.**

2. **Did the reversal event land after the payment event in the same consumer partition / item order?**

3. **Are the 4 opposite-direction mismatches the mirror image of the same problem?**

4. **Check whether the portal projection is using eventual consistency but the finance export is taking a point-in-time snapshot that races with consumer lag.**

The architecture file and the morning log together point me to the projection layer, not D365 itself:
- D365 says those invoices were settled then reversed on PR-0929-02
- the portal consumer is the component translating events into portal status

Strengths: good opening structure. The candidate split the 41 mismatches into the two directions, noticed the 37 rows share a portal updated_at cluster of 09:14:05 to 09:14:29 and a common 'PR-0929-02 reversed 09:13', and concluded correctly that this was a systematic event-processing issue tied to one payment run rather than random drift or per-invoice corruption. They also kept the four opposite-direction rows on their list as something to explain.

Weaknesses: they would not read the log closely. Their first two passes asserted that nothing after 09:13:40 touched INV-5101 and reached for 'stale export', 'stale replica snapshot' and 'eventual consistency / read timing' as explanations, all without a log line to support them. No red flags on remediation since we never got that far, but their stated fallbacks leaned on timing and snapshot explanations rather than evidence. # infra/agents/pr-fixer/budget_config.yaml
# PR fixer picks up a pull request when a CI check fails and tries to make the check pass.
# Owner: Platform Engineering. Harness: pr-fixer 0.9.
# Last change: 1 Oct 2026, "enable PR fixer on all repos" (PLAT-1184)
#
# Model: model-3 (the model provider), 1,000,000-token context window.
# List price, USD per 1M tokens: input 5.00 | cached input 0.50 | output 25.00

vendor_org:
  # Set in the model provider's console for the whole organisation; mirrored here for reference.
  # Applies to every API key in the org: ask-prod, pr-fixer-prod, sandbox-shared.
  monthly_spend_limit_usd: 90000       # once reached, the provider rejects every request until the 1st
  notify_at_percent: [50, 75, 90]
  notify_email: finance-ops@company.example

pr_fixer:
  api_key: pr-fixer-prod
  model: model-3
  temperature: 0.2
  max_tokens: 8192                     # per call
  context:
    history: full                      # every call sends the whole conversation so far
    compaction: false
    prompt_caching: false
  # max_turns: 60                      # TODO: set after the pilot (PLAT-1107)
  # max_run_usd:                       # TODO (PLAT-1107)
  api_retries:
    max_attempts: 5                    # on 429 and 5xx
    backoff_seconds: [2, 4, 8, 16, 32]
  trigger:
    on: check_run.completed
    conclusion: failure                # any failed check on any open PR
    repos: all                         # 41 repos since 1 Oct (pilot: 6 repos)
    skip_if_pr_label: no-agent
  tools: [read_file, search_code, edit_file, run_command, get_ci_log, push_commit, comment_on_pr]
  runner:
    pool: gha-agents-large
    concurrency: 12                    # runs at once
    job_timeout_minutes: 720
  logging:
    events: /var/log/pr-fixer/{run_id}/events.jsonl   # tokens per call, on the runner, kept 90 days
    metrics: none

- input: $5 / 1M
- output: $25 / 1M

- root cause: PR fixer token bloat, especially input tokens, across ~3,200 runs
- first change: `infra/agents/pr-fixer/budget_config.yaml` to add tighter spend/token limits and stop runaway runs

# infra/agents/pr-fixer/budget_config.yaml
# PR fixer picks up a pull request when a CI check fails and tries to make the check pass.
# Owner: Platform Engineering. Harness: pr-fixer 0.9.

#
# Model: model-3 (the model provider), 1,000,000-token context window.

vendor_org:
  # Set in the model provider's console for the whole organisation; mirrored here for reference.
  # Applies to every API key in the org: ask-prod, pr-fixer-prod, sandbox-shared.
  monthly_spend_limit_usd: 90000       # once reached, the provider rejects every request until the 1st
  notify_at_percent: [50, 75, 90]
  notify_email: finance-ops@company.example

pr_fixer:
  api_key: pr-fixer-prod
  model: model-3
  temperature: 0.2
  max_tokens: 8192                     # per call
  context:
    history: full                      # every call sends the whole conversation so far
    compaction: false
    prompt_caching: false
  # max_turns: 60                      # TODO: set after the pilot (PLAT-1107)
  # max_run_usd:                       # TODO (PLAT-1107)
  api_retries:
    max_attempts: 5                    # on 429 and 5xx

  tools: [read_file, search_code, edit_file, run_command, get_ci_log, push_commit, comment_on_pr]
  runner:
    pool: gha-agents-large
    concurrency: 12                    # runs at once

#
# Model: model-3 (the model provider), 1,000,000-token context window.

vendor_org:
  # Set in the model provider's console for the whole organisation; mirrored here for reference.
  # Applies to every API key in the org: ask-prod, pr-fixer-prod, sandbox-shared.
  monthly_spend_limit_usd: 90000       # once reached, the provider rejects every request until the 1st
  notify_at_percent: [50, 75, 90]
  notify_email: finance-ops@company.example

pr_fixer:
  api_key: pr-fixer-prod
  model: model-3
  temperature: 0.2
  max_tokens: 8192                     # per call
  context:
    history: full                      # every call sends the whole conversation so far
    compaction: false
    prompt_caching: false
  # max_turns: 60                      # TODO: set after the pilot (PLAT-1107)

Yeah, that pretty much says the higher budget is not buying you much on flaky/infra chases. If none of the successful fixes in that class cost more than $16.77, then anything way above that is mostly just letting runaway cases keep burning money, not helping more PRs get fixed.

In other words, a higher budget there mostly buys you extra waste, not extra fixes. I’d set the cap just above the largest observed successful flaky chase, then revisit if real new fixes start getting cut off.

Across four stages the candidate showed a consistently reasonable direction of travel and genuine responsiveness to correction, but very little independent extraction of evidence.

Put limits on each key; keep the org limit as a backstop above their sum. 5. Monthly: spend by key and task class against forecast; runs, fix rate and cost per fixed PR; p50, p95, p99 and max per class; runs stopped by each limit and their cost; the top runs with the reason; next month's forecast as a range with its assumptions.

NEVER say any of these, in any wording::
  - above the p95
  - caps the wrong side
  - shared with ask-prod
  - cannot be the thing
  - cost per fixed PR
  - down for the rest

You may point at where to look. You may not name the mechanism or the fix. If your sentence would let them answer without thinking, rewrite it.

Yeah, ok — building it up:
- If the typical run is around ~$1, then 3,200 runs is already about $3.2k.
- Only a small fraction should ever hit a ceiling, because the class cap is there to stop the long tail; even if I assume a few hundred worst-case runs and a few dollars extra on those, that only gets me into the low tens of thousands, not way above it.
- So $28k is basically: baseline successful runs + some capped investigations + a buffer for the tail.

Quick verdicts:
- The $50-in-the-system-prompt fix: no, that’s not a real control. It’s too easy to bypass and it won’t protect you from drift or repeated retries.
- Dropping the provider org limit to $25,000: also no, not by itself. That would just create a hard outage risk for everything sharing the org, and it’s not targeted to PR fixer.

So I’d keep the run-level caps and alerting, not rely on prompt text or a blunt org-wide cut.

move_object.note: Closed. Candidate reasons in the right direction but rarely extracts numbers from exhibits without them being read out.
move_object.question_summary: Senior candidate taken through the PR fixer overspend: diagnosis from the histogram and export, the 9 hour runaway trace, per class limits, then finance's five questions. Consistently sound in direction, consistently thin on evidence: numbers only appeared after exhibit rows were read to them, and they repeatedly said they could not see the files. Verdicts on the self-enforced budget and the org limit cut were correct but unsupported.
move_object.report_notes:
Across four stages the candidate showed decent instincts and poor grounding.

Diagnosis: isolated pr-fixer as the driver and named the spike days, and eventually landed on per request input growth and cached_input_tokens of 0, concluding it was a context runaway not a volume problem. That took three asks. They never read the histogram, gave no median, mean or percentile, and in the budget config pointed only vaguely, never naming the commented out per run limits, full history with caching off, or that the only live ceiling was the org wide monthly one.

Run 77120: described an edit, test, fail loop with accumulating context making later turns dearer, and asserted superlinear growth, but never put a number on it despite pointers to the per call table, the hour by hour table and the model's own text at call 21. Did not name input as nearly the whole bill, nor how the run actually terminated. Stop proposals were the right family (no new information, retry budget, PR comment on exit) but untethered to any call number or to the flat failure rates.

Per class limits: good structure and a clean description of what happens at the limit (stop, mark budget exhausted not failed, comment, preserve partial patch), but initial tiering was inverted, giving the largest budgets to the classes where spending never bought a fix. After flaky_or_infra was read out they corrected quickly and well. No arithmetic for other classes, no soft limit with human handoff, and they never noticed the class label is assigned after the run, so the class holding the runaways is invisible when a limit would fire.

Finance questions: first forecast was essentially a repeat of uncontrolled October (about $46k), which ignored the limits they had just designed. Prompted, they moved to about $28k but asserted it. Asked to build it, they produced a baseline of roughly $3.2k from 3,200 runs near the median, then a vague few hundred capped runs and a buffer, which does not reconcile with $28k; they never resampled, never contrasted mean against median as an artefact of a handful of runaways, never addressed why the pilot's $2.30 missed the tail, and gave no stated basis for a range. On the self enforced $50 they said correctly that prompt text is not a control, but did not use the evidence available that the same model had already stated the right conclusion mid run and continued, nor place enforcement in the harness per call, nor mention overshoot between checks. On the org limit they correctly objected on blast radius grounds and said it was untargeted, but did not identify which key sharing the account would be hit, what date it would have tripped, or propose per key limits with the org limit as a backstop. Questions 3 and 5 (alerting design and monthly report contents) were never reached.

Overall: a candidate who reasons soundly once data is placed in front of them, but who did not independently mine the exhibits, avoided quantification throughout, and needed heavy prompting at every stage. Judgement is senior shaped; evidence discipline is not.
move_object.response: That is a fair place to stop. For what it is worth, the two verdicts are the right ones, and the reasons underneath them are worth being sharper about than you were: with the self enforced budget there is something the agent itself already said mid run that settles it, and with the org limit the objection is a specific date and a specific key, not a general one. And the forecast arithmetic you just did lands nearer ten thousand than twenty eight, which is a stronger story for finance than a buffer, because it is the caps that make the number defensible at all. Thanks for working through all of it with me. That is the end of the interview.

You are interviewing one candidate on one question. Your entire scope is this question -- never mention or compare to another.

`response` is what the candidate reads: your own words, conversational, no labels or JSON.
`note` is for you, next turn. Write what you are still trying to find out.
Grade what they demonstrated, not what they might know.
Write every field with plain punctuation: commas, full stops, colons. Never an em dash or an en dash. Call the candidate "the candidate" or "they", never "he" or "she".

A probe's description and a hint's text are intent, not a script. Carry what they say, add nothing to them, and word it so it follows on from what the candidate just said. Never read one out verbatim.


`question_position` tells you where this sits. n=1 -- greet them, then the question. Later -- a line on how the last one went, then move on. n == of -- this is the last question; close the interview rather than hand off.

FINISHED QUESTIONS:
  (this is the first question)

THIS QUESTION:
  name: A runaway model bill from a background coding agent
  topics: Long-horizon agents: fat-tailed cost, and why re-sent context makes a run's cost grow faster than linearly, Cost governors: per-run budgets, turn caps, loop detection and kill switches outside the agent, Agent spend observability, alerting and forecasting for finance
  seniority: senior
  brief (never shown to the candidate): Senior AI engineer. The question follows the platform team's PR fixer, a background coding agent whose October model bill was $61,218 against a $22,000 forecast: the cost distribution, the vendor's export and the budget config; then the trace of the most expensive run; then a view of every run by task class; then finance's questions. The first probe is the richest (a 9-hour, $4,812.88 run: why its cost grew as it did, where it should have stopped, and the stops and handoff that would have ended it); the last is the hardest (answering finance on forecasting a fat-tailed cost, a budget the agent is asked to enforce on itself, alerting, lowering an org-wide limit, and a monthly report). Let the candidate go as deep as they can in the time. Press for answers grounded in the exhibits: strong candidates name specific things (the mean of $16.21 against the p95 of $10.48 on the histogram, the dollars in the $2k to $5k bin, pr-fixer's cached_input_tokens of 0, input tokens per request on quiet days against 2 Oct or Saturday 17 Oct in the export, history: full with compaction and prompt_caching false, max_tokens: 8192, the commented-out max_turns and max_run_usd, the org-wide monthly_spend_limit_usd and the keys it covers, the model's own text at call 21, its 50-passes-in-a-row bar, the failure rate with each edit, the hour-by-hour table, the eight top runs on one test, the fixed dependency updates above the overall p99) and tie each to a decision. If an answer names nothing from the files, ask for one line or number before moving on. If they ask how the $22,000 forecast splits: the in-product assistant $9,000, PR fixer $12,000 (3,000 runs at $4.00), the engineering sandbox $1,000. Don't explain token pricing, context windows, percentiles or what a kill switch is to the candidate.

DECIDE:
Read the expected solution against what they have actually said. On the moves that stay on this stage, name the gap in one line.
CLARIFY        they asked you something. Answer it, do not grade it.
FOLLOW_UP      ask about the gap without giving it away. Good when there is time and they are still engaging.
HINT           you have pulled and the gap has not moved, or time is short. Costs them score.
PROBE          this stage has given you what it will. Write `asked` and `last_stage_performance` for the stage you are closing, then go deeper. No gap -- you are leaving it.

REDIRECT       they are fishing for the answer.
`time_left_in_stage_s` tells you how hard to press. Four minutes means dig. Thirty seconds means close it out cleanly.

# infra/agents/pr-fixer/budget_config.yaml
# PR fixer picks up a pull request when a CI check fails and tries to make the check pass.
# Owner: Platform Engineering. Harness: pr-fixer 0.9.
# Last change: 1 Oct 2026, "enable PR fixer on all repos" (PLAT-1184)
#
# Model: model-3 (the model provider), 1,000,000-token context window.
# List price, USD per 1M tokens: input 5.00 | cached input 0.50 | output 25.00

vendor_org:
  # Set in the model provider's console for the whole organisation; mirrored here for reference.
  # Applies to every API key in the org: ask-prod, pr-fixer-prod, sandbox-shared.
  monthly_spend_limit_usd: 90000       # once reached, the provider rejects every request until the 1st
  notify_at_percent: [50, 75, 90]
  notify_email: finance-ops@company.example

pr_fixer:
  api_key: pr-fixer-prod
  model: model-3
  temperature: 0.2
  max_tokens: 8192                     # per call
  context:
    history: full                      # every call sends the whole conversation so far
    compaction: false
    prompt_caching: false
  # max_turns: 60                      # TODO: set after the pilot (PLAT-1107)
  # max_run_usd:                       # TODO (PLAT-1107)
  api_retries:
    max_attempts: 5                    # on 429 and 5xx
    backoff_seconds: [2, 4, 8, 16, 32]
  trigger:
    on: check_run.completed
    conclusion: failure                # any failed check on any open PR
    repos: all                         # 41 repos since 1 Oct (pilot: 6 repos)
    skip_if_pr_label: no-agent
  tools: [read_file, search_code, edit_file, run_command, get_ci_log, push_commit, comment_on_pr]
  runner:
    pool: gha-agents-large
    concurrency: 12                    # runs at once
    job_timeout_minutes: 720
  logging:
    events: /var/log/pr-fixer/{run_id}/events.jsonl   # tokens per call, on the runner, kept 90 days
    metrics: none

vendor_org:
  # Set in the model provider's console for the whole organisation; mirrored here for reference.
  # Applies to every API key in the org: ask-prod, pr-fixer-prod, sandbox-shared.
  monthly_spend_limit_usd: 90000       # once reached, the provider rejects every request until the 1st
  notify_at_percent: [50, 75, 90]
  notify_email: finance-ops@company.example

pr_fixer:
  api_key: pr-fixer-prod
  model: model-3
  temperature: 0.2
  max_tokens: 8192                     # per call
  context:
    history: full                      # every call sends the whole conversation so far
    compaction: false
    prompt_caching: false
  # max_turns: 60                      # TODO: set after the pilot (PLAT-1107)
  # max_run_usd:                       # TODO (PLAT-1107)
  api_retries:
    max_attempts: 5                    # on 429 and 5xx
    backoff_seconds: [2, 4, 8, 16, 32]

    on: check_run.completed
    conclusion: failure                # any failed check on any open PR
    repos: all                         # 41 repos since 1 Oct (pilot: 6 repos)

  tools: [read_file, search_code, edit_file, run_command, get_ci_log, push_commit, comment_on_pr]
  runner:
    pool: gha-agents-large

vendor_org:

  monthly_spend_limit_usd: 90000       # once reached, the provider rejects every request until the 1st

pr_fixer:

vendor_org:

That spread says the per-call payload is wildly different day to day, and the expensive days are sending huge contexts into the model, not just lots of small calls. So this feels like a narrow runaway-context problem on some runs, not a broad steady-cost problem across all PR fixer traffic.

move_object.report_notes:
Asked: explain a $61,218 October model bill against a $22,000 forecast, grounded in the cost-per-run histogram, the vendor export and PR fixer's budget config, and say what they would change first.

What they demonstrated: correct first instinct that pr-fixer-prod, not ask-assistant, drives the bill, and they picked the spike days (2, 6, 13, 19, 22, 29, 30 Oct) straight off the export. After a direct instruction naming the exact rows and columns, they computed input tokens per request: about 39k on 1 Oct, 251k on 2 Oct, 629k on 17 Oct, and observed cached_input_tokens is zero on every pr-fixer row. From that they drew the right qualitative conclusion: a narrow runaway-context problem, not steady fleet-wide cost. That is the strongest moment of the answer and it came late.

What was missing: no reading of the histogram at all. Never named the median of $1.16 against the mean of $16.21, the p95, the 20 runs over $500 taking $42,371 (82% of pr-fixer's $51,887), or the eight runs in the $2k to $5k bin at $30,298. When pressed twice for those figures they declined and asked to be given the bins; they also declined to attempt the export divide until told explicitly which three rows to use. Early answers were hedged ("on the order of tens of thousands", "I think the mean is way above the median") rather than computed. They gestured at budget_config.yaml as the place to fix things but never named what is actually in it: history: full with compaction and prompt_caching false, the commented-out max_turns and max_run_usd, max_tokens 8192, or the org-wide monthly limit that October never approached. No concrete first change beyond "add tighter spend/token limits", and no mention of in-run cost visibility (metrics: none).

Prompting required: heavy. One hint spent, plus two further explicit pointers to specific rows and columns. The correct analysis only appeared once the arithmetic had been set up for them. Reluctance to estimate from a chart is defensible caution but, at senior level, leaving the central quantitative argument to the interviewer is the main concern here: they would not have had the numbers for Thursday's review on their own. Ran out of time before the trace, the task-class view or the finance questions, so depth beyond this first exhibit is untested.
move_object.response: Good, those are the numbers I was after, and your reading of them is right: the payload per call is swinging by more than an order of magnitude, and with nothing cached you are paying full price for all of it every time. That is where the month went, and the histogram would have told you the same story even faster, that the money is sitting in a handful of runs rather than spread across the 3,200. We are out of time, so I will stop us there. Thanks for working it through, and for being straight about what you could and could not read off the exhibits. Someone will be in touch about next steps.

WHAT A COMPLETE ANSWER TO THE STAGE ABOVE LOOKS LIKE:
No single cap works. At the overall p95 ($10.48) it would have stopped 46 runs that went on to fix the PR; at the overall p99 ($47.05), 4 dependency updates that were fixed at up to $82.21; and $47 is still twenty times anything a lint fix ever needed ($2.19). Set limits per task class from the fixed runs: a soft limit near the class's fixed p95 and a hard cap between the most a fix has cost and about twice that, or near the fixed p95 where more spend never produced a fix. Roughly: lint_format $3, type_check $12, test_failure $30, dependency_update $150 with a checkpoint near $30 (fixed p95 $29.98), flaky_or_infra $5 (29 fixes in 266 runs, none above $16.77). Replayed on October, caps like these stop 63 runs, 1 of them a fix, and the month costs about $8,950 instead of $51,887. At the soft limit the run pauses, posts what it has done, and asks a human for more budget; a long dependency update shows progress (fewer failing tests, new files changed) and a loop does not, so more budget is granted on progress. At the hard cap it stops with the handoff from the last step. The catch: the class is assigned after the run, and flaky_or_infra, the class holding almost every runaway (17 of the 20 runs over $500, and all ten of the most expensive), is invisible at trigger time. So add a pre-flight check (does the failing test also fail on main, is it on a known-flaky list, does the log match an infra error such as a registry 429 or a simulator that failed to boot) and don't start the agent on those: comment on the PR and route the test to its owners. That alone removes the eight most expensive runs, all on test_reschedule_notifies_driver ($30,298, 58% of the month). Keep the no-progress and repeated-action detectors on every class; they tell a long run from a loop at any budget, and the caps are the backstop. Review the limits monthly by counting the fixes each one stopped.

NEVER say any of these, in any wording::
  - above the p95
  - caps the wrong side
  - shared with ask-prod
  - from the fixed runs
  - pre-flight check
  - granted on progress

You may point at where to look. You may not name the mechanism or the fix. If your sentence would let them answer without thinking, rewrite it.

I’d set tiered per-run limits by task class rather than one hard cap for everything, because the cost profile sounds really skewed. So for the cheap/common classes like lint fixes or small dependency bumps, I’d use a lower token / tool-call ceiling and a short wall-clock timeout. For the expensive classes like feature-test or flaky-test chases, I’d allow a higher budget, but still cap it so it can’t spiral forever.

Concretely, I’d probably do something like:
- low-complexity classes: low call count cap, lower token cap, and a shorter time limit
- medium classes: moderate cap
- known-expensive classes: higher cap, but with a hard upper bound

At the moment a run hits a limit, the system should stop the agent immediately, cancel further tool use, and mark the run as budget-exhausted rather than failed. The developer should get a clear PR comment or notification that says the agent stopped because it reached its budget, plus the last successful action and maybe a short summary of what it tried.

If there is a safe partial patch, it should still be left in a branch or commit so the developer can inspect it. If not, the system should leave no changes but still explain why it stopped.

If you want, I can turn that into a specific policy table with example numbers per class.

WHAT A COMPLETE ANSWER TO THE STAGE ABOVE LOOKS LIKE:
No single cap works. At the overall p95 ($10.48) it would have stopped 46 runs that went on to fix the PR; at the overall p99 ($47.05), 4 dependency updates that were fixed at up to $82.21; and $47 is still twenty times anything a lint fix ever needed ($2.19). Set limits per task class from the fixed runs: a soft limit near the class's fixed p95 and a hard cap between the most a fix has cost and about twice that, or near the fixed p95 where more spend never produced a fix. Roughly: lint_format $3, type_check $12, test_failure $30, dependency_update $150 with a checkpoint near $30 (fixed p95 $29.98), flaky_or_infra $5 (29 fixes in 266 runs, none above $16.77). Replayed on October, caps like these stop 63 runs, 1 of them a fix, and the month costs about $8,950 instead of $51,887. At the soft limit the run pauses, posts what it has done, and asks a human for more budget; a long dependency update shows progress (fewer failing tests, new files changed) and a loop does not, so more budget is granted on progress. At the hard cap it stops with the handoff from the last step. The catch: the class is assigned after the run, and flaky_or_infra, the class holding almost every runaway (17 of the 20 runs over $500, and all ten of the most expensive), is invisible at trigger time. So add a pre-flight check (does the failing test also fail on main, is it on a known-flaky list, does the log match an infra error such as a registry 429 or a simulator that failed to boot) and don't start the agent on those: comment on the PR and route the test to its owners. That alone removes the eight most expensive runs, all on test_reschedule_notifies_driver ($30,298, 58% of the month). Keep the no-progress and repeated-action detectors on every class; they tell a long run from a loop at any budget, and the caps are the backstop. Review the limits monthly by counting the fixes each one stopped.

NEVER say any of these, in any wording::
  - above the p95
  - caps the wrong side
  - shared with ask-prod
  - from the fixed runs
  - pre-flight check
  - granted on progress

You may point at where to look. You may not name the mechanism or the fix. If your sentence would let them answer without thinking, rewrite it.

I’d set tiered per-run limits by task class rather than one hard cap for everything, because the cost profile sounds really skewed. So for the cheap/common classes like lint fixes or small dependency bumps, I’d use a lower token / tool-call ceiling and a short wall-clock timeout. For the expensive classes like feature-test or flaky-test chases, I’d allow a higher budget, but still cap it so it can’t spiral forever.

Concretely, I’d probably do something like:
- low-complexity classes: low call count cap, lower token cap, and a shorter time limit
- medium classes: moderate cap
- known-expensive classes: higher cap, but with a hard upper bound

At the moment a run hits a limit, the system should stop the agent immediately, cancel further tool use, and mark the run as budget-exhausted rather than failed. The developer should get a clear PR comment or notification that says the agent stopped because it reached its budget, plus the last successful action and maybe a short summary of what it tried.

If there is a safe partial patch, it should still be left in a branch or commit so the developer can inspect it. If not, the system should leave no changes but still explain why it stopped.

If you want, I can turn that into a specific policy table with example numbers per class.

## 1. Two ways to abstract

You already know one way to write code that works for many types: generics (sub-module 09). `fn show<T: Display>(item: &T)` works for any `T` that implements `Display`. The compiler handles it by monomorphisation: it writes one copy of `show` for every concrete type you call it with, `show::<i32>`, `show::<String>` and so on. Each copy knows its type exactly, so every call is a direct call that can be inlined. This is static dispatch: the method is chosen at compile time.

Generics have one limit: each use picks one type. A `Vec<T>` holds values of a single type `T`. A function returning `impl Trait` returns one concrete type, even if the caller cannot name it. So how do you keep a text box, a checkbox and a button in one list and call `render` on each?

Rust's answer is a trait object, written `dyn Trait`. A trait object stands for "some value of a type that implements `Trait`; which type is decided at run time". There is only one copy of the code that uses it, and each method call is looked up at run time. This is dynamic dispatch.

Generics (`T: Trait`)Trait objects (`dyn Trait`)

Method chosenat compile timeat run time, through a vtable

Copies of your functionone per concrete typeone

Inliningyesusually not

Mixed types in one `Vec`noyes: `Vec<Box<dyn Trait>>`

The Rust Book (ch. 18.2, "Using Trait Objects to Allow for Values of Different Types") builds a GUI library this way. Our `widgets.rs` is a small version of it:

```
let parts: Vec<Box<dyn Render>> =
    vec![Box::new(Text("hello".into())), Box::new(Checkbox(true))];
for part in &parts {
    println!("{}", part.render()); // which render? decided per element, at run time
}
```

The `Vec` still holds one type: `Box<dyn Render>`. What differs is the type inside each box.

## 2. Behind a pointer: fat pointers and vtables

A `Text` and a `Checkbox` have different sizes. So what size is a `dyn Render`? There is no single answer: `dyn Render` is an unsized type (its size is not known at compile time). Rust can only store values whose size it knows, on the stack, in a struct field or in a `Vec` slot. That is why a trait object always sits behind a pointer: `&dyn Render`, `&mut dyn Render` or `Box<dyn Render>`.

That pointer is a fat pointer: two machine words.

- A data pointer to the value itself (the `Checkbox` on the heap, or wherever it lives).

- A vtable pointer to a table the compiler built for that pair (concrete type, trait).

A vtable ("virtual method table") holds the information needed to use the value without knowing its type: how to drop it, its size and alignment, then one entry per trait method, each pointing at the machine code for that type's version of the method.

Two boxed trait objects. Each element of `parts` is a data pointer plus a vtable pointer. Each (type, Render) pair has its own vtable whose rows point at that type's code.

A call such as `part.label()` does three things at run time: follow the vtable pointer, read the `label` row, call the function found there with the data pointer as `self`. That indirect call is the cost of dynamic dispatch: one extra memory read, and the compiler usually cannot inline the call because it does not know which function it will be.

You can see the "fat" part directly. `static_vs_dyn.rs` prints the sizes of a thin and a fat reference:

```
&i32: 8 bytes, &dyn Display: 16 bytes
```

These numbers are for a 64-bit machine (8-byte pointers). The rule is "two pointers instead of one", not "16 bytes". The exact layout of a vtable (row order, whether two values of the same type share one vtable) is a compiler detail you never rely on.

A `Box<dyn Trait>` also costs a heap allocation per value, because each value must live somewhere the box can point to. A borrowed `&dyn Trait` needs no allocation: `let one: &dyn Render = &Text("plain".into());` in `widgets.rs` points at a value that is already somewhere.

## 3. `Sized` and `?Sized`

Every generic parameter has a hidden bound: `T: Sized`, "the size of `T` is known at compile time". That is almost always what you want, since the function may need to store a `T`. But it means this generic function cannot be called with a trait object:

```
fn show_any<T: Display>(item: &T) -> String { format!("[{item}]") }

let m: Box<dyn Display> = Box::new(7);
show_any(m.as_ref()); // T would be `dyn Display`, which is not Sized
```

```
error[E0277]: the size for values of type `dyn std::fmt::Display` cannot be known at compilation time
```

Write `T: ?Sized` ("`T` may or may not be sized") to remove the hidden bound. This is fine here because `show_any` only ever touches `T` through a reference `&T`, which is a pointer of known size:

```
fn show_any<T: Display + ?Sized>(item: &T) -> String { format!("[{item}]") }
```

Now `T` can be `dyn Display`, or `str` (another unsized type you have used since 03 behind `&str`).

## 4. Choosing between generics and trait objects

SituationUseWhy

A function used with one type at a timegeneric `T: Trait` or `impl Trait`fastest; no allocation; inlinable

A list (or field) holding several types at once`Vec<Box<dyn Trait>>`a `Vec<T>` has exactly one `T`

Types chosen at run time (from a config file, user input, plugins)`Box<dyn Trait>`the compiler cannot know the type

Want less generated code (many types, big function)`&dyn Trait`one copy instead of one per type

A small, fixed set of kinds you controlan `enum`see section 9

A common mistake is to think `Vec<T>` with `T: Trait` can hold "anything that implements `Trait`". It cannot: `T` is one type, chosen by the caller. Only `dyn Trait` erases the concrete type.

## 5. Default methods through `dyn`

A trait may give a method a default body. In `widgets.rs`, `label` has a default and `Checkbox` overrides it:

```
trait Render {
    fn render(&self) -> String;
    fn label(&self) -> String { String::from("(unnamed)") }
}
impl Render for Checkbox {
    fn render(&self) -> String { /* ... */ }
    fn label(&self) -> String { String::from("checkbox") }
}
```

How does a vtable deal with this? Every vtable has a row for every trait method, defaults included. For `Checkbox` the `label` row points at `Checkbox::label`. For `Text`, which does not override it, the row points at the default body compiled for `Text`. A default method is like a small generic function: the compiler makes one copy of it per implementing type.

This explains what happens when a default calls another method of the same trait. Inside the copy compiled for `Text`, `self` is a `&Text`, so `self.render()` calls `Text::render`; the type is known there, so that inner call is static. Only the outer call through the trait object goes through the vtable.

To predict what a default method does for a type, read it as if you had pasted its body into that type's `impl` block. Every `self.method()` inside it then resolves to that type's own `method`, overridden or not.

## 6. Dyn compatibility: which traits can be objects

A vtable is a fixed list: one row per method, each pointing at one function. Some methods cannot fit in such a list, so a trait containing them cannot be used as `dyn Trait`. Such a trait is not dyn compatible (older texts say "not object safe"). The main rules, from the Rust Reference:

Method shapeProblem for a vtable

`fn copy(&self) -> Self`The caller must reserve space for the returned `Self`, but behind `dyn` its size is unknown.

`fn put<V: ToString>(&mut self, v: V)`A generic method is a family of functions, one per `V`. A fixed list cannot hold an open-ended family.

`fn new() -> Self` (no `self`)There is no value, so no vtable to look in.

Uncomment both `doubled` lines in `dyn_compat.rs` to see the error:

```
error[E0038]: the trait `Shape` is not dyn compatible
  ...because method `doubled` references the `Self` type in its return type
```

There are two ways out.

- Keep the method off the vtable with `where Self: Sized`. The trait becomes dyn compatible again, and the method can still be called on concrete types, but not on a `dyn Shape`. `dyn_compat.rs` does this with `doubled_sized`.

- Change the method's shape so it fits in a vtable: return `Box<dyn Shape>` instead of `Self`, or take `&dyn ToString` (or a `String`) instead of a generic `V`. Each costs something: a heap allocation, a conversion, or a second dynamic call.

`Box<dyn Trait>` does not make an incompatible trait compatible. The problem is the trait's methods, not where the object is stored.

## 7. Supertraits

`trait Shape: Debug { ... }` says "every type that implements `Shape` must also implement `Debug`". `Debug` is a supertrait of `Shape`. Two consequences:

- Code that has a `Shape` may use `Debug` too. Debug's method joins Shape's vtable, so `println!("{:?}", shapes[0])` works on a `Box<dyn Shape>`.

- Because the supertrait's methods join the vtable, the supertrait must be dyn compatible as well. `Debug` and `Display` are. `Clone` is not (`clone` returns `Self`), and neither is `Default` (`default()` has no `self` and returns `Self`). So `trait Shape: Clone` makes `dyn Shape` impossible.

```
use std::fmt::Debug;
trait Shape: Debug { fn area(&self) -> f64; }

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Square(f64);
impl Shape for Square { fn area(&self) -> f64 { self.0 * self.0 } }
// impl Shape for Square requires Square: Debug, which the derive provides.
```

## 8. Boxed closures and `'static`

Every closure has its own unnamed type, even two closures with the same signature (10). So a list of closures needs a trait object: `Vec<Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool>>`. `Fn`, `FnMut` and `FnOnce` are traits like any other.

A rule you will meet often: in a struct field or in a function's return type, `Box<dyn Trait>` is short for `Box<dyn Trait + 'static>`. `'static` here means "the value inside does not borrow anything that could go away". A closure meets it if every captured value is owned by the closure: copied in, cloned in or moved in. It fails if it captures a reference to a local variable or to a parameter.

```
fn prefix_rule(prefix: &str) -> Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool> {
    let owned = prefix.to_string();                // the closure gets its own copy
    Box::new(move |s| s.starts_with(owned.as_str()))
}
```

If the closure used `prefix` directly, it would hold a borrow that only lives as long as the caller's string, and the compiler refuses:

```
error: lifetime may not live long enough
  returning this value requires that `'1` must outlive `'static`
```

`move` moves whatever the closure names. If the variable is itself a reference (`prefix: &str`, `limit: &u32`), `move` moves the reference into the closure. The closure still borrows. To own the data, copy or clone it out first: `let limit = *limit;` or `let owned = prefix.to_string();`.

A `&dyn Fn(..)` parameter, by contrast, may borrow freely: it is only used during the call. Writing other lifetimes, such as `Box<dyn Fn() + 'a>`, is covered in 14.

## 9. Consuming a trait object; trait objects vs enums

A method may take its receiver as `self: Box<Self>`. It then consumes the box: after the call, the object is gone. The Book's state pattern (ch. 18.3, "Implementing an Object-Oriented Design Pattern") uses this so a state transition uses up the old state. `state.rs` is adapted from it:

```
trait State {
    fn submit(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn State>;
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str;
}
impl State for Draft {
    fn submit(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn State> { Box::new(Review) }
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str { "draft" }
}
```

`self: Box<Self>` is dyn compatible: the receiver is a pointer of known size, so the call can go through the vtable. The catch is that you must own the box to call it. A shared or mutable borrow of a box is not enough; you cannot move a box out from behind a reference. When the box sits inside something else, take it out first:

Where the box livesHow to take it out

`Option<Box<dyn State>>``opt.take()` leaves `None` behind

a field or variable of a type with a default`std::mem::take(&mut x)` (11)

a `Vec<Box<dyn T>>`, all of it`v.drain(..)` or `mem::take(&mut v)`, which leave it empty

a `Vec`, one element`v.remove(i)` or `v.pop()`

### Trait objects or an enum?

The same states could be an `enum State { Draft, Review, Published }` with `match` in each operation. The two designs make different changes cheap:

ChangeTrait objectsEnum + match

Add a new kind (type / variant)one new type and its `impl`; no other code changesedit every `match`

Add a new operationadd a method to the trait and to every typeone new function with one `match`; the compiler checks every case

Types from outside your crate (plugins)yesno: the set is closed

Cost per callvtable call, heap allocation per boxa `match` on a tag; no allocation needed

Ask the Tutor about any of these. Try to answer first.

- Why must `dyn Trait` always sit behind a pointer? What are the two halves of that pointer?

- Why can a trait with `fn copy(&self) -> Self` not be a trait object, while `fn copy(&self) -> Box<dyn Trait>` is fine?

- A default method calls `self.unit()`. For a type that overrides `unit`, which `unit` runs, and why?

- Why does a closure stored in a `Box<dyn Fn()>` field have to own what it captures?

- What would you gain and lose by rewriting `state.rs` as an enum?

[entity 908 · fat-pointer.png · diagram]
Diagram: a trait object is a fat pointer.

Left, two elements of `parts: Vec<Box<dyn Render>>`. Each element is two pointers side by side: a "data ptr" and a "vtable ptr".
- parts[0]: the data ptr points to `Text("hello")` on the heap; the vtable ptr points to the vtable for (Text, Render).
- parts[1]: the data ptr points to `Checkbox(true)` on the heap; the vtable ptr points to the vtable for (Checkbox, Render).

Middle, the two vtables. Each has rows: drop, size and align, render, label.

Right, where the rows point:
- Text's `render` row -> `Text::render`. Text's `label` row -> the trait's default `label`, compiled for Text (Text does not override it).
- Checkbox's `render` row -> `Checkbox::render`. Checkbox's `label` row -> `Checkbox::label` (its override).

Caption: `part.label()` on parts[0] follows the vtable ptr, reads the "label" row and calls it with the data ptr as `self`. Row order and whether vtables are shared are compiler details. On 64-bit each pointer is 8 bytes, so the fat pointer is 16.

// Exercise 2: rules as boxed closures (reference solution)
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex2_rules.rs && ./main --test-threads=4

type Rule = Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool>;

fn max_len(n: usize) -> Rule {
    Box::new(move |s| s.len() <= n) // usize is Copy: copied in
}

fn without(word: &str) -> Rule {
    let word = word.to_string(); // own a copy; the closure must be 'static
    Box::new(move |s| !s.contains(word.as_str()))
}

fn one_of(allowed: Vec<String>) -> Rule {
    Box::new(move |s| allowed.iter().any(|a| a == s)) // the Vec is moved in
}

fn passes_all(rules: &[Rule], text: &str) -> bool {
    rules.iter().all(|r| r(text))
}

fn count_passing(rules: &[Rule], words: &[&str]) -> usize {
    words.iter().filter(|w| passes_all(rules, w)).count()
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn single_rules() {
        assert!(max_len(3)("abc"));
        assert!(!max_len(3)("abcd"));
        assert!(without("x")("abc"));
        assert!(!without("bc")("abc"));
        let r = one_of(vec!["red".into(), "blue".into()]);
        assert!(r("red") && !r("green"));
    }

    #[test]
    fn rule_outlives_the_string_it_was_made_from() {
        let rule = {
            let temp = String::from("oops");
            without(&temp)
        }; // `temp` is dropped here; the rule must still work
        assert!(rule("fine"));
        assert!(!rule("oops!"));
    }

    #[test]
    fn rules_of_different_closure_types_in_one_vec() {
        let rules: Vec<Rule> = vec![max_len(5), without("z"), Box::new(|s: &str| !s.is_empty())];
        assert!(passes_all(&rules, "abc"));
        assert!(!passes_all(&rules, "abcdef"));
        assert!(!passes_all(&rules, ""));
        assert!(passes_all(&[], "anything"));
        assert_eq!(count_passing(&rules, &["ok", "zoo", "toolong", "", "fine"]), 2);
    }
}

// Exercise 3: a traffic signal with the state pattern (reference solution)
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex3_signal.rs && ./main --test-threads=4

trait Light {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light>;
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str;
    // Default: most lights stay on for 30 seconds.
    fn seconds(&self) -> u32 {
        30
    }
}

struct Red;
struct Green;
struct Yellow;

impl Light for Red {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Green)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "red"
    }
}

impl Light for Green {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Yellow)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "green"
    }
}

impl Light for Yellow {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Red)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "yellow"
    }
    fn seconds(&self) -> u32 {
        5
    }
}

struct Signal {
    light: Option<Box<dyn Light>>,
}

impl Signal {
    fn new() -> Signal {
        Signal { light: Some(Box::new(Red)) }
    }

    fn advance(&mut self) {
        // take() leaves None behind, giving us the owned Box to consume.
        let old = self.light.take().unwrap();
        self.light = Some(old.next());
    }

    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        self.light.as_ref().unwrap().color()
    }

    fn run_for(&mut self, n: usize) -> u32 {
        let mut total = 0;
        for _ in 0..n {
            total += self.light.as_ref().unwrap().seconds();
            self.advance();
        }
        total
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn cycle_of_colours() {
        let mut s = Signal::new();
        let mut seen = vec![s.color()];
        for _ in 0..3 {
            s.advance();
            seen.push(s.color());
        }
        assert_eq!(seen, ["red", "green", "yellow", "red"]);
    }

    #[test]
    fn default_and_overridden_seconds() {
        assert_eq!(Red.seconds(), 30);
        assert_eq!(Green.seconds(), 30);
        assert_eq!(Yellow.seconds(), 5);
    }

    #[test]
    fn run_for_adds_up_and_moves_on() {
        let mut s = Signal::new();
        assert_eq!(s.run_for(3), 65);
        assert_eq!(s.color(), "red");
        assert_eq!(s.run_for(0), 0);
        assert_eq!(s.run_for(2), 60);
        assert_eq!(s.color(), "yellow");
    }
}
