// Exercise 2: rules as boxed closures (reference solution)
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex2_rules.rs && ./main --test-threads=4

type Rule = Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool>;

fn max_len(n: usize) -> Rule {
    Box::new(move |s| s.len() <= n) // usize is Copy: copied in
}

fn without(word: &str) -> Rule {
    let word = word.to_string(); // own a copy; the closure must be 'static
    Box::new(move |s| !s.contains(word.as_str()))
}

fn one_of(allowed: Vec<String>) -> Rule {
    Box::new(move |s| allowed.iter().any(|a| a == s)) // the Vec is moved in
}

fn passes_all(rules: &[Rule], text: &str) -> bool {
    rules.iter().all(|r| r(text))
}

fn count_passing(rules: &[Rule], words: &[&str]) -> usize {
    words.iter().filter(|w| passes_all(rules, w)).count()
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn single_rules() {
        assert!(max_len(3)("abc"));
        assert!(!max_len(3)("abcd"));
        assert!(without("x")("abc"));
        assert!(!without("bc")("abc"));
        let r = one_of(vec!["red".into(), "blue".into()]);
        assert!(r("red") && !r("green"));
    }

    #[test]
    fn rule_outlives_the_string_it_was_made_from() {
        let rule = {
            let temp = String::from("oops");
            without(&temp)
        }; // `temp` is dropped here; the rule must still work
        assert!(rule("fine"));
        assert!(!rule("oops!"));
    }

    #[test]
    fn rules_of_different_closure_types_in_one_vec() {
        let rules: Vec<Rule> = vec![max_len(5), without("z"), Box::new(|s: &str| !s.is_empty())];
        assert!(passes_all(&rules, "abc"));
        assert!(!passes_all(&rules, "abcdef"));
        assert!(!passes_all(&rules, ""));
        assert!(passes_all(&[], "anything"));
        assert_eq!(count_passing(&rules, &["ok", "zoo", "toolong", "", "fine"]), 2);
    }
}

// Exercise 3: a traffic signal with the state pattern (reference solution)
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex3_signal.rs && ./main --test-threads=4

trait Light {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light>;
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str;
    // Default: most lights stay on for 30 seconds.
    fn seconds(&self) -> u32 {
        30
    }
}

struct Red;
struct Green;
struct Yellow;

impl Light for Red {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Green)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "red"
    }
}

impl Light for Green {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Yellow)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "green"
    }
}

impl Light for Yellow {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Red)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "yellow"
    }
    fn seconds(&self) -> u32 {
        5
    }
}

struct Signal {
    light: Option<Box<dyn Light>>,
}

impl Signal {
    fn new() -> Signal {
        Signal { light: Some(Box::new(Red)) }
    }

    fn advance(&mut self) {
        // take() leaves None behind, giving us the owned Box to consume.
        let old = self.light.take().unwrap();
        self.light = Some(old.next());
    }

    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        self.light.as_ref().unwrap().color()
    }

    fn run_for(&mut self, n: usize) -> u32 {
        let mut total = 0;
        for _ in 0..n {
            total += self.light.as_ref().unwrap().seconds();
            self.advance();
        }
        total
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn cycle_of_colours() {
        let mut s = Signal::new();
        let mut seen = vec![s.color()];
        for _ in 0..3 {
            s.advance();
            seen.push(s.color());
        }
        assert_eq!(seen, ["red", "green", "yellow", "red"]);
    }

    #[test]
    fn default_and_overridden_seconds() {
        assert_eq!(Red.seconds(), 30);
        assert_eq!(Green.seconds(), 30);
        assert_eq!(Yellow.seconds(), 5);
    }

    #[test]
    fn run_for_adds_up_and_moves_on() {
        let mut s = Signal::new();
        assert_eq!(s.run_for(3), 65);
        assert_eq!(s.color(), "red");
        assert_eq!(s.run_for(0), 0);
        assert_eq!(s.run_for(2), 60);
        assert_eq!(s.color(), "yellow");
    }
}

messages.content:
I’d trace it as two separate flows: the settings page render, and the save action.

For the settings page, `app/settings/page.tsx` is a server component. It does `await getSettings()` and passes those values into `SettingsForm`. So on a normal request, the page is rendering from whatever `lib/settings` returns at request time, not from local component state. The form itself is in `app/settings/settings-form.tsx`, and it’s a client component that just seeds inputs with the server-provided values.

The save path is `app/settings/actions.ts`. The `saveSettings` server action parses the form, then calls `putSettings(parsed.values)`, and returns a saved state. So the update should be happening through the API there.

The key reason the new values don’t show up after reload is almost certainly caching of the server-side `getSettings()` fetch. In this setup the app is built once and then run in three separate `next start` containers, each with its own `.next` cache. If `lib/settings` is using `fetch()` with default caching behavior inside a server component, Next can serve a cached response per container rather than going back to the admin API on the next page load. Since the containers don’t share a cache, you can also get inconsistent behavior depending on which container handles the request.

So the stale read is in the read path, not the write path:
- `app/settings/page.tsx` reads settings through `getSettings()`.
- `app/settings/actions.ts` writes with `putSettings()`.
- The bug is likely in `lib/settings.ts` / `lib/settings` where the fetch to `GET /settings` is being cached, and there’s no invalidation after `PUT /settings`.

That also lines up with the “everyone sees old values” symptom: the source of truth in the API changed, but the Next app keeps reusing an old cached result until the cache is busted or a container happens to miss it.

On the header name issue, the account badge is driven by `app/account-provider.tsx`, which fetches `/api/account` client-side after mount, and `app/api/account/route.ts` calls `getAccountSummary(sid)`. If that route or its underlying lib is cached incorrectly, one user’s account payload could leak into another user’s header. I’d inspect `lib/account` and the route for any default cache behavior as well.

messages.content:
If it were just a reused cached fetch, I’d expect the access log for the admin API to show the initial GET /settings once, and then no further upstream GET /settings when people reload the settings page — because the app would keep serving the cached result from its own layer. You wouldn’t expect a fresh GET /settings to suddenly appear only because somebody visited /orders.

The marker difference in the build output is the bigger clue. A different marker beside /settings than beside /orders usually means the route was classified differently at build time — for example, /settings was rendered as a dynamic route or had a runtime data dependency, while /orders was handled in a way that can be cached/optimized differently. So the /settings upstream call likely was not happening on every browser request in the way a normal uncached server read would. It was being executed at build time or at first render generation time, then reused until some unrelated navigation caused a fresh render path to run.

So, putting them together: the stale behavior doesn’t look like a simple missing revalidation after PUT; it looks like the settings page’s data fetch was baked into the build/render output, and the later GET /settings at 09:26:40 suggests the upstream call was triggered by a separate render event, not by the settings page reload itself.

messages.content:
Right — with the legend, the circle is the static/fully pre-rendered route and the `ƒ` is the dynamic one.

So in this app, `/orders` is the `ƒ` route and `/settings` is the circle route. That fits the log pair at 09:26:40/09:26:41: a request to `/orders` can trigger a fresh server render path, and then the settings data shows up as part of that render lifecycle, rather than `/settings` itself being re-fetched on every reload.

What makes `app/orders/page.tsx` dynamic is that it reads `searchParams` and uses them to compute the page/filter state. It also calls `getOrders(...)` on each request. That shape keeps it in the dynamic category. By contrast, `app/settings/page.tsx` just does `await getSettings()` and renders a form from that data, with no per-request URL state driving the page.

On the save path, `app/settings/actions.ts` does `await putSettings(parsed.values);` and then immediately returns `{ status: 'saved', savedAt: new Date().toISOString() }`.

So no — there’s nothing after the PUT that invalidates or refreshes the settings page data for the next reload. There’s no `revalidatePath`, no cache busting, no redirect, no follow-up read. The action updates the API, but the next `/settings` request will still serve whatever the page’s cached/static data path has already baked in unless something else forces regeneration.

getAccountSummary(sid) wraps api('/me', bearer sid) in unstable_cache(fn, ['account-summary'], { revalidate: 60 }). unstable_cache keys an entry by its keyParts plus the stringified function and the arguments of the call. The cached function takes no arguments and sid is only read inside it: the source text contains the name sid but never its value, so sid is not in the key. There is one entry per container, account-summary, shared by every request and every user; it sits in that instance's server cache (on disk under .next/cache) for 60 seconds. Whoever fills it first is shown to everyone: all four read u_311. After 60 seconds the first caller is still served the stale entry while a background refresh runs with their own sid, and from then on everyone sees that person, which is why all four changed together. React cache() in lib/session.ts is the opposite: it is request-scoped, deduping within one server render and reset for each request, so it is safe for per-user values. unstable_cache persists across requests (the docs say across deployments too), which is why it leaks between users. The boundary: AccountBadge is a client component that only renders what /api/account returns; the identity is chosen on the server, in the route handler reading the shared cache. The same value drives canEdit in settings-form.tsx, so an editor can lose the Save button and a viewer can be given it. Fix: do not keep identity in a cross-request cache.   - decided by the route

  - request-scoped

I’d look in `lib/account.ts` and check the wrapper around the `/me` fetch. The important bit is the cache key it uses when it stores the result. If that wrapper is only keyed by something like the endpoint or a generic label, and the session id isn’t part of that key, then all sessions hitting the same container would collapse onto one cached account response.

So: no, if the session id is not included there, that means the container is memoizing `getAccountSummary` across users. Four different people can land on the same answer because the first `/me` result gets reused for everyone on that container until the entry changes or expires. When it flips a minute later, that would just mean the cached entry was replaced by a different session’s response on that same container.

WHAT A COMPLETE ANSWER TO THE STAGE ABOVE LOOKS LIKE:
A Server Action is a public endpoint: the form compiles to a POST to the page's route carrying a Next-Action id, and anyone who can send that POST can run it. The id is in the page's HTML for anyone who can load the page, and the replay copies it. Without a cookie the proxy answers 307 to SSO, because proxy.ts only checks that a sid cookie exists. With the made-up sid=x the page loads, the POST returns HTTP 200 with status saved, and the audit shows refundApprovalLimit 10000 written by service:admin-console. What stops a viewer in the UI is the proxy (presence only, not who or which role) and canEdit in settings-form.tsx (the Save button is not rendered and the inputs are disabled), which runs in the browser and comes from /api/account, itself the shared identity from the last stage. Nothing runs inside saveSettings: no session lookup, no role check. The API cannot catch it either: every write is signed with the service token (auth=service), so it never learns who saved. The HTTP 500 is the framework's CSRF defence: Next.js compares the Origin header's host with the Host (or X-Forwarded-Host) header and aborts the action before it runs, so nothing was written. That stops a hostile page in a browser, but it is not authorization: a script can send no Origin, as the first POST did. Fix: in saveSettings read the sid cookie with cookies(), resolve the user per request (not through the shared cache), and refuse anyone who is not an editor (throw or return an error; forbidden() needs the experimental authInterrupts flag); keep the server-side parseSettings validation; ideally pass the user's identity to the API so writes are attributable and the API can enforce the role too.

NEVER say any of these, in any wording::
  - baked in at build
  - no revalidation call
  - decided by the route
  - public endpoint
  - role check
  - not authorization

A 200 from a replayed save tells me the write path is trusting the request too much — it isn’t being restricted to the browser UI or to a specific user role in any strong way. The fact that a made-up session cookie can reach the save action means the server action is relying on the cookie/session at request time, not on some client-only guard.

The 500 from a different Origin is the bigger clue on the protection side: there’s some server-side origin / CSRF-style check in front of the PUT, so a cross-site replay gets blocked before it can actually write. In other words, the thing standing between a stranger and that PUT is not an authorization gate in the settings action itself, but the request provenance check enforced by the framework or proxy layer.

So I’d summarize it as: the actual writer is anyone who can present a valid-enough session to the server action, and the defense against a random third-party site is origin checking/CSRF protection, not an explicit role check in `saveSettings`.

A Server Action is a public endpoint: the form compiles to a POST to the page's route carrying a Next-Action id, and anyone who can send that POST can run it. The id is in the page's HTML for anyone who can load the page, and the replay copies it. Without a cookie the proxy answers 307 to SSO, because proxy.ts only checks that a sid cookie exists. With the made-up sid=x the page loads, the POST returns HTTP 200 with status saved, and the audit shows refundApprovalLimit 10000 written by service:admin-console. What stops a viewer in the UI is the proxy (presence only, not who or which role) and canEdit in settings-form.tsx (the Save button is not rendered and the inputs are disabled), which runs in the browser and comes from /api/account, itself the shared identity from the last stage. Nothing runs inside saveSettings: no session lookup, no role check. The API cannot catch it either: every write is signed with the service token (auth=service), so it never learns who saved. The HTTP 500 is the framework's CSRF defence: Next.js compares the Origin header's host with the Host (or X-Forwarded-Host) header and aborts the action before it runs, so nothing was written. # Proposed fix for the stale settings problem

Author: a teammate on the squad. Please review before I open the PR.

## What I changed
Two one-line edits, nothing else.

**1. app/layout.tsx** (the root layout, so it covers every page):

```diff
+export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic';
+
 export const metadata: Metadata = { title: 'Admin console' };
```

**2. app/settings/actions.ts**, in the save action:

```diff
+import { revalidatePath } from 'next/cache';
 import { parseSettings, putSettings } from '@/lib/settings';
 ...
   await putSettings(parsed.values);
+  revalidatePath('/', 'layout');

   return { status: 'saved', savedAt: new Date().toISOString() };
```

## Why I think it works
After the change the whole app is dynamic, so there is no stale prerender to serve,
and `revalidatePath('/', 'layout')` clears the router cache for every route after a
save. I rebuilt and ran it: after a save, a reload shows the new values.

### Build route table, after the change
```
Route (app)
┌ ƒ /_not-found
├ ƒ /api/account
├ ƒ /orders
└ ƒ /settings
```

### Load test on /settings
How I ran it: one `next start` on my laptop, before and after the change, each run
`npx autocannon -c 20 -d 20` (20 connections for 20 seconds) on /settings with an
editor's cookie, against the staging admin API (its GET /settings takes about 120 ms).
Upstream calls counted from the API's access log during each run.

|                              | before        | after         |
|------------------------------|---------------|---------------|
| requests / sec (average)     | 4,048         | 159           |
| latency (median / average)   | 4 ms / 4.49 ms  | 124 ms / 125.07 ms |
| requests in 20 s             | 81k           | 3k            |
| upstream GET /settings       | 0             | 3,181         |
| upstream GET /me             | 0             | 0             |

WHAT A COMPLETE ANSWER TO THE STAGE ABOVE LOOKS LIKE:
The change works for the editor but at a high price. Throughput falls about 25 times (4,048 to 159 requests a second), latency rises from about 4 ms to about 125 ms, and upstream GET /settings goes from 0 to 3,181 in 20 seconds, about one per request. The latency is now the API's 120 ms plus rendering, and 20 connections over 0.125 s is about 160 a second: every view of the console becomes load on the settings API, for a value that changes a few times a week. GET /me stays at 0, and the change does not touch the wrong-name bug: force-dynamic in the root layout does not change the /api/account route handler, and the unstable_cache key is the same (verified: still one user for all four sessions). revalidatePath('/', 'layout') purges the client router cache and invalidates all cached data on every save; with every route dynamic there is little left for it to clear, and on its own it would have fixed /settings, far too broadly. Instead: keep /settings static. In saveSettings call revalidatePath('/settings'), or, since several routes read settings, tag the fetch (next: { tags: ['settings'] }, optionally with cache: 'force-cache' so /orders reads the data cache instead of the API on every request) and call updateTag('settings'). updateTag gives read-your-own-writes: the entry expires at once and the action's own response already carries the new value (verified: circle /settings kept, the action response had the new value, the next request regenerated it). revalidateTag('settings', 'max') serves stale while it refreshes, for route handlers or webhooks. Three containers: the default cache is per instance (memory plus local disk), and updateTag on one instance does not reach the others (verified with two next start copies: the second kept the old value, and with force-cache its /orders too). Either give all instances a shared cache handler (cacheHandler in next.config backed by shared storage, cacheMaxMemorySize: 0) with tag coordination across instances (refreshTags for cacheHandlers), or accept a short time-based revalidate. Also fix the action's authorization and the identity cache.

NEVER say any of these, in any wording::
  - baked in at build
  - no revalidation call
  - decided by the route
  - one per request
  - read-your-own-writes
  - per instance

I’d be cautious about approving that as-is.

The `force-dynamic` on `/settings` does address the stale page symptom in a brute-force way, and `revalidatePath('/', 'layout')` will certainly kick the tree, but I wouldn’t love shipping a fix that depends on global layout revalidation for what is really a settings-data problem. Across three independent containers behind round-robin, that kind of invalidation is only as good as the instance that receives it — each container has its own `.next` state, so you don’t get a single shared cache to invalidate.

I can’t honestly read back the teammate’s before/after numbers because I don’t have the contents of `teammate-fix.md` here. If you paste the table, I can comment on the counts directly.

What I’d ship instead is something more targeted:
- make the settings page read dynamically from the API on each request, or use a cache policy tied to the settings data itself rather than the whole layout;
- after `putSettings`, invalidate the specific settings data source, not the entire app shell;
- if the app is using any memoization around `/me` or `/settings`, key it by the session or remove it for per-user data.

In short: fix the exact data path, not the whole layout, and don’t rely on cross-container cache invalidation as the main mechanism.

CREATE OR REPLACE PACKAGE BODY xxap_uninv_accr_pkg AS
-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- XX AP Uninvoiced Receipts Accrual (XXAP_UNINV_ACCR)
-- Month end: expense receipts delivered in the period and not yet invoiced,
-- written to XXAP_UNINV_ACCR_LINES for the accrual journal.
-- Run by the close team from XX Payables Close (all operating units).
-- v2.1  03-2024  : expense accounts only
-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

  PROCEDURE run (errbuf        OUT VARCHAR2,
                 retcode       OUT VARCHAR2,
                 p_period_name IN  VARCHAR2) IS

    CURSOR c_receipts (cp_start DATE, cp_end DATE) IS
      SELECT rt.transaction_id,
             rt.quantity,
             rt.po_unit_price,
             pd.code_combination_id,
             pd.org_id,
             ph.segment1  po_number,
             ph.vendor_id
        FROM rcv_transactions  rt,
             po_distributions  pd,
             po_headers        ph
       WHERE rt.transaction_type       = 'DELIVER'
         AND rt.transaction_date      >= cp_start
         AND rt.transaction_date       < cp_end + 1
         AND pd.po_distribution_id     = rt.po_distribution_id
         AND pd.accrue_on_receipt_flag = 'N'
         AND ph.po_header_id           = pd.po_header_id;

    l_start    DATE;
    l_end      DATE;
    l_billed   NUMBER;
    l_account  gl_code_combinations.segment3%TYPE;
    l_rows     PLS_INTEGER := 0;
    l_written  PLS_INTEGER := 0;
  BEGIN
    mo_global.init('PO');

    SELECT start_date, end_date
      INTO l_start, l_end
      FROM gl_periods
     WHERE period_set_name = 'XX_CALENDAR'
       AND period_name     = p_period_name;

    DELETE FROM xxap_uninv_accr_lines
     WHERE period_name = p_period_name;

    FOR r IN c_receipts (l_start, l_end) LOOP

      -- quantity already invoiced against this receipt
      SELECT NVL(SUM(aid.quantity_invoiced), 0)
        INTO l_billed
        FROM ap_invoice_distributions aid
       WHERE aid.rcv_transaction_id = r.transaction_id;

      -- natural account of the charge account
      SELECT gcc.segment3
        INTO l_account
        FROM gl_code_combinations gcc
       WHERE gcc.code_combination_id = r.code_combination_id;

      IF l_account BETWEEN '5000' AND '7999'          -- expense accounts only
         AND r.quantity > l_billed THEN
        INSERT INTO xxap_uninv_accr_lines
          (period_name, org_id, po_number, vendor_id, rcv_transaction_id,
           natural_account, code_combination_id, uninvoiced_qty, accrual_amount,
           created_by, creation_date)
        VALUES
          (p_period_name, r.org_id, r.po_number, r.vendor_id, r.transaction_id,
           l_account, r.code_combination_id, r.quantity - l_billed,
           ROUND((r.quantity - l_billed) * r.po_unit_price, 2),
           fnd_global.user_id, SYSDATE);
        l_written := l_written + 1;
      END IF;

      l_rows := l_rows + 1;
      IF MOD(l_rows, 500) = 0 THEN
        COMMIT;
      END IF;
    END LOOP;

    COMMIT;
    fnd_file.put_line(fnd_file.log, l_rows || ' receipt lines read, ' || l_written || ' accrual lines written');
    retcode := '0';
  EXCEPTION
    WHEN OTHERS THEN
      ROLLBACK;
      errbuf  := SQLERRM;
      retcode := '2';
  END run;

END xxap_uninv_accr_pkg;
/

CREATE OR REPLACE PACKAGE BODY xxap_uninv_accr_pkg AS
-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- XX AP Uninvoiced Receipts Accrual (XXAP_UNINV_ACCR)
-- Month end: expense receipts delivered in the period and not yet invoiced,
-- written to XXAP_UNINV_ACCR_LINES for the accrual journal.
-- Run by the close team from XX Payables Close (all operating units).
-- v2.1  03-2024  : expense accounts only
-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

  PROCEDURE run (errbuf        OUT VARCHAR2,
                 retcode       OUT VARCHAR2,
                 p_period_name IN  VARCHAR2) IS

    CURSOR c_receipts (cp_start DATE, cp_end DATE) IS
      SELECT rt.transaction_id,
             rt.quantity,
             rt.po_unit_price,
             pd.code_combination_id,
             pd.org_id,
             ph.segment1  po_number,
             ph.vendor_id
        FROM rcv_transactions  rt,
             po_distributions  pd,
             po_headers        ph
       WHERE rt.transaction_type       = 'DELIVER'
         AND rt.transaction_date      >= cp_start
         AND rt.transaction_date       < cp_end + 1
         AND pd.po_distribution_id     = rt.po_distribution_id
         AND pd.accrue_on_receipt_flag = 'N'
         AND ph.po_header_id           = pd.po_header_id;

    l_start    DATE;
    l_end      DATE;
    l_billed   NUMBER;
    l_account  gl_code_combinations.segment3%TYPE;
    l_rows     PLS_INTEGER := 0;
    l_written  PLS_INTEGER := 0;
  BEGIN
    mo_global.init('PO');

    SELECT start_date, end_date
      INTO l_start, l_end
      FROM gl_periods
     WHERE period_set_name = 'XX_CALENDAR'
       AND period_name     = p_period_name;

    DELETE FROM xxap_uninv_accr_lines
     WHERE period_name = p_period_name;

    FOR r IN c_receipts (l_start, l_end) LOOP

      -- quantity already invoiced against this receipt
      SELECT NVL(SUM(aid.quantity_invoiced), 0)
        INTO l_billed
        FROM ap_invoice_distributions aid
       WHERE aid.rcv_transaction_id = r.transaction_id;

      -- natural account of the charge account
      SELECT gcc.segment3
        INTO l_account
        FROM gl_code_combinations gcc
       WHERE gcc.code_combination_id = r.code_combination_id;

      IF l_account BETWEEN '5000' AND '7999'          -- expense accounts only
         AND r.quantity > l_billed THEN
        INSERT INTO xxap_uninv_accr_lines
          (period_name, org_id, po_number, vendor_id, rcv_transaction_id,
           natural_account, code_combination_id, uninvoiced_qty, accrual_amount,
           created_by, creation_date)
        VALUES
          (p_period_name, r.org_id, r.po_number, r.vendor_id, r.transaction_id,
           l_account, r.code_combination_id, r.quantity - l_billed,
           ROUND((r.quantity - l_billed) * r.po_unit_price, 2),
           fnd_global.user_id, SYSDATE);
        l_written := l_written + 1;
      END IF;

      l_rows := l_rows + 1;
      IF MOD(l_rows, 500) = 0 THEN
        COMMIT;
      END IF;
    END LOOP;

    COMMIT;
    fnd_file.put_line(fnd_file.log, l_rows || ' receipt lines read, ' || l_written || ' accrual lines written');
    retcode := '0';
  EXCEPTION
    WHEN OTHERS THEN
      ROLLBACK;
      errbuf  := SQLERRM;
      retcode := '2';
  END run;

END xxap_uninv_accr_pkg;
/

move_object.report_notes:
Scenario: 300 purchase orders stuck In Process with empty worklists after a Friday AME change.

Strengths. The candidate went straight to the workflow's own state rather than guessing, read the activity and status correctly, and concluded the items were errored at the approver step rather than waiting on a notification or the mailer. They ruled the mailer out as the blocker at that point without any prompting. They connected the error to Friday's AME rule and the twelve new cost centres on their own, and correctly identified a null owner mapping as the cause. On remediation they proposed retrying the errored activity in batch through Workflow, and were explicit and unprompted that the purchase orders themselves must not be recreated or resubmitted, which is the key safety point here. They also named sensible risks: duplicate notifications, retrying only the failed activity, auditing each item afterwards.

Gaps. The single purchase order test before mass action did not appear until I asked for it; their first answer jumped straight to the fix. The range of alternative remedies (fallback approver, default role, temporary rule override) likewise only came out on request. The weakest point was the tail of the question: for items that were neither errored nor notified, they attributed it to mailer lag twice, proposing to restart the mailer and resend notifications, even after I told them no notification record existed. They only reached the deferred queue and the background engine after I pointed specifically at how the engine handles activities it does not run on the spot, and even then the answer was tentative and mixed in some vague references to item type launchers and engine tables. Verification after the retries was thin and generic until pulled: status transition and worklist check, nothing on confirming the items reached the notification activity until asked.

Prompting required. Diagnosis: none. Fix: one pull for validation and alternatives. Final deferred processing stage: three pulls plus a sharpened restatement, and the answer still arrived only partially formed. No scripted hint was spent.

Overall. Solid production support diagnostic instincts and good judgement about what not to touch, which matters at senior level. Operational completeness after the fix is where this falls short of senior: the discipline of test then act then confirm, and the background engine as part of routine Workflow operations, were not held independently. Communication is persistently terse note form and needs drawing out.
move_object.response:
That's it, that's where I was pointing. Those ones are parked for later processing rather than broken, and it takes the scheduled engine run to pick them up, so it's worth knowing how often that's set to run in a given environment before you promise a buyer a timeline.

That's everything I had, so let's stop there. Thanks for working through both of these. Your diagnosis on this one was genuinely quick: reading the workflow state first and tying it back to the Friday rule change was the right instinct, and you were clear from the start about leaving the purchase orders themselves alone. Someone will be in touch with you about next steps. Thanks for your time today.

CREATE OR REPLACE PACKAGE BODY xxap_uninv_accr_pkg AS
-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- XX AP Uninvoiced Receipts Accrual (XXAP_UNINV_ACCR)
-- Month end: expense receipts delivered in the period and not yet invoiced,
-- written to XXAP_UNINV_ACCR_LINES for the accrual journal.
-- Run by the close team from XX Payables Close (all operating units).
-- v2.1  03-2024  : expense accounts only
-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

  PROCEDURE run (errbuf        OUT VARCHAR2,
                 retcode       OUT VARCHAR2,
                 p_period_name IN  VARCHAR2) IS

    CURSOR c_receipts (cp_start DATE, cp_end DATE) IS
      SELECT rt.transaction_id,
             rt.quantity,
             rt.po_unit_price,
             pd.code_combination_id,
             pd.org_id,
             ph.segment1  po_number,
             ph.vendor_id
        FROM rcv_transactions  rt,
             po_distributions  pd,
             po_headers        ph
       WHERE rt.transaction_type       = 'DELIVER'
         AND rt.transaction_date      >= cp_start
         AND rt.transaction_date       < cp_end + 1
         AND pd.po_distribution_id     = rt.po_distribution_id
         AND pd.accrue_on_receipt_flag = 'N'
         AND ph.po_header_id           = pd.po_header_id;

    l_start    DATE;
    l_end      DATE;
    l_billed   NUMBER;
    l_account  gl_code_combinations.segment3%TYPE;
    l_rows     PLS_INTEGER := 0;
    l_written  PLS_INTEGER := 0;
  BEGIN
    mo_global.init('PO');

    SELECT start_date, end_date
      INTO l_start, l_end
      FROM gl_periods
     WHERE period_set_name = 'XX_CALENDAR'
       AND period_name     = p_period_name;

    DELETE FROM xxap_uninv_accr_lines
     WHERE period_name = p_period_name;

    FOR r IN c_receipts (l_start, l_end) LOOP

      -- quantity already invoiced against this receipt
      SELECT NVL(SUM(aid.quantity_invoiced), 0)
        INTO l_billed
        FROM ap_invoice_distributions aid
       WHERE aid.rcv_transaction_id = r.transaction_id;

      -- natural account of the charge account
      SELECT gcc.segment3
        INTO l_account
        FROM gl_code_combinations gcc
       WHERE gcc.code_combination_id = r.code_combination_id;

      IF l_account BETWEEN '5000' AND '7999'          -- expense accounts only
         AND r.quantity > l_billed THEN
        INSERT INTO xxap_uninv_accr_lines
          (period_name, org_id, po_number, vendor_id, rcv_transaction_id,
           natural_account, code_combination_id, uninvoiced_qty, accrual_amount,
           created_by, creation_date)
        VALUES
          (p_period_name, r.org_id, r.po_number, r.vendor_id, r.transaction_id,
           l_account, r.code_combination_id, r.quantity - l_billed,
           ROUND((r.quantity - l_billed) * r.po_unit_price, 2),
           fnd_global.user_id, SYSDATE);
        l_written := l_written + 1;
      END IF;

      l_rows := l_rows + 1;
      IF MOD(l_rows, 500) = 0 THEN
        COMMIT;
      END IF;
    END LOOP;

    COMMIT;
    fnd_file.put_line(fnd_file.log, l_rows || ' receipt lines read, ' || l_written || ' accrual lines written');
    retcode := '0';
  EXCEPTION
    WHEN OTHERS THEN
      ROLLBACK;
      errbuf  := SQLERRM;
      retcode := '2';
  END run;

END xxap_uninv_accr_pkg;
/

WHAT A COMPLETE ANSWER TO THE STAGE ABOVE LOOKS LIKE:
The package reads SEGMENT3 as the natural account and keeps only 5000-7999 ('expense accounts only'). That holds for the corporate chart of accounts (Company.CostCentre.Account.Intercompany), used by the US and UK ledgers. India's ledger uses its own structure, Company.Account.CostCentre.Location.Intercompany, where the account is SEGMENT2 and SEGMENT3 is the cost centre. So for India the filter keeps receipts by cost centre, not by account: India's 'accounts' 5010, 5020, 6040 and 7100 in the summary are cost centres, and every expense receipt charged to a cost centre outside 5000-7999 is missing, about 62% of India's accrual. Parity passed because the old program had the same bug: matching a wrong reference proves nothing, and India's accruals for June, July and August were understated in GL. That has to be raised with finance now, not just fixed in code. The fix: never hard-code a segment number. Find each operating unit's ledger and chart of accounts (HR_OPERATING_UNITS or the OU's ledger, then GL_LEDGERS.CHART_OF_ACCOUNTS_ID), find the natural-account segment from the flexfield qualifier GL_ACCOUNT (FND_FLEX_APIS.GET_SEGMENT_COLUMN or the segment qualifier setup), and select expense accounts by account type (GL_CODE_COMBINATIONS.ACCOUNT_TYPE = 'E') rather than by number range. Better still, drive the accrual from Purchasing setup instead of account ranges. Also good: the natural-account column in the output must come from the same derivation, and a test case per chart of accounts belongs in the regression pack.

NEVER say any of these, in any wording::
  - rows times cost
  - ORACLE_PROCESS_ID
  - queue time
  - SEGMENT2
  - same bug
  - GL_ACCOUNT

You may point at where to look. You may not name the mechanism or the fix. If your sentence would let them answer without thinking, rewrite it.

Likely hardcoded expense filter. `segment3 BETWEEN '5000' AND '7999'` drops India NAT accounts. Matching June/July/August only proves old vs new same bug. If India only went live in Aug, the bad mapping only appears there. Need flexfield/COA mapping, not just totals.

move_object.note_text:
## Order to follow
- Lesson sections in order, then `places.rs` and `syntax.rs`, then `ex1_scores.rs`, `ex2_slices.rs`, `ex3_slots.rs`.

## `while let` stopping rule
- `while let Some(top) = stack.pop()` tests the pattern at the start of every iteration.
- Match succeeds: body runs. Match fails: loop ends right there, no else branch.
- With `vec![10, 20]`: pops 20, then 10, then `None` fails the pattern, so body runs twice.

## Binding modes (through a reference)
- `if let Slot::Full { label, count } = first` where `first: &Slot`: non-reference pattern on a reference, so fields bind by reference (`&String`, `&u32`). This is the default binding mode.
- `if let &Slot::Full { count, .. } = first`: the `&` pattern matches the reference itself, so Copy fields bind by value (`u32`).
- Matching a place by value, like `*first` or `slots[0]`, needs `ref` / `ref mut` to borrow instead of moving.
- Through `&mut`, fields bind as `&mut`, so `*count += 10` changes the slot in place.
- Edition 2024: if the pattern is already borrowing implicitly, writing `ref` inside it is an error.

## `matches!`
- `matches!(value, pattern)` just turns a pattern test into a `bool`. The lesson examples are enough.
move_object.note_title: Patterns: order, while let, binding modes
move_object.response: Added a summary to your notes: the study order, how `while let` stops with `stack.pop()`, the binding mode cases through `&` and `&mut` plus the edition 2024 `ref` rule, and a line on `matches!`. Kuch aur add karna ho to bolo.

messages.content: Haan, mere hisaab se `while let` me pattern fail hone par Rust pehle last matched value ko destructure karke cleanup karta hai, isliye `stack.pop()` se loop tabhi rukta hai jab `None` aata hai aur previous `Some` ki value ek extra time borrow ho jaati hai. Iska matlab `while let Some(top) = stack.pop()` me `top` practically last element ka reference hota hai, copy nahi. Yeh sahi hai na? Phir `matches!` bhi kya internally same temporary borrow logic use karta hai?

move_object.note: Explained default binding mode only applies when scrutinee is a reference; pop() gives owned Option<i32>. Next: maybe TRY type-forcing line or assess.
move_object.response:
Rule yeh hai: default binding mode tabhi reference deta hai jab **scrutinee khud ek reference ho** (jaise `&Slot` ko `Slot::Full {..}` se match karna). `stack.pop()` ka return type `Option<i32>` hai, reference nahi. Toh pattern `Some(top)` us owned value ke andar ghusta hai aur `top: i32` banta hai, owned (yahan Copy bhi).

`println!("{top}")` me koi ownership issue nahi, kyunki `i32` Copy hai; aur agar `String` hota to bhi `println!` sirf borrow karta hai.

Ulta case socho: `for x in &vec![1,2]` me `x` kya hoga, aur kyun?

fn classify(pair: (i32, i32)) -> String {
    match pair {
        (0, 0) => String::from("origin"),
        (x, 0) | (0, x) if x < 0 => format!("negative axis {x}"),
        (x, 0) | (0, x) => format!("axis {x}"),
        (x, y) if x == y => format!("diagonal {x}"),
        (n @ 1..=9, _) => format!("small first {n}"),
        _ => String::from("other"),
    }
}

fn main() {
    for p in [(0, 0), (0, -3), (5, 0), (4, 4), (7, 2), (12, 1), (-2, -2)] {
        println!("{p:?} -> {}", classify(p));
    }
}

(0, -3) -> negative axis -3

(4, 4) -> diagonal 4

In this exact set, the visible output text for those two lines stays the same, so no printed line changes. The important diff is only which arm gets picked. If there were some pair like `(0,0)` it still stays origin because the first arm is exact and comes before any guard if kept that way. More generally only pairs satisfying that diagonal condition can be affected.

(3) For `(5, 0)`: it checks arms in order.
- `(0, 0)` no, not same.
- `(x, 0) | (0, x) if x < 0` yes shape matches `(x,0)` with `x = 5`, but guard `x < 0` is false, so reject.

fn route(cmd: &String, fallback: &str) -> String {

        fallback => format!("fallback {fallback}"),
        other => format!("unknown {other}"),
    }
}

    for word in ["stop", "run", "wait", "jump"] {
        println!("{}", route(&String::from(word), default));
    }

enum Signal {
    Level(u8),
    Pulse { width: u8, repeat: bool },
    Off,

fn describe(signal: &Signal) -> String {
    match signal {

        Signal::Level(101..=255) => String::from("high level"),
        Signal::Pulse { repeat: true, .. } => String::from("repeating pulse"),
        Signal::Pulse { width, repeat: false } if *width > 10 => format!("wide pulse {width}"),
    }
}

    let items = [Signal::Level(0), Signal::Level(150), Signal::Pulse { width: 20, repeat: false }, Signal::Off];
    for s in &items {
        println!("{}", describe(s));

Yep. The match is missing a catch for some `Level(_)` values, cause ranges dont cover all u8 values.

(1) No arm covers: `Signal::Level(2..=100)` and `Signal::Level(100)`? wait, more exact: all `Signal::Level` values from `2` through `100`, plus `100` itself, and also `100` is in there, so the uncovered set is `Signal::Level(2..=100)` with `100` included; also `Signal::Level(100)` is just part of that. The other variants are covered.

(2) The guarded `Pulse` arm counts for nothing in exhaustiveness checking because the guard is not trusted to always be true. So even though the pattern shape is `Signal::Pulse { width, repeat: false }`, the compiler treats it as not fully covering Pulse values, since the guard could fail.

        Signal::Level(1..=99) => String::from("low level"),
        Signal::Level(100..=100) => String::from("high level"),

        Signal::Pulse { repeat: true, .. } => String::from("repeating pulse"),
        Signal::Pulse { width, repeat: false } if *width > 10 => format!("wide pulse {width}"),
        Signal::Pulse { width, repeat: false } => format!("narrow pulse {width}"),

}

No, this will not compile.

Rust cannot make a `dyn Store` here because `Store` is not object-safe: the method `put` has a generic type parameter, `fn put<V: ToString>(...)`. A trait object needs a single fixed vtable, but a generic method would need a separate function for every possible `V`, which does not fit into one vtable.

Two fixes:
1. Remove the generic parameter and take a concrete type such as `&str` or `String`.
   - Cost: less flexibility; callers must convert values before calling `put`.
2. Keep flexibility but make `put` take a trait object or enum, for example `&dyn ToString`, `Box<dyn ToString>`, or a custom enum of allowed value types.
   - Cost: dynamic dispatch and/or allocation, plus usually loss of ownership simplicity or the need to clone/format values.

trait Store {
    fn get(&self, key: &str) -> Option<String>;
    fn put<V: ToString>(&mut self, key: &str, value: V);
}

struct MemStore {
    pairs: Vec<(String, String)>,
}

impl Store for MemStore {
    fn get(&self, key: &str) -> Option<String> {
        self.pairs.iter().find(|(k, _)| k == key).map(|(_, v)| v.clone())
    }
    fn put<V: ToString>(&mut self, key: &str, value: V) {
        self.pairs.push((key.to_string(), value.to_string()));
    }
}

fn fill(store: &mut dyn Store) {
    store.put("size", 3);
    store.put("mode", "fast");
}

fn main() {
    let mut store = MemStore { pairs: Vec::new() };
    fill(&mut store);
    println!("{:?} {:?}", store.get("size"), store.get("mode"));
}

struct Filters {
    rules: Vec<Box<dyn Fn(u32) -> bool>>,
}

impl Filters {
    fn add_limit(&mut self, limit: &u32) {
        self.rules.push(Box::new(move |n| n <= *limit));
    }

    fn passes(&self, n: u32) -> bool {
        self.rules.iter().all(|rule| rule(n))
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut filters = Filters { rules: Vec::new() };
    filters.rules.push(Box::new(|n| n % 2 == 0));
    let limit = 10;
    filters.add_limit(&limit);
    let items = [4, 7, 12, 8];
    let kept: Vec<u32> = items.into_iter().filter(|&n| filters.passes(n)).collect();
    println!("{kept:?}");
}

trait Store {
    fn get(&self, key: &str) -> Option<String>;
    fn put<V: ToString>(&mut self, key: &str, value: V);
}

struct MemStore {
    pairs: Vec<(String, String)>,
}

impl Store for MemStore {
    fn get(&self, key: &str) -> Option<String> {
        self.pairs.iter().find(|(k, _)| k == key).map(|(_, v)| v.clone())
    }
    fn put<V: ToString>(&mut self, key: &str, value: V) {
        self.pairs.push((key.to_string(), value.to_string()));
    }
}

fn fill<S: Store>(store: &mut S) {
    store.put("size", 3);
    store.put("mode", "fast");
}

fn main() {
    let mut store = MemStore { pairs: Vec::new() };
    fill(&mut store);
    println!("{:?} {:?}", store.get("size"), store.get("mode"));
}

Nope, `Store` is not object-safe, so `&mut dyn Store` wont compile. Rust cant make one vtable cause `put` has a generic type param `V: ToString`; vtables need monomorphic method slots, but generic methods get monomorphized per `V`, so no single fn ptr to stick in the table.

Two fixes:
1) Change `put` to `fn put(&mut self, key: &str, value: &str)` or `String`. Cost: less flexible, callers must pre-convert.
2) Make the generic method non-dyn and keep the trait for `get` only, or use an enum/boxed trait object for values. Cost: you lose one neat `dyn Store` API, and the storage becomes more verbose / may allocate.

trait Store {
    fn get(&self, key: &str) -> Option<String>;
    fn put<V: ToString>(&mut self, key: &str, value: V);
}

struct MemStore {
    pairs: Vec<(String, String)>,
}

impl Store for MemStore {
    fn get(&self, key: &str) -> Option<String> {
        self.pairs.iter().find(|(k, _)| k == key).map(|(_, v)| v.clone())
    }
    fn put<V: ToString>(&mut self, key: &str, value: V) {
        self.pairs.push((key.to_string(), value.to_string()));
    }
}

fn fill(store: &mut dyn Store) {
    store.put("size", 3);
    store.put("mode", "fast");
}

fn main() {
    let mut store = MemStore { pairs: Vec::new() };
    fill(&mut store);
    println!("{:?} {:?}", store.get("size"), store.get("mode"));
}

struct Filters {
    rules: Vec<Box<dyn Fn(u32) -> bool>>,
}

impl Filters {
    fn add_limit(&mut self, limit: &u32) {
        self.rules.push(Box::new(move |n| n <= *limit));
    }

    fn passes(&self, n: u32) -> bool {
        self.rules.iter().all(|rule| rule(n))
    }
}

fn main() {

    let items = [4, 7, 12, 8];
    let kept: Vec<u32> = items.into_iter().filter(|&n| filters.passes(n)).collect();
    println!("{kept:?}");
}

How you examine:

fn shape(items: &[i32]) -> String {
    match items {
        [] => String::from("empty"),
        [x] => format!("one: {x}"),
        [first, .., last] if first == last => format!("same ends: {first}"),
        [first, rest @ ..] => format!("{first} then {} more", rest.len()),

}

// Count how many times a value is bigger than the one before it.
// Use a slice pattern and recursion. No indexing with [i].
fn rises(items: &[i32]) -> u32 {
    match items {
        [] | [_] => 0,
        [prev, next, rest @ ..] => {
            let count = if next > prev { 1 } else { 0 };
            count + rises(&items[1..])
        }
    }
}

Yep — I'd start by treating this like a workflow break right after the AME rule change, bc the symptom is very specific: 300 POs all sit in **IN PROCESS**, and the workflow item activity is **PO_AME_APPRV_PROCESS / GET_NEXT_APPROVER = ERROR** for all 300, while **NOTIFY_APPROVER = 0**. So the issue is almost certainly **before** notification, not in the mailer itself.

How I'd trace it:

1. **Confirm scope and isolate the break point**
   - Look at a few of the stuck PO workflow items, not just the summary.
   - Check the item key / PO number and the current activity status in WF tables or Workflow Monitor.
   - Since all 300 are failing at **GET_NEXT_APPROVER**, I'd focus there first.

2. **Inspect the AME rule that changed on Friday**
   - The new rule `XX_PO_COST_CENTER_OWNER` routes to `XX_CC_OWNER_PERSON_ID` on the charge account's cost centre.
   - I’d verify the rule logic for the new 12 cost centres created at 17:45.
   - Main question: do those new cost centres have a valid owner person id populated? If not, AME may be returning no approver or erroring when it tries to derive one.

3. **Check the data for affected POs**
   - Pick one PO from the stuck batch and inspect the charge account / cost centre.
   - Verify whether `XX_CC_OWNER_PERSON_ID` exists and maps to an active HR person / valid approver.
   - Also check if the owner is end-dated, not in the approver chain, or otherwise not eligible.

4. **Reproduce in AME / debug the transaction**
   - Run the AME test / transaction evaluation for one of the POs.
   - See whether the rule returns an exception, null approver list, or invalid participant.
   - If the workflow activity is erroring, I'd look at the error text on the item — it should tell us if it’s a bad SQL, missing person, invalid role, etc.

5. **Correlate with the timing**
   - The issue starts after the 17:30 rule deployment, and before the 19:00 mailer restart.
   - Since **NOTIFY_APPROVER = 0**, the mailer restart is probly not the root cause for this batch.
   - The likely break is the AME rule deployment plus new cost centre data.

6. **Look for a systemic pattern**
   - Because all 300 are affected, this is more likely a config/data issue than a single bad PO.
   - I’d compare a good PO from before Friday vs a bad PO after Friday to see what changed in account coding.

7. **Fix / workaround**
   - If the new cost centres are missing owners, populate `XX_CC_OWNER_PERSON_ID` or correct the mapping.
   - If the rule is too strict, add fallback approver logic for unmapped cost centres.
   - After that, bounce/retry the workflow items or re-run the approval process for the stuck POs.

So in short: I'd prove it’s failing inside **AME GET_NEXT_APPROVER**, then check the new cost centre ownership data introduced on Friday, because that lines up exactly with the first bad approvals and the complete lack of notifications.

CREATE OR REPLACE PACKAGE BODY xxap_uninv_accr_pkg AS
-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- XX AP Uninvoiced Receipts Accrual (XXAP_UNINV_ACCR)
-- Month end: expense receipts delivered in the period and not yet invoiced,
-- written to XXAP_UNINV_ACCR_LINES for the accrual journal.
-- Run by the close team from XX Payables Close (all operating units).
-- v2.1  03-2024  : expense accounts only
-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

  PROCEDURE run (errbuf        OUT VARCHAR2,
                 retcode       OUT VARCHAR2,
                 p_period_name IN  VARCHAR2) IS

    CURSOR c_receipts (cp_start DATE, cp_end DATE) IS
      SELECT rt.transaction_id,
             rt.quantity,
             rt.po_unit_price,
             pd.code_combination_id,
             pd.org_id,
             ph.segment1  po_number,
             ph.vendor_id
        FROM rcv_transactions  rt,
             po_distributions  pd,
             po_headers        ph
       WHERE rt.transaction_type       = 'DELIVER'
         AND rt.transaction_date      >= cp_start
         AND rt.transaction_date       < cp_end + 1
         AND pd.po_distribution_id     = rt.po_distribution_id
         AND pd.accrue_on_receipt_flag = 'N'
         AND ph.po_header_id           = pd.po_header_id;

    l_start    DATE;
    l_end      DATE;
    l_billed   NUMBER;
    l_account  gl_code_combinations.segment3%TYPE;
    l_rows     PLS_INTEGER := 0;
    l_written  PLS_INTEGER := 0;
  BEGIN
    mo_global.init('PO');

    SELECT start_date, end_date
      INTO l_start, l_end
      FROM gl_periods
     WHERE period_set_name = 'XX_CALENDAR'
       AND period_name     = p_period_name;

    DELETE FROM xxap_uninv_accr_lines
     WHERE period_name = p_period_name;

    FOR r IN c_receipts (l_start, l_end) LOOP

      -- quantity already invoiced against this receipt
      SELECT NVL(SUM(aid.quantity_invoiced), 0)
        INTO l_billed
        FROM ap_invoice_distributions aid
       WHERE aid.rcv_transaction_id = r.transaction_id;

      -- natural account of the charge account
      SELECT gcc.segment3
        INTO l_account
        FROM gl_code_combinations gcc
       WHERE gcc.code_combination_id = r.code_combination_id;

      IF l_account BETWEEN '5000' AND '7999'          -- expense accounts only
         AND r.quantity > l_billed THEN
        INSERT INTO xxap_uninv_accr_lines
          (period_name, org_id, po_number, vendor_id, rcv_transaction_id,
           natural_account, code_combination_id, uninvoiced_qty, accrual_amount,
           created_by, creation_date)
        VALUES
          (p_period_name, r.org_id, r.po_number, r.vendor_id, r.transaction_id,
           l_account, r.code_combination_id, r.quantity - l_billed,
           ROUND((r.quantity - l_billed) * r.po_unit_price, 2),
           fnd_global.user_id, SYSDATE);
        l_written := l_written + 1;
      END IF;

      l_rows := l_rows + 1;
      IF MOD(l_rows, 500) = 0 THEN
        COMMIT;
      END IF;
    END LOOP;

    COMMIT;
    fnd_file.put_line(fnd_file.log, l_rows || ' receipt lines read, ' || l_written || ' accrual lines written');
    retcode := '0';
  EXCEPTION
    WHEN OTHERS THEN
      ROLLBACK;
      errbuf  := SQLERRM;
      retcode := '2';
  END run;

END xxap_uninv_accr_pkg;
/

CREATE OR REPLACE PACKAGE BODY xxap_uninv_accr_pkg AS
-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- XX AP Uninvoiced Receipts Accrual (XXAP_UNINV_ACCR)
-- Month end: expense receipts delivered in the period and not yet invoiced,
-- written to XXAP_UNINV_ACCR_LINES for the accrual journal.
-- Run by the close team from XX Payables Close (all operating units).
-- v2.1  03-2024  : expense accounts only
-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

  PROCEDURE run (errbuf        OUT VARCHAR2,
                 retcode       OUT VARCHAR2,
                 p_period_name IN  VARCHAR2) IS

    CURSOR c_receipts (cp_start DATE, cp_end DATE) IS
      SELECT rt.transaction_id,
             rt.quantity,
             rt.po_unit_price,
             pd.code_combination_id,
             pd.org_id,
             ph.segment1  po_number,
             ph.vendor_id
        FROM rcv_transactions  rt,
             po_distributions  pd,
             po_headers        ph
       WHERE rt.transaction_type       = 'DELIVER'
         AND rt.transaction_date      >= cp_start
         AND rt.transaction_date       < cp_end + 1
         AND pd.po_distribution_id     = rt.po_distribution_id
         AND pd.accrue_on_receipt_flag = 'N'
         AND ph.po_header_id           = pd.po_header_id;

    l_start    DATE;
    l_end      DATE;
    l_billed   NUMBER;
    l_account  gl_code_combinations.segment3%TYPE;
    l_rows     PLS_INTEGER := 0;
    l_written  PLS_INTEGER := 0;
  BEGIN
    mo_global.init('PO');

    SELECT start_date, end_date
      INTO l_start, l_end
      FROM gl_periods
     WHERE period_set_name = 'XX_CALENDAR'
       AND period_name     = p_period_name;

    DELETE FROM xxap_uninv_accr_lines
     WHERE period_name = p_period_name;

    FOR r IN c_receipts (l_start, l_end) LOOP

      -- quantity already invoiced against this receipt
      SELECT NVL(SUM(aid.quantity_invoiced), 0)
        INTO l_billed
        FROM ap_invoice_distributions aid
       WHERE aid.rcv_transaction_id = r.transaction_id;

      -- natural account of the charge account
      SELECT gcc.segment3
        INTO l_account
        FROM gl_code_combinations gcc
       WHERE gcc.code_combination_id = r.code_combination_id;

      IF l_account BETWEEN '5000' AND '7999'          -- expense accounts only
         AND r.quantity > l_billed THEN
        INSERT INTO xxap_uninv_accr_lines
          (period_name, org_id, po_number, vendor_id, rcv_transaction_id,
           natural_account, code_combination_id, uninvoiced_qty, accrual_amount,
           created_by, creation_date)
        VALUES
          (p_period_name, r.org_id, r.po_number, r.vendor_id, r.transaction_id,
           l_account, r.code_combination_id, r.quantity - l_billed,
           ROUND((r.quantity - l_billed) * r.po_unit_price, 2),
           fnd_global.user_id, SYSDATE);
        l_written := l_written + 1;
      END IF;

      l_rows := l_rows + 1;
      IF MOD(l_rows, 500) = 0 THEN
        COMMIT;
      END IF;
    END LOOP;

    COMMIT;
    fnd_file.put_line(fnd_file.log, l_rows || ' receipt lines read, ' || l_written || ' accrual lines written');
    retcode := '0';
  EXCEPTION
    WHEN OTHERS THEN
      ROLLBACK;
      errbuf  := SQLERRM;
      retcode := '2';
  END run;

END xxap_uninv_accr_pkg;
/

WHAT A COMPLETE ANSWER TO THE STAGE ABOVE LOOKS LIKE:
No statement is slow; the statements run too many times. The SUM on AP_INVOICE_DISTRIBUTIONS ran 1,412,806 times at about 9.7 ms each (13,720 s, 92% of the 14,961 s run), mostly single-block reads (1.9 million db file sequential read waits): one index probe on AP_INVOICE_DISTRIBUTIONS_N17 plus one table block per receipt line. The GL_CODE_COMBINATIONS lookup ran 1,412,806 times (610 s) and the INSERT 331,020 times (403 s); the driving cursor itself took only 180 s. The plan's FILTER on MO_GLOB_ORG_ACCESS_TMP is the multi-org security predicate, paid on every execution. 1.4 million executions is India's volume: before June the same loop ran about 95,000 times, which is the old 10 minutes. The fix is the shape of the program, not one statement: one set-based statement that reads the period's deliveries once, joins to invoiced quantities aggregated once per receipt (GROUP BY rcv_transaction_id, as an inline view or a join), joins GL_CODE_COMBINATIONS instead of looking it up, and writes the result with a single INSERT ... SELECT (at minimum BULK COLLECT with FORALL). In batch code, read the _ALL tables with an explicit org_id filter taken from the operating units the request may process, rather than paying the security predicate per row; drop the commits inside the loop. Expected run: a few passes over about 1.4 million rows with hash joins, minutes rather than hours. Proof: run old and new against the same clone snapshot and compare line by line (period, org, receipt, quantity, amount); every difference explained.

NEVER say any of these, in any wording::
  - rows times cost
  - ORACLE_PROCESS_ID
  - queue time
  - too many times
  - GROUP BY rcv_transaction_id
  - set-based statement

You may point at where to look. You may not name the mechanism or the fix. If your sentence would let them answer without thinking, rewrite it.

Right, that tkprof is pretty clear: the runtime is overwhelmingly spent in the two row-by-row SQLs inside the loop, not in the loop control itself.

From the package body, the hot path is `FOR r IN c_receipts (...) LOOP` in `xxap_uninv_accr_pkg`, with a per-row `SELECT NVL(SUM(aid.quantity_invoiced), 0)` from `ap_invoice_distributions` and a per-row `SELECT gcc.segment3` from `gl_code_combinations`.

What the tkprof says:
- `AP_INVOICE_DISTRIBUTIONS` sum query executed 1,412,806 times and took the vast majority of elapsed time. That is the real bottleneck.
- The `GL_CODE_COMBINATIONS` lookup also executed 1,412,806 times, but it is much cheaper; still, it is classic row-by-row overhead.
- So the problem is not the cursor fetch or the insert, it is the nested SQL per receipt.

What I’d change:
1. Eliminate the per-row `SUM(quantity_invoiced)` lookup by joining or pre-aggregating `ap_invoice_distributions` once for the whole receipt set.
2. Eliminate the per-row `gl_code_combinations` lookup by joining `gl_code_combinations` in the cursor itself, since you already have `code_combination_id`.
3. Process the receipt set in set-based SQL, ideally inserting directly into `xxap_uninv_accr_lines` from a single `INSERT ... SELECT` with the invoiced quantity aggregated in an inline view.
4. Keep the 500-row commit only if you must, but the real fix is removing the 1.4M scalar queries.

So on the back of tkprof, I’d rewrite this package to be set-based, not iterative. The current code is doing about 2.8 million SQL calls for 1.4 million rows, which is exactly why it fell from 10 minutes to 4 hours when volume grew.

  candidate: Right, that tkprof is pretty clear: the runtime is overwhelmingly spent in the two row-by-row SQLs inside the loop, not in the loop control itself.

From the package body, the hot path is `FOR r IN c_receipts (...) LOOP` in `xxap_uninv_accr_pkg`, with a per-row `SELECT NVL(SUM(aid.quantity_invoiced), 0)` from `ap_invoice_distributions` and a per-row `SELECT gcc.segment3` from `gl_code_combinations`.

What the tkprof says:
- `AP_INVOICE_DISTRIBUTIONS` sum query executed 1,412,806 times and took the vast majority of elapsed time. That is the real bottleneck.
- The `GL_CODE_COMBINATIONS` lookup also executed 1,412,806 times, but it is much cheaper; still, it is classic row-by-row overhead.
- So the problem is not the cursor fetch or the insert, it is the nested SQL per receipt.

What I’d change:
1. Eliminate the per-row `SUM(quantity_invoiced)` lookup by joining or pre-aggregating `ap_invoice_distributions` once for the whole receipt set.
2. Eliminate the per-row `gl_code_combinations` lookup by joining `gl_code_combinations` in the cursor itself, since you already have `code_combination_id`.
3. Process the receipt set in set-based SQL, ideally inserting directly into `xxap_uninv_accr_lines` from a single `INSERT ... SELECT` with the invoiced quantity aggregated in an inline view.
4. Keep the 500-row commit only if you must, but the real fix is removing the 1.4M scalar queries.

So on the back of tkprof, I’d rewrite this package to be set-based, not iterative. The current code is doing about 2.8 million SQL calls for 1.4 million rows, which is exactly why it fell from 10 minutes to 4 hours when volume grew.
  ai: Good, that is the shape of it. Before we leave the trace, go one level down into the row source for that SUM rather than the call totals. There is a line in there that I would not expect to see in the plan of a query against invoice distributions. What do you make of it, and does it change what your rewrite has to do?

WHAT A COMPLETE ANSWER TO THE STAGE ABOVE LOOKS LIKE:
No statement is slow; the statements run too many times. The SUM on AP_INVOICE_DISTRIBUTIONS ran 1,412,806 times at about 9.7 ms each (13,720 s, 92% of the 14,961 s run), mostly single-block reads (1.9 million db file sequential read waits): one index probe on AP_INVOICE_DISTRIBUTIONS_N17 plus one table block per receipt line. The GL_CODE_COMBINATIONS lookup ran 1,412,806 times (610 s) and the INSERT 331,020 times (403 s); the driving cursor itself took only 180 s. The plan's FILTER on MO_GLOB_ORG_ACCESS_TMP is the multi-org security predicate, paid on every execution. 1.4 million executions is India's volume: before June the same loop ran about 95,000 times, which is the old 10 minutes. The fix is the shape of the program, not one statement: one set-based statement that reads the period's deliveries once, joins to invoiced quantities aggregated once per receipt (GROUP BY rcv_transaction_id, as an inline view or a join), joins GL_CODE_COMBINATIONS instead of looking it up, and writes the result with a single INSERT ... SELECT (at minimum BULK COLLECT with FORALL). In batch code, read the _ALL tables with an explicit org_id filter taken from the operating units the request may process, rather than paying the security predicate per row; drop the commits inside the loop. Expected run: a few passes over about 1.4 million rows with hash joins, minutes rather than hours. Proof: run old and new against the same clone snapshot and compare line by line (period, org, receipt, quantity, amount); every difference explained.

NEVER say any of these, in any wording::
  - rows times cost
  - ORACLE_PROCESS_ID
  - queue time
  - too many times
  - GROUP BY rcv_transaction_id
  - set-based statement

You may point at where to look. You may not name the mechanism or the fix. If your sentence would let them answer without thinking, rewrite it.

Yeah, that line is the `MO_GLOB_ORG_ACCESS_TMP` access under the SUM query. I would read that as MOAC org-security being injected into what looks like a simple lookup on `AP_INVOICE_DISTRIBUTIONS`. So the query is not just doing `RCV_TRANSACTION_ID = :B1`, it is also checking org access every single time, which is extra overhead and it explains why the fetch side is so expensive.

It does not really change the rewrite direction, but it does change how I’d be careful about it:
- I would still get rid of the row-by-row SUM in the loop.
- But in the rewrite I’d make sure the set-based SQL preserves the same MOAC visibility, either by running in the proper org context or by joining/aggregating in a way that stays inside the same security model.
- I would not try to bypass that security check unless we had explicit sign-off, because it is there for a reason.

So no, it doesn’t change the fact that this wants a set-based rewrite. It just tells me the current scalar query is paying an org-security tax 1.4 million times, and the new SQL has to be designed with MOAC in mind.

2. Eliminate the per-row `gl_code_combinations` lookup by joining `gl_code_combinations` in the cursor itself, since you already have `code_combination_id`.

WHAT A COMPLETE ANSWER TO THE STAGE ABOVE LOOKS LIKE:
No statement is slow; the statements run too many times. The SUM on AP_INVOICE_DISTRIBUTIONS ran 1,412,806 times at about 9.7 ms each (13,720 s, 92% of the 14,961 s run), mostly single-block reads (1.9 million db file sequential read waits): one index probe on AP_INVOICE_DISTRIBUTIONS_N17 plus one table block per receipt line. The GL_CODE_COMBINATIONS lookup ran 1,412,806 times (610 s) and the INSERT 331,020 times (403 s); the driving cursor itself took only 180 s. The plan's FILTER on MO_GLOB_ORG_ACCESS_TMP is the multi-org security predicate, paid on every execution. 1.4 million executions is India's volume: before June the same loop ran about 95,000 times, which is the old 10 minutes. The fix is the shape of the program, not one statement: one set-based statement that reads the period's deliveries once, joins to invoiced quantities aggregated once per receipt (GROUP BY rcv_transaction_id, as an inline view or a join), joins GL_CODE_COMBINATIONS instead of looking it up, and writes the result with a single INSERT ... SELECT (at minimum BULK COLLECT with FORALL). In batch code, read the _ALL tables with an explicit org_id filter taken from the operating units the request may process, rather than paying the security predicate per row; drop the commits inside the loop. Expected run: a few passes over about 1.4 million rows with hash joins, minutes rather than hours. Yeah, that line is the `MO_GLOB_ORG_ACCESS_TMP` access under the SUM query. I would read that as MOAC org-security being injected into what looks like a simple lookup on `AP_INVOICE_DISTRIBUTIONS`. So the query is not just doing `RCV_TRANSACTION_ID = :B1`, it is also checking org access every single time, which is extra overhead and it explains why the fetch side is so expensive.

It does not really change the rewrite direction, but it does change how I’d be careful about it:
- I would still get rid of the row-by-row SUM in the loop.
- But in the rewrite I’d make sure the set-based SQL preserves the same MOAC visibility, either by running in the proper org context or by joining/aggregating in a way that stays inside the same security model.
- I would not try to bypass that security check unless we had explicit sign-off, because it is there for a reason.

So no, it doesn’t change the fact that this wants a set-based rewrite. It just tells me the current scalar query is paying an org-security tax 1.4 million times, and the new SQL has to be designed with MOAC in mind.

  - SEGMENT2

  - GL_ACCOUNT

I’d suspect the rewrite is now set-based, but it’s still using the wrong accounting context for India’s COA. In the package body, the account filter is `l_account BETWEEN '5000' AND '7999'` after reading `gcc.segment3` from `gl_code_combinations` — that works only if `segment3` is the natural account in both charts. If India’s chart uses a different segment layout, or the natural account is not in segment3, then India’s expense receipts will be undercounted or filtered wrong. So the India total coming out low is probably because the rewritten SQL/logic is still tied to the US-style COA structure, and India’s expense account is being read from the wrong segment or not classified as an expense at all.

Why the parity test missed it: you said you ran old vs new on the same clone for June/July/August and matched line for line. That only proves the rewrite preserves the existing logic, not that the existing logic is correct for India. If the clone was taken before India’s real production setup was fully represented, or if the test cases only exercised the original operating units / COA structure, then the bad COA mapping in India would never be exposed. In other words, parity with the legacy code is not enough here — both old and new can be consistently wrong for India.

Then I’d re-run India-specific cases against actual India receipts and compare to the controller’s expected accrual, not just old-vs-new parity.

WHAT A COMPLETE ANSWER TO THE STAGE ABOVE LOOKS LIKE:
2 h 41 min still misses the 20:00 cut-off (18:00 plus 2 h 41 is 20:41, before any queueing): the covering index lowers the cost of each execution, but all 1.4 million executions remain, and the INSERT, the lookup and the security predicate are untouched. Statistics: EBS supports statistics gathered only through FND_STATS or the Gather Schema / Table Statistics programs, not DBMS_STATS directly; and METHOD_OPT SIZE 1 removes the histograms FND_STATS maintains for the columns listed in FND_HISTOGRAM_COLS, so plans of standard AP and PO programs can change the night before close. The index: AP_INVOICE_DISTRIBUTIONS_ALL is written all day by invoice entry, import, validation and accounting, all of which now maintain one more index, and standard SQL may start choosing it. It is a customization on a standard table: named XX, registered, documented, and re-checked after every patch (a patch can rebuild or change the table). The hint names an index, so it silently stops working if the index is renamed or dropped. Before either change reaches production: a run on a production-sized clone with production statistics; old vs new output compared on the same snapshot, US and UK identical, India deliberately different and reconciled independently (to the GL accrual account balance or the standard Uninvoiced Receipts Report for India); the run time measured end to end; approval as a change with a rollback; and a fallback for close night. A pragmatic plan for Tuesday: freeze the DBA change except perhaps the index if the clone proves it harmless; get the rewrite through a focused UAT this week; on close night run the old program early (or per operating unit, US and UK first) and the rewrite in parallel for comparison; tell finance about India's understatement.

  - rows times cost
  - ORACLE_PROCESS_ID
  - queue time
  - FND_STATS
  - FND_HISTOGRAM_COLS
  - still misses

I’d push back a bit, politely but firmly. The DBA fix may be lower risk than a full rewrite, but it is still changing a month-end close program that already showed functional risk on India, so I wouldn’t take either change straight to prod on the 29th without evidence.

What I’d say back:
- I understand the urgency and I agree the 2 lookup hot spots are the immediate perf issue in `xxap_uninv_accr_pkg`.
- But a pure performance change can still alter results if it changes join order, org-security behavior, or the row set being aggregated.
- We already found one functional gap in the rewrite path: India COA mapping / account derivation. So I do not want a “low risk” label to override testing.
- If the DBA team’s patch is only on the SQL access path, fine, but we still need proof that it returns exactly the same accrual lines for every operating unit, including India.

What I’d need before either change goes to prod:
1. Side-by-side result proof
- run original vs DBA patch vs rewrite on the same clone
- compare output by period, org_id, po_number, rcv_transaction_id, amount
- include India, not just the older OUs

2. Functional sign-off
- AP / close team confirms totals are right for June, July, August, and a current India sample
- confirm the India discrepancy is addressed, not just runtime

3. Performance evidence
- tkprof / trace for the DBA patch showing the two hot SQLs are materially reduced
- overall runtime under the close SLA with margin, not just barely under 20:00

4. Security / MOAC check
- ensure the change does not bypass `MO_GLOBAL` org access behavior that the current query is using
- especially important because the trace showed `MO_GLOB_ORG_ACCESS_TMP` in the SUM query path

5. Controlled deployment plan
- one-off deployment window
- backup/rollback script ready
- request id and validation query list prepared
- support on call during the first run

So my answer is: I’m not blocking the DBA fix, but I am blocking a blind Tuesday-night prod move unless we can prove both performance and correctness, with India in scope. If they can get me a clean clone run, same-output parity, and AP sign-off, then I’d be comfortable with the lower-risk patch going first — but not on trust alone.

WHAT A COMPLETE ANSWER TO THE STAGE ABOVE LOOKS LIKE:
2 h 41 min still misses the 20:00 cut-off (18:00 plus 2 h 41 is 20:41, before any queueing): the covering index lowers the cost of each execution, but all 1.4 million executions remain, and the INSERT, the lookup and the security predicate are untouched. Statistics: EBS supports statistics gathered only through FND_STATS or the Gather Schema / Table Statistics programs, not DBMS_STATS directly; and METHOD_OPT SIZE 1 removes the histograms FND_STATS maintains for the columns listed in FND_HISTOGRAM_COLS, so plans of standard AP and PO programs can change the night before close. The index: AP_INVOICE_DISTRIBUTIONS_ALL is written all day by invoice entry, import, validation and accounting, all of which now maintain one more index, and standard SQL may start choosing it. It is a customization on a standard table: named XX, registered, documented, and re-checked after every patch (a patch can rebuild or change the table). The hint names an index, so it silently stops working if the index is renamed or dropped. Before either change reaches production: a run on a production-sized clone with production statistics; old vs new output compared on the same snapshot, US and UK identical, India deliberately different and reconciled independently (to the GL accrual account balance or the standard Uninvoiced Receipts Report for India); the run time measured end to end; approval as a change with a rollback; and a fallback for close night. A pragmatic plan for Tuesday: freeze the DBA change except perhaps the index if the clone proves it harmless; get the rewrite through a focused UAT this week; on close night run the old program early (or per operating unit, US and UK first) and the rewrite in parallel for comparison; tell finance about India's understatement.

  - rows times cost

  - queue time
  - FND_STATS
  - FND_HISTOGRAM_COLS

Yes — from the script itself I’d refuse at least one thing on sight.

1) The index
If they are proposing a new index just to speed the AP invoice lookup, I would want to see exactly what table, columns, and naming it uses. If it’s on a busy AP table and not clearly aligned to the predicate `RCV_TRANSACTION_ID = :B1`, I’d be cautious. But an index alone is not an automatic no.

2) The hinted statement
This is the bigger red flag. A hint hard-codes a plan, and on a close program I would not accept a forced plan change without proof it is safe across volumes and orgs. In particular, if the hint is doing something like forcing nested loops or a specific index, I’d refuse that on sight until we’ve proven it against the clone. Hints are brittle, and this code already depends on MOAC org filtering, so I don’t want a plan frozen blindly.

3) The statistics call
If they are calling `DBMS_STATS` or similar in the production deploy script, I’d also push back hard. I would not want ad hoc stats gathering bundled into a one-off close fix unless it’s very narrowly scoped and agreed. Stats changes can affect lots of other EBS SQL, not just this package.

So, the thing I’d refuse immediately is the hinted statement, and probably the stats call as well if it’s broad rather than targeted. The index might be acceptable if it is surgical and justified.

On the arithmetic: if UAT is saying the program is about 6 minutes, and they want to go in production Tuesday night for a 20:00 close window after an 18:00 start, then the program itself would fit with a lot of headroom. But that is only the program runtime. It does not prove the whole close window is safe, because we still need deploy time, post-change validation, and any concurrent manager queueing. So 6 minutes against a 2-hour window looks fine on paper, but it is not enough by itself to justify a same-night move without extra buffer.
