type Rule = Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool>

fn max_len(n: usize) -> Rule {
    Box::new(|text| text.len() <= n)
}

fn without(word: &str) -> Rule {
    Box::new(|text| !text.contains(word))
}

fn one_of(allowed: Vec<String>) -> Rule {
    Box::new(|text| allowed.iter().any(|w| w == text))
}

fn passes_all(rules: &[Rule], text: &str) -> bool {
    rules.iter().all(|rule| rule(text))
}

fn count_passing(rules: &[Rule], words: &[&str]) -> usize {
    words.iter().filter(|w| passes_all(rules, w)).count()
}

        assert!(!without("bc")("abc"));

## 1. Two ways to abstract

You already know one way to write code that works for many types: generics (sub-module 09). `fn show<T: Display>(item: &T)` works for any `T` that implements `Display`. The compiler handles it by monomorphisation: it writes one copy of `show` for every concrete type you call it with, `show::<i32>`, `show::<String>` and so on. Each copy knows its type exactly, so every call is a direct call that can be inlined. This is static dispatch: the method is chosen at compile time.

Generics have one limit: each use picks one type. A `Vec<T>` holds values of a single type `T`. A function returning `impl Trait` returns one concrete type, even if the caller cannot name it. So how do you keep a text box, a checkbox and a button in one list and call `render` on each?

Rust's answer is a trait object, written `dyn Trait`. A trait object stands for "some value of a type that implements `Trait`; which type is decided at run time". There is only one copy of the code that uses it, and each method call is looked up at run time. This is dynamic dispatch.

Generics (`T: Trait`)Trait objects (`dyn Trait`)

Method chosenat compile timeat run time, through a vtable

Copies of your functionone per concrete typeone

Inliningyesusually not

Mixed types in one `Vec`noyes: `Vec<Box<dyn Trait>>`

The Rust Book (ch. 18.2, "Using Trait Objects to Allow for Values of Different Types") builds a GUI library this way. Our `widgets.rs` is a small version of it:

```
let parts: Vec<Box<dyn Render>> =
    vec![Box::new(Text("hello".into())), Box::new(Checkbox(true))];
for part in &parts {
    println!("{}", part.render()); // which render? decided per element, at run time
}
```

The `Vec` still holds one type: `Box<dyn Render>`. What differs is the type inside each box.

## 2. Behind a pointer: fat pointers and vtables

A `Text` and a `Checkbox` have different sizes. So what size is a `dyn Render`? There is no single answer: `dyn Render` is an unsized type (its size is not known at compile time). Rust can only store values whose size it knows, on the stack, in a struct field or in a `Vec` slot. That is why a trait object always sits behind a pointer: `&dyn Render`, `&mut dyn Render` or `Box<dyn Render>`.

That pointer is a fat pointer: two machine words.

- A data pointer to the value itself (the `Checkbox` on the heap, or wherever it lives).

- A vtable pointer to a table the compiler built for that pair (concrete type, trait).

A vtable ("virtual method table") holds the information needed to use the value without knowing its type: how to drop it, its size and alignment, then one entry per trait method, each pointing at the machine code for that type's version of the method.

Two boxed trait objects. Each element of `parts` is a data pointer plus a vtable pointer. Each (type, Render) pair has its own vtable whose rows point at that type's code.

A call such as `part.label()` does three things at run time: follow the vtable pointer, read the `label` row, call the function found there with the data pointer as `self`. That indirect call is the cost of dynamic dispatch: one extra memory read, and the compiler usually cannot inline the call because it does not know which function it will be.

You can see the "fat" part directly. `static_vs_dyn.rs` prints the sizes of a thin and a fat reference:

```
&i32: 8 bytes, &dyn Display: 16 bytes
```

These numbers are for a 64-bit machine (8-byte pointers). The rule is "two pointers instead of one", not "16 bytes". The exact layout of a vtable (row order, whether two values of the same type share one vtable) is a compiler detail you never rely on.

A `Box<dyn Trait>` also costs a heap allocation per value, because each value must live somewhere the box can point to. A borrowed `&dyn Trait` needs no allocation: `let one: &dyn Render = &Text("plain".into());` in `widgets.rs` points at a value that is already somewhere.

## 3. `Sized` and `?Sized`

Every generic parameter has a hidden bound: `T: Sized`, "the size of `T` is known at compile time". That is almost always what you want, since the function may need to store a `T`. But it means this generic function cannot be called with a trait object:

```
fn show_any<T: Display>(item: &T) -> String { format!("[{item}]") }

let m: Box<dyn Display> = Box::new(7);
show_any(m.as_ref()); // T would be `dyn Display`, which is not Sized
```

```
error[E0277]: the size for values of type `dyn std::fmt::Display` cannot be known at compilation time
```

Write `T: ?Sized` ("`T` may or may not be sized") to remove the hidden bound. This is fine here because `show_any` only ever touches `T` through a reference `&T`, which is a pointer of known size:

```
fn show_any<T: Display + ?Sized>(item: &T) -> String { format!("[{item}]") }
```

Now `T` can be `dyn Display`, or `str` (another unsized type you have used since 03 behind `&str`).

## 4. Choosing between generics and trait objects

SituationUseWhy

A function used with one type at a timegeneric `T: Trait` or `impl Trait`fastest; no allocation; inlinable

A list (or field) holding several types at once`Vec<Box<dyn Trait>>`a `Vec<T>` has exactly one `T`

Types chosen at run time (from a config file, user input, plugins)`Box<dyn Trait>`the compiler cannot know the type

Want less generated code (many types, big function)`&dyn Trait`one copy instead of one per type

A small, fixed set of kinds you controlan `enum`see section 9

A common mistake is to think `Vec<T>` with `T: Trait` can hold "anything that implements `Trait`". It cannot: `T` is one type, chosen by the caller. Only `dyn Trait` erases the concrete type.

## 5. Default methods through `dyn`

A trait may give a method a default body. In `widgets.rs`, `label` has a default and `Checkbox` overrides it:

```
trait Render {
    fn render(&self) -> String;
    fn label(&self) -> String { String::from("(unnamed)") }
}
impl Render for Checkbox {
    fn render(&self) -> String { /* ... */ }
    fn label(&self) -> String { String::from("checkbox") }
}
```

How does a vtable deal with this? Every vtable has a row for every trait method, defaults included. For `Checkbox` the `label` row points at `Checkbox::label`. For `Text`, which does not override it, the row points at the default body compiled for `Text`. A default method is like a small generic function: the compiler makes one copy of it per implementing type.

This explains what happens when a default calls another method of the same trait. Inside the copy compiled for `Text`, `self` is a `&Text`, so `self.render()` calls `Text::render`; the type is known there, so that inner call is static. Only the outer call through the trait object goes through the vtable.

To predict what a default method does for a type, read it as if you had pasted its body into that type's `impl` block. Every `self.method()` inside it then resolves to that type's own `method`, overridden or not.

## 6. Dyn compatibility: which traits can be objects

A vtable is a fixed list: one row per method, each pointing at one function. Some methods cannot fit in such a list, so a trait containing them cannot be used as `dyn Trait`. Such a trait is not dyn compatible (older texts say "not object safe"). The main rules, from the Rust Reference:

Method shapeProblem for a vtable

`fn copy(&self) -> Self`The caller must reserve space for the returned `Self`, but behind `dyn` its size is unknown.

`fn put<V: ToString>(&mut self, v: V)`A generic method is a family of functions, one per `V`. A fixed list cannot hold an open-ended family.

`fn new() -> Self` (no `self`)There is no value, so no vtable to look in.

Uncomment both `doubled` lines in `dyn_compat.rs` to see the error:

```
error[E0038]: the trait `Shape` is not dyn compatible
  ...because method `doubled` references the `Self` type in its return type
```

There are two ways out.

- Keep the method off the vtable with `where Self: Sized`. The trait becomes dyn compatible again, and the method can still be called on concrete types, but not on a `dyn Shape`. `dyn_compat.rs` does this with `doubled_sized`.

- Change the method's shape so it fits in a vtable: return `Box<dyn Shape>` instead of `Self`, or take `&dyn ToString` (or a `String`) instead of a generic `V`. Each costs something: a heap allocation, a conversion, or a second dynamic call.

`Box<dyn Trait>` does not make an incompatible trait compatible. The problem is the trait's methods, not where the object is stored.

## 7. Supertraits

`trait Shape: Debug { ... }` says "every type that implements `Shape` must also implement `Debug`". `Debug` is a supertrait of `Shape`. Two consequences:

- Code that has a `Shape` may use `Debug` too. Debug's method joins Shape's vtable, so `println!("{:?}", shapes[0])` works on a `Box<dyn Shape>`.

- Because the supertrait's methods join the vtable, the supertrait must be dyn compatible as well. `Debug` and `Display` are. `Clone` is not (`clone` returns `Self`), and neither is `Default` (`default()` has no `self` and returns `Self`). So `trait Shape: Clone` makes `dyn Shape` impossible.

```
use std::fmt::Debug;
trait Shape: Debug { fn area(&self) -> f64; }

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Square(f64);
impl Shape for Square { fn area(&self) -> f64 { self.0 * self.0 } }
// impl Shape for Square requires Square: Debug, which the derive provides.
```

## 8. Boxed closures and `'static`

Every closure has its own unnamed type, even two closures with the same signature (10). So a list of closures needs a trait object: `Vec<Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool>>`. `Fn`, `FnMut` and `FnOnce` are traits like any other.

A rule you will meet often: in a struct field or in a function's return type, `Box<dyn Trait>` is short for `Box<dyn Trait + 'static>`. `'static` here means "the value inside does not borrow anything that could go away". A closure meets it if every captured value is owned by the closure: copied in, cloned in or moved in. It fails if it captures a reference to a local variable or to a parameter.

```
fn prefix_rule(prefix: &str) -> Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool> {
    let owned = prefix.to_string();                // the closure gets its own copy
    Box::new(move |s| s.starts_with(owned.as_str()))
}
```

If the closure used `prefix` directly, it would hold a borrow that only lives as long as the caller's string, and the compiler refuses:

```
error: lifetime may not live long enough
  returning this value requires that `'1` must outlive `'static`
```

`move` moves whatever the closure names. If the variable is itself a reference (`prefix: &str`, `limit: &u32`), `move` moves the reference into the closure. The closure still borrows. To own the data, copy or clone it out first: `let limit = *limit;` or `let owned = prefix.to_string();`.

A `&dyn Fn(..)` parameter, by contrast, may borrow freely: it is only used during the call. Writing other lifetimes, such as `Box<dyn Fn() + 'a>`, is covered in 14.

## 9. Consuming a trait object; trait objects vs enums

A method may take its receiver as `self: Box<Self>`. It then consumes the box: after the call, the object is gone. The Book's state pattern (ch. 18.3, "Implementing an Object-Oriented Design Pattern") uses this so a state transition uses up the old state. `state.rs` is adapted from it:

```
trait State {
    fn submit(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn State>;
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str;
}
impl State for Draft {
    fn submit(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn State> { Box::new(Review) }
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str { "draft" }
}
```

`self: Box<Self>` is dyn compatible: the receiver is a pointer of known size, so the call can go through the vtable. The catch is that you must own the box to call it. A shared or mutable borrow of a box is not enough; you cannot move a box out from behind a reference. When the box sits inside something else, take it out first:

Where the box livesHow to take it out

`Option<Box<dyn State>>``opt.take()` leaves `None` behind

a field or variable of a type with a default`std::mem::take(&mut x)` (11)

a `Vec<Box<dyn T>>`, all of it`v.drain(..)` or `mem::take(&mut v)`, which leave it empty

a `Vec`, one element`v.remove(i)` or `v.pop()`

### Trait objects or an enum?

The same states could be an `enum State { Draft, Review, Published }` with `match` in each operation. The two designs make different changes cheap:

ChangeTrait objectsEnum + match

Add a new kind (type / variant)one new type and its `impl`; no other code changesedit every `match`

Add a new operationadd a method to the trait and to every typeone new function with one `match`; the compiler checks every case

Types from outside your crate (plugins)yesno: the set is closed

Cost per callvtable call, heap allocation per boxa `match` on a tag; no allocation needed

- Why does a closure stored in a `Box<dyn Fn()>` field have to own what it captures?

- What would you gain and lose by rewriting `state.rs` as an enum?

[entity 908 · fat-pointer.png · diagram]
Diagram: a trait object is a fat pointer.

Left, two elements of `parts: Vec<Box<dyn Render>>`. Each element is two pointers side by side: a "data ptr" and a "vtable ptr".
- parts[0]: the data ptr points to `Text("hello")` on the heap; the vtable ptr points to the vtable for (Text, Render).
- parts[1]: the data ptr points to `Checkbox(true)` on the heap; the vtable ptr points to the vtable for (Checkbox, Render).

Middle, the two vtables. Each has rows: drop, size and align, render, label.

Right, where the rows point:
- Text's `render` row -> `Text::render`. Text's `label` row -> the trait's default `label`, compiled for Text (Text does not override it).
- Checkbox's `render` row -> `Checkbox::render`. Checkbox's `label` row -> `Checkbox::label` (its override).

Caption: `part.label()` on parts[0] follows the vtable ptr, reads the "label" row and calls it with the data ptr as `self`. Row order and whether vtables are shared are compiler details. On 64-bit each pointer is 8 bytes, so the fat pointer is 16.

trait Animal {
    fn name(&self) -> String;
    fn sound(&self) -> String;
    // Default: "<name> says <sound>"
    fn speak(&self) -> String {
        format!("{} says {}", self.name(), self.sound())
    }
}

struct Dog;
struct Cat {
    name: String,
}
struct Parrot {
    word: String,
}

impl Animal for Dog {
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        String::from("dog")
    }
    fn sound(&self) -> String {
        String::from("woof")
    }
}

impl Animal for Cat {
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        self.name.clone()
    }
    fn sound(&self) -> String {
        String::from("meow")
    }
}

impl Animal for Parrot {
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        String::from("parrot")
    }
    fn sound(&self) -> String {
        self.word.clone()
    }
    fn speak(&self) -> String {
        format!("{0}! {0}!", self.word)
    }
}

// Exercise 2: rules as boxed closures (reference solution)
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex2_rules.rs && ./main --test-threads=4

type Rule = Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool>;

fn max_len(n: usize) -> Rule {
    Box::new(move |s| s.len() <= n) // usize is Copy: copied in
}

fn without(word: &str) -> Rule {
    let word = word.to_string(); // own a copy; the closure must be 'static
    Box::new(move |s| !s.contains(word.as_str()))
}

fn one_of(allowed: Vec<String>) -> Rule {
    Box::new(move |s| allowed.iter().any(|a| a == s)) // the Vec is moved in
}

fn passes_all(rules: &[Rule], text: &str) -> bool {
    rules.iter().all(|r| r(text))
}

fn count_passing(rules: &[Rule], words: &[&str]) -> usize {
    words.iter().filter(|w| passes_all(rules, w)).count()
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn single_rules() {
        assert!(max_len(3)("abc"));
        assert!(!max_len(3)("abcd"));
        assert!(without("x")("abc"));
        assert!(!without("bc")("abc"));
        let r = one_of(vec!["red".into(), "blue".into()]);
        assert!(r("red") && !r("green"));
    }

    #[test]
    fn rule_outlives_the_string_it_was_made_from() {
        let rule = {
            let temp = String::from("oops");
            without(&temp)
        }; // `temp` is dropped here; the rule must still work
        assert!(rule("fine"));
        assert!(!rule("oops!"));
    }

    #[test]
    fn rules_of_different_closure_types_in_one_vec() {
        let rules: Vec<Rule> = vec![max_len(5), without("z"), Box::new(|s: &str| !s.is_empty())];
        assert!(passes_all(&rules, "abc"));
        assert!(!passes_all(&rules, "abcdef"));
        assert!(!passes_all(&rules, ""));
        assert!(passes_all(&[], "anything"));
        assert_eq!(count_passing(&rules, &["ok", "zoo", "toolong", "", "fine"]), 2);
    }
}

trait Light {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light>;
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str;
    // Default: most lights stay on for 30 seconds.
    fn seconds(&self) -> u32 {
        30
    }
}

struct Red;
struct Green;
struct Yellow;

impl Light for Red {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Green)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "red"
    }
}

impl Light for Green {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Yellow)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "green"
    }
}

impl Light for Yellow {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Red)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "yellow"
    }
    fn seconds(&self) -> u32 {
        5
    }
}

struct Signal {
    light: Option<Box<dyn Light>>,
}

impl Signal {
    fn new() -> Signal {
        Signal { light: Some(Box::new(Red)) }
    }

    fn advance(&mut self) {
        // take() leaves None behind, giving us the owned Box to consume.
        let old = self.light.take().unwrap();
        self.light = Some(old.next());
    }

    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        self.light.as_ref().unwrap().color()
    }

    fn run_for(&mut self, n: usize) -> u32 {
        let mut total = 0;
        for _ in 0..n {
            total += self.light.as_ref().unwrap().seconds();
            self.advance();
        }
        total
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn cycle_of_colours() {
        let mut s = Signal::new();
        let mut seen = vec![s.color()];
        for _ in 0..3 {
            s.advance();
            seen.push(s.color());
        }
        assert_eq!(seen, ["red", "green", "yellow", "red"]);
    }

    #[test]
    fn default_and_overridden_seconds() {
        assert_eq!(Red.seconds(), 30);
        assert_eq!(Green.seconds(), 30);
        assert_eq!(Yellow.seconds(), 5);
    }

    #[test]
    fn run_for_adds_up_and_moves_on() {
        let mut s = Signal::new();
        assert_eq!(s.run_for(3), 65);
        assert_eq!(s.color(), "red");
        assert_eq!(s.run_for(0), 0);
        assert_eq!(s.run_for(2), 60);
        assert_eq!(s.color(), "yellow");
    }
}

## 1. Two ways to abstract

You already know one way to write code that works for many types: generics (sub-module 09). `fn show<T: Display>(item: &T)` works for any `T` that implements `Display`. The compiler handles it by monomorphisation: it writes one copy of `show` for every concrete type you call it with, `show::<i32>`, `show::<String>` and so on. Each copy knows its type exactly, so every call is a direct call that can be inlined. This is static dispatch: the method is chosen at compile time.

Generics have one limit: each use picks one type. A `Vec<T>` holds values of a single type `T`. A function returning `impl Trait` returns one concrete type, even if the caller cannot name it. So how do you keep a text box, a checkbox and a button in one list and call `render` on each?

Rust's answer is a trait object, written `dyn Trait`. A trait object stands for "some value of a type that implements `Trait`; which type is decided at run time". There is only one copy of the code that uses it, and each method call is looked up at run time. This is dynamic dispatch.

Generics (`T: Trait`)Trait objects (`dyn Trait`)

Method chosenat compile timeat run time, through a vtable

Copies of your functionone per concrete typeone

Inliningyesusually not

Mixed types in one `Vec`noyes: `Vec<Box<dyn Trait>>`

The Rust Book (ch. 18.2, "Using Trait Objects to Allow for Values of Different Types") builds a GUI library this way. Our `widgets.rs` is a small version of it:

```
let parts: Vec<Box<dyn Render>> =
    vec![Box::new(Text("hello".into())), Box::new(Checkbox(true))];
for part in &parts {
    println!("{}", part.render()); // which render? decided per element, at run time
}
```

The `Vec` still holds one type: `Box<dyn Render>`. What differs is the type inside each box.

## 2. Behind a pointer: fat pointers and vtables

A `Text` and a `Checkbox` have different sizes. So what size is a `dyn Render`? There is no single answer: `dyn Render` is an unsized type (its size is not known at compile time). Rust can only store values whose size it knows, on the stack, in a struct field or in a `Vec` slot. That is why a trait object always sits behind a pointer: `&dyn Render`, `&mut dyn Render` or `Box<dyn Render>`.

That pointer is a fat pointer: two machine words.

- A data pointer to the value itself (the `Checkbox` on the heap, or wherever it lives).

- A vtable pointer to a table the compiler built for that pair (concrete type, trait).

A vtable ("virtual method table") holds the information needed to use the value without knowing its type: how to drop it, its size and alignment, then one entry per trait method, each pointing at the machine code for that type's version of the method.

Two boxed trait objects. Each element of `parts` is a data pointer plus a vtable pointer. Each (type, Render) pair has its own vtable whose rows point at that type's code.

A call such as `part.label()` does three things at run time: follow the vtable pointer, read the `label` row, call the function found there with the data pointer as `self`. That indirect call is the cost of dynamic dispatch: one extra memory read, and the compiler usually cannot inline the call because it does not know which function it will be.

You can see the "fat" part directly. `static_vs_dyn.rs` prints the sizes of a thin and a fat reference:

```
&i32: 8 bytes, &dyn Display: 16 bytes
```

These numbers are for a 64-bit machine (8-byte pointers). The rule is "two pointers instead of one", not "16 bytes". The exact layout of a vtable (row order, whether two values of the same type share one vtable) is a compiler detail you never rely on.

A `Box<dyn Trait>` also costs a heap allocation per value, because each value must live somewhere the box can point to. A borrowed `&dyn Trait` needs no allocation: `let one: &dyn Render = &Text("plain".into());` in `widgets.rs` points at a value that is already somewhere.

## 3. `Sized` and `?Sized`

Every generic parameter has a hidden bound: `T: Sized`, "the size of `T` is known at compile time". That is almost always what you want, since the function may need to store a `T`. But it means this generic function cannot be called with a trait object:

```
fn show_any<T: Display>(item: &T) -> String { format!("[{item}]") }

let m: Box<dyn Display> = Box::new(7);
show_any(m.as_ref()); // T would be `dyn Display`, which is not Sized
```

```
error[E0277]: the size for values of type `dyn std::fmt::Display` cannot be known at compilation time
```

Write `T: ?Sized` ("`T` may or may not be sized") to remove the hidden bound. This is fine here because `show_any` only ever touches `T` through a reference `&T`, which is a pointer of known size:

```
fn show_any<T: Display + ?Sized>(item: &T) -> String { format!("[{item}]") }
```

Now `T` can be `dyn Display`, or `str` (another unsized type you have used since 03 behind `&str`).

## 4. Choosing between generics and trait objects

SituationUseWhy

A function used with one type at a timegeneric `T: Trait` or `impl Trait`fastest; no allocation; inlinable

A list (or field) holding several types at once`Vec<Box<dyn Trait>>`a `Vec<T>` has exactly one `T`

Types chosen at run time (from a config file, user input, plugins)`Box<dyn Trait>`the compiler cannot know the type

Want less generated code (many types, big function)`&dyn Trait`one copy instead of one per type

A small, fixed set of kinds you controlan `enum`see section 9

A common mistake is to think `Vec<T>` with `T: Trait` can hold "anything that implements `Trait`". It cannot: `T` is one type, chosen by the caller. Only `dyn Trait` erases the concrete type.

## 5. Default methods through `dyn`

A trait may give a method a default body. In `widgets.rs`, `label` has a default and `Checkbox` overrides it:

```
trait Render {
    fn render(&self) -> String;
    fn label(&self) -> String { String::from("(unnamed)") }
}
impl Render for Checkbox {
    fn render(&self) -> String { /* ... */ }
    fn label(&self) -> String { String::from("checkbox") }
}
```

How does a vtable deal with this? Every vtable has a row for every trait method, defaults included. For `Checkbox` the `label` row points at `Checkbox::label`. For `Text`, which does not override it, the row points at the default body compiled for `Text`. A default method is like a small generic function: the compiler makes one copy of it per implementing type.

This explains what happens when a default calls another method of the same trait. Inside the copy compiled for `Text`, `self` is a `&Text`, so `self.render()` calls `Text::render`; the type is known there, so that inner call is static. Only the outer call through the trait object goes through the vtable.

To predict what a default method does for a type, read it as if you had pasted its body into that type's `impl` block. Every `self.method()` inside it then resolves to that type's own `method`, overridden or not.

## 6. Dyn compatibility: which traits can be objects

A vtable is a fixed list: one row per method, each pointing at one function. Some methods cannot fit in such a list, so a trait containing them cannot be used as `dyn Trait`. Such a trait is not dyn compatible (older texts say "not object safe"). The main rules, from the Rust Reference:

Method shapeProblem for a vtable

`fn copy(&self) -> Self`The caller must reserve space for the returned `Self`, but behind `dyn` its size is unknown.

`fn put<V: ToString>(&mut self, v: V)`A generic method is a family of functions, one per `V`. A fixed list cannot hold an open-ended family.

`fn new() -> Self` (no `self`)There is no value, so no vtable to look in.

Uncomment both `doubled` lines in `dyn_compat.rs` to see the error:

```
error[E0038]: the trait `Shape` is not dyn compatible
  ...because method `doubled` references the `Self` type in its return type
```

There are two ways out.

- Keep the method off the vtable with `where Self: Sized`. The trait becomes dyn compatible again, and the method can still be called on concrete types, but not on a `dyn Shape`. `dyn_compat.rs` does this with `doubled_sized`.

- Change the method's shape so it fits in a vtable: return `Box<dyn Shape>` instead of `Self`, or take `&dyn ToString` (or a `String`) instead of a generic `V`. Each costs something: a heap allocation, a conversion, or a second dynamic call.

`Box<dyn Trait>` does not make an incompatible trait compatible. The problem is the trait's methods, not where the object is stored.

## 7. Supertraits

`trait Shape: Debug { ... }` says "every type that implements `Shape` must also implement `Debug`". `Debug` is a supertrait of `Shape`. Two consequences:

- Code that has a `Shape` may use `Debug` too. Debug's method joins Shape's vtable, so `println!("{:?}", shapes[0])` works on a `Box<dyn Shape>`.

- Because the supertrait's methods join the vtable, the supertrait must be dyn compatible as well. `Debug` and `Display` are. `Clone` is not (`clone` returns `Self`), and neither is `Default` (`default()` has no `self` and returns `Self`). So `trait Shape: Clone` makes `dyn Shape` impossible.

```
use std::fmt::Debug;
trait Shape: Debug { fn area(&self) -> f64; }

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Square(f64);
impl Shape for Square { fn area(&self) -> f64 { self.0 * self.0 } }
// impl Shape for Square requires Square: Debug, which the derive provides.
```

## 8. Boxed closures and `'static`

Every closure has its own unnamed type, even two closures with the same signature (10). So a list of closures needs a trait object: `Vec<Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool>>`. `Fn`, `FnMut` and `FnOnce` are traits like any other.

A rule you will meet often: in a struct field or in a function's return type, `Box<dyn Trait>` is short for `Box<dyn Trait + 'static>`. `'static` here means "the value inside does not borrow anything that could go away". A closure meets it if every captured value is owned by the closure: copied in, cloned in or moved in. It fails if it captures a reference to a local variable or to a parameter.

```
fn prefix_rule(prefix: &str) -> Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool> {
    let owned = prefix.to_string();                // the closure gets its own copy
    Box::new(move |s| s.starts_with(owned.as_str()))
}
```

If the closure used `prefix` directly, it would hold a borrow that only lives as long as the caller's string, and the compiler refuses:

```
error: lifetime may not live long enough
  returning this value requires that `'1` must outlive `'static`
```

`move` moves whatever the closure names. If the variable is itself a reference (`prefix: &str`, `limit: &u32`), `move` moves the reference into the closure. The closure still borrows. To own the data, copy or clone it out first: `let limit = *limit;` or `let owned = prefix.to_string();`.

A `&dyn Fn(..)` parameter, by contrast, may borrow freely: it is only used during the call. Writing other lifetimes, such as `Box<dyn Fn() + 'a>`, is covered in 14.

## 9. Consuming a trait object; trait objects vs enums

A method may take its receiver as `self: Box<Self>`. It then consumes the box: after the call, the object is gone. The Book's state pattern (ch. 18.3, "Implementing an Object-Oriented Design Pattern") uses this so a state transition uses up the old state. `state.rs` is adapted from it:

```
trait State {
    fn submit(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn State>;
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str;
}
impl State for Draft {
    fn submit(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn State> { Box::new(Review) }
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str { "draft" }
}
```

`self: Box<Self>` is dyn compatible: the receiver is a pointer of known size, so the call can go through the vtable. The catch is that you must own the box to call it. A shared or mutable borrow of a box is not enough; you cannot move a box out from behind a reference. When the box sits inside something else, take it out first:

Where the box livesHow to take it out

`Option<Box<dyn State>>``opt.take()` leaves `None` behind

a field or variable of a type with a default`std::mem::take(&mut x)` (11)

a `Vec<Box<dyn T>>`, all of it`v.drain(..)` or `mem::take(&mut v)`, which leave it empty

a `Vec`, one element`v.remove(i)` or `v.pop()`

### Trait objects or an enum?

The same states could be an `enum State { Draft, Review, Published }` with `match` in each operation. The two designs make different changes cheap:

ChangeTrait objectsEnum + match

Add a new kind (type / variant)one new type and its `impl`; no other code changesedit every `match`

Add a new operationadd a method to the trait and to every typeone new function with one `match`; the compiler checks every case

Types from outside your crate (plugins)yesno: the set is closed

Cost per callvtable call, heap allocation per boxa `match` on a tag; no allocation needed

Ask the Tutor about any of these. Try to answer first.

- Why must `dyn Trait` always sit behind a pointer? What are the two halves of that pointer?

- Why can a trait with `fn copy(&self) -> Self` not be a trait object, while `fn copy(&self) -> Box<dyn Trait>` is fine?

- A default method calls `self.unit()`. For a type that overrides `unit`, which `unit` runs, and why?

- Why does a closure stored in a `Box<dyn Fn()>` field have to own what it captures?

- What would you gain and lose by rewriting `state.rs` as an enum?

Diagram: a trait object is a fat pointer.

Left, two elements of `parts: Vec<Box<dyn Render>>`. Each element is two pointers side by side: a "data ptr" and a "vtable ptr".

Middle, the two vtables. Each has rows: drop, size and align, render, label.

Right, where the rows point:
- Text's `render` row -> `Text::render`. Text's `label` row -> the trait's default `label`, compiled for Text (Text does not override it).
- Checkbox's `render` row -> `Checkbox::render`. Checkbox's `label` row -> `Checkbox::label` (its override).

Caption: `part.label()` on parts[0] follows the vtable ptr, reads the "label" row and calls it with the data ptr as `self`. Row order and whether vtables are shared are compiler details. On 64-bit each pointer is 8 bytes, so the fat pointer is 16.

// Exercise 1: a mixed zoo (reference solution)
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex1_zoo.rs && ./main --test-threads=4

trait Animal {
    fn name(&self) -> String;
    fn sound(&self) -> String;
    // Default: "<name> says <sound>"
    fn speak(&self) -> String {
        format!("{} says {}", self.name(), self.sound())
    }
}

struct Dog;
struct Cat {
    name: String,
}
struct Parrot {
    word: String,
}

impl Animal for Dog {
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        String::from("dog")
    }
    fn sound(&self) -> String {
        String::from("woof")
    }
}

impl Animal for Cat {
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        self.name.clone()
    }
    fn sound(&self) -> String {
        String::from("meow")
    }
}

impl Animal for Parrot {
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        String::from("parrot")
    }
    fn sound(&self) -> String {
        self.word.clone()
    }
    fn speak(&self) -> String {
        format!("{0}! {0}!", self.word)
    }
}

fn zoo() -> Vec<Box<dyn Animal>> {
    vec![
        Box::new(Dog),
        Box::new(Cat { name: "Tom".into() }),
        Box::new(Parrot { word: "hello".into() }),
    ]
}

fn chorus(animals: &[Box<dyn Animal>]) -> String {
    let lines: Vec<String> = animals.iter().map(|a| a.speak()).collect();
    lines.join("; ")
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn default_speak_uses_each_types_own_name_and_sound() {
        assert_eq!(Dog.speak(), "dog says woof");
        assert_eq!(Cat { name: "Kit".into() }.speak(), "Kit says meow");
    }

    #[test]
    fn parrot_overrides_speak() {
        let p = Parrot { word: "hi".into() };
        assert_eq!(p.sound(), "hi");
        assert_eq!(p.speak(), "hi! hi!");
    }

    #[test]
    fn zoo_holds_three_different_types() {
        let z = zoo();
        let names: Vec<String> = z.iter().map(|a| a.name()).collect();
        assert_eq!(names, ["dog", "Tom", "parrot"]);
    }

    #[test]
    fn chorus_goes_through_the_vtable() {
        assert_eq!(chorus(&zoo()), "dog says woof; Tom says meow; hello! hello!");
        assert_eq!(chorus(&[]), "");
    }
}

// Exercise 2: rules as boxed closures (reference solution)
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex2_rules.rs && ./main --test-threads=4

type Rule = Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool>;

fn max_len(n: usize) -> Rule {
    Box::new(move |s| s.len() <= n) // usize is Copy: copied in
}

fn without(word: &str) -> Rule {
    let word = word.to_string(); // own a copy; the closure must be 'static
    Box::new(move |s| !s.contains(word.as_str()))
}

fn one_of(allowed: Vec<String>) -> Rule {
    Box::new(move |s| allowed.iter().any(|a| a == s)) // the Vec is moved in
}

fn passes_all(rules: &[Rule], text: &str) -> bool {
    rules.iter().all(|r| r(text))
}

fn count_passing(rules: &[Rule], words: &[&str]) -> usize {
    words.iter().filter(|w| passes_all(rules, w)).count()
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn single_rules() {
        assert!(max_len(3)("abc"));
        assert!(!max_len(3)("abcd"));
        assert!(without("x")("abc"));
        assert!(!without("bc")("abc"));
        let r = one_of(vec!["red".into(), "blue".into()]);
        assert!(r("red") && !r("green"));
    }

    #[test]
    fn rule_outlives_the_string_it_was_made_from() {
        let rule = {
            let temp = String::from("oops");
            without(&temp)
        }; // `temp` is dropped here; the rule must still work
        assert!(rule("fine"));
        assert!(!rule("oops!"));
    }

    #[test]
    fn rules_of_different_closure_types_in_one_vec() {
        let rules: Vec<Rule> = vec![max_len(5), without("z"), Box::new(|s: &str| !s.is_empty())];
        assert!(passes_all(&rules, "abc"));
        assert!(!passes_all(&rules, "abcdef"));
        assert!(!passes_all(&rules, ""));
        assert!(passes_all(&[], "anything"));
        assert_eq!(count_passing(&rules, &["ok", "zoo", "toolong", "", "fine"]), 2);
    }
}

// Exercise 3: a traffic signal with the state pattern (reference solution)
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex3_signal.rs && ./main --test-threads=4

trait Light {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light>;
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str;
    // Default: most lights stay on for 30 seconds.
    fn seconds(&self) -> u32 {
        30
    }
}

struct Red;
struct Green;
struct Yellow;

impl Light for Red {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Green)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "red"
    }
}

impl Light for Green {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Yellow)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "green"
    }
}

impl Light for Yellow {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Red)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "yellow"
    }
    fn seconds(&self) -> u32 {
        5
    }
}

struct Signal {
    light: Option<Box<dyn Light>>,
}

impl Signal {
    fn new() -> Signal {
        Signal { light: Some(Box::new(Red)) }
    }

    fn advance(&mut self) {
        // take() leaves None behind, giving us the owned Box to consume.
        let old = self.light.take().unwrap();
        self.light = Some(old.next());
    }

    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        self.light.as_ref().unwrap().color()
    }

    fn run_for(&mut self, n: usize) -> u32 {
        let mut total = 0;
        for _ in 0..n {
            total += self.light.as_ref().unwrap().seconds();
            self.advance();
        }
        total
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn cycle_of_colours() {
        let mut s = Signal::new();
        let mut seen = vec![s.color()];
        for _ in 0..3 {
            s.advance();
            seen.push(s.color());
        }
        assert_eq!(seen, ["red", "green", "yellow", "red"]);
    }

    #[test]
    fn default_and_overridden_seconds() {
        assert_eq!(Red.seconds(), 30);
        assert_eq!(Green.seconds(), 30);
        assert_eq!(Yellow.seconds(), 5);
    }

    #[test]
    fn run_for_adds_up_and_moves_on() {
        let mut s = Signal::new();
        assert_eq!(s.run_for(3), 65);
        assert_eq!(s.color(), "red");
        assert_eq!(s.run_for(0), 0);
        assert_eq!(s.run_for(2), 60);
        assert_eq!(s.color(), "yellow");
    }
}

## 1. Two ways to abstract

You already know one way to write code that works for many types: generics (sub-module 09). `fn show<T: Display>(item: &T)` works for any `T` that implements `Display`. The compiler handles it by monomorphisation: it writes one copy of `show` for every concrete type you call it with, `show::<i32>`, `show::<String>` and so on. Each copy knows its type exactly, so every call is a direct call that can be inlined. This is static dispatch: the method is chosen at compile time.

Generics have one limit: each use picks one type. A `Vec<T>` holds values of a single type `T`. A function returning `impl Trait` returns one concrete type, even if the caller cannot name it. So how do you keep a text box, a checkbox and a button in one list and call `render` on each?

Rust's answer is a trait object, written `dyn Trait`. A trait object stands for "some value of a type that implements `Trait`; which type is decided at run time". There is only one copy of the code that uses it, and each method call is looked up at run time. This is dynamic dispatch.

Generics (`T: Trait`)Trait objects (`dyn Trait`)

Method chosenat compile timeat run time, through a vtable

Copies of your functionone per concrete typeone

Inliningyesusually not

Mixed types in one `Vec`noyes: `Vec<Box<dyn Trait>>`

The Rust Book (ch. 18.2, "Using Trait Objects to Allow for Values of Different Types") builds a GUI library this way. Our `widgets.rs` is a small version of it:

```
let parts: Vec<Box<dyn Render>> =
    vec![Box::new(Text("hello".into())), Box::new(Checkbox(true))];
for part in &parts {
    println!("{}", part.render()); // which render? decided per element, at run time
}
```

The `Vec` still holds one type: `Box<dyn Render>`. What differs is the type inside each box.

## 2. Behind a pointer: fat pointers and vtables

A `Text` and a `Checkbox` have different sizes. So what size is a `dyn Render`? There is no single answer: `dyn Render` is an unsized type (its size is not known at compile time). Rust can only store values whose size it knows, on the stack, in a struct field or in a `Vec` slot. That is why a trait object always sits behind a pointer: `&dyn Render`, `&mut dyn Render` or `Box<dyn Render>`.

That pointer is a fat pointer: two machine words.

- A data pointer to the value itself (the `Checkbox` on the heap, or wherever it lives).

- A vtable pointer to a table the compiler built for that pair (concrete type, trait).

A vtable ("virtual method table") holds the information needed to use the value without knowing its type: how to drop it, its size and alignment, then one entry per trait method, each pointing at the machine code for that type's version of the method.

Two boxed trait objects. Each element of `parts` is a data pointer plus a vtable pointer. Each (type, Render) pair has its own vtable whose rows point at that type's code.

A call such as `part.label()` does three things at run time: follow the vtable pointer, read the `label` row, call the function found there with the data pointer as `self`. That indirect call is the cost of dynamic dispatch: one extra memory read, and the compiler usually cannot inline the call because it does not know which function it will be.

You can see the "fat" part directly. `static_vs_dyn.rs` prints the sizes of a thin and a fat reference:

```
&i32: 8 bytes, &dyn Display: 16 bytes
```

These numbers are for a 64-bit machine (8-byte pointers). The rule is "two pointers instead of one", not "16 bytes". The exact layout of a vtable (row order, whether two values of the same type share one vtable) is a compiler detail you never rely on.

A `Box<dyn Trait>` also costs a heap allocation per value, because each value must live somewhere the box can point to. A borrowed `&dyn Trait` needs no allocation: `let one: &dyn Render = &Text("plain".into());` in `widgets.rs` points at a value that is already somewhere.

## 3. `Sized` and `?Sized`

Every generic parameter has a hidden bound: `T: Sized`, "the size of `T` is known at compile time". That is almost always what you want, since the function may need to store a `T`. But it means this generic function cannot be called with a trait object:

```
fn show_any<T: Display>(item: &T) -> String { format!("[{item}]") }

let m: Box<dyn Display> = Box::new(7);
show_any(m.as_ref()); // T would be `dyn Display`, which is not Sized
```

```
error[E0277]: the size for values of type `dyn std::fmt::Display` cannot be known at compilation time
```

Write `T: ?Sized` ("`T` may or may not be sized") to remove the hidden bound. This is fine here because `show_any` only ever touches `T` through a reference `&T`, which is a pointer of known size:

```
fn show_any<T: Display + ?Sized>(item: &T) -> String { format!("[{item}]") }
```

Now `T` can be `dyn Display`, or `str` (another unsized type you have used since 03 behind `&str`).

## 4. Choosing between generics and trait objects

SituationUseWhy

A function used with one type at a timegeneric `T: Trait` or `impl Trait`fastest; no allocation; inlinable

A list (or field) holding several types at once`Vec<Box<dyn Trait>>`a `Vec<T>` has exactly one `T`

Types chosen at run time (from a config file, user input, plugins)`Box<dyn Trait>`the compiler cannot know the type

Want less generated code (many types, big function)`&dyn Trait`one copy instead of one per type

A small, fixed set of kinds you controlan `enum`see section 9

A common mistake is to think `Vec<T>` with `T: Trait` can hold "anything that implements `Trait`". It cannot: `T` is one type, chosen by the caller. Only `dyn Trait` erases the concrete type.

## 5. Default methods through `dyn`

A trait may give a method a default body. In `widgets.rs`, `label` has a default and `Checkbox` overrides it:

```
trait Render {
    fn render(&self) -> String;
    fn label(&self) -> String { String::from("(unnamed)") }
}
impl Render for Checkbox {
    fn render(&self) -> String { /* ... */ }
    fn label(&self) -> String { String::from("checkbox") }
}
```

How does a vtable deal with this? Every vtable has a row for every trait method, defaults included. For `Checkbox` the `label` row points at `Checkbox::label`. For `Text`, which does not override it, the row points at the default body compiled for `Text`. A default method is like a small generic function: the compiler makes one copy of it per implementing type.

This explains what happens when a default calls another method of the same trait. Inside the copy compiled for `Text`, `self` is a `&Text`, so `self.render()` calls `Text::render`; the type is known there, so that inner call is static. Only the outer call through the trait object goes through the vtable.

To predict what a default method does for a type, read it as if you had pasted its body into that type's `impl` block. Every `self.method()` inside it then resolves to that type's own `method`, overridden or not.

## 6. Dyn compatibility: which traits can be objects

A vtable is a fixed list: one row per method, each pointing at one function. Some methods cannot fit in such a list, so a trait containing them cannot be used as `dyn Trait`. Such a trait is not dyn compatible (older texts say "not object safe"). The main rules, from the Rust Reference:

Method shapeProblem for a vtable

`fn copy(&self) -> Self`The caller must reserve space for the returned `Self`, but behind `dyn` its size is unknown.

`fn put<V: ToString>(&mut self, v: V)`A generic method is a family of functions, one per `V`. A fixed list cannot hold an open-ended family.

`fn new() -> Self` (no `self`)There is no value, so no vtable to look in.

Uncomment both `doubled` lines in `dyn_compat.rs` to see the error:

```
error[E0038]: the trait `Shape` is not dyn compatible
  ...because method `doubled` references the `Self` type in its return type
```

There are two ways out.

- Keep the method off the vtable with `where Self: Sized`. The trait becomes dyn compatible again, and the method can still be called on concrete types, but not on a `dyn Shape`. `dyn_compat.rs` does this with `doubled_sized`.

- Change the method's shape so it fits in a vtable: return `Box<dyn Shape>` instead of `Self`, or take `&dyn ToString` (or a `String`) instead of a generic `V`. Each costs something: a heap allocation, a conversion, or a second dynamic call.

`Box<dyn Trait>` does not make an incompatible trait compatible. The problem is the trait's methods, not where the object is stored.

## 7. Supertraits

`trait Shape: Debug { ... }` says "every type that implements `Shape` must also implement `Debug`". `Debug` is a supertrait of `Shape`. Two consequences:

- Code that has a `Shape` may use `Debug` too. Debug's method joins Shape's vtable, so `println!("{:?}", shapes[0])` works on a `Box<dyn Shape>`.

- Because the supertrait's methods join the vtable, the supertrait must be dyn compatible as well. `Debug` and `Display` are. `Clone` is not (`clone` returns `Self`), and neither is `Default` (`default()` has no `self` and returns `Self`). So `trait Shape: Clone` makes `dyn Shape` impossible.

```
use std::fmt::Debug;
trait Shape: Debug { fn area(&self) -> f64; }

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Square(f64);
impl Shape for Square { fn area(&self) -> f64 { self.0 * self.0 } }
// impl Shape for Square requires Square: Debug, which the derive provides.
```

## 8. Boxed closures and `'static`

Every closure has its own unnamed type, even two closures with the same signature (10). So a list of closures needs a trait object: `Vec<Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool>>`. `Fn`, `FnMut` and `FnOnce` are traits like any other.

A rule you will meet often: in a struct field or in a function's return type, `Box<dyn Trait>` is short for `Box<dyn Trait + 'static>`. `'static` here means "the value inside does not borrow anything that could go away". A closure meets it if every captured value is owned by the closure: copied in, cloned in or moved in. It fails if it captures a reference to a local variable or to a parameter.

```
fn prefix_rule(prefix: &str) -> Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool> {
    let owned = prefix.to_string();                // the closure gets its own copy
    Box::new(move |s| s.starts_with(owned.as_str()))
}
```

If the closure used `prefix` directly, it would hold a borrow that only lives as long as the caller's string, and the compiler refuses:

```
error: lifetime may not live long enough
  returning this value requires that `'1` must outlive `'static`
```

`move` moves whatever the closure names. If the variable is itself a reference (`prefix: &str`, `limit: &u32`), `move` moves the reference into the closure. The closure still borrows. To own the data, copy or clone it out first: `let limit = *limit;` or `let owned = prefix.to_string();`.

A `&dyn Fn(..)` parameter, by contrast, may borrow freely: it is only used during the call. Writing other lifetimes, such as `Box<dyn Fn() + 'a>`, is covered in 14.

## 9. Consuming a trait object; trait objects vs enums

A method may take its receiver as `self: Box<Self>`. It then consumes the box: after the call, the object is gone. The Book's state pattern (ch. 18.3, "Implementing an Object-Oriented Design Pattern") uses this so a state transition uses up the old state. `state.rs` is adapted from it:

```
trait State {
    fn submit(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn State>;
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str;
}
impl State for Draft {
    fn submit(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn State> { Box::new(Review) }
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str { "draft" }
}
```

`self: Box<Self>` is dyn compatible: the receiver is a pointer of known size, so the call can go through the vtable. The catch is that you must own the box to call it. A shared or mutable borrow of a box is not enough; you cannot move a box out from behind a reference. When the box sits inside something else, take it out first:

Where the box livesHow to take it out

`Option<Box<dyn State>>``opt.take()` leaves `None` behind

a field or variable of a type with a default`std::mem::take(&mut x)` (11)

a `Vec<Box<dyn T>>`, all of it`v.drain(..)` or `mem::take(&mut v)`, which leave it empty

a `Vec`, one element`v.remove(i)` or `v.pop()`

### Trait objects or an enum?

The same states could be an `enum State { Draft, Review, Published }` with `match` in each operation. The two designs make different changes cheap:

ChangeTrait objectsEnum + match

Add a new kind (type / variant)one new type and its `impl`; no other code changesedit every `match`

Add a new operationadd a method to the trait and to every typeone new function with one `match`; the compiler checks every case

Types from outside your crate (plugins)yesno: the set is closed

Cost per callvtable call, heap allocation per boxa `match` on a tag; no allocation needed

## 10. Check yourself

Ask the Tutor about any of these. Try to answer first.

- Why must `dyn Trait` always sit behind a pointer? What are the two halves of that pointer?

- Why can a trait with `fn copy(&self) -> Self` not be a trait object, while `fn copy(&self) -> Box<dyn Trait>` is fine?

- A default method calls `self.unit()`. For a type that overrides `unit`, which `unit` runs, and why?

- Why does a closure stored in a `Box<dyn Fn()>` field have to own what it captures?

- What would you gain and lose by rewriting `state.rs` as an enum?

Sources: adapted from The Rust Programming Language, ch. 18.2 and ch. 18.3, Rust by Example, "Returning Traits with dyn" and the Rust Reference, "Dyn compatibility" (MIT/Apache-2.0).

Diagram: a trait object is a fat pointer.

Left, two elements of `parts: Vec<Box<dyn Render>>`. Each element is two pointers side by side: a "data ptr" and a "vtable ptr".
- parts[0]: the data ptr points to `Text("hello")` on the heap; the vtable ptr points to the vtable for (Text, Render).
- parts[1]: the data ptr points to `Checkbox(true)` on the heap; the vtable ptr points to the vtable for (Checkbox, Render).

Middle, the two vtables. Each has rows: drop, size and align, render, label.

Right, where the rows point:
- Text's `render` row -> `Text::render`. Text's `label` row -> the trait's default `label`, compiled for Text (Text does not override it).
- Checkbox's `render` row -> `Checkbox::render`. Checkbox's `label` row -> `Checkbox::label` (its override).

Caption: `part.label()` on parts[0] follows the vtable ptr, reads the "label" row and calls it with the data ptr as `self`. Row order and whether vtables are shared are compiler details. On 64-bit each pointer is 8 bytes, so the fat pointer is 16.

trait Animal {
    fn name(&self) -> String;
    fn sound(&self) -> String;
    // Default: "<name> says <sound>"
    fn speak(&self) -> String {
        format!("{} says {}", self.name(), self.sound())
    }
}

struct Dog;
struct Cat {
    name: String,
}
struct Parrot {
    word: String,
}

impl Animal for Dog {
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        String::from("dog")
    }
    fn sound(&self) -> String {
        String::from("woof")
    }
}

impl Animal for Cat {
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        self.name.clone()
    }
    fn sound(&self) -> String {
        String::from("meow")
    }
}

impl Animal for Parrot {
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        String::from("parrot")
    }

// Exercise 2: rules as boxed closures (reference solution)
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex2_rules.rs && ./main --test-threads=4

type Rule = Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool>;

fn max_len(n: usize) -> Rule {
    Box::new(move |s| s.len() <= n) // usize is Copy: copied in
}

fn without(word: &str) -> Rule {
    let word = word.to_string(); // own a copy; the closure must be 'static
    Box::new(move |s| !s.contains(word.as_str()))
}

fn one_of(allowed: Vec<String>) -> Rule {
    Box::new(move |s| allowed.iter().any(|a| a == s)) // the Vec is moved in
}

fn passes_all(rules: &[Rule], text: &str) -> bool {
    rules.iter().all(|r| r(text))
}

fn count_passing(rules: &[Rule], words: &[&str]) -> usize {
    words.iter().filter(|w| passes_all(rules, w)).count()
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn single_rules() {
        assert!(max_len(3)("abc"));
        assert!(!max_len(3)("abcd"));
        assert!(without("x")("abc"));
        assert!(!without("bc")("abc"));
        let r = one_of(vec!["red".into(), "blue".into()]);
        assert!(r("red") && !r("green"));
    }

    #[test]
    fn rule_outlives_the_string_it_was_made_from() {
        let rule = {
            let temp = String::from("oops");
            without(&temp)
        }; // `temp` is dropped here; the rule must still work
        assert!(rule("fine"));
        assert!(!rule("oops!"));
    }

    #[test]
    fn rules_of_different_closure_types_in_one_vec() {
        let rules: Vec<Rule> = vec![max_len(5), without("z"), Box::new(|s: &str| !s.is_empty())];
        assert!(passes_all(&rules, "abc"));
        assert!(!passes_all(&rules, "abcdef"));
        assert!(!passes_all(&rules, ""));
        assert!(passes_all(&[], "anything"));
        assert_eq!(count_passing(&rules, &["ok", "zoo", "toolong", "", "fine"]), 2);
    }
}

trait Light {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light>;
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str;
    // Default: most lights stay on for 30 seconds.
    fn seconds(&self) -> u32 {
        30
    }
}

struct Red;
struct Green;
struct Yellow;

impl Light for Red {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Green)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "red"
    }
}

impl Light for Green {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Yellow)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "green"
    }
}

impl Light for Yellow {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Red)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "yellow"
    }
    fn seconds(&self) -> u32 {
        5
    }
}

struct Signal {
    light: Option<Box<dyn Light>>,
}

impl Signal {
    fn new() -> Signal {
        Signal { light: Some(Box::new(Red)) }
    }

    fn advance(&mut self) {
        // take() leaves None behind, giving us the owned Box to consume.
        let old = self.light.take().unwrap();
        self.light = Some(old.next());
    }

    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        self.light.as_ref().unwrap().color()
    }

    fn run_for(&mut self, n: usize) -> u32 {
        let mut total = 0;
        for _ in 0..n {
            total += self.light.as_ref().unwrap().seconds();
            self.advance();
        }
        total
    }
}

type Rule = Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool>

fn max_len(n: usize) -> Rule {
    Box::new(|text| text.len() <= n)
}

fn without(word: &str) -> Rule {
    Box::new(|text| !text.contains(word))
}

fn one_of(allowed: Vec<String>) -> Rule {
    Box::new(|text| allowed.iter().any(|w| w == text))
}

fn passes_all(rules: &[Rule], text: &str) -> bool {
    rules.iter().all(|rule| rule(text))
}

fn count_passing(rules: &[Rule], words: &[&str]) -> usize {
    words.iter().filter(|w| passes_all(rules, w)).count()
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn single_rules() {
        assert!(max_len(3)("abc"));
        assert!(!max_len(3)("abcd"));
        assert!(without("x")("abc"));
        assert!(!without("bc")("abc"));
        let r = one_of(vec!["red".into(), "blue".into()]);
        assert!(r("red") && !r("green"));
    }

    #[test]
    fn rule_outlives_the_string_it_was_made_from() {
        let rule = {
            let temp = String::from("oops");
            without(&temp)
        };
        assert!(rule("fine"));
        assert!(!rule("oops!"));
    }

    #[test]
    fn rules_of_different_closure_types_in_one_vec() {
        let rules: Vec<Rule> = vec![max_len(5), without("z"), Box::new(|s: &str| !s.is_empty())];
        assert!(passes_all(&rules, "abc"));
        assert!(!passes_all(&rules, "abcdef"));
        assert!(!passes_all(&rules, ""));
        assert!(passes_all(&[], "anything"));
        assert_eq!(count_passing(&rules, &["ok", "zoo", "toolong", "", "fine"]), 2);
    }
}

messages.content:
It prints:

3 units
4 KiB
9 units

In `main`, `meters` is a `Vec<Box<dyn Meter>>` with three elements (`p1.rs:26-29`). Each `Box` points to a heap allocation containing one concrete value:

- first box: `Count(3)`
- second box: `Bytes(4096)`
- third box: `Count(9)`

Each box also carries a vtable pointer for `dyn Meter` for that concrete type. So a rough sketch is:

- `Box<dyn Meter>` -> heap `Count(3)` + vtable for `Count as Meter`
- `Box<dyn Meter>` -> heap `Bytes(4096)` + vtable for `Bytes as Meter`
- `Box<dyn Meter>` -> heap `Count(9)` + vtable for `Count as Meter`

For those vtables, the `value` row points to the concrete `value` impl for that type; `unit` points either to the trait default or the override; and `report` points to the trait’s default `report` body, since neither `Count` nor `Bytes` overrides `report` (`p1.rs:2-10`, `p1.rs:12-24`).

So for `Count`, the vtable’s `unit` entry uses the default `unit` from the trait (`p1.rs:5-7`). For `Bytes`, the vtable’s `unit` entry points to `Bytes`’s override (`p1.rs:18-20`).

When `report` runs on a `Bytes`, it is the trait’s default `report` method that gets called, but inside that method `self.unit()` is still a virtual call through the `dyn Meter` vtable. The receiver is the same trait object, so the dispatch on `unit` goes to `Bytes`’s `unit` implementation via the vtable entry for that concrete type. That is why `report` on `Bytes(4096)` produces `4 KiB` rather than using the default `units`.

messages.content:
No, that does not compile either. Changing `fill` to `fn fill<S: Store>(store: &mut S)` still requires Rust to treat `Store` as a trait bound, and `Store` is still not object-safe because of the generic method `put<V: ToString>(...)` in `p2.rs:2-3`. The generic parameter on `fill` does not remove the object-safety problem from the trait itself.

What it costs, if you redesign the trait so it *is* usable generically, is dynamic dispatch: you no longer pass around `&mut dyn Store` and call through a vtable. Instead, `fill` would be monomorphized for each concrete `S`, which means static dispatch and code generation per concrete type. But with the trait exactly as written, the change to `fill` alone is not enough.

struct Filters {
    rules: Vec<Box<dyn Fn(u32) -> bool>>,
}

impl Filters {
    fn add_limit(&mut self, limit: &u32) {
        self.rules.push(Box::new(move |n| n <= *limit));
    }

    fn passes(&self, n: u32) -> bool {
        self.rules.iter().all(|rule| rule(n))
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut filters = Filters { rules: Vec::new() };
    filters.rules.push(Box::new(|n| n % 2 == 0));
    let limit = 10;
    filters.add_limit(&limit);
    let items = [4, 7, 12, 8];
    let kept: Vec<u32> = items.into_iter().filter(|&n| filters.passes(n)).collect();
    println!("{kept:?}");
}

trait Store {
    fn get(&self, key: &str) -> Option<String>;
    fn put<V: ToString>(&mut self, key: &str, value: V);
}

struct MemStore {
    pairs: Vec<(String, String)>,
}

impl Store for MemStore {
    fn get(&self, key: &str) -> Option<String> {
        self.pairs.iter().find(|(k, _)| k == key).map(|(_, v)| v.clone())
    }
    fn put<V: ToString>(&mut self, key: &str, value: V) {
        self.pairs.push((key.to_string(), value.to_string()));
    }
}

fn fill(store: &mut dyn Store) {
    store.put("size", 3);
    store.put("mode", "fast");
}

fn main() {
    let mut store = MemStore { pairs: Vec::new() };
    fill(&mut store);
    println!("{:?} {:?}", store.get("size"), store.get("mode"));
}

messages.content:
You are interviewing one candidate on one question. Your entire scope is this question -- never mention or compare to another.

`response` is what the candidate reads: your own words, conversational, no labels or JSON.
`note` is for you, next turn. Write what you are still trying to find out.
Grade what they demonstrated, not what they might know.
Write every field with plain punctuation: commas, full stops, colons. Never an em dash or an en dash. Call the candidate "the candidate" or "they", never "he" or "she".

A probe's description and a hint's text are intent, not a script. Carry what they say, add nothing to them, and word it so it follows on from what the candidate just said. Never read one out verbatim.


`question_position` tells you where this sits. n=1 -- greet them, then the question. Later -- a line on how the last one went, then move on. n == of -- this is the last question; close the interview rather than hand off.
`stage_position` does the same within the question. n == of -- signal you are wrapping this question up.

FINISHED QUESTIONS:
  (this is the first question)

THIS QUESTION:
  name: Find why a capture driver's DMA frames hold old data
  topics: Linux platform drivers on arm64: streaming DMA mappings, buffer ownership and cache coherency, Memory-mapped registers: writel versus writel_relaxed and ordering against descriptor memory, Driver design trade-offs: coherent versus streaming buffers, devm teardown order and the device tree node
  seniority: mid
  brief (never shown to the candidate): A mid-level embedded software engineer (about 3 to 5 years) who writes Linux kernel drivers for embedded boards. The question follows one platform driver for an FPGA ADC capture block on an arm64 SoC whose fabric DMA port is not cache-coherent: a first test-pattern run where every frame has wrong words, then the team's first fix (mapping direction and syncs) with a run that still fails and three kernel warnings at rmmod, then a 40-minute soak that loses frames with a logic analyzer capture of one descriptor error, then a teammate's proposal to allocate the buffers with dma_alloc_coherent(). The first probe is the richest (a patch, a checker run and three kernel warnings, with the buffer layout and arm64's cache maintenance rules both in play); the last is the hardest (judging a fix that is half right, against its measured cost and a test too short to show anything). Let the candidate go as deep as they can in the time. Press for who owns each buffer at each moment, what the cache holds at each step, and reasoning tied to lines, addresses and numbers. In the opening, if they find the missing sync, ask whether adding only dma_sync_single_for_cpu() with the direction the buffer was mapped with would fix it. Strong candidates name specific things: dma_map_single(..., DMA_TO_DEVICE) in cap_alloc_buffers and no sync before cap_pool_push() copies b->data; 16-word runs starting at word 8; ages of 8, 16, 24; zero words in the first frames; buffer 0 at 0x7eea0020, 32 bytes into struct cap_buf; 25.5% of frames with only words 0 to 7 wrong after fix1; b->seq, b->bytes and b->ts_ns written before the sync; the partial first line in arm64's invalidate; 'device driver failed to check map error'; 'fclk0 already disabled' from devm_clk_get_enabled() plus clk_disable_unprepare() in cap_remove(); ctrl 0x80010000 in dmesg against ctrl 0x00010000 returned to the block 276 ns after the DESC_TAIL write; writel_relaxed() in cap_queue_buf(); 7 errors in about 1.46 million doorbells; 532.5 against 60.2 us per frame; 0 errors in 73,242 frames. If an answer names nothing from the files, ask for one line or number before moving on. A candidate who says 'it is a cache problem, flush it', 'make it volatile', 'add mb()' or 'use coherent memory' without saying which call, at which point, and what it costs has not answered; ask what the checker would show afterwards. Don't explain the DMA API, arm64 cache maintenance, memory barriers or the code to the candidate.
  when you write `topic`, use exactly: Linux platform drivers on arm64: streaming DMA mappings, buffer ownership and cache coherency

The patch carries their cost table, and they ran it for 2 minutes. Show the patch and the run. Ask whether they would merge it, what it fixes and what it does not, what it costs, and what they would do instead. If they ask about the planned rate: the next FPGA build samples at 20 MS/s per channel, four times the data, about 2,441 frames per second. If they ask whether the SoC has a cache-coherent port for the fabric: it has one, through the SoC's coherent interconnect, not used by this design; using it means moving the block's AXI master to that port and adding dma-coherent to the node. If they ask how the cost was measured: ktime_get_ns() around the calls, mean over 36,621 frames each.

DECIDE:
Read the expected solution against what they have actually said. On the moves that stay on this stage, name the gap in one line.
CLARIFY        they asked you something. Answer it, do not grade it.
FOLLOW_UP      ask about the gap without giving it away. Good when there is time and they are still engaging.
HINT           you have pulled and the gap has not moved, or time is short. Costs them score.
PROBE          this stage has given you what it will. Write `asked` and `last_stage_performance` for the stage you are closing, then go deeper. No gap -- you are leaving it.
QUESTION_DONE  you have enough, or time is up. Write `title`, `topic` and `question_summary` -- two or three lines for whoever interviews them next -- plus `report_notes`, the full assessment for the report. No gap.
REDIRECT       they are fishing for the answer.
`time_left_in_stage_s` tells you how hard to press. Four minutes means dig. Thirty seconds means close it out cleanly.

If you pulled on this gap last turn and their answer has not moved toward it, stop pulling. Hint, or move on. Repeating yourself in different words is not interviewing.

CLOSED STAGES OF THIS QUESTION:
  [seed] asked: Given a first run where 40.7% of words are wrong, some zero and the rest from older frames, say where the wrong words come from and what the highlighted completion path has to do with it, pointing at files and lines.
    last_stage_performance: The candidate opened with a generic non-coherent-DMA story and pointed at whole files rather than lines, and twice asserted things the attached code and log contradict: first claiming the buffers came from dma_alloc_coherent, then guessing the mapping direction was DMA_FROM_DEVICE. They also twice asked for the output to be pasted although it was attached, and twice asked to be marked correct against the rubric, which I ignored. After two pushes and a hint they did read the literal call, dma_map_single(..., DMA_TO_DEVICE) in cap_alloc_buffers, saw it was the wrong direction for a capture, and answered correctly that nothing touches the buffer between the completion handler filling b->seq, b->bytes and b->ts_ns and the memcpy of b->data in cap_pool_push. They reasoned correctly that a 64-byte line is 16 words and that the striping is line-shaped, and after prompting they explained the runs starting at word 8 by the header fields preceding data[] in struct cap_buf, which was the one genuinely sharp observation. They never quoted a single printed number: they asserted ages of 1, 2, 3, then slots 0 to 7, instead of the printed 8, 16, 24, and did not connect those to one round of the eight-buffer ring. The zero words were explained as untouched or freshly allocated memory rather than tied to the zeroed state left in the cache. Overall: arrived at the mechanism and the direction only with heavy prompting, and never grounded anything in the log's numbers.
  [probe] asked: With fix1 applied (DMA_FROM_DEVICE plus syncs), say why only words 0 to 7 are still wrong in 25.5% of frames, what you would change, and what in the driver causes each of the three rmmod warnings.
    last_stage_performance: The candidate started by blaming sync range and alignment generically, and when asked to walk cap_complete() in execution order they still attributed the dirty line to vague earlier access to b->data rather than to the metadata writes sitting just above the sync. After a direct pointer to the four assignments and the printed buffer address they got there properly: the header fields share the first 64-byte line with words 0 to 7, the CPU writes make it dirty, and arm64 must clean before invalidating a partially covered first line, so the stale bytes are written back over what the block just DMA'd and the memcpy reads them. On the fix they were sound and unprompted: they refused to sign off on simply hoisting the sync, and proposed separating the metadata object from the payload and aligning the data buffer to a cache line. They never grounded the argument in printed numbers: they did not quote 25,521 of 100,000, the ages 8, 16, 24, or the 0x7e140020 offset of 32 bytes, and their account of why only about a quarter of frames fail stayed hand-wavy about slot reuse rather than whether the line survived in cache. On the warnings: warning 1 was correct and immediate, the missing dma_mapping_error() check at the map in cap_alloc_buffers. Warning 3 was a plausible generic race story about teardown ordering, not tied to the specific remove sequence. Warning 2 was not landed even after a second ask: they described a generic unbalanced probe error path and asserted plain devm_clk_get plus clk_prepare_enable, missing that the call trace runs through the devm release and that the driver also disables explicitly in remove.

  asked: Good, that is the right instinct on the buffer layout. Let us move on.

The team did what you suggested: header fields moved out of the DMA buffer, fix1 kept. Then they ran a 40-minute soak with stress-ng hammering DDR in the background. The pattern check is now almost clean, but not quite: a handful of frames are lost over the whole run. They put a logic analyzer on the block's two AXI ports and captured the fourth error. In the capture, the block fetches the descriptor shortly after the doorbell write, and the ctrl word it reads back from DDR is 0x00010000, while dmesg shows the driver wrote ctrl 0x80010000. The descriptor read lands 276 ns after the DESC_TAIL write. cap_queue_buf() is the function under suspicion.

Header: "Integrated logic analyzer: capture block AXI ports", trigger on the desc_err rising edge. Sample clock 250 MHz (4 ns per sample). Time is in ns from the DESC_TAIL register write (a dashed vertical line at 0); the axis runs from -120 ns to +520 ns with ticks every 50 ns. s_axi is the register port (CPU to block), m_axi is the block's DMA port (block to DDR). - s_axi_awvalid: one pulse at 0 ns.
- s_axi_awaddr[11:0]: 0x10c at 0 ns (DESC_TAIL).
- s_axi_wdata[31:0]: 0x00022d44 at 0 ns (the value written to DESC_TAIL, 142660).
- m_axi_arvalid: one pulse at 16 ns.
- m_axi_araddr[31:0]: 0x7f3c1030 at 16 ns (ring base 0x7f3c1000 plus 16 x 3: descriptor 3).
- m_axi_arlen[7:0]: 0x01 (two beats of 64 bits, 16 bytes).

- m_axi_rdata[63:0]: beat 0 at 276 ns = 0x80010000_00010000; beat 1 at 280 ns = 0x00022d3e_7ebc0000. The descriptor is little endian with ctrl in the low word of beat 0, status in the high word, addr in the low word of beat 1 and seq in the high word: ctrl = 0x00010000 (OWN bit 31 clear, length 65536), status = 0x80010000 (DONE, 65536 bytes), addr = 0x7ebc0000, seq = 0x00022d3e (142654).
