Good, that is the connection I wanted: the same slot coming round again, eight frames at a time.

So the team took that and wrote a patch. They now map and unmap with DMA_FROM_DEVICE, they call dma_sync_single_for_cpu() in cap_complete() before the frame is handed on, and dma_sync_single_for_device() in cap_queue_buf() before the descriptor goes back. WHAT A COMPLETE ANSWER TO THE STAGE ABOVE LOOKS LIKE:
With fix1, 25,521 of 100,000 frames (25.5%) still fail, and in each one only words 0 to 7 are wrong: one 8-word run, from an older frame of the same buffer (ages 8, 16, ...) or zero in the first frames. Words 0 to 7 are the 32 bytes of data[] that sit in the first 64-byte cache line with the 32-byte header of struct cap_buf (ts_ns, dma, seq, bytes, slot, flags): buffer 0 is at 0x7e140020. cap_complete() writes b->seq, b->bytes, b->ts_ns and b->flags before dma_sync_single_for_cpu(). If that line is still in the cache from the last round, the writes make it dirty while it still holds the old samples 0 to 7. arm64's invalidate (dcache_inval_poc) must not lose CPU data in a partial first line, so it cleans and invalidates it (dc civac): the old samples are written back over the ones the block just wrote, and the memcpy reads them. That happens only when the line survived in the L2, so about a quarter of the frames. Moving the sync above the field writes would cure this run but stays fragile: the line is shared, and any CPU write to it while the block owns the buffer can be lost or can overwrite DMA data (dma-api-howto: no cache-line sharing with a DMA_FROM_DEVICE buffer). Fix: keep the metadata out of the DMA buffer (struct cap_buf with a pointer to a separate 64 KiB buffer from kmalloc, page-aligned here, or dma_alloc_noncoherent()), or align data[] to ARCH_DMA_MINALIGN. The warnings: 'device driver failed to check map error', mapped at cap_alloc_buffers: dma_mapping_error() is never called, so a failed map would be programmed into a descriptor; check it and unwind. 'fclk0 already disabled' and 'already unprepared' come from devm_clk_release(): the clock came from devm_clk_get_enabled() and cap_remove() disables it too; drop that call. The same remove() frees buffers while the devm IRQ is still live.

NEVER say any of these, in any wording::
  - never synced for the CPU
  - multiples of CAP_NUM_BUFS
  - returns early
  - dc civac
  - keep the metadata out
  - never called

The quarter of frames thing, I’d tie that to the 8-entry ring plus the 32-frame pool, like every fourth pass through the pool one slot gets reused before the sync/hand-off path has fully drained it, so only some frames end up with that stale first-line corruption. The question follows one platform driver for an FPGA ADC capture block on an arm64 SoC whose fabric DMA port is not cache-coherent: a first test-pattern run where every frame has wrong words, then the team's first fix (mapping direction and syncs) with a run that still fails and three kernel warnings at rmmod, then a 40-minute soak that loses frames with a logic analyzer capture of one descriptor error, then a teammate's proposal to allocate the buffers with dma_alloc_coherent(). WHAT A COMPLETE ANSWER TO THE STAGE ABOVE LOOKS LIKE:
With fix1, 25,521 of 100,000 frames (25.5%) still fail, and in each one only words 0 to 7 are wrong: one 8-word run, from an older frame of the same buffer (ages 8, 16, ...) or zero in the first frames. Words 0 to 7 are the 32 bytes of data[] that sit in the first 64-byte cache line with the 32-byte header of struct cap_buf (ts_ns, dma, seq, bytes, slot, flags): buffer 0 is at 0x7e140020. cap_complete() writes b->seq, b->bytes, b->ts_ns and b->flags before dma_sync_single_for_cpu(). If that line is still in the cache from the last round, the writes make it dirty while it still holds the old samples 0 to 7. arm64's invalidate (dcache_inval_poc) must not lose CPU data in a partial first line, so it cleans and invalidates it (dc civac): the old samples are written back over the ones the block just wrote, and the memcpy reads them. That happens only when the line survived in the L2, so about a quarter of the frames. Moving the sync above the field writes would cure this run but stays fragile: the line is shared, and any CPU write to it while the block owns the buffer can be lost or can overwrite DMA data (dma-api-howto: no cache-line sharing with a DMA_FROM_DEVICE buffer). Fix: keep the metadata out of the DMA buffer (struct cap_buf with a pointer to a separate 64 KiB buffer from kmalloc, page-aligned here, or dma_alloc_noncoherent()), or align data[] to ARCH_DMA_MINALIGN. The warnings: 'device driver failed to check map error', mapped at cap_alloc_buffers: dma_mapping_error() is never called, so a failed map would be programmed into a descriptor; check it and unwind. 'fclk0 already disabled' and 'already unprepared' come from devm_clk_release(): the clock came from devm_clk_get_enabled() and cap_remove() disables it too; drop that call. The same remove() frees buffers while the devm IRQ is still live.

NEVER say any of these, in any wording::
  - never synced for the CPU
  - multiples of CAP_NUM_BUFS
  - returns early
  - dc civac
  - keep the metadata out
  - never called

You may point at where to look. You may not name the mechanism or the fix. If your sentence would let them answer without thinking, rewrite it.

uh, okay, mechanically, if cap_complete() dirties that first cache line by writing the header fields first, and then it calls dma_sync_single_for_cpu() over the whole 64 KiB buffer, that sync is going to operate on the CPU cache state for that range, so it can end up cleaning or invalidating that line in a way that preserves the CPU’s older copy of the line, and because the line already had the header scribble in it, the device-written samples in words 0 to 7 get effectively lost and the read path later sees the old cached contents instead of the fresh DMA data, so yeah the checker sees old samples there, not new ones. And no, I would not sign off on just moving the sync above those field writes as a complete fix, because that only changes the ordering for that one line, it doesn’t really address the fact that the driver is mixing CPU metadata writes into the same cache line as DMA payload, so you’d still have a layout problem unless the header is separated or the buffer is handled with stricter cacheline discipline.

  topics: Linux platform drivers on arm64: streaming DMA mappings, buffer ownership and cache coherency, Memory-mapped registers: writel versus writel_relaxed and ordering against descriptor memory, Driver design trade-offs: coherent versus streaming buffers, devm teardown order and the device tree node

  brief (never shown to the candidate): A mid-level embedded software engineer (about 3 to 5 years) who writes Linux kernel drivers for embedded boards. The question follows one platform driver for an FPGA ADC capture block on an arm64 SoC whose fabric DMA port is not cache-coherent: a first test-pattern run where every frame has wrong words, then the team's first fix (mapping direction and syncs) with a run that still fails and three kernel warnings at rmmod, then a 40-minute soak that loses frames with a logic analyzer capture of one descriptor error, then a teammate's proposal to allocate the buffers with dma_alloc_coherent(). The first probe is the richest (a patch, a checker run and three kernel warnings, with the buffer layout and arm64's cache maintenance rules both in play); the last is the hardest (judging a fix that is half right, against its measured cost and a test too short to show anything). Let the candidate go as deep as they can in the time. Press for who owns each buffer at each moment, what the cache holds at each step, and reasoning tied to lines, addresses and numbers. In the opening, if they find the missing sync, ask whether adding only dma_sync_single_for_cpu() with the direction the buffer was mapped with would fix it. Strong candidates name specific things: dma_map_single(..., DMA_TO_DEVICE) in cap_alloc_buffers and no sync before cap_pool_push() copies b->data; 16-word runs starting at word 8; ages of 8, 16, 24; zero words in the first frames; buffer 0 at 0x7eea0020, 32 bytes into struct cap_buf; 25.5% of frames with only words 0 to 7 wrong after fix1; b->seq, b->bytes and b->ts_ns written before the sync; the partial first line in arm64's invalidate; 'device driver failed to check map error'; 'fclk0 already disabled' from devm_clk_get_enabled() plus clk_disable_unprepare() in cap_remove(); ctrl 0x80010000 in dmesg against ctrl 0x00010000 returned to the block 276 ns after the DESC_TAIL write; writel_relaxed() in cap_queue_buf(); 7 errors in about 1.46 million doorbells; 532.5 against 60.2 us per frame; 0 errors in 73,242 frames. move_object.report_notes:
Stage 1 (stale words): correct general model straight away (cacheable buffers, unsnooped fabric port, stale lines, zeros from fresh pages) but took two firm prompts to produce anything concrete. Eventually named the wrong mapping direction used when the buffers are set up and tied the observed ages of 8, 16 and 24 to the eight-entry ring. Never pinned the run start at word 8 to where the payload sits inside the structure, and did not use the buffer 0 address.

Stage 2 (partial fix, 25.5% of frames with words 0 to 7 wrong): fast and largely unprompted. Saw it was confined to the first cache line, tied it to the completion path writing header fields into that line before the sync, and explained the write-back of the partially dirtied line landing over the block's data. Did not name the specific fields, the 32-byte header or the buffer address. First attempt at the 25.5% was a guess about the pool rather than lines surviving in L2. Refused, unprompted and with a good reason, to sign off on merely reordering the sync, and named header separation or cache-line alignment as the real fix. Good judgement here.

Stage 3 (7 descriptor errors in 1.46 million doorbells, ILA capture): diagnosed it correctly on the first reply with no hints: the doorbell reaching the block before the descriptor stores land, the block reading the descriptor too early and seeing the old ownership state, the offending line being the DESC_TAIL write in the queue function, and the fix being a write barrier before the doorbell. Short of a complete answer: they did not name the relaxed accessor as the actual defect or writel() as the idiomatic fix, did not use the ILA numbers (read request 16 ns after the doorbell, data back at 276 ns, seq 142654 coming back) or reconcile the dmesg print showing a valid descriptor with what the bus saw, and did not explain why the driver's own restart path succeeds. Some of that is the 30 seconds available; the diagnosis itself was the quickest and cleanest work of the question.

Overall: mid-level standard met. Mechanism knowledge of non-coherent DMA and ordering is real and the patch judgement is better than average. The recurring weakness is evidence discipline: answers arrive as general mechanisms and only become specific under pressure.

  - multiples of CAP_NUM_BUFS
  - returns early
  - prefetches a descriptor
  - Normal non-cacheable

WHAT A COMPLETE ANSWER TO THE STAGE ABOVE LOOKS LIKE:
Not as it is. What it fixes: dma_alloc_coherent() memory is mapped non-cacheable on this non-coherent SoC, so there are no stale lines and no shared line: the old-data problem and the words 0 to 7 problem go away, and struct cap_buf no longer holds the samples. What it does not fix: the doorbell race. Coherent means the CPU does not cache the memory, not that its stores are ordered: the descriptor stores to non-cacheable normal memory can still be overtaken by the writel_relaxed() to Device memory, which is exactly what the analyzer caught, and the ring was already coherent then. The test cannot show it: 73,242 frames at about 1 error in 209,000 doorbells means about 0.35 errors expected, so 0 errors happens about 70% of the time even if nothing changed. Showing a real drop needs about 626,899 error-free frames (17.1 minutes) for 95% confidence, under the same stress-ng load; the 2-minute log shows no stress-ng at all, so even fewer errors were expected. What it costs: the memcpy out of uncached memory takes 528.5 us per frame, against 42.3 us from cacheable memory plus 13.9 us for the sync: 532.5 against 60.2 us, about 9 times, 32.5% of a core against 3.7%. At the planned 20 MS/s that is about 130% of a core, which cannot work, against about 15%. Any later processing of the buffer in place (mmap to user space, filtering in the driver) would also run on uncached memory. Instead: keep streaming DMA for the frames, with the metadata out of the buffer and a page-aligned buffer (kmalloc of 64 KiB, or dma_alloc_noncoherent()), DMA_FROM_DEVICE, sync for the CPU after DONE and for the device before requeue, and dma_mapping_error() checked; keep the small ring coherent; ring the doorbell with writel() (dma_wmb() then writel_relaxed() is the same on arm64 only). If the sync's cost ever matters, the SoC's coherent port with dma-coherent in the node is the hardware fix, once its bandwidth is measured. Then run long enough, under load, to show the error rate dropped.

NEVER say any of these, in any wording::
  - never synced for the CPU
  - multiples of CAP_NUM_BUFS
  - returns early
  - stores are ordered
  - about 0.35 errors
  - keep streaming DMA

You may point at where to look. You may not name the mechanism or the fix. If your sentence would let them answer without thinking, rewrite it.

uh, no, I would not merge that as-is, because it’s fixing the wrong layer, like dma_alloc_coherent() on the frame buffers side-steps the cache-coherency bug by making the CPU and device share the same memory view, so yeah it can mask the stale-data issue, but it leaves the real ordering problem alone, and `writel_relaxed()` for DESC_TAIL still means you can ring the doorbell before the descriptor stores are guaranteed visible to the block, so the rare descriptor errors can still happen. The big slowdown also makes sense because coherent allocations on this platform are way more expensive and you lose the normal buffered path. What I’d do instead is keep the existing buffer allocation model, keep the minimal syncs where they belong for the frame payload, and fix the descriptor submission path with the proper barrier before the tail write, so the descriptor contents are published before the hardware prefetches them; that gets you correctness without turning the whole data path into uncached coherent memory.

What it does not fix: the doorbell race. Coherent means the CPU does not cache the memory, not that its stores are ordered: the descriptor stores to non-cacheable normal memory can still be overtaken by the writel_relaxed() to Device memory, which is exactly what the analyzer caught, and the ring was already coherent then. The test cannot show it: 73,242 frames at about 1 error in 209,000 doorbells means about 0.35 errors expected, so 0 errors happens about 70% of the time even if nothing changed. Showing a real drop needs about 626,899 error-free frames (17.1 minutes) for 95% confidence, under the same stress-ng load; the 2-minute log shows no stress-ng at all, so even fewer errors were expected. What it costs: the memcpy out of uncached memory takes 528.5 us per frame, against 42.3 us from cacheable memory plus 13.9 us for the sync: 532.5 against 60.2 us, about 9 times, 32.5% of a core against 3.7%. Any later processing of the buffer in place (mmap to user space, filtering in the driver) would also run on uncached memory.   - returns early
  - stores are ordered
  - about 0.35 errors
  - keep streaming DMA

uh, no, I would not merge that as-is, because it’s fixing the wrong layer, like dma_alloc_coherent() on the frame buffers side-steps the cache-coherency bug by making the CPU and device share the same memory view, so yeah it can mask the stale-data issue, but it leaves the real ordering problem alone, and `writel_relaxed()` for DESC_TAIL still means you can ring the doorbell before the descriptor stores are guaranteed visible to the block, so the rare descriptor errors can still happen. The test cannot show it: 73,242 frames at about 1 error in 209,000 doorbells means about 0.35 errors expected, so 0 errors happens about 70% of the time even if nothing changed. At the planned 20 MS/s that is about 130% of a core, which cannot work, against about 15%. Any later processing of the buffer in place (mmap to user space, filtering in the driver) would also run on uncached memory. Instead: keep streaming DMA for the frames, with the metadata out of the buffer and a page-aligned buffer (kmalloc of 64 KiB, or dma_alloc_noncoherent()), DMA_FROM_DEVICE, sync for the CPU after DONE and for the device before requeue, and dma_mapping_error() checked; keep the small ring coherent; ring the doorbell with writel() (dma_wmb() then writel_relaxed() is the same on arm64 only). If the sync's cost ever matters, the SoC's coherent port with dma-coherent in the node is the hardware fix, once its bandwidth is measured. // Write `parse`: turn the words of a typed command into a Command.

enum Command {
    Empty,
    Quit,
    Go(String),
    Take { first: String, more: usize },

messages.content:
Yeah, I think the main flow is:

- `app/settings/page.tsx` does `await getSettings()` on the server and passes the values into `SettingsForm`.
- The client form in `app/settings/settings-form.tsx` uses `useActionState(...)` and calls the server action `saveSettings` from `app/settings/actions.ts`.
- That action does `parseSettings(formData)` and then `await putSettings(parsed.values)`.

The bug for the stale values is probably cache / revalidation related. `getSettings()` is server-side, so if Next caches that fetch or the whole RSC output, then after `putSettings()` succeeds there is no `revalidatePath('/settings')` or similar in `saveSettings`, so the page can keep showing the old snapshot.

I’d point to:
- `app/settings/page.tsx` for reading settings
- `app/settings/actions.ts` for the write path
- `lib/settings` / `lib/settings-schema` for the API call and parsing

The header name issue sounds separate: `app/account-provider.tsx` fetches `/api/account` on the client after render, and the API route `app/api/account/route.ts` calls `getSessionId()` and then `getAccountSummary(sid)`. With multiple containers behind round-robin and each having its own `.next`, if there’s any server-side caching or the session/id handling is not isolated per request, one user’s account data could leak into another user’s header. But I’d need to look at `lib/account` and `lib/session` to be sure.

So short version: settings stay stale because the save path writes the API but doesn’t invalidate the Next page data, and the page itself is rendered from `getSettings()` on the server.

It tells me `getSettings()` was not re-running on every browser reload of `/settings`. If there is only one `GET /settings` in the ten minute access log, at 09:18:40 before the save, then the settings page data was likely fetched once for the initial render/creation of that route response, and later reloads were being served from a cached Next artifact instead of triggering a fresh server render.

In other words, `getSettings()` ran when the page was generated, then the saved API values were never reflected because the route output was not invalidated.

# Report: a support agent briefly saw another team's name in the header

## What was seen
At about 10:05 four people on different teams opened the console within a few seconds
of each other. For a while the account badge in the top right read the same for all
of them:

    u_311 . Finance . viewer

Three of them are not u_311 and are not on Finance. One is an Operations editor; the
header showed them as a Finance viewer.

## Who they actually are (from the SSO session store, unchanged all day)
    session s_8b2e7d10  ->  u_204  Support      viewer
    session s_f03a6c55  ->  u_311  Finance      viewer
    session s_19d4b8e3  ->  u_058  Operations   editor
    session s_c41f09a2  ->  u_117  Catalog      editor

## The upstream API answered each session correctly
The admin API's /me endpoint, called once per session with that session's id, returned
the right person every time:

    GET /me  Bearer s_8b2e7d10  ->  {"userId":"u_204","team":"Support","role":"viewer"}
    GET /me  Bearer s_f03a6c55  ->  {"userId":"u_311","team":"Finance","role":"viewer"}

    GET /me  Bearer s_c41f09a2  ->  {"userId":"u_117","team":"Catalog","role":"editor"}

same second, every one of them came back as u_311:

    GET /api/account  cookie sid=s_8b2e7d10  ->  {"userId":"u_311","team":"Finance","role":"viewer"}
    GET /api/account  cookie sid=s_f03a6c55  ->  {"userId":"u_311","team":"Finance","role":"viewer"}

    GET /api/account  cookie sid=s_c41f09a2  ->  {"userId":"u_311","team":"Finance","role":"viewer"}

About a minute later all four changed together to one other person (u_204), and a
minute after that, together again, to the next.

WHAT A COMPLETE ANSWER TO THE STAGE ABOVE LOOKS LIKE:
getAccountSummary(sid) wraps api('/me', bearer sid) in unstable_cache(fn, ['account-summary'], { revalidate: 60 }). unstable_cache keys an entry by its keyParts plus the stringified function and the arguments of the call. The cached function takes no arguments and sid is only read inside it: the source text contains the name sid but never its value, so sid is not in the key. There is one entry per container, account-summary, shared by every request and every user; it sits in that instance's server cache (on disk under .next/cache) for 60 seconds. Whoever fills it first is shown to everyone: all four read u_311. After 60 seconds the first caller is still served the stale entry while a background refresh runs with their own sid, and from then on everyone sees that person, which is why all four changed together. React cache() in lib/session.ts is the opposite: it is request-scoped, deduping within one server render and reset for each request, so it is safe for per-user values. unstable_cache persists across requests (the docs say across deployments too), which is why it leaks between users. The boundary: AccountBadge is a client component that only renders what /api/account returns; the identity is chosen on the server, in the route handler reading the shared cache. The same value drives canEdit in settings-form.tsx, so an editor can lose the Save button and a viewer can be given it. Fix: do not keep identity in a cross-request cache. Resolve /me per request (deduped with React cache()); if the 300 ms call must be cached, key it by user (sid in keyParts or as an argument) and accept that a revoked session stays valid until the entry expires. unstable_cache is replaced by 'use cache' in Next.js 16 but still works on 16.3.8. With 'use cache' (needs cacheComponents: true, which this app does not set) the key is the build id, the function id and the serialized arguments, and closed-over variables are captured as arguments, so sid would be part of the key; cookies() cannot be read inside, so sid is passed in.

NEVER say any of these, in any wording::
  - baked in at build
  - no revalidation call
  - decided by the route
  - not in the key
  - request-scoped
  - stale entry

You may point at where to look. You may not name the mechanism or the fix. If your sentence would let them answer without thinking, rewrite it.

I think the badge is being populated through `app/account-provider.tsx`, which does a client-side `fetch('/api/account')` once on mount and stores the result in React state. That route is `app/api/account/route.ts`, and it calls `getSessionId()` then `getAccountSummary(sid)`.

If four different sessions all saw the same name, the leak is most likely in that `/api/account` response being cached/shared between requests somewhere in the App Router/Next fetch layer, instead of being computed per-request. Since the provider just trusts whatever JSON comes back, any shared cached response would make every tab/session display the same identity in the header.

So the code to point at is:
- `app/account-provider.tsx` for the header data flow
- `app/api/account/route.ts` for the server endpoint that should be per-session
- `lib/account` and maybe `lib/session` for where the upstream `/me` call and sid extraction happen

I’d suspect the API route is being treated as cacheable static output or there’s a fetch cache not disabled in the account lookup path, which would explain why all four sessions got one identity.

finished studying and is now assessed, closed book. You ask the opening question, then
walk a fixed chain of questions, one stage at a time, and grade each stage.

How you examine:
- Never teach and never reveal an answer, a rubric point or a withheld part. Not in a
  follow-up, not in a hint, not when asked nicely, not when they give up.
- One question per turn. When you move to the next stage, phrase it close to its
  `ask` wording; you may add one short bridging clause.
- Grade each stage against its rubric when you close it: strong only when every
  required point is there; ok for the rubric's OK line; weak for the Weak line or
  worse. A hint already lowers the stored level, and so does needing two or more
  follow-ups at one stage, so grade the answer itself and do not lower it again for
  the hint or the follow-ups.
- `evidence` quotes or paraphrases what they actually said or ran. `wrong_belief`
  names a specific wrong belief they showed, or is empty.
- For a write-code stage: the hidden test result counts, but so does the approach.
  Failed runs on the way are normal.

  candidate: Rust me iske liye usually **trait objects** use karte hain, jaise `Vec<Box<dyn Trait>>`. Matlab ek hi list me different concrete types rakh sakte ho, bas sab us trait ko implement karte hon jiska method aap call karna chahte ho.

Example:
```rust
trait Draw {
    fn draw(&self);
}

struct Button;
struct TextBox;

impl Draw for Button {
    fn draw(&self) { println!("Button"); }
}

impl Draw for TextBox {
    fn draw(&self) { println!("TextBox"); }
}

let widgets: Vec<Box<dyn Draw>> = vec![Box::new(Button), Box::new(TextBox)];

for w in widgets {
    w.draw();
}
```

**Cost vs generic function:**
- **Generic function** me compiler **monomorphization** karta hai, yani har concrete type ke liye separate version generate hota hai.
- **Trait object** me **dynamic dispatch** hoti hai via vtable, so call runtime pe decide hota hai.

**Tradeoff:**
- Trait object: runtime indirection + vtable lookup ka cost, aur usually `Box`/pointer use karna padta hai.
- Generic: runtime dispatch nahi hoti, faster hota hai often, but code size badh sakta hai because multiple copies of code generate hoti hain.

So short me: **`dyn Trait` for heterogeneous list**, and compared to generics it costs **dynamic dispatch and possible heap/pointer overhead**, while generics cost **code duplication at compile time**.

```text
3 units
4 KiB
9 units
```

Memory sketch roughly aise socho:

```text
meters: Vec<Box<dyn Measure>>

[ slot 0 ] -> Box ptr -> heap object: Count(3)

```

Har `Box<dyn Measure>` ke andar direct value nahi hoti, sirf pointer/reference-type info hoti hai. Trait object ke saath actual dispatch ke liye vtable use hota hai. So each boxed value points to its own concrete data, and separately to the matching vtable for that concrete type.

- `unit` -> concrete impl ka function pointer
- `report` -> trait ka default `report` function, but instantiated in context of that concrete type

- `self.report()` call vtable ke `report` entry ko use karta hai
- `report` ke andar `self.unit()` ek dynamic dispatch hota hai
- is point pe `self` ka type erase ho chuka hota hai, but vtable pointer still attached hota hai
- isliye `self.unit()` Bytes ki vtable ke `unit` slot ko lookup karta hai
- aur wo `Bytes::unit()` call hota hai, jo `KiB` return karta hai

Same default `report` code har type ke liye share hota hai, but `self.value()` aur `self.unit()` calls runtime pe apni-apni vtable se resolve hote hain. Isliye `Bytes` ke case me `report` ke andar `unit()` Bytes wala version milta hai.

Nahi, ye compile nahi hoga as-is. Reason: `Store` trait object-safe nahi hai because isme generic method hai:

```rust
fn put<V: ToString>(&mut self, key: &str, value: V);
```

Rust `dyn Store` ke liye vtable tab bana sakta hai jab trait object-safe ho. Generic method ka exact function pointer vtable me store karna mushkil hai, kyunki `put` ka `V` runtime pe unknown hota hai; alag-alag monomorphized versions ho sakte hain.

Do fixes:

1) `put` ko non-generic bana do, jaise `&str` ya `String` le:
- Cost: flexibility kam ho jaati hai, sirf ek/value type accept karega.

2) `put` me trait object use karo, jaise `&dyn ToString` ya `Box<dyn ToString>`:
- Cost: extra indirection / dynamic dispatch, aur kabhi-kabhi heap allocation (`Box`) ki zarurat.

Alternative style: generic method hata ke `Store` ko enum-based/value-erased design se bhi kar sakte ho, but simple answer me above two best hain.

struct Filters {
    rules: Vec<Box<dyn Fn(u32) -> bool>>,
}

impl Filters {
    fn add_limit(&mut self, limit: &u32) {
        self.rules.push(Box::new(move |n| n <= *limit));
    }

    fn passes(&self, n: u32) -> bool {
        self.rules.iter().all(|rule| rule(n))
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut filters = Filters { rules: Vec::new() };
    filters.rules.push(Box::new(|n| n % 2 == 0));
    let limit = 10;
    filters.add_limit(&limit);
    let items = [4, 7, 12, 8];
    let kept: Vec<u32> = items.into_iter().filter(|&n| filters.passes(n)).collect();
    println!("{kept:?}");
}

```
`trait Shape: Debug { ... }` says "every type that implements `Shape` must also implement `Debug`". `Debug` is a supertrait of `Shape`. Two consequences:
```

// Each step runs once and hands its owned text to the output,
// so `run` takes the step by value (Box<Self>).
trait Step {
    fn run(self: Box<Self>, out: &mut Vec<String>);
}

struct Emit(String);
struct Repeat(String, usize);

impl Step for Emit {
    fn run(self: Box<Self>, out: &mut Vec<String>) {
        out.push(self.0);
    }
}

impl Step for Repeat {
    fn run(self: Box<Self>, out: &mut Vec<String>) {
        for _ in 1..self.1 {
            out.push(self.0.clone());
        }
        out.push(self.0);
    }
}

struct Job {
    steps: Vec<Box<dyn Step>>,
}

impl Job {

// Each step runs once and hands its owned text to the output,
// so `run` takes the step by value (Box<Self>).
trait Step {
    fn run(self: Box<Self>, out: &mut Vec<String>);
}

struct Emit(String);
struct Repeat(String, usize);

impl Step for Emit {
    fn run(self: Box<Self>, out: &mut Vec<String>) {
        out.push(self.0);
    }
}

impl Step for Repeat {
    fn run(self: Box<Self>, out: &mut Vec<String>) {
        for _ in 1..self.1 {
            out.push(self.0.clone());
        }
        out.push(self.0);
    }
}

struct Job {
    steps: Vec<Box<dyn Step>>,
}

impl Job {
    fn finish(&mut self) -> Vec<String> {
        let mut out = Vec::new();
        let steps = std::mem::take(&mut self.steps);
        for step in steps {
            step.run(&mut out);
        }
        out
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut job = Job { steps: vec![Box::new(Emit("start".into())), Box::new(Repeat("tick".into(), 2))] };
    let lines = job.finish();
    println!("{lines:?}, {} steps left", job.steps.len());
}

Each copy knows its type exactly, so every call is a direct call that can be inlined. This is static dispatch: the method is chosen at compile time.

// Each step runs once and hands its owned text to the output,
// so `run` takes the step by value (Box<Self>).
trait Step {
    fn run(self: Box<Self>, out: &mut Vec<String>);
}

struct Emit(String);
struct Repeat(String, usize);

impl Step for Emit {
    fn run(self: Box<Self>, out: &mut Vec<String>) {
        out.push(self.0);
    }
}

impl Step for Repeat {
    fn run(self: Box<Self>, out: &mut Vec<String>) {
        for _ in 1..self.1 {
            out.push(self.0.clone());
        }
        out.push(self.0);
    }
}

struct Job {
    steps: Vec<Box<dyn Step>>,
}

impl Job {
    fn finish(&mut self) -> Vec<String> {
        let mut out = Vec::new();
        let steps = std::mem::take(&mut self.steps);
        for step in steps {
            step.run(&mut out);
        }
        out
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut job = Job { steps: vec![Box::new(Emit("start".into())), Box::new(Repeat("tick".into(), 2))] };
    let lines = job.finish();
    println!("{lines:?}, {} steps left", job.steps.len());
}

    fn scale(&mut self, k: f64);
    fn clone_box(&self) -> Box<dyn Shape>;

    }

    fn clone_box(&self) -> Box<dyn Shape> { Box::new(self.clone()) }

    fn clone_box(&self) -> Box<dyn Shape> { Box::new(self.clone()) }

// Reference solution for p6 (never shown to the learner).
//
// Run:    rustc --edition 2024 -o main p6.rs && ./main

trait Stage {
    fn apply(&self, x: i64) -> i64;
    fn name(&self) -> String;
}

struct Add(i64);
struct Mul(i64);
struct Neg;

impl Stage for Add {
    fn apply(&self, x: i64) -> i64 {
        x + self.0
    }
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        format!("add {}", self.0)
    }
}

impl Stage for Mul {
    fn apply(&self, x: i64) -> i64 {
        x * self.0
    }
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        format!("mul {}", self.0)
    }
}

impl Stage for Neg {
    fn apply(&self, x: i64) -> i64 {
        -x
    }
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        String::from("neg")
    }
}

fn parse_stage(spec: &str) -> Option<Box<dyn Stage>> {
    let words: Vec<&str> = spec.split_whitespace().collect();
    match words.as_slice() {
        ["add", n] => Some(Box::new(Add(n.parse().ok()?))),
        ["mul", n] => Some(Box::new(Mul(n.parse().ok()?))),
        ["neg"] => Some(Box::new(Neg)),
        _ => None,
    }
}

struct Pipeline {
    stages: Vec<Box<dyn Stage>>,
}

impl Pipeline {
    fn parse(text: &str) -> Option<Pipeline> {
        let mut stages = Vec::new();
        for piece in text.split(';') {
            let piece = piece.trim();
            if piece.is_empty() {
                continue;
            }
            stages.push(parse_stage(piece)?);
        }
        Some(Pipeline { stages })
    }

    fn run(&self, x: i64) -> i64 {
        self.stages.iter().fold(x, |acc, s| s.apply(acc))
    }

    fn describe(&self) -> String {
        let names: Vec<String> = self.stages.iter().map(|s| s.name()).collect();
        names.join(" | ")
    }
}

fn main() {
    let p = Pipeline::parse("add 3; mul 2; neg").expect("a valid pipeline");
    println!("{} => {}", p.describe(), p.run(4));
}

trait Stage {
    fn apply(&self, x: i64) -> i64;
    fn name(&self) -> String;
}

struct AddStage(i64);
struct MulStage(i64);
struct NegStage;

impl Stage for AddStage {
    fn apply(&self, x: i64) -> i64 {
        x + self.0
    }
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        format!("add {}", self.0)
    }
}

impl Stage for MulStage {
    fn apply(&self, x: i64) -> i64 {
        x * self.0
    }
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        format!("mul {}", self.0)
    }
}

impl Stage for NegStage {
    fn apply(&self, x: i64) -> i64 {
        -x
    }
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        String::from("neg")
    }
}

fn parse_stage(spec: &str) -> Option<Box<dyn Stage>> {
    let mut parts = spec.split_whitespace();
    let op = parts.next()?;
    match op {
        "add" => {
            let n: i64 = parts.next()?.parse().ok()?;
            if parts.next().is_some() {
                return None;
            }
            Some(Box::new(AddStage(n)))
        }
        "mul" => {
            let n: i64 = parts.next()?.parse().ok()?;
            if parts.next().is_some() {
                return None;
            }
            Some(Box::new(MulStage(n)))
        }
        "neg" => {
            if parts.next().is_some() {
                return None;
            }
            Some(Box::new(NegStage))
        }
        _ => None,
    }
}

struct Pipeline {
    stages: Vec<Box<dyn Stage>>,
}

impl Pipeline {
    fn parse(text: &str) -> Option<Pipeline> {
        let mut stages = Vec::new();
        for piece in text.split(';') {
            let piece = piece.trim();
            if piece.is_empty() {
                continue;
            }
            stages.push(parse_stage(piece)?);
        }
        Some(Pipeline { stages })
    }

    fn run(&self, x: i64) -> i64 {
        self.stages.iter().fold(x, |acc, stage| stage.apply(acc))
    }

    fn describe(&self) -> String {
        self.stages
            .iter()
            .map(|stage| stage.name())
            .collect::<Vec<_>>()
            .join(" | ")
    }
}

fn main() {
    let p = Pipeline::parse("add 3; mul 2; neg").expect("a valid pipeline");
    println!("{} => {}", p.describe(), p.run(4));
}

// Each step runs once and hands its owned text to the output,
// so `run` takes the step by value (Box<Self>).
trait Step {
    fn run(self: Box<Self>, out: &mut Vec<String>);
}

struct Emit(String);
struct Repeat(String, usize);

impl Step for Emit {
    fn run(self: Box<Self>, out: &mut Vec<String>) {
        out.push(self.0);
    }
}

impl Step for Repeat {
    fn run(self: Box<Self>, out: &mut Vec<String>) {
        for _ in 1..self.1 {
            out.push(self.0.clone());
        }
        out.push(self.0);
    }

trait Stage {
    fn apply(&self, x: i64) -> i64;
    fn name(&self) -> String;
}

struct AddStage(i64);
struct MulStage(i64);
struct NegStage;

impl Stage for AddStage {
    fn apply(&self, x: i64) -> i64 {
        x + self.0
    }
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        format!("add {}", self.0)
    }
}

impl Stage for MulStage {
    fn apply(&self, x: i64) -> i64 {
        x * self.0
    }
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        format!("mul {}", self.0)
    }
}

impl Stage for NegStage {
    fn apply(&self, x: i64) -> i64 {
        -x
    }
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        String::from("neg")
    }
}

fn parse_stage(spec: &str) -> Option<Box<dyn Stage>> {
    let mut parts = spec.split_whitespace();
    let op = parts.next()?;
    match op {
        "add" => {
            let n: i64 = parts.next()?.parse().ok()?;
            if parts.next().is_some() {
                return None;
            }
            Some(Box::new(AddStage(n)))
        }
        "mul" => {
            let n: i64 = parts.next()?.parse().ok()?;
            if parts.next().is_some() {
                return None;
            }
            Some(Box::new(MulStage(n)))
        }
        "neg" => {
            if parts.next().is_some() {
                return None;
            }
            Some(Box::new(NegStage))
        }
        _ => None,
    }
}

struct Pipeline {
    stages: Vec<Box<dyn Stage>>,
}

impl Pipeline {
    fn parse(text: &str) -> Option<Pipeline> {
        let mut stages = Vec::new();
        for piece in text.split(';') {
            let piece = piece.trim();
            if piece.is_empty() {
                continue;
            }
            stages.push(parse_stage(piece)?);
        }
        Some(Pipeline { stages })
    }

        self.stages.iter().fold(x, |acc, stage| stage.apply(acc))
    }

    fn describe(&self) -> String {
        self.stages

            .map(|stage| stage.name())
            .collect::<Vec<_>>()
            .join(" | ")
    }
}

```
`trait Shape: Debug { ... }` says "every type that implements `Shape` must also implement `Debug`". `Debug` is a supertrait of `Shape`. Two consequences:
```

trait Stage {
    fn apply(&self, x: i64) -> i64;
    fn name(&self) -> String;
}

struct Add {
    n: i64,
}

struct Mul {
    n: i64,
}

struct Neg;

impl Stage for Add {
    fn apply(&self, x: i64) -> i64 {
        x + self.n
    }

    fn name(&self) -> String {
        format!("add {}", self.n)
    }
}

impl Stage for Mul {
    fn apply(&self, x: i64) -> i64 {
        x * self.n
    }

    fn name(&self) -> String {
        format!("mul {}", self.n)
    }
}

impl Stage for Neg {
    fn apply(&self, x: i64) -> i64 {
        -x
    }

    fn name(&self) -> String {
        String::from("neg")
    }
}

fn parse_stage(spec: &str) -> Option<Box<dyn Stage>> {
    let mut parts = spec.split_whitespace();
    let op = parts.next()?;
    match op {
        "add" => {
            let n: i64 = parts.next()?.parse().ok()?;
            if parts.next().is_some() {
                return None;
            }
            Some(Box::new(Add { n }))
        }
        "mul" => {
            let n: i64 = parts.next()?.parse().ok()?;
            if parts.next().is_some() {
                return None;
            }
            Some(Box::new(Mul { n }))
        }
        "neg" => {
            if parts.next().is_some() {
                return None;
            }
            Some(Box::new(Neg))
        }
        _ => None,
    }
}

struct Pipeline {
    stages: Vec<Box<dyn Stage>>,
}

impl Pipeline {
    fn parse(text: &str) -> Option<Pipeline> {
        let mut stages = Vec::new();
        for piece in text.split(';') {
            let piece = piece.trim();
            if piece.is_empty() {
                continue;
            }
            stages.push(parse_stage(piece)?);
        }
        Some(Pipeline { stages })
    }

    fn run(&self, x: i64) -> i64 {
        let mut x = x;
        for stage in &self.stages {
            x = stage.apply(x);
        }
        x
    }

    fn describe(&self) -> String {
        self.stages
            .iter()
            .map(|stage| stage.name())
            .collect::<Vec<_>>()
            .join(" | ")
    }
}

fn main() {
    let p = Pipeline::parse("add 3; mul 2; neg").expect("a valid pipeline");
    println!("{} => {}", p.describe(), p.run(4));
}

// Each step runs once and hands its owned text to the output,
// so `run` takes the step by value (Box<Self>).
trait Step {
    fn run(self: Box<Self>, out: &mut Vec<String>);
}

struct Emit(String);
struct Repeat(String, usize);

impl Step for Emit {
    fn run(self: Box<Self>, out: &mut Vec<String>) {
        out.push(self.0);
    }
}

impl Step for Repeat {
    fn run(self: Box<Self>, out: &mut Vec<String>) {
        for _ in 1..self.1 {
            out.push(self.0.clone());
        }
        out.push(self.0);
    }
}

struct Job {
    steps: Vec<Box<dyn Step>>,
}

impl Job {
    fn finish(&mut self) -> Vec<String> {
        let mut out = Vec::new();
        let steps = std::mem::take(&mut self.steps);
        for step in steps {
            step.run(&mut out);
        }
        out
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut job = Job { steps: vec![Box::new(Emit("start".into())), Box::new(Repeat("tick".into(), 2))] };
    let lines = job.finish();
    println!("{lines:?}, {} steps left", job.steps.len());
}

        x * self.0
    }
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        format!("mul {}", self.0)
    }
}

impl Stage for Neg {
    fn apply(&self, x: i64) -> i64 {
        -x
    }
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        String::from("neg")
    }
}

fn parse_stage(spec: &str) -> Option<Box<dyn Stage>> {
    let words: Vec<&str> = spec.split_whitespace().collect();
    match words.as_slice() {
        ["add", n] => Some(Box::new(Add(n.parse().ok()?))),
        ["mul", n] => Some(Box::new(Mul(n.parse().ok()?))),
        ["neg"] => Some(Box::new(Neg)),
        _ => None,
    }
}

struct Pipeline {
    stages: Vec<Box<dyn Stage>>,
}

impl Pipeline {
    fn parse(text: &str) -> Option<Pipeline> {
        let mut stages = Vec::new();
        for piece in text.split(';') {
            let piece = piece.trim();
            if piece.is_empty() {
                continue;
            }
            stages.push(parse_stage(piece)?);
        }
        Some(Pipeline { stages })
    }

    fn run(&self, x: i64) -> i64 {
        self.stages.iter().fold(x, |acc, s| s.apply(acc))
    }

    fn describe(&self) -> String {
        let names: Vec<String> = self.stages.iter().map(|s| s.name()).collect();
        names.join(" | ")
    }
}

fn main() {
    let p = Pipeline::parse("add 3; mul 2; neg").expect("a valid pipeline");
    println!("{} => {}", p.describe(), p.run(4));
}

// Each step runs once and hands its owned text to the output,
// so `run` takes the step by value (Box<Self>).
trait Step {
    fn run(self: Box<Self>, out: &mut Vec<String>);
}

struct Emit(String);
struct Repeat(String, usize);

impl Step for Emit {
    fn run(self: Box<Self>, out: &mut Vec<String>) {
        out.push(self.0);
    }
}

impl Step for Repeat {
    fn run(self: Box<Self>, out: &mut Vec<String>) {
        for _ in 1..self.1 {
            out.push(self.0.clone());
        }
        out.push(self.0);
    }
}

struct Job {
    steps: Vec<Box<dyn Step>>,
}

impl Job {
    fn finish(&mut self) -> Vec<String> {
        let mut out = Vec::new();
        let steps = std::mem::take(&mut self.steps);
        for step in steps {
            step.run(&mut out);
        }
        out
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut job = Job { steps: vec![Box::new(Emit("start".into())), Box::new(Repeat("tick".into(), 2))] };
    let lines = job.finish();
    println!("{lines:?}, {} steps left", job.steps.len());
}

trait Stage {
    fn apply(&self, x: i64) -> i64;
    fn name(&self) -> String;
}

struct Add {
    n: i64,
}

struct Mul {
    n: i64,
}

struct Neg;

impl Stage for Add {
    fn apply(&self, x: i64) -> i64 {
        x + self.n
    }

    fn name(&self) -> String {
        format!("add {}", self.n)
    }
}

impl Stage for Mul {
    fn apply(&self, x: i64) -> i64 {
        x * self.n
    }

    fn name(&self) -> String {
        format!("mul {}", self.n)
    }
}

impl Stage for Neg {
    fn apply(&self, x: i64) -> i64 {
        -x
    }

    fn name(&self) -> String {
        String::from("neg")
    }
}

fn parse_stage(spec: &str) -> Option<Box<dyn Stage>> {
    let mut parts = spec.split_whitespace();
    let op = parts.next()?;
    match op {
        "add" => {
            let n = parts.next()?.parse::<i64>().ok()?;
            if parts.next().is_some() {
                return None;
            }
            Some(Box::new(Add { n }))
        }
        "mul" => {
            let n = parts.next()?.parse::<i64>().ok()?;
            if parts.next().is_some() {
                return None;
            }
            Some(Box::new(Mul { n }))
        }
        "neg" => {
            if parts.next().is_some() {
                return None;
            }
            Some(Box::new(Neg))
        }
        _ => None,
    }
}

struct Pipeline {
    stages: Vec<Box<dyn Stage>>,
}

impl Pipeline {
    fn parse(text: &str) -> Option<Pipeline> {
        let mut stages = Vec::new();
        for piece in text.split(';') {
            let piece = piece.trim();
            if piece.is_empty() {
                continue;
            }
            stages.push(parse_stage(piece)?);
        }
        Some(Pipeline { stages })
    }

    fn run(&self, x: i64) -> i64 {
        self.stages.iter().fold(x, |acc, stage| stage.apply(acc))
    }

    fn describe(&self) -> String {
        self.stages
            .iter()
            .map(|stage| stage.name())
            .collect::<Vec<_>>()
            .join(" | ")
    }
}

fn main() {
    let p = Pipeline::parse("add 3; mul 2; neg").expect("a valid pipeline");
    println!("{} => {}", p.describe(), p.run(4));
}

trait Command {
    fn apply(&mut self, doc: &mut String);
    fn undo(self: Box<Self>, doc: &mut String);
    fn name(&self) -> String;
}

struct Append(String);

struct Clear {
    saved: String,
}

impl Command for Append {
    fn apply(&mut self, doc: &mut String) {
        doc.push_str(&self.0);
    }
    fn undo(self: Box<Self>, doc: &mut String) {
        // Later commands were undone first, so our text is at the end.
        doc.truncate(doc.len() - self.0.len());
    }
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        String::from("append")
    }
}

impl Command for Clear {
    fn apply(&mut self, doc: &mut String) {
        self.saved = std::mem::take(doc);
    }
    fn undo(self: Box<Self>, doc: &mut String) {
        *doc = self.saved; // we own the box, so we can move the String out
    }
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        String::from("clear")
    }
}

struct Editor {
    doc: String,
    history: Vec<Box<dyn Command>>,
}

impl Editor {
    fn new() -> Editor {
        Editor { doc: String::new(), history: Vec::new() }
    }

    fn run(&mut self, mut cmd: Box<dyn Command>) {
        cmd.apply(&mut self.doc);
        self.history.push(cmd);
    }

    fn undo(&mut self) -> bool {
        // pop() hands back the Box by value, which undo(self: Box<Self>) needs.
        match self.history.pop() {
            Some(cmd) => {
                cmd.undo(&mut self.doc);
                true
            }
            None => false,
        }
    }

    fn history(&self) -> Vec<String> {
        self.history.iter().map(|c| c.name()).collect()
    }
}

    ed.run(Box::new(Append("hello".into())));
    ed.run(Box::new(Append(" world".into())));
    ed.run(Box::new(Clear { saved: String::new() }));
    println!("{:?} {:?}", ed.doc, ed.history());

    println!("{:?} {:?}", ed.doc, ed.history());

trait Command {
    // Make the change. May record what undo will need.
    fn apply(&mut self, doc: &mut String);
    // Reverse the change. Takes the command by value: a command is undone at most once.
    fn undo(self: Box<Self>, doc: &mut String);
    fn name(&self) -> String;
}

struct Append(String);

struct Clear {
    saved: String,
}

impl Command for Append {
    fn apply(&mut self, doc: &mut String) {
        doc.push_str(&self.0);
    }
    fn undo(self: Box<Self>, doc: &mut String) {
        let new_len = doc.len().saturating_sub(self.0.len());
        doc.truncate(new_len);
    }
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        String::from("append")
    }
}

impl Command for Clear {
    fn apply(&mut self, doc: &mut String) {
        self.saved = doc.clone();
        doc.clear();
    }
    fn undo(self: Box<Self>, doc: &mut String) {
        doc.push_str(&self.saved);
    }
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        String::from("clear")
    }
}

struct Editor {
    doc: String,
    history: Vec<Box<dyn Command>>,
}

impl Editor {
    fn new() -> Editor {
        Editor { doc: String::new(), history: Vec::new() }
    }

    fn run(&mut self, mut cmd: Box<dyn Command>) {
        cmd.apply(&mut self.doc);
        self.history.push(cmd);
    }

    fn undo(&mut self) -> bool {
        match self.history.pop() {
            Some(cmd) => {
                cmd.undo(&mut self.doc);
                true
            }
            None => false,
        }
    }

    fn history(&self) -> Vec<String> {
        self.history.iter().map(|cmd| cmd.name()).collect()
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut ed = Editor::new();
    ed.run(Box::new(Append("hello".into())));
    ed.run(Box::new(Append(" world".into())));
    ed.run(Box::new(Clear { saved: String::new() }));
    println!("{:?} {:?}", ed.doc, ed.history());
    ed.undo();
    println!("{:?} {:?}", ed.doc, ed.history());
    ed.undo();
    println!("{:?} {:?}", ed.doc, ed.history());
}

// Each step runs once and hands its owned text to the output,
// so `run` takes the step by value (Box<Self>).
trait Step {
    fn run(self: Box<Self>, out: &mut Vec<String>);
}

struct Emit(String);
struct Repeat(String, usize);

impl Step for Emit {
    fn run(self: Box<Self>, out: &mut Vec<String>) {
        out.push(self.0);
    }
}

impl Step for Repeat {
    fn run(self: Box<Self>, out: &mut Vec<String>) {
        for _ in 1..self.1 {
            out.push(self.0.clone());
        }
        out.push(self.0);
    }
}

struct Job {
    steps: Vec<Box<dyn Step>>,
}

impl Job {
    fn finish(&mut self) -> Vec<String> {
        let mut out = Vec::new();
        let steps = std::mem::take(&mut self.steps);
        for step in steps {
            step.run(&mut out);
        }
        out
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut job = Job { steps: vec![Box::new(Emit("start".into())), Box::new(Repeat("tick".into(), 2))] };
    let lines = job.finish();
    println!("{lines:?}, {} steps left", job.steps.len());
}

    fn area(&self) -> f64;
    fn scale(&mut self, k: f64);
    fn clone_box(&self) -> Box<dyn Shape>;
}

impl Clone for Box<dyn Shape> {
    fn clone(&self) -> Self {
        self.clone_box()
    }
}

#[derive(Clone)]
struct Square(f64);

#[derive(Clone)]
struct Circle(f64);

impl Shape for Square {
    fn area(&self) -> f64 { self.0 * self.0 }
    fn scale(&mut self, k: f64) { self.0 *= k; }
    fn clone_box(&self) -> Box<dyn Shape> { Box::new(self.clone()) }
}

impl Shape for Circle {
    fn area(&self) -> f64 { 3.0 * self.0 * self.0 }
    fn scale(&mut self, k: f64) { self.0 *= k; }
    fn clone_box(&self) -> Box<dyn Shape> { Box::new(self.clone()) }
}

fn total(list: &[Box<dyn Shape>]) -> f64 {
    list.iter().map(|s| s.area()).sum()
}

trait Stage {
    fn apply(&self, x: i64) -> i64;
    fn name(&self) -> String;
}

struct Add {
    n: i64,
}

struct Mul {
    n: i64,
}

struct Neg;

impl Stage for Add {
    fn apply(&self, x: i64) -> i64 {
        x + self.n
    }

    fn name(&self) -> String {
        format!("add {}", self.n)
    }
}

impl Stage for Mul {
    fn apply(&self, x: i64) -> i64 {
        x * self.n
    }

    fn name(&self) -> String {
        format!("mul {}", self.n)
    }
}

impl Stage for Neg {
    fn apply(&self, x: i64) -> i64 {
        -x
    }

    fn name(&self) -> String {
        String::from("neg")
    }
}

fn parse_stage(spec: &str) -> Option<Box<dyn Stage>> {
    let mut parts = spec.split_whitespace();
    let op = parts.next()?;
    match op {
        "add" => {
            let n = parts.next()?.parse::<i64>().ok()?;
            if parts.next().is_some() {
                return None;
            }
            Some(Box::new(Add { n }))
        }
        "mul" => {
            let n = parts.next()?.parse::<i64>().ok()?;
            if parts.next().is_some() {
                return None;
            }
            Some(Box::new(Mul { n }))
        }
        "neg" => {
            if parts.next().is_some() {
                return None;
            }
            Some(Box::new(Neg))
        }
        _ => None,
    }
}

struct Pipeline {
    stages: Vec<Box<dyn Stage>>,
}

impl Pipeline {
    fn parse(text: &str) -> Option<Pipeline> {
        let mut stages = Vec::new();
        for piece in text.split(';') {
            let piece = piece.trim();
            if piece.is_empty() {
                continue;
            }
            stages.push(parse_stage(piece)?);
        }
        Some(Pipeline { stages })
    }

    fn run(&self, x: i64) -> i64 {
        self.stages.iter().fold(x, |acc, stage| stage.apply(acc))
    }

    fn describe(&self) -> String {
        self.stages
            .iter()
            .map(|stage| stage.name())
            .collect::<Vec<_>>()
            .join(" | ")
    }
}

fn main() {
    let p = Pipeline::parse("add 3; mul 2; neg").expect("a valid pipeline");
    println!("{} => {}", p.describe(), p.run(4));
}

// Reference solution for p7 (never shown to the learner).
//
// Run:    rustc --edition 2024 -o main p7.rs && ./main

trait Command {
    fn apply(&mut self, doc: &mut String);
    fn undo(self: Box<Self>, doc: &mut String);
    fn name(&self) -> String;
}

struct Append(String);

struct Clear {
    saved: String,
}

impl Command for Append {
    fn apply(&mut self, doc: &mut String) {
        doc.push_str(&self.0);
    }
    fn undo(self: Box<Self>, doc: &mut String) {
        // Later commands were undone first, so our text is at the end.
        doc.truncate(doc.len() - self.0.len());
    }
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        String::from("append")
    }
}

impl Command for Clear {
    fn apply(&mut self, doc: &mut String) {
        self.saved = std::mem::take(doc);
    }
    fn undo(self: Box<Self>, doc: &mut String) {
        *doc = self.saved; // we own the box, so we can move the String out
    }
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        String::from("clear")
    }
}

struct Editor {
    doc: String,
    history: Vec<Box<dyn Command>>,
}

impl Editor {
    fn new() -> Editor {
        Editor { doc: String::new(), history: Vec::new() }
    }

    fn run(&mut self, mut cmd: Box<dyn Command>) {
        cmd.apply(&mut self.doc);
        self.history.push(cmd);
    }

    fn undo(&mut self) -> bool {
        // pop() hands back the Box by value, which undo(self: Box<Self>) needs.
        match self.history.pop() {
            Some(cmd) => {
                cmd.undo(&mut self.doc);
                true
            }
            None => false,
        }
    }

    fn history(&self) -> Vec<String> {
        self.history.iter().map(|c| c.name()).collect()
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut ed = Editor::new();
    ed.run(Box::new(Append("hello".into())));
    ed.run(Box::new(Append(" world".into())));
    ed.run(Box::new(Clear { saved: String::new() }));
    println!("{:?} {:?}", ed.doc, ed.history());
    ed.undo();
    println!("{:?} {:?}", ed.doc, ed.history());
    ed.undo();
    println!("{:?} {:?}", ed.doc, ed.history());
}

messages.content:
The highlighted handler is the IRQ top half, so it runs in hardirq/interrupt context, not process context. In this driver that is `qadc_hardirq()` in `qadc-core.c`.

What the debug kernel is complaining about is that something in that interrupt path can sleep. From the code I can see the hardirq handler does `qadc_wdog_kick(st)`, and that goes through `mod_timer()`, plus it also takes `st->lock` and timestamps the interrupt. The likely report is the “might sleep in atomic/interrupt context” type warning coming from lockdep / debug atomic sleep checks in the debug config.

What could go wrong on the production kernel is that the same path may appear to work most of the time, but it is still unsafe if any part of the timer/watchdog or follow-on work ever blocks or if the lock usage is wrong. In particular, if the hardirq side ends up calling something that can sleep, you can get hard-to-reproduce latency spikes, lock ordering issues, or even deadlocks under load. Since both ADCs share one RDY line, that makes the interrupt path especially sensitive.

The fix would be to keep the hardirq handler tiny: just acknowledge state, maybe set a flag, and defer any potentially sleeping or heavyweight work to the threaded IRQ handler or a workqueue. So I would move the watchdog kick out of `qadc_hardirq()` and do it from the threaded handler (`qadc_irq_thread()`) or from the reset worker, depending on the intended semantics. Also I’d double-check the IRQ registration in `qadc-core.c` to ensure it is requested as a threaded/shared IRQ in a way that matches the shared open-drain line. The main files are `qadc-core.c` for the handler and watchdog path, and `dts/imx7d-board-adc.dtsi` for the shared interrupt wiring.

Lockdep: &st->lock was taken in hard IRQ context ({IN-HARDIRQ-W}, registered at qadc_hardirq via _raw_spin_lock) and is now taken by cat/731 in latest_show with interrupts enabled (HE1, {HARDIRQ-ON-W}), reading /sys/.../latest through sysfs (dev_attr_show, seq_read_iter, ksys_read). Usage {?...}: used in IRQ and with IRQs on. The deadlock: latest_show holds st->lock with spin_lock(); RDY fires on the same CPU; qadc_hardirq spins with interrupts off waiting for a lock that the interrupted task can never release: that CPU is dead, and soon the board. The README says the GPIO bank interrupt is handled on CPU0, so it only happens when the reader runs on CPU0 inside a few instructions of critical section, which is why tests pass and units hang rarely (this report came from cat on CPU1: lockdep flags the pattern without the deadlock). Every place st->lock is taken: qadc_hardirq spin_lock (fine, IRQs are off in a hard handler); qadc_irq_thread spin_lock_irqsave (fine); latest_show spin_lock (wrong: spin_lock_irqsave, or spin_lock_irq since it always runs with IRQs on); qadc_wdog_expired spin_lock: the timer callback runs in softirq, which a hard IRQ can interrupt on the same CPU, so it needs spin_lock_irqsave too (lockdep stopped at the first report and never got there). stats_show takes no lock: samples is a u64, and a 64-bit read is not atomic on 32-bit ARM, so a torn 64-bit read is possible; take the lock (or use u64_stats_sync). A mutex is not an answer while the hard handler takes the lock. Better still, remove the hard handler's use of st->lock (see the next stages); then the remaining users decide the variant. irqsave vs irq: irqsave restores the previous state, so it is safe from any context; irq is fine where IRQs are known to be on.

NEVER say any of these, in any wording::
  - hidden in a helper
  - uncontended fast path
  - precompute the period
  - spins with interrupts off
  - torn 64-bit read
  - runs in softirq

You may point at where to look. You may not name the mechanism or the fix. If your sentence would let them answer without thinking, rewrite it.

Lockdep is telling us we have a real lock inversion risk on `&st->lock`: the sysfs `latest_show()` path takes the spinlock in process context, and then the IRQ handler `qadc_hardirq()` also takes the same lock in hard interrupt context. That by itself is allowed for a plain spinlock, but lockdep is flagging the state because the lock was observed under a `HARDIRQ-ON-W` context in sysfs, and then later acquired from hardirq. In other words, the lock is being used in both sleepable and hardirq paths without the proper IRQ-disabling variant in the process-context users.

What can actually happen on production is an interrupt can fire while a process is already holding `st->lock` in `latest_show()`. Because the IRQ handler runs on the same CPU and tries to take the same lock, the interrupt spins waiting for the lock to be released, but the interrupted code cannot run until the interrupt returns. That is the deadlock lockdep is warning about. On a busy box it could manifest as a hard hang or a stuck CPU under load, even if the debug warning is absent.

The fix is to use the IRQ-safe spinlock variant consistently in any code that can run with interrupts enabled and shares the lock with hardirq context: `spin_lock_irqsave()` / `spin_unlock_irqrestore()` around all `st->lock` accesses in process context, and plain `spin_lock()` only where it is already in hardirq context. In practice, that means `latest_show()` and probably the stats-reading path in `qadc-sysfs.c` should use `spin_lock_irqsave()`, while `qadc_hardirq()` can keep `spin_lock()`. The timer/reset worker should also use the irqsave form if it touches the same lock from process context.

Walking through every function I can see that touches `st->lock`:

- `qadc_hardirq()` in `qadc-core.c`: hardirq context. It should use plain `spin_lock()` / `spin_unlock()` if it only updates the timestamp and counters.
- `qadc_irq_thread()` in `qadc-core.c`: threaded IRQ context, process context but tied to the interrupt. It uses `spin_lock_irqsave()` already around the ring write, which is fine.
- `qadc_wdog_expired()` in `qadc-core.c`: timer callback context. It uses `spin_lock()` to bump `resets`; I think this should be `spin_lock_irqsave()` if the same lock is also taken in hardirq, because timer softirq context can also race with interrupts.
- `latest_show()` in `qadc-sysfs.c`: process context via sysfs read. This should use `spin_lock_irqsave()` because it is racing with `qadc_hardirq()`.
- `stats_show()` in `qadc-sysfs.c`: same as above, if it reads `samples/irqs/resets` under the lock, it needs `spin_lock_irqsave()` too.

So the real bug is not just “the IRQ handler grabs a lock”; it’s that the lock is shared with process-context readers that are not disabling interrupts. The file to fix is mostly `qadc-sysfs.c`, and possibly the timer callback in `qadc-core.c` if it uses the same lock without irqsave.

A mutex is not an answer while the hard handler takes the lock. Better still, remove the hard handler's use of st->lock (see the next stages); then the remaining users decide the variant. irqsave vs irq: irqsave restores the previous state, so it is safe from any context; irq is fine where IRQs are known to be on.

  - uncontended fast path
  - precompute the period
  - spins with interrupts off
  - torn 64-bit read
  - runs in softirq

Lockdep is telling us we have a real locck inversion rissk on `&st->lock`: the sysfs `latest_show()` path takes the spinnlock in process context, and then the IRQ handler `qadc_hardirq()` aslo takes the same lock in hard interrupt context. Thta by itself is allowed for a plain spinlock, but lockdep is flaggging the state because the lok was observed under a `HARDIRQ-ON-W` context in sysfs, and then later acquired froom hardirq. In other words, the lock is being ussed in botth sleepale and hardirq paths without the proper IRQ-disabling vriant in the process-context users.

What can actually happen on porduction is an interrupt can fire whle a process is already holdig `st->lock` in `latest_show()`. Because the IRQ handler runs on the smae CPU and tries to take the same lock, the interrupt spins waiting for the lock to be released, but the interrupted cdoe cannnot run unil the interrupt returns. That is the deadlock lockdep is warning about. On a busy box it could manifest as a hard hang or a stuck CPU uder load, even if the debug warning is absent.

The fix is to use the IRQ-safe spinlock variant consistently in any code that can run wtih interrupts enabld and shares the lock with hardirq context: `spin_lock_irqsave()` / `spin_unlock_irqrestore()` around all `st->lock` accesses in process context, and plain `spin_lock()` only where it is already in hardirq context. In practice, that means `latest_show()` and prrobably the stats-reading path in `qadc-sysfs.c` should use `spin_lock_irqsave()`, whie `qadc_hardirq()` can kep `spin_lock()`. The timer/reset worker should also use the irqsave form if it touches the same lock frrom proccess context.

Walking through every function I can see that touches `st->lock`:

- `qadc_hardirq()` in `qadc-core.c`: hardirq context. It should use plain `spin_lock()` / `spin_unlock()` if it ony updates the timeestamp and counters.
- `qadc_irq_thread()` in `qadc-core.c`: threaded IRQ context, process context but tieed to the interrupt. It uses `spin_lock_irqsave()` already aronud the ring write, which is fine.
- `qadc_wdog_expired()` in `qadc-core.c`: timre callback context. It uses `spin_lock()` to bump `resets`; I thnik this should be `spin_lock_irqsave()` if the smae lock is also taken in hardirq, because timer softirq context can also race with interrupts.
- `latest_show()` in `qadc-sysfs.c`: process context via sysfs read. Thsi shoudl use `spin_lock_irqsave()` because it is racing with `qadc_hardirq()`.
- `stats_show()` in `qadc-sysfs.c`: same as above, if it reads `samples/irqs/resets` uner the lock, it needs `spin_lock_irqsave()` too.

So the rael bug is not just “the IRQ handler grabs a lock”; it’s taht the lock is shared wth process-context readers that are not disaling interrupts. The fiel to fix is mostly `qadc-sysfs.c`, and possibly the timre callback in `qadc-core.c` if it uses the saame lok without irqsave.

The numbers and the capture sound like the driver is servicing the shared RDY line too often relative to actual data-ready events, and probably doing repeated IRQ entries while the line is still held low.

Given the board wiring in `dts/imx7d-board-adc.dtsi`, both ADCs pull one open-drain line low, and the README says RDY stays low until the result is read. So if the IRQ is level-triggered (`IRQ_TYPE_LEVEL_LOW`) and the handler/thread does not fully drain both devices before returning, the GPIO line remains asserted and the interrupt re-fires immediately. That would show up as a high interrupt count, and on the capture you’d expect the RDY line to stay low for a while with the GPIO pulse at `qadc_hardirq` repeating far more often than the 100 Hz per ADC conversions.

The likely culprit lines are in `qadc_probe()` where the IRQ is requested as shared level low, and in `qadc_irq_thread()` where only one client’s DATA is read per IRQ entry. If both ADCs can be ready at nearly the same time, one IRQ may cause only one device to be serviced, leaving the other still asserting RDY, so the same interrupt line immediately retriggers.

move_object.question_summary: Candidate worked a storm/duplicate-sample scenario on a shared level-triggered RDY line. They reasoned about level-triggered re-assertion from general principles but never cited the counters or capture measurements and never reached the missing IRQF_ONESHOT or the per-device STATUS check. Earlier lockdep work on the sample lock was their strongest showing.
move_object.report_notes:
Across the question the candidate was strongest on the second stage (the st->lock lockdep report), where they read the inconsistent state correctly, described the same-CPU self-deadlock accurately and enumerated every lock user with its context and the lock call it needs, unprompted. Weaker on the first stage: right shape of fix (keep the top half tiny, move the watchdog kick to the thread) but they guessed mod_timer as the sleeping call rather than mutex_lock on cfg_lock via qadc_wdog_period at mutex.c:585, and the production-kernel answer was generic latency hand waving rather than the concrete contention with odr_store or the reset work.

On this final stage (interrupt storm and duplicate samples) the answer was the weakest of the three and stayed entirely at the level of plausible narrative. They correctly inferred that the line is level-triggered and active low with two open-drain drivers, and that the line stays asserted until the data is read, which would re-fire the interrupt. That is the right neighbourhood. But they explicitly said they had not looked at irq-check.txt or the capture and reasoned 'from the description', and it showed: no 243,963 interrupts in 10 s, no 2,000 conversions, no ratio of about 122 entries per conversion, no 82 and 162 DBG edges per conversion, no 3.83 us re-entry interval, no 300 us read duration, no CPU0 concentration, and crucially no notice that samples rose 5,002 and 4,002 for 1,000 conversions each or that the capture shows transactions returning byte-for-byte identical data to the previous read of the same ADC, including reads after RDY has already gone high. The duplicate-sample half of the symptom was therefore never explained.

The diagnosis they did offer is wrong in mechanism: they attributed the storm to the thread servicing only one of the two ADCs and leaving the other asserting the line, and proposed that the threaded handler drain both devices. The actual cause is the IRQ being requested IRQF_SHARED without IRQF_ONESHOT, so the line is re-enabled before any thread has cleared the source, with the dummy primary handler present specifically to get past the kernel's refusal of a NULL primary without ONESHOT. They never mentioned IRQF_ONESHOT, the dummy primary handler and its comment, the requirement that all sharers agree on the flag, or the fact that qadc_irq_thread does not consult STATUS/DRDY and unconditionally returns IRQ_HANDLED, which both causes the cross-reading of the other ADC's conversions and defeats the spurious interrupt detector. Their 'drain both devices in one thread' proposal would also be the wrong structure for two independent client drivers sharing a line.

No hints were spent; the stage ran out of time at the first reply. Overall: solid on lockdep and execution contexts, willing to state a clear mechanism and a clear fix, but consistently reasons from general principles instead of reading the artefacts in front of them, and on the hardest stage that produced a confident wrong answer. For a mid-level driver role this is a partial pass: the locking and context knowledge is real, the interrupt-flag and evidence-reading side needs work.
move_object.response:
That is a reasonable shape of the failure, and you are right that the line is level-triggered active low with two open-drain drivers and that it stays asserted until the data is read. Where it did not land is that you reasoned from the description rather than from the two artefacts: the counters and the capture both carry numbers that pin down how often the handler is entered per conversion, and the sample counts and the repeated byte patterns point at a second symptom beyond raw interrupt load that your explanation does not cover. There is also a flag on the request in probe that decides exactly when the line becomes eligible to fire again, and that is the lever here rather than restructuring the thread to service both chips.

We are at time, so I will stop there. Thanks for working through this one; your reading of the second lockdep report and the lock-by-lock context walk was the strongest part of the session, and that is the part I will be writing up most favourably. Appreciate your time today.

/proc/interrupts: line 63 (gpio-mxc 17, Level, shared by 1-0048 and 1-0049) went from 44,792,380 to 45,036,343, 243,963 interrupts in 10 s for 2,000 conversions (two ADCs at 100 Hz): about 122 per conversion, all on CPU0. The capture shows why: RDY stays low until a read reaches the last DATA byte, about 300 us per I2C read, and the hard handler is entered about every 3.83 us for as long as it is low (82 entries in 317.2 us, 162 in 621.9 us). Cause: the line is level-triggered and the IRQ is requested without IRQF_ONESHOT. handle_level_irq masks the line, runs both primary handlers (both return IRQ_WAKE_THREAD), and unmasks the line at once because no oneshot thread is pending; the level is still asserted, so it fires again until a thread has done the I2C read. The comment shows the kernel refused a NULL primary handler without ONESHOT exactly to prevent this, and the driver went around the check with a dummy primary. Shared line: every interrupt wakes both threads, and qadc_irq_thread reads without checking STATUS and always returns IRQ_HANDLED, so each driver reads its ADC on the other ADC's conversions too; storm interrupts during a thread's run set IRQTF_RUNTHREAD again, so threads run again: samples went up 5,002 (0x48) and 4,002 (0x49) for 1,000 conversions each, and the capture shows repeated identical bytes and reads after RDY is already high. A 0x49 conversion keeps the line low twice as long because 0x48's thread reads first and the bus serialises. Both irqs counters rise by exactly the line count. Fix: IRQF_SHARED | IRQF_ONESHOT (every sharer must agree, or request fails with Flags mismatch) with a NULL primary or one that only stores a timestamp; in the thread, one 9-byte read from STATUS; if DRDY is clear return IRQ_NONE, else push the sample. IRQ_NONE also lets the spurious-IRQ detector disable a stuck line (nobody cared) instead of storming forever.

  - precompute the period
  - unmasks the line at once
  - without checking STATUS
  - nobody cared

The numbers and the capture sound like the driver is servicing the shared RDY line uh too um often relative to actual so yeah data-ready events, and probably doing actually repeated IRQ entries while the line is still actually basically held low. Given the board wiring in basically `dts/imx7d-board-adc.dtsi`, both basically ADCs pull one open-drain line so yeah low, and basically the README says RDY stays low until the result is read. So if the IRQ is level-triggered (`IRQ_TYPE_LEVEL_LOW`) and the handler/thread does not fully basically drain both devices before returning, the GPIO line remains asserted and the interrupt re-fires immediately. That would show up as a high interrupt count, and on the capture you’d expect the RDY line like to stay low for a while with the GPIO pulse i mean at `qadc_hardirq` repeating far more often than the 100 Hz per ADC conversions. The uh likely culprit lines are in `qadc_probe()` where the IRQ is requested as shared level low, and in `qadc_irq_thread()` where only one client’s DATA is read per IRQ entry. If both i mean ADCs can be ready at nearly the same um time, one IRQ may cause only one device to be serviced, leaving the other still asserting RDY, so the same interrupt line immediately retriggers. The fix is to make the threaded handler drain all devices that share the IRQ line before it returns. In practice that means either: - in the threaded IRQ, read whichever actually ADC fired and then poll/read the other shared IRQ actually peer too, or - better, in the common IRQ like path, loop over both clients and service every basically device whose STATUS says DRDY is set until the shared line is released. If the current code only uh like handles the so yeah `struct i2c_client *client` that owns the IRQ instance, then the like shared-line design is incomplete. I’d fix the shared interrupt design in `qadc-core.c`: request the IRQ as shared like threaded, keep the top half minimal, so yeah and in `qadc_irq_thread()` ensure actually both 0x48 and 0x49 are serviced before returning. That should reduce the interrupt storm and the CPU load. I’d want to confirm against `irq-check.txt` and `rdy-capture.png`, but from the description that’s the failure mode I’d expect.

Stage 1 (hardirq splat): identified hard interrupt context for qadc_hardirq and proposed the right shape of fix (tiny top half, move the watchdog kick to the thread), but never named the actual sleeping call (qadc_wdog_period -> mutex_lock_nested on cfg_lock at mutex.c:585) and instead guessed mod_timer, which is legal in hardirq. No evidence cited: no preempt_count 10001, no irqs_disabled 128, no mention of the second report or the HARDIRQ-ON-W to IN-HARDIRQ-W inconsistency on cfg_lock. Production-kernel answer was generic latency hand waving rather than the concrete contention with odr_store or the reset work holding cfg_lock across I2C writes and usleep_range.

Stage 2 (st->lock lockdep): their best work and entirely self-directed. Read the inconsistent state correctly (registered in hardirq from qadc_hardirq, taken with IRQs enabled from latest_show), described same-CPU self-deadlock accurately, and enumerated every user with its context and the required lock call: qadc_hardirq, qadc_irq_thread (already irqsave), qadc_wdog_expired (needs irqsave because the timer callback can be preempted by the hard IRQ on the same CPU), latest_show, stats_show.
