Stage 3 (interrupt storm): weakest. They correctly connected IRQ_TYPE_LEVEL_LOW and the open-drain shared line to re-triggering while RDY is held low, and correctly predicted the shape of the capture (DBG pulses far more often than 100 Hz). But the diagnosis was wrong in substance: they attributed the storm to the thread servicing only one device per IRQ, leaving the peer asserting RDY, and proposed draining both ADCs in the thread. They never reached IRQF_ONESHOT or the missing-oneshot unmask behaviour, never noticed the probe comment about the dummy primary handler working around the NULL-primary check, and never addressed the thread returning IRQ_HANDLED without checking STATUS, so they missed the duplicate-sample half of the problem entirely. No number from irq-check.txt was quoted: not the 243,963 interrupts in 10 s, not the 122 per conversion, not samples rising 5,002 and 4,002 against 1,000 conversions each, not the 82 and 162 DBG entries or the 3.83 us spacing, and not the repeated identical byte patterns in the I2C decode that are the direct evidence of duplicate reads. They closed by saying they would want to confirm against the two files, having had both in front of them.

Overall: solid grasp of kernel execution contexts and spinlock discipline, which is the mid-level core and which they demonstrated without prompting. Materially weaker on interrupt-line mechanics (level-triggered flow, ONESHOT, shared-line demultiplexing via STATUS and IRQ_NONE). The recurring pattern across all three stages is reasoning from remembered principles rather than from the artefacts supplied; when the principle happens to fit they are good, and when it does not they do not let the data correct them. The final stage on judging the teammate's rework and teardown ordering was not reached. No hints were used at any stage.

That is a reasonable instinct about the level-triggered line staying asserted, and you are right that the fix lives between the probe request and the thread. I will say the mechanism is a bit more specific than one device being left unserviced, and the counters in irq-check.txt would have pushed you towards it: the sample counts and the per-conversion handler entries do not line up the way your model predicts. Worth going back to how a level IRQ with a threaded handler gets masked and unmasked, and what the thread owes the core when it cannot tell whether its own device fired.

We are out of time, so I will stop there. Thanks for working through it, and for talking out loud the way you did on the lock audit in particular, that part was clear and well organised. Someone will be in touch about next steps.

## 1. Closures

Adapted from The Rust Programming Language, ch 13.1-13.2, and Rust by Example (Closures, Capturing, As input parameters, Iterators), MIT/Apache-2.0.

A closure is a function you write inline, without a name, that can use the variables around it:

```
let limit = 10;
let over = |x: i32| x > limit;     // reads `limit` from the surrounding scope
println!("{}", over(12));          // true
let add_one = |x| x + 1;           // parameter and return types inferred
```

- Parameters go between bars: `|x|`, `|a, b|`, or `||` for none. The body is one expression or a `{ ... }` block.

- Types are usually inferred. They are fixed by the first use: after `add_one(5)`, calling `add_one(2.5)` is a type error.

- A `fn` item cannot read local variables of the function around it; a closure can. That is the whole point.

Parameters are patterns. Iterator methods often hand a closure a reference. A pattern can unpack it:

```
let temps = [18, 23, 31];
// iter() yields &i32; filter passes a reference to that, so its closure gets &&i32.
let warm: Vec<&i32> = temps.iter().filter(|&&t| t > 20).collect();  // t: i32
let doubled: Vec<i32> = temps.iter().map(|&t| t * 2).collect();       // t: i32
let hot: Vec<usize> = temps.iter().enumerate()
    .filter(|(_, t)| **t > 25).map(|(i, _)| i).collect();              // tuples too
```

## 2. How a closure captures

A closure captures each outside variable it uses in the weakest way its body needs:

Body doesCaptured asWhile the closure is alive

reads the variableshared borrow `&T`others may read it too

changes itmutable borrow `&mut T`nobody else may use it

moves it out (gives it away, drops it)by value `T`it now belongs to the closure

The borrow rules from 03 apply to these captures. A closure that holds `&mut count` blocks every other use of `count` until the closure's last use:

```
let mut count = 0;
let mut bump = || count += 1;   // captures &mut count
bump();
println!("{count}");            // error: bump is used again below
bump();
```

```
error[E0502]: cannot borrow `count` as immutable because it is also borrowed as mutable
  |     let mut bump = || count += 1;
  |                    -- ----- first borrow occurs due to use of `count` in closure
  |                    |
  |                    mutable borrow occurs here
  |     println!("{count}");
  |                ^^^^^ immutable borrow occurs here
  |     bump();
  |     ---- mutable borrow later used here
```

Move the `println!` after the last `bump()` and it compiles: the borrow ends when the closure is last used.

Fields, not whole structs. Since edition 2021, a closure that uses `stats.hits` captures only that field. Other fields of `stats` stay free to use while the closure is alive. (Older editions captured the whole struct.) Part 4 of `capture.rs` shows it.

## 3. `move`

Writing `move` before the bars makes the closure take ownership of every variable it uses, even ones it only reads:

```
let label = String::from("total");
let owned = move || println!("owned: {label}");
owned();
// println!("{label}");  // error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `label`
```

You need `move` when the closure must outlive the variables it uses: a closure returned from a function (section 5), or one sent to another thread (18).

With a `Copy` value (integers, `bool`, `char`, `f64`), `move` copies it into the closure. The closure then works on its own copy, and the outside variable never sees the changes:

```
let mut fuel = 50.0;
let mut burn = move || { fuel -= 10.0; fuel };   // burn owns a copy of fuel
println!("{} {}", burn(), burn());              // 40 30
println!("{fuel}");                             // 50: the outer fuel was never touched
```

## 4. Fn, FnMut and FnOnce

Every closure implements one or more of three traits. Which ones depends on what the body does with its captures, not on whether you wrote `move`:

TraitThe body...Can be called

`Fn`only reads its capturesany number of times, even through a shared reference

`FnMut`changes a capturemany times, but each call needs exclusive (`&mut`) access to the closure

`FnOnce`moves a capture outonce: the first call uses the captured value up

capture-and-traits.png: what the body does picks the trait; Fn sits inside FnMut, inside FnOnce.

The traits nest: every `Fn` closure is also `FnMut` and `FnOnce`, and every `FnMut` is also `FnOnce`. So a function that asks for `FnOnce` accepts anything; one that asks for `Fn` accepts only closures that do not mutate or move out.

A `move` closure that only reads a `String` is still `Fn`: it owns the string, but calling it does not use the string up. `move` changes how captures are stored, not which trait you get.

## 5. Closures as parameters and return values

Take a closure with `impl Fn...` or a generic bound, exactly like any other trait (09):

```
fn call_twice<F: Fn() -> usize>(f: F) -> usize {
    f() + f()
}
fn call_twice_mut<F: FnMut()>(mut f: F) {   // note `mut f`
    f();
    f();
}
fn call_once<F: FnOnce() -> String>(f: F) -> String {
    f()                                    // f is used up here
}
```

Calling an `FnMut` needs `&mut` access to the closure value (its captured state changes), so the parameter or variable that holds it must be declared `mut`. Calling an `FnOnce` consumes it, so it can be called only once in the function body.

Std examples: `Option::unwrap_or_else` takes an `FnOnce` (called at most once); `sort_by_key` takes an `FnMut` (called many times, may count or record).

### Returning a closure

```
fn make_adder(step: i32) -> impl Fn(i32) -> i32 {
    let base = step * 10;
    move |x| x + base + step
}
```

The returned closure is called after `make_adder` has returned, when `base` and `step` no longer exist. Without `move` it would borrow them:

```
error[E0373]: closure may outlive the current function, but it borrows `base`, which is owned by the current function
  |     |x| x + base + step
  |     ^^^     ---- `base` is borrowed here
  |     |
  |     may outlive borrowed value `base`
note: closure is returned here
```

The return type must name the right trait too: a closure whose body changes its captures is `FnMut`, so the function must say `-> impl FnMut(...)`, and the caller must store it in a `let mut` binding to call it.

## 6. The Iterator trait and the three ways to iterate

An iterator is any value that implements one required method:

```
trait Iterator {
    type Item;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item>;   // Some(item), or None when done
    // ...plus dozens of provided methods (map, filter, sum, ...)
}
```

A collection gives you three iterators, which differ in the item type:

CallItem type for a `Vec<T>`The Vec afterwardsSame as

`v.iter()``&T`untouched`for x in &v`

`v.iter_mut()``&mut T`changed in place`for x in &mut v`

`v.into_iter()``T`consumed (moved)`for x in v`

A `for` loop calls `into_iter()` on whatever you give it, which is why `for x in v` consumes `v` while `for x in &v` only borrows it. `iterators.rs` shows all three.

## 7. Adapters are lazy, consumers pull

Adapters take an iterator and return a new one: `map`, `filter`, `take(n)`, `skip(n)`, `take_while`, `zip`, `enumerate`, `rev`, `step_by`, `copied`/`cloned`. Building one runs no closure. Consumers call `next` until they are done: `collect`, `sum`, `count`, `fold`, `any`, `position`, and a `for` loop.

iterator-pipeline.png: requests travel right to left, items left to right, one at a time.

An adapter chain with no consumer does nothing, and the compiler warns you:

```
warning: unused `Map` that must be used
  |     v.iter().map(|s| s * 2);
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  = note: iterators are lazy and do nothing unless consumed
```

When the consumer asks for an item, the request travels back through the chain to the source, and the item comes forward through every stage before the next item is fetched. A `filter` keeps asking for items until one passes. A `take(n)` stops asking once it has handed out `n` items, so the stages before it never see the rest.

`zip` pairs two iterators. It asks the left one first and stops as soon as the left one returns `None` (this order is documented). `skip(n)` drops the first `n` items of the iterator it is called on, and only that one.

`sum` and `collect` can produce several types, so the result type must be written somewhere: `let total: i32 = v.iter().sum();` or `.collect::<Vec<_>>()`.

## 8. What `collect` can build

ItemsTarget typeResult

`T``Vec<T>`a vector

`(K, V)``HashMap<K, V>`a map from pairs

`char``String`a string

`Result<T, E>``Result<Vec<T>, E>``Ok(vec)`, or the first `Err` (stops there)

You cannot collect owned values from references: `v.iter()` yields `&String`, so `.collect::<Vec<String>>()` fails with E0277 ("cannot be built from an iterator over elements of type `&String`"). Either collect references (`Vec<&String>`), copy them (`.cloned()`, or `.copied()` for `Copy` types), or start from `into_iter()` to get owned items.

## 9. Writing your own iterator

Put the state in a struct and implement `next`. Every adapter and consumer then works on it for free:

```
struct Countdown { left: u32 }

impl Iterator for Countdown {
    type Item = u32;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u32> {
        if self.left == 0 {
            None
        } else {
            self.left -= 1;
            Some(self.left + 1)
        }
    }
}
let ticks: Vec<u32> = Countdown { left: 3 }.collect();   // [3, 2, 1]
```

Iterator chains are not slower than loops in an optimised (`--release`) build: the compiler inlines the closures and produces the same machine code as a hand-written loop. Debug builds, which the runner uses, are slower for both.

# capture-and-traits.png

Left, three boxes: "body only reads a capture (captured as &T)", "body changes a capture (captured as &mut T)", "body moves a capture out (captured as T)".
Right, three nested rounded sets: the outer set "FnOnce: can be called at least once" contains "FnMut: can be called many times", which contains "Fn: many times, even shared", with the note "every Fn is also FnMut and FnOnce; every FnMut is also FnOnce".
Arrows: reads goes to Fn, changes goes to FnMut, moves out goes to FnOnce.
Footer: `move` changes HOW captures are stored (owned instead of borrowed), not WHICH trait you get: a `move` closure that only reads is still Fn.

[entity 867 · iterator-pipeline.png · diagram]
# iterator-pipeline.png

Five boxes left to right: `iter()`, `filter(..)`, `map(..)`, `take(2)`, `collect()`.
Dark arrows above point right to left, labelled "next()?" (requests travel right to left). Green arrows below point left to right: "Some(item) travels left to right, one item at a time".
Numbered notes:
1. Adapters (filter, map, take, zip, skip, enumerate, rev) only build a value. Nothing runs yet.
2. A consumer (collect, sum, fold, count, any, a for loop) calls next() and work starts.
3. One item passes the whole chain before the next item is fetched.
4. filter keeps asking the stage before it until an item passes (or None).
5. When take has handed out its count, it stops asking: earlier stages never see the rest.

pub fn apply_n(f: impl Fn(i32) -> i32, n: usize, x: i32) -> i32 {
    let mut v = x;
    for _ in 0..n {
        v = f(v);
    }
    v
}

pub fn compose<F, G>(f: F, g: G) -> impl Fn(i32) -> i32
where
    F: Fn(i32) -> i32,
    G: Fn(i32) -> i32,
{
    move |x| g(f(x)) // move: the closure must own f and g, they outlive this call
}

pub fn keep_words(text: &str, keep: impl Fn(&str) -> bool) -> Vec<String> {
    text.split_whitespace().filter(|w| keep(w)).map(|w| w.to_string()).collect()
}

mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn apply_several_times() {
        assert_eq!(apply_n(|v| v * 2, 3, 1), 8);
        assert_eq!(apply_n(|v| v - 1, 0, 5), 5);
    }

    #[test]
    fn apply_with_captured_step() {
        let step = 7;
        assert_eq!(apply_n(|v| v + step, 2, 0), 14);
    }

        let h = compose(|v| v + 1, |v| v * 10);
        assert_eq!(h(2), 30);

    }

        let h = compose(move |v| v + offset, |v| -v);
        assert_eq!(h(1), -101);
    }

// Reference solution for exercise 3 (Tutor only; never shown to the learner).
pub struct Fib {
    a: u64,
    b: u64,
}

impl Fib {
    pub fn new() -> Fib {
        Fib { a: 0, b: 1 }
    }
}

impl Iterator for Fib {
    type Item = u64;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u64> {
        let out = self.a;
        self.a = self.b;
        self.b += out;
        Some(out)
    }
}

pub fn first_fib(n: usize) -> Vec<u64> {
    Fib::new().take(n).collect()
}

pub fn even_fib_sum_below(limit: u64) -> u64 {
    Fib::new().take_while(|&x| x < limit).filter(|x| x % 2 == 0).sum()
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn next_by_hand() {
        let mut f = Fib::new();
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(0));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(1));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(1));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(2));
    }

    #[test]
    fn first_few() {
        assert_eq!(first_fib(7), vec![0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8]);
        assert!(first_fib(0).is_empty());
    }

    #[test]
    fn even_sum() {
        assert_eq!(even_fib_sum_below(10), 10); // 0 + 2 + 8
        assert_eq!(even_fib_sum_below(100), 44); // + 34
    }
}

How you teach:
- One idea per turn. A few sentences, then hand the turn back.
- Ask before telling: when a question can lead them to the idea, ask it.
- Ground everything in the files in front of them. Point at real lines (POINT), or

- You do not know the assessment questions and must not guess at them. If they ask

- Their notes and past gaps are their own words and earlier results. Use them to aim

## 1. Closures

Adapted from The Rust Programming Language, ch 13.1-13.2, and Rust by Example (Closures, Capturing, As input parameters, Iterators), MIT/Apache-2.0.

A closure is a function you write inline, without a name, that can use the variables around it:

```
let limit = 10;
let over = |x: i32| x > limit;     // reads `limit` from the surrounding scope
println!("{}", over(12));          // true
let add_one = |x| x + 1;           // parameter and return types inferred
```

- Parameters go between bars: `|x|`, `|a, b|`, or `||` for none. The body is one expression or a `{ ... }` block.

- Types are usually inferred. They are fixed by the first use: after `add_one(5)`, calling `add_one(2.5)` is a type error.

- A `fn` item cannot read local variables of the function around it; a closure can. That is the whole point.

Parameters are patterns. Iterator methods often hand a closure a reference. A pattern can unpack it:

```
let temps = [18, 23, 31];
// iter() yields &i32; filter passes a reference to that, so its closure gets &&i32.
let warm: Vec<&i32> = temps.iter().filter(|&&t| t > 20).collect();  // t: i32
let doubled: Vec<i32> = temps.iter().map(|&t| t * 2).collect();       // t: i32
let hot: Vec<usize> = temps.iter().enumerate()
    .filter(|(_, t)| **t > 25).map(|(i, _)| i).collect();              // tuples too
```

## 2. How a closure captures

A closure captures each outside variable it uses in the weakest way its body needs:

Body doesCaptured asWhile the closure is alive

reads the variableshared borrow `&T`others may read it too

changes itmutable borrow `&mut T`nobody else may use it

moves it out (gives it away, drops it)by value `T`it now belongs to the closure

The borrow rules from 03 apply to these captures. A closure that holds `&mut count` blocks every other use of `count` until the closure's last use:

```
let mut count = 0;
let mut bump = || count += 1;   // captures &mut count
bump();
println!("{count}");            // error: bump is used again below
bump();
```

```
error[E0502]: cannot borrow `count` as immutable because it is also borrowed as mutable
  |     let mut bump = || count += 1;
  |                    -- ----- first borrow occurs due to use of `count` in closure
  |                    |
  |                    mutable borrow occurs here
  |     println!("{count}");
  |                ^^^^^ immutable borrow occurs here
  |     bump();
  |     ---- mutable borrow later used here
```

Move the `println!` after the last `bump()` and it compiles: the borrow ends when the closure is last used.

Fields, not whole structs. Since edition 2021, a closure that uses `stats.hits` captures only that field. Other fields of `stats` stay free to use while the closure is alive. (Older editions captured the whole struct.) Part 4 of `capture.rs` shows it.

## 3. `move`

Writing `move` before the bars makes the closure take ownership of every variable it uses, even ones it only reads:

```
let label = String::from("total");
let owned = move || println!("owned: {label}");
owned();
// println!("{label}");  // error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `label`
```

You need `move` when the closure must outlive the variables it uses: a closure returned from a function (section 5), or one sent to another thread (18).

With a `Copy` value (integers, `bool`, `char`, `f64`), `move` copies it into the closure. The closure then works on its own copy, and the outside variable never sees the changes:

```
let mut fuel = 50.0;
let mut burn = move || { fuel -= 10.0; fuel };   // burn owns a copy of fuel
println!("{} {}", burn(), burn());              // 40 30
println!("{fuel}");                             // 50: the outer fuel was never touched
```

## 4. Fn, FnMut and FnOnce

Every closure implements one or more of three traits. Which ones depends on what the body does with its captures, not on whether you wrote `move`:

TraitThe body...Can be called

`Fn`only reads its capturesany number of times, even through a shared reference

`FnMut`changes a capturemany times, but each call needs exclusive (`&mut`) access to the closure

`FnOnce`moves a capture outonce: the first call uses the captured value up

capture-and-traits.png: what the body does picks the trait; Fn sits inside FnMut, inside FnOnce.

The traits nest: every `Fn` closure is also `FnMut` and `FnOnce`, and every `FnMut` is also `FnOnce`. So a function that asks for `FnOnce` accepts anything; one that asks for `Fn` accepts only closures that do not mutate or move out.

A `move` closure that only reads a `String` is still `Fn`: it owns the string, but calling it does not use the string up. `move` changes how captures are stored, not which trait you get.

## 5. Closures as parameters and return values

Take a closure with `impl Fn...` or a generic bound, exactly like any other trait (09):

```
fn call_twice<F: Fn() -> usize>(f: F) -> usize {
    f() + f()
}
fn call_twice_mut<F: FnMut()>(mut f: F) {   // note `mut f`
    f();
    f();
}
fn call_once<F: FnOnce() -> String>(f: F) -> String {
    f()                                    // f is used up here
}
```

Calling an `FnMut` needs `&mut` access to the closure value (its captured state changes), so the parameter or variable that holds it must be declared `mut`. Calling an `FnOnce` consumes it, so it can be called only once in the function body.

Std examples: `Option::unwrap_or_else` takes an `FnOnce` (called at most once); `sort_by_key` takes an `FnMut` (called many times, may count or record).

### Returning a closure

```
fn make_adder(step: i32) -> impl Fn(i32) -> i32 {
    let base = step * 10;
    move |x| x + base + step
}
```

The returned closure is called after `make_adder` has returned, when `base` and `step` no longer exist. Without `move` it would borrow them:

```
error[E0373]: closure may outlive the current function, but it borrows `base`, which is owned by the current function
  |     |x| x + base + step
  |     ^^^     ---- `base` is borrowed here
  |     |
  |     may outlive borrowed value `base`
note: closure is returned here
```

The return type must name the right trait too: a closure whose body changes its captures is `FnMut`, so the function must say `-> impl FnMut(...)`, and the caller must store it in a `let mut` binding to call it.

## 6. The Iterator trait and the three ways to iterate

An iterator is any value that implements one required method:

```
trait Iterator {
    type Item;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item>;   // Some(item), or None when done
    // ...plus dozens of provided methods (map, filter, sum, ...)
}
```

A collection gives you three iterators, which differ in the item type:

CallItem type for a `Vec<T>`The Vec afterwardsSame as

`v.iter()``&T`untouched`for x in &v`

`v.iter_mut()``&mut T`changed in place`for x in &mut v`

`v.into_iter()``T`consumed (moved)`for x in v`

A `for` loop calls `into_iter()` on whatever you give it, which is why `for x in v` consumes `v` while `for x in &v` only borrows it. `iterators.rs` shows all three.

## 7. Adapters are lazy, consumers pull

Adapters take an iterator and return a new one: `map`, `filter`, `take(n)`, `skip(n)`, `take_while`, `zip`, `enumerate`, `rev`, `step_by`, `copied`/`cloned`. Building one runs no closure. Consumers call `next` until they are done: `collect`, `sum`, `count`, `fold`, `any`, `position`, and a `for` loop.

iterator-pipeline.png: requests travel right to left, items left to right, one at a time.

An adapter chain with no consumer does nothing, and the compiler warns you:

```
warning: unused `Map` that must be used
  |     v.iter().map(|s| s * 2);
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  = note: iterators are lazy and do nothing unless consumed
```

When the consumer asks for an item, the request travels back through the chain to the source, and the item comes forward through every stage before the next item is fetched. A `filter` keeps asking for items until one passes. A `take(n)` stops asking once it has handed out `n` items, so the stages before it never see the rest.

`zip` pairs two iterators. It asks the left one first and stops as soon as the left one returns `None` (this order is documented). `skip(n)` drops the first `n` items of the iterator it is called on, and only that one.

`sum` and `collect` can produce several types, so the result type must be written somewhere: `let total: i32 = v.iter().sum();` or `.collect::<Vec<_>>()`.

## 8. What `collect` can build

ItemsTarget typeResult

`T``Vec<T>`a vector

`(K, V)``HashMap<K, V>`a map from pairs

`char``String`a string

`Result<T, E>``Result<Vec<T>, E>``Ok(vec)`, or the first `Err` (stops there)

You cannot collect owned values from references: `v.iter()` yields `&String`, so `.collect::<Vec<String>>()` fails with E0277 ("cannot be built from an iterator over elements of type `&String`"). Either collect references (`Vec<&String>`), copy them (`.cloned()`, or `.copied()` for `Copy` types), or start from `into_iter()` to get owned items.

## 9. Writing your own iterator

Put the state in a struct and implement `next`. Every adapter and consumer then works on it for free:

```
struct Countdown { left: u32 }

impl Iterator for Countdown {
    type Item = u32;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u32> {
        if self.left == 0 {
            None
        } else {
            self.left -= 1;
            Some(self.left + 1)
        }
    }
}
let ticks: Vec<u32> = Countdown { left: 3 }.collect();   // [3, 2, 1]
```

Iterator chains are not slower than loops in an optimised (`--release`) build: the compiler inlines the closures and produces the same machine code as a hand-written loop. Debug builds, which the runner uses, are slower for both.

## 10. Practice

- `ex1_compose.rs`: closures as arguments and a returned closure.

- `ex2_chains.rs`: replace loops with one chain each.

- `ex3_fib.rs`: your own iterator plus `take` and `take_while`.

## 11. Check yourself

- Why does adding `move` to a closure that only reads a `String` not make it FnOnce?

- In `v.iter().map(f).filter(g).collect()`, which closure runs first for the second element?

- When should a function take `impl FnMut` instead of `impl Fn`, and what does the caller have to change?

- What item type does `iter_mut()` give for a `Vec<String>`?

# capture-and-traits.png

Left, three boxes: "body only reads a capture (captured as &T)", "body changes a capture (captured as &mut T)", "body moves a capture out (captured as T)".
Right, three nested rounded sets: the outer set "FnOnce: can be called at least once" contains "FnMut: can be called many times", which contains "Fn: many times, even shared", with the note "every Fn is also FnMut and FnOnce; every FnMut is also FnOnce".
Arrows: reads goes to Fn, changes goes to FnMut, moves out goes to FnOnce.
Footer: `move` changes HOW captures are stored (owned instead of borrowed), not WHICH trait you get: a `move` closure that only reads is still Fn.

[entity 867 · iterator-pipeline.png · diagram]
# iterator-pipeline.png

Five boxes left to right: `iter()`, `filter(..)`, `map(..)`, `take(2)`, `collect()`.
Dark arrows above point right to left, labelled "next()?" (requests travel right to left). Green arrows below point left to right: "Some(item) travels left to right, one item at a time".
Numbered notes:
1. Adapters (filter, map, take, zip, skip, enumerate, rev) only build a value. Nothing runs yet.
2. A consumer (collect, sum, fold, count, any, a for loop) calls next() and work starts.
3. One item passes the whole chain before the next item is fetched.
4. filter keeps asking the stage before it until an item passes (or None).
5. When take has handed out its count, it stops asking: earlier stages never see the rest.

// Reference solution for exercise 3 (Tutor only; never shown to the learner).
pub struct Fib {
    a: u64,
    b: u64,
}

impl Fib {
    pub fn new() -> Fib {
        Fib { a: 0, b: 1 }
    }
}

impl Iterator for Fib {
    type Item = u64;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u64> {
        let out = self.a;
        self.a = self.b;
        self.b += out;
        Some(out)
    }
}

pub fn first_fib(n: usize) -> Vec<u64> {
    Fib::new().take(n).collect()
}

pub fn even_fib_sum_below(limit: u64) -> u64 {
    Fib::new().take_while(|&x| x < limit).filter(|x| x % 2 == 0).sum()
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn next_by_hand() {
        let mut f = Fib::new();
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(0));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(1));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(1));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(2));
    }

    #[test]
    fn first_few() {
        assert_eq!(first_fib(7), vec![0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8]);
        assert!(first_fib(0).is_empty());
    }

    #[test]
    fn even_sum() {
        assert_eq!(even_fib_sum_below(10), 10); // 0 + 2 + 8
        assert_eq!(even_fib_sum_below(100), 44); // + 34
    }
}

## 1. Closures

Adapted from The Rust Programming Language, ch 13.1-13.2, and Rust by Example (Closures, Capturing, As input parameters, Iterators), MIT/Apache-2.0.

A closure is a function you write inline, without a name, that can use the variables around it:

```
let limit = 10;
let over = |x: i32| x > limit;     // reads `limit` from the surrounding scope
println!("{}", over(12));          // true
let add_one = |x| x + 1;           // parameter and return types inferred
```

- Parameters go between bars: `|x|`, `|a, b|`, or `||` for none. The body is one expression or a `{ ... }` block.

- Types are usually inferred. They are fixed by the first use: after `add_one(5)`, calling `add_one(2.5)` is a type error.

- A `fn` item cannot read local variables of the function around it; a closure can. That is the whole point.

Parameters are patterns. Iterator methods often hand a closure a reference. A pattern can unpack it:

```
let temps = [18, 23, 31];
// iter() yields &i32; filter passes a reference to that, so its closure gets &&i32.
let warm: Vec<&i32> = temps.iter().filter(|&&t| t > 20).collect();  // t: i32
let doubled: Vec<i32> = temps.iter().map(|&t| t * 2).collect();       // t: i32
let hot: Vec<usize> = temps.iter().enumerate()
    .filter(|(_, t)| **t > 25).map(|(i, _)| i).collect();              // tuples too
```

## 2. How a closure captures

A closure captures each outside variable it uses in the weakest way its body needs:

Body doesCaptured asWhile the closure is alive

reads the variableshared borrow `&T`others may read it too

changes itmutable borrow `&mut T`nobody else may use it

moves it out (gives it away, drops it)by value `T`it now belongs to the closure

The borrow rules from 03 apply to these captures. A closure that holds `&mut count` blocks every other use of `count` until the closure's last use:

```
let mut count = 0;
let mut bump = || count += 1;   // captures &mut count
bump();
println!("{count}");            // error: bump is used again below
bump();
```

```
error[E0502]: cannot borrow `count` as immutable because it is also borrowed as mutable
  |     let mut bump = || count += 1;
  |                    -- ----- first borrow occurs due to use of `count` in closure
  |                    |
  |                    mutable borrow occurs here
  |     println!("{count}");
  |                ^^^^^ immutable borrow occurs here
  |     bump();
  |     ---- mutable borrow later used here
```

Move the `println!` after the last `bump()` and it compiles: the borrow ends when the closure is last used.

Fields, not whole structs. Since edition 2021, a closure that uses `stats.hits` captures only that field. Other fields of `stats` stay free to use while the closure is alive. (Older editions captured the whole struct.) Part 4 of `capture.rs` shows it.

## 3. `move`

Writing `move` before the bars makes the closure take ownership of every variable it uses, even ones it only reads:

```
let label = String::from("total");
let owned = move || println!("owned: {label}");
owned();
// println!("{label}");  // error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `label`
```

You need `move` when the closure must outlive the variables it uses: a closure returned from a function (section 5), or one sent to another thread (18).

With a `Copy` value (integers, `bool`, `char`, `f64`), `move` copies it into the closure. The closure then works on its own copy, and the outside variable never sees the changes:

```
let mut fuel = 50.0;
let mut burn = move || { fuel -= 10.0; fuel };   // burn owns a copy of fuel
println!("{} {}", burn(), burn());              // 40 30
println!("{fuel}");                             // 50: the outer fuel was never touched
```

## 4. Fn, FnMut and FnOnce

Every closure implements one or more of three traits. Which ones depends on what the body does with its captures, not on whether you wrote `move`:

TraitThe body...Can be called

`Fn`only reads its capturesany number of times, even through a shared reference

`FnMut`changes a capturemany times, but each call needs exclusive (`&mut`) access to the closure

`FnOnce`moves a capture outonce: the first call uses the captured value up

capture-and-traits.png: what the body does picks the trait; Fn sits inside FnMut, inside FnOnce.

The traits nest: every `Fn` closure is also `FnMut` and `FnOnce`, and every `FnMut` is also `FnOnce`. So a function that asks for `FnOnce` accepts anything; one that asks for `Fn` accepts only closures that do not mutate or move out.

A `move` closure that only reads a `String` is still `Fn`: it owns the string, but calling it does not use the string up. `move` changes how captures are stored, not which trait you get.

## 5. Closures as parameters and return values

Take a closure with `impl Fn...` or a generic bound, exactly like any other trait (09):

```
fn call_twice<F: Fn() -> usize>(f: F) -> usize {
    f() + f()
}
fn call_twice_mut<F: FnMut()>(mut f: F) {   // note `mut f`
    f();
    f();
}
fn call_once<F: FnOnce() -> String>(f: F) -> String {
    f()                                    // f is used up here
}
```

Calling an `FnMut` needs `&mut` access to the closure value (its captured state changes), so the parameter or variable that holds it must be declared `mut`. Calling an `FnOnce` consumes it, so it can be called only once in the function body.

Std examples: `Option::unwrap_or_else` takes an `FnOnce` (called at most once); `sort_by_key` takes an `FnMut` (called many times, may count or record).

### Returning a closure

```
fn make_adder(step: i32) -> impl Fn(i32) -> i32 {
    let base = step * 10;
    move |x| x + base + step
}
```

The returned closure is called after `make_adder` has returned, when `base` and `step` no longer exist. Without `move` it would borrow them:

```
error[E0373]: closure may outlive the current function, but it borrows `base`, which is owned by the current function
  |     |x| x + base + step
  |     ^^^     ---- `base` is borrowed here
  |     |
  |     may outlive borrowed value `base`
note: closure is returned here
```

The return type must name the right trait too: a closure whose body changes its captures is `FnMut`, so the function must say `-> impl FnMut(...)`, and the caller must store it in a `let mut` binding to call it.

## 6. The Iterator trait and the three ways to iterate

An iterator is any value that implements one required method:

```
trait Iterator {
    type Item;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item>;   // Some(item), or None when done
    // ...plus dozens of provided methods (map, filter, sum, ...)
}
```

A collection gives you three iterators, which differ in the item type:

CallItem type for a `Vec<T>`The Vec afterwardsSame as

`v.iter()``&T`untouched`for x in &v`

`v.iter_mut()``&mut T`changed in place`for x in &mut v`

`v.into_iter()``T`consumed (moved)`for x in v`

A `for` loop calls `into_iter()` on whatever you give it, which is why `for x in v` consumes `v` while `for x in &v` only borrows it. `iterators.rs` shows all three.

## 7. Adapters are lazy, consumers pull

Adapters take an iterator and return a new one: `map`, `filter`, `take(n)`, `skip(n)`, `take_while`, `zip`, `enumerate`, `rev`, `step_by`, `copied`/`cloned`. Building one runs no closure. Consumers call `next` until they are done: `collect`, `sum`, `count`, `fold`, `any`, `position`, and a `for` loop.

iterator-pipeline.png: requests travel right to left, items left to right, one at a time.

An adapter chain with no consumer does nothing, and the compiler warns you:

```
warning: unused `Map` that must be used
  |     v.iter().map(|s| s * 2);
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  = note: iterators are lazy and do nothing unless consumed
```

When the consumer asks for an item, the request travels back through the chain to the source, and the item comes forward through every stage before the next item is fetched. A `filter` keeps asking for items until one passes. A `take(n)` stops asking once it has handed out `n` items, so the stages before it never see the rest.

`zip` pairs two iterators. It asks the left one first and stops as soon as the left one returns `None` (this order is documented). `skip(n)` drops the first `n` items of the iterator it is called on, and only that one.

`sum` and `collect` can produce several types, so the result type must be written somewhere: `let total: i32 = v.iter().sum();` or `.collect::<Vec<_>>()`.

## 8. What `collect` can build

ItemsTarget typeResult

`T``Vec<T>`a vector

`(K, V)``HashMap<K, V>`a map from pairs

`char``String`a string

`Result<T, E>``Result<Vec<T>, E>``Ok(vec)`, or the first `Err` (stops there)

You cannot collect owned values from references: `v.iter()` yields `&String`, so `.collect::<Vec<String>>()` fails with E0277 ("cannot be built from an iterator over elements of type `&String`"). Either collect references (`Vec<&String>`), copy them (`.cloned()`, or `.copied()` for `Copy` types), or start from `into_iter()` to get owned items.

## 9. Writing your own iterator

Put the state in a struct and implement `next`. Every adapter and consumer then works on it for free:

```
struct Countdown { left: u32 }

impl Iterator for Countdown {
    type Item = u32;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u32> {
        if self.left == 0 {
            None
        } else {
            self.left -= 1;
            Some(self.left + 1)
        }
    }
}
let ticks: Vec<u32> = Countdown { left: 3 }.collect();   // [3, 2, 1]
```

Iterator chains are not slower than loops in an optimised (`--release`) build: the compiler inlines the closures and produces the same machine code as a hand-written loop. Debug builds, which the runner uses, are slower for both.

[entity 861 · capture-and-traits.png · diagram]
# capture-and-traits.png

Left, three boxes: "body only reads a capture (captured as &T)", "body changes a capture (captured as &mut T)", "body moves a capture out (captured as T)".
Right, three nested rounded sets: the outer set "FnOnce: can be called at least once" contains "FnMut: can be called many times", which contains "Fn: many times, even shared", with the note "every Fn is also FnMut and FnOnce; every FnMut is also FnOnce".
Arrows: reads goes to Fn, changes goes to FnMut, moves out goes to FnOnce.
Footer: `move` changes HOW captures are stored (owned instead of borrowed), not WHICH trait you get: a `move` closure that only reads is still Fn.

[entity 867 · iterator-pipeline.png · diagram]
# iterator-pipeline.png

Five boxes left to right: `iter()`, `filter(..)`, `map(..)`, `take(2)`, `collect()`.
Dark arrows above point right to left, labelled "next()?" (requests travel right to left). Green arrows below point left to right: "Some(item) travels left to right, one item at a time".
Numbered notes:
1. Adapters (filter, map, take, zip, skip, enumerate, rev) only build a value. Nothing runs yet.
2. A consumer (collect, sum, fold, count, any, a for loop) calls next() and work starts.
3. One item passes the whole chain before the next item is fetched.
4. filter keeps asking the stage before it until an item passes (or None).
5. When take has handed out its count, it stops asking: earlier stages never see the rest.

pub struct Fib {

## 1. Closures

Adapted from The Rust Programming Language, ch 13.1-13.2, and Rust by Example (Closures, Capturing, As input parameters, Iterators), MIT/Apache-2.0.

A closure is a function you write inline, without a name, that can use the variables around it:

```
let limit = 10;
let over = |x: i32| x > limit;     // reads `limit` from the surrounding scope
println!("{}", over(12));          // true
let add_one = |x| x + 1;           // parameter and return types inferred
```

- Parameters go between bars: `|x|`, `|a, b|`, or `||` for none. The body is one expression or a `{ ... }` block.

- Types are usually inferred. They are fixed by the first use: after `add_one(5)`, calling `add_one(2.5)` is a type error.

- A `fn` item cannot read local variables of the function around it; a closure can. That is the whole point.

Parameters are patterns. Iterator methods often hand a closure a reference. A pattern can unpack it:

```
let temps = [18, 23, 31];
// iter() yields &i32; filter passes a reference to that, so its closure gets &&i32.
let warm: Vec<&i32> = temps.iter().filter(|&&t| t > 20).collect();  // t: i32
let doubled: Vec<i32> = temps.iter().map(|&t| t * 2).collect();       // t: i32
let hot: Vec<usize> = temps.iter().enumerate()
    .filter(|(_, t)| **t > 25).map(|(i, _)| i).collect();              // tuples too
```

## 2. How a closure captures

A closure captures each outside variable it uses in the weakest way its body needs:

Body doesCaptured asWhile the closure is alive

reads the variableshared borrow `&T`others may read it too

changes itmutable borrow `&mut T`nobody else may use it

moves it out (gives it away, drops it)by value `T`it now belongs to the closure

The borrow rules from 03 apply to these captures. A closure that holds `&mut count` blocks every other use of `count` until the closure's last use:

```
let mut count = 0;
let mut bump = || count += 1;   // captures &mut count
bump();
println!("{count}");            // error: bump is used again below
bump();
```

```
error[E0502]: cannot borrow `count` as immutable because it is also borrowed as mutable
  |     let mut bump = || count += 1;
  |                    -- ----- first borrow occurs due to use of `count` in closure
  |                    |
  |                    mutable borrow occurs here
  |     println!("{count}");
  |                ^^^^^ immutable borrow occurs here
  |     bump();
  |     ---- mutable borrow later used here
```

Move the `println!` after the last `bump()` and it compiles: the borrow ends when the closure is last used.

Fields, not whole structs. Since edition 2021, a closure that uses `stats.hits` captures only that field. Other fields of `stats` stay free to use while the closure is alive. (Older editions captured the whole struct.) Part 4 of `capture.rs` shows it.

## 3. `move`

Writing `move` before the bars makes the closure take ownership of every variable it uses, even ones it only reads:

```
let label = String::from("total");
let owned = move || println!("owned: {label}");
owned();
// println!("{label}");  // error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `label`
```

You need `move` when the closure must outlive the variables it uses: a closure returned from a function (section 5), or one sent to another thread (18).

With a `Copy` value (integers, `bool`, `char`, `f64`), `move` copies it into the closure. The closure then works on its own copy, and the outside variable never sees the changes:

```
let mut fuel = 50.0;
let mut burn = move || { fuel -= 10.0; fuel };   // burn owns a copy of fuel
println!("{} {}", burn(), burn());              // 40 30
println!("{fuel}");                             // 50: the outer fuel was never touched
```

## 4. Fn, FnMut and FnOnce

Every closure implements one or more of three traits. Which ones depends on what the body does with its captures, not on whether you wrote `move`:

TraitThe body...Can be called

`Fn`only reads its capturesany number of times, even through a shared reference

`FnMut`changes a capturemany times, but each call needs exclusive (`&mut`) access to the closure

`FnOnce`moves a capture outonce: the first call uses the captured value up

capture-and-traits.png: what the body does picks the trait; Fn sits inside FnMut, inside FnOnce.

The traits nest: every `Fn` closure is also `FnMut` and `FnOnce`, and every `FnMut` is also `FnOnce`. So a function that asks for `FnOnce` accepts anything; one that asks for `Fn` accepts only closures that do not mutate or move out.

A `move` closure that only reads a `String` is still `Fn`: it owns the string, but calling it does not use the string up. `move` changes how captures are stored, not which trait you get.

## 5. Closures as parameters and return values

Take a closure with `impl Fn...` or a generic bound, exactly like any other trait (09):

```
fn call_twice<F: Fn() -> usize>(f: F) -> usize {
    f() + f()
}
fn call_twice_mut<F: FnMut()>(mut f: F) {   // note `mut f`
    f();
    f();
}
fn call_once<F: FnOnce() -> String>(f: F) -> String {
    f()                                    // f is used up here
}
```

Calling an `FnMut` needs `&mut` access to the closure value (its captured state changes), so the parameter or variable that holds it must be declared `mut`. Calling an `FnOnce` consumes it, so it can be called only once in the function body.

Std examples: `Option::unwrap_or_else` takes an `FnOnce` (called at most once); `sort_by_key` takes an `FnMut` (called many times, may count or record).

### Returning a closure

```
fn make_adder(step: i32) -> impl Fn(i32) -> i32 {
    let base = step * 10;
    move |x| x + base + step
}
```

The returned closure is called after `make_adder` has returned, when `base` and `step` no longer exist. Without `move` it would borrow them:

```
error[E0373]: closure may outlive the current function, but it borrows `base`, which is owned by the current function
  |     |x| x + base + step
  |     ^^^     ---- `base` is borrowed here
  |     |
  |     may outlive borrowed value `base`
note: closure is returned here
```

The return type must name the right trait too: a closure whose body changes its captures is `FnMut`, so the function must say `-> impl FnMut(...)`, and the caller must store it in a `let mut` binding to call it.

## 6. The Iterator trait and the three ways to iterate

An iterator is any value that implements one required method:

```
trait Iterator {
    type Item;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item>;   // Some(item), or None when done
    // ...plus dozens of provided methods (map, filter, sum, ...)
}
```

A collection gives you three iterators, which differ in the item type:

CallItem type for a `Vec<T>`The Vec afterwardsSame as

`v.iter()``&T`untouched`for x in &v`

`v.iter_mut()``&mut T`changed in place`for x in &mut v`

`v.into_iter()``T`consumed (moved)`for x in v`

A `for` loop calls `into_iter()` on whatever you give it, which is why `for x in v` consumes `v` while `for x in &v` only borrows it. `iterators.rs` shows all three.

## 7. Adapters are lazy, consumers pull

Adapters take an iterator and return a new one: `map`, `filter`, `take(n)`, `skip(n)`, `take_while`, `zip`, `enumerate`, `rev`, `step_by`, `copied`/`cloned`. Building one runs no closure. Consumers call `next` until they are done: `collect`, `sum`, `count`, `fold`, `any`, `position`, and a `for` loop.

iterator-pipeline.png: requests travel right to left, items left to right, one at a time.

An adapter chain with no consumer does nothing, and the compiler warns you:

```
warning: unused `Map` that must be used
  |     v.iter().map(|s| s * 2);
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  = note: iterators are lazy and do nothing unless consumed
```

When the consumer asks for an item, the request travels back through the chain to the source, and the item comes forward through every stage before the next item is fetched. A `filter` keeps asking for items until one passes. A `take(n)` stops asking once it has handed out `n` items, so the stages before it never see the rest.

`zip` pairs two iterators. It asks the left one first and stops as soon as the left one returns `None` (this order is documented). `skip(n)` drops the first `n` items of the iterator it is called on, and only that one.

`sum` and `collect` can produce several types, so the result type must be written somewhere: `let total: i32 = v.iter().sum();` or `.collect::<Vec<_>>()`.

## 8. What `collect` can build

ItemsTarget typeResult

`T``Vec<T>`a vector

`(K, V)``HashMap<K, V>`a map from pairs

`char``String`a string

`Result<T, E>``Result<Vec<T>, E>``Ok(vec)`, or the first `Err` (stops there)

You cannot collect owned values from references: `v.iter()` yields `&String`, so `.collect::<Vec<String>>()` fails with E0277 ("cannot be built from an iterator over elements of type `&String`"). Either collect references (`Vec<&String>`), copy them (`.cloned()`, or `.copied()` for `Copy` types), or start from `into_iter()` to get owned items.

## 9. Writing your own iterator

Put the state in a struct and implement `next`. Every adapter and consumer then works on it for free:

```
struct Countdown { left: u32 }

impl Iterator for Countdown {
    type Item = u32;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u32> {
        if self.left == 0 {
            None
        } else {
            self.left -= 1;
            Some(self.left + 1)
        }
    }
}
let ticks: Vec<u32> = Countdown { left: 3 }.collect();   // [3, 2, 1]
```

Iterator chains are not slower than loops in an optimised (`--release`) build: the compiler inlines the closures and produces the same machine code as a hand-written loop. Debug builds, which the runner uses, are slower for both.

## 10. Practice

- `ex1_compose.rs`: closures as arguments and a returned closure.

- `ex2_chains.rs`: replace loops with one chain each.

- `ex3_fib.rs`: your own iterator plus `take` and `take_while`.

## 11. Check yourself

- Why does adding `move` to a closure that only reads a `String` not make it FnOnce?

- In `v.iter().map(f).filter(g).collect()`, which closure runs first for the second element?

- When should a function take `impl FnMut` instead of `impl Fn`, and what does the caller have to change?

- What item type does `iter_mut()` give for a `Vec<String>`?

# capture-and-traits.png

Left, three boxes: "body only reads a capture (captured as &T)", "body changes a capture (captured as &mut T)", "body moves a capture out (captured as T)".
Right, three nested rounded sets: the outer set "FnOnce: can be called at least once" contains "FnMut: can be called many times", which contains "Fn: many times, even shared", with the note "every Fn is also FnMut and FnOnce; every FnMut is also FnOnce".
Arrows: reads goes to Fn, changes goes to FnMut, moves out goes to FnOnce.
Footer: `move` changes HOW captures are stored (owned instead of borrowed), not WHICH trait you get: a `move` closure that only reads is still Fn.

[entity 867 · iterator-pipeline.png · diagram]
# iterator-pipeline.png

Five boxes left to right: `iter()`, `filter(..)`, `map(..)`, `take(2)`, `collect()`.
Dark arrows above point right to left, labelled "next()?" (requests travel right to left). Green arrows below point left to right: "Some(item) travels left to right, one item at a time".
Numbered notes:
1. Adapters (filter, map, take, zip, skip, enumerate, rev) only build a value. Nothing runs yet.
2. A consumer (collect, sum, fold, count, any, a for loop) calls next() and work starts.
3. One item passes the whole chain before the next item is fetched.
4. filter keeps asking the stage before it until an item passes (or None).
5. When take has handed out its count, it stops asking: earlier stages never see the rest.

// Reference solution for exercise 3 (Tutor only; never shown to the learner).
pub struct Fib {
    a: u64,
    b: u64,
}

impl Fib {
    pub fn new() -> Fib {
        Fib { a: 0, b: 1 }
    }
}

impl Iterator for Fib {
    type Item = u64;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u64> {
        let out = self.a;
        self.a = self.b;
        self.b += out;
        Some(out)
    }
}

pub fn first_fib(n: usize) -> Vec<u64> {
    Fib::new().take(n).collect()
}

pub fn even_fib_sum_below(limit: u64) -> u64 {
    Fib::new().take_while(|&x| x < limit).filter(|x| x % 2 == 0).sum()
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn next_by_hand() {
        let mut f = Fib::new();
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(0));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(1));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(1));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(2));
    }

    #[test]
    fn first_few() {
        assert_eq!(first_fib(7), vec![0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8]);
        assert!(first_fib(0).is_empty());
    }

    #[test]
    fn even_sum() {
        assert_eq!(even_fib_sum_below(10), 10); // 0 + 2 + 8
        assert_eq!(even_fib_sum_below(100), 44); // + 34
    }
}

## 1. Closures

Adapted from The Rust Programming Language, ch 13.1-13.2, and Rust by Example (Closures, Capturing, As input parameters, Iterators), MIT/Apache-2.0.

A closure is a function you write inline, without a name, that can use the variables around it:

```
let limit = 10;
let over = |x: i32| x > limit;     // reads `limit` from the surrounding scope
println!("{}", over(12));          // true
let add_one = |x| x + 1;           // parameter and return types inferred
```

- Parameters go between bars: `|x|`, `|a, b|`, or `||` for none. The body is one expression or a `{ ... }` block.

- Types are usually inferred. They are fixed by the first use: after `add_one(5)`, calling `add_one(2.5)` is a type error.

- A `fn` item cannot read local variables of the function around it; a closure can. That is the whole point.

Parameters are patterns. Iterator methods often hand a closure a reference. A pattern can unpack it:

```
let temps = [18, 23, 31];
// iter() yields &i32; filter passes a reference to that, so its closure gets &&i32.
let warm: Vec<&i32> = temps.iter().filter(|&&t| t > 20).collect();  // t: i32
let doubled: Vec<i32> = temps.iter().map(|&t| t * 2).collect();       // t: i32
let hot: Vec<usize> = temps.iter().enumerate()
    .filter(|(_, t)| **t > 25).map(|(i, _)| i).collect();              // tuples too
```

## 2. How a closure captures

A closure captures each outside variable it uses in the weakest way its body needs:

Body doesCaptured asWhile the closure is alive

reads the variableshared borrow `&T`others may read it too

changes itmutable borrow `&mut T`nobody else may use it

moves it out (gives it away, drops it)by value `T`it now belongs to the closure

The borrow rules from 03 apply to these captures. A closure that holds `&mut count` blocks every other use of `count` until the closure's last use:

```
let mut count = 0;
let mut bump = || count += 1;   // captures &mut count
bump();
println!("{count}");            // error: bump is used again below
bump();
```

```
error[E0502]: cannot borrow `count` as immutable because it is also borrowed as mutable
  |     let mut bump = || count += 1;
  |                    -- ----- first borrow occurs due to use of `count` in closure
  |                    |
  |                    mutable borrow occurs here
  |     println!("{count}");
  |                ^^^^^ immutable borrow occurs here
  |     bump();
  |     ---- mutable borrow later used here
```

Move the `println!` after the last `bump()` and it compiles: the borrow ends when the closure is last used.

Fields, not whole structs. Since edition 2021, a closure that uses `stats.hits` captures only that field. Other fields of `stats` stay free to use while the closure is alive. (Older editions captured the whole struct.) Part 4 of `capture.rs` shows it.

## 3. `move`

Writing `move` before the bars makes the closure take ownership of every variable it uses, even ones it only reads:

```
let label = String::from("total");
let owned = move || println!("owned: {label}");
owned();
// println!("{label}");  // error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `label`
```

You need `move` when the closure must outlive the variables it uses: a closure returned from a function (section 5), or one sent to another thread (18).

With a `Copy` value (integers, `bool`, `char`, `f64`), `move` copies it into the closure. The closure then works on its own copy, and the outside variable never sees the changes:

```
let mut fuel = 50.0;
let mut burn = move || { fuel -= 10.0; fuel };   // burn owns a copy of fuel
println!("{} {}", burn(), burn());              // 40 30
println!("{fuel}");                             // 50: the outer fuel was never touched
```

## 4. Fn, FnMut and FnOnce

Every closure implements one or more of three traits. Which ones depends on what the body does with its captures, not on whether you wrote `move`:

TraitThe body...Can be called

`Fn`only reads its capturesany number of times, even through a shared reference

`FnMut`changes a capturemany times, but each call needs exclusive (`&mut`) access to the closure

`FnOnce`moves a capture outonce: the first call uses the captured value up

capture-and-traits.png: what the body does picks the trait; Fn sits inside FnMut, inside FnOnce.

The traits nest: every `Fn` closure is also `FnMut` and `FnOnce`, and every `FnMut` is also `FnOnce`. So a function that asks for `FnOnce` accepts anything; one that asks for `Fn` accepts only closures that do not mutate or move out.

A `move` closure that only reads a `String` is still `Fn`: it owns the string, but calling it does not use the string up. `move` changes how captures are stored, not which trait you get.

## 5. Closures as parameters and return values

Take a closure with `impl Fn...` or a generic bound, exactly like any other trait (09):

```
fn call_twice<F: Fn() -> usize>(f: F) -> usize {
    f() + f()
}
fn call_twice_mut<F: FnMut()>(mut f: F) {   // note `mut f`
    f();
    f();
}
fn call_once<F: FnOnce() -> String>(f: F) -> String {
    f()                                    // f is used up here
}
```

Calling an `FnMut` needs `&mut` access to the closure value (its captured state changes), so the parameter or variable that holds it must be declared `mut`. Calling an `FnOnce` consumes it, so it can be called only once in the function body.

Std examples: `Option::unwrap_or_else` takes an `FnOnce` (called at most once); `sort_by_key` takes an `FnMut` (called many times, may count or record).

### Returning a closure

```
fn make_adder(step: i32) -> impl Fn(i32) -> i32 {
    let base = step * 10;
    move |x| x + base + step
}
```

The returned closure is called after `make_adder` has returned, when `base` and `step` no longer exist. Without `move` it would borrow them:

```
error[E0373]: closure may outlive the current function, but it borrows `base`, which is owned by the current function
  |     |x| x + base + step
  |     ^^^     ---- `base` is borrowed here
  |     |
  |     may outlive borrowed value `base`
note: closure is returned here
```

The return type must name the right trait too: a closure whose body changes its captures is `FnMut`, so the function must say `-> impl FnMut(...)`, and the caller must store it in a `let mut` binding to call it.

## 6. The Iterator trait and the three ways to iterate

An iterator is any value that implements one required method:

```
trait Iterator {
    type Item;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item>;   // Some(item), or None when done
    // ...plus dozens of provided methods (map, filter, sum, ...)
}
```

A collection gives you three iterators, which differ in the item type:

CallItem type for a `Vec<T>`The Vec afterwardsSame as

`v.iter()``&T`untouched`for x in &v`

`v.iter_mut()``&mut T`changed in place`for x in &mut v`

`v.into_iter()``T`consumed (moved)`for x in v`

A `for` loop calls `into_iter()` on whatever you give it, which is why `for x in v` consumes `v` while `for x in &v` only borrows it. `iterators.rs` shows all three.

## 7. Adapters are lazy, consumers pull

Adapters take an iterator and return a new one: `map`, `filter`, `take(n)`, `skip(n)`, `take_while`, `zip`, `enumerate`, `rev`, `step_by`, `copied`/`cloned`. Building one runs no closure. Consumers call `next` until they are done: `collect`, `sum`, `count`, `fold`, `any`, `position`, and a `for` loop.

iterator-pipeline.png: requests travel right to left, items left to right, one at a time.

An adapter chain with no consumer does nothing, and the compiler warns you:

```
warning: unused `Map` that must be used
  |     v.iter().map(|s| s * 2);
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  = note: iterators are lazy and do nothing unless consumed
```

When the consumer asks for an item, the request travels back through the chain to the source, and the item comes forward through every stage before the next item is fetched. A `filter` keeps asking for items until one passes. A `take(n)` stops asking once it has handed out `n` items, so the stages before it never see the rest.

`zip` pairs two iterators. It asks the left one first and stops as soon as the left one returns `None` (this order is documented). `skip(n)` drops the first `n` items of the iterator it is called on, and only that one.

`sum` and `collect` can produce several types, so the result type must be written somewhere: `let total: i32 = v.iter().sum();` or `.collect::<Vec<_>>()`.

## 8. What `collect` can build

ItemsTarget typeResult

`T``Vec<T>`a vector

You cannot collect owned values from references: `v.iter()` yields `&String`, so `.collect::<Vec<String>>()` fails with E0277 ("cannot be built from an iterator over elements of type `&String`"). ## 9. Writing your own iterator

Put the state in a struct and implement `next`. Every adapter and consumer then works on it for free:

```
struct Countdown { left: u32 }

impl Iterator for Countdown {
    type Item = u32;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u32> {
        if self.left == 0 {
            None
        } else {
            self.left -= 1;
            Some(self.left + 1)
        }
    }
}
let ticks: Vec<u32> = Countdown { left: 3 }.collect();   // [3, 2, 1]
```

Iterator chains are not slower than loops in an optimised (`--release`) build: the compiler inlines the closures and produces the same machine code as a hand-written loop. Debug builds, which the runner uses, are slower for both.

# capture-and-traits.png

Left, three boxes: "body only reads a capture (captured as &T)", "body changes a capture (captured as &mut T)", "body moves a capture out (captured as T)".
Right, three nested rounded sets: the outer set "FnOnce: can be called at least once" contains "FnMut: can be called many times", which contains "Fn: many times, even shared", with the note "every Fn is also FnMut and FnOnce; every FnMut is also FnOnce".
Arrows: reads goes to Fn, changes goes to FnMut, moves out goes to FnOnce.
Footer: `move` changes HOW captures are stored (owned instead of borrowed), not WHICH trait you get: a `move` closure that only reads is still Fn.

[entity 867 · iterator-pipeline.png · diagram]
# iterator-pipeline.png

Five boxes left to right: `iter()`, `filter(..)`, `map(..)`, `take(2)`, `collect()`.
Dark arrows above point right to left, labelled "next()?" (requests travel right to left). Green arrows below point left to right: "Some(item) travels left to right, one item at a time".
Numbered notes:
1. Adapters (filter, map, take, zip, skip, enumerate, rev) only build a value. Nothing runs yet.
2. A consumer (collect, sum, fold, count, any, a for loop) calls next() and work starts.
3. One item passes the whole chain before the next item is fetched.
4. filter keeps asking the stage before it until an item passes (or None).
5. When take has handed out its count, it stops asking: earlier stages never see the rest.

pub struct Fib {
    a: u64,
    b: u64,
}

impl Fib {
    pub fn new() -> Fib {
        Fib { a: 0, b: 1 }
    }
}

impl Iterator for Fib {
    type Item = u64;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u64> {
        let out = self.a;
        self.a = self.b;
        self.b += out;
        Some(out)
    }
}

pub fn first_fib(n: usize) -> Vec<u64> {
    Fib::new().take(n).collect()
}

pub fn even_fib_sum_below(limit: u64) -> u64 {
    Fib::new().take_while(|&x| x < limit).filter(|x| x % 2 == 0).sum()
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn next_by_hand() {
        let mut f = Fib::new();
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(0));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(1));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(1));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(2));
    }

    #[test]
    fn first_few() {
        assert_eq!(first_fib(7), vec![0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8]);
        assert!(first_fib(0).is_empty());
    }

    #[test]
    fn even_sum() {
        assert_eq!(even_fib_sum_below(10), 10); // 0 + 2 + 8
        assert_eq!(even_fib_sum_below(100), 44); // + 34
    }
}

## 1. Closures

Adapted from The Rust Programming Language, ch 13.1-13.2, and Rust by Example (Closures, Capturing, As input parameters, Iterators), MIT/Apache-2.0.

A closure is a function you write inline, without a name, that can use the variables around it:

```
let limit = 10;
let over = |x: i32| x > limit;     // reads `limit` from the surrounding scope
println!("{}", over(12));          // true
let add_one = |x| x + 1;           // parameter and return types inferred
```

- Parameters go between bars: `|x|`, `|a, b|`, or `||` for none. The body is one expression or a `{ ... }` block.

- Types are usually inferred. They are fixed by the first use: after `add_one(5)`, calling `add_one(2.5)` is a type error.

- A `fn` item cannot read local variables of the function around it; a closure can. That is the whole point.

Parameters are patterns. Iterator methods often hand a closure a reference. A pattern can unpack it:

```
let temps = [18, 23, 31];
// iter() yields &i32; filter passes a reference to that, so its closure gets &&i32.
let warm: Vec<&i32> = temps.iter().filter(|&&t| t > 20).collect();  // t: i32
let doubled: Vec<i32> = temps.iter().map(|&t| t * 2).collect();       // t: i32
let hot: Vec<usize> = temps.iter().enumerate()
    .filter(|(_, t)| **t > 25).map(|(i, _)| i).collect();              // tuples too
```

## 2. How a closure captures

A closure captures each outside variable it uses in the weakest way its body needs:

Body doesCaptured asWhile the closure is alive

reads the variableshared borrow `&T`others may read it too

changes itmutable borrow `&mut T`nobody else may use it

moves it out (gives it away, drops it)by value `T`it now belongs to the closure

The borrow rules from 03 apply to these captures. A closure that holds `&mut count` blocks every other use of `count` until the closure's last use:

```
let mut count = 0;
let mut bump = || count += 1;   // captures &mut count
bump();
println!("{count}");            // error: bump is used again below
bump();
```

```
error[E0502]: cannot borrow `count` as immutable because it is also borrowed as mutable
  |     let mut bump = || count += 1;
  |                    -- ----- first borrow occurs due to use of `count` in closure
  |                    |
  |                    mutable borrow occurs here
  |     println!("{count}");
  |                ^^^^^ immutable borrow occurs here
  |     bump();
  |     ---- mutable borrow later used here
```

Move the `println!` after the last `bump()` and it compiles: the borrow ends when the closure is last used.

Fields, not whole structs. Since edition 2021, a closure that uses `stats.hits` captures only that field. Other fields of `stats` stay free to use while the closure is alive. (Older editions captured the whole struct.) Part 4 of `capture.rs` shows it.

## 3. `move`

Writing `move` before the bars makes the closure take ownership of every variable it uses, even ones it only reads:

```
let label = String::from("total");
let owned = move || println!("owned: {label}");
owned();
// println!("{label}");  // error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `label`
```

You need `move` when the closure must outlive the variables it uses: a closure returned from a function (section 5), or one sent to another thread (18).

With a `Copy` value (integers, `bool`, `char`, `f64`), `move` copies it into the closure. The closure then works on its own copy, and the outside variable never sees the changes:

```
let mut fuel = 50.0;
let mut burn = move || { fuel -= 10.0; fuel };   // burn owns a copy of fuel
println!("{} {}", burn(), burn());              // 40 30
println!("{fuel}");                             // 50: the outer fuel was never touched
```

## 4. Fn, FnMut and FnOnce

Every closure implements one or more of three traits. Which ones depends on what the body does with its captures, not on whether you wrote `move`:

TraitThe body...Can be called

`Fn`only reads its capturesany number of times, even through a shared reference

`FnMut`changes a capturemany times, but each call needs exclusive (`&mut`) access to the closure

`FnOnce`moves a capture outonce: the first call uses the captured value up

capture-and-traits.png: what the body does picks the trait; Fn sits inside FnMut, inside FnOnce.

The traits nest: every `Fn` closure is also `FnMut` and `FnOnce`, and every `FnMut` is also `FnOnce`. So a function that asks for `FnOnce` accepts anything; one that asks for `Fn` accepts only closures that do not mutate or move out.

A `move` closure that only reads a `String` is still `Fn`: it owns the string, but calling it does not use the string up. `move` changes how captures are stored, not which trait you get.

## 5. Closures as parameters and return values

Take a closure with `impl Fn...` or a generic bound, exactly like any other trait (09):

```
fn call_twice<F: Fn() -> usize>(f: F) -> usize {
    f() + f()
}
fn call_twice_mut<F: FnMut()>(mut f: F) {   // note `mut f`
    f();
    f();
}
fn call_once<F: FnOnce() -> String>(f: F) -> String {
    f()                                    // f is used up here
}
```

Calling an `FnMut` needs `&mut` access to the closure value (its captured state changes), so the parameter or variable that holds it must be declared `mut`. Calling an `FnOnce` consumes it, so it can be called only once in the function body.

Std examples: `Option::unwrap_or_else` takes an `FnOnce` (called at most once); `sort_by_key` takes an `FnMut` (called many times, may count or record).

### Returning a closure

```
fn make_adder(step: i32) -> impl Fn(i32) -> i32 {
    let base = step * 10;
    move |x| x + base + step
}
```

The returned closure is called after `make_adder` has returned, when `base` and `step` no longer exist. Without `move` it would borrow them:

```
error[E0373]: closure may outlive the current function, but it borrows `base`, which is owned by the current function
  |     |x| x + base + step
  |     ^^^     ---- `base` is borrowed here
  |     |
  |     may outlive borrowed value `base`
note: closure is returned here
```

The return type must name the right trait too: a closure whose body changes its captures is `FnMut`, so the function must say `-> impl FnMut(...)`, and the caller must store it in a `let mut` binding to call it.

## 6. The Iterator trait and the three ways to iterate

An iterator is any value that implements one required method:

```
trait Iterator {
    type Item;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item>;   // Some(item), or None when done
    // ...plus dozens of provided methods (map, filter, sum, ...)
}
```

A collection gives you three iterators, which differ in the item type:

CallItem type for a `Vec<T>`The Vec afterwardsSame as

`v.iter()``&T`untouched`for x in &v`

`v.iter_mut()``&mut T`changed in place`for x in &mut v`

`v.into_iter()``T`consumed (moved)`for x in v`

A `for` loop calls `into_iter()` on whatever you give it, which is why `for x in v` consumes `v` while `for x in &v` only borrows it. `iterators.rs` shows all three.

## 7. Adapters are lazy, consumers pull

Adapters take an iterator and return a new one: `map`, `filter`, `take(n)`, `skip(n)`, `take_while`, `zip`, `enumerate`, `rev`, `step_by`, `copied`/`cloned`. Building one runs no closure. Consumers call `next` until they are done: `collect`, `sum`, `count`, `fold`, `any`, `position`, and a `for` loop.

iterator-pipeline.png: requests travel right to left, items left to right, one at a time.

An adapter chain with no consumer does nothing, and the compiler warns you:

```
warning: unused `Map` that must be used
  |     v.iter().map(|s| s * 2);
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  = note: iterators are lazy and do nothing unless consumed
```

When the consumer asks for an item, the request travels back through the chain to the source, and the item comes forward through every stage before the next item is fetched. A `filter` keeps asking for items until one passes. A `take(n)` stops asking once it has handed out `n` items, so the stages before it never see the rest.

`zip` pairs two iterators. It asks the left one first and stops as soon as the left one returns `None` (this order is documented). `skip(n)` drops the first `n` items of the iterator it is called on, and only that one.

`sum` and `collect` can produce several types, so the result type must be written somewhere: `let total: i32 = v.iter().sum();` or `.collect::<Vec<_>>()`.

## 8. What `collect` can build

ItemsTarget typeResult

`T``Vec<T>`a vector

`(K, V)``HashMap<K, V>`a map from pairs

`char``String`a string

`Result<T, E>``Result<Vec<T>, E>``Ok(vec)`, or the first `Err` (stops there)

You cannot collect owned values from references: `v.iter()` yields `&String`, so `.collect::<Vec<String>>()` fails with E0277 ("cannot be built from an iterator over elements of type `&String`"). Either collect references (`Vec<&String>`), copy them (`.cloned()`, or `.copied()` for `Copy` types), or start from `into_iter()` to get owned items.

## 9. Writing your own iterator

Put the state in a struct and implement `next`. Every adapter and consumer then works on it for free:

```
struct Countdown { left: u32 }

impl Iterator for Countdown {
    type Item = u32;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u32> {
        if self.left == 0 {
            None
        } else {
            self.left -= 1;
            Some(self.left + 1)
        }
    }
}
let ticks: Vec<u32> = Countdown { left: 3 }.collect();   // [3, 2, 1]
```

Iterator chains are not slower than loops in an optimised (`--release`) build: the compiler inlines the closures and produces the same machine code as a hand-written loop. Debug builds, which the runner uses, are slower for both.

## 10. Practice

- `ex1_compose.rs`: closures as arguments and a returned closure.

- `ex2_chains.rs`: replace loops with one chain each.

- `ex3_fib.rs`: your own iterator plus `take` and `take_while`.

## 11. Check yourself

- Why does adding `move` to a closure that only reads a `String` not make it FnOnce?

- In `v.iter().map(f).filter(g).collect()`, which closure runs first for the second element?

- When should a function take `impl FnMut` instead of `impl Fn`, and what does the caller have to change?

- What item type does `iter_mut()` give for a `Vec<String>`?

[entity 861 · capture-and-traits.png · diagram]
# capture-and-traits.png

Left, three boxes: "body only reads a capture (captured as &T)", "body changes a capture (captured as &mut T)", "body moves a capture out (captured as T)".
Right, three nested rounded sets: the outer set "FnOnce: can be called at least once" contains "FnMut: can be called many times", which contains "Fn: many times, even shared", with the note "every Fn is also FnMut and FnOnce; every FnMut is also FnOnce".
Arrows: reads goes to Fn, changes goes to FnMut, moves out goes to FnOnce.
Footer: `move` changes HOW captures are stored (owned instead of borrowed), not WHICH trait you get: a `move` closure that only reads is still Fn.

[entity 867 · iterator-pipeline.png · diagram]
# iterator-pipeline.png

Five boxes left to right: `iter()`, `filter(..)`, `map(..)`, `take(2)`, `collect()`.
Dark arrows above point right to left, labelled "next()?" (requests travel right to left). Green arrows below point left to right: "Some(item) travels left to right, one item at a time".
Numbered notes:
1. Adapters (filter, map, take, zip, skip, enumerate, rev) only build a value. Nothing runs yet.
2. A consumer (collect, sum, fold, count, any, a for loop) calls next() and work starts.
3. One item passes the whole chain before the next item is fetched.
4. filter keeps asking the stage before it until an item passes (or None).
5. When take has handed out its count, it stops asking: earlier stages never see the rest.

pub fn apply_n(f: impl Fn(i32) -> i32, n: usize, x: i32) -> i32 {
    let mut v = x;
    for _ in 0..n {
        v = f(v);
    }

pub fn compose<F, G>(f: F, g: G) -> impl Fn(i32) -> i32
where
    F: Fn(i32) -> i32,
    G: Fn(i32) -> i32,
{
    move |x| g(f(x)) // move: the closure must own f and g, they outlive this call
}

// Reference solution for exercise 3 (Tutor only; never shown to the learner).
pub struct Fib {
    a: u64,
    b: u64,
}

impl Fib {
    pub fn new() -> Fib {
        Fib { a: 0, b: 1 }
    }
}

impl Iterator for Fib {
    type Item = u64;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u64> {
        let out = self.a;
        self.a = self.b;
        self.b += out;
        Some(out)
    }
}

pub fn first_fib(n: usize) -> Vec<u64> {
    Fib::new().take(n).collect()
}

pub fn even_fib_sum_below(limit: u64) -> u64 {
    Fib::new().take_while(|&x| x < limit).filter(|x| x % 2 == 0).sum()
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn next_by_hand() {
        let mut f = Fib::new();
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(0));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(1));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(1));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(2));
    }

    #[test]
    fn first_few() {
        assert_eq!(first_fib(7), vec![0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8]);
        assert!(first_fib(0).is_empty());
    }

    #[test]
    fn even_sum() {
        assert_eq!(even_fib_sum_below(10), 10); // 0 + 2 + 8
        assert_eq!(even_fib_sum_below(100), 44); // + 34
    }
}
