WHAT A COMPLETE ANSWER TO THE STAGE ABOVE LOOKS LIKE:
Lockdep: &st->lock was taken in hard IRQ context ({IN-HARDIRQ-W}, registered at qadc_hardirq via _raw_spin_lock) and is now taken by cat/731 in latest_show with interrupts enabled (HE1, {HARDIRQ-ON-W}), reading /sys/.../latest through sysfs (dev_attr_show, seq_read_iter, ksys_read). Usage {?...}: used in IRQ and with IRQs on. The deadlock: latest_show holds st->lock with spin_lock(); RDY fires on the same CPU; qadc_hardirq spins with interrupts off waiting for a lock that the interrupted task can never release: that CPU is dead, and soon the board. The README says the GPIO bank interrupt is handled on CPU0, so it only happens when the reader runs on CPU0 inside a few instructions of critical section, which is why tests pass and units hang rarely (this report came from cat on CPU1: lockdep flags the pattern without the deadlock). Every place st->lock is taken: qadc_hardirq spin_lock (fine, IRQs are off in a hard handler); qadc_irq_thread spin_lock_irqsave (fine); latest_show spin_lock (wrong: spin_lock_irqsave, or spin_lock_irq since it always runs with IRQs on); qadc_wdog_expired spin_lock: the timer callback runs in softirq, which a hard IRQ can interrupt on the same CPU, so it needs spin_lock_irqsave too (lockdep stopped at the first report and never got there). stats_show takes no lock: samples is a u64, and a 64-bit read is not atomic on 32-bit ARM, so a torn 64-bit read is possible; take the lock (or use u64_stats_sync). A mutex is not an answer while the hard handler takes the lock. Better still, remove the hard handler's use of st->lock (see the next stages); then the remaining users decide the variant. irqsave vs irq: irqsave restores the previous state, so it is safe from any context; irq is fine where IRQs are known to be on.

NEVER say any of these, in any wording::
  - hidden in a helper
  - uncontended fast path
  - precompute the period
  - spins with interrupts off
  - torn 64-bit read
  - runs in softirq

You may point at where to look. You may not name the mechanism or the fix. If your sentence would let them answer without thinking, rewrite it.

Haan, yeh second report ka essence ye hai ki `latest_show` sysfs read path me lockdep / might-sleep warning aa raha hai because it’s taking a lock in a context where sleeping/locking order unsafe ho sakta hai. `latest_show` `/sys/.../latest` attribute ka `.show` handler hai in `qadc-sysfs.c`, aur woh likely `st->lock` ya `cfg_lock` ke around sample/ring state read karta hai. Debug kernel me lockdep isliye print karta hai because sysfs read can run concurrently with IRQ thread / reset work, aur agar show handler spinlock ke andar koi slow operation ya nested lock order hit karta hai, it triggers.

What can go wrong on production: nothing gets printed, but the bug can still show up as missed samples, stale `latest` reads, or a hard-to-reproduce deadlock/starvation if `latest_show` races with the IRQ thread updating the ring or with reset work reconfiguring the ADC. Since tools/qadc-mon.sh polls both devices every 100 ms, it can increase the probability of hitting the race, especially on the shared IRQ line.

Fix I’d do: make `latest_show` a pure snapshot path. Take only the minimal spinlock needed to copy the already-stored sample fields into locals, then release it before formatting to `buf`. No I2C, no sleeping, no mutex under spinlock. If the current code grabs `cfg_lock` from sysfs and then touches ring state or vice versa, I’d split that: use `cfg_lock` only for ODR/config access, and `st->lock` only for ring/counter snapshot. Also keep lock ordering consistent everywhere, i.e. never take `st->lock` while holding `cfg_lock` in one path and the opposite order in another. The relevant files are `qadc-sysfs.c` for `latest_show`, and `qadc-core.c` for the IRQ thread / reset worker that updates the same state.

WHAT A COMPLETE ANSWER TO THE STAGE ABOVE LOOKS LIKE:
/proc/interrupts: line 63 (gpio-mxc 17, Level, shared by 1-0048 and 1-0049) went from 44,792,380 to 45,036,343, 243,963 interrupts in 10 s for 2,000 conversions (two ADCs at 100 Hz): about 122 per conversion, all on CPU0. The capture shows why: RDY stays low until a read reaches the last DATA byte, about 300 us per I2C read, and the hard handler is entered about every 3.83 us for as long as it is low (82 entries in 317.2 us, 162 in 621.9 us). Cause: the line is level-triggered and the IRQ is requested without IRQF_ONESHOT. handle_level_irq masks the line, runs both primary handlers (both return IRQ_WAKE_THREAD), and unmasks the line at once because no oneshot thread is pending; the level is still asserted, so it fires again until a thread has done the I2C read. The comment shows the kernel refused a NULL primary handler without ONESHOT exactly to prevent this, and the driver went around the check with a dummy primary. Shared line: every interrupt wakes both threads, and qadc_irq_thread reads without checking STATUS and always returns IRQ_HANDLED, so each driver reads its ADC on the other ADC's conversions too; storm interrupts during a thread's run set IRQTF_RUNTHREAD again, so threads run again: samples went up 5,002 (0x48) and 4,002 (0x49) for 1,000 conversions each, and the capture shows repeated identical bytes and reads after RDY is already high. A 0x49 conversion keeps the line low twice as long because 0x48's thread reads first and the bus serialises. Both irqs counters rise by exactly the line count. Fix: IRQF_SHARED | IRQF_ONESHOT (every sharer must agree, or request fails with Flags mismatch) with a NULL primary or one that only stores a timestamp; in the thread, one 9-byte read from STATUS; if DRDY is clear return IRQ_NONE, else push the sample. IRQ_NONE also lets the spurious-IRQ detector disable a stuck line (nobody cared) instead of storming forever.

NEVER say any of these, in any wording::
  - hidden in a helper
  - uncontended fast path
  - precompute the period
  - unmasks the line at once
  - without checking STATUS
  - nobody cared

messages.content:
Nahi, main is patch ko approve nahi karunga as-is.

Jo results aapne diye, unse clear hai ki interrupt side wala issue improve hua hai: 10 s me 2001 IRQs aur dono ADCs ke sample counts ka 2001 rise hona matlab shared RDY line par each conversion pe thread wake ho raha hai, aur sampling path ka functional part chal raha hai. Yeh expected direction hai for 1000 Hz per ADC + shared line.

Lekin unbind loop warnings serious hain. `preempt_count = 101` + `call_timer_fn` backtrace ka matlab timer callback fire ho raha hai while teardown path me something still live hai. Aur `devres_release_group` ke time "freeing active timer" complaint tells me `qadc_remove()` ya devm teardown order wrong hai: timer/work/IRQ ka lifetime device release ke saath safely quiesce nahi ho raha. Iska production impact real hai — unbind/remove ke baad use-after-free, stray timer callback, ya delayed work hitting freed `struct qadc`.

Stall test ka FAIL bhi important hai: only `1-0048` ko stop karne par resets 0->0 ka matlab watchdog recovery us ADC ke missing conversions par trigger nahi hua, at least as observed by the test. So watchdog path either armed nahi hai, or `qadc_wdog_kick()` / expiry/reset logic single-device stall ko detect nahi kar raha in the patched version.

Main `remove()` ko is driver ke liye is order me likhta:
1. First, prevent new IRQs and new work from entering: `disable_irq(client->irq)`/`disable_irq_nosync()` as appropriate, or otherwise stop the threaded handler from re-arming the watchdog.
2. Delete the watchdog timer synchronously: `del_timer_sync(&st->wdog)`.
3. Cancel pending reset work: `cancel_work_sync(&st->reset_work)`.
4. Then free the IRQ: `free_irq(client->irq, st)` if not fully devm-managed.
5. Only after all asynchronous callbacks are gone, let devres release the rest.

If the driver is using devm for IRQ allocation, I’d still keep explicit quiesce in `remove()` because devm cleanup order alone is clearly not enough here.

On the hard-handler vs thread split, I’d keep it strict:
- Hard handler (`qadc_hardirq()`): minimal, non-sleeping bookkeeping only — timestamp, irq counter, maybe arm a defer mechanism. No I2C, no mutex, no timer teardown, no reset.
- Thread (`qadc_irq_thread()`): do the sleeping I2C read, parse samples, update ring buffer, and kick watchdog at the end if that’s the design.
- Watchdog/reset work: only in timer/workqueue context, never from hardirq.

So my line is: anything that can sleep or can race with teardown goes to thread/work; hardirq stays tiny. Given the active-timer warning and the failed stall test, this patch is not yet safe enough for production.

Relevant places are `qadc-core.c` around `qadc_hardirq()`, `qadc_irq_thread()`, watchdog timer/work (`qadc_wdog_expired()`, `qadc_reset_work()`), and `qadc_remove()`; plus `qadc-sysfs.c` only if the patch touched sysfs locking.

move_object.question_summary: Mid-level candidate on a qadc ADC driver: interrupt context, locking and teardown. They reasoned competently about driver structure from the source and named IRQF_ONESHOT with IRQF_SHARED as the storm fix, but across all four stages they never worked from the attached logs, patch or captures, saying they could not see them, so almost every specific finding was missed. Next interviewer should check whether attachment reading was a tooling problem or an approach problem.
move_object.report_notes:
Across the whole question the candidate worked from the source and from general kernel knowledge, never from the attached evidence. At every stage they either said the file was not visible or paraphrased what they expected it to say, so not one line, counter or lockdep state was ever quoted: not preempt_count 10001 or irqs_disabled 128, not mutex.c:585, not the HARDIRQ-ON-W to IN-HARDIRQ-W state on cfg_lock, not cat/731 and HE1, not 243,963 interrupts in 10 s or the 82 and 162 handler entries per conversion, not the ODEBUG free active timer_list from devres_release_group, not preempt_count 101 with call_timer_fn.

What they did demonstrate: a correct mental model of the hard handler and thread split, correct identification that a level-low shared line stays asserted until the data read completes and therefore re-fires, and the central correction of IRQF_SHARED plus IRQF_ONESHOT with the DRDY release tied to the final DATA byte. That was the strongest moment of the interview. They also refused to approve the teammate's patch and read the headline numbers sensibly, correctly concluding the interrupt side was now behaving at 2,001 per 10 s.

On the final stage the diagnosis went wrong in a way that matters. They read the 2215 splat as a teardown race and explained it as the watchdog firing during unbind, when the log is plainly from the stall test and the actual cause is the patch converting st->lock from a spinlock to a mutex, which qadc_wdog_expired then takes from a timer callback, with lockdep's SOFTIRQ-ON-W to IN-SOFTIRQ-W report naming it. Pointed directly at the function and told it was nowhere near an unbind, they correctly said timer callback and cannot sleep, but still did not connect it to the mutex conversion or to the lock at all, instead inventing nested timer manipulation inside the callback that the patch does not contain. Their proposed fix, callback only schedules work, happens to point in a useful direction but was reached without reading what was broken.

Teardown ordering was partly right by instinct (quiesce before release, explicit quiesce in remove rather than trusting devres) but they did not identify that the devm IRQ is freed only after remove returns, so the thread can re-arm the timer after the sync delete, nor that cancel_work_sync before deleting the timer is the wrong order, nor that disable_irq would wrongly affect the other ADC on the shared line. They also missed, across both the storm stage and the final stage, that the threads return IRQ_HANDLED without consulting STATUS, which is why each ADC's watchdog is kicked by the other and why the single-device stall test behaves as it does; they noted the FAIL but attributed it vaguely to the watchdog not being armed. The stale timestamp now taken in the thread was not mentioned.

Prompting required was heavy: four stages, repeated requests to quote a line or number that went unmet, and a direct pointer to the function and timeframe on the last stage that still did not move the answer to the lock. Net: sound general kernel instincts and one solid correct call on IRQF_ONESHOT, but no demonstrated ability to debug from the evidence in front of them, which is the core of the job.
move_object.response: That is time, so let us stop there. You have the context right: it is a timer callback, and sleeping is not allowed there. The part that did not land is what specifically the patch made that callback do inside that context, and it is sitting right in the diff rather than in the reset machinery. One broader note from the whole session: a lot of your reasoning came from the source and from general principle rather than from the logs and captures attached to each stage, and the specific numbers and lockdep states in them were where most of the answers lived. Worth checking whether those were genuinely not rendering for you, because that is the kind of thing to flag early. Thanks for working through it, that is the end of the interview.

move_object.report_notes:
Asked: how they would locate where 300 POs submitted since Friday are stuck in approval, with a snapshot of POAPPRV activity statuses and Friday's change log provided.

The candidate's first answer was a plausible investigation order in the abstract (compare PO rows against workflow item errors, trace AME output on a single PO, check the owner attribute, check mailer and engine logs) but it did not use the evidence already in front of them, and it kept the notification mailer in play as a live thread. After one prompt pointing them back at the snapshot, they correctly identified that all 300 sit in ERROR at GET_NEXT_APPROVER and explicitly parked the mailer as secondary. That is the right conclusion but it was prompted, not volunteered, and they did not articulate why the ERROR status rules out the worklist and mailer explanations rather than simply deprioritising them.

Not demonstrated: any connection between the errored approver step and Friday's AME rule deployment or the 12 new cost centres; no mention of testing the rule on a single PO before retrying in bulk, the Workflow Background Process, or monitoring for errored approval items. No red flags: they never proposed touching PO or workflow tables directly, and did not reach for a mailer restart as a fix.

Overall: sound instincts on where to look, but slow to read the diagnostic data supplied and did not get to a diagnosis within the time. Assessment limited to the opening stage.
move_object.response: That's the right read, and parking the mailer is the correct call. We're out of time on this one, so let's stop there. Thanks, you got to the workflow engine as the primary thread, which is where this one lives. Appreciate you talking it through.

move_object.report_notes:
Scenario: 300 purchase orders In Process, nothing in worklists, after a Friday AME rule change.

Diagnosis: opened with a generic checklist (workflow tables, AME trace, mailer, engine logs) and needed two pushes before actually reading the data in front of them. Once pushed, read it correctly: all 300 errored at the approver resolution activity, which means no notification was ever created, so the worklist and the mailer are both red herrings. Linked it to the new cost centres without being handed the link.

Remediation: strong here. Immediately identified the missing cost centre owner data and gave the right menu of fixes (load the owner data, correct the attribute source, or a fallback approver). Needed one push to convert that into an ordered plan, then produced a sound one: seed one cost centre, rerun a single PO, confirm the approver list resolves, then bulk load and retry the rest. Never once suggested updating PO or workflow tables directly, which is the main trap in this scenario.

Final stage: asked how to clear the remaining 299 and what to watch. Answered correctly in a single line: bulk reprocess the workflow items, watch the approver activity move through to notified, and watch for fresh application errors. Did not name the retry mechanism explicitly or mention the background process for deferred activities, but the shape of the answer was right and the monitoring instinct was sound.

Overall: the technical judgement is there and the safety instincts are good. The weakness is communication and initiative: answers were consistently telegraphic, and the key reasoning at each stage arrived only after a prompt rather than being offered. They also never named who owns the data fix or how the AME rule gets validated beyond the one test PO, which matters at senior level on production support. No hints were needed.
move_object.response: That is the right shape, and watching for fresh errors on the retry rather than assuming the data fix covered every case is the correct instinct. That is where I will leave it. Thanks for working through it: your diagnosis was sound and you stayed well away from touching the underlying tables, which is the thing that usually goes wrong in this scenario. One piece of feedback to take away: say more. Most of your reasoning was correct but it only came out when I pushed for it, and on production support the person on the bridge call needs to hear it unprompted. Thanks for your time today.

Diagnosis: sound but led. Opened with a generic checklist (workflow tables, AME trace, mailer, logs) and needed two pushes to actually read the data in front of them. Once pushed, correctly identified all 300 in ERROR at the approver resolution activity, dismissed the mailer and worklist as irrelevant because no notification exists before that point, and tied the failure to Friday's AME rule plus the new cost centres.

Remediation: strong instincts on the fix menu (populate owner data, correct the attribute source, or a fallback approver) and a sensible running order after one push: seed one cost centre, rerun one PO, verify the approver list, then bulk load and retry. Never proposed updating PO or workflow tables directly, and when challenged drew the right distinction between retrying the errored workflow item and resubmitting the documents, which is the key senior judgement in this scenario.

Final stage: weakest part. On the bulk retry they described watching for status transitions and new errors, but when presented with items neither errored nor notified they first blamed the mailer, which contradicted their own earlier reasoning that no notification exists yet. After an explicit redirect to the activity state they recognised the activity had not run, and only on a further push named the background workflow process and checking it is running. They got there without the formal hint, but with three successive pulls.

Overall: the technical model is correct and the production instincts are safe, but the candidate consistently waited to be steered rather than driving the diagnosis, and answers were so compressed that ownership, validation beyond a single test PO, and verification sweeps were never volunteered. Competent senior-adjacent performance with a real gap in independent structuring and communication.

Overall you landed on the right diagnosis and, importantly, the right remediation: retrying the workflow items rather than resubmitting the documents, and never touching the underlying tables. The main thing I would push you on is driving more of that reasoning yourself and talking through it out loud, since several of the key steps only came out after I nudged. Thanks for working through it with me, that is everything from my side.

THIS SUB-MODULE: Closures and iterators. ITS SKILLS:
  F4: closures and capture (Fn, FnMut, FnOnce, move)
  F5: iterators and adapters (lazy, consuming, iter/iter_mut/into_iter)

THE FILES THEY CAN SEE (code shown with line numbers):
[entity 882 · Lesson · lesson]
## 1. Closures

Adapted from The Rust Programming Language, ch 13.1-13.2, and Rust by Example (Closures, Capturing, As input parameters, Iterators), MIT/Apache-2.0.

A closure is a function you write inline, without a name, that can use the variables around it:

```
let limit = 10;
let over = |x: i32| x > limit;     // reads `limit` from the surrounding scope
println!("{}", over(12));          // true
let add_one = |x| x + 1;           // parameter and return types inferred
```

- Parameters go between bars: `|x|`, `|a, b|`, or `||` for none. The body is one expression or a `{ ... }` block.

- Types are usually inferred. They are fixed by the first use: after `add_one(5)`, calling `add_one(2.5)` is a type error.

- A `fn` item cannot read local variables of the function around it; a closure can. That is the whole point.

Parameters are patterns. Iterator methods often hand a closure a reference. A pattern can unpack it:

```
let temps = [18, 23, 31];
// iter() yields &i32; filter passes a reference to that, so its closure gets &&i32.
let warm: Vec<&i32> = temps.iter().filter(|&&t| t > 20).collect();  // t: i32
let doubled: Vec<i32> = temps.iter().map(|&t| t * 2).collect();       // t: i32
let hot: Vec<usize> = temps.iter().enumerate()
    .filter(|(_, t)| **t > 25).map(|(i, _)| i).collect();              // tuples too
```

## 2. How a closure captures

A closure captures each outside variable it uses in the weakest way its body needs:

Body doesCaptured asWhile the closure is alive

reads the variableshared borrow `&T`others may read it too

changes itmutable borrow `&mut T`nobody else may use it

moves it out (gives it away, drops it)by value `T`it now belongs to the closure

The borrow rules from 03 apply to these captures. A closure that holds `&mut count` blocks every other use of `count` until the closure's last use:

```
let mut count = 0;
let mut bump = || count += 1;   // captures &mut count
bump();
println!("{count}");            // error: bump is used again below
bump();
```

```
error[E0502]: cannot borrow `count` as immutable because it is also borrowed as mutable
  |     let mut bump = || count += 1;
  |                    -- ----- first borrow occurs due to use of `count` in closure
  |                    |
  |                    mutable borrow occurs here
  |     println!("{count}");
  |                ^^^^^ immutable borrow occurs here
  |     bump();
  |     ---- mutable borrow later used here
```

Move the `println!` after the last `bump()` and it compiles: the borrow ends when the closure is last used.

Fields, not whole structs. Since edition 2021, a closure that uses `stats.hits` captures only that field. Other fields of `stats` stay free to use while the closure is alive. (Older editions captured the whole struct.) Part 4 of `capture.rs` shows it.

## 3. `move`

Writing `move` before the bars makes the closure take ownership of every variable it uses, even ones it only reads:

```
let label = String::from("total");
let owned = move || println!("owned: {label}");
owned();
// println!("{label}");  // error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `label`
```

You need `move` when the closure must outlive the variables it uses: a closure returned from a function (section 5), or one sent to another thread (18).

With a `Copy` value (integers, `bool`, `char`, `f64`), `move` copies it into the closure. The closure then works on its own copy, and the outside variable never sees the changes:

```
let mut fuel = 50.0;
let mut burn = move || { fuel -= 10.0; fuel };   // burn owns a copy of fuel
println!("{} {}", burn(), burn());              // 40 30
println!("{fuel}");                             // 50: the outer fuel was never touched
```

## 4. Fn, FnMut and FnOnce

Every closure implements one or more of three traits. Which ones depends on what the body does with its captures, not on whether you wrote `move`:

TraitThe body...Can be called

`Fn`only reads its capturesany number of times, even through a shared reference

`FnMut`changes a capturemany times, but each call needs exclusive (`&mut`) access to the closure

`FnOnce`moves a capture outonce: the first call uses the captured value up

capture-and-traits.png: what the body does picks the trait; Fn sits inside FnMut, inside FnOnce.

The traits nest: every `Fn` closure is also `FnMut` and `FnOnce`, and every `FnMut` is also `FnOnce`. So a function that asks for `FnOnce` accepts anything; one that asks for `Fn` accepts only closures that do not mutate or move out.

A `move` closure that only reads a `String` is still `Fn`: it owns the string, but calling it does not use the string up. `move` changes how captures are stored, not which trait you get.

## 5. Closures as parameters and return values

Take a closure with `impl Fn...` or a generic bound, exactly like any other trait (09):

```
fn call_twice<F: Fn() -> usize>(f: F) -> usize {
    f() + f()
}
fn call_twice_mut<F: FnMut()>(mut f: F) {   // note `mut f`
    f();
    f();
}
fn call_once<F: FnOnce() -> String>(f: F) -> String {
    f()                                    // f is used up here
}
```

Calling an `FnMut` needs `&mut` access to the closure value (its captured state changes), so the parameter or variable that holds it must be declared `mut`. Calling an `FnOnce` consumes it, so it can be called only once in the function body.

Std examples: `Option::unwrap_or_else` takes an `FnOnce` (called at most once); `sort_by_key` takes an `FnMut` (called many times, may count or record).

### Returning a closure

```
fn make_adder(step: i32) -> impl Fn(i32) -> i32 {
    let base = step * 10;
    move |x| x + base + step
}
```

The returned closure is called after `make_adder` has returned, when `base` and `step` no longer exist. Without `move` it would borrow them:

```
error[E0373]: closure may outlive the current function, but it borrows `base`, which is owned by the current function
  |     |x| x + base + step
  |     ^^^     ---- `base` is borrowed here
  |     |
  |     may outlive borrowed value `base`
note: closure is returned here
```

The return type must name the right trait too: a closure whose body changes its captures is `FnMut`, so the function must say `-> impl FnMut(...)`, and the caller must store it in a `let mut` binding to call it.

## 6. The Iterator trait and the three ways to iterate

An iterator is any value that implements one required method:

```
trait Iterator {
    type Item;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item>;   // Some(item), or None when done
    // ...plus dozens of provided methods (map, filter, sum, ...)
}
```

A collection gives you three iterators, which differ in the item type:

CallItem type for a `Vec<T>`The Vec afterwardsSame as

`v.iter()``&T`untouched`for x in &v`

`v.iter_mut()``&mut T`changed in place`for x in &mut v`

`v.into_iter()``T`consumed (moved)`for x in v`

A `for` loop calls `into_iter()` on whatever you give it, which is why `for x in v` consumes `v` while `for x in &v` only borrows it. `iterators.rs` shows all three.

## 7. Adapters are lazy, consumers pull

Adapters take an iterator and return a new one: `map`, `filter`, `take(n)`, `skip(n)`, `take_while`, `zip`, `enumerate`, `rev`, `step_by`, `copied`/`cloned`. Building one runs no closure. Consumers call `next` until they are done: `collect`, `sum`, `count`, `fold`, `any`, `position`, and a `for` loop.

iterator-pipeline.png: requests travel right to left, items left to right, one at a time.

An adapter chain with no consumer does nothing, and the compiler warns you:

```
warning: unused `Map` that must be used
  |     v.iter().map(|s| s * 2);
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  = note: iterators are lazy and do nothing unless consumed
```

When the consumer asks for an item, the request travels back through the chain to the source, and the item comes forward through every stage before the next item is fetched. A `filter` keeps asking for items until one passes. A `take(n)` stops asking once it has handed out `n` items, so the stages before it never see the rest.

`zip` pairs two iterators. It asks the left one first and stops as soon as the left one returns `None` (this order is documented). `skip(n)` drops the first `n` items of the iterator it is called on, and only that one.

`sum` and `collect` can produce several types, so the result type must be written somewhere: `let total: i32 = v.iter().sum();` or `.collect::<Vec<_>>()`.

## 8. What `collect` can build

ItemsTarget typeResult

`T``Vec<T>`a vector

`(K, V)``HashMap<K, V>`a map from pairs

`char``String`a string

`Result<T, E>``Result<Vec<T>, E>``Ok(vec)`, or the first `Err` (stops there)

You cannot collect owned values from references: `v.iter()` yields `&String`, so `.collect::<Vec<String>>()` fails with E0277 ("cannot be built from an iterator over elements of type `&String`"). Either collect references (`Vec<&String>`), copy them (`.cloned()`, or `.copied()` for `Copy` types), or start from `into_iter()` to get owned items.

## 9. Writing your own iterator

Put the state in a struct and implement `next`. Every adapter and consumer then works on it for free:

```
struct Countdown { left: u32 }

impl Iterator for Countdown {
    type Item = u32;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u32> {
        if self.left == 0 {
            None
        } else {
            self.left -= 1;
            Some(self.left + 1)
        }
    }
}
let ticks: Vec<u32> = Countdown { left: 3 }.collect();   // [3, 2, 1]
```

Iterator chains are not slower than loops in an optimised (`--release`) build: the compiler inlines the closures and produces the same machine code as a hand-written loop. Debug builds, which the runner uses, are slower for both.

# capture-and-traits.png

Left, three boxes: "body only reads a capture (captured as &T)", "body changes a capture (captured as &mut T)", "body moves a capture out (captured as T)".
Right, three nested rounded sets: the outer set "FnOnce: can be called at least once" contains "FnMut: can be called many times", which contains "Fn: many times, even shared", with the note "every Fn is also FnMut and FnOnce; every FnMut is also FnOnce".
Arrows: reads goes to Fn, changes goes to FnMut, moves out goes to FnOnce.
Footer: `move` changes HOW captures are stored (owned instead of borrowed), not WHICH trait you get: a `move` closure that only reads is still Fn.

[entity 867 · iterator-pipeline.png · diagram]
# iterator-pipeline.png

Five boxes left to right: `iter()`, `filter(..)`, `map(..)`, `take(2)`, `collect()`.
Dark arrows above point right to left, labelled "next()?" (requests travel right to left). Green arrows below point left to right: "Some(item) travels left to right, one item at a time".
Numbered notes:
1. Adapters (filter, map, take, zip, skip, enumerate, rev) only build a value. Nothing runs yet.
2. A consumer (collect, sum, fold, count, any, a for loop) calls next() and work starts.
3. One item passes the whole chain before the next item is fetched.
4. filter keeps asking the stage before it until an item passes (or None).
5. When take has handed out its count, it stops asking: earlier stages never see the rest.

pub fn apply_n(f: impl Fn(i32) -> i32, n: usize, x: i32) -> i32 {
    let mut v = x;
    for _ in 0..n {
        v = f(v);
    }
    v
}

pub fn compose<F, G>(f: F, g: G) -> impl Fn(i32) -> i32
where
    F: Fn(i32) -> i32,
    G: Fn(i32) -> i32,
{
    move |x| g(f(x)) // move: the closure must own f and g, they outlive this call
}

pub fn keep_words(text: &str, keep: impl Fn(&str) -> bool) -> Vec<String> {
    text.split_whitespace().filter(|w| keep(w)).map(|w| w.to_string()).collect()
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn apply_several_times() {
        assert_eq!(apply_n(|v| v * 2, 3, 1), 8);
        assert_eq!(apply_n(|v| v - 1, 0, 5), 5);
    }

    #[test]
    fn apply_with_captured_step() {
        let step = 7;
        assert_eq!(apply_n(|v| v + step, 2, 0), 14);
    }

    #[test]
    fn compose_runs_f_then_g() {
        let h = compose(|v| v + 1, |v| v * 10);
        assert_eq!(h(2), 30);
        assert_eq!(h(0), 10);
    }

    #[test]
    fn compose_with_captures() {
        let offset = 100;
        let h = compose(move |v| v + offset, |v| -v);
        assert_eq!(h(1), -101);
    }

    #[test]
    fn keeps_matching_words() {
        assert_eq!(keep_words("a bb ccc", |w| w.len() > 1), vec!["bb", "ccc"]);
        let banned = "x";
        assert_eq!(keep_words("x y x z", |w| w != banned), vec!["y", "z"]);
    }
}

pub fn sum_even_squares(v: &[i32]) -> i32 {
    v.iter().filter(|&&x| x % 2 == 0).map(|x| x * x).sum()
}

pub fn char_lengths(words: &[&str]) -> Vec<usize> {
    words.iter().map(|w| w.chars().count()).collect()
}

pub fn shout_all(words: Vec<String>) -> Vec<String> {
    words.into_iter().map(|w| w.to_uppercase()).collect()
}

pub fn negative_positions(v: &[i32]) -> Vec<usize> {
    v.iter().enumerate().filter(|(_, x)| **x < 0).map(|(i, _)| i).collect()
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn even_squares() {
        assert_eq!(sum_even_squares(&[1, 2, 3, 4]), 20);
        assert_eq!(sum_even_squares(&[]), 0);
        assert_eq!(sum_even_squares(&[-2, 5]), 4);
    }

    #[test]
    fn lengths_in_chars() {
        assert_eq!(char_lengths(&["ab", "été", ""]), vec![2, 3, 0]);
    }

    #[test]
    fn shouting() {
        let v = vec![String::from("hi"), String::from("straße")];
        assert_eq!(shout_all(v), vec!["HI", "STRASSE"]);
    }

    #[test]
    fn negatives() {
        assert_eq!(negative_positions(&[3, -1, 0, -7]), vec![1, 3]);
        assert!(negative_positions(&[1, 2]).is_empty());
    }
}

// Reference solution for exercise 3 (Tutor only; never shown to the learner).
pub struct Fib {
    a: u64,
    b: u64,
}

impl Fib {
    pub fn new() -> Fib {
        Fib { a: 0, b: 1 }
    }
}

impl Iterator for Fib {
    type Item = u64;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u64> {
        let out = self.a;
        self.a = self.b;
        self.b += out;
        Some(out)
    }
}

pub fn first_fib(n: usize) -> Vec<u64> {
    Fib::new().take(n).collect()
}

pub fn even_fib_sum_below(limit: u64) -> u64 {
    Fib::new().take_while(|&x| x < limit).filter(|x| x % 2 == 0).sum()
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn next_by_hand() {
        let mut f = Fib::new();
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(0));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(1));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(1));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(2));
    }

    #[test]
    fn first_few() {
        assert_eq!(first_fib(7), vec![0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8]);
        assert!(first_fib(0).is_empty());
    }

    #[test]
    fn even_sum() {
        assert_eq!(even_fib_sum_below(10), 10); // 0 + 2 + 8
        assert_eq!(even_fib_sum_below(100), 44); // + 34
    }
}

## 1. Closures

Adapted from The Rust Programming Language, ch 13.1-13.2, and Rust by Example (Closures, Capturing, As input parameters, Iterators), MIT/Apache-2.0.

A closure is a function you write inline, without a name, that can use the variables around it:

```
let limit = 10;
let over = |x: i32| x > limit;     // reads `limit` from the surrounding scope
println!("{}", over(12));          // true
let add_one = |x| x + 1;           // parameter and return types inferred
```

- Parameters go between bars: `|x|`, `|a, b|`, or `||` for none. The body is one expression or a `{ ... }` block.

- Types are usually inferred. They are fixed by the first use: after `add_one(5)`, calling `add_one(2.5)` is a type error.

- A `fn` item cannot read local variables of the function around it; a closure can. That is the whole point.

Parameters are patterns. Iterator methods often hand a closure a reference. A pattern can unpack it:

```
let temps = [18, 23, 31];
// iter() yields &i32; filter passes a reference to that, so its closure gets &&i32.
let warm: Vec<&i32> = temps.iter().filter(|&&t| t > 20).collect();  // t: i32
let doubled: Vec<i32> = temps.iter().map(|&t| t * 2).collect();       // t: i32
let hot: Vec<usize> = temps.iter().enumerate()
    .filter(|(_, t)| **t > 25).map(|(i, _)| i).collect();              // tuples too
```

## 2. How a closure captures

A closure captures each outside variable it uses in the weakest way its body needs:

Body doesCaptured asWhile the closure is alive

reads the variableshared borrow `&T`others may read it too

changes itmutable borrow `&mut T`nobody else may use it

moves it out (gives it away, drops it)by value `T`it now belongs to the closure

The borrow rules from 03 apply to these captures. A closure that holds `&mut count` blocks every other use of `count` until the closure's last use:

```
let mut count = 0;
let mut bump = || count += 1;   // captures &mut count
bump();
println!("{count}");            // error: bump is used again below
bump();
```

```
error[E0502]: cannot borrow `count` as immutable because it is also borrowed as mutable
  |     let mut bump = || count += 1;
  |                    -- ----- first borrow occurs due to use of `count` in closure
  |                    |
  |                    mutable borrow occurs here
  |     println!("{count}");
  |                ^^^^^ immutable borrow occurs here
  |     bump();
  |     ---- mutable borrow later used here
```

Move the `println!` after the last `bump()` and it compiles: the borrow ends when the closure is last used.

Fields, not whole structs. Since edition 2021, a closure that uses `stats.hits` captures only that field. Other fields of `stats` stay free to use while the closure is alive. (Older editions captured the whole struct.) Part 4 of `capture.rs` shows it.

## 3. `move`

Writing `move` before the bars makes the closure take ownership of every variable it uses, even ones it only reads:

```
let label = String::from("total");
let owned = move || println!("owned: {label}");
owned();
// println!("{label}");  // error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `label`
```

You need `move` when the closure must outlive the variables it uses: a closure returned from a function (section 5), or one sent to another thread (18).

With a `Copy` value (integers, `bool`, `char`, `f64`), `move` copies it into the closure. The closure then works on its own copy, and the outside variable never sees the changes:

```
let mut fuel = 50.0;
let mut burn = move || { fuel -= 10.0; fuel };   // burn owns a copy of fuel
println!("{} {}", burn(), burn());              // 40 30
println!("{fuel}");                             // 50: the outer fuel was never touched
```

## 4. Fn, FnMut and FnOnce

Every closure implements one or more of three traits. Which ones depends on what the body does with its captures, not on whether you wrote `move`:

TraitThe body...Can be called

`Fn`only reads its capturesany number of times, even through a shared reference

`FnMut`changes a capturemany times, but each call needs exclusive (`&mut`) access to the closure

`FnOnce`moves a capture outonce: the first call uses the captured value up

capture-and-traits.png: what the body does picks the trait; Fn sits inside FnMut, inside FnOnce.

The traits nest: every `Fn` closure is also `FnMut` and `FnOnce`, and every `FnMut` is also `FnOnce`. So a function that asks for `FnOnce` accepts anything; one that asks for `Fn` accepts only closures that do not mutate or move out.

A `move` closure that only reads a `String` is still `Fn`: it owns the string, but calling it does not use the string up. `move` changes how captures are stored, not which trait you get.

## 5. Closures as parameters and return values

Take a closure with `impl Fn...` or a generic bound, exactly like any other trait (09):

```
fn call_twice<F: Fn() -> usize>(f: F) -> usize {
    f() + f()
}
fn call_twice_mut<F: FnMut()>(mut f: F) {   // note `mut f`
    f();
    f();
}
fn call_once<F: FnOnce() -> String>(f: F) -> String {
    f()                                    // f is used up here
}
```

Calling an `FnMut` needs `&mut` access to the closure value (its captured state changes), so the parameter or variable that holds it must be declared `mut`. Calling an `FnOnce` consumes it, so it can be called only once in the function body.

Std examples: `Option::unwrap_or_else` takes an `FnOnce` (called at most once); `sort_by_key` takes an `FnMut` (called many times, may count or record).

### Returning a closure

```
fn make_adder(step: i32) -> impl Fn(i32) -> i32 {
    let base = step * 10;
    move |x| x + base + step
}
```

The returned closure is called after `make_adder` has returned, when `base` and `step` no longer exist. Without `move` it would borrow them:

```
error[E0373]: closure may outlive the current function, but it borrows `base`, which is owned by the current function
  |     |x| x + base + step
  |     ^^^     ---- `base` is borrowed here
  |     |
  |     may outlive borrowed value `base`
note: closure is returned here
```

The return type must name the right trait too: a closure whose body changes its captures is `FnMut`, so the function must say `-> impl FnMut(...)`, and the caller must store it in a `let mut` binding to call it.

## 6. The Iterator trait and the three ways to iterate

An iterator is any value that implements one required method:

```
trait Iterator {
    type Item;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item>;   // Some(item), or None when done
    // ...plus dozens of provided methods (map, filter, sum, ...)
}
```

A collection gives you three iterators, which differ in the item type:

CallItem type for a `Vec<T>`The Vec afterwardsSame as

`v.iter()``&T`untouched`for x in &v`

`v.iter_mut()``&mut T`changed in place`for x in &mut v`

`v.into_iter()``T`consumed (moved)`for x in v`

A `for` loop calls `into_iter()` on whatever you give it, which is why `for x in v` consumes `v` while `for x in &v` only borrows it. `iterators.rs` shows all three.

## 7. Adapters are lazy, consumers pull

Adapters take an iterator and return a new one: `map`, `filter`, `take(n)`, `skip(n)`, `take_while`, `zip`, `enumerate`, `rev`, `step_by`, `copied`/`cloned`. Building one runs no closure. Consumers call `next` until they are done: `collect`, `sum`, `count`, `fold`, `any`, `position`, and a `for` loop.

iterator-pipeline.png: requests travel right to left, items left to right, one at a time.

An adapter chain with no consumer does nothing, and the compiler warns you:

```
warning: unused `Map` that must be used
  |     v.iter().map(|s| s * 2);
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  = note: iterators are lazy and do nothing unless consumed
```

When the consumer asks for an item, the request travels back through the chain to the source, and the item comes forward through every stage before the next item is fetched. A `filter` keeps asking for items until one passes. A `take(n)` stops asking once it has handed out `n` items, so the stages before it never see the rest.

`zip` pairs two iterators. It asks the left one first and stops as soon as the left one returns `None` (this order is documented). `skip(n)` drops the first `n` items of the iterator it is called on, and only that one.

`sum` and `collect` can produce several types, so the result type must be written somewhere: `let total: i32 = v.iter().sum();` or `.collect::<Vec<_>>()`.

## 8. What `collect` can build

ItemsTarget typeResult

`T``Vec<T>`a vector

`(K, V)``HashMap<K, V>`a map from pairs

`char``String`a string

`Result<T, E>``Result<Vec<T>, E>``Ok(vec)`, or the first `Err` (stops there)

You cannot collect owned values from references: `v.iter()` yields `&String`, so `.collect::<Vec<String>>()` fails with E0277 ("cannot be built from an iterator over elements of type `&String`"). Either collect references (`Vec<&String>`), copy them (`.cloned()`, or `.copied()` for `Copy` types), or start from `into_iter()` to get owned items.

## 9. Writing your own iterator

Put the state in a struct and implement `next`. Every adapter and consumer then works on it for free:

```
struct Countdown { left: u32 }

impl Iterator for Countdown {
    type Item = u32;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u32> {
        if self.left == 0 {
            None
        } else {
            self.left -= 1;
            Some(self.left + 1)
        }
    }
}
let ticks: Vec<u32> = Countdown { left: 3 }.collect();   // [3, 2, 1]
```

Iterator chains are not slower than loops in an optimised (`--release`) build: the compiler inlines the closures and produces the same machine code as a hand-written loop. Debug builds, which the runner uses, are slower for both.

## 10. Practice

- `ex1_compose.rs`: closures as arguments and a returned closure.

- `ex2_chains.rs`: replace loops with one chain each.

- `ex3_fib.rs`: your own iterator plus `take` and `take_while`.

## 11. Check yourself

- Why does adding `move` to a closure that only reads a `String` not make it FnOnce?

- In `v.iter().map(f).filter(g).collect()`, which closure runs first for the second element?

- When should a function take `impl FnMut` instead of `impl Fn`, and what does the caller have to change?

- What item type does `iter_mut()` give for a `Vec<String>`?

# capture-and-traits.png

Left, three boxes: "body only reads a capture (captured as &T)", "body changes a capture (captured as &mut T)", "body moves a capture out (captured as T)".
Right, three nested rounded sets: the outer set "FnOnce: can be called at least once" contains "FnMut: can be called many times", which contains "Fn: many times, even shared", with the note "every Fn is also FnMut and FnOnce; every FnMut is also FnOnce".
Arrows: reads goes to Fn, changes goes to FnMut, moves out goes to FnOnce.
Footer: `move` changes HOW captures are stored (owned instead of borrowed), not WHICH trait you get: a `move` closure that only reads is still Fn.

[entity 867 · iterator-pipeline.png · diagram]
# iterator-pipeline.png

Five boxes left to right: `iter()`, `filter(..)`, `map(..)`, `take(2)`, `collect()`.
Dark arrows above point right to left, labelled "next()?" (requests travel right to left). Green arrows below point left to right: "Some(item) travels left to right, one item at a time".
Numbered notes:
1. Adapters (filter, map, take, zip, skip, enumerate, rev) only build a value. Nothing runs yet.
2. A consumer (collect, sum, fold, count, any, a for loop) calls next() and work starts.
3. One item passes the whole chain before the next item is fetched.
4. filter keeps asking the stage before it until an item passes (or None).
5. When take has handed out its count, it stops asking: earlier stages never see the rest.

pub struct Fib {
    a: u64,
    b: u64,
}

impl Fib {
    pub fn new() -> Fib {
        Fib { a: 0, b: 1 }
    }
}

impl Iterator for Fib {
    type Item = u64;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u64> {
        let out = self.a;
        self.a = self.b;
        self.b += out;
        Some(out)
    }
}

pub fn first_fib(n: usize) -> Vec<u64> {
    Fib::new().take(n).collect()
}

pub fn even_fib_sum_below(limit: u64) -> u64 {
    Fib::new().take_while(|&x| x < limit).filter(|x| x % 2 == 0).sum()
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn next_by_hand() {
        let mut f = Fib::new();
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(0));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(1));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(1));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(2));
    }

    fn first_few() {
        assert_eq!(first_fib(7), vec![0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8]);
        assert!(first_fib(0).is_empty());
    }

    fn even_sum() {
        assert_eq!(even_fib_sum_below(10), 10); // 0 + 2 + 8

## 1. Closures

Adapted from The Rust Programming Language, ch 13.1-13.2, and Rust by Example (Closures, Capturing, As input parameters, Iterators), MIT/Apache-2.0.

A closure is a function you write inline, without a name, that can use the variables around it:

```
let limit = 10;
let over = |x: i32| x > limit;     // reads `limit` from the surrounding scope
println!("{}", over(12));          // true
let add_one = |x| x + 1;           // parameter and return types inferred
```

- Parameters go between bars: `|x|`, `|a, b|`, or `||` for none. The body is one expression or a `{ ... }` block.

- Types are usually inferred. They are fixed by the first use: after `add_one(5)`, calling `add_one(2.5)` is a type error.

- A `fn` item cannot read local variables of the function around it; a closure can. That is the whole point.

Parameters are patterns. Iterator methods often hand a closure a reference. A pattern can unpack it:

```
let temps = [18, 23, 31];
// iter() yields &i32; filter passes a reference to that, so its closure gets &&i32.
let warm: Vec<&i32> = temps.iter().filter(|&&t| t > 20).collect();  // t: i32
let doubled: Vec<i32> = temps.iter().map(|&t| t * 2).collect();       // t: i32
let hot: Vec<usize> = temps.iter().enumerate()
    .filter(|(_, t)| **t > 25).map(|(i, _)| i).collect();              // tuples too
```

## 2. How a closure captures

A closure captures each outside variable it uses in the weakest way its body needs:

Body doesCaptured asWhile the closure is alive

reads the variableshared borrow `&T`others may read it too

changes itmutable borrow `&mut T`nobody else may use it

moves it out (gives it away, drops it)by value `T`it now belongs to the closure

The borrow rules from 03 apply to these captures. A closure that holds `&mut count` blocks every other use of `count` until the closure's last use:

```
let mut count = 0;
let mut bump = || count += 1;   // captures &mut count
bump();
println!("{count}");            // error: bump is used again below
bump();
```

```
error[E0502]: cannot borrow `count` as immutable because it is also borrowed as mutable
  |     let mut bump = || count += 1;
  |                    -- ----- first borrow occurs due to use of `count` in closure
  |                    |
  |                    mutable borrow occurs here
  |     println!("{count}");
  |                ^^^^^ immutable borrow occurs here
  |     bump();
  |     ---- mutable borrow later used here
```

Move the `println!` after the last `bump()` and it compiles: the borrow ends when the closure is last used.

Fields, not whole structs. Since edition 2021, a closure that uses `stats.hits` captures only that field. Other fields of `stats` stay free to use while the closure is alive. (Older editions captured the whole struct.) Part 4 of `capture.rs` shows it.

## 3. `move`

Writing `move` before the bars makes the closure take ownership of every variable it uses, even ones it only reads:

```
let label = String::from("total");
let owned = move || println!("owned: {label}");
owned();
// println!("{label}");  // error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `label`
```

You need `move` when the closure must outlive the variables it uses: a closure returned from a function (section 5), or one sent to another thread (18).

With a `Copy` value (integers, `bool`, `char`, `f64`), `move` copies it into the closure. The closure then works on its own copy, and the outside variable never sees the changes:

```
let mut fuel = 50.0;
let mut burn = move || { fuel -= 10.0; fuel };   // burn owns a copy of fuel
println!("{} {}", burn(), burn());              // 40 30
println!("{fuel}");                             // 50: the outer fuel was never touched
```

## 4. Fn, FnMut and FnOnce

Every closure implements one or more of three traits. Which ones depends on what the body does with its captures, not on whether you wrote `move`:

TraitThe body...Can be called

`Fn`only reads its capturesany number of times, even through a shared reference

`FnMut`changes a capturemany times, but each call needs exclusive (`&mut`) access to the closure

`FnOnce`moves a capture outonce: the first call uses the captured value up

capture-and-traits.png: what the body does picks the trait; Fn sits inside FnMut, inside FnOnce.

The traits nest: every `Fn` closure is also `FnMut` and `FnOnce`, and every `FnMut` is also `FnOnce`. So a function that asks for `FnOnce` accepts anything; one that asks for `Fn` accepts only closures that do not mutate or move out.

A `move` closure that only reads a `String` is still `Fn`: it owns the string, but calling it does not use the string up. `move` changes how captures are stored, not which trait you get.

## 5. Closures as parameters and return values

Take a closure with `impl Fn...` or a generic bound, exactly like any other trait (09):

```
fn call_twice<F: Fn() -> usize>(f: F) -> usize {
    f() + f()
}
fn call_twice_mut<F: FnMut()>(mut f: F) {   // note `mut f`
    f();
    f();
}
fn call_once<F: FnOnce() -> String>(f: F) -> String {
    f()                                    // f is used up here
}
```

Calling an `FnMut` needs `&mut` access to the closure value (its captured state changes), so the parameter or variable that holds it must be declared `mut`. Calling an `FnOnce` consumes it, so it can be called only once in the function body.

Std examples: `Option::unwrap_or_else` takes an `FnOnce` (called at most once); `sort_by_key` takes an `FnMut` (called many times, may count or record).

### Returning a closure

```
fn make_adder(step: i32) -> impl Fn(i32) -> i32 {
    let base = step * 10;
    move |x| x + base + step
}
```

The returned closure is called after `make_adder` has returned, when `base` and `step` no longer exist. Without `move` it would borrow them:

```
error[E0373]: closure may outlive the current function, but it borrows `base`, which is owned by the current function
  |     |x| x + base + step
  |     ^^^     ---- `base` is borrowed here
  |     |
  |     may outlive borrowed value `base`
note: closure is returned here
```

The return type must name the right trait too: a closure whose body changes its captures is `FnMut`, so the function must say `-> impl FnMut(...)`, and the caller must store it in a `let mut` binding to call it.

## 6. The Iterator trait and the three ways to iterate

An iterator is any value that implements one required method:

```
trait Iterator {
    type Item;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item>;   // Some(item), or None when done
    // ...plus dozens of provided methods (map, filter, sum, ...)
}
```

A collection gives you three iterators, which differ in the item type:

CallItem type for a `Vec<T>`The Vec afterwardsSame as

`v.iter()``&T`untouched`for x in &v`

`v.iter_mut()``&mut T`changed in place`for x in &mut v`

`v.into_iter()``T`consumed (moved)`for x in v`

A `for` loop calls `into_iter()` on whatever you give it, which is why `for x in v` consumes `v` while `for x in &v` only borrows it. `iterators.rs` shows all three.

## 7. Adapters are lazy, consumers pull

Adapters take an iterator and return a new one: `map`, `filter`, `take(n)`, `skip(n)`, `take_while`, `zip`, `enumerate`, `rev`, `step_by`, `copied`/`cloned`. Building one runs no closure. Consumers call `next` until they are done: `collect`, `sum`, `count`, `fold`, `any`, `position`, and a `for` loop.

iterator-pipeline.png: requests travel right to left, items left to right, one at a time.

An adapter chain with no consumer does nothing, and the compiler warns you:

```
warning: unused `Map` that must be used
  |     v.iter().map(|s| s * 2);
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  = note: iterators are lazy and do nothing unless consumed
```

When the consumer asks for an item, the request travels back through the chain to the source, and the item comes forward through every stage before the next item is fetched. A `filter` keeps asking for items until one passes. A `take(n)` stops asking once it has handed out `n` items, so the stages before it never see the rest.

`zip` pairs two iterators. It asks the left one first and stops as soon as the left one returns `None` (this order is documented). `skip(n)` drops the first `n` items of the iterator it is called on, and only that one.

`sum` and `collect` can produce several types, so the result type must be written somewhere: `let total: i32 = v.iter().sum();` or `.collect::<Vec<_>>()`.

## 8. What `collect` can build

ItemsTarget typeResult

`T``Vec<T>`a vector

`(K, V)``HashMap<K, V>`a map from pairs

`char``String`a string

`Result<T, E>``Result<Vec<T>, E>``Ok(vec)`, or the first `Err` (stops there)

You cannot collect owned values from references: `v.iter()` yields `&String`, so `.collect::<Vec<String>>()` fails with E0277 ("cannot be built from an iterator over elements of type `&String`"). Either collect references (`Vec<&String>`), copy them (`.cloned()`, or `.copied()` for `Copy` types), or start from `into_iter()` to get owned items.

## 9. Writing your own iterator

Put the state in a struct and implement `next`. Every adapter and consumer then works on it for free:

```
struct Countdown { left: u32 }

impl Iterator for Countdown {
    type Item = u32;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u32> {
        if self.left == 0 {
            None
        } else {
            self.left -= 1;
            Some(self.left + 1)
        }
    }
}
let ticks: Vec<u32> = Countdown { left: 3 }.collect();   // [3, 2, 1]
```

Iterator chains are not slower than loops in an optimised (`--release`) build: the compiler inlines the closures and produces the same machine code as a hand-written loop. Debug builds, which the runner uses, are slower for both.

# iterator-pipeline.png

Five boxes left to right: `iter()`, `filter(..)`, `map(..)`, `take(2)`, `collect()`.
Dark arrows above point right to left, labelled "next()?" (requests travel right to left). Green arrows below point left to right: "Some(item) travels left to right, one item at a time".
Numbered notes:
1. Adapters (filter, map, take, zip, skip, enumerate, rev) only build a value. Nothing runs yet.
2. A consumer (collect, sum, fold, count, any, a for loop) calls next() and work starts.
3. One item passes the whole chain before the next item is fetched.
4. filter keeps asking the stage before it until an item passes (or None).
5. When take has handed out its count, it stops asking: earlier stages never see the rest.

pub fn apply_n(f: impl Fn(i32) -> i32, n: usize, x: i32) -> i32 {

pub fn compose<F, G>(f: F, g: G) -> impl Fn(i32) -> i32
where
    F: Fn(i32) -> i32,
    G: Fn(i32) -> i32,
{
    move |x| g(f(x)) // move: the closure must own f and g, they outlive this call
}

    text.split_whitespace().filter(|w| keep(w)).map(|w| w.to_string()).collect()
}

pub struct Fib {
    a: u64,
    b: u64,
}

impl Fib {
    pub fn new() -> Fib {
        Fib { a: 0, b: 1 }
    }
}

impl Iterator for Fib {
    type Item = u64;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u64> {
        let out = self.a;
        self.a = self.b;
        self.b += out;
        Some(out)
    }
}

pub fn first_fib(n: usize) -> Vec<u64> {
    Fib::new().take(n).collect()
}

pub fn even_fib_sum_below(limit: u64) -> u64 {
    Fib::new().take_while(|&x| x < limit).filter(|x| x % 2 == 0).sum()
}

#[cfg(test)]

    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn next_by_hand() {
        let mut f = Fib::new();
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(0));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(1));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(1));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(2));
    }

    fn first_few() {
        assert_eq!(first_fib(7), vec![0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8]);
        assert!(first_fib(0).is_empty());

## 1. Closures

Adapted from The Rust Programming Language, ch 13.1-13.2, and Rust by Example (Closures, Capturing, As input parameters, Iterators), MIT/Apache-2.0.

A closure is a function you write inline, without a name, that can use the variables around it:

```
let limit = 10;
let over = |x: i32| x > limit;     // reads `limit` from the surrounding scope
println!("{}", over(12));          // true
let add_one = |x| x + 1;           // parameter and return types inferred
```

- Parameters go between bars: `|x|`, `|a, b|`, or `||` for none. The body is one expression or a `{ ... }` block.

- Types are usually inferred. They are fixed by the first use: after `add_one(5)`, calling `add_one(2.5)` is a type error.

- A `fn` item cannot read local variables of the function around it; a closure can. That is the whole point.

Parameters are patterns. Iterator methods often hand a closure a reference. A pattern can unpack it:

```
let temps = [18, 23, 31];
// iter() yields &i32; filter passes a reference to that, so its closure gets &&i32.
let warm: Vec<&i32> = temps.iter().filter(|&&t| t > 20).collect();  // t: i32
let doubled: Vec<i32> = temps.iter().map(|&t| t * 2).collect();       // t: i32
let hot: Vec<usize> = temps.iter().enumerate()
    .filter(|(_, t)| **t > 25).map(|(i, _)| i).collect();              // tuples too
```

## 2. How a closure captures

A closure captures each outside variable it uses in the weakest way its body needs:

Body doesCaptured asWhile the closure is alive

reads the variableshared borrow `&T`others may read it too

changes itmutable borrow `&mut T`nobody else may use it

moves it out (gives it away, drops it)by value `T`it now belongs to the closure

The borrow rules from 03 apply to these captures. A closure that holds `&mut count` blocks every other use of `count` until the closure's last use:

```
let mut count = 0;
let mut bump = || count += 1;   // captures &mut count
bump();
println!("{count}");            // error: bump is used again below
bump();
```

```
error[E0502]: cannot borrow `count` as immutable because it is also borrowed as mutable
  |     let mut bump = || count += 1;
  |                    -- ----- first borrow occurs due to use of `count` in closure
  |                    |
  |                    mutable borrow occurs here
  |     println!("{count}");
  |                ^^^^^ immutable borrow occurs here
  |     bump();
  |     ---- mutable borrow later used here
```

Move the `println!` after the last `bump()` and it compiles: the borrow ends when the closure is last used.

Fields, not whole structs. Since edition 2021, a closure that uses `stats.hits` captures only that field. Other fields of `stats` stay free to use while the closure is alive. (Older editions captured the whole struct.) Part 4 of `capture.rs` shows it.

## 3. `move`

Writing `move` before the bars makes the closure take ownership of every variable it uses, even ones it only reads:

```
let label = String::from("total");
let owned = move || println!("owned: {label}");
owned();
// println!("{label}");  // error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `label`
```

You need `move` when the closure must outlive the variables it uses: a closure returned from a function (section 5), or one sent to another thread (18).

With a `Copy` value (integers, `bool`, `char`, `f64`), `move` copies it into the closure. The closure then works on its own copy, and the outside variable never sees the changes:

```
let mut fuel = 50.0;
let mut burn = move || { fuel -= 10.0; fuel };   // burn owns a copy of fuel
println!("{} {}", burn(), burn());              // 40 30
println!("{fuel}");                             // 50: the outer fuel was never touched
```

## 4. Fn, FnMut and FnOnce

Every closure implements one or more of three traits. Which ones depends on what the body does with its captures, not on whether you wrote `move`:

TraitThe body...Can be called

`Fn`only reads its capturesany number of times, even through a shared reference

`FnMut`changes a capturemany times, but each call needs exclusive (`&mut`) access to the closure

`FnOnce`moves a capture outonce: the first call uses the captured value up

capture-and-traits.png: what the body does picks the trait; Fn sits inside FnMut, inside FnOnce.

The traits nest: every `Fn` closure is also `FnMut` and `FnOnce`, and every `FnMut` is also `FnOnce`. So a function that asks for `FnOnce` accepts anything; one that asks for `Fn` accepts only closures that do not mutate or move out.

A `move` closure that only reads a `String` is still `Fn`: it owns the string, but calling it does not use the string up. `move` changes how captures are stored, not which trait you get.

## 5. Closures as parameters and return values

Take a closure with `impl Fn...` or a generic bound, exactly like any other trait (09):

```
fn call_twice<F: Fn() -> usize>(f: F) -> usize {
    f() + f()
}
fn call_twice_mut<F: FnMut()>(mut f: F) {   // note `mut f`
    f();
    f();
}
fn call_once<F: FnOnce() -> String>(f: F) -> String {
    f()                                    // f is used up here
}
```

Calling an `FnMut` needs `&mut` access to the closure value (its captured state changes), so the parameter or variable that holds it must be declared `mut`. Calling an `FnOnce` consumes it, so it can be called only once in the function body.

Std examples: `Option::unwrap_or_else` takes an `FnOnce` (called at most once); `sort_by_key` takes an `FnMut` (called many times, may count or record).

### Returning a closure

```
fn make_adder(step: i32) -> impl Fn(i32) -> i32 {
    let base = step * 10;
    move |x| x + base + step
}
```

The returned closure is called after `make_adder` has returned, when `base` and `step` no longer exist. Without `move` it would borrow them:

```
error[E0373]: closure may outlive the current function, but it borrows `base`, which is owned by the current function
  |     |x| x + base + step
  |     ^^^     ---- `base` is borrowed here
  |     |
  |     may outlive borrowed value `base`
note: closure is returned here
```

The return type must name the right trait too: a closure whose body changes its captures is `FnMut`, so the function must say `-> impl FnMut(...)`, and the caller must store it in a `let mut` binding to call it.

## 6. The Iterator trait and the three ways to iterate

An iterator is any value that implements one required method:

```
trait Iterator {
    type Item;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item>;   // Some(item), or None when done
    // ...plus dozens of provided methods (map, filter, sum, ...)
}
```

A collection gives you three iterators, which differ in the item type:

CallItem type for a `Vec<T>`The Vec afterwardsSame as

`v.iter()``&T`untouched`for x in &v`

`v.iter_mut()``&mut T`changed in place`for x in &mut v`

`v.into_iter()``T`consumed (moved)`for x in v`

A `for` loop calls `into_iter()` on whatever you give it, which is why `for x in v` consumes `v` while `for x in &v` only borrows it. `iterators.rs` shows all three.

## 7. Adapters are lazy, consumers pull

Adapters take an iterator and return a new one: `map`, `filter`, `take(n)`, `skip(n)`, `take_while`, `zip`, `enumerate`, `rev`, `step_by`, `copied`/`cloned`. Building one runs no closure. Consumers call `next` until they are done: `collect`, `sum`, `count`, `fold`, `any`, `position`, and a `for` loop.

iterator-pipeline.png: requests travel right to left, items left to right, one at a time.

An adapter chain with no consumer does nothing, and the compiler warns you:

```
warning: unused `Map` that must be used
  |     v.iter().map(|s| s * 2);
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  = note: iterators are lazy and do nothing unless consumed
```

When the consumer asks for an item, the request travels back through the chain to the source, and the item comes forward through every stage before the next item is fetched. A `filter` keeps asking for items until one passes. A `take(n)` stops asking once it has handed out `n` items, so the stages before it never see the rest.

`zip` pairs two iterators. It asks the left one first and stops as soon as the left one returns `None` (this order is documented). `skip(n)` drops the first `n` items of the iterator it is called on, and only that one.

`sum` and `collect` can produce several types, so the result type must be written somewhere: `let total: i32 = v.iter().sum();` or `.collect::<Vec<_>>()`.

## 8. What `collect` can build

ItemsTarget typeResult

`T``Vec<T>`a vector

`(K, V)``HashMap<K, V>`a map from pairs

`char``String`a string

`Result<T, E>``Result<Vec<T>, E>``Ok(vec)`, or the first `Err` (stops there)

You cannot collect owned values from references: `v.iter()` yields `&String`, so `.collect::<Vec<String>>()` fails with E0277 ("cannot be built from an iterator over elements of type `&String`"). Either collect references (`Vec<&String>`), copy them (`.cloned()`, or `.copied()` for `Copy` types), or start from `into_iter()` to get owned items.

## 9. Writing your own iterator

Put the state in a struct and implement `next`. Every adapter and consumer then works on it for free:

```
struct Countdown { left: u32 }

impl Iterator for Countdown {
    type Item = u32;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u32> {
        if self.left == 0 {
            None
        } else {
            self.left -= 1;
            Some(self.left + 1)
        }
    }
}
let ticks: Vec<u32> = Countdown { left: 3 }.collect();   // [3, 2, 1]
```

Iterator chains are not slower than loops in an optimised (`--release`) build: the compiler inlines the closures and produces the same machine code as a hand-written loop. Debug builds, which the runner uses, are slower for both.

## 10. Practice

- `ex1_compose.rs`: closures as arguments and a returned closure.

- `ex2_chains.rs`: replace loops with one chain each.

- `ex3_fib.rs`: your own iterator plus `take` and `take_while`.

## 11. Check yourself

- Why does adding `move` to a closure that only reads a `String` not make it FnOnce?

- In `v.iter().map(f).filter(g).collect()`, which closure runs first for the second element?

- When should a function take `impl FnMut` instead of `impl Fn`, and what does the caller have to change?

- What item type does `iter_mut()` give for a `Vec<String>`?

# capture-and-traits.png

Left, three boxes: "body only reads a capture (captured as &T)", "body changes a capture (captured as &mut T)", "body moves a capture out (captured as T)".
Right, three nested rounded sets: the outer set "FnOnce: can be called at least once" contains "FnMut: can be called many times", which contains "Fn: many times, even shared", with the note "every Fn is also FnMut and FnOnce; every FnMut is also FnOnce".
Arrows: reads goes to Fn, changes goes to FnMut, moves out goes to FnOnce.
Footer: `move` changes HOW captures are stored (owned instead of borrowed), not WHICH trait you get: a `move` closure that only reads is still Fn.

[entity 867 · iterator-pipeline.png · diagram]
# iterator-pipeline.png

Five boxes left to right: `iter()`, `filter(..)`, `map(..)`, `take(2)`, `collect()`.
Dark arrows above point right to left, labelled "next()?" (requests travel right to left). Green arrows below point left to right: "Some(item) travels left to right, one item at a time".
Numbered notes:
1. Adapters (filter, map, take, zip, skip, enumerate, rev) only build a value. Nothing runs yet.
2. A consumer (collect, sum, fold, count, any, a for loop) calls next() and work starts.
3. One item passes the whole chain before the next item is fetched.
4. filter keeps asking the stage before it until an item passes (or None).
5. When take has handed out its count, it stops asking: earlier stages never see the rest.

pub struct Fib {
    a: u64,
    b: u64,
}

impl Fib {
    pub fn new() -> Fib {
        Fib { a: 0, b: 1 }
    }
}

impl Iterator for Fib {
    type Item = u64;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u64> {
        let out = self.a;
        self.a = self.b;
        self.b += out;
        Some(out)
    }
}

pub fn first_fib(n: usize) -> Vec<u64> {
    Fib::new().take(n).collect()
}

pub fn even_fib_sum_below(limit: u64) -> u64 {
    Fib::new().take_while(|&x| x < limit).filter(|x| x % 2 == 0).sum()
}
