## 1. Closures

Adapted from The Rust Programming Language, ch 13.1-13.2, and Rust by Example (Closures, Capturing, As input parameters, Iterators), MIT/Apache-2.0.

A closure is a function you write inline, without a name, that can use the variables around it:

```
let limit = 10;
let over = |x: i32| x > limit;     // reads `limit` from the surrounding scope
println!("{}", over(12));          // true
let add_one = |x| x + 1;           // parameter and return types inferred
```

- Parameters go between bars: `|x|`, `|a, b|`, or `||` for none. The body is one expression or a `{ ... }` block.

- Types are usually inferred. They are fixed by the first use: after `add_one(5)`, calling `add_one(2.5)` is a type error.

- A `fn` item cannot read local variables of the function around it; a closure can. That is the whole point.

Parameters are patterns. Iterator methods often hand a closure a reference. A pattern can unpack it:

```
let temps = [18, 23, 31];
// iter() yields &i32; filter passes a reference to that, so its closure gets &&i32.
let warm: Vec<&i32> = temps.iter().filter(|&&t| t > 20).collect();  // t: i32
let doubled: Vec<i32> = temps.iter().map(|&t| t * 2).collect();       // t: i32
let hot: Vec<usize> = temps.iter().enumerate()
    .filter(|(_, t)| **t > 25).map(|(i, _)| i).collect();              // tuples too
```

## 2. How a closure captures

A closure captures each outside variable it uses in the weakest way its body needs:

Body doesCaptured asWhile the closure is alive

reads the variableshared borrow `&T`others may read it too

changes itmutable borrow `&mut T`nobody else may use it

moves it out (gives it away, drops it)by value `T`it now belongs to the closure

The borrow rules from 03 apply to these captures. A closure that holds `&mut count` blocks every other use of `count` until the closure's last use:

```
let mut count = 0;
let mut bump = || count += 1;   // captures &mut count
bump();
println!("{count}");            // error: bump is used again below
bump();
```

```
error[E0502]: cannot borrow `count` as immutable because it is also borrowed as mutable
  |     let mut bump = || count += 1;
  |                    -- ----- first borrow occurs due to use of `count` in closure
  |                    |
  |                    mutable borrow occurs here
  |     println!("{count}");
  |                ^^^^^ immutable borrow occurs here
  |     bump();
  |     ---- mutable borrow later used here
```

Move the `println!` after the last `bump()` and it compiles: the borrow ends when the closure is last used.

Fields, not whole structs. Since edition 2021, a closure that uses `stats.hits` captures only that field. Other fields of `stats` stay free to use while the closure is alive. (Older editions captured the whole struct.) Part 4 of `capture.rs` shows it.

## 3. `move`

Writing `move` before the bars makes the closure take ownership of every variable it uses, even ones it only reads:

```
let label = String::from("total");
let owned = move || println!("owned: {label}");
owned();
// println!("{label}");  // error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `label`
```

You need `move` when the closure must outlive the variables it uses: a closure returned from a function (section 5), or one sent to another thread (18).

With a `Copy` value (integers, `bool`, `char`, `f64`), `move` copies it into the closure. The closure then works on its own copy, and the outside variable never sees the changes:

```
let mut fuel = 50.0;
let mut burn = move || { fuel -= 10.0; fuel };   // burn owns a copy of fuel
println!("{} {}", burn(), burn());              // 40 30
println!("{fuel}");                             // 50: the outer fuel was never touched
```

## 4. Fn, FnMut and FnOnce

Every closure implements one or more of three traits. Which ones depends on what the body does with its captures, not on whether you wrote `move`:

TraitThe body...Can be called

`Fn`only reads its capturesany number of times, even through a shared reference

`FnMut`changes a capturemany times, but each call needs exclusive (`&mut`) access to the closure

`FnOnce`moves a capture outonce: the first call uses the captured value up

capture-and-traits.png: what the body does picks the trait; Fn sits inside FnMut, inside FnOnce.

The traits nest: every `Fn` closure is also `FnMut` and `FnOnce`, and every `FnMut` is also `FnOnce`. So a function that asks for `FnOnce` accepts anything; one that asks for `Fn` accepts only closures that do not mutate or move out.

A `move` closure that only reads a `String` is still `Fn`: it owns the string, but calling it does not use the string up. `move` changes how captures are stored, not which trait you get.

## 5. Closures as parameters and return values

Take a closure with `impl Fn...` or a generic bound, exactly like any other trait (09):

```
fn call_twice<F: Fn() -> usize>(f: F) -> usize {
    f() + f()
}
fn call_twice_mut<F: FnMut()>(mut f: F) {   // note `mut f`
    f();
    f();
}
fn call_once<F: FnOnce() -> String>(f: F) -> String {
    f()                                    // f is used up here
}
```

Calling an `FnMut` needs `&mut` access to the closure value (its captured state changes), so the parameter or variable that holds it must be declared `mut`. Calling an `FnOnce` consumes it, so it can be called only once in the function body.

Std examples: `Option::unwrap_or_else` takes an `FnOnce` (called at most once); `sort_by_key` takes an `FnMut` (called many times, may count or record).

### Returning a closure

```
fn make_adder(step: i32) -> impl Fn(i32) -> i32 {
    let base = step * 10;
    move |x| x + base + step
}
```

The returned closure is called after `make_adder` has returned, when `base` and `step` no longer exist. Without `move` it would borrow them:

```
error[E0373]: closure may outlive the current function, but it borrows `base`, which is owned by the current function
  |     |x| x + base + step
  |     ^^^     ---- `base` is borrowed here
  |     |
  |     may outlive borrowed value `base`
note: closure is returned here
```

The return type must name the right trait too: a closure whose body changes its captures is `FnMut`, so the function must say `-> impl FnMut(...)`, and the caller must store it in a `let mut` binding to call it.

## 6. The Iterator trait and the three ways to iterate

An iterator is any value that implements one required method:

```
trait Iterator {
    type Item;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item>;   // Some(item), or None when done
    // ...plus dozens of provided methods (map, filter, sum, ...)
}
```

A collection gives you three iterators, which differ in the item type:

CallItem type for a `Vec<T>`The Vec afterwardsSame as

`v.iter()``&T`untouched`for x in &v`

`v.iter_mut()``&mut T`changed in place`for x in &mut v`

`v.into_iter()``T`consumed (moved)`for x in v`

A `for` loop calls `into_iter()` on whatever you give it, which is why `for x in v` consumes `v` while `for x in &v` only borrows it. `iterators.rs` shows all three.

## 7. Adapters are lazy, consumers pull

Adapters take an iterator and return a new one: `map`, `filter`, `take(n)`, `skip(n)`, `take_while`, `zip`, `enumerate`, `rev`, `step_by`, `copied`/`cloned`. Building one runs no closure. Consumers call `next` until they are done: `collect`, `sum`, `count`, `fold`, `any`, `position`, and a `for` loop.

iterator-pipeline.png: requests travel right to left, items left to right, one at a time.

An adapter chain with no consumer does nothing, and the compiler warns you:

```
warning: unused `Map` that must be used
  |     v.iter().map(|s| s * 2);
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  = note: iterators are lazy and do nothing unless consumed
```

When the consumer asks for an item, the request travels back through the chain to the source, and the item comes forward through every stage before the next item is fetched. A `filter` keeps asking for items until one passes. A `take(n)` stops asking once it has handed out `n` items, so the stages before it never see the rest.

`zip` pairs two iterators. It asks the left one first and stops as soon as the left one returns `None` (this order is documented). `skip(n)` drops the first `n` items of the iterator it is called on, and only that one.

`sum` and `collect` can produce several types, so the result type must be written somewhere: `let total: i32 = v.iter().sum();` or `.collect::<Vec<_>>()`.

## 8. What `collect` can build

ItemsTarget typeResult

`T``Vec<T>`a vector

`(K, V)``HashMap<K, V>`a map from pairs

`char``String`a string

`Result<T, E>``Result<Vec<T>, E>``Ok(vec)`, or the first `Err` (stops there)

You cannot collect owned values from references: `v.iter()` yields `&String`, so `.collect::<Vec<String>>()` fails with E0277 ("cannot be built from an iterator over elements of type `&String`"). Either collect references (`Vec<&String>`), copy them (`.cloned()`, or `.copied()` for `Copy` types), or start from `into_iter()` to get owned items.

## 9. Writing your own iterator

Put the state in a struct and implement `next`. Every adapter and consumer then works on it for free:

```
struct Countdown { left: u32 }

impl Iterator for Countdown {
    type Item = u32;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u32> {
        if self.left == 0 {
            None
        } else {
            self.left -= 1;
            Some(self.left + 1)
        }
    }
}
let ticks: Vec<u32> = Countdown { left: 3 }.collect();   // [3, 2, 1]
```

Iterator chains are not slower than loops in an optimised (`--release`) build: the compiler inlines the closures and produces the same machine code as a hand-written loop. Debug builds, which the runner uses, are slower for both.

# capture-and-traits.png

Left, three boxes: "body only reads a capture (captured as &T)", "body changes a capture (captured as &mut T)", "body moves a capture out (captured as T)".
Right, three nested rounded sets: the outer set "FnOnce: can be called at least once" contains "FnMut: can be called many times", which contains "Fn: many times, even shared", with the note "every Fn is also FnMut and FnOnce; every FnMut is also FnOnce".
Arrows: reads goes to Fn, changes goes to FnMut, moves out goes to FnOnce.
Footer: `move` changes HOW captures are stored (owned instead of borrowed), not WHICH trait you get: a `move` closure that only reads is still Fn.

# iterator-pipeline.png

Five boxes left to right: `iter()`, `filter(..)`, `map(..)`, `take(2)`, `collect()`.
Dark arrows above point right to left, labelled "next()?" (requests travel right to left). Green arrows below point left to right: "Some(item) travels left to right, one item at a time".
Numbered notes:
1. Adapters (filter, map, take, zip, skip, enumerate, rev) only build a value. Nothing runs yet.
2. A consumer (collect, sum, fold, count, any, a for loop) calls next() and work starts.
3. One item passes the whole chain before the next item is fetched.
4. filter keeps asking the stage before it until an item passes (or None).
5. When take has handed out its count, it stops asking: earlier stages never see the rest.

pub fn compose<F, G>(f: F, g: G) -> impl Fn(i32) -> i32
where
    F: Fn(i32) -> i32,
    G: Fn(i32) -> i32,
{
    move |x| g(f(x)) // move: the closure must own f and g, they outlive this call
}

// Reference solution for exercise 3 (Tutor only; never shown to the learner).
pub struct Fib {
    a: u64,
    b: u64,
}

impl Fib {
    pub fn new() -> Fib {
        Fib { a: 0, b: 1 }
    }
}

impl Iterator for Fib {
    type Item = u64;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u64> {
        let out = self.a;
        self.a = self.b;
        self.b += out;
        Some(out)
    }
}

pub fn first_fib(n: usize) -> Vec<u64> {
    Fib::new().take(n).collect()
}

pub fn even_fib_sum_below(limit: u64) -> u64 {
    Fib::new().take_while(|&x| x < limit).filter(|x| x % 2 == 0).sum()
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn next_by_hand() {
        let mut f = Fib::new();
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(0));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(1));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(1));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(2));
    }

    #[test]
    fn first_few() {
        assert_eq!(first_fib(7), vec![0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8]);
        assert!(first_fib(0).is_empty());
    }

    #[test]
    fn even_sum() {
        assert_eq!(even_fib_sum_below(10), 10); // 0 + 2 + 8
        assert_eq!(even_fib_sum_below(100), 44); // + 34
    }
}

A closure can be `move`-capturing and still be `Fn`. `move` only changes how captures are stored (owned instead of borrowed), not which trait you get.

## 1. Closures

Adapted from The Rust Programming Language, ch 13.1-13.2, and Rust by Example (Closures, Capturing, As input parameters, Iterators), MIT/Apache-2.0.

A closure is a function you write inline, without a name, that can use the variables around it:

```
let limit = 10;
let over = |x: i32| x > limit;     // reads `limit` from the surrounding scope
println!("{}", over(12));          // true
let add_one = |x| x + 1;           // parameter and return types inferred
```

- Parameters go between bars: `|x|`, `|a, b|`, or `||` for none. The body is one expression or a `{ ... }` block.

- Types are usually inferred. They are fixed by the first use: after `add_one(5)`, calling `add_one(2.5)` is a type error.

- A `fn` item cannot read local variables of the function around it; a closure can. That is the whole point.

Parameters are patterns. Iterator methods often hand a closure a reference. A pattern can unpack it:

```
let temps = [18, 23, 31];
// iter() yields &i32; filter passes a reference to that, so its closure gets &&i32.
let warm: Vec<&i32> = temps.iter().filter(|&&t| t > 20).collect();  // t: i32
let doubled: Vec<i32> = temps.iter().map(|&t| t * 2).collect();       // t: i32
let hot: Vec<usize> = temps.iter().enumerate()
    .filter(|(_, t)| **t > 25).map(|(i, _)| i).collect();              // tuples too
```

## 2. How a closure captures

A closure captures each outside variable it uses in the weakest way its body needs:

Body doesCaptured asWhile the closure is alive

reads the variableshared borrow `&T`others may read it too

changes itmutable borrow `&mut T`nobody else may use it

moves it out (gives it away, drops it)by value `T`it now belongs to the closure

The borrow rules from 03 apply to these captures. A closure that holds `&mut count` blocks every other use of `count` until the closure's last use:

```
let mut count = 0;
let mut bump = || count += 1;   // captures &mut count
bump();
println!("{count}");            // error: bump is used again below
bump();
```

```
error[E0502]: cannot borrow `count` as immutable because it is also borrowed as mutable
  |     let mut bump = || count += 1;
  |                    -- ----- first borrow occurs due to use of `count` in closure
  |                    |
  |                    mutable borrow occurs here
  |     println!("{count}");
  |                ^^^^^ immutable borrow occurs here
  |     bump();
  |     ---- mutable borrow later used here
```

Move the `println!` after the last `bump()` and it compiles: the borrow ends when the closure is last used.

Fields, not whole structs. Since edition 2021, a closure that uses `stats.hits` captures only that field. Other fields of `stats` stay free to use while the closure is alive. (Older editions captured the whole struct.) Part 4 of `capture.rs` shows it.

## 3. `move`

Writing `move` before the bars makes the closure take ownership of every variable it uses, even ones it only reads:

```
let label = String::from("total");
let owned = move || println!("owned: {label}");
owned();
// println!("{label}");  // error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `label`
```

You need `move` when the closure must outlive the variables it uses: a closure returned from a function (section 5), or one sent to another thread (18).

With a `Copy` value (integers, `bool`, `char`, `f64`), `move` copies it into the closure. The closure then works on its own copy, and the outside variable never sees the changes:

```
let mut fuel = 50.0;
let mut burn = move || { fuel -= 10.0; fuel };   // burn owns a copy of fuel
println!("{} {}", burn(), burn());              // 40 30
println!("{fuel}");                             // 50: the outer fuel was never touched
```

## 4. Fn, FnMut and FnOnce

Every closure implements one or more of three traits. Which ones depends on what the body does with its captures, not on whether you wrote `move`:

TraitThe body...Can be called

`Fn`only reads its capturesany number of times, even through a shared reference

`FnMut`changes a capturemany times, but each call needs exclusive (`&mut`) access to the closure

`FnOnce`moves a capture outonce: the first call uses the captured value up

capture-and-traits.png: what the body does picks the trait; Fn sits inside FnMut, inside FnOnce.

The traits nest: every `Fn` closure is also `FnMut` and `FnOnce`, and every `FnMut` is also `FnOnce`. So a function that asks for `FnOnce` accepts anything; one that asks for `Fn` accepts only closures that do not mutate or move out.

A `move` closure that only reads a `String` is still `Fn`: it owns the string, but calling it does not use the string up. `move` changes how captures are stored, not which trait you get.

## 5. Closures as parameters and return values

Take a closure with `impl Fn...` or a generic bound, exactly like any other trait (09):

```
fn call_twice<F: Fn() -> usize>(f: F) -> usize {
    f() + f()
}
fn call_twice_mut<F: FnMut()>(mut f: F) {   // note `mut f`
    f();
    f();
}
fn call_once<F: FnOnce() -> String>(f: F) -> String {
    f()                                    // f is used up here
}
```

Calling an `FnMut` needs `&mut` access to the closure value (its captured state changes), so the parameter or variable that holds it must be declared `mut`. Calling an `FnOnce` consumes it, so it can be called only once in the function body.

Std examples: `Option::unwrap_or_else` takes an `FnOnce` (called at most once); `sort_by_key` takes an `FnMut` (called many times, may count or record).

### Returning a closure

```
fn make_adder(step: i32) -> impl Fn(i32) -> i32 {
    let base = step * 10;
    move |x| x + base + step
}
```

The returned closure is called after `make_adder` has returned, when `base` and `step` no longer exist. Without `move` it would borrow them:

```
error[E0373]: closure may outlive the current function, but it borrows `base`, which is owned by the current function
  |     |x| x + base + step
  |     ^^^     ---- `base` is borrowed here
  |     |
  |     may outlive borrowed value `base`
note: closure is returned here
```

The return type must name the right trait too: a closure whose body changes its captures is `FnMut`, so the function must say `-> impl FnMut(...)`, and the caller must store it in a `let mut` binding to call it.

## 6. The Iterator trait and the three ways to iterate

An iterator is any value that implements one required method:

```
trait Iterator {
    type Item;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item>;   // Some(item), or None when done
    // ...plus dozens of provided methods (map, filter, sum, ...)
}
```

A collection gives you three iterators, which differ in the item type:

CallItem type for a `Vec<T>`The Vec afterwardsSame as

`v.iter()``&T`untouched`for x in &v`

`v.iter_mut()``&mut T`changed in place`for x in &mut v`

`v.into_iter()``T`consumed (moved)`for x in v`

A `for` loop calls `into_iter()` on whatever you give it, which is why `for x in v` consumes `v` while `for x in &v` only borrows it. `iterators.rs` shows all three.

## 7. Adapters are lazy, consumers pull

Adapters take an iterator and return a new one: `map`, `filter`, `take(n)`, `skip(n)`, `take_while`, `zip`, `enumerate`, `rev`, `step_by`, `copied`/`cloned`. Building one runs no closure. Consumers call `next` until they are done: `collect`, `sum`, `count`, `fold`, `any`, `position`, and a `for` loop.

iterator-pipeline.png: requests travel right to left, items left to right, one at a time.

An adapter chain with no consumer does nothing, and the compiler warns you:

```
warning: unused `Map` that must be used
  |     v.iter().map(|s| s * 2);
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  = note: iterators are lazy and do nothing unless consumed
```

When the consumer asks for an item, the request travels back through the chain to the source, and the item comes forward through every stage before the next item is fetched. A `filter` keeps asking for items until one passes. A `take(n)` stops asking once it has handed out `n` items, so the stages before it never see the rest.

`zip` pairs two iterators. It asks the left one first and stops as soon as the left one returns `None` (this order is documented). `skip(n)` drops the first `n` items of the iterator it is called on, and only that one.

`sum` and `collect` can produce several types, so the result type must be written somewhere: `let total: i32 = v.iter().sum();` or `.collect::<Vec<_>>()`.

## 8. What `collect` can build

ItemsTarget typeResult

`T``Vec<T>`a vector

You cannot collect owned values from references: `v.iter()` yields `&String`, so `.collect::<Vec<String>>()` fails with E0277 ("cannot be built from an iterator over elements of type `&String`"). ## 9. Writing your own iterator

Put the state in a struct and implement `next`. Every adapter and consumer then works on it for free:

```
struct Countdown { left: u32 }

impl Iterator for Countdown {
    type Item = u32;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u32> {
        if self.left == 0 {
            None
        } else {
            self.left -= 1;
            Some(self.left + 1)
        }
    }
}
let ticks: Vec<u32> = Countdown { left: 3 }.collect();   // [3, 2, 1]
```

Iterator chains are not slower than loops in an optimised (`--release`) build: the compiler inlines the closures and produces the same machine code as a hand-written loop. Debug builds, which the runner uses, are slower for both.

# capture-and-traits.png

Left, three boxes: "body only reads a capture (captured as &T)", "body changes a capture (captured as &mut T)", "body moves a capture out (captured as T)".
Right, three nested rounded sets: the outer set "FnOnce: can be called at least once" contains "FnMut: can be called many times", which contains "Fn: many times, even shared", with the note "every Fn is also FnMut and FnOnce; every FnMut is also FnOnce".
Arrows: reads goes to Fn, changes goes to FnMut, moves out goes to FnOnce.
Footer: `move` changes HOW captures are stored (owned instead of borrowed), not WHICH trait you get: a `move` closure that only reads is still Fn.

[entity 867 · iterator-pipeline.png · diagram]
# iterator-pipeline.png

Five boxes left to right: `iter()`, `filter(..)`, `map(..)`, `take(2)`, `collect()`.
Dark arrows above point right to left, labelled "next()?" (requests travel right to left). Green arrows below point left to right: "Some(item) travels left to right, one item at a time".
Numbered notes:
1. Adapters (filter, map, take, zip, skip, enumerate, rev) only build a value. Nothing runs yet.
2. A consumer (collect, sum, fold, count, any, a for loop) calls next() and work starts.
3. One item passes the whole chain before the next item is fetched.
4. filter keeps asking the stage before it until an item passes (or None).
5. When take has handed out its count, it stops asking: earlier stages never see the rest.

pub struct Fib {
    a: u64,
    b: u64,
}

impl Fib {
    pub fn new() -> Fib {
        Fib { a: 0, b: 1 }
    }
}

impl Iterator for Fib {
    type Item = u64;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u64> {
        let out = self.a;
        self.a = self.b;
        self.b += out;
        Some(out)
    }
}

pub fn first_fib(n: usize) -> Vec<u64> {
    Fib::new().take(n).collect()
}

pub fn even_fib_sum_below(limit: u64) -> u64 {
    Fib::new().take_while(|&x| x < limit).filter(|x| x % 2 == 0).sum()
}

### move does not mean FnOnce · 2 Nov

A closure can be `move`-capturing and still be `Fn`. `move` only changes how captures are stored (owned instead of borrowed), not which trait you get.

The trait comes from what each call does:
- only reads its captures: `Fn`
- changes a capture: `FnMut`
- moves a capture out or consumes it during the call: `FnOnce`

Example: `fn make_adder(step: i32) -> impl Fn(i32) -> i32 { let base = step * 10; move |x| x + base + step }` owns `base` and `step` but only reads them, so it stays `Fn` and can be called many times.

## 1. Closures

Adapted from The Rust Programming Language, ch 13.1-13.2, and Rust by Example (Closures, Capturing, As input parameters, Iterators), MIT/Apache-2.0.

A closure is a function you write inline, without a name, that can use the variables around it:

```
let limit = 10;
let over = |x: i32| x > limit;     // reads `limit` from the surrounding scope
println!("{}", over(12));          // true
let add_one = |x| x + 1;           // parameter and return types inferred
```

- Parameters go between bars: `|x|`, `|a, b|`, or `||` for none. The body is one expression or a `{ ... }` block.

- Types are usually inferred. They are fixed by the first use: after `add_one(5)`, calling `add_one(2.5)` is a type error.

- A `fn` item cannot read local variables of the function around it; a closure can. That is the whole point.

Parameters are patterns. Iterator methods often hand a closure a reference. A pattern can unpack it:

```
let temps = [18, 23, 31];
// iter() yields &i32; filter passes a reference to that, so its closure gets &&i32.
let warm: Vec<&i32> = temps.iter().filter(|&&t| t > 20).collect();  // t: i32
let doubled: Vec<i32> = temps.iter().map(|&t| t * 2).collect();       // t: i32
let hot: Vec<usize> = temps.iter().enumerate()
    .filter(|(_, t)| **t > 25).map(|(i, _)| i).collect();              // tuples too
```

## 2. How a closure captures

A closure captures each outside variable it uses in the weakest way its body needs:

Body doesCaptured asWhile the closure is alive

reads the variableshared borrow `&T`others may read it too

changes itmutable borrow `&mut T`nobody else may use it

moves it out (gives it away, drops it)by value `T`it now belongs to the closure

The borrow rules from 03 apply to these captures. A closure that holds `&mut count` blocks every other use of `count` until the closure's last use:

```
let mut count = 0;
let mut bump = || count += 1;   // captures &mut count
bump();
println!("{count}");            // error: bump is used again below
bump();
```

```
error[E0502]: cannot borrow `count` as immutable because it is also borrowed as mutable
  |     let mut bump = || count += 1;
  |                    -- ----- first borrow occurs due to use of `count` in closure
  |                    |
  |                    mutable borrow occurs here
  |     println!("{count}");
  |                ^^^^^ immutable borrow occurs here
  |     bump();
  |     ---- mutable borrow later used here
```

Move the `println!` after the last `bump()` and it compiles: the borrow ends when the closure is last used.

Fields, not whole structs. Since edition 2021, a closure that uses `stats.hits` captures only that field. Other fields of `stats` stay free to use while the closure is alive. (Older editions captured the whole struct.) Part 4 of `capture.rs` shows it.

## 3. `move`

Writing `move` before the bars makes the closure take ownership of every variable it uses, even ones it only reads:

```
let label = String::from("total");
let owned = move || println!("owned: {label}");
owned();
// println!("{label}");  // error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `label`
```

You need `move` when the closure must outlive the variables it uses: a closure returned from a function (section 5), or one sent to another thread (18).

With a `Copy` value (integers, `bool`, `char`, `f64`), `move` copies it into the closure. The closure then works on its own copy, and the outside variable never sees the changes:

```
let mut fuel = 50.0;
let mut burn = move || { fuel -= 10.0; fuel };   // burn owns a copy of fuel
println!("{} {}", burn(), burn());              // 40 30
println!("{fuel}");                             // 50: the outer fuel was never touched
```

## 4. Fn, FnMut and FnOnce

Every closure implements one or more of three traits. Which ones depends on what the body does with its captures, not on whether you wrote `move`:

TraitThe body...Can be called

`Fn`only reads its capturesany number of times, even through a shared reference

`FnMut`changes a capturemany times, but each call needs exclusive (`&mut`) access to the closure

`FnOnce`moves a capture outonce: the first call uses the captured value up

capture-and-traits.png: what the body does picks the trait; Fn sits inside FnMut, inside FnOnce.

The traits nest: every `Fn` closure is also `FnMut` and `FnOnce`, and every `FnMut` is also `FnOnce`. So a function that asks for `FnOnce` accepts anything; one that asks for `Fn` accepts only closures that do not mutate or move out.

A `move` closure that only reads a `String` is still `Fn`: it owns the string, but calling it does not use the string up. `move` changes how captures are stored, not which trait you get.

## 5. Closures as parameters and return values

Take a closure with `impl Fn...` or a generic bound, exactly like any other trait (09):

```
fn call_twice<F: Fn() -> usize>(f: F) -> usize {
    f() + f()
}
fn call_twice_mut<F: FnMut()>(mut f: F) {   // note `mut f`
    f();
    f();
}
fn call_once<F: FnOnce() -> String>(f: F) -> String {
    f()                                    // f is used up here
}
```

Calling an `FnMut` needs `&mut` access to the closure value (its captured state changes), so the parameter or variable that holds it must be declared `mut`. Calling an `FnOnce` consumes it, so it can be called only once in the function body.

Std examples: `Option::unwrap_or_else` takes an `FnOnce` (called at most once); `sort_by_key` takes an `FnMut` (called many times, may count or record).

### Returning a closure

```
fn make_adder(step: i32) -> impl Fn(i32) -> i32 {
    let base = step * 10;
    move |x| x + base + step
}
```

The returned closure is called after `make_adder` has returned, when `base` and `step` no longer exist. Without `move` it would borrow them:

```
error[E0373]: closure may outlive the current function, but it borrows `base`, which is owned by the current function
  |     |x| x + base + step
  |     ^^^     ---- `base` is borrowed here
  |     |
  |     may outlive borrowed value `base`
note: closure is returned here
```

The return type must name the right trait too: a closure whose body changes its captures is `FnMut`, so the function must say `-> impl FnMut(...)`, and the caller must store it in a `let mut` binding to call it.

## 6. The Iterator trait and the three ways to iterate

An iterator is any value that implements one required method:

```
trait Iterator {
    type Item;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item>;   // Some(item), or None when done
    // ...plus dozens of provided methods (map, filter, sum, ...)
}
```

A collection gives you three iterators, which differ in the item type:

CallItem type for a `Vec<T>`The Vec afterwardsSame as

`v.iter()``&T`untouched`for x in &v`

`v.iter_mut()``&mut T`changed in place`for x in &mut v`

`v.into_iter()``T`consumed (moved)`for x in v`

A `for` loop calls `into_iter()` on whatever you give it, which is why `for x in v` consumes `v` while `for x in &v` only borrows it. `iterators.rs` shows all three.

## 7. Adapters are lazy, consumers pull

Adapters take an iterator and return a new one: `map`, `filter`, `take(n)`, `skip(n)`, `take_while`, `zip`, `enumerate`, `rev`, `step_by`, `copied`/`cloned`. Building one runs no closure. Consumers call `next` until they are done: `collect`, `sum`, `count`, `fold`, `any`, `position`, and a `for` loop.

iterator-pipeline.png: requests travel right to left, items left to right, one at a time.

An adapter chain with no consumer does nothing, and the compiler warns you:

```
warning: unused `Map` that must be used
  |     v.iter().map(|s| s * 2);
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  = note: iterators are lazy and do nothing unless consumed
```

When the consumer asks for an item, the request travels back through the chain to the source, and the item comes forward through every stage before the next item is fetched. A `filter` keeps asking for items until one passes. A `take(n)` stops asking once it has handed out `n` items, so the stages before it never see the rest.

`zip` pairs two iterators. It asks the left one first and stops as soon as the left one returns `None` (this order is documented). `skip(n)` drops the first `n` items of the iterator it is called on, and only that one.

`sum` and `collect` can produce several types, so the result type must be written somewhere: `let total: i32 = v.iter().sum();` or `.collect::<Vec<_>>()`.

## 8. What `collect` can build

ItemsTarget typeResult

`T``Vec<T>`a vector

`(K, V)``HashMap<K, V>`a map from pairs

`char``String`a string

`Result<T, E>``Result<Vec<T>, E>``Ok(vec)`, or the first `Err` (stops there)

You cannot collect owned values from references: `v.iter()` yields `&String`, so `.collect::<Vec<String>>()` fails with E0277 ("cannot be built from an iterator over elements of type `&String`"). Either collect references (`Vec<&String>`), copy them (`.cloned()`, or `.copied()` for `Copy` types), or start from `into_iter()` to get owned items.

## 9. Writing your own iterator

Put the state in a struct and implement `next`. Every adapter and consumer then works on it for free:

```
struct Countdown { left: u32 }

impl Iterator for Countdown {
    type Item = u32;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u32> {
        if self.left == 0 {
            None
        } else {
            self.left -= 1;
            Some(self.left + 1)
        }
    }
}
let ticks: Vec<u32> = Countdown { left: 3 }.collect();   // [3, 2, 1]
```

Iterator chains are not slower than loops in an optimised (`--release`) build: the compiler inlines the closures and produces the same machine code as a hand-written loop. Debug builds, which the runner uses, are slower for both.

## 10. Practice

- `ex1_compose.rs`: closures as arguments and a returned closure.

- `ex2_chains.rs`: replace loops with one chain each.

- `ex3_fib.rs`: your own iterator plus `take` and `take_while`.

## 11. Check yourself

- Why does adding `move` to a closure that only reads a `String` not make it FnOnce?

- In `v.iter().map(f).filter(g).collect()`, which closure runs first for the second element?

- When should a function take `impl FnMut` instead of `impl Fn`, and what does the caller have to change?

- What item type does `iter_mut()` give for a `Vec<String>`?

# capture-and-traits.png

Left, three boxes: "body only reads a capture (captured as &T)", "body changes a capture (captured as &mut T)", "body moves a capture out (captured as T)".
Right, three nested rounded sets: the outer set "FnOnce: can be called at least once" contains "FnMut: can be called many times", which contains "Fn: many times, even shared", with the note "every Fn is also FnMut and FnOnce; every FnMut is also FnOnce".
Arrows: reads goes to Fn, changes goes to FnMut, moves out goes to FnOnce.
Footer: `move` changes HOW captures are stored (owned instead of borrowed), not WHICH trait you get: a `move` closure that only reads is still Fn.

[entity 867 · iterator-pipeline.png · diagram]
# iterator-pipeline.png

Five boxes left to right: `iter()`, `filter(..)`, `map(..)`, `take(2)`, `collect()`.
Dark arrows above point right to left, labelled "next()?" (requests travel right to left). Green arrows below point left to right: "Some(item) travels left to right, one item at a time".
Numbered notes:
1. Adapters (filter, map, take, zip, skip, enumerate, rev) only build a value. Nothing runs yet.
2. A consumer (collect, sum, fold, count, any, a for loop) calls next() and work starts.
3. One item passes the whole chain before the next item is fetched.
4. filter keeps asking the stage before it until an item passes (or None).
5. When take has handed out its count, it stops asking: earlier stages never see the rest.

pub struct Fib {
    a: u64,
    b: u64,
}

impl Fib {
    pub fn new() -> Fib {
        Fib { a: 0, b: 1 }
    }
}

impl Iterator for Fib {
    type Item = u64;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u64> {
        let out = self.a;
        self.a = self.b;
        self.b += out;
        Some(out)
    }
}

pub fn first_fib(n: usize) -> Vec<u64> {
    Fib::new().take(n).collect()
}

pub fn even_fib_sum_below(limit: u64) -> u64 {
    Fib::new().take_while(|&x| x < limit).filter(|x| x % 2 == 0).sum()
}

### move does not mean FnOnce · 2 Nov

A closure can be `move`-capturing and still be `Fn`. `move` only changes how captures are stored (owned instead of borrowed), not which trait you get.

The trait comes from what each call does:
- only reads its captures: `Fn`
- changes a capture: `FnMut`
- moves a capture out or consumes it during the call: `FnOnce`

Example: `fn make_adder(step: i32) -> impl Fn(i32) -> i32 { let base = step * 10; move |x| x + base + step }` owns `base` and `step` but only reads them, so it stays `Fn` and can be called many times.

## 1. Closures

Adapted from The Rust Programming Language, ch 13.1-13.2, and Rust by Example (Closures, Capturing, As input parameters, Iterators), MIT/Apache-2.0.

A closure is a function you write inline, without a name, that can use the variables around it:

```
let limit = 10;
let over = |x: i32| x > limit;     // reads `limit` from the surrounding scope
println!("{}", over(12));          // true
let add_one = |x| x + 1;           // parameter and return types inferred
```

- Parameters go between bars: `|x|`, `|a, b|`, or `||` for none. The body is one expression or a `{ ... }` block.

- Types are usually inferred. They are fixed by the first use: after `add_one(5)`, calling `add_one(2.5)` is a type error.

- A `fn` item cannot read local variables of the function around it; a closure can. That is the whole point.

Parameters are patterns. Iterator methods often hand a closure a reference. A pattern can unpack it:

```
let temps = [18, 23, 31];
// iter() yields &i32; filter passes a reference to that, so its closure gets &&i32.
let warm: Vec<&i32> = temps.iter().filter(|&&t| t > 20).collect();  // t: i32
let doubled: Vec<i32> = temps.iter().map(|&t| t * 2).collect();       // t: i32
let hot: Vec<usize> = temps.iter().enumerate()
    .filter(|(_, t)| **t > 25).map(|(i, _)| i).collect();              // tuples too
```

## 2. How a closure captures

A closure captures each outside variable it uses in the weakest way its body needs:

Body doesCaptured asWhile the closure is alive

reads the variableshared borrow `&T`others may read it too

changes itmutable borrow `&mut T`nobody else may use it

moves it out (gives it away, drops it)by value `T`it now belongs to the closure

The borrow rules from 03 apply to these captures. A closure that holds `&mut count` blocks every other use of `count` until the closure's last use:

```
let mut count = 0;
let mut bump = || count += 1;   // captures &mut count
bump();
println!("{count}");            // error: bump is used again below
bump();
```

```
error[E0502]: cannot borrow `count` as immutable because it is also borrowed as mutable
  |     let mut bump = || count += 1;
  |                    -- ----- first borrow occurs due to use of `count` in closure
  |                    |
  |                    mutable borrow occurs here
  |     println!("{count}");
  |                ^^^^^ immutable borrow occurs here
  |     bump();
  |     ---- mutable borrow later used here
```

Move the `println!` after the last `bump()` and it compiles: the borrow ends when the closure is last used.

Fields, not whole structs. Since edition 2021, a closure that uses `stats.hits` captures only that field. Other fields of `stats` stay free to use while the closure is alive. (Older editions captured the whole struct.) Part 4 of `capture.rs` shows it.

## 3. `move`

Writing `move` before the bars makes the closure take ownership of every variable it uses, even ones it only reads:

```
let label = String::from("total");
let owned = move || println!("owned: {label}");
owned();
// println!("{label}");  // error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `label`
```

You need `move` when the closure must outlive the variables it uses: a closure returned from a function (section 5), or one sent to another thread (18).

With a `Copy` value (integers, `bool`, `char`, `f64`), `move` copies it into the closure. The closure then works on its own copy, and the outside variable never sees the changes:

```
let mut fuel = 50.0;
let mut burn = move || { fuel -= 10.0; fuel };   // burn owns a copy of fuel
println!("{} {}", burn(), burn());              // 40 30
println!("{fuel}");                             // 50: the outer fuel was never touched
```

## 4. Fn, FnMut and FnOnce

Every closure implements one or more of three traits. Which ones depends on what the body does with its captures, not on whether you wrote `move`:

TraitThe body...Can be called

`Fn`only reads its capturesany number of times, even through a shared reference

`FnMut`changes a capturemany times, but each call needs exclusive (`&mut`) access to the closure

`FnOnce`moves a capture outonce: the first call uses the captured value up

capture-and-traits.png: what the body does picks the trait; Fn sits inside FnMut, inside FnOnce.

The traits nest: every `Fn` closure is also `FnMut` and `FnOnce`, and every `FnMut` is also `FnOnce`. So a function that asks for `FnOnce` accepts anything; one that asks for `Fn` accepts only closures that do not mutate or move out.

A `move` closure that only reads a `String` is still `Fn`: it owns the string, but calling it does not use the string up. `move` changes how captures are stored, not which trait you get.

## 5. Closures as parameters and return values

Take a closure with `impl Fn...` or a generic bound, exactly like any other trait (09):

```
fn call_twice<F: Fn() -> usize>(f: F) -> usize {
    f() + f()
}
fn call_twice_mut<F: FnMut()>(mut f: F) {   // note `mut f`
    f();
    f();
}
fn call_once<F: FnOnce() -> String>(f: F) -> String {
    f()                                    // f is used up here
}
```

Calling an `FnMut` needs `&mut` access to the closure value (its captured state changes), so the parameter or variable that holds it must be declared `mut`. Calling an `FnOnce` consumes it, so it can be called only once in the function body.

Std examples: `Option::unwrap_or_else` takes an `FnOnce` (called at most once); `sort_by_key` takes an `FnMut` (called many times, may count or record).

### Returning a closure

```
fn make_adder(step: i32) -> impl Fn(i32) -> i32 {
    let base = step * 10;
    move |x| x + base + step
}
```

The returned closure is called after `make_adder` has returned, when `base` and `step` no longer exist. Without `move` it would borrow them:

```
error[E0373]: closure may outlive the current function, but it borrows `base`, which is owned by the current function
  |     |x| x + base + step
  |     ^^^     ---- `base` is borrowed here
  |     |
  |     may outlive borrowed value `base`
note: closure is returned here
```

The return type must name the right trait too: a closure whose body changes its captures is `FnMut`, so the function must say `-> impl FnMut(...)`, and the caller must store it in a `let mut` binding to call it.

## 6. The Iterator trait and the three ways to iterate

An iterator is any value that implements one required method:

```
trait Iterator {
    type Item;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item>;   // Some(item), or None when done
    // ...plus dozens of provided methods (map, filter, sum, ...)
}
```

A collection gives you three iterators, which differ in the item type:

CallItem type for a `Vec<T>`The Vec afterwardsSame as

`v.iter()``&T`untouched`for x in &v`

`v.iter_mut()``&mut T`changed in place`for x in &mut v`

`v.into_iter()``T`consumed (moved)`for x in v`

A `for` loop calls `into_iter()` on whatever you give it, which is why `for x in v` consumes `v` while `for x in &v` only borrows it. `iterators.rs` shows all three.

## 7. Adapters are lazy, consumers pull

Adapters take an iterator and return a new one: `map`, `filter`, `take(n)`, `skip(n)`, `take_while`, `zip`, `enumerate`, `rev`, `step_by`, `copied`/`cloned`. Building one runs no closure. Consumers call `next` until they are done: `collect`, `sum`, `count`, `fold`, `any`, `position`, and a `for` loop.

iterator-pipeline.png: requests travel right to left, items left to right, one at a time.

An adapter chain with no consumer does nothing, and the compiler warns you:

```
warning: unused `Map` that must be used
  |     v.iter().map(|s| s * 2);
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  = note: iterators are lazy and do nothing unless consumed
```

When the consumer asks for an item, the request travels back through the chain to the source, and the item comes forward through every stage before the next item is fetched. A `filter` keeps asking for items until one passes. A `take(n)` stops asking once it has handed out `n` items, so the stages before it never see the rest.

`zip` pairs two iterators. It asks the left one first and stops as soon as the left one returns `None` (this order is documented). `skip(n)` drops the first `n` items of the iterator it is called on, and only that one.

`sum` and `collect` can produce several types, so the result type must be written somewhere: `let total: i32 = v.iter().sum();` or `.collect::<Vec<_>>()`.

## 8. What `collect` can build

ItemsTarget typeResult

`T``Vec<T>`a vector

`(K, V)``HashMap<K, V>`a map from pairs

`char``String`a string

`Result<T, E>``Result<Vec<T>, E>``Ok(vec)`, or the first `Err` (stops there)

You cannot collect owned values from references: `v.iter()` yields `&String`, so `.collect::<Vec<String>>()` fails with E0277 ("cannot be built from an iterator over elements of type `&String`"). Either collect references (`Vec<&String>`), copy them (`.cloned()`, or `.copied()` for `Copy` types), or start from `into_iter()` to get owned items.

## 9. Writing your own iterator

Put the state in a struct and implement `next`. Every adapter and consumer then works on it for free:

```
struct Countdown { left: u32 }

impl Iterator for Countdown {
    type Item = u32;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u32> {
        if self.left == 0 {
            None
        } else {
            self.left -= 1;
            Some(self.left + 1)
        }
    }
}
let ticks: Vec<u32> = Countdown { left: 3 }.collect();   // [3, 2, 1]
```

Iterator chains are not slower than loops in an optimised (`--release`) build: the compiler inlines the closures and produces the same machine code as a hand-written loop. Debug builds, which the runner uses, are slower for both.

# capture-and-traits.png

Left, three boxes: "body only reads a capture (captured as &T)", "body changes a capture (captured as &mut T)", "body moves a capture out (captured as T)".
Right, three nested rounded sets: the outer set "FnOnce: can be called at least once" contains "FnMut: can be called many times", which contains "Fn: many times, even shared", with the note "every Fn is also FnMut and FnOnce; every FnMut is also FnOnce".
Arrows: reads goes to Fn, changes goes to FnMut, moves out goes to FnOnce.
Footer: `move` changes HOW captures are stored (owned instead of borrowed), not WHICH trait you get: a `move` closure that only reads is still Fn.

# iterator-pipeline.png

Five boxes left to right: `iter()`, `filter(..)`, `map(..)`, `take(2)`, `collect()`.
Dark arrows above point right to left, labelled "next()?" (requests travel right to left). Green arrows below point left to right: "Some(item) travels left to right, one item at a time".
Numbered notes:
1. Adapters (filter, map, take, zip, skip, enumerate, rev) only build a value. Nothing runs yet.
2. A consumer (collect, sum, fold, count, any, a for loop) calls next() and work starts.
3. One item passes the whole chain before the next item is fetched.
4. filter keeps asking the stage before it until an item passes (or None).
5. When take has handed out its count, it stops asking: earlier stages never see the rest.

where
    F: Fn(i32) -> i32,
    G: Fn(i32) -> i32,
{

pub struct Fib {
    a: u64,
    b: u64,
}

impl Fib {
    pub fn new() -> Fib {
        Fib { a: 0, b: 1 }
    }
}

impl Iterator for Fib {
    type Item = u64;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u64> {
        let out = self.a;
        self.a = self.b;
        self.b += out;
        Some(out)
    }
}

pub fn first_fib(n: usize) -> Vec<u64> {
    Fib::new().take(n).collect()
}

pub fn even_fib_sum_below(limit: u64) -> u64 {
    Fib::new().take_while(|&x| x < limit).filter(|x| x % 2 == 0).sum()
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn next_by_hand() {
        let mut f = Fib::new();
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(0));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(1));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(1));
        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(2));
    }

    #[test]
    fn first_few() {
        assert_eq!(first_fib(7), vec![0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8]);
        assert!(first_fib(0).is_empty());
    }

    #[test]
    fn even_sum() {
        assert_eq!(even_fib_sum_below(10), 10); // 0 + 2 + 8
        assert_eq!(even_fib_sum_below(100), 44); // + 34
    }
}

### move does not mean FnOnce · 2 Nov

A closure can be `move`-capturing and still be `Fn`. `move` only changes how captures are stored (owned instead of borrowed), not which trait you get.

The trait comes from what each call does:
- only reads its captures: `Fn`
- changes a capture: `FnMut`
- moves a capture out or consumes it during the call: `FnOnce`

Example: `fn make_adder(step: i32) -> impl Fn(i32) -> i32 { let base = step * 10; move |x| x + base + step }` owns `base` and `step` but only reads them, so it stays `Fn` and can be called many times.

## 1. Closures

Adapted from The Rust Programming Language, ch 13.1-13.2, and Rust by Example (Closures, Capturing, As input parameters, Iterators), MIT/Apache-2.0.

A closure is a function you write inline, without a name, that can use the variables around it:

```
let limit = 10;
let over = |x: i32| x > limit;     // reads `limit` from the surrounding scope
println!("{}", over(12));          // true
let add_one = |x| x + 1;           // parameter and return types inferred
```

- Parameters go between bars: `|x|`, `|a, b|`, or `||` for none. The body is one expression or a `{ ... }` block.

- Types are usually inferred. They are fixed by the first use: after `add_one(5)`, calling `add_one(2.5)` is a type error.

- A `fn` item cannot read local variables of the function around it; a closure can. That is the whole point.

Parameters are patterns. Iterator methods often hand a closure a reference. A pattern can unpack it:

```
let temps = [18, 23, 31];
// iter() yields &i32; filter passes a reference to that, so its closure gets &&i32.
let warm: Vec<&i32> = temps.iter().filter(|&&t| t > 20).collect();  // t: i32
let doubled: Vec<i32> = temps.iter().map(|&t| t * 2).collect();       // t: i32
let hot: Vec<usize> = temps.iter().enumerate()
    .filter(|(_, t)| **t > 25).map(|(i, _)| i).collect();              // tuples too
```

## 2. How a closure captures

A closure captures each outside variable it uses in the weakest way its body needs:

Body doesCaptured asWhile the closure is alive

reads the variableshared borrow `&T`others may read it too

changes itmutable borrow `&mut T`nobody else may use it

moves it out (gives it away, drops it)by value `T`it now belongs to the closure

The borrow rules from 03 apply to these captures. A closure that holds `&mut count` blocks every other use of `count` until the closure's last use:

```
let mut count = 0;
let mut bump = || count += 1;   // captures &mut count
bump();
println!("{count}");            // error: bump is used again below
bump();
```

```
error[E0502]: cannot borrow `count` as immutable because it is also borrowed as mutable
  |     let mut bump = || count += 1;
  |                    -- ----- first borrow occurs due to use of `count` in closure
  |                    |
  |                    mutable borrow occurs here
  |     println!("{count}");
  |                ^^^^^ immutable borrow occurs here
  |     bump();
  |     ---- mutable borrow later used here
```

Move the `println!` after the last `bump()` and it compiles: the borrow ends when the closure is last used.

Fields, not whole structs. Since edition 2021, a closure that uses `stats.hits` captures only that field. Other fields of `stats` stay free to use while the closure is alive. (Older editions captured the whole struct.) Part 4 of `capture.rs` shows it.

## 3. `move`

Writing `move` before the bars makes the closure take ownership of every variable it uses, even ones it only reads:

```
let label = String::from("total");
let owned = move || println!("owned: {label}");
owned();
// println!("{label}");  // error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `label`
```

You need `move` when the closure must outlive the variables it uses: a closure returned from a function (section 5), or one sent to another thread (18).

With a `Copy` value (integers, `bool`, `char`, `f64`), `move` copies it into the closure. The closure then works on its own copy, and the outside variable never sees the changes:

```
let mut fuel = 50.0;
let mut burn = move || { fuel -= 10.0; fuel };   // burn owns a copy of fuel
println!("{} {}", burn(), burn());              // 40 30
println!("{fuel}");                             // 50: the outer fuel was never touched
```

## 4. Fn, FnMut and FnOnce

Every closure implements one or more of three traits. Which ones depends on what the body does with its captures, not on whether you wrote `move`:

TraitThe body...Can be called

`Fn`only reads its capturesany number of times, even through a shared reference

`FnMut`changes a capturemany times, but each call needs exclusive (`&mut`) access to the closure

`FnOnce`moves a capture outonce: the first call uses the captured value up

capture-and-traits.png: what the body does picks the trait; Fn sits inside FnMut, inside FnOnce.

The traits nest: every `Fn` closure is also `FnMut` and `FnOnce`, and every `FnMut` is also `FnOnce`. So a function that asks for `FnOnce` accepts anything; one that asks for `Fn` accepts only closures that do not mutate or move out.

A `move` closure that only reads a `String` is still `Fn`: it owns the string, but calling it does not use the string up. `move` changes how captures are stored, not which trait you get.

## 5. Closures as parameters and return values

Take a closure with `impl Fn...` or a generic bound, exactly like any other trait (09):

```
fn call_twice<F: Fn() -> usize>(f: F) -> usize {
    f() + f()
}
fn call_twice_mut<F: FnMut()>(mut f: F) {   // note `mut f`
    f();
    f();
}
fn call_once<F: FnOnce() -> String>(f: F) -> String {
    f()                                    // f is used up here
}
```

Calling an `FnMut` needs `&mut` access to the closure value (its captured state changes), so the parameter or variable that holds it must be declared `mut`. Calling an `FnOnce` consumes it, so it can be called only once in the function body.

Std examples: `Option::unwrap_or_else` takes an `FnOnce` (called at most once); `sort_by_key` takes an `FnMut` (called many times, may count or record).

### Returning a closure

```
fn make_adder(step: i32) -> impl Fn(i32) -> i32 {
    let base = step * 10;
    move |x| x + base + step
}
```

The returned closure is called after `make_adder` has returned, when `base` and `step` no longer exist. Without `move` it would borrow them:

```
error[E0373]: closure may outlive the current function, but it borrows `base`, which is owned by the current function
  |     |x| x + base + step
  |     ^^^     ---- `base` is borrowed here
  |     |
  |     may outlive borrowed value `base`
note: closure is returned here
```

The return type must name the right trait too: a closure whose body changes its captures is `FnMut`, so the function must say `-> impl FnMut(...)`, and the caller must store it in a `let mut` binding to call it.

## 6. The Iterator trait and the three ways to iterate

An iterator is any value that implements one required method:

```
trait Iterator {
    type Item;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item>;   // Some(item), or None when done
    // ...plus dozens of provided methods (map, filter, sum, ...)
}
```

A collection gives you three iterators, which differ in the item type:

CallItem type for a `Vec<T>`The Vec afterwardsSame as

`v.iter()``&T`untouched`for x in &v`

A `for` loop calls `into_iter()` on whatever you give it, which is why `for x in v` consumes `v` while `for x in &v` only borrows it. `iterators.rs` shows all three.

## 7. Adapters are lazy, consumers pull

Adapters take an iterator and return a new one: `map`, `filter`, `take(n)`, `skip(n)`, `take_while`, `zip`, `enumerate`, `rev`, `step_by`, `copied`/`cloned`. Building one runs no closure. Consumers call `next` until they are done: `collect`, `sum`, `count`, `fold`, `any`, `position`, and a `for` loop.

iterator-pipeline.png: requests travel right to left, items left to right, one at a time.

An adapter chain with no consumer does nothing, and the compiler warns you:

```
warning: unused `Map` that must be used
  |     v.iter().map(|s| s * 2);
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  = note: iterators are lazy and do nothing unless consumed
```

When the consumer asks for an item, the request travels back through the chain to the source, and the item comes forward through every stage before the next item is fetched. A `filter` keeps asking for items until one passes. A `take(n)` stops asking once it has handed out `n` items, so the stages before it never see the rest.

`zip` pairs two iterators. It asks the left one first and stops as soon as the left one returns `None` (this order is documented). `skip(n)` drops the first `n` items of the iterator it is called on, and only that one.

`sum` and `collect` can produce several types, so the result type must be written somewhere: `let total: i32 = v.iter().sum();` or `.collect::<Vec<_>>()`.

## 8. What `collect` can build

ItemsTarget typeResult

`T``Vec<T>`a vector

`(K, V)``HashMap<K, V>`a map from pairs

`char``String`a string

`Result<T, E>``Result<Vec<T>, E>``Ok(vec)`, or the first `Err` (stops there)

You cannot collect owned values from references: `v.iter()` yields `&String`, so `.collect::<Vec<String>>()` fails with E0277 ("cannot be built from an iterator over elements of type `&String`"). Either collect references (`Vec<&String>`), copy them (`.cloned()`, or `.copied()` for `Copy` types), or start from `into_iter()` to get owned items.

## 9. Writing your own iterator

Put the state in a struct and implement `next`. Every adapter and consumer then works on it for free:

```
struct Countdown { left: u32 }

impl Iterator for Countdown {
    type Item = u32;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u32> {
        if self.left == 0 {
            None
        } else {
            self.left -= 1;
            Some(self.left + 1)
        }
    }
}
let ticks: Vec<u32> = Countdown { left: 3 }.collect();   // [3, 2, 1]
```

Iterator chains are not slower than loops in an optimised (`--release`) build: the compiler inlines the closures and produces the same machine code as a hand-written loop. Debug builds, which the runner uses, are slower for both.

# capture-and-traits.png

Left, three boxes: "body only reads a capture (captured as &T)", "body changes a capture (captured as &mut T)", "body moves a capture out (captured as T)".
Right, three nested rounded sets: the outer set "FnOnce: can be called at least once" contains "FnMut: can be called many times", which contains "Fn: many times, even shared", with the note "every Fn is also FnMut and FnOnce; every FnMut is also FnOnce".
Arrows: reads goes to Fn, changes goes to FnMut, moves out goes to FnOnce.
Footer: `move` changes HOW captures are stored (owned instead of borrowed), not WHICH trait you get: a `move` closure that only reads is still Fn.

[entity 867 · iterator-pipeline.png · diagram]
# iterator-pipeline.png

Five boxes left to right: `iter()`, `filter(..)`, `map(..)`, `take(2)`, `collect()`.
Dark arrows above point right to left, labelled "next()?" (requests travel right to left). Green arrows below point left to right: "Some(item) travels left to right, one item at a time".
Numbered notes:
1. Adapters (filter, map, take, zip, skip, enumerate, rev) only build a value. Nothing runs yet.
2. A consumer (collect, sum, fold, count, any, a for loop) calls next() and work starts.
3. One item passes the whole chain before the next item is fetched.
4. filter keeps asking the stage before it until an item passes (or None).
5. When take has handed out its count, it stops asking: earlier stages never see the rest.

pub struct Fib {
    a: u64,
    b: u64,
}

impl Fib {
    pub fn new() -> Fib {
        Fib { a: 0, b: 1 }
    }
}

impl Iterator for Fib {
    type Item = u64;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u64> {
        let out = self.a;
        self.a = self.b;
        self.b += out;
        Some(out)
    }
}

pub fn first_fib(n: usize) -> Vec<u64> {
    Fib::new().take(n).collect()
}

pub fn even_fib_sum_below(limit: u64) -> u64 {
    Fib::new().take_while(|&x| x < limit).filter(|x| x % 2 == 0).sum()
}

        assert_eq!(f.next(), Some(2));

### move does not mean FnOnce · 2 Nov

A closure can be `move`-capturing and still be `Fn`. `move` only changes how captures are stored (owned instead of borrowed), not which trait you get.

The trait comes from what each call does:
- only reads its captures: `Fn`
- changes a capture: `FnMut`
- moves a capture out or consumes it during the call: `FnOnce`

Example: `fn make_adder(step: i32) -> impl Fn(i32) -> i32 { let base = step * 10; move |x| x + base + step }` owns `base` and `step` but only reads them, so it stays `Fn` and can be called many times.

Make that visible: add a println inside the collect step so you see the interleaving.

With fix1, 25,521 of 100,000 frames (25.5%) still fail, and in each one only words 0 to 7 are wrong: one 8-word run, from an older frame of the same buffer (ages 8, 16, ...) or zero in the first frames. Words 0 to 7 are the 32 bytes of data[] that sit in the first 64-byte cache line with the 32-byte header of struct cap_buf (ts_ns, dma, seq, bytes, slot, flags): buffer 0 is at 0x7e140020. cap_complete() writes b->seq, b->bytes, b->ts_ns and b->flags before dma_sync_single_for_cpu(). If that line is still in the cache from the last round, the writes make it dirty while it still holds the old samples 0 to 7. arm64's invalidate (dcache_inval_poc) must not lose CPU data in a partial first line, so it cleans and invalidates it (dc civac): the old samples are written back over the ones the block just wrote, and the memcpy reads them. That happens only when the line survived in the L2, so about a quarter of the frames. Moving the sync above the field writes would cure this run but stays fragile: the line is shared, and any CPU write to it while the block owns the buffer can be lost or can overwrite DMA data (dma-api-howto: no cache-line sharing with a DMA_FROM_DEVICE buffer). Fix: keep the metadata out of the DMA buffer (struct cap_buf with a pointer to a separate 64 KiB buffer from kmalloc, page-aligned here, or dma_alloc_noncoherent()), or align data[] to ARCH_DMA_MINALIGN. The warnings: 'device driver failed to check map error', mapped at cap_alloc_buffers: dma_mapping_error() is never called, so a failed map would be programmed into a descriptor; check it and unwind. 'fclk0 already disabled' and 'already unprepared' come from devm_clk_release(): the clock came from devm_clk_get_enabled() and cap_remove() disables it too; drop that call. The same remove() frees buffers while the devm IRQ is still live.

  - never synced for the CPU
  - multiples of CAP_NUM_BUFS
  - returns early
  - dc civac
  - keep the metadata out
  - never called

With fix1, 25,521 of 100,000 frames (25.5%) still fail, and in each one only words 0 to 7 are wrong: one 8-word run, from an older frame of the same buffer (ages 8, 16, ...) or zero in the first frames. Words 0 to 7 are the 32 bytes of data[] that sit in the first 64-byte cache line with the 32-byte header of struct cap_buf (ts_ns, dma, seq, bytes, slot, flags): buffer 0 is at 0x7e140020. cap_complete() writes b->seq, b->bytes, b->ts_ns and b->flags before dma_sync_single_for_cpu(). If that line is still in the cache from the last round, the writes make it dirty while it still holds the old samples 0 to 7. arm64's invalidate (dcache_inval_poc) must not lose CPU data in a partial first line, so it cleans and invalidates it (dc civac): the old samples are written back over the ones the block just wrote, and the memcpy reads them. That happens only when the line survived in the L2, so about a quarter of the frames. Moving the sync above the field writes would cure this run but stays fragile: the line is shared, and any CPU write to it while the block owns the buffer can be lost or can overwrite DMA data (dma-api-howto: no cache-line sharing with a DMA_FROM_DEVICE buffer). Fix: keep the metadata out of the DMA buffer (struct cap_buf with a pointer to a separate 64 KiB buffer from kmalloc, page-aligned here, or dma_alloc_noncoherent()), or align data[] to ARCH_DMA_MINALIGN. The warnings: 'device driver failed to check map error', mapped at cap_alloc_buffers: dma_mapping_error() is never called, so a failed map would be programmed into a descriptor; check it and unwind. 'fclk0 already disabled' and 'already unprepared' come from devm_clk_release(): the clock came from devm_clk_get_enabled() and cap_remove() disables it too; drop that call. The same remove() frees buffers while the devm IRQ is still live.

  - never synced for the CPU
  - multiples of CAP_NUM_BUFS
  - returns early
  - dc civac
  - keep the metadata out
  - never called

Stage 1 (seed): reached the mechanism unprompted, non-snooped fabric master plus cacheable buffers and a CPU read through cache in the pool copy, named both files and the right remedy family. Needed two prompts to actually read dma_map_single's direction, initially asserting DMA_FROM_DEVICE; once corrected, reasoned correctly that a for_cpu sync with DMA_TO_DEVICE only cleans and does not invalidate. Did not use any of the checker's numbers (16 word runs, runs starting at word 8, ages 8/16/24, buffer address).

Stage 2 (fix1 patch, checker run, three rmmod warnings): partial. Correctly spotted that words 0 to 7 point at a single first cache line, and flagged cap_complete()'s sync placement as suspect, but explained it as descriptor ring versus payload mapping, which is not what the log shows. Did not identify that the 32 byte header of struct cap_buf shares the first 64 byte line with data[0..7] (buffer 0 at 0x7e140020), did not note that cap_complete() writes b->seq, b->bytes, b->ts_ns before the sync, and did not reason about what arm64 does with a partly covered first line. WHAT A COMPLETE ANSWER TO THE STAGE ABOVE LOOKS LIKE:
capcheck finds no bad words but 7 gaps of one frame each, and dmesg has 7 'descriptor N not owned by the block' lines, each printing ctrl 0x80010000 (OWN set), status 0 and seq 0: when the driver looks, the descriptor is valid. The ILA shows why: 16 ns after the DESC_TAIL write (0x00022d44) the block reads descriptor 3 at 0x7f3c1030 and gets ctrl 0x00010000 and status 0x80010000 with seq 142654, the values the block itself wrote back when it finished that frame, not what cap_queue_buf() wrote. The block prefetches a descriptor as soon as DESC_TAIL moves (README), so the doorbell must not reach it before the descriptor stores reach DDR. cap_queue_buf() writes the descriptor into dma_alloc_coherent() memory, which is Normal non-cacheable on this non-coherent SoC, then rings the doorbell with writel_relaxed(): with no barrier, the store to Device memory can be seen before the earlier stores to normal memory, and with stress-ng loading DDR the descriptor stores had not reached DDR when the block's read did (its data came back 276 ns after the doorbell). The comment's reason (keep the doorbell cheap) is the wrong trade: this is the one write that needs ordering. The block aborts the frame in progress, so each error loses one frame; the restart in cap_desc_error() succeeds because it runs microseconds later, when the descriptor is long in DDR (and it uses writel()). Fix: writel(cd->queued, ...) in cap_queue_buf(). On arm64 writel() is dma_wmb() (dmb oshst) then the store, which orders the descriptor stores before the doorbell; dma_wmb() followed by writel_relaxed() emits the same instructions on arm64, but memory-barriers.txt says the dma_*() barriers give no ordering against MMIO, so portable code uses writel() (or wmb() before writel_relaxed()); wmb() (dsb st) also works but costs more. device-io.rst asks for a comment that explains why a relaxed accessor is safe. 7 in 1,464,851 doorbells is about 1 in 209,000, rare enough to pass short tests.

NEVER say any of these, in any wording::
  - never synced for the CPU
  - multiples of CAP_NUM_BUFS
  - returns early
  - prefetches a descriptor
  - Normal non-cacheable
  - dmb oshst

You may point at where to look. You may not name the mechanism or the fix. If your sentence would let them answer without thinking, rewrite it.

Posted stale descriptor. CPU write not visible yet when doorbell rang.

`cap_queue_buf()` — write `DESC_TAIL` before the descriptor store is fully pushed out.

Fix: DMA sync / wmb before doorbell, e.g. write desc, `dma_sync_single_for_device()` or `wmb()`, then MMIO tail write.

move_object.question_summary: Worked a non-coherent arm64 capture driver bug across three stages: stale frame data, surviving first-line corruption plus rmmod warnings, and a soak-test descriptor race. Consistently reaches the right mechanism fast but answers in two or three asserted lines, almost never citing an address, count or specific API call from the material unless pushed. Strongest on cause, weakest on evidence and on costing a fix.
move_object.report_notes:
Stage 1 (seed): identified the mechanism immediately and unprompted: cacheable buffers written by a non-snooped fabric master, CPU reading through the cache in the pool copy, hence stale lines and kzalloc zeros. Named both relevant files and the right remedy family. Needed two prompts to actually read the mapping direction: asserted FROM_DEVICE, corrected to TO_DEVICE only after being told to reread, then correctly concluded a for_cpu sync with that direction only cleans and does not invalidate. Used none of the checker's evidence: nothing on the 16 word runs, the runs starting at word 8, the ages of 8, 16, 24, or the buffer 0 address showing data[] 32 bytes into the struct.

Stage 2 (probe, first line plus rmmod warnings): partly there. Correctly saw the surviving corruption was confined to the first cache line and that the completion path syncs while the CPU is still touching that line, but attributed the sharing to the descriptor ring rather than to the header fields of the buffer struct itself. Did not derive the layout from the printed address, did not name the fields written just before the sync, did not reason about a partly covered first line or why that yields roughly a quarter of frames. Proposed a generic split of ring and payload mappings rather than moving metadata off the line or aligning the data array. Of the three rmmod warnings: the map error check was exactly right including its location; the clock pair was broadly right as a double disable in remove but without naming the devm helper that forms the other half; the third was guessed as a double free rather than read as the matching unprepare.

Stage 3 (probe, soak descriptor race): reached the correct diagnosis in one short reply with no hints: stale descriptor, CPU descriptor store not yet visible in DDR when the doorbell reached the block, cap_queue_buf named as the function, fix as a barrier or sync before the MMIO tail write. That is the core of the expected answer and it came fast. What was absent, as in earlier stages, was any engagement with the evidence or the specifics: did not name the relaxed accessor on the doorbell line as the actual offending line, did not contrast the values the block read with the values dmesg prints for the same descriptor, did not say which barrier is correct for coherent descriptor memory against Device memory ordering or why writel is the portable choice over a dma sync on non-cacheable coherent allocations (their suggested dma_sync_single_for_device is not the right tool for a dma_alloc_coherent ring and they did not notice), did not explain why each error costs exactly one frame or why the driver's own restart path succeeds, and did not use the rate (7 in about 1.46 million doorbells) to explain why short tests pass.

Overall: strong, quick instincts for the right mechanism in a non-coherent DMA setting, and no wasted words. But the work is asserted rather than derived; across all three stages the candidate almost never quoted a line, address, count or percentage from the material, and when a detail mattered (the mapping direction, the struct layout, the accessor used for the doorbell) it was either skipped or got wrong until prompted. At mid level I would want the diagnosis backed by the evidence, and the fix named down to the exact call with its cost. The ownership reasoning is there in outline; the precision is not. The fourth stage, judging a coherent-buffer proposal against its measured cost, was not reached.
move_object.response:
That is the right picture, and you got to it fast: the doorbell overtook the descriptor stores, so the block read back its own completion values rather than the ones the driver had just written. We are out of time on this one, so I will stop you there.

One thing to carry forward from all three parts: your instinct for the mechanism was good every time, but the answers would land much harder if you pinned them to the actual evidence on the page, the exact accessor on the suspect line, the values in the capture against the ones in dmesg, the error rate against the test length. That is the difference between a plausible diagnosis and one a reviewer can merge. Thanks, let us move on.

capture: allocate the frame buffers with dma_alloc_coherent()

The streaming mapping keeps biting us: first stale cache lines everywhere,
then words 0 to 7 wrong in 26% of frames after fix1, and the
descriptor errors from the soak. Coherent memory removes the whole class:

- no cache lines to go stale, so no dma_sync_*() calls to get wrong;
- struct cap_buf no longer shares memory with the samples;
- the descriptor ring is already coherent, and with the buffers coherent
  too nothing the block reads sits in a cache, so the doorbell can stay
  writel_relaxed().

Tested on the board, test pattern on, 2 minutes (73,242 frames):
0 bad words, 0 gaps, 0 descriptor errors (capcheck_coherent_2min.log).

Cost, measured with ktime_get_ns() around the calls in cap_complete(),
mean over 36,621 frames (60 s) each:

                                fix1 (streaming)   this patch (coherent)
  dma_sync_single_for_cpu()         13.9 us                -
  memcpy() into the read pool       42.3 us           528.5 us
  cap_complete() total              60.2 us           532.5 us
  IRQ thread, % of one core          3.7 %             32.5 %

32.5% of one A53 at 610 frames/s is affordable, and the code is simpler.

capture: allocate the frame buffers with dma_alloc_coherent()

The streaming mapping keeps biting us: first stale cache lines everywhere,
then words 0 to 7 wrong in 26% of frames after fix1, and the
descriptor errors from the soak. Coherent memory removes the whole class:

- no cache lines to go stale, so no dma_sync_*() calls to get wrong;
- struct cap_buf no longer shares memory with the samples;
- the descriptor ring is already coherent, and with the buffers coherent
  too nothing the block reads sits in a cache, so the doorbell can stay
  writel_relaxed().

Tested on the board, test pattern on, 2 minutes (73,242 frames):
0 bad words, 0 gaps, 0 descriptor errors (capcheck_coherent_2min.log).

Cost, measured with ktime_get_ns() around the calls in cap_complete(),
mean over 36,621 frames (60 s) each:

                                fix1 (streaming)   this patch (coherent)
  dma_sync_single_for_cpu()         13.9 us                -
  memcpy() into the read pool       42.3 us           528.5 us
  cap_complete() total              60.2 us           532.5 us
  IRQ thread, % of one core          3.7 %             32.5 %

32.5% of one A53 at 610 frames/s is affordable, and the code is simpler.

index f758c5d..9b4848e 100644
--- a/capture.h
+++ b/capture.h
@@ -23,15 +23,15 @@

-/* One capture buffer: the block writes the samples into data[] */
+/* One capture buffer: the block writes the samples into data */
 struct cap_buf {
 	u64 ts_ns;		/* completion time, set by the IRQ thread */
-	dma_addr_t dma;		/* bus address of data[] */
+	void *data;		/* CAP_FRAME_BYTES, dma_alloc_coherent() */
+	dma_addr_t dma;		/* bus address of data */
 	u32 seq;		/* frame number, from the descriptor */
 	u32 bytes;		/* bytes written, from the descriptor */
 	u32 slot;		/* index in the ring */
 	u32 flags;
-	u8 data[];
 };
 
 #define CAP_BUF_ERR		BIT(0)
diff --git a/capture_dma.c b/capture_dma.c
index 7864f1e..6ebe65d 100644
--- a/capture_dma.c
+++ b/capture_dma.c
@@ -31,13 +31,17 @@ int cap_alloc_buffers(struct cap_dev *cd)
 	for (i = 0; i < CAP_NUM_BUFS; i++) {
 		struct cap_buf *b;
 
-		b = kzalloc(sizeof(*b) + CAP_FRAME_BYTES, GFP_KERNEL);
+		b = kzalloc(sizeof(*b), GFP_KERNEL);
 		if (!b)
 			goto err;
 
+		b->data = dma_alloc_coherent(cd->dev, CAP_FRAME_BYTES, &b->dma,
+					     GFP_KERNEL);
+		if (!b->data) {
+			kfree(b);
+			goto err;
+		}
 		b->slot = i;
-		b->dma = dma_map_single(cd->dev, b->data, CAP_FRAME_BYTES,
-					DMA_FROM_DEVICE);
 		cd->bufs[i] = b;
 	}
 
@@ -57,7 +61,7 @@ void cap_free_buffers(struct cap_dev *cd)
 
 		if (!b)
 			continue;
-		dma_unmap_single(cd->dev, b->dma, CAP_FRAME_BYTES, DMA_FROM_DEVICE);
+		dma_free_coherent(cd->dev, CAP_FRAME_BYTES, b->data, b->dma);
 		kfree(b);
 		cd->bufs[i] = NULL;
 	}
@@ -74,17 +78,13 @@ static void cap_queue_buf(struct cap_dev *cd, unsigned int idx)
 	struct cap_desc *d = &cd->ring[idx];
 	struct cap_buf *b = cd->bufs[idx];
 
-	/* the block owns the buffer again */
-	dma_sync_single_for_device(cd->dev, b->dma, CAP_FRAME_BYTES,
-				   DMA_FROM_DEVICE);
-
 	d->addr = cpu_to_le32(b->dma);
 	d->seq = 0;
 	d->status = 0;
 	d->ctrl = cpu_to_le32(CAP_DESC_OWN | CAP_FRAME_BYTES);
 
 	cd->queued++;
-	/* once per frame: keep the doorbell cheap */
+	/* ring and buffers are coherent (uncached): nothing to order */
 	writel_relaxed(cd->queued, cd->base + CAP_REG_DESC_TAIL);
 }
 
@@ -168,8 +168,6 @@ static void cap_complete(struct cap_dev *cd, unsigned int idx)
 	b->ts_ns = ktime_get_ns();
 	b->flags = (status & CAP_DESC_ERR) ? CAP_BUF_ERR : 0;
 
-	/* the CPU owns the buffer until cap_queue_buf() */
-	dma_sync_single_for_cpu(cd->dev, b->dma, CAP_FRAME_BYTES, DMA_FROM_DEVICE);
 	cap_pool_push(cd, b);
 	cd->stats.frames++;
