// Exercise 2: rules as boxed closures (reference solution)
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex2_rules.rs && ./main --test-threads=4

type Rule = Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool>;

fn max_len(n: usize) -> Rule {
    Box::new(move |s| s.len() <= n) // usize is Copy: copied in
}

fn without(word: &str) -> Rule {
    let word = word.to_string(); // own a copy; the closure must be 'static
    Box::new(move |s| !s.contains(word.as_str()))
}

fn one_of(allowed: Vec<String>) -> Rule {
    Box::new(move |s| allowed.iter().any(|a| a == s)) // the Vec is moved in
}

fn passes_all(rules: &[Rule], text: &str) -> bool {
    rules.iter().all(|r| r(text))
}

fn count_passing(rules: &[Rule], words: &[&str]) -> usize {
    words.iter().filter(|w| passes_all(rules, w)).count()
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn single_rules() {
        assert!(max_len(3)("abc"));
        assert!(!max_len(3)("abcd"));
        assert!(without("x")("abc"));
        assert!(!without("bc")("abc"));
        let r = one_of(vec!["red".into(), "blue".into()]);
        assert!(r("red") && !r("green"));
    }

    #[test]
    fn rule_outlives_the_string_it_was_made_from() {
        let rule = {
            let temp = String::from("oops");
            without(&temp)
        }; // `temp` is dropped here; the rule must still work
        assert!(rule("fine"));
        assert!(!rule("oops!"));
    }

    #[test]
    fn rules_of_different_closure_types_in_one_vec() {
        let rules: Vec<Rule> = vec![max_len(5), without("z"), Box::new(|s: &str| !s.is_empty())];
        assert!(passes_all(&rules, "abc"));
        assert!(!passes_all(&rules, "abcdef"));
        assert!(!passes_all(&rules, ""));
        assert!(passes_all(&[], "anything"));
        assert_eq!(count_passing(&rules, &["ok", "zoo", "toolong", "", "fine"]), 2);
    }
}

    fn color(&self) -> &'static str;
    // Default: most lights stay on for 30 seconds.
    fn seconds(&self) -> u32 {
        30
    }

struct Red;
struct Green;
struct Yellow;

impl Light for Red {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Green)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "red"
    }
}

impl Light for Green {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Yellow)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "green"
    }
}

impl Light for Yellow {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Red)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "yellow"
    }
    fn seconds(&self) -> u32 {
        5
    }
}

struct Signal {
    light: Option<Box<dyn Light>>,
}

impl Signal {
    fn new() -> Signal {
        Signal { light: Some(Box::new(Red)) }
    }

    fn advance(&mut self) {
        // take() leaves None behind, giving us the owned Box to consume.
        let old = self.light.take().unwrap();
        self.light = Some(old.next());
    }

    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        self.light.as_ref().unwrap().color()
    }

    fn run_for(&mut self, n: usize) -> u32 {
        let mut total = 0;
        for _ in 0..n {
            total += self.light.as_ref().unwrap().seconds();
            self.advance();
        }
        total
    }
}

## 5. Default methods through `dyn`
A trait may give a method a default body. In `widgets.rs`, `label` has a default and `Checkbox` overrides it:

```
trait Render {
    fn render(&self) -> String;
    fn label(&self) -> String { String::from("(unnamed)") }
}
impl Render for Checkbox {
    fn render(&self) -> String { /* ... */ }
    fn label(&self) -> String { String::from("checkbox") }
}
```

How does a vtable deal with this? Every vtable has a row for every trait method, defaults included. For `Checkbox` the `label` row points at `Checkbox::label`. For `Text`, which does not override it, the row points at the default body compiled for `Text`. A default method is like a small generic function: the compiler makes one copy of it per implementing type.

## 4. Choosing between generics and trait objects
SituationUseWhy

A function used with one type at a timegeneric `T: Trait` or `impl Trait`fastest; no allocation; inlinable

## 1. Two ways to abstract
You already know one way to write code that works for many types: generics (sub-module 09). `fn show<T: Display>(item: &T)` works for any `T` that implements `Display`. ## 1. Two ways to abstract

You already know one way to write code that works for many types: generics (sub-module 09). `fn show<T: Display>(item: &T)` works for any `T` that implements `Display`. The compiler handles it by monomorphisation: it writes one copy of `show` for every concrete type you call it with, `show::<i32>`, `show::<String>` and so on. Each copy knows its type exactly, so every call is a direct call that can be inlined. This is static dispatch: the method is chosen at compile time.

Generics have one limit: each use picks one type. A `Vec<T>` holds values of a single type `T`. A function returning `impl Trait` returns one concrete type, even if the caller cannot name it. So how do you keep a text box, a checkbox and a button in one list and call `render` on each?

Rust's answer is a trait object, written `dyn Trait`. A trait object stands for "some value of a type that implements `Trait`; which type is decided at run time". There is only one copy of the code that uses it, and each method call is looked up at run time. This is dynamic dispatch.

Generics (`T: Trait`)Trait objects (`dyn Trait`)

Method chosenat compile timeat run time, through a vtable

Copies of your functionone per concrete typeone

Inliningyesusually not

Mixed types in one `Vec`noyes: `Vec<Box<dyn Trait>>`

The Rust Book (ch. 18.2, "Using Trait Objects to Allow for Values of Different Types") builds a GUI library this way. Our `widgets.rs` is a small version of it:

```
let parts: Vec<Box<dyn Render>> =
    vec![Box::new(Text("hello".into())), Box::new(Checkbox(true))];
for part in &parts {
    println!("{}", part.render()); // which render? decided per element, at run time
}
```

The `Vec` still holds one type: `Box<dyn Render>`. What differs is the type inside each box.

## 2. Behind a pointer: fat pointers and vtables

A `Text` and a `Checkbox` have different sizes. So what size is a `dyn Render`? There is no single answer: `dyn Render` is an unsized type (its size is not known at compile time). Rust can only store values whose size it knows, on the stack, in a struct field or in a `Vec` slot. That is why a trait object always sits behind a pointer: `&dyn Render`, `&mut dyn Render` or `Box<dyn Render>`.

That pointer is a fat pointer: two machine words.

- A data pointer to the value itself (the `Checkbox` on the heap, or wherever it lives).

- A vtable pointer to a table the compiler built for that pair (concrete type, trait).

A vtable ("virtual method table") holds the information needed to use the value without knowing its type: how to drop it, its size and alignment, then one entry per trait method, each pointing at the machine code for that type's version of the method.

Two boxed trait objects. Each element of `parts` is a data pointer plus a vtable pointer. Each (type, Render) pair has its own vtable whose rows point at that type's code.

A call such as `part.label()` does three things at run time: follow the vtable pointer, read the `label` row, call the function found there with the data pointer as `self`. That indirect call is the cost of dynamic dispatch: one extra memory read, and the compiler usually cannot inline the call because it does not know which function it will be.

You can see the "fat" part directly. `static_vs_dyn.rs` prints the sizes of a thin and a fat reference:

```
&i32: 8 bytes, &dyn Display: 16 bytes
```

These numbers are for a 64-bit machine (8-byte pointers). The rule is "two pointers instead of one", not "16 bytes". The exact layout of a vtable (row order, whether two values of the same type share one vtable) is a compiler detail you never rely on.

A `Box<dyn Trait>` also costs a heap allocation per value, because each value must live somewhere the box can point to. A borrowed `&dyn Trait` needs no allocation: `let one: &dyn Render = &Text("plain".into());` in `widgets.rs` points at a value that is already somewhere.

## 3. `Sized` and `?Sized`

Every generic parameter has a hidden bound: `T: Sized`, "the size of `T` is known at compile time". That is almost always what you want, since the function may need to store a `T`. But it means this generic function cannot be called with a trait object:

```
fn show_any<T: Display>(item: &T) -> String { format!("[{item}]") }

let m: Box<dyn Display> = Box::new(7);
show_any(m.as_ref()); // T would be `dyn Display`, which is not Sized
```

```
error[E0277]: the size for values of type `dyn std::fmt::Display` cannot be known at compilation time
```

Write `T: ?Sized` ("`T` may or may not be sized") to remove the hidden bound. This is fine here because `show_any` only ever touches `T` through a reference `&T`, which is a pointer of known size:

```
fn show_any<T: Display + ?Sized>(item: &T) -> String { format!("[{item}]") }
```

Now `T` can be `dyn Display`, or `str` (another unsized type you have used since 03 behind `&str`).

## 4. Choosing between generics and trait objects

SituationUseWhy

A function used with one type at a timegeneric `T: Trait` or `impl Trait`fastest; no allocation; inlinable

A list (or field) holding several types at once`Vec<Box<dyn Trait>>`a `Vec<T>` has exactly one `T`

Types chosen at run time (from a config file, user input, plugins)`Box<dyn Trait>`the compiler cannot know the type

Want less generated code (many types, big function)`&dyn Trait`one copy instead of one per type

A small, fixed set of kinds you controlan `enum`see section 9

A common mistake is to think `Vec<T>` with `T: Trait` can hold "anything that implements `Trait`". It cannot: `T` is one type, chosen by the caller. Only `dyn Trait` erases the concrete type.

## 5. Default methods through `dyn`

A trait may give a method a default body. In `widgets.rs`, `label` has a default and `Checkbox` overrides it:

```
trait Render {
    fn render(&self) -> String;
    fn label(&self) -> String { String::from("(unnamed)") }
}
impl Render for Checkbox {
    fn render(&self) -> String { /* ... */ }
    fn label(&self) -> String { String::from("checkbox") }
}
```

How does a vtable deal with this? Every vtable has a row for every trait method, defaults included. For `Checkbox` the `label` row points at `Checkbox::label`. For `Text`, which does not override it, the row points at the default body compiled for `Text`. A default method is like a small generic function: the compiler makes one copy of it per implementing type.

This explains what happens when a default calls another method of the same trait. Inside the copy compiled for `Text`, `self` is a `&Text`, so `self.render()` calls `Text::render`; the type is known there, so that inner call is static. Only the outer call through the trait object goes through the vtable.

To predict what a default method does for a type, read it as if you had pasted its body into that type's `impl` block. Every `self.method()` inside it then resolves to that type's own `method`, overridden or not.

## 6. Dyn compatibility: which traits can be objects

A vtable is a fixed list: one row per method, each pointing at one function. Some methods cannot fit in such a list, so a trait containing them cannot be used as `dyn Trait`. Such a trait is not dyn compatible (older texts say "not object safe"). The main rules, from the Rust Reference:

Method shapeProblem for a vtable

`fn copy(&self) -> Self`The caller must reserve space for the returned `Self`, but behind `dyn` its size is unknown.

`fn put<V: ToString>(&mut self, v: V)`A generic method is a family of functions, one per `V`. A fixed list cannot hold an open-ended family.

`fn new() -> Self` (no `self`)There is no value, so no vtable to look in.

Uncomment both `doubled` lines in `dyn_compat.rs` to see the error:

```
error[E0038]: the trait `Shape` is not dyn compatible
  ...because method `doubled` references the `Self` type in its return type
```

There are two ways out.

- Keep the method off the vtable with `where Self: Sized`. The trait becomes dyn compatible again, and the method can still be called on concrete types, but not on a `dyn Shape`. `dyn_compat.rs` does this with `doubled_sized`.

- Change the method's shape so it fits in a vtable: return `Box<dyn Shape>` instead of `Self`, or take `&dyn ToString` (or a `String`) instead of a generic `V`. Each costs something: a heap allocation, a conversion, or a second dynamic call.

`Box<dyn Trait>` does not make an incompatible trait compatible. The problem is the trait's methods, not where the object is stored.

## 7. Supertraits

`trait Shape: Debug { ... }` says "every type that implements `Shape` must also implement `Debug`". `Debug` is a supertrait of `Shape`. Two consequences:

- Code that has a `Shape` may use `Debug` too. Debug's method joins Shape's vtable, so `println!("{:?}", shapes[0])` works on a `Box<dyn Shape>`.

- Because the supertrait's methods join the vtable, the supertrait must be dyn compatible as well. `Debug` and `Display` are. `Clone` is not (`clone` returns `Self`), and neither is `Default` (`default()` has no `self` and returns `Self`). So `trait Shape: Clone` makes `dyn Shape` impossible.

```
use std::fmt::Debug;
trait Shape: Debug { fn area(&self) -> f64; }

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Square(f64);
impl Shape for Square { fn area(&self) -> f64 { self.0 * self.0 } }
// impl Shape for Square requires Square: Debug, which the derive provides.
```

## 8. Boxed closures and `'static`

Every closure has its own unnamed type, even two closures with the same signature (10). So a list of closures needs a trait object: `Vec<Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool>>`. `Fn`, `FnMut` and `FnOnce` are traits like any other.

A rule you will meet often: in a struct field or in a function's return type, `Box<dyn Trait>` is short for `Box<dyn Trait + 'static>`. `'static` here means "the value inside does not borrow anything that could go away". A closure meets it if every captured value is owned by the closure: copied in, cloned in or moved in. It fails if it captures a reference to a local variable or to a parameter.

```
fn prefix_rule(prefix: &str) -> Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool> {
    let owned = prefix.to_string();                // the closure gets its own copy
    Box::new(move |s| s.starts_with(owned.as_str()))
}
```

If the closure used `prefix` directly, it would hold a borrow that only lives as long as the caller's string, and the compiler refuses:

```
error: lifetime may not live long enough
  returning this value requires that `'1` must outlive `'static`
```

`move` moves whatever the closure names. If the variable is itself a reference (`prefix: &str`, `limit: &u32`), `move` moves the reference into the closure. The closure still borrows. To own the data, copy or clone it out first: `let limit = *limit;` or `let owned = prefix.to_string();`.

A `&dyn Fn(..)` parameter, by contrast, may borrow freely: it is only used during the call. Writing other lifetimes, such as `Box<dyn Fn() + 'a>`, is covered in 14.

## 9. Consuming a trait object; trait objects vs enums

A method may take its receiver as `self: Box<Self>`. It then consumes the box: after the call, the object is gone. The Book's state pattern (ch. 18.3, "Implementing an Object-Oriented Design Pattern") uses this so a state transition uses up the old state. `state.rs` is adapted from it:

```
trait State {
    fn submit(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn State>;
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str;
}
impl State for Draft {
    fn submit(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn State> { Box::new(Review) }
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str { "draft" }
}
```

`self: Box<Self>` is dyn compatible: the receiver is a pointer of known size, so the call can go through the vtable. The catch is that you must own the box to call it. A shared or mutable borrow of a box is not enough; you cannot move a box out from behind a reference. When the box sits inside something else, take it out first:

Where the box livesHow to take it out

`Option<Box<dyn State>>``opt.take()` leaves `None` behind

a field or variable of a type with a default`std::mem::take(&mut x)` (11)

a `Vec<Box<dyn T>>`, all of it`v.drain(..)` or `mem::take(&mut v)`, which leave it empty

a `Vec`, one element`v.remove(i)` or `v.pop()`

### Trait objects or an enum?

The same states could be an `enum State { Draft, Review, Published }` with `match` in each operation. The two designs make different changes cheap:

ChangeTrait objectsEnum + match

Add a new kind (type / variant)one new type and its `impl`; no other code changesedit every `match`

Add a new operationadd a method to the trait and to every typeone new function with one `match`; the compiler checks every case

Types from outside your crate (plugins)yesno: the set is closed

Cost per callvtable call, heap allocation per boxa `match` on a tag; no allocation needed

Ask the Tutor about any of these. Try to answer first.

- Why must `dyn Trait` always sit behind a pointer? What are the two halves of that pointer?

- Why can a trait with `fn copy(&self) -> Self` not be a trait object, while `fn copy(&self) -> Box<dyn Trait>` is fine?

- A default method calls `self.unit()`. For a type that overrides `unit`, which `unit` runs, and why?

- Why does a closure stored in a `Box<dyn Fn()>` field have to own what it captures?

Left, two elements of `parts: Vec<Box<dyn Render>>`. Each element is two pointers side by side: a "data ptr" and a "vtable ptr".

- Text's `render` row -> `Text::render`. Text's `label` row -> the trait's default `label`, compiled for Text (Text does not override it).

trait Animal {
    fn name(&self) -> String;
    fn sound(&self) -> String;
    // Default: "<name> says <sound>"
    fn speak(&self) -> String {
        format!("{} says {}", self.name(), self.sound())
    }
}

struct Dog;
struct Cat {
    name: String,
}
struct Parrot {
    word: String,
}

impl Animal for Dog {
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        String::from("dog")
    }
    fn sound(&self) -> String {
        String::from("woof")
    }
}

impl Animal for Cat {
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        self.name.clone()
    }
    fn sound(&self) -> String {
        String::from("meow")
    }
}

impl Animal for Parrot {
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        String::from("parrot")
    }
    fn sound(&self) -> String {
        self.word.clone()
    }

// Exercise 2: rules as boxed closures (reference solution)
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex2_rules.rs && ./main --test-threads=4

type Rule = Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool>;

fn max_len(n: usize) -> Rule {
    Box::new(move |s| s.len() <= n) // usize is Copy: copied in
}

fn without(word: &str) -> Rule {
    let word = word.to_string(); // own a copy; the closure must be 'static
    Box::new(move |s| !s.contains(word.as_str()))
}

fn one_of(allowed: Vec<String>) -> Rule {
    Box::new(move |s| allowed.iter().any(|a| a == s)) // the Vec is moved in
}

fn passes_all(rules: &[Rule], text: &str) -> bool {
    rules.iter().all(|r| r(text))
}

fn count_passing(rules: &[Rule], words: &[&str]) -> usize {
    words.iter().filter(|w| passes_all(rules, w)).count()
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn single_rules() {
        assert!(max_len(3)("abc"));
        assert!(!max_len(3)("abcd"));
        assert!(without("x")("abc"));
        assert!(!without("bc")("abc"));
        let r = one_of(vec!["red".into(), "blue".into()]);
        assert!(r("red") && !r("green"));
    }

    #[test]
    fn rule_outlives_the_string_it_was_made_from() {
        let rule = {
            let temp = String::from("oops");
            without(&temp)
        }; // `temp` is dropped here; the rule must still work
        assert!(rule("fine"));
        assert!(!rule("oops!"));
    }

    #[test]
    fn rules_of_different_closure_types_in_one_vec() {
        let rules: Vec<Rule> = vec![max_len(5), without("z"), Box::new(|s: &str| !s.is_empty())];
        assert!(passes_all(&rules, "abc"));
        assert!(!passes_all(&rules, "abcdef"));
        assert!(!passes_all(&rules, ""));
        assert!(passes_all(&[], "anything"));
        assert_eq!(count_passing(&rules, &["ok", "zoo", "toolong", "", "fine"]), 2);
    }

trait Light {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light>;
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str;
    // Default: most lights stay on for 30 seconds.
    fn seconds(&self) -> u32 {
        30
    }
}

struct Red;
struct Green;
struct Yellow;

impl Light for Red {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Green)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "red"
    }
}

impl Light for Green {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Yellow)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "green"
    }
}

impl Light for Yellow {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Red)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "yellow"
    }
    fn seconds(&self) -> u32 {
        5
    }
}

struct Signal {
    light: Option<Box<dyn Light>>,
}

impl Signal {
    fn new() -> Signal {
        Signal { light: Some(Box::new(Red)) }
    }

    fn advance(&mut self) {
        // take() leaves None behind, giving us the owned Box to consume.
        let old = self.light.take().unwrap();
        self.light = Some(old.next());
    }

    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        self.light.as_ref().unwrap().color()
    }

    fn run_for(&mut self, n: usize) -> u32 {
        let mut total = 0;
        for _ in 0..n {
            total += self.light.as_ref().unwrap().seconds();
            self.advance();
        }
        total
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn cycle_of_colours() {
        let mut s = Signal::new();
        let mut seen = vec![s.color()];
        for _ in 0..3 {
            s.advance();
            seen.push(s.color());
        }
        assert_eq!(seen, ["red", "green", "yellow", "red"]);
    }

    fn default_and_overridden_seconds() {
        assert_eq!(Red.seconds(), 30);
        assert_eq!(Green.seconds(), 30);
        assert_eq!(Yellow.seconds(), 5);
    }

        assert_eq!(s.run_for(0), 0);

fn classify(pair: (i32, i32)) -> String {
    match pair {
        (0, 0) => String::from("origin"),
        (x, 0) | (0, x) if x < 0 => format!("negative axis {x}"),
        (x, 0) | (0, x) => format!("axis {x}"),

        (n @ 1..=9, _) => format!("small first {n}"),
        _ => String::from("other"),
    }
}

const STOP: &str = "stop";

fn route(cmd: &String, fallback: &str) -> String {
    match cmd.as_str() {
        STOP => String::from("halt"),
        c @ ("go" | "run") => format!("move ({c})"),
        c if c == fallback => format!("fallback {fallback}"),
        other => format!("unknown {other}"),
    }
}

fn main() {
    let default = "wait";
    for word in ["stop", "run", "wait", "jump"] {
        println!("{}", route(&String::from(word), default));
    }
}

const STOP: &str = "stop";

fn route(cmd: &String, fallback: &str) -> String {
    match cmd.as_str() {
        STOP => String::from("halt"),
        c @ ("go" | "run") => format!("move ({c})"),
        c if c == fallback => format!("fallback {fallback}"),
        other => format!("unknown {other}"),
    }
}

fn main() {
    let default = "wait";
    for word in ["stop", "run", "wait", "jump"] {
        println!("{}", route(&String::from(word), default));
    }
}

enum Signal {
    Level(u8),
    Pulse { width: u8, repeat: bool },
    Off,
}

fn describe(signal: &Signal) -> String {
    match signal {
        Signal::Off => String::from("off"),
        Signal::Level(0) => String::from("level zero"),
        Signal::Level(1..=99) => String::from("low level"),
        Signal::Level(100) => String::from("medium level"),
        Signal::Level(101..=255) => String::from("high level"),
        Signal::Pulse { repeat: true, .. } => String::from("repeating pulse"),
        Signal::Pulse { width, repeat: false } if *width > 10 => format!("wide pulse {width}"),
        Signal::Pulse { .. } => String::from("pulse"),
    }
}

fn main() {
    let items = [Signal::Level(0), Signal::Level(150), Signal::Pulse { width: 20, repeat: false }, Signal::Off];
    for s in &items {
        println!("{}", describe(s));
    }
}

    match items {

fn route(cmd: &String, fallback: &str) -> String {
    match cmd.as_str() {
        STOP => String::from("halt"),
        c @ ("go" | "run") => format!("move ({c})"),
        c if c == fallback => format!("fallback {fallback}"),
        other => format!("unknown {other}"),
    }
}

fn main() {

    for word in ["stop", "run", "wait", "jump"] {
        println!("{}", route(&String::from(word), default));
    }
}

enum Signal {
    Level(u8),
    Pulse { width: u8, repeat: bool },
    Off,
}

fn describe(signal: &Signal) -> String {
    match signal {
        Signal::Off => String::from("off"),
        Signal::Level(0) => String::from("level zero"),
        Signal::Level(1..=99) => String::from("low level"),
        Signal::Level(100) => String::from("medium level"),
        Signal::Level(101..=255) => String::from("high level"),
        Signal::Pulse { repeat: true, .. } => String::from("repeating pulse"),
        Signal::Pulse { width, repeat: false } if *width > 10 => format!("wide pulse {width}"),
        Signal::Pulse { .. } => String::from("pulse"),
    }
}

    let items = [Signal::Level(0), Signal::Level(150), Signal::Pulse { width: 20, repeat: false }, Signal::Off];
    for s in &items {

The bill is mostly explained by PR fixer, and specifically by how often it ran and how expensive each run is at model-3 list price.

From the billing export, PR fixer is the dominant spend line every day in October. The daily rows in the export show PR fixer using roughly 1.6k–3.4k requests/day for most of the month, with spend often in the low thousands per day (for example 2026-10-02: $4,363.98; 2026-10-06: $3,934.70; 2026-10-13: $4,109.35). Over the month that adds up to the bulk of the $61,218 bill.

The config explains why. In `infra/agents/pr-fixer/budget_config.yaml`, PR fixer is configured to use `model-3`, and the comments say the model price is $5/M input tokens and $25/M output tokens. That’s a very expensive output rate for a background fixer agent.

The histogram you attached also suggests PR fixer has a long tail: most runs are cheap, but there are enough very expensive runs to drive the total up. The export supports that too: output tokens are huge on PR fixer runs—often 400k–700k+ output tokens per day. Since output is priced at $25/M, output dominates the bill.

Back-of-the-envelope: October PR fixer usage is about 3,200 runs. The export shows roughly 61.1M input tokens and about 13.9M output tokens for PR fixer across the month, which at list price is on the order of the reported spend. So this isn’t a mystery bill; it’s volume plus an expensive model plus high output.

What I would change first: cap PR fixer’s output and reduce its model cost. Concretely, I’d first change `infra/agents/pr-fixer/budget_config.yaml` to move PR fixer off `model-3` or at least lower the allowed completion budget / truncate the agent’s loop so it can’t emit hundreds of thousands of tokens per run. If I had to pick one immediate lever, I’d reduce PR fixer’s max output and stop it from doing long iterative fixes on every failed CI run.

So the short answer is: the bill is driven by PR fixer’s high run count, expensive model, and especially output tokens; first change the PR fixer config to constrain or downgrade the model and hard-limit output per run.

The bill is mostly explained by PR fixer, and specifically by how often it ran and how expensive each run is at model-3 list price.

From the billing export, PR fixer is the dominant spend line every day in October. The daily rows in the export show PR fixer using roughly 1.6k–3.4k requests/day for most of the month, with spend often in the low thousands per day (for example 2026-10-02: $4,363.98; 2026-10-06: $3,934.70; 2026-10-13: $4,109.35). Over the month that adds up to the bulk of the $61,218 bill.

The config explains why. In `infra/agents/pr-fixer/budget_config.yaml`, PR fixer is configured to use `model-3`, and the comments say the model price is $5/M input tokens and $25/M output tokens. That’s a very expensive output rate for a background fixer agent.

The histogram you attached also suggests PR fixer has a long tail: most runs are cheap, but there are enough very expensive runs to drive the total up. The export supports that too: output tokens are huge on PR fixer runs—often 400k–700k+ output tokens per day. Since output is priced at $25/M, output dominates the bill.

Back-of-the-envelope: October PR fixer usage is about 3,200 runs. The export shows roughly 61.1M input tokens and about 13.9M output tokens for PR fixer across the month, which at list price is on the order of the reported spend. So this isn’t a mystery bill; it’s volume plus an expensive model plus high output.

What I would change first: cap PR fixer’s output and reduce its model cost. Concretely, I’d first change `infra/agents/pr-fixer/budget_config.yaml` to move PR fixer off `model-3` or at least lower the allowed completion budget / truncate the agent’s loop so it can’t emit hundreds of thousands of tokens per run. If I had to pick one immediate lever, I’d reduce PR fixer’s max output and stop it from doing long iterative fixes on every failed CI run.

So the short answer is: the bill is driven by PR fixer’s high run count, expensive model, and especially output tokens; first change the PR fixer config to constrain or downgrade the model and hard-limit output per run.

WHAT A COMPLETE ANSWER TO THE STAGE ABOVE LOOKS LIKE:
Each call re-sends the whole conversation (history: full, no compaction, no caching) and adds a few hundred tokens to it, so call t costs roughly a + b·t and the run costs about the square of its length. Call 1 sent 18,922 tokens ($0.098), call 1,000 sent 545,542 ($2.73), call 1,859 sent 999,715 ($5.00). Hour 9 cost $743.31 for 155 calls against $154.72 for 290 in hour 1: fewer calls, 4.8 times the money. Input was $4,802.13 of $4,812.88. It ended only when the prompt passed 1,000,000 tokens: an unhandled API error, no commit, no comment, sandbox deleted. It should have stopped at call 21 ($3.48, under 4 minutes): the model said the failure was intermittent and not the PR's (the PR touches billing; the test fails 38 of 266 runs on main). The system prompt ('keep going until every check is green', 'do not ask for help') gave it no permitted way to stop, and its own bar, 50 passes in a row at a 14% failure rate, has a chance of 0.857^50, about 0.04%. No edit moved the failure rate (13.7%, 15.5%, 12.1% against 14.3%), and there was no new working-tree state after call 57. Stops, in the harness, checked before every call: a per-run budget ($10 fires at call 49, 9 minutes; $47.05 at call 144, 29 minutes); a turn cap and a wall clock (60 minutes still costs $154.72, hour 1 on page 2); no progress, such as 50 calls with no new working-tree state (call 107, $29.96); a repeated-action breaker (5 identical calls fires at call 11, a fair flakiness check, so it should pause and ask, not kill); compaction under a context cap. A graceful stop: stop calling the model, build the handoff from the log (edits tried, failure rate with each, fails on main too), post it on PR #3318, flag the test to its owners, keep the branch, record the run as stopped by budget rather than an error. Better still, check against main before starting.

NEVER say any of these, in any wording::
  - above the p95
  - caps the wrong side
  - shared with ask-prod
  - square of its length
  - no permitted way
  - stopped by budget

You may point at where to look. You may not name the mechanism or the fix. If your sentence would let them answer without thinking, rewrite it.

The growth pattern is consistent with a runaway loop where PR fixer kept re-reading and re-scanning the repo after each failed attempt, so the input context kept expanding while the run accumulated more calls. The important part is that the cost rises because each turn adds more repository state, CI output, and prior diffs into the prompt, so the per-request input size balloons over time rather than staying flat.

For this run, the stop point should have been after a bounded number of repair attempts on PR #3318 once the same failure was being re-encountered. A hard stop should have been set in the PR fixer agent configuration, at the agent-level execution loop in `infra/agents/pr-fixer/budget_config.yaml`, by lowering the per-run request cap / max iterations so the fixer cannot keep cycling for nine hours on one PR. If I had to name the exact control, it should be the max-call / max-iteration stop for the fixer workflow, set low enough to terminate after the first few unsuccessful edit + CI cycles.

Each call re-sends the whole conversation (history: full, no compaction, no caching) and adds a few hundred tokens to it, so call t costs roughly a + b·t and the run costs about the square of its length. Call 1 sent 18,922 tokens ($0.098), call 1,000 sent 545,542 ($2.73), call 1,859 sent 999,715 ($5.00). Hour 9 cost $743.31 for 155 calls against $154.72 for 290 in hour 1: fewer calls, 4.8 times the money. Input was $4,802.13 of $4,812.88. It ended only when the prompt passed 1,000,000 tokens: an unhandled API error, no commit, no comment, sandbox deleted. It should have stopped at call 21 ($3.48, under 4 minutes): the model said the failure was intermittent and not the PR's (the PR touches billing; the test fails 38 of 266 runs on main). The system prompt ('keep going until every check is green', 'do not ask for help') gave it no permitted way to stop, and its own bar, 50 passes in a row at a 14% failure rate, has a chance of 0.857^50, about 0.04%. No edit moved the failure rate (13.7%, 15.5%, 12.1% against 14.3%), and there was no new working-tree state after call 57.   - no permitted way

The prompt is being filled by the accumulated conversation state, not fresh file reads: the agent keeps appending its own prior tool outputs, CI logs, intermediate reasoning, and increasingly large edit/search results into the context. So even after no new files were read, the running transcript kept growing until it hit the near-1M token context window.

WHAT A COMPLETE ANSWER TO THE STAGE ABOVE LOOKS LIKE:
No single cap works. At the overall p95 ($10.48) it would have stopped 46 runs that went on to fix the PR; at the overall p99 ($47.05), 4 dependency updates that were fixed at up to $82.21; and $47 is still twenty times anything a lint fix ever needed ($2.19). Set limits per task class from the fixed runs: a soft limit near the class's fixed p95 and a hard cap between the most a fix has cost and about twice that, or near the fixed p95 where more spend never produced a fix. Roughly: lint_format $3, type_check $12, test_failure $30, dependency_update $150 with a checkpoint near $30 (fixed p95 $29.98), flaky_or_infra $5 (29 fixes in 266 runs, none above $16.77). Replayed on October, caps like these stop 63 runs, 1 of them a fix, and the month costs about $8,950 instead of $51,887. At the soft limit the run pauses, posts what it has done, and asks a human for more budget; a long dependency update shows progress (fewer failing tests, new files changed) and a loop does not, so more budget is granted on progress. At the hard cap it stops with the handoff from the last step. The catch: the class is assigned after the run, and flaky_or_infra, the class holding almost every runaway (17 of the 20 runs over $500, and all ten of the most expensive), is invisible at trigger time. So add a pre-flight check (does the failing test also fail on main, is it on a known-flaky list, does the log match an infra error such as a registry 429 or a simulator that failed to boot) and don't start the agent on those: comment on the PR and route the test to its owners. That alone removes the eight most expensive runs, all on test_reschedule_notifies_driver ($30,298, 58% of the month). Keep the no-progress and repeated-action detectors on every class; they tell a long run from a loop at any budget, and the caps are the backstop. Review the limits monthly by counting the fixes each one stopped.

NEVER say any of these, in any wording::
  - above the p95
  - caps the wrong side
  - shared with ask-prod
  - from the fixed runs
  - pre-flight check
  - granted on progress

You may point at where to look. You may not name the mechanism or the fix. If your sentence would let them answer without thinking, rewrite it.

I’d set a layered budget with a hard per-run token cap, a hard per-run call cap, and a short wall-clock timeout, then fail closed when any one is hit.

Given the shape of the October distribution, I would start with something like:
- max tool calls: 25–40 per run
- max input tokens: low hundreds of thousands, not anywhere near 1M
- max wall time: perhaps 30–45 minutes

The key is to place the token cap low enough that a runaway like run 77120 gets cut off after the first repeated cycle, but high enough that a normal fixer has room for a read/log/patch/retest loop.

At the moment a run hits a limit, the agent should stop immediately, write a concise status comment on the PR saying it hit its automation budget and could not complete the fix, and preserve whatever partial diff it has already produced. It should not keep iterating, and it should not keep reloading context. If there is a plausible partial change, it can leave that for a human to inspect; otherwise it should leave the PR untouched and report the blocking failure.

Since the run starts knowing only the repo, failing check name, and the check log, I’d bias the initial budget toward a small number of read/search cycles and one or two edit/test cycles, then stop early if the same failure repeats.

No single cap works. At the overall p95 ($10.48) it would have stopped 46 runs that went on to fix the PR; at the overall p99 ($47.05), 4 dependency updates that were fixed at up to $82.21; and $47 is still twenty times anything a lint fix ever needed ($2.19). Roughly: lint_format $3, type_check $12, test_failure $30, dependency_update $150 with a checkpoint near $30 (fixed p95 $29.98), flaky_or_infra $5 (29 fixes in 266 runs, none above $16.77). Replayed on October, caps like these stop 63 runs, 1 of them a fix, and the month costs about $8,950 instead of $51,887. At the soft limit the run pauses, posts what it has done, and asks a human for more budget; a long dependency update shows progress (fewer failing tests, new files changed) and a loop does not, so more budget is granted on progress. At the hard cap it stops with the handoff from the last step. The catch: the class is assigned after the run, and flaky_or_infra, the class holding almost every runaway (17 of the 20 runs over $500, and all ten of the most expensive), is invisible at trigger time. I’d set class-specific limits, not one universal cap. For the fixed runs, I’d take the upper envelope per class from the distribution and set each class’s budget just above the worst historical successful fix, so lint can stay tight while dependency updates get more room. move_object.report_notes:
Three stages covered. Seed: opened with volume plus expensive model plus output tokens, which was the wrong read, and the arithmetic offered was loose; when asked to price a single export row they were fast and exact ($4,344.24 input against $19.74 output, 250,677 input tokens per request on 2 Oct against 39,192 on 1 Oct) and correctly flipped to an input blowup. They did not read the histogram as fat-tailed, did not connect growth to full history being re-sent with cached_input_tokens at 0, and did not notice the config bounds nothing per run; their first change stayed vague.

Probe 1 (the 9-hour run): first read was wrong (repo re-scanning); after being pointed at read_file appearing 4 times they corrected cleanly to the growing transcript hitting the context ceiling, but never priced the curve from the exhibit (no use of call 1 at 18,922 tokens against call 1,859 at 999,715, no hour-by-hour figures, no note that input was $4,802.13 of $4,812.88 or that the run ended on an unhandled provider error). Stop point moved from 'a few cycles' to 'around call 6', the right region but a guess: they did not use the model's own text at call 21, the 50-consecutive-passes bar, or the flat 14.3% failure rate. They placed the cap inside the agent's own config rather than outside it. Unprompted, they gave a decent handoff: leave the PR unchanged and comment that the fix failed.

Probe 2 (setting limits from the per-class view): first answer was a single global cap for all five classes, set by intuition (25 to 40 calls, 30 to 45 minutes, 'low hundreds of thousands' of tokens), with no reference to the table. The stop behaviour they described was good and detailed: halt, comment on the PR, preserve partial diff, do not keep iterating. After a direct push to read the fixed runs per class and the footnote, they moved to per-class limits set just above the worst historical successful fix in each class, which is the right shape, but named not a single number from the exhibit: no $2.19 for lint, no $82.21 for a fixed dependency update, no $16.77 ceiling on flaky fixes, no use of the 46 fixed runs above the overall p95 or the 4 above the p99 to show why one cap fails. They did register that the class label is assigned after the run and correctly refused to use it as a start-of-run selector, proposing a conservative class-agnostic first stage and a mid-run switch; they did not reach screening the failing check before dispatch (does it also fail on main, infra error in the log), and so never saw that the eight runs on one test, $30,298 and 58% of the month, were avoidable by never starting. No soft-limit-plus-human-top-up, no progress signal to distinguish a long run from a loop, no replay of what caps would have saved.

Overall: good instincts on failure handling and graceful stops, and genuinely quick arithmetic when pointed at a row. The recurring weakness is evidential: three times the first answer was an off-the-shelf diagnosis, and each time it took a direct pointer to a specific line before they engaged with the data. Prompting required was substantial at every stage.
move_object.response: That is the right shape, and I am going to stop you there since we are out of time on this one. You got to class-specific limits and you were right not to lean on a label that only exists after the fact. What I would have liked to hear underneath that is the actual numbers from the table: the most a fix ever cost in each class is sitting right there, and it is what turns your envelope idea into something you could ship on Monday. The other thread worth pulling, had we had longer, is whether some of those runs should have been started at all, given what the log tells you up front. Thanks for working through it, that was a good session.

## 1. Two ways to abstract

You already know one way to write code that works for many types: generics (sub-module 09). `fn show<T: Display>(item: &T)` works for any `T` that implements `Display`. The compiler handles it by monomorphisation: it writes one copy of `show` for every concrete type you call it with, `show::<i32>`, `show::<String>` and so on. Each copy knows its type exactly, so every call is a direct call that can be inlined. This is static dispatch: the method is chosen at compile time.

Generics have one limit: each use picks one type. A `Vec<T>` holds values of a single type `T`. A function returning `impl Trait` returns one concrete type, even if the caller cannot name it. So how do you keep a text box, a checkbox and a button in one list and call `render` on each?

Rust's answer is a trait object, written `dyn Trait`. A trait object stands for "some value of a type that implements `Trait`; which type is decided at run time". There is only one copy of the code that uses it, and each method call is looked up at run time. This is dynamic dispatch.

Generics (`T: Trait`)Trait objects (`dyn Trait`)

Method chosenat compile timeat run time, through a vtable

Copies of your functionone per concrete typeone

Inliningyesusually not

Mixed types in one `Vec`noyes: `Vec<Box<dyn Trait>>`

The Rust Book (ch. 18.2, "Using Trait Objects to Allow for Values of Different Types") builds a GUI library this way. Our `widgets.rs` is a small version of it:

```
let parts: Vec<Box<dyn Render>> =
    vec![Box::new(Text("hello".into())), Box::new(Checkbox(true))];
for part in &parts {
    println!("{}", part.render()); // which render? decided per element, at run time
}
```

The `Vec` still holds one type: `Box<dyn Render>`. What differs is the type inside each box.

## 2. Behind a pointer: fat pointers and vtables

A `Text` and a `Checkbox` have different sizes. So what size is a `dyn Render`? There is no single answer: `dyn Render` is an unsized type (its size is not known at compile time). Rust can only store values whose size it knows, on the stack, in a struct field or in a `Vec` slot. That is why a trait object always sits behind a pointer: `&dyn Render`, `&mut dyn Render` or `Box<dyn Render>`.

That pointer is a fat pointer: two machine words.

- A data pointer to the value itself (the `Checkbox` on the heap, or wherever it lives).

- A vtable pointer to a table the compiler built for that pair (concrete type, trait).

A vtable ("virtual method table") holds the information needed to use the value without knowing its type: how to drop it, its size and alignment, then one entry per trait method, each pointing at the machine code for that type's version of the method.

Two boxed trait objects. Each element of `parts` is a data pointer plus a vtable pointer. Each (type, Render) pair has its own vtable whose rows point at that type's code.

A call such as `part.label()` does three things at run time: follow the vtable pointer, read the `label` row, call the function found there with the data pointer as `self`. That indirect call is the cost of dynamic dispatch: one extra memory read, and the compiler usually cannot inline the call because it does not know which function it will be.

You can see the "fat" part directly. `static_vs_dyn.rs` prints the sizes of a thin and a fat reference:

```
&i32: 8 bytes, &dyn Display: 16 bytes
```

These numbers are for a 64-bit machine (8-byte pointers). The rule is "two pointers instead of one", not "16 bytes". The exact layout of a vtable (row order, whether two values of the same type share one vtable) is a compiler detail you never rely on.

A `Box<dyn Trait>` also costs a heap allocation per value, because each value must live somewhere the box can point to. A borrowed `&dyn Trait` needs no allocation: `let one: &dyn Render = &Text("plain".into());` in `widgets.rs` points at a value that is already somewhere.

## 3. `Sized` and `?Sized`

Every generic parameter has a hidden bound: `T: Sized`, "the size of `T` is known at compile time". That is almost always what you want, since the function may need to store a `T`. But it means this generic function cannot be called with a trait object:

```
fn show_any<T: Display>(item: &T) -> String { format!("[{item}]") }

let m: Box<dyn Display> = Box::new(7);
show_any(m.as_ref()); // T would be `dyn Display`, which is not Sized
```

```
error[E0277]: the size for values of type `dyn std::fmt::Display` cannot be known at compilation time
```

Write `T: ?Sized` ("`T` may or may not be sized") to remove the hidden bound. This is fine here because `show_any` only ever touches `T` through a reference `&T`, which is a pointer of known size:

```
fn show_any<T: Display + ?Sized>(item: &T) -> String { format!("[{item}]") }
```

Now `T` can be `dyn Display`, or `str` (another unsized type you have used since 03 behind `&str`).

## 4. Choosing between generics and trait objects

SituationUseWhy

A function used with one type at a timegeneric `T: Trait` or `impl Trait`fastest; no allocation; inlinable

A list (or field) holding several types at once`Vec<Box<dyn Trait>>`a `Vec<T>` has exactly one `T`

Types chosen at run time (from a config file, user input, plugins)`Box<dyn Trait>`the compiler cannot know the type

Want less generated code (many types, big function)`&dyn Trait`one copy instead of one per type

A small, fixed set of kinds you controlan `enum`see section 9

A common mistake is to think `Vec<T>` with `T: Trait` can hold "anything that implements `Trait`". It cannot: `T` is one type, chosen by the caller. Only `dyn Trait` erases the concrete type.

## 5. Default methods through `dyn`

A trait may give a method a default body. In `widgets.rs`, `label` has a default and `Checkbox` overrides it:

```
trait Render {
    fn render(&self) -> String;
    fn label(&self) -> String { String::from("(unnamed)") }
}
impl Render for Checkbox {
    fn render(&self) -> String { /* ... */ }
    fn label(&self) -> String { String::from("checkbox") }
}
```

How does a vtable deal with this? Every vtable has a row for every trait method, defaults included. For `Checkbox` the `label` row points at `Checkbox::label`. For `Text`, which does not override it, the row points at the default body compiled for `Text`. A default method is like a small generic function: the compiler makes one copy of it per implementing type.

This explains what happens when a default calls another method of the same trait. Inside the copy compiled for `Text`, `self` is a `&Text`, so `self.render()` calls `Text::render`; the type is known there, so that inner call is static. Only the outer call through the trait object goes through the vtable.

To predict what a default method does for a type, read it as if you had pasted its body into that type's `impl` block. Every `self.method()` inside it then resolves to that type's own `method`, overridden or not.

## 6. Dyn compatibility: which traits can be objects

A vtable is a fixed list: one row per method, each pointing at one function. Some methods cannot fit in such a list, so a trait containing them cannot be used as `dyn Trait`. Such a trait is not dyn compatible (older texts say "not object safe"). The main rules, from the Rust Reference:

Method shapeProblem for a vtable

`fn copy(&self) -> Self`The caller must reserve space for the returned `Self`, but behind `dyn` its size is unknown.

`fn put<V: ToString>(&mut self, v: V)`A generic method is a family of functions, one per `V`. A fixed list cannot hold an open-ended family.

`fn new() -> Self` (no `self`)There is no value, so no vtable to look in.

Uncomment both `doubled` lines in `dyn_compat.rs` to see the error:

```
error[E0038]: the trait `Shape` is not dyn compatible
  ...because method `doubled` references the `Self` type in its return type
```

There are two ways out.

- Keep the method off the vtable with `where Self: Sized`. The trait becomes dyn compatible again, and the method can still be called on concrete types, but not on a `dyn Shape`. `dyn_compat.rs` does this with `doubled_sized`.

- Change the method's shape so it fits in a vtable: return `Box<dyn Shape>` instead of `Self`, or take `&dyn ToString` (or a `String`) instead of a generic `V`. Each costs something: a heap allocation, a conversion, or a second dynamic call.

`Box<dyn Trait>` does not make an incompatible trait compatible. The problem is the trait's methods, not where the object is stored.

## 7. Supertraits

`trait Shape: Debug { ... }` says "every type that implements `Shape` must also implement `Debug`". `Debug` is a supertrait of `Shape`. Two consequences:

- Code that has a `Shape` may use `Debug` too. Debug's method joins Shape's vtable, so `println!("{:?}", shapes[0])` works on a `Box<dyn Shape>`.

- Because the supertrait's methods join the vtable, the supertrait must be dyn compatible as well. `Debug` and `Display` are. `Clone` is not (`clone` returns `Self`), and neither is `Default` (`default()` has no `self` and returns `Self`). So `trait Shape: Clone` makes `dyn Shape` impossible.

```
use std::fmt::Debug;
trait Shape: Debug { fn area(&self) -> f64; }

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Square(f64);
impl Shape for Square { fn area(&self) -> f64 { self.0 * self.0 } }
// impl Shape for Square requires Square: Debug, which the derive provides.
```

## 8. Boxed closures and `'static`

Every closure has its own unnamed type, even two closures with the same signature (10). So a list of closures needs a trait object: `Vec<Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool>>`. `Fn`, `FnMut` and `FnOnce` are traits like any other.

A rule you will meet often: in a struct field or in a function's return type, `Box<dyn Trait>` is short for `Box<dyn Trait + 'static>`. `'static` here means "the value inside does not borrow anything that could go away". A closure meets it if every captured value is owned by the closure: copied in, cloned in or moved in. It fails if it captures a reference to a local variable or to a parameter.

```
fn prefix_rule(prefix: &str) -> Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool> {
    let owned = prefix.to_string();                // the closure gets its own copy
    Box::new(move |s| s.starts_with(owned.as_str()))
}
```

If the closure used `prefix` directly, it would hold a borrow that only lives as long as the caller's string, and the compiler refuses:

```
error: lifetime may not live long enough
  returning this value requires that `'1` must outlive `'static`
```

`move` moves whatever the closure names. If the variable is itself a reference (`prefix: &str`, `limit: &u32`), `move` moves the reference into the closure. The closure still borrows. To own the data, copy or clone it out first: `let limit = *limit;` or `let owned = prefix.to_string();`.

A `&dyn Fn(..)` parameter, by contrast, may borrow freely: it is only used during the call. Writing other lifetimes, such as `Box<dyn Fn() + 'a>`, is covered in 14.

## 9. Consuming a trait object; trait objects vs enums

A method may take its receiver as `self: Box<Self>`. It then consumes the box: after the call, the object is gone. The Book's state pattern (ch. 18.3, "Implementing an Object-Oriented Design Pattern") uses this so a state transition uses up the old state. `state.rs` is adapted from it:

```
trait State {
    fn submit(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn State>;
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str;
}
impl State for Draft {
    fn submit(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn State> { Box::new(Review) }
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str { "draft" }
}
```

`self: Box<Self>` is dyn compatible: the receiver is a pointer of known size, so the call can go through the vtable. The catch is that you must own the box to call it. A shared or mutable borrow of a box is not enough; you cannot move a box out from behind a reference. When the box sits inside something else, take it out first:

Where the box livesHow to take it out

`Option<Box<dyn State>>``opt.take()` leaves `None` behind

a field or variable of a type with a default`std::mem::take(&mut x)` (11)

a `Vec<Box<dyn T>>`, all of it`v.drain(..)` or `mem::take(&mut v)`, which leave it empty

a `Vec`, one element`v.remove(i)` or `v.pop()`

### Trait objects or an enum?

The same states could be an `enum State { Draft, Review, Published }` with `match` in each operation. The two designs make different changes cheap:

ChangeTrait objectsEnum + match

Add a new kind (type / variant)one new type and its `impl`; no other code changesedit every `match`

Add a new operationadd a method to the trait and to every typeone new function with one `match`; the compiler checks every case

Types from outside your crate (plugins)yesno: the set is closed

Cost per callvtable call, heap allocation per boxa `match` on a tag; no allocation needed

## 10. Check yourself

Ask the Tutor about any of these. Try to answer first.

- Why must `dyn Trait` always sit behind a pointer? What are the two halves of that pointer?

- Why can a trait with `fn copy(&self) -> Self` not be a trait object, while `fn copy(&self) -> Box<dyn Trait>` is fine?

- A default method calls `self.unit()`. For a type that overrides `unit`, which `unit` runs, and why?

- Why does a closure stored in a `Box<dyn Fn()>` field have to own what it captures?

- What would you gain and lose by rewriting `state.rs` as an enum?

Sources: adapted from The Rust Programming Language, ch. 18.2 and ch. 18.3, Rust by Example, "Returning Traits with dyn" and the Rust Reference, "Dyn compatibility" (MIT/Apache-2.0).

[entity 908 · fat-pointer.png · diagram]
Diagram: a trait object is a fat pointer.

Left, two elements of `parts: Vec<Box<dyn Render>>`. Each element is two pointers side by side: a "data ptr" and a "vtable ptr".
- parts[0]: the data ptr points to `Text("hello")` on the heap; the vtable ptr points to the vtable for (Text, Render).
- parts[1]: the data ptr points to `Checkbox(true)` on the heap; the vtable ptr points to the vtable for (Checkbox, Render).

Middle, the two vtables. Each has rows: drop, size and align, render, label.

Right, where the rows point:
- Text's `render` row -> `Text::render`. Text's `label` row -> the trait's default `label`, compiled for Text (Text does not override it).
- Checkbox's `render` row -> `Checkbox::render`. Checkbox's `label` row -> `Checkbox::label` (its override).

Caption: `part.label()` on parts[0] follows the vtable ptr, reads the "label" row and calls it with the data ptr as `self`. Row order and whether vtables are shared are compiler details. On 64-bit each pointer is 8 bytes, so the fat pointer is 16.

// Exercise 1: a mixed zoo (reference solution)
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex1_zoo.rs && ./main --test-threads=4

trait Animal {
    fn name(&self) -> String;
    fn sound(&self) -> String;
    // Default: "<name> says <sound>"
    fn speak(&self) -> String {
        format!("{} says {}", self.name(), self.sound())
    }
}

struct Dog;
struct Cat {
    name: String,
}
struct Parrot {
    word: String,
}

impl Animal for Dog {
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        String::from("dog")
    }
    fn sound(&self) -> String {
        String::from("woof")
    }
}

impl Animal for Cat {
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        self.name.clone()
    }
    fn sound(&self) -> String {
        String::from("meow")
    }
}

impl Animal for Parrot {
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        String::from("parrot")
    }
    fn sound(&self) -> String {
        self.word.clone()
    }
    fn speak(&self) -> String {
        format!("{0}! {0}!", self.word)
    }
}

fn zoo() -> Vec<Box<dyn Animal>> {
    vec![
        Box::new(Dog),
        Box::new(Cat { name: "Tom".into() }),
        Box::new(Parrot { word: "hello".into() }),
    ]
}

fn chorus(animals: &[Box<dyn Animal>]) -> String {
    let lines: Vec<String> = animals.iter().map(|a| a.speak()).collect();
    lines.join("; ")
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn default_speak_uses_each_types_own_name_and_sound() {
        assert_eq!(Dog.speak(), "dog says woof");
        assert_eq!(Cat { name: "Kit".into() }.speak(), "Kit says meow");
    }

    #[test]
    fn parrot_overrides_speak() {
        let p = Parrot { word: "hi".into() };
        assert_eq!(p.sound(), "hi");
        assert_eq!(p.speak(), "hi! hi!");
    }

    #[test]
    fn zoo_holds_three_different_types() {
        let z = zoo();
        let names: Vec<String> = z.iter().map(|a| a.name()).collect();
        assert_eq!(names, ["dog", "Tom", "parrot"]);
    }

    #[test]
    fn chorus_goes_through_the_vtable() {
        assert_eq!(chorus(&zoo()), "dog says woof; Tom says meow; hello! hello!");
        assert_eq!(chorus(&[]), "");
    }
}

type Rule = Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool>;

fn max_len(n: usize) -> Rule {
    Box::new(move |s| s.len() <= n) // usize is Copy: copied in
}

fn without(word: &str) -> Rule {
    let word = word.to_string(); // own a copy; the closure must be 'static
    Box::new(move |s| !s.contains(word.as_str()))
}

fn one_of(allowed: Vec<String>) -> Rule {
    Box::new(move |s| allowed.iter().any(|a| a == s)) // the Vec is moved in
}

fn passes_all(rules: &[Rule], text: &str) -> bool {
    rules.iter().all(|r| r(text))
}

fn count_passing(rules: &[Rule], words: &[&str]) -> usize {
    words.iter().filter(|w| passes_all(rules, w)).count()
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn single_rules() {
        assert!(max_len(3)("abc"));
        assert!(!max_len(3)("abcd"));
        assert!(without("x")("abc"));
        assert!(!without("bc")("abc"));
        let r = one_of(vec!["red".into(), "blue".into()]);
        assert!(r("red") && !r("green"));
    }

    #[test]
    fn rule_outlives_the_string_it_was_made_from() {
        let rule = {
            let temp = String::from("oops");
            without(&temp)
        }; // `temp` is dropped here; the rule must still work
        assert!(rule("fine"));
        assert!(!rule("oops!"));
    }

    #[test]
    fn rules_of_different_closure_types_in_one_vec() {
        let rules: Vec<Rule> = vec![max_len(5), without("z"), Box::new(|s: &str| !s.is_empty())];
        assert!(passes_all(&rules, "abc"));
        assert!(!passes_all(&rules, "abcdef"));
        assert!(!passes_all(&rules, ""));
        assert!(passes_all(&[], "anything"));
        assert_eq!(count_passing(&rules, &["ok", "zoo", "toolong", "", "fine"]), 2);
    }
}

// Exercise 3: a traffic signal with the state pattern (reference solution)
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex3_signal.rs && ./main --test-threads=4

trait Light {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light>;
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str;
    // Default: most lights stay on for 30 seconds.
    fn seconds(&self) -> u32 {
        30
    }
}

struct Red;
struct Green;
struct Yellow;

impl Light for Red {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Green)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "red"
    }
}

impl Light for Green {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Yellow)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "green"
    }
}

impl Light for Yellow {
    fn next(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn Light> {
        Box::new(Red)
    }
    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        "yellow"
    }
    fn seconds(&self) -> u32 {
        5
    }
}

struct Signal {
    light: Option<Box<dyn Light>>,
}

impl Signal {
    fn new() -> Signal {
        Signal { light: Some(Box::new(Red)) }
    }

    fn advance(&mut self) {
        // take() leaves None behind, giving us the owned Box to consume.
        let old = self.light.take().unwrap();
        self.light = Some(old.next());
    }

    fn color(&self) -> &'static str {
        self.light.as_ref().unwrap().color()
    }

    fn run_for(&mut self, n: usize) -> u32 {
        let mut total = 0;
        for _ in 0..n {
            total += self.light.as_ref().unwrap().seconds();
            self.advance();
        }
        total
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn cycle_of_colours() {
        let mut s = Signal::new();
        let mut seen = vec![s.color()];
        for _ in 0..3 {
            s.advance();
            seen.push(s.color());
        }
        assert_eq!(seen, ["red", "green", "yellow", "red"]);
    }

    #[test]
    fn default_and_overridden_seconds() {
        assert_eq!(Red.seconds(), 30);
        assert_eq!(Green.seconds(), 30);
        assert_eq!(Yellow.seconds(), 5);
    }

    #[test]
    fn run_for_adds_up_and_moves_on() {
        let mut s = Signal::new();
        assert_eq!(s.run_for(3), 65);
        assert_eq!(s.color(), "red");
        assert_eq!(s.run_for(0), 0);
        assert_eq!(s.run_for(2), 60);
        assert_eq!(s.color(), "yellow");
    }
}

## 1. Two ways to abstract

You already know one way to write code that works for many types: generics (sub-module 09). `fn show<T: Display>(item: &T)` works for any `T` that implements `Display`. The compiler handles it by monomorphisation: it writes one copy of `show` for every concrete type you call it with, `show::<i32>`, `show::<String>` and so on. Each copy knows its type exactly, so every call is a direct call that can be inlined. This is static dispatch: the method is chosen at compile time.

Generics have one limit: each use picks one type. A `Vec<T>` holds values of a single type `T`. A function returning `impl Trait` returns one concrete type, even if the caller cannot name it. So how do you keep a text box, a checkbox and a button in one list and call `render` on each?

Rust's answer is a trait object, written `dyn Trait`. A trait object stands for "some value of a type that implements `Trait`; which type is decided at run time". There is only one copy of the code that uses it, and each method call is looked up at run time. This is dynamic dispatch.

Generics (`T: Trait`)Trait objects (`dyn Trait`)

Method chosenat compile timeat run time, through a vtable

Copies of your functionone per concrete typeone

Inliningyesusually not

Mixed types in one `Vec`noyes: `Vec<Box<dyn Trait>>`

The Rust Book (ch. 18.2, "Using Trait Objects to Allow for Values of Different Types") builds a GUI library this way. Our `widgets.rs` is a small version of it:

```
let parts: Vec<Box<dyn Render>> =
    vec![Box::new(Text("hello".into())), Box::new(Checkbox(true))];
for part in &parts {
    println!("{}", part.render()); // which render? decided per element, at run time
}
```

The `Vec` still holds one type: `Box<dyn Render>`. What differs is the type inside each box.

## 2. Behind a pointer: fat pointers and vtables

A `Text` and a `Checkbox` have different sizes. So what size is a `dyn Render`? There is no single answer: `dyn Render` is an unsized type (its size is not known at compile time). Rust can only store values whose size it knows, on the stack, in a struct field or in a `Vec` slot. That is why a trait object always sits behind a pointer: `&dyn Render`, `&mut dyn Render` or `Box<dyn Render>`.

That pointer is a fat pointer: two machine words.

- A data pointer to the value itself (the `Checkbox` on the heap, or wherever it lives).

- A vtable pointer to a table the compiler built for that pair (concrete type, trait).

A vtable ("virtual method table") holds the information needed to use the value without knowing its type: how to drop it, its size and alignment, then one entry per trait method, each pointing at the machine code for that type's version of the method.

Two boxed trait objects. Each element of `parts` is a data pointer plus a vtable pointer. Each (type, Render) pair has its own vtable whose rows point at that type's code.

A call such as `part.label()` does three things at run time: follow the vtable pointer, read the `label` row, call the function found there with the data pointer as `self`. That indirect call is the cost of dynamic dispatch: one extra memory read, and the compiler usually cannot inline the call because it does not know which function it will be.

You can see the "fat" part directly. `static_vs_dyn.rs` prints the sizes of a thin and a fat reference:

```
&i32: 8 bytes, &dyn Display: 16 bytes
```

These numbers are for a 64-bit machine (8-byte pointers). The rule is "two pointers instead of one", not "16 bytes". The exact layout of a vtable (row order, whether two values of the same type share one vtable) is a compiler detail you never rely on.

A `Box<dyn Trait>` also costs a heap allocation per value, because each value must live somewhere the box can point to. A borrowed `&dyn Trait` needs no allocation: `let one: &dyn Render = &Text("plain".into());` in `widgets.rs` points at a value that is already somewhere.

## 3. `Sized` and `?Sized`

Every generic parameter has a hidden bound: `T: Sized`, "the size of `T` is known at compile time". That is almost always what you want, since the function may need to store a `T`. But it means this generic function cannot be called with a trait object:

```
fn show_any<T: Display>(item: &T) -> String { format!("[{item}]") }

let m: Box<dyn Display> = Box::new(7);
show_any(m.as_ref()); // T would be `dyn Display`, which is not Sized
```

```
error[E0277]: the size for values of type `dyn std::fmt::Display` cannot be known at compilation time
```

Write `T: ?Sized` ("`T` may or may not be sized") to remove the hidden bound. This is fine here because `show_any` only ever touches `T` through a reference `&T`, which is a pointer of known size:

```
fn show_any<T: Display + ?Sized>(item: &T) -> String { format!("[{item}]") }
```

Now `T` can be `dyn Display`, or `str` (another unsized type you have used since 03 behind `&str`).

## 4. Choosing between generics and trait objects

SituationUseWhy

A function used with one type at a timegeneric `T: Trait` or `impl Trait`fastest; no allocation; inlinable

A list (or field) holding several types at once`Vec<Box<dyn Trait>>`a `Vec<T>` has exactly one `T`

Types chosen at run time (from a config file, user input, plugins)`Box<dyn Trait>`the compiler cannot know the type

Want less generated code (many types, big function)`&dyn Trait`one copy instead of one per type

A small, fixed set of kinds you controlan `enum`see section 9

A common mistake is to think `Vec<T>` with `T: Trait` can hold "anything that implements `Trait`". It cannot: `T` is one type, chosen by the caller. Only `dyn Trait` erases the concrete type.

## 5. Default methods through `dyn`

A trait may give a method a default body. In `widgets.rs`, `label` has a default and `Checkbox` overrides it:

```
trait Render {
    fn render(&self) -> String;
    fn label(&self) -> String { String::from("(unnamed)") }
}
impl Render for Checkbox {
    fn render(&self) -> String { /* ... */ }
    fn label(&self) -> String { String::from("checkbox") }
}
```

How does a vtable deal with this? Every vtable has a row for every trait method, defaults included. For `Checkbox` the `label` row points at `Checkbox::label`. For `Text`, which does not override it, the row points at the default body compiled for `Text`. A default method is like a small generic function: the compiler makes one copy of it per implementing type.

This explains what happens when a default calls another method of the same trait. Inside the copy compiled for `Text`, `self` is a `&Text`, so `self.render()` calls `Text::render`; the type is known there, so that inner call is static. Only the outer call through the trait object goes through the vtable.

To predict what a default method does for a type, read it as if you had pasted its body into that type's `impl` block. Every `self.method()` inside it then resolves to that type's own `method`, overridden or not.

## 6. Dyn compatibility: which traits can be objects

A vtable is a fixed list: one row per method, each pointing at one function. Some methods cannot fit in such a list, so a trait containing them cannot be used as `dyn Trait`. Such a trait is not dyn compatible (older texts say "not object safe"). The main rules, from the Rust Reference:

Method shapeProblem for a vtable

`fn copy(&self) -> Self`The caller must reserve space for the returned `Self`, but behind `dyn` its size is unknown.

`fn put<V: ToString>(&mut self, v: V)`A generic method is a family of functions, one per `V`. A fixed list cannot hold an open-ended family.

`fn new() -> Self` (no `self`)There is no value, so no vtable to look in.

Uncomment both `doubled` lines in `dyn_compat.rs` to see the error:

```
error[E0038]: the trait `Shape` is not dyn compatible
  ...because method `doubled` references the `Self` type in its return type
```

There are two ways out.

- Keep the method off the vtable with `where Self: Sized`. The trait becomes dyn compatible again, and the method can still be called on concrete types, but not on a `dyn Shape`. `dyn_compat.rs` does this with `doubled_sized`.

- Change the method's shape so it fits in a vtable: return `Box<dyn Shape>` instead of `Self`, or take `&dyn ToString` (or a `String`) instead of a generic `V`. Each costs something: a heap allocation, a conversion, or a second dynamic call.

`Box<dyn Trait>` does not make an incompatible trait compatible. The problem is the trait's methods, not where the object is stored.

## 7. Supertraits

`trait Shape: Debug { ... }` says "every type that implements `Shape` must also implement `Debug`". `Debug` is a supertrait of `Shape`. Two consequences:

- Code that has a `Shape` may use `Debug` too. Debug's method joins Shape's vtable, so `println!("{:?}", shapes[0])` works on a `Box<dyn Shape>`.

- Because the supertrait's methods join the vtable, the supertrait must be dyn compatible as well. `Debug` and `Display` are. `Clone` is not (`clone` returns `Self`), and neither is `Default` (`default()` has no `self` and returns `Self`). So `trait Shape: Clone` makes `dyn Shape` impossible.

```
use std::fmt::Debug;
trait Shape: Debug { fn area(&self) -> f64; }

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Square(f64);
impl Shape for Square { fn area(&self) -> f64 { self.0 * self.0 } }
// impl Shape for Square requires Square: Debug, which the derive provides.
```

## 8. Boxed closures and `'static`

Every closure has its own unnamed type, even two closures with the same signature (10). So a list of closures needs a trait object: `Vec<Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool>>`. `Fn`, `FnMut` and `FnOnce` are traits like any other.

A rule you will meet often: in a struct field or in a function's return type, `Box<dyn Trait>` is short for `Box<dyn Trait + 'static>`. `'static` here means "the value inside does not borrow anything that could go away". A closure meets it if every captured value is owned by the closure: copied in, cloned in or moved in. It fails if it captures a reference to a local variable or to a parameter.

```
fn prefix_rule(prefix: &str) -> Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool> {
    let owned = prefix.to_string();                // the closure gets its own copy
    Box::new(move |s| s.starts_with(owned.as_str()))
}
```

If the closure used `prefix` directly, it would hold a borrow that only lives as long as the caller's string, and the compiler refuses:

```
error: lifetime may not live long enough
  returning this value requires that `'1` must outlive `'static`
```

`move` moves whatever the closure names. If the variable is itself a reference (`prefix: &str`, `limit: &u32`), `move` moves the reference into the closure. The closure still borrows. To own the data, copy or clone it out first: `let limit = *limit;` or `let owned = prefix.to_string();`.

A `&dyn Fn(..)` parameter, by contrast, may borrow freely: it is only used during the call. Writing other lifetimes, such as `Box<dyn Fn() + 'a>`, is covered in 14.

## 9. Consuming a trait object; trait objects vs enums

A method may take its receiver as `self: Box<Self>`. It then consumes the box: after the call, the object is gone. The Book's state pattern (ch. 18.3, "Implementing an Object-Oriented Design Pattern") uses this so a state transition uses up the old state. `state.rs` is adapted from it:

```
trait State {
    fn submit(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn State>;
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str;
}
impl State for Draft {
    fn submit(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn State> { Box::new(Review) }
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str { "draft" }
}
```

`self: Box<Self>` is dyn compatible: the receiver is a pointer of known size, so the call can go through the vtable. The catch is that you must own the box to call it. A shared or mutable borrow of a box is not enough; you cannot move a box out from behind a reference. When the box sits inside something else, take it out first:

Where the box livesHow to take it out

`Option<Box<dyn State>>``opt.take()` leaves `None` behind

a field or variable of a type with a default`std::mem::take(&mut x)` (11)

a `Vec<Box<dyn T>>`, all of it`v.drain(..)` or `mem::take(&mut v)`, which leave it empty

a `Vec`, one element`v.remove(i)` or `v.pop()`

### Trait objects or an enum?

The same states could be an `enum State { Draft, Review, Published }` with `match` in each operation. The two designs make different changes cheap:

ChangeTrait objectsEnum + match

Add a new kind (type / variant)one new type and its `impl`; no other code changesedit every `match`

Add a new operationadd a method to the trait and to every typeone new function with one `match`; the compiler checks every case

Types from outside your crate (plugins)yesno: the set is closed

Cost per callvtable call, heap allocation per boxa `match` on a tag; no allocation needed

Ask the Tutor about any of these. Try to answer first.

- Why must `dyn Trait` always sit behind a pointer? What are the two halves of that pointer?

- Why can a trait with `fn copy(&self) -> Self` not be a trait object, while `fn copy(&self) -> Box<dyn Trait>` is fine?

- A default method calls `self.unit()`. For a type that overrides `unit`, which `unit` runs, and why?

- Why does a closure stored in a `Box<dyn Fn()>` field have to own what it captures?

- What would you gain and lose by rewriting `state.rs` as an enum?

[entity 908 · fat-pointer.png · diagram]
Diagram: a trait object is a fat pointer.

Left, two elements of `parts: Vec<Box<dyn Render>>`. Each element is two pointers side by side: a "data ptr" and a "vtable ptr".
- parts[0]: the data ptr points to `Text("hello")` on the heap; the vtable ptr points to the vtable for (Text, Render).
- parts[1]: the data ptr points to `Checkbox(true)` on the heap; the vtable ptr points to the vtable for (Checkbox, Render).

Middle, the two vtables. Each has rows: drop, size and align, render, label.

Right, where the rows point:
- Text's `render` row -> `Text::render`. Text's `label` row -> the trait's default `label`, compiled for Text (Text does not override it).
- Checkbox's `render` row -> `Checkbox::render`. Checkbox's `label` row -> `Checkbox::label` (its override).

Caption: `part.label()` on parts[0] follows the vtable ptr, reads the "label" row and calls it with the data ptr as `self`. Row order and whether vtables are shared are compiler details. On 64-bit each pointer is 8 bytes, so the fat pointer is 16.
